BMW Group receives prestigious technology award for Gen6 high-voltage battery in China
24.09.2026 Press Release
Gen6 high-voltage battery recognised as a “Global New Energy Vehicle Innovative Technology” at the 2026 World New Energy Vehicle Congress (WNEVC) in China. The award recognises the BMW Group’s holistic approach to innovation, focusing on safety, efficiency, sustainability and customer benefits. The Gen6 high-voltage battery is a key technology of the Neue Klasse.
Press Contact.
Lisa Aigner
BMW Group


Tel: +49-151-601-30526





send an e-mail


Author.
Lisa Aigner
BMW Group


This article in other PressClubs
Munich/Haikou. The BMW Group has received the “Global New Energy Vehicle Innovative Technology” award at the 2026 World New Energy Vehicle Congress (WNEVC) in China. The judges recognised the key technologies of the BMW Gen6 high-voltage battery based on the new BMW round cells with a high-nickel cathode. In doing so, they paid tribute to the BMW Group’s innovative achievements in the field of electric drive technologies and its holistic approach to the development of high-voltage batteries. The BMW Group is the only automotive manufacturer from outside China to receive one of the WNEVC’s prestigious technology awards.
“We are very proud to receive this international award for our Gen6 high-voltage battery. It confirms our long-term approach of combining technological innovation with the highest standards of quality and safety and genuine customer relevance. With the Neue Klasse, we are setting new benchmarks in this area,” says Jochen Goller, member of the Board of Management of BMW AG responsible for Customer, Brands, Sales.
The Gen6 high-voltage battery reflects the BMW Group’s comprehensive battery expertise, bringing together the company’s own development and production expertise across the entire value chain – from cell chemistry and the development and production of the high-voltage battery through to its integration into the vehicle. As a key technology of the Neue Klasse, it lays the foundation for greater range, faster charging and a new dimension of long-distance electric capabilities. Designed as a global offering, it meets the highest safety requirements worldwide.
The award was presented during the WNEVC, one of the world’s leading platforms for the future of electromobility. This marks the fifth consecutive year – and the sixth time overall – that the BMW Group has been recognised for technological innovation at the congress.
A technological leap for the Neue Klasse
The sixth generation of BMW eDrive technology forms the technological foundation of the Neue Klasse and will be introduced gradually across the BMW Group’s entire fully-electric portfolio. In making the leap from the fifth to the sixth generation, the BMW Group filed patent applications for more than 500 innovations.
“The Gen6 high-voltage battery represents a technological leap across all customer-relevant features. Its innovative, flat design with cylindrical cells paves the way for greater range and faster charging, while maintaining the highest level of safety. As a core technology of the Neue Klasse, it forms the foundation for fully-electric driving pleasure across the entire BMW portfolio,” says Thomas Engelhardt, Senior Vice President Development High-Voltage Batteries, Charging at the BMW Group.
The fundamentally new high-voltage battery concept combines the new BMW round cells, the in-house-developed Energy Master hardware and software, and the systematic integration of the battery into the vehicle architecture to create a holistic system. This allows range, charging speed, efficiency, sustainability and driving dynamics to be refined and optimised together as an integrated system.
The entire Gen6 high-voltage battery portfolio is designed for an 800-volt architecture and enables bidirectional charging capabilities. The cells are integrated directly into the high-voltage battery without a module structure. This cell-to-pack design enables high energy density at battery level and ensures efficient use of the available installation space.
Innovation across the entire value chain
Safety was the highest priority in the development of the Gen6 high-voltage battery. The new round cells feature a steel housing and integrated safety mechanisms. The BMW Group’s in-house cell expertise also ensures continuous scientific and technical validation throughout the entire development process. The high-voltage battery features a multi-stage insulation concept, as well as comprehensive thermal and energy management.
Another element of this innovation is the Energy Master, with both hardware and software developed in-house by BMW. Mounted on the high-voltage battery, it manages the energy flow, supplies power to the e-drives and the vehicle’s electrical system, and serves as the interface for data from the high-voltage battery. It therefore ensures efficient and safe battery operation. In conjunction with the available installation space and vehicle interfaces, it also provides flexibility: It is compatible with both 400-volt and 800-volt charging infrastructure and enables bidirectional charging. At the same time, the overall system has been designed for technology openness, allowing other cell technologies to be integrated.
Questions & answers
What is the World New Energy Vehicle Congress (WNEVC)?
The World New Energy Vehicle Congress (WNEVC) is an annual conference held in China focusing on electromobility and new energy vehicles. Representatives from industry, academia and the political sector discuss current developments and future trends in the sector. The BMW Group has already been recognised by the Congress for technological innovation for the fifth consecutive year and the sixth time overall.
What did the BMW Group receive the award for?
The BMW Group received the “Global New Energy Vehicle Innovative Technology” award for the key technologies of its Gen6 high-voltage battery, based on the new BMW round cells with a high-nickel cathode. The award honours the BMW Group’s holistic approach to innovation in the areas of safety, efficiency, sustainability and customer benefits.
What distinguishes the Gen6 high-voltage battery?
The Gen6 high-voltage battery combines new BMW round cells, an 800-volt architecture, the Energy Master, with both hardware and software developed in-house , and its consistent integration into the vehicle architecture. The system was developed to improve range, charging performance, efficiency and sustainability simultaneously.

articles.title: Columbia residents concerned as W.R. Grace tests recycling technology

articles.article_title: Columbia residents concerned as W.R. Grace tests recycling technology
articles.heading: Columbia residents concerned as W.R. Grace tests recycling technology
authors: The Washington Post News Service & Syndicate
articles.summary: W.R. Grace & Co. is piloting advanced plastic recycling technology in Maryland, sparking safety concerns from nearby Columbia residents.
articles.content:
Columbia residents concerned as W.R. Grace tests recycling technology
Key takeaways:
- W.R. Grace operates pilot recycling machine in Building 30
- Residents near Cedar Creek development express health and safety worries
- Grace claims emissions are minimal and technology reduces waste
- Stop Grace Coalition challenges permit and transparency
The contraption sits in Building No. 30, a nondescript brick facility on the fenced-off campus of W.R. Grace & Co., a major manufacturer of specialty chemicals and materials.
To a nonscientist, it looks like it came out of the movie “Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory.” The 24-by-32-foot maze of chambers, gaskets, gauges and pipes has jokingly been nicknamed Martha by some of the technicians who run it. The company hopes it will improve the way plastic gets recycled around the globe.
Next door to Grace’s sprawling Maryland headquarters is Cedar Creek, a tidy subdivision in Columbia, about 30 miles from Washington. On a recent afternoon, moms chatted in driveways, kids rode bikes and played tag, and some neighbors said they feared Grace’s contraption could be putting them in danger.
“We were trying to move to a safe environment,” said Shamieka Preston, who settled with her family four years ago in an airy home about 400 feet from Grace’s property line, in part to escape California’s wildfire smoke. Instead, she said, they have lived with constant worry and occasional wafts of acrid air. “It gets stuck in your throat,” she said. “It’s awful.”
Grace executives said concerns about emissions from its pilot plastics-recycling operation are unfounded. The company went through a two-year permitting, zoning and technical review with county and state officials, they said, and operates safely.
The dispute unfolding in this community between Washington and Baltimore has put two visions of recycling in conflict. One side says new technologies are urgently needed, the other that the risks are too high. They disagree over whether Grace has a workable solution – and whether the experimental process it is using, and hopes to sell, belongs in a suburban setting at all.
Many residents moved to Cedar Creek after its roughly 180 homes and townhouses were built about six years ago, drawn by its green space, good schools and proximity to two major cities. Many said they knew little about Grace or what it does on its large campus, which has been a fixture since the 1950s. The development housing Grace’s opponents was built, in part, on land the company once owned.
In February, Grace began operating its pilot machine to test whether its new technology works and can be commercially viable.
“We’re developing technology that is meant to help the world recycle more plastics,” said Thomas Deman, president of Grace’s performance catalyst solutions division. He said the method uses less energy and reduces costs, emissions and waste compared with other forms of recycling.
Grace has previously referred to the process it uses as “pyrolysis,” including in a 2024 letter to Maryland officials, but says that technical chemistry term is no longer an accurate description.
Grace executives and scientists likened their process to taking apart Legos: Heat and a company-made catalyst break plastic into molecular building blocks that, Grace says, can be reused to make food packaging, detergent bottles, storage bins and auto parts.
Inside Building 30, technicians load tiny plastic pellets into a funnel, mix them with the catalyst and heat them with electricity. The resulting liquids and gases are separated and studied.
The company says it takes extensive measures to address emissions. Gases from its machine pass through an air-pollution control device that is designed to reduce 99.9 percent of volatile organic compounds before emissions are released through a stack, according to Grace officials. Those emissions “are so minimal they flow through a ⅜-inch tube – about the size of a drinking straw,” the company said in legal filings.
The liquids are collected in 55-gallon drums and sent to a waste treatment facility, the company said.
Grace said it is in “dozens of customer discussions” to sell the technology for use at refineries and petrochemical facilities and does not plan to manufacture plastics at its Columbia site.
“If we want to get to 100 percent recycling in the world, you need this type of technology,” Deman said. “The old, traditional way of melting is not enough.”
Grace is among several companies pursuing what the industry calls “advanced recycling,” in which plastics are broken down into raw materials or chemical components. Half the states in the U.S. have passed legislation regulating it as a manufacturing process, according to the American Chemistry Council, an industry group.
Some environmental groups and scientists counter that such chemical recycling actually recycles little, while potentially releasing hazardous pollutants. The Natural Resources Defense Council calls it a “toxic trap.”
Opponents also say the efforts fail to address what they consider the bigger challenge. “This isn’t solving the problem of there being too much plastic in the world,” said Maher Akremi, a coordinator for Clean Water Action, an environmental advocacy group. “This is them greenwashing the problem.”
Jonah Erlebacher, a professor at Johns Hopkins University’s materials science and engineering department, said the dispute between Grace and some of its neighbors reflects a tension between companies promoting new technologies and people fearful of a chemical process developed, essentially, “behind a curtain.”
“On some level, I get it, because Grace isn’t being transparent,” he said. But Erlebacher said pollution from Grace’s pilot machine is “likely a small drop in the bucket” compared with that from vehicles.
In legal filings, Grace said that because its pilot recycling project is highly confidential, some details relating to emissions that it submitted to state officials were “trade secrets.” Disclosing that information to the public would allow “competitors to recreate the project, thus destroying the future value of Grace’s licenses for that technology,” the company said in court papers.
A group of neighbors who oppose the project – including doctors, lawyers, bankers, teachers, tech executives and scientists, as well as federal government employees and consultants – formed the Stop Grace Coalition. They say they were blindsided by Grace’s plans for the operation in Building 30.
Coalition members contend that Grace has not disclosed enough about the plastics it processes, its chemical catalyst or the pollutants the machine could emit. They also say that the Maryland Department of the Environment has not sufficiently scrutinized Grace’s pilot project.
Over the past year, the coalition has held protests, pressed state regulators to revoke Grace’s permit, lobbied local politicians to intervene, and filed zoning appeals with county officials and the courts in an effort to shut down the machine.
Lisa Krausz, who co-leads the coalition, said Grace’s technology is “not what environmental regulators and political leaders think it is.”
“It has negative health impacts,” Krausz said. “We’re dealing with something far more serious than people understand.”
Veena Singla, an environmental health scientist at the University of California at San Francisco, and five other scientists and experts wrote an 18-page letter this month arguing that the state had not adequately protected the community’s health when it issued Grace’s permit.
“Pollutants are coming out,” Singla said. “What we are not seeing is monitoring on chemicals of concern, like dioxins,” which are highly toxic compounds that can form in processing plastics and raise the risks of cancer, diabetes and reproductive, cardiovascular and developmental problems.
State officials disagreed, saying they issued the permit last summer after a thorough examination. The Maryland Department of the Environment said Grace had met “all legal air emissions standards” and that it is “satisfied that there will be no adverse impact to public health or the environment.” Officials said the agency would do “periodic inspections” of the Grace facility and require Grace to hire an independent third party to test the emissions from stacks at its building.
“Protecting the health of nearby residents is our top priority, and we’re following the science and the law to do just that,” department spokesman Jay Apperson said in an email.
Even if they cannot stop the operation, coalition members say they will press state and local officials to do more to regulate any pollutants and try to persuade the Maryland environmental officials to deny Grace’s permit when it comes up for renewal in 2029.
Founded in the late 1870s by Irish-born businessman William Russell Grace, the company began in Peru as a shipping business and later expanded into specialty chemicals.
The firm drew national media attention in the 1980s after families alleged that a plant it owned had contaminated drinking water in Woburn, Massachusetts, causing leukemia and deaths. The area was named by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency as a Superfund site, and the case inspired the book “A Civil Action,” made into a movie starring John Travolta. In the 2000s, the company underwent bankruptcy restructuring after thousands of asbestos-related claims were filed against a former mining operation it ran in Libby, Montana.
Grace said it is working with other companies and agencies to clean up the property in Woburn and that the site has since been redeveloped. The company emerged from bankruptcy with a “renewed focus” on operational excellence, it said, adding that it has a decades-long track record of safe research and development at its Columbia campus.
Grace now has 4,200 employees in 20 countries, including roughly 500 in Columbia, and produces catalysts, chemicals and other materials used in making such items as toothpaste, makeup, cooking oil, renewable fuels, food packaging and pharmaceuticals.
The company’s pilot recycling project is permitted to run up to 16 hours a day, five days a week, and neighbors said it has brought noise and odors.
“Some mornings when they start up, it sounds like 20 airplanes having their engines starting at the same time,” said Preston, who is a co-leader in the Stop Grace Coalition.
Golash Adadey, a financial consultant to the federal government whose backyard borders Grace’s property, said the company repaired a broken exhaust system on its land after he complained about noise several years ago. It stopped for a time, he said, but about a month ago, he said, he began hearing a louder and more consistent noise. He said Grace did not respond to his latest complaint.
“It’s a humming noise,” Adadey said. “It’s like a factory sound. It goes on day and night. You can’t open the windows to sleep.”
Grace said it had received no noise or odor complaints about its recycling pilot from residents. Company officials said state regulators investigated reports of smells in the area but found nothing.
A Maryland Department of the Environment spokesperson said in an email that the agency received four odor complaints from May to July and their investigations found Grace’s plastic recycling machine was not operating during four of the six events reported in those complaints. The spokesperson said the department also did “an unannounced inspection” in late July and detected no odors at Grace’s facility or in the neighborhood.
Some residents have chosen to leave. David Askwith and his wife sold their Cedar Creek home after efforts to try to stop Grace’s pilot failed.
“Not knowing what was going into the air made me highly concerned,” said Askwith, who moved about 15 miles away. “We didn’t want to deal with pollution.”
Residents also fear an accident. René Maldonado, a retired chemist who lives nearby, said automated shutdown equipment might not protect neighbors from a chemical release, fire or explosion.
“By the time a shutdown actually occurs,” Maldonado said, “any mishap will already have impacted the residents because we live so close by.”
Grace said the lab has “multiple layers of safety,” including systems that immediately shut down the unit if any operating conditions stray from the normal range.
Preston said when she first came to Columbia and was house hunting, she drove by and saw the company’s name on its building. “The sign outside just said Grace,” she said. “We thought it was a church.” She later heard it was the corporate headquarters for a company that made paint. Years later, when she learned of the company’s plans for a recycling pilot, Preston said, she was stunned – and the fight became personal.
Her son told her that although their family could afford to move, it “wasn’t fair that other kids might not be able to,” she recalled.
“He said, ‘It’s up to you adults. You need to figure this out,’ ” Preston said. And so, she said, she’s trying. “I’m just a mom, trying to fight a big chemical company.”

Lisa Krausz, who co-leads the coalition, said Grace’s technology is “not what environmental regulators and political leaders think it is.”

“It has negative health impacts,” Krausz said. “We’re dealing with something far more serious than people understand.”

Veena Singla, an environmental health scientist at the University of California at San Francisco, and five other scientists and experts wrote an 18-page letter this month arguing that the state had not adequately protected the community’s health when it issued Grace’s permit.

“Pollutants are coming out,” Singla said. “What we are not seeing is monitoring on chemicals of concern, like dioxins,” which are highly toxic compounds that can form in processing plastics and raise the risks of cancer, diabetes and reproductive, cardiovascular and developmental problems.

State officials disagreed, saying they issued the permit last summer after a thorough examination. The Maryland Department of the Environment said Grace had met “all legal air emissions standards” and that it is “satisfied that there will be no adverse impact to public health or the environment.” Officials said the agency would do “periodic inspections” of the Grace facility and require Grace to hire an independent third party to test the emissions from stacks at its building.

“Protecting the health of nearby residents is our top priority, and we’re following the science and the law to do just that,” department spokesman Jay Apperson said in an email.

Even if they cannot stop the operation, coalition members say they will press state and local officials to do more to regulate any pollutants and try to persuade the Maryland environmental officials to deny Grace’s permit when it comes up for renewal in 2029.

Founded in the late 1870s by Irish-born businessman William Russell Grace, the company began in Peru as a shipping business and later expanded into specialty chemicals.

The firm drew national media attention in the 1980s after families alleged that a plant it owned had contaminated drinking water in Woburn, Massachusetts, causing leukemia and deaths. The area was named by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency as a Superfund site, and the case inspired the book “A Civil Action,” made into a movie starring John Travolta. In the 2000s, the company underwent bankruptcy restructuring after thousands of asbestos-related claims were filed against a former mining operation it ran in Libby, Montana.

Grace said it is working with other companies and agencies to clean up the property in Woburn and that the site has since been redeveloped. The company emerged from bankruptcy with a “renewed focus” on operational excellence, it said, adding that it has a decades-long track record of safe research and development at its Columbia campus.

Grace now has 4,200 employees in 20 countries, including roughly 500 in Columbia, and produces catalysts, chemicals and other materials used in making such items as toothpaste, makeup, cooking oil, renewable fuels, food packaging and pharmaceuticals.

The company’s pilot recycling project is permitted to run up to 16 hours a day, five days a week, and neighbors said it has brought noise and odors.

“Some mornings when they start up, it sounds like 20 airplanes having their engines starting at the same time,” said Preston, who is a co-leader in the Stop Grace Coalition.

Golash Adadey, a financial consultant to the federal government whose backyard borders Grace’s property, said the company repaired a broken exhaust system on its land after he complained about noise several years ago. It stopped for a time, he said, but about a month ago, he said, he began hearing a louder and more consistent noise. He said Grace did not respond to his latest complaint.

“It’s a humming noise,” Adadey said. “It’s like a factory sound. It goes on day and night. You can’t open the windows to sleep.”

Grace said it had received no noise or odor complaints about its recycling pilot from residents. Company officials said state regulators investigated reports of smells in the area but found nothing.

A Maryland Department of the Environment spokesperson said in an email that the agency received four odor complaints from May to July and their investigations found Grace’s plastic recycling machine was not operating during four of the six events reported in those complaints. The spokesperson said the department also did “an unannounced inspection” in late July and detected no odors at Grace’s facility or in the neighborhood.

Some residents have chosen to leave. David Askwith and his wife sold their Cedar Creek home after efforts to try to stop Grace’s pilot failed.

“Not knowing what was going into the air made me highly concerned,” said Askwith, who moved about 15 miles away. “We didn’t want to deal with pollution.”

Residents also fear an accident. René Maldonado, a retired chemist who lives nearby, said automated shutdown equipment might not protect neighbors from a chemical release, fire or explosion.

“By the time a shutdown actually occurs,” Maldonado said, “any mishap will already have impacted the residents because we live so close by.”

Grace said the lab has “multiple layers of safety,” including systems that immediately shut down the unit if any operating conditions stray from the normal range.

Preston said when she first came to Columbia and was house hunting, she drove by and saw the company’s name on its building. “The sign outside just said Grace,” she said. “We thought it was a church.” She later heard it was the corporate headquarters for a company that made paint. Years later, when she learned of the company’s plans for a recycling pilot, Preston said, she was stunned – and the fight became personal.

Her son told her that although their family could afford to move, it “wasn’t fair that other kids might not be able to,” she recalled.

“He said, ‘It’s up to you adults. You need to figure this out,’ ” Preston said. And so, she said, she’s trying. “I’m just a mom, trying to fight a big chemical company.”

articles.title: In radiology, AI is blurring the line between technology development and clinical practice
articles.description: In radiology, AI is blurring the line between technology development and clinical practice STAT
articles.description_html: In radiology, AI is blurring the line between technology development and clinical practice  STAT
articles.article_title: In radiology, AI is blurring the line between technology development and clinical practice
articles.heading: In radiology, AI is blurring the line between technology development and clinical practice
articles.summary: A new wave of radiology practices are aggressively embracing AI: developing and deploying it in-house, and marketing themselves as 'AI-native.'
articles.content:
A decade ago, machine learning scientist and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton made a proclamation that still puts radiologists on edge.
“If you work as a radiologist,” the so-called godfather of artificial intelligence said at a conference, “you’re like a coyote that’s already over the edge of the cliff, but hasn’t yet looked down.” Deep learning was getting so good, so fast, said Hinton, that “people should stop training radiologists now.” In five years — ten, max — AI would do better than radiologists, he predicted.
The clock has run out on that prediction. But the field of radiology isn’t just staring at its shoes, waiting to see how technology upends the profession. Instead, a growing number of radiology practices, in particular outpatient and teleradiology groups, are aggressively embracing AI: developing and acquiring their own tech, deploying it in-house, and marketing their “AI-native” capabilities to radiologist employees and hospital customers alike.

articles.title: Know the new technology rules before heading into the field
articles.description: Know the new technology rules before heading into the field Coeur d'Alene Press
articles.description_html: Know the new technology rules before heading into the field  Coeur d'Alene Press
articles.article_title: Know the new technology rules before heading into the field
articles.heading: Know the new technology rules before heading into the field
articles.summary: Know the new technology rules before heading into the field Coeur d'Alene Press
articles.content:
Know the new technology rules before heading into the field
Hunters heading into this year’s hunting seasons should be aware of technology rule changes after the legislature passed new legislation earlier this year.
The Idaho Legislature passed House Bill 939, addressing the use of advanced technology during big game and game bird hunting seasons. The legislation follows extensive discussion about the role of technology in hunting and establishes statutory restrictions hunters need to understand before heading into the field.
Between Aug. 30 and Dec. 31, 2026, it is unlawful to use any of the following technologies for hunting or scouting all deer, elk, pronghorn, mountain goat, bighorn sheep, moose, black bear, and game birds:
Thermal imaging technology
Night vision technology
Transmitting trail cameras on land owned by the federal government, the state of Idaho, or a local government within the state
Drone aircraft or other unmanned aircraft systems
The only exceptions for these technologies being used are:
Hunting wolves, mountain lions, or predatory wildlife (coyotes, jackrabbits, skunks, weasels, starlings, raccoons, and rattlesnakes)
Retrieving wounded game animals or game birds
Monitoring traps
The law includes specific provisions and exceptions, so hunters should not assume that all technology is prohibited or that the same rules apply to every species.
Hunters should review Pages 95-96 of the 2026 Idaho Big Game Seasons and Rules booklet to understand how the law applies to their hunt.
“Technology continues to change how people hunt and interact with wildlife,” said Legislative and Community Engagement Coordinator Ellary Tucker Williams. “It is imperative that hunters understand the laws that apply to their hunt and make sure they are using technology legally and responsibly.”
Fish and Game encourages hunters to stay informed about changes to hunting laws and regulations. IDFG staff can help explain how the law applies to specific hunting situations, but hunters are responsible for knowing and following the laws and regulations that apply to their hunt.
For more information, visit Fish and Game’s website or contact a local Fish and Game office.

articles.title: Chattanooga Schools Begin K–12 Quantum Technology Curriculum
articles.description: Chattanooga Schools Begin K–12 Quantum Technology Curriculum The Quantum Insider
articles.description_html: Chattanooga Schools Begin K–12 Quantum Technology Curriculum  The Quantum Insider
articles.article_title: Chattanooga Schools Begin K–12 Quantum Technology Curriculum
articles.heading: Chattanooga Schools Begin K–12 Quantum Technology Curriculum
articles.summary: TN QuantumWorks has begun a K–12 pilot in 13 Hamilton County schools to introduce quantum concepts and careers.
articles.content:
Insider Brief
- TN QuantumWorks has begun a K–12 pilot in 13 Hamilton County, Tennessee schools to introduce quantum concepts and careers as EPB launches its quantum computer.
- The curriculum uses age-specific hands-on activities, from light and patterns in elementary classes to simulations of superposition, entanglement, quantum security and hardware comparisons in later grades.
- Project leaders will use teacher and student feedback to assess classroom fit, engagement and state-standards alignment before expanding the Tennessee workforce-development initiative.
PRESS RELEASE — As EPB launches its quantum computer, the TN QuantumWorks K–12 quantum technology and career awareness curriculum is now being implemented in Hamilton County classrooms. Announced earlier this year, the curriculum includes programs for four age groups: grades K–2, grades 3–5, middle school, and high school. TN QuantumWorks is designed to help build the local workforce needed to support the community’s growing quantum technology initiatives.
Participating teachers completed professional development and received hands-on activity kits to support classroom implementation. Sample activities include elementary students exploring basic quantum concepts through light, patterns and other age-appropriate hands-on activities; middle school students using coins, paired cards and even cereal to model quantum technology, superposition and entanglement; and high school students simulating quantum security, comparing quantum hardware and exploring quantum-related careers.
Selected by Hamilton County Schools in coordination with TN QuantumWorks partners, the 13 pilot schools represent elementary, middle and high school grade levels across the district.
The pilot is intentionally starting with a focused group of educators so project leaders can gather feedback before future expansion. Pilot goals include assessing lesson appropriateness by age group, student engagement, alignment with Tennessee state standards and fit with Hamilton County Schools’ adopted curriculum and scope and sequence.
“This curriculum is about both understanding quantum technology and seeing what it could make possible,” said Dr. Dane Boyington, CTO of Thinking Media, creators of the TN QuantumWorks. “We want students to learn the science in age-appropriate ways, but we also want them to see themselves in the careers and opportunities that may grow from it.”
Participating teachers and specialists include Onica Monroe, Mary Avans, Sierra Magee, Taylor Eller, Courtney Smoker, Hayden White, Rachel DeFriese, Jenn Riley, Kim Elbkidze, Forest Shober, Manika Dant and Timothy Alexander, with support from Anthony Goad, Angie Mullins and Kelsey Oliver as content leads.
Several pilot teachers, including Kim Elbkidze, Forest Shober and Rachel DeFriese, also completed QCaMP, a quantum professional development program for K-12 educators developed by Sandia National Laboratories and brought to Chattanooga by the Chattanooga Quantum Collaborative.
“TN QuantumWorks gives Hamilton County Schools teachers and students a chance to help shape how quantum education can work in real classrooms,” said Dr. Justin Robertson, Superintendent of Hamilton County Schools. “This pilot is about making emerging technology accessible and helping students connect what they are learning today with the careers and opportunities of the future.”
TN QuantumWorks is funded through support from the Tennessee Department of Labor and Workforce Development, with CQC serving as the state awardee and initiative lead. The curriculum was conceived and developed by Sheila and Dr. Dane Boyington of Thinking Media, and the pilot is being implemented in coordination with Hamilton County Schools, UTC and EPB.
“We do not have time to wait for the future to arrive before preparing students for it,” said Commissioner Deniece Thomas of the Tennessee Department of Labor and Workforce Development. “In a few short months, TN QuantumWorks has moved from announcement to classroom readiness, with curriculum developed, teachers selected and trained, and students now preparing to explore quantum technology and related career pathways.”
The pilot also includes plans to identify a small number of students in the spring for accelerated opportunities connected to time on the quantum computer at EPB.
“TN QuantumWorks demonstrates how quickly Tennessee can move when curriculum expertise, classroom leadership, state support and quantum infrastructure come together,” said Charlie Brock, CEO of the Chattanooga Quantum Collaborative. “CQC is proud to support the integration of those pieces so this pilot connects to a larger education and workforce pathway.”
Participating Pilot Schools
Grades K-2: East Side Elementary, Lookout Mountain Elementary, Middle Valley Elementary
Grades 3-5: Daisy Elementary, Calvin Donaldson Elementary, Wolftever Creek Elementary
Middle Schools: Soddy Daisy Middle School, Hunter Middle School, Red Bank Middle School
High Schools: University High, Ooltewah High School, Tyner Academy, Signal Mountain High

articles.description: Microsoft Strengthens Its Commitment to the Middle East by Investing in Technology, Digital Resilience and People Microsoft Source
articles.description_html: Microsoft Strengthens Its Commitment to the Middle East by Investing in Technology, Digital Resilience and People  Microsoft Source
articles.article_title: Microsoft Strengthens Its Commitment to the Middle East by Investing in Technology, Digital Resilience and People - Source EMEA
articles.heading: Microsoft Strengthens Its Commitment to the Middle East by Investing in Technology, Digital Resilience and People
articles.summary: Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith and Microsoft Middle East and Africa President Naim Yazbeck today announced a new framework reinforcing Microsoft’s long-term commitment to the Middle East, focused on technology, digital resilience and people.
articles.content:
Microsoft Strengthens Its Commitment to the Middle East by Investing in Technology, Digital Resilience and People
New framework builds on more than 35 years of partnership with the region, backed by plans to invest more than $10 billion between now and 2030.
In the image (L-R): Mr. Nick Tsilas, Assistant General Counsel, Corporate, External and Legal Affairs, Middle East, Microsoft, H.E. Dr. Mohamed Al Kuwaiti, Head of Cyber Security for the UAE Government, H.E. Fahad bin Hamad Al Sulaiti, Director General of Qatar Fund for Development (QFFD), Dr. Khalid bin Fahad Al Khater, President and Founder of New Ground Research, Qatar, Mr. Naim Yazbeck, President, Middle East and Africa, Microsoft, Mr. Jacob Helberg, U.S. Under Secretary of State (E), Mr. Brad Smith, Vice Chair and President, Microsoft, H.E. Sheikh Dr. Meshaal Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah, Director General,Kuwait Direct Investment Promotion Authority (KDIPA), H.E. Abdulla Ahmed Balalaa, Assistant Minister of Foreign Affairs for Energy and Sustainability for the UAE Government, Mr. Jameel Aljaber, Counselor at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Saudi Arabia, Ms. Carol Ann Browne, Vice President and Chief of Staff at Microsoft Corporate, External and Legal Affairs, Ms. Maitha Alsuwaidi, Chief of Strategy & Business Microsoft Middle East and Africa
Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith and Microsoft Middle East and Africa President Naim Yazbeck today announced a new framework reinforcing Microsoft’s long-term commitment to the Middle East, focused on technology, digital resilience and people.
Unveiled at a round table on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York and attended by senior government representatives from Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, the framework includes plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses across the region between now and 2030.
Across the Middle East, governments are pursuing one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations. Realizing this ambition will require digital resilience as a cornerstone, strengthening continuity and recovery, protecting critical data and services, and building trust through stronger cybersecurity.
“Microsoft’s economic ties to the Middle East run deep, and our commitment to the region has always been, and will remain, steadfast. As AI reshapes economies around the world, the Middle East has an important opportunity to lead. Our responsibility is not only to invest in the technology that enables that progress, but to help provide the digital resilience, security and continuity it depends on. This new framework reflects that responsibility and our determination to help the region translate AI ambition into enduring economic and societal benefit,” said Brad Smith, Vice Chair and President, Microsoft.
Naim Yazbeck, President, Microsoft Middle East and Africa, added: “Microsoft has been part of the Middle East’s transformation for more than 35 years, and we’re committed to being here for decades to come. Countries across the region aren’t waiting for the future of AI to be written elsewhere – they’re helping shape it themselves, and our role is to be a long-term partner in that journey. These tangible initiatives expand our commitment as innovation accelerates and national visions advance, strengthening digital resilience, maintaining business continuity and creating lasting opportunity across the region.”
This commitment reflects Microsoft’s belief that every country should be able to benefit from the world’s leading AI and cloud technologies while maintaining confidence in the security, resilience and sovereignty of its digital infrastructure. From now until 2030, Microsoft will pursue the following initiatives with its partners in the region:
Technology
- Expanding cloud and AI infrastructure across the region. Microsoft plans to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses across the Middle East between now and 2030, expanding capacity and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
- Deepening partnerships with national AI champions. Microsoft is expanding strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations – including HUMAIN, G42, QAI and the Government of Kuwait – alongside digital-government initiatives such as TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait.
Digital Resilience
- Creating a Middle East Digital Resilience initiative. Building on lessons from recent regional disruption, Microsoft will make digital resilience a cornerstone of its Middle East strategy – helping organizations strengthen continuity and recovery through resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance and enablement programs.
- Investing in subsea and terrestrial connectivity. Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, building on existing investments including the SeaMeWe-6 subsea cable system, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
- Strengthening data protection, privacy and business continuity. Microsoft will expand data-protection, sovereignty and business-continuity commitments, making them available to eligible governments and customers across the region, backed by Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud and Project Digital Shield.
- Expanding cybersecurity cooperation. Microsoft is deepening partnerships with national cybersecurity authorities across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, supported by a network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in each country.
- Advancing responsible AI through governance and inclusion. Microsoft will expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation (RAIFF), co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), to support responsible AI practices and evaluation tools across the region.
People
- Investing in talent for the AI economy. Building on its existing commitment to help skill more than 4.2 million people across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE by 2030, Microsoft will continue investing in AI skills, workforce readiness and public-sector capability building – including through Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia.
- Helping education communities prepare learners for the AI era. Microsoft is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the Middle East to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education. This includes supporting AI literacy, helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning, and sharing practical guidance for responsible AI use in educational settings
- Empowering workers in the AI economy. We will partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders to help people adapt to changing workplace demands. Our focus is on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development that helps countries build competitive economies and create new opportunities for workers in an AI-enabled future.
As a long-term technology partner to governments, businesses, educators and communities, Microsoft brings together global-scale cloud and AI infrastructure, trusted security and resilience capabilities, and deep local partnerships to help countries advance their national visions. The company will continue working alongside the region to turn AI ambition into lasting economic growth, stronger public services and new opportunities for people.
For additional details, read Brad Smith’s full blog [here].

Building on lessons from recent regional disruption, Microsoft will make digital resilience a cornerstone of its Middle East strategy – helping organizations strengthen continuity and recovery through resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance and enablement programs.
  • Investing in subsea and terrestrial connectivity. Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, building on existing investments including the SeaMeWe-6 subsea cable system, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
  • Strengthening data protection, privacy and business continuity. Microsoft will expand data-protection, sovereignty and business-continuity commitments, making them available to eligible governments and customers across the region, backed by Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud and Project Digital Shield.
  • Expanding cybersecurity cooperation. Microsoft is deepening partnerships with national cybersecurity authorities across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, supported by a network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in each country.
  • Advancing responsible AI through governance and inclusion. Microsoft will expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation (RAIFF), co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), to support responsible AI practices and evaluation tools across the region.

People

  • Investing in talent for the AI economy. Building on its existing commitment to help skill more than 4.2 million people across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE by 2030, Microsoft will continue investing in AI skills, workforce readiness and public-sector capability building – including through Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia.
  • Helping education communities prepare learners for the AI era. Microsoft is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the Middle East to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education. This includes supporting AI literacy, helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning, and sharing practical guidance for responsible AI use in educational settings
  • Empowering workers in the AI economy. We will partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders to help people adapt to changing workplace demands. Our focus is on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development that helps countries build competitive economies and create new opportunities for workers in an AI-enabled future.

As a long-term technology partner to governments, businesses, educators and communities, Microsoft brings together global-scale cloud and AI infrastructure, trusted security and resilience capabilities, and deep local partnerships to help countries advance their national visions. The company will continue working alongside the region to turn AI ambition into lasting economic growth, stronger public services and new opportunities for people.

For additional details, read Brad Smith’s full blog [here].

articles.heading: Tech leaders to UN: For the sake of humanity, please control the AI technology we created
authors: SETH BORENSTEIN and JENNIFER PELTZ, Associated Press
articles.summary: UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The heads of major artificial intelligence firms pleaded with the United Nations on Wednesday to save the world or at least its people — by somehow regulating the fast-expandi…
articles.content:
UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The heads of major artificial intelligence firms pleaded with the United Nations on Wednesday to save the world or at least its people — by somehow regulating the fast-expanding technology that they have been designing.
“If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” said Dario Amodei, chief executive officer of Anthropic. And from his competitor Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, came this assessment: “We could lose control of the future to AI.”
Both said the countries of the world, through the U.N. Security Council, where they testified Wednesday, have to set safeguards of some kind to prevent the technology from getting too powerful to rein in.
They also called for the world to make sure that the power of AI isn’t concentrated in one company or country. They also touted the benefits of the technology for bettering humanity and what Altman called “giving people more power over their own lives.”
Those tech leaders “are telling us in stark terms that it cannot be left to them to prevent disaster from befalling the world,” British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said at the Security Council. “We cannot ignore them because they are right.’’
AI will be at the heart of G20 discussions
Miliband said when the U.K. leads the G20 next year, it will put controlling AI at the heart of discussions, looking for a single set of global standards “to insure that AI development is safe.”
But, the United States said: Don’t do it.
Worries about control of AI are “not a reason to pause its further development or to constrain it with new global governance structure,” said White House Science Adviser Michael Kratsios. “We want you, our allies and partners, to share in the benefits of this technology.”
The U.S. and China are jostling for AI dominance — and Chinese U.N. Ambassador Fu Cong emphasized that all countries should be able to choose AI technology as they see fit.
He warned against “banding together into a petty us-vs.-them clique in the tech sector and forcing other countries to take sides” and enabling unnamed major powers that he described as seeking “digital hegemony.” He called on countries instead to promote open-source models — China’s approach to the technology.
For most of the world leaders, one key question about AI is this: Who should control life-and-death decisions — human or machine?
Amodei, Altman and Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue, who spoke via a glitchy remote connection, spoke with the U.N.’s most powerful council because they and world leaders are trying to figure out not just whether to control AI, but by whom, how it could possibly be done and when it might be just too late.
The day before, U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of “killer robots.” Experts and European leaders said that’s not hyperbole but something that’s either already a grim reality or perilously close.
Amodei called on world leaders to agree on not letting AI build biological weapons, figure out how to verify what models have the capability to do and “establish common standards” for testing and for loss of control and misuse.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, whose country convened Wednesday’s meeting, compared the current state of AI to both the runaway computer HAL9000 in the movie “2001: A Space Odyssey” and the dawn of the atomic age.
“Just as with the atom back then, the international community must now regulate AI in order to make the most of its potential and avoid the worst,” Barrot said.
Other leaders and nations are paying close attention to AI
His wasn’t the only concern expressed during this high-profile U.N. meeting week.
“We must not allow the cost of today’s hesitation to become tomorrow’s catastrophe,” said Liberian UN Ambassador Lewis G. Brown II.
Ukrainian President President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, speaking at the General Assembly, said some kind of human control over machines must achieved soon. Otherwise, he said, for his country — at war for 4½ years — it may be just too late.
“There is already a real possibility that AI, not only people, will begin to decide what happens on the battlefield. And we need peace before we reach that point,” Zelenskyy said.
Last month, a Russian drone seemingly using AI “autonomously made a targeting decision that killed three Ukrainians. Killer robots are technically easy to build, and they are real. We should not be under any illusions otherwise,” Kentaro Toyama, an information technology professor at the University of Michigan, said in an email.
Data scientist Rumman Chowdhury, co-founder of the accountability nonprofit Humane Intelligence, said the idea of killer robots “evokes a science-fiction villain, when the question I want the public to ask is much more concrete: Who authorized a machine to select and attack a target, under what constraints, and who answers for the result?”
The U.N. meeting unfolded as Chinese President Xi Jinping headed to Washington for a much-anticipated state visit. AI interests are looking to what comes out of Xi’s discussions with U.S. President Donald Trump. Earlier, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the two countries had discussed a potential new “notification mechanism” for AI incidents that could impact national security.
But on Tuesday, Trump, lauding AI as “superintelligence,” said the United States would reject efforts to control the technology as it tries to win the development race with China. Kratsios was the one of the few who used that term in the Security Council.
Meanwhile, regional groups in Europe, Asia and elsewhere also are trying to coordinate AI policies, and various nations — and even subcomponents, such as U.S. states — are crafting their own.
___
Farnoush Amiri, Edith M. Lederer and Jennifer McDermott contributed to this report from the United Nations.
___

articles.title: Europe’s technology backbone is becoming a cyber target
articles.description: Europe’s technology backbone is becoming a cyber target Help Net Security
articles.description_html: Europe’s technology backbone is becoming a cyber target  Help Net Security
articles.article_title: Europe’s technology backbone is becoming a cyber target - Help Net Security
articles.heading: Europe’s technology backbone is becoming a cyber target
articles.summary: EU companies endure cyber threats from DDoS attacks, ransomware, supply chain breaches, phishing and growing misuse of AI systems.
articles.content:
Europe’s technology backbone is becoming a cyber target
Disruptive attacks on public-facing services, financially motivated cybercrime and compromises of shared technology providers are increasing cybersecurity risks across Europe.
ENISA’s Threat Landscape 2026 identifies cybercrime, state-linked activity, foreign information manipulation and interference, hacktivism and vulnerability exploitation as key threats. Geopolitical developments influence attackers’ targets, and interconnected digital systems allow disruption to spread across organizations.
Breakdown of incident types impacting the EU (Source: ENISA)
ENISA analyzed 8,257 incidents recorded between January 1 and December 31, 2025. The agency collected the data mainly from open sources, along with anonymized information shared by EU member states and members of the ENISA Cyber Partnership Programme.
“The ENISA threat landscape is more than a list of cybersecurity threats affecting the EU and how they are distributed around sectors and entities. The analysis highlights how threats become more interconnected and how threat groups spread their impact across the larger map of digital services and infrastructures. Being aware of such underlying dynamics is key if we want to implement the right solutions and maintain a high level of resilience across our digital economy,” said ENISA’s Executive Director Juhan Lepassaar.
DDoS attacks accounted for 51.3% of recorded incidents, followed by unauthorized access at 39.5%. Hacktivist groups were linked to much of the DDoS activity targeting government websites and online services. Ransomware remained a major source of disruption across the EU.
Attacks on shared technology services widen impact
Cybercriminals continued to target third-party providers, cloud environments and software supply chains. Reliance on an affected supplier can expose organizations even when their own systems have not been directly compromised.
Incidents involved compromised software, repositories and browser extensions, along with attacks on widely used software libraries and packages. Organizations can become exposed when they incorporate these components into their systems.
Technology providers are attractive targets because their systems may connect to multiple customers. An intrusion at one supplier can interrupt services or give attackers access to other parts of a digital supply chain.
ENISA cited a ransomware attack on a Swedish IT supplier that affected around 200 municipalities and regional authorities. The attack disrupted systems used for human resources reporting, demonstrating how a breach at one company can affect customers that depend on its services.
Public administration remains the most targeted sector
Public administration accounted for 31.8% of recorded incidents, making it the most affected sector. Business services followed at 8.5%, transport at 8%, manufacturing at 6.9%, and finance and banking at 5.6%.
DDoS attacks represented 81.8% of incidents affecting public administration. Attackers repeatedly targeted government websites and online portals in connection with elections, law enforcement operations and geopolitical developments, including Russia’s war against Ukraine and conflicts in the Middle East.
Of financially motivated incidents affecting public administration, data breaches accounted for 38.4%. Ransomware claims represented 36% and primarily affected municipalities.
State-linked groups continued to target ministries, diplomatic organizations and other government institutions for cyberespionage. Their broader operations across the EU also focused on strategic intelligence collection and possible intellectual property theft.
Business services, the second-most affected sector, included consulting firms, legal services, hospitality businesses, broadcast media companies and other commercial providers. Unauthorized access accounted for 56.7% of incidents affecting the sector, followed by DDoS attacks at 38%.
Ransomware deployments accounted for 54% of recorded unauthorized-access incidents affecting business services. Data breaches represented 26.5%.
Phishing and software vulnerabilities as common entry points
Phishing accounted for 77.8% of the social engineering techniques identified in incidents targeting the EU. ENISA also observed increased use of ClickFix, a technique that tricks people into running malicious commands presented as instructions for resolving a computer problem.
Attackers continued to exploit software vulnerabilities to enter systems. The agency identified an intrusion method in 5.2% of unauthorized-access incidents. Vulnerability exploitation accounted for 60.4% of that subset, meaning the figure does not represent all such attacks.
Other campaigns used trusted messaging platforms, including Signal and WhatsApp, to initiate personalized contact. Targets were guided through legitimate authentication processes that gave attackers full access to compromised devices.
AI could accelerate cyberattacks
Cybercriminals and state-linked groups used AI to support phishing, fraud, reconnaissance, malicious code development and post-exploitation activity. AI tools helped operators create tailored messages, write scripts and increase the speed of existing techniques.
Groups involved in foreign information manipulation and interference used AI-generated text, audio and video to produce content, translate it into multiple languages and distribute it to larger audiences.
AI applications have become targets because they may connect to sensitive files, credentials, browser sessions and development environments. A compromised application could provide a route into trusted systems. AI-linked development tools and software supply chains create additional opportunities for attackers seeking access to organizations and their customers.
ENISA expects advanced models to enable more stages of the attack process. Increased automation could expand the speed and scale of cyber activity and make malicious operations harder to detect. Threat groups may also experiment with systems capable of performing parts of an attack with limited human involvement.

articles.title: AI in the newsroom: It’s here, but needs guardrails
articles.description: AI in the newsroom: It’s here, but needs guardrails The Chestnut Hill Local
articles.description_html: AI in the newsroom: It’s here, but needs guardrails  The Chestnut Hill Local
articles.article_title: AI in the newsroom: It’s here, but needs guardrails - The Chestnut Hill Local
articles.heading: AI in the newsroom: It’s here, but needs guardrails
articles.summary: The reality is this: Artificial intelligence is already well out of the box. While there should be clear guardrails — our elected officials are perilously perched behind the eightball on this — AI is here to stay.
articles.content:
by Jeff Meade
Posted 9/24/26
I tapped out my first news stories at the Hatboro Public Spirit on a bulky Olivetti-Underwood manual typewriter roughly the size and weight of a 1970 Buick Regal. We typed our stories on cheap, thin gray sheets of newsprint and edited them with thick pencils — the kind you might have used back in the day to keep score at a bowling alley.
The sleek IBM Selectric was my next technological advance, but I wasn’t satisfied. I longed to land a job at the Courier Times in Levittown, where they used computers.
Be careful what you wish for.
Those “advanced” computers were actually IBM …

Those “advanced” computers were actually IBM “dumb” terminals, hooked up to a huge, finicky mainframe housed in a hyper-refrigerated room in the back of the building, tended to by a hive of nerdy acolytes.
We called our dumb computers “tubes,” and they were down more than they were up. Usually on deadline.
I was the newsroom liaison whose job it was to call the worker bees in the refrigerated room to ask whether we were down. You could usually tell we were down because the screens would freeze, but having one person to make the call saved the nerds the trouble of having to respond to multiple phone calls from ticked-off news editors.
I developed a suitably high-tech means for spreading the bad news. I purchased a wind-up monkey with a tin drum, and when everyone in the newsroom heard the monkey banging away, they knew for sure that we were down.
The technology never improved much while I was on staff, but I was on hand to be one of the first users of the TRS-80 Model 100, a comparatively primitive notebook computer with a horizontal screen roughly the size of four or five postage stamps end to end. It worked better than the tubes.
A few years later, along came the first desktops. My first personal computer purchase was an IBM 286. First, that is, if you don’t include the Commodore 64 that was mainly good for playing games of pong.
Laptops were next up, and I was an early adopter. By this time, it became clear that the internet was going to take over the world, and it kind of did. It was also apparent that my old friends in print were losing their jobs to the new technology.
It was the first time I had heard the term “creative destruction,” which to my mind meant that the new technology might create new jobs, but it could also cost my old friends in newspapers theirs.
Now, here we are with the next new technology, and we read about Jacob Coxon, a resigned researcher at the AI company Anthropic, who says some working in the field believe AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Talk about your creative destruction.
Set aside for a moment Coxon’s doomsday scenario. (If you can.) Artificial intelligence has been associated with a number of suicides — lonely people who previewed their own doomsday scenarios with a nonjudgmental chatbot. If you’re the parent of a kid who has succumbed, that’s plenty apocalyptic enough.
AI has even been associated with several murders. For example, a 17-year-old in Middlesex County, Massachusetts, is recently alleged to have employed a chatbot to search for “theoretical ideas or fantasy stories” about the killing of his mother and younger brother. The teen has pleaded not guilty.
There are far less lethal uses of AI, but no less concerning. Some college students use AI to cheat. In 2024, the web service Turnitin suggested that of 200 million papers reviewed by the service, more than 22 million were at least 20 percent generated by AI, and that more than six million were mostly written — 80 percent or more of the total text — by AI.
And we’ve just begun to talk about AI’s unquenchable thirst for electrical and computing power, requiring the construction of massive data center complexes. You’ve been reading about that in the Local.
Yet, the reality is this: Artificial intelligence is already well out of the box. While there should be clear guardrails — our elected officials are perilously perched behind the eightball on this — AI is here to stay.
Not surprisingly, the ethical use of AI is hotly debated in the Fourth Estate.
At 75, I remain an unrepentant geek. I spend a good deal of time on OpenAI’s ChatGPT, and to a lesser extent Anthropic’s Claude — perhaps more than I should — trying to figure out how artificial intelligence might aid the cause of local journalism.
Here’s what I’ve learned.
A chatbot will write a whole story, soup to nuts, if you let it. Provide it with a few salient facts and feed it a couple of juicy quotes. ChatGPT will do a fair bit of research on its own and crank out a 2,000-word think piece in minutes, or less. The average reader might never know the difference. That’s a clear violation of journalistic ethics.
On the other hand, a chatbot can compile research with blinding speed, and that can save a reporter hours of online digging. It can fact-check. It can make useful suggestions. (You thought of this, but did you think of that?) It can crank out static and interactive graphics. (Although if you’re not careful, they can all look the same.)
My overall sense of the newsroom might be characterized in the following way: Not so fast, Jeff. And caution, when it comes to AI, is well advised.
But my own take is this: AI is one more tool to come along in my career, a career shaped by evolutionary technology at every step along the way. If nothing else, AI’s facility with numbers makes it an intriguing potential resource for data journalism, an enterprise that otherwise might not be available to a small local paper with a bare-bones budget.
There must be clear ethical guidelines for the use of AI in the newsroom, and we are talking about that in depth. We should be open about what those guidelines are. We should be absolutely transparent about its use in anything we publish.
But artificial intelligence is here, and we should use it.

I was the newsroom liaison whose job it was to call the worker bees in the refrigerated room to ask whether we were down. You could usually tell we were down because the screens would freeze, but having one person to make the call saved the nerds the trouble of having to respond to multiple phone calls from ticked-off news editors.

I developed a suitably high-tech means for spreading the bad news. I purchased a wind-up monkey with a tin drum, and when everyone in the newsroom heard the monkey banging away, they knew for sure that we were down.

The technology never improved much while I was on staff, but I was on hand to be one of the first users of the TRS-80 Model 100, a comparatively primitive notebook computer with a horizontal screen roughly the size of four or five postage stamps end to end. It worked better than the tubes.

A few years later, along came the first desktops. My first personal computer purchase was an IBM 286. First, that is, if you don’t include the Commodore 64 that was mainly good for playing games of pong.

Laptops were next up, and I was an early adopter. By this time, it became clear that the internet was going to take over the world, and it kind of did. It was also apparent that my old friends in print were losing their jobs to the new technology.

It was the first time I had heard the term “creative destruction,” which to my mind meant that the new technology might create new jobs, but it could also cost my old friends in newspapers theirs.

Now, here we are with the next new technology, and we read about Jacob Coxon, a resigned researcher at the AI company Anthropic, who says some working in the field believe AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Talk about your creative destruction.

Set aside for a moment Coxon’s doomsday scenario. (If you can.) Artificial intelligence has been associated with a number of suicides — lonely people who previewed their own doomsday scenarios with a nonjudgmental chatbot. If you’re the parent of a kid who has succumbed, that’s plenty apocalyptic enough.

AI has even been associated with several murders. For example, a 17-year-old in Middlesex County, Massachusetts, is recently alleged to have employed a chatbot to search for “theoretical ideas or fantasy stories” about the killing of his mother and younger brother. The teen has pleaded not guilty.

There are far less lethal uses of AI, but no less concerning. Some college students use AI to cheat. In 2024, the web service Turnitin suggested that of 200 million papers reviewed by the service, more than 22 million were at least 20 percent generated by AI, and that more than six million were mostly written — 80 percent or more of the total text — by AI.

And we’ve just begun to talk about AI’s unquenchable thirst for electrical and computing power, requiring the construction of massive data center complexes. You’ve been reading about that in the Local.

Yet, the reality is this: Artificial intelligence is already well out of the box. While there should be clear guardrails — our elected officials are perilously perched behind the eightball on this — AI is here to stay.

Not surprisingly, the ethical use of AI is hotly debated in the Fourth Estate.

At 75, I remain an unrepentant geek. I spend a good deal of time on OpenAI’s ChatGPT, and to a lesser extent Anthropic’s Claude — perhaps more than I should — trying to figure out how artificial intelligence might aid the cause of local journalism.

Here’s what I’ve learned.

A chatbot will write a whole story, soup to nuts, if you let it. Provide it with a few salient facts and feed it a couple of juicy quotes. ChatGPT will do a fair bit of research on its own and crank out a 2,000-word think piece in minutes, or less. The average reader might never know the difference. That’s a clear violation of journalistic ethics.

On the other hand, a chatbot can compile research with blinding speed, and that can save a reporter hours of online digging. It can fact-check. It can make useful suggestions. (You thought of this, but did you think of that?) It can crank out static and interactive graphics. (Although if you’re not careful, they can all look the same.)

My overall sense of the newsroom might be characterized in the following way: Not so fast, Jeff. And caution, when it comes to AI, is well advised.

But my own take is this: AI is one more tool to come along in my career, a career shaped by evolutionary technology at every step along the way. If nothing else, AI’s facility with numbers makes it an intriguing potential resource for data journalism, an enterprise that otherwise might not be available to a small local paper with a bare-bones budget.

There must be clear ethical guidelines for the use of AI in the newsroom, and we are talking about that in depth. We should be open about what those guidelines are. We should be absolutely transparent about its use in anything we publish.

But artificial intelligence is here, and we should use it.
