articles.article_title: Student Technology Council aims to represent students on technological issues
articles.heading: Student Technology Council aims to represent students on technological issues
articles.summary: STC is currently a 20-member council and includes students from across schools and organizations within the University.
articles.content:
As technology becomes an increasingly important part of student life, the University and organizations across Grounds are finding ways to adapt. The Student Technology Council is one of these organizations, and fourth-year Data Science student Kayla Kim was named its inaugural chair at the beginning of the academic year.
STC is currently a 20-member council and includes students from across schools and organizations within the University. It was originally founded as a collaboration between the Sloane Lab, the Karsh Institute of Democracy and the Digital Technology for Democracy Lab. Its founding mission was to serve as a legislative body where students can elect fellow students to represent them in discussions surrounding technology on Grounds. Originally intended to be an individual Special Status Organization, Kim said it has since shifted its goals to incorporating with a larger overarching SSO, such as Student Council.
STC is divided into two teams, the Policy team and the Projects team, with each working together to best represent the student body, Kim said. The Policy team is headed by third-year Batten student Hafsah Zaman, who explained it as the “backend” part of STC, which works to provide recommendations and policy memos to University administrators based on student opinions.
“What we're trying to do going forward is [make] a standard for a lot of different tech policies [for] what we think should happen [at the University],” Zaman said. “That's taking student feedback, and also looking at what other schools are doing in terms of a bunch of different things like [artificial intelligence], data privacy concerns, things like that.”
On the other side, the Projects team is led by third-year College student Rishi Chandra, who said they provide more direct dialogue with administrators and University technology partners. Chandra said the team works closely with the Policy team’s recommendations to accurately represent the student body.
“We’re going to be coordinating with our administrative partners, making sure student voice is translated from the actual student body and then presented to the administrators,” Chandra said.
One of the main advantages STC has, Chandra and Zaman agreed, is its diverse nature. They said that not only do students represent many of the University’s different schools and majors, but they are also in many different extracurricular clubs and organizations. They explained this can further increase STC’s outreach efforts and bring a unique perspective to general body meetings concerning technological issues at the University.
“The cool thing about STC is all of the students were selected from many different departments and different fields. We have a lot of artistic students, and so we're trying to balance that idea of art and data with AI,” Chandra said.
Currently, STC’s focus has been on traditional issues such as AI and data protection. However, it is also using a sandboxing process, where new technologies such as apps and websites are tested to make sure of their usefulness. He said the two teams work closely together to make decisions on these issues, with Policy focusing more on research and Projects on front-end interactions with administrators and partners. However, he described this structure as fluid, with both teams taking note of what works and what does not for future cohorts of STC leadership.
Kim said her original interest in chairing STC stemmed from noticing a lack of student input when the University launches new technology products. Notably, many students expressed dissatisfaction with Wahoo Eats, which was an online food ordering application released in the fall of 2025 to replace Grubhub. The University has since switched back to Grubhub, but Kim said decisions like these are ones she hopes STC can be a part of before problems arise for students.
But first, Kim said, students need to know that STC exists in the first place. Zaman views this as one of the chief goals of the Policy team during her year as lead and said she has several ideas for the year on how to increase this outreach to the community. Some of these are traditional — such as student surveys and town halls — and some are more innovative — like creating a Substack to explain University-wide technological changes to students in a digestible format.
“Not creating what we think the issues are, but actually gauging what the students think the issues are … We actually will need to ask the students, ‘What do you guys think are problems in terms of technology at U.Va.?’” Zaman said.
Another goal of Kim’s during her year as chair is to integrate STC as a branch of Student Council, as she said she believes it could provide STC with immediate benefits.
Kim said that incorporating STC into Student Council would allow STC to report directly to students through Student Council general body assemblies, which would give students immediate access to STC and their current discussions as well as providing them with structural benefits such as the Student Council newsletter.
“The … branch idea … [is that] there will be public immediate access to what the STC is doing,” Kim said. “A set Technology Council representative at the [Student Council] general body meetings … would get our voice out there.”
STC operates as a hybrid organization, with the students working in tandem with University administrators and professors to develop recommendations and policy memos for technological decisions. One of these faculty advisors, Data Science Prof. Aaron Martin, said he believes STC can give students a voice when it comes to the technology the University uses.
“The idea that students can engage more closely on [technological] issues to provide their perspectives and student body perspective more broadly, I thought was something innovative and different,” Martin said.
Martin described his role as a support position, where he leverages his experience in technology policy to provide STC guidance on the most pressing technology-related issues facing American universities, and society more generally, today. Additionally, he explained that he counsels students on what is achievable within an institution such as the University when it comes to policy change and advocacy. Still, he said he wants to maintain the students’ independence when it comes to STC and not have it be something professors take over.
“I was keen to get involved, but also mindful that this is their thing, not mine. I’m happy to take a backseat role and … provide some steering, but I really want this to be something that they drive and take ownership of,” Martin said.
Kim also explained that the long-term goal for STC is still student self-governance despite this current hybrid model, which involves students, professors and administrators working together to provide recommendations to the University. One of the main challenges during her first term, Kim cited, will be demonstrating that despite this hybrid model, the STC does actually represent student voices.
“The hybrid model of our organization in its early infancy phase might seem like an issue to people, and I’m hoping to communicate with others that yes, we are hybrid right now. We're working with … other faculty,” Kim said. “I feel like people will push back on that, saying, ‘This is not student self-governance,’ but I want to remind them that … we're right now [just] starting out.”
Ultimately, Kim said that as technological decisions gain more importance in students’ lives, she said she hopes that the STC can continue to protect and prioritize student voices.
“I would like the students to see [themselves] as the … guardians of their technological rights … as their voice, their direct voice, with administrators on what they believe should be implemented around them,” Kim said.
Solomon Ross-Milligan is a staff writer on the news desk from Charlottesville. He is a second-year College student.

articles.article_title: Trackdown: Dallas police use DNA technology to solve decades-old cases
articles.heading: Trackdown: Dallas police use DNA technology to solve decades-old cases
articles.summary: The Dallas Police Department is utilizing modern DNA technology and investigative genetic genealogy to crack thousands of unsolved cold cases, successfully identifying killers in murders dating back to the 1980s.
articles.content:
Trackdown: Dallas police use DNA technology to solve decades-old cases
DALLAS - Dallas has thousands of unsolved murder cases, but with modern DNA technology, detectives at the Dallas Police Department are solving decades-long cold cases.
Finding a suspect
What we know:
Detective Andrea Isom and the Dallas Police Department's Cold Case Unit are working to track down suspects using DNA technology that did not exist when the crimes occurred.
This includes a DNA database containing DNA taken from people who have been arrested, as well as investigative genetic genealogy, using DNA left at a crime scene decades ago to map biological relationships and find a suspect.
September is National Cold Case Awareness Month.
Breaking Through Cold Cases
Modern day technology has led to the arrest of Willie Jones 44 years after Virginia White was sexually assaulted and strangled to death in 1981. Earlier this year, Marvin Lee Holloway was identified through DNA as the killer in the 1986 murder of Ruby Battee. Holloway was already in prison for a sexual assault.
What we don't know:
The unit has made major breakthroughs. However, thousands of unsolved cases still remain in storage boxes underground.
What they're saying:
"I'm just picking up what the last detective started," Detective Isom said. "Most of the time, they did fantastic work. I'm just doing the last 10% that didn't exist for them." She called genetic genealogy "the new frontier for investigations."
"We arrested an individual from a 1981 case before I was born," Isom said. "It feels good knowing you can still catch them. People thought they got away with it, but now they will face justice."
"Every case matters," Isom said. "We want to solve every single case we can. They killed someone, and they deserve to answer for it in court."
What's next:
Next week, units from across North Texas will meet to share information and techniques on solving cold cases.
The Source: The information in this article comes from an interview with Detective Andrea Isom.

articles.content:
AI leaders warn UN of risks as technology develops
- Leaders of AI companies warn of risks associated with rapid AI development and call for international cooperation at the UN Security Council.
Leaders of artificial intelligence (AI) companies appealed for international cooperation on the technology at the UN Security Council on Wednesday.
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the current moment in AI development called for "extreme care" as developers reached a crossroads.
"We have a choice in front of us. AI can either be more like a new Renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray."
Altman said there were two major risks with AI.
"First, we could lose control of the future to AI. The risk is that it moves so fast that people can no longer follow what's happening or intervene when needed. This would obviously be terrible," he said.
"In the other direction, these systems could concentrate too much power in too few hands. No one person or company or country should be able to use the most powerful AI models to impose their worldview on everyone else."
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei told the meeting AI is the most important global security issue facing the world today.
"If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole," he said.
Amodei called for a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models.
The warnings came after a high-profile hacking incident in which OpenAI software broke out of a secure testing environment during a trial and independently accessed systems belonging to AI company Hugging Face.
Following the incident, major US AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic said they were prepared to slow the development of the technology, something critics had long called for.
In recent years, Amodei has repeatedly warned of risks of AI development and has at times been sharply criticized for this by some in the AI industry. One argument in the United States, backed by US President Donald Trump and the White House, is the race with China for AI supremacy.

articles.heading: U.S. Senate holds hearing on automated license plate reader technology
articles.summary: Executives from all four major ALPR companies were invited to testify before a Senate subcommittee, and all of them declined to do so.
articles.content:
U.S. Senate holds hearing on automated license plate reader technology
GREEN BAY, Wis. (WBAY) - As a growing number of communities across our area terminate their contract with Flock, members of the U.S. Senate met on Wednesday to examine allegations of police abuse and the potential need for safeguards.
Executives from all four major companies that sell automatic license plate reader (ALPR) technology, including Flock, were invited to testify before a Senate subcommittee, and all of them declined to do so.
During the hearing, the subcommittee did hear from several other people, including Lindsey Isaacs, who was falsely accused in a car crash where three people died in Florida based on information from an ALPR camera.
Her testimony has become the focal point for the congressional scrutiny against cameras like the ones used by Flock.
The black Dodge Durango Isaacs drove was pinged by a camera three miles from the scene around the time of the crash.
However, witnesses described a maroon Durango, and investigators only relied on the data from the camera.
She told members of the subcommittee how she was then arrested and jailed for 13 days despite having nothing to do with the crash.
“I was terrified. I was facing the possibility of spending the rest of my life in prison for a crash I knew I had not been involved in. I did not know if I would ever get out of jail. At my lowest point, I didn’t want to be alive,” said Isaacs.
Illinois senator Dick Durbin also wanted to know if the cameras are being used in cooperation with ICE investigations, to which he was told it’s possible.
“Looking at it in the immigration context is horrifying, but they’ve done the same with people who go to gun ranges. This really is non-partisan. It is: come up with the group you want to target, and with this level of technology, targeting them is fairly easy,” said Chad Marlow, a senior policy counsel with the ACLU.
In our area, several communities have announced the end of their contracts with Flock, including Winnebago, Fond du Lac, and Waupaca counties.
Green Bay police will continue to use the technology but say that additional safeguards are in place to restrict access and prevent misuse.

articles.heading: The hour before the school bus: How connected technology can help calm the morning rush
articles.summary: How smart-home technology can calm the morning rush, helping families automate routines, reduce distractions and start the day with confidence.
articles.content:
The hour before the kids leave for school can be a scramble for even the most organized families.
Lunches are being packed. A permission slip is sitting unsigned on the kitchen counter. The dog still needs to go outside. Parents are watching the clock while mentally juggling pickup schedules, after-school activities and their own morning commute.
It's not usually one big problem that creates stress. It's dozens of small decisions competing for attention at the same time.
Did someone lock the back door? Are the lights still on upstairs? Will the house be comfortable when everyone gets home? What if I forget something important?
As families look for ways to simplify busy routines during the school year, many are turning to connected technology to automate everyday tasks and reduce some of the mental load of managing a household.
"Understanding your routine and being able to adapt to it is really important for us at ADT," said James Knox, ADT's Director of Product Management. "Our goal is to recognize when something falls outside a home's normal routine and help homeowners decide whether action is needed."
That philosophy reflects a broader shift in how families use smart-home technology. Instead of simply monitoring what happens at home, connected devices can help households prepare for the day ahead, automate recurring tasks and reduce the number of things parents need to think about before walking out the door.
Here are three ways connected technology can help make hectic mornings a little easier.
Put routine tasks on autopilot
During a busy morning, every task someone doesn't have to remember is one less thing competing for attention.
Connected-home automations can help handle many of the small actions that often become last-minute worries. Families can schedule lights to turn off after everyone leaves, automatically arm their system as the house empties or adjust temperatures before the day begins.
Using the ADT+ app, homeowners can create routines around how their family actually lives, with schedules that differ between weekdays, weekends and school breaks.
Rather than wondering whether the house was secured while rushing from school drop-off to work, parents can have confidence that those tasks happened automatically.
Stay connected without constant check-ins
Even during the morning rush, families are rarely all moving on the same schedule.
One child may leave early for band practice. A teenager might miss the bus and head back home. A grandparent could stop by while everyone is away.
Connected cameras and video doorbells can help families stay informed without requiring texts, calls or constant check-ins.
Through the ADT+ app, homeowners can receive notifications from devices such as doorbell cameras and see who's at the door from virtually anywhere. Two-way audio also allows family members to communicate with visitors or children who arrive home later in the day.
For households that regularly coordinate with trusted family members, caregivers or service providers, Trusted Neighbor† can simplify access by allowing temporary or scheduled entry directly through the ADT+ app.
The result is fewer interruptions and more visibility into what's happening at home throughout the day.
Catch the things busy mornings make easy to miss
The faster a morning moves, the easier it is to overlook something.
A garage door gets left open. A window that's normally closed remains open after everyone leaves. A routine part of the morning simply doesn't happen.
The ADT+ app's Unusual Activity Alerts feature is designed to identify activity that falls outside a home's normal patterns and draw attention to situations that may deserve a second look. Using information from connected devices such as ADT door and window sensors, the feature can help surface issues that might otherwise go unnoticed.
According to Knox, the objective isn't to create more alerts. It's to help homeowners focus on the alerts that matter most.
"The most effective smart-home experiences aren't the ones that create the most notifications," Knox said. "They're the ones that help homeowners quickly understand what matters and decide whether action is needed."
When a busy day becomes something more
Sometimes, however, a situation requires more than a notification. That's where professional monitoring provides an additional layer of support.
ADT's network of company-operated monitoring centers is staffed 24/7/365 by trained professionals who can help when alarm events occur* — whether you’re home or not.
For Knox, that's where technology and people work best together.
"Professional monitoring gives homeowners reassurance that someone is looking out for them,” Knox said. “It provides confidence that support is available when human expertise and response are needed.”
A calmer start to the day
No technology can eliminate the realities of family life. There will still be forgotten lunchboxes, last-minute schedule changes and mornings when everyone is running late.
But when fewer routine tasks require attention, families can spend less time worrying about what they may have forgotten and more time focusing on getting where they need to go.
Sometimes peace of mind doesn't come from adding more information. It comes from having fewer things to think about before the school bus arrives.
ADT products that help support busy families
- ADT Door/Window Sensor: Helps parents stay aware of doors and windows that may have been left open during a rushed morning.
- ADT Smart Light Bulb: Parents can check that lights were turned off for the day or program them to automatically turn on before family members arrive home.
- Google Nest Doorbell (wired, 3rd gen): Allows parents to see who's at the door, receive notifications, and use two-way audio to check in from virtually anywhere.
- Google Nest Learning Thermostat (4th gen): Can automatically adjust temperatures when the house is empty and before it fills up again.
Visit ADT.com to start putting together your ideal professionally installed or ADT Blu DIY security system.

Familiar face detection is not to be used as definitive identification, and is not available on Nest cameras used in Illinois. Customer is responsible to inform their trusted individuals of any dangerous conditions existing at the premises.

Did someone lock the back door? Are the lights still on upstairs? Will the house be comfortable when everyone gets home? What if I forget something important?

As families look for ways to simplify busy routines during the school year, many are turning to connected technology to automate everyday tasks and reduce some of the mental load of managing a household.

"Understanding your routine and being able to adapt to it is really important for us at ADT," said James Knox, ADT's Director of Product Management. "Our goal is to recognize when something falls outside a home's normal routine and help homeowners decide whether action is needed."

That philosophy reflects a broader shift in how families use smart-home technology. Instead of simply monitoring what happens at home, connected devices can help households prepare for the day ahead, automate recurring tasks and reduce the number of things parents need to think about before walking out the door.

Here are three ways connected technology can help make hectic mornings a little easier.

Put routine tasks on autopilot

During a busy morning, every task someone doesn't have to remember is one less thing competing for attention.

Connected-home automations can help handle many of the small actions that often become last-minute worries. Families can schedule lights to turn off after everyone leaves, automatically arm their system as the house empties or adjust temperatures before the day begins.

Using the ADT+ app, homeowners can create routines around how their family actually lives, with schedules that differ between weekdays, weekends and school breaks.

Rather than wondering whether the house was secured while rushing from school drop-off to work, parents can have confidence that those tasks happened automatically.

Stay connected without constant check-ins

Even during the morning rush, families are rarely all moving on the same schedule.

One child may leave early for band practice. A teenager might miss the bus and head back home. A grandparent could stop by while everyone is away.

Connected cameras and video doorbells can help families stay informed without requiring texts, calls or constant check-ins.

Through the ADT+ app, homeowners can receive notifications from devices such as doorbell cameras and see who's at the door from virtually anywhere. Two-way audio also allows family members to communicate with visitors or children who arrive home later in the day.

For households that regularly coordinate with trusted family members, caregivers or service providers, Trusted Neighbor† can simplify access by allowing temporary or scheduled entry directly through the ADT+ app.

The result is fewer interruptions and more visibility into what's happening at home throughout the day.

Catch the things busy mornings make easy to miss

The faster a morning moves, the easier it is to overlook something.

A garage door gets left open. A window that's normally closed remains open after everyone leaves. A routine part of the morning simply doesn't happen.

The ADT+ app's Unusual Activity Alerts feature is designed to identify activity that falls outside a home's normal patterns and draw attention to situations that may deserve a second look. Using information from connected devices such as ADT door and window sensors, the feature can help surface issues that might otherwise go unnoticed.

According to Knox, the objective isn't to create more alerts. It's to help homeowners focus on the alerts that matter most.

"The most effective smart-home experiences aren't the ones that create the most notifications," Knox said. "They're the ones that help homeowners quickly understand what matters and decide whether action is needed."

When a busy day becomes something more

Sometimes, however, a situation requires more than a notification. That's where professional monitoring provides an additional layer of support.

ADT's network of company-operated monitoring centers is staffed 24/7/365 by trained professionals who can help when alarm events occur* — whether you’re home or not.

For Knox, that's where technology and people work best together.

"Professional monitoring gives homeowners reassurance that someone is looking out for them,” Knox said. “It provides confidence that support is available when human expertise and response are needed.”

A calmer start to the day

No technology can eliminate the realities of family life. There will still be forgotten lunchboxes, last-minute schedule changes and mornings when everyone is running late.

But when fewer routine tasks require attention, families can spend less time worrying about what they may have forgotten and more time focusing on getting where they need to go.

Sometimes peace of mind doesn't come from adding more information. It comes from having fewer things to think about before the school bus arrives.

ADT products that help support busy families
  • ADT Door/Window Sensor: Helps parents stay aware of doors and windows that may have been left open during a rushed morning.
  • ADT Smart Light Bulb: Parents can check that lights were turned off for the day or program them to automatically turn on before family members arrive home.
  • Google Nest Doorbell (wired, 3rd gen): Allows parents to see who's at the door, receive notifications, and use two-way audio to check in from virtually anywhere.
  • Google Nest Learning Thermostat (4th gen): Can automatically adjust temperatures when the house is empty and before it fills up again.

articles.title: Naperville police officer used Flock technology for stalking, records show
articles.description: Naperville police officer used Flock technology for stalking, records show Chicago Tribune
articles.description_html: Naperville police officer used Flock technology for stalking, records show  Chicago Tribune
articles.article_title: Naperville police officer used Flock technology for stalking, records show
articles.heading: Naperville police officer used Flock technology for stalking, records show
articles.summary: A Naperville police officer used Flock Safety license plate reader technology to track a girlfriend and her ex-fiance, documents show.
articles.content:
A Naperville police officer used Flock Safety license plate reader technology to track a girlfriend and her ex-fiance, according to documents obtained in a Freedom of Information Act request filed by the Naperville Sun.
Oscar Maldonado, who no longer works for the Naperville Police Department, tracked license plates for non-police-related matters hundreds of times between June 18, 2025, and Sept. 15, 2025, records show. When the department received a citizen complaint about the cameras’ misuse, an investigation was conducted.
Maldonado was placed on administrative leave while an internal investigation was done, and ultimately resigned in May prior to the conclusion of the probe, according to a statement from Naperville Police Chief Jason Arres.
Naperville police contacted the Will County sheriff’s office to conduct an independent criminal investigation, which was later turned over to the state’s attorney’s office. A representative for the prosecutor’s office said they could not confirm or deny any investigation being done by their staff.
Automated license plate readers — increasingly synonymous with Flock, though there are other brands on the market — photograph license plates and other identifiers of passing vehicles. Police officers can use the data obtained for investigations.
However, a growing number of officers in the Chicago area and across the country have been accused of searching those databases for personal reasons. Civil liberties activists say they fear law enforcement agencies could use the cameras to work with immigration officials or to surveil law-abiding citizens.
As allegations of misuse mount, police departments and lawmakers are grappling with how to prevent the cameras’ misuse.
“The Naperville Police Department has and will continue to develop strong policies and auditing procedures around these sensitive systems and hold individuals accountable for any misuse,” Arres wrote in the statement. “This is precisely the approach we took in this instance and the standard we are committed to upholding for our community going forward.”
The department updated its internal policy on automated license plate reader usage earlier this month, which now includes a new section on the auditing process. Naperville police also reported both Maldonado’s resignation and internal investigation to the Illinois Law Enforcement and Training Standards Board.
According to the documents obtained in the FOIA request, Maldonado began using Flock to track the woman and her ex-fiance shortly after entering into a relationship with the woman.
In his interrogation with the police department, Maldonado said he did not use the technology for a criminal case involving the woman or her ex-fiance but for personal reasons.
When asked why he used Flock to look up the license plates, Maldonado said it was for the safety of the woman he was seeing, himself and his family.
According to both the internal investigation and his attorney, Patty Kalkanis, there were times when Maldonado felt threatened by the ex-fiance, including multiple incidents in which the ex-fiance allegedly tracked Maldonado.
“It wasn’t our client stalking him and our client being the aggressor. We believe that … Mr. Maldonado was only trying to protect himself,” Kalkanis said.
However, the police investigation casts doubt on Maldonado’s explanation, citing instances in which Maldonado used Flock despite there being no clear threat to his own safety, his family’s or the woman he was seeing.
It also notes that despite the concerning behavior, Maldonado never reported these incidents to law enforcement. He also conceded during the interrogation that the information he obtained would have done little to no good in protecting his family as he wasn’t home.
The police’s internal report found Maldonado violated multiple department regulations, including abusing his authority and breaking the department’s code of ethics.
“(T)here is a preponderance of the evidence that shows Maldonado did commit the crime of official misconduct,” the report said. “Evidence shows that Maldonado performed acts in excess of lawful authority, being the use of FLOCK, with intent to obtain personal advantage.”
But Kalkanis disputes the claim that Maldonado’s actions rise to the level of official misconduct due to a lack of state legislative clarity regarding Flock misuse.
“This is Illinois case law and it is very clear that it is not breaking the law using Flock right now. … There is no law to have been broken. Maybe a violation of an employee manual but I think that’s about as far as it can go,” Kalkanis said.
Other criminal charges, such as stalking, could be possible. Last year, the ex-fiance filed a stalking no contact order against Maldonado, but that case was later dropped and the two agreed to enter into an order to stay away from each other, Kalkanis said.
“Any complaining witness or alleged victim can go to the state’s attorney’s office and say, ‘X, Y and Z happened so charge them’ and the state’s attorney has a job whether to proceed on their word with maybe little to no evidence or not,” she said.
When asked if Maldonado had any regrets about how he used the Flock system, Kalkanis said the only regret he may have is not informing a supervisor sooner about what was going on.
“I think that’s the only regret he has. He does not have a regret using the tools and the resources he has to protect himself and his family,” she said.
Chicago Tribune staff writers Rebecca Johnson and Lila Hempel-Edgers contributed to this report.
cstein@chicagotribune.com

articles.title: At UN, tech chiefs urge caution in AI development
articles.description: At UN, tech chiefs urge caution in AI development Yahoo
articles.description_html: At UN, tech chiefs urge caution in AI development  Yahoo
articles.article_title: At UN, tech chiefs urge caution in AI development
articles.heading: At UN, tech chiefs urge caution in AI development
articles.summary: Leaders of major AI firms told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that the technology calls for heightened vigilance, with Anthropic's CEO pledging to slow down where needed to ensure the safety of ...
articles.content:
At UN, tech chiefs urge caution in AI development
Leaders of major AI firms told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that the technology calls for heightened vigilance, with Anthropic's CEO pledging to slow down where needed to ensure the safety of new releases.
"This moment calls for extreme care," OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in New York at an emergency meeting of the 15-member council.
He warned that as AI systems become more capable and autonomous, they could move faster than institutions or concentrate power into too few hands.
Altman was among industry leaders briefing the council following weeks of global headlines about the risks of uncontrollable artificial intelligence and calls for a slowdown, which have been resisted by US President Donald Trump.
"The industry must not accept too much technological risk just because the benefits are too great and important to slow down," Altman told the United Nations' top body.
He also urged governments to work with each other and the industry on decisions shaping the technology's future.
"In our history, there have been times where countries who compete and don't always like each other very much still come together for shared interests and the collective good in the face of a powerful new technology," he said.
"We believe this must be one of those times," he added.
- Slowing down -
Speaking after Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said his company understands that as AI models become more powerful, "even more stringent standards of safety will be required."
He said Anthropic aims to improve its ability to prevent misuse of the technology.
"We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," Amodei said in a video feed.
"If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole," Amodei added.
Other speakers included Clement Delangue of Hugging Face, which was the target of a recent cyberattack by autonomous OpenAI software.
This marked the first in a series of incidents that have raised alarm bells over the rapidly evolving technology.
In early September, Jacob Coxon, a researcher who worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic, decided to leave the industry and accused both companies of "gambling with our lives" in the race to develop AI models capable of self-improvement.
- 'Middle path' -
The executives' remarks come shortly before Trump is due to welcome Chinese leader Xi Jinping, hosting him for a summit where AI will be on the agenda.
On Wednesday, Altman said his company would try to walk a "middle path."
"We don't want to fall into the trap of blind optimism," but he cautioned against falling into "doomerism" too.
Yoshua Bengio, the Canadian computer scientist considered one of the founders of AI, told the Security Council that "more and more people are rightly worried about recent advances."
"We must channel that concern into productive action," he said.
Delangue of Hugging Face noted that while his company was targeted by AI, it also used the technology to fend off the attacks. "The world needs open-source AI more than ever to defend itself."
Altman, Amodei and several other leading AI executives have been calling for global oversight of the technology.
OpenAI has urged the United States to lead a global effort on establishing standards for AI, noting that its industry is at the technical frontier.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Tuesday that Britain would launch an effort to set up global AI standards during its 2027 G20 presidency.
France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot similarly urged joint action within the UN framework and with companies to set rules for a new era.
But diplomatic efforts could clash with the US position.
Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, said rapid advancement is not a reason to pause AI's development or constrain it with new governance structures.
Trump on Tuesday rejected international regulation of AI, calling such proposals a "globalist scheme."
bys/msp

articles.title: Prince William County, Va., Taps a New Technology Director
articles.description: Prince William County, Va., Taps a New Technology Director GovTech
articles.description_html: Prince William County, Va., Taps a New Technology Director  GovTech
articles.article_title: Prince William County, Va., Taps a New Technology Director
articles.heading: Prince William County, Va., Taps a New Technology Director
articles.summary: Duane Prophet brings more than 25 years of local gov tech experience from adjacent Prince George’s County, Md., to Prince William County, Va., as its incoming director of IT.
articles.content:
Following a national search, the county has appointed Duane Prophet as director of its Department of Information Technology. He will start Monday, taking on a job that covers many parts of the county’s technology operation, including cybersecurity, computer systems, digital services, cloud technology and newer tech.
Prophet has spent much of his career roughly 50 miles away in Prince George’s County, Md., where he rose through the organization during more than 25 years in government technology. He started as an entry-level clerk before moving into technology and leadership positions. Prophet also worked more than 13 years at Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission, an agency serving two counties.
Most recently, Prophet was Prince George’s County’s director of digital government. In 2025, he also served as acting CIO and chaired the county’s AI Task Force. He holds a bachelor’s degree in information systems management from the University of Maryland and has several professional technology certifications.
His move to Prince William County comes after Mancini resigned in February, following nearly nine years as its CIO. He left behind an IT operation that went through major changes during his time at the helm, including upgrades to its computer and communications systems, and improvements in cybersecurity and digital services.
During his tenure, Prince William County also ranked No. 1 among counties with populations from 250,000-499,999, in the Center for Digital Government’s* 2023 Digital Counties Survey.
Prophet will now take over that technology operation and continue its work, connecting with leaders on planning and modernization as the county continues to update its systems.
County Executive Chris Shorter pointed to Prophet’s experience in local government as an important part of his appointment in an announcement Tuesday and said he brings “extensive experience in using technology to strengthen government operations.”
For Prophet, the move is an opportunity to work with the county’s technology team, he said in a statement, on “resilient, innovative and customer-focused solutions” for employees and residents.
*The Center for Digital Government is part of e.Republic, Government Technology's parent company.

articles.title: Caroline Board of Supervisors approve Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center
articles.description: Caroline Board of Supervisors approve Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center Fredericksburg Free Press
articles.description_html: Caroline Board of Supervisors approve Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center  Fredericksburg Free Press
articles.article_title: Caroline Board of Supervisors approve Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center – Fredericksburg Free Press
articles.heading: Caroline Board of Supervisors approve Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center
articles.summary: Caroline Board of Supervisors approve Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center Fredericksburg Free Press
articles.content:
by

The Caroline County Board of Supervisors and community members shared varying viewpoints when it came to a proposed massive industrial park called the Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center.

During a board public hearing on Tuesday, Western Caroline District Supervisor Jeff Black expressed concerns about increased traffic along U.S. Route 1 and the fact that no end-user has been determined for the facility.

Bowling Green District Supervisor Jeff Sili doesn’t believe the road infrastructure can handle the development, while other officials were optimistic about the economic benefits and community projects that developer Luck Stone proposed in exchange for rezoning 916 acres from Rural Preservation to Industrial in the Reedy Church magisterial district.

Bishop Duane Fields Sr., pastor of Oxford Mount Zion Baptist Church, said the board’s decision should be an easy one when considering that Luck Stone is planning to facilitate the construction of a community center for his church, a waterpark at Lowe-Massie Park in the Dawn area, and provide assistance to Jericho Baptist Church, Carmel Baptist Church, and The Carmel School.

“Tonight, I’m asking this board to consider the needs of this district and the future we are creating for the next generation,” Fields said. “Some are asking you to preserve land. I’m asking you to preserve lives. Reedy Church doesn’t need to be managed into stagnation. We need help facilitating our progress.”

In the end, the board voted 4-2 to approve the rezoning as a large flock of Oxford Mount Zion members rejoiced.

Black and Sili cast the dissenting votes. Board Chair Clay Forehand (Madison District), along with Nancy Long (Port Royal District), Floyd Thomas (Mattaponi District), and Reginald Underwood (Reedy Church) voted in favor of the project.

The vote came less than a month after the county’s planning commission voted 3-1 to recommend denial , in large part because no end user has been determined. Charlie Payne, an attorney representing Luck Stone, told the planning commission in July that the vision is for a “typical industrial park” with logistics, distribution, warehousing, manufacturing, and research and development offices. At full capacity in 2031, 5.6 million square feet of building space is projected.

Caroline Director of Public Utilities Joey Schiebel said there is sufficient water for the project, and Underwood asserted that electricity isn’t a concern either.

“They need to shut the hell up, saying there’s not enough water, because that’s not true,” Underwood said. “There is enough electricity. I think utilities are there. So, stop that conversation. Let’s speak about the benefits of this project.”

Those benefits include 1,800 jobs and $15 million in annual projected revenue for the county at full buildout.

Del. Nicole Cole, D-Spotsylvania, attended the public hearing and spoke in favor of the project, citing a potential boost in tax revenue in an area that is “underserved.”

Cole said the construction of the community center and industrial park allows her to entice resources to the county because they’ll have a location in which to operate. Brian Freeman, a Caroline native who specializes in assisting people suffering from drug addiction, said the community center would help prevent childhood traumas that lead to people turning to substance abuse.

Michael Dreiling, the leader of the Virginia Economic Development Partnership Real Estate Solutions team, stressed that recruiting businesses is a lot easier when property is already zoned. Dreiling noted that the VEDP put together real-estate packages for some of the largest projects in Virginia, including L3Harris Technologies in Northern Virginia, AstraZeneca in Albemarle County, and Lego in Chesterfield County. He said large economic development projects like Luck Stone is presenting can be “transformational” for any community.

“What I’ve heard tonight is one of the best cases for the work that we do at the state level that I’ve heard in the last four and a half years that I’ve been in the role that I serve,” Dreiling said. “These opportunities are not going to properties that are not zoned. They have to be fully zoned and proffered. We have not seen a large-scale opportunity go to a single unzoned property in the last four and a half years.”

Reedy Church District resident Kevin Collins, who is planning to compete with Planning Commissioner J.D. Young for Underwood’s board of supervisors’ seat in 2027, said the project is transformational for all the wrong reasons.

“We need to step back and ask a very basic question: ‘Does this project belong here?’” Collins said. “Not whether it can be engineered, not whether roads can eventually be widened, not whether the property can technically be rezoned, but whether transforming more than 1,000 acres of rural land into a massive industrial development is appropriate for this part of the county. I believe it is not. This is not just another business park. The scale of this proposal would fundamentally change this area forever.”

The project area includes several parcels located between Jericho Road and U.S. Route 1 and along Zion Road and Oxford Road.

The supervisors voted 6-0 in August 2024 to approve the Comprehensive Plan amendment to change the land use in that area from Rural Transition to Industrial. Underwood said “nobody twisted our arm” to vote for the amendment.

Still, Black and Sili aren’t sold that the Luck Stone project is good for the area. Black cited a traffic study showing the project will increase daily trips on U.S. Route 1 from 5,500 to 14,778. He also noted that Rappahannock Electric Cooperative is moving its headquarters to the Route 1 area, that Pendleton subdivision is constantly building homes, and that it’s already difficult leaving Lake Caroline to reach the U.S. 1 highway.

“I have major concerns with Route 1 being an absolute nightmare as far as traffic is concerned,” Black said.

However, Underwood and Thomas espoused the benefits of the project, including revised proffers that include a five-mile public walking trail, a $300,000 contribution to a splash pad at Lowe-Massie Park, $100,000 to the Career and Technical Education program at Caroline High School, and the OMZBC community center to provide an outlet for youth, adults, and seniors.

Thomas said former Caroline Superintendent Stanley Jones, a deacon at OMZBC, assured him that church officials would not allow a company to take advantage of them.

“I believe Mr. Jones, and I think the biggest thing is this gives people hope,” Thomas said. “And I think hope is something we don’t have enough of right now. You heard the young lady talk about her son needing tutoring. I believe this community center will provide tutoring.

“There is also going to be a daycare there. Do you know how important it is to be able to drop your kid off somewhere safely and go to work? I know a lot of y’all are doing what I did. You’re driving up to D.C. where the good jobs are. We’re going to make it so the good jobs are here now.”

articles.article_title: Five officers face charges after Indiana police department finds ALPR technology misuse
articles.heading: Five officers face charges after Indiana police department finds ALPR technology misuse
articles.summary: In August and September, internal audits at the the Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department found potential misuse of the license plate reader technology, police say.
articles.content:
Five officers face charges after Indiana police department finds ALPR technology misuse
The reported misuse happened before the department’s new ALPR policy, police say
INDIANAPOLIS (WNDU) - Four suspended officers and one former officer with the Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department (IMPD) were accused of fraud and official misconduct after reportedly misusing automatic license plate reader (ALPR) technology.
Michael Rogers, Cassandra Crawley, Matthew Binford and another unnamed officer were all suspended and recommended for termination. The unnamed officer’s identity has not been released because the warrant is sealed.
Abigail Cramer resigned from IMPD after the officers were placed on administrative duty following the investigation’s preliminary findings.
In August and September, internal audits found potential ALPR misuse, according to IMPD. The police department investigated, and all five officers were placed on administrative duty with no police powers or access to ALPR systems.
According to IMPD, the reported misuse happened before the department’s new ALPR policy, which requires every ALPR user to sign the policy to keep access.
IMPD said it has implemented stronger auditing to more quickly identify and investigate potential license plate reader misuse.

Five officers face charges after Indiana police department finds ALPR technology misuse

The reported misuse happened before the department’s new ALPR policy, police say

INDIANAPOLIS (WNDU) - Four suspended officers and one former officer with the Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department (IMPD) were accused of fraud and official misconduct after reportedly misusing automatic license plate reader (ALPR) technology.

Michael Rogers, Cassandra Crawley, Matthew Binford and another unnamed officer were all suspended and recommended for termination. The unnamed officer’s identity has not been released because the warrant is sealed.

Abigail Cramer resigned from IMPD after the officers were placed on administrative duty following the investigation’s preliminary findings.

articles.title: NACS hires Paul Ziv as vice president of technology

articles.description_html: NACS hires Paul Ziv as vice president of technology  CSP Daily News
articles.article_title: NACS hires Paul Ziv as vice president of technology
articles.heading: NACS hires Paul Ziv as vice president of technology
articles.summary: Convenience-store association also promotes Bob Hughes to senior vice president of supplier relations, expositions and meetings
articles.content:
Paul Ziv has joined the National Association of Convenience Stores (NACS) as its new vice president of technology. In this newly created position, Ziv will lead technology strategy and the development of digital capabilities across NACS and its affiliated organizations, including TruAge, NACS said.
“NACS has a huge focus on accelerating innovation and guiding priorities to help unlock new sources of value across the global convenience and fuel retailing industry, and we are thrilled to bring on Paul to help us build our internal and external capabilities to take us there,” said NACS President and CEO Frank Gleeson. “Paul brings the experience to turn that ambition into practical capabilities that support our teams, members and partners.”
Prior to his new position, Ziv served as vice president of emerging technology and operations for TruAge. Before that, he was vice president of information technology for AnswerNet, overseeing a 100-person team responsible for software development and innovation, programming, infrastructure and quality assurance.
Ziv also served in multiple leadership roles at March of Dimes, including as vice president and associate chief operating officer. He also has industry experience, previously serving as senior network administrator at Atlanta-based RaceTrac Inc.
Alexandria, Virginia-based NACS also promoted Bob Hughes to its senior vice president of supplier relations, expositions and meetings.
Hughes joined NACS nearly 25 years ago as a director of expositions. Since then, NACS has enhanced its supplier relations and expanded its meetings and events portfolio, NACS said in a news release.
Hughes has led engagement of NACS’ 1,8000 supplier members, with a particular focus on cultivating the Hunter Club. His team has helped make the NACS Show one of the Top 50 tradeshows by expo size in the country, NACS said.
“This promotion reflects the trust Bob’s built across our industry, and the importance of our supplier partners,” Gleeson said. “We have an ambitious set of objectives moving forward in growing the NACS Show and overall member engagement, and I am excited about how Bob and his team will continue to elevate the NACS offer to the benefit of our industry.”

articles.title: Heads of AI firms tell UN Security Council that it could be a risk to all humanity
articles.description: Heads of AI firms tell UN Security Council that it could be a risk to all humanity Spectrum News
articles.description_html: Heads of AI firms tell UN Security Council that it could be a risk to all humanity  Spectrum News
articles.article_title: Heads of AI firms tell UN Security Council that it could risk all humanity
articles.heading: Heads of AI firms tell UN Security Council that it could be a risk to all humanity
articles.summary: THey pleaded with the United Nations on Wednesday to set controls over the burgeoning technology they are designing in order to save the world
articles.content:
UNITED NATIONS — The heads of major artificial intelligence firms pleaded with the United Nations on Wednesday to set controls over the burgeoning technology they are designing in order to save the world — or, at least, its people.
“If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” said Dario Amodei, the chief executive officer of Anthropic.
“We could lose control of the future to AI,” said his competitor, Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI.
Both said the countries of the world, though the U.N. Security Council, where they testified Wednesday afternoon, have to set safeguards, which would be actual controls to prevent the technology from getting too powerful to rein in. They also called for the world to make sure that the power of AI isn’t concentrated in one company or country.
For world leaders, one key question about AI is this: Who should control life-and-death decisions — human or machine?
The United Nations Security Council on Wednesday huddled with top technology leaders to figure out if the increasing abilities and pervasiveness of artificial intelligence should be controlled and, if so, by who. Other lingering questions: How could it be done? When might it be just too late?
The day before, U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of “killer robots.” Experts and European leaders said that’s not hyperbole but something that’s already a reality or at least perilously close.

articles.heading: Growing the next generation of technology talent
articles.summary: Almost $90K GenCyber grant will fund Missouri State’s next cyber camp.
articles.content:
What began as a small summer outreach effort in summer 2024 is growing into a larger investment in Southwest Missouri’s next generation of technology talent.
Missouri State University’s department of information technology and cybersecurity (ITC) has received an $89,868.98 GenCyber grant to expand cybersecurity education and outreach for middle and high school students.
The grant is awarded through GenCyber, a National Security Agency (NSA)-supported initiative that promotes cybersecurity education and helps inspire the next generation of cybersecurity professionals.
Dr. Xiang Guo, head of ITC, serves as program director and principal investigator for the project. Dr. Zhiguo Yang, professor of ITC, is the lead instructor and co-investigator, with co-investigators Jason Speer, senior instructor, and Conner Wilkinson, instructor.
The award will support a new GenCyber summer camp on campus planned for Aug. 16-20, 2027. The camp will allow up to 30 students to gain hands-on experience with cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and robotics while reducing financial barriers to participation. Grant funding will support equipment, supplies, faculty instruction and student counselors.
“We want to help our community and the next generation be technology ready,” said Yang. “When high school and middle school students get early exposure to advanced robotics and AI technology, they have an opportunity to understand these technologies, discover their interests and explore career paths they may not have considered before.”
Where it began
The GenCyber award is the latest step in a cybersecurity outreach effort years in the making at Missouri State.
ITC first gained experience working with younger learners through Cyber Cubs. Over three summers, faculty and student counselors developed lessons, tested hands-on activities and learned how to introduce cybersecurity, coding and robotics to students with varying levels of technology experience.
The work provided more than a successful summer camp. It gave the department a tested curriculum, lesson plans, photos, testimonials and a proven ability to deliver cybersecurity education to young learners.
At the same time, ITC strengthened its academic cybersecurity infrastructure. Missouri State established its Center of Academic Excellence in Cybersecurity Operations, Research and Engagement and earned the National Security Agency’s Center of Academic Excellence in Cyber Defense (CAE-CD) designation in 2025. The designation recognizes institutions that meet national standards for cybersecurity education, with community outreach forming part of the broader mission of the CAE-CD program.
Those initiatives led to the next step: GenCyber, a program available only to academic institutions with a current CAE-CD designation.
“These milestones were not separate accomplishments, but part of a deliberate progression,” said Guo. “Each step builds a stronger foundation for what comes next, but the goal has always been bigger than the program itself. It’s about using what we’ve built to give back to the community and create more opportunities for the next generation.”
Putting GenCyber in motion
The new camp will move students from learning cybersecurity concepts to applying them to systems they can build, test and see in action.
Students will explore defense-in-depth; confidentiality, integrity and availability; adversarial thinking; and secure system design. They will reinforce those concepts through applying them with physical computing and robotics challenges.
One planned project brings several of those ideas together in an autonomous or semi-autonomous building patrol security system. Student teams will work with a quadruped, design patrol routes and explore how cameras can identify potential physical security concerns. They will also examine how the system could detect suspicious Wi-Fi access points.
Programming experience is preferred but not required for the GenCyber Camp. Rather than making coding a barrier, the curriculum teaches students to think through logic, system design and how different technologies work together to solve security problems.
“We want campers to focus on the design, figuring out what their program needs to do to solve the problem,” Yang said.
How to participate
Registration details for the 2027 GenCyber Camp will be announced when available. Students and families across Missouri interested in the program can visit the Association for Business Information Students website.

articles.title: ‘I miss old Google’: readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AI
articles.description: ‘I miss old Google’: readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AI The Guardian
articles.description_html: ‘I miss old Google’: readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AI  The Guardian
articles.article_title: ‘I miss old Google’: readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AI
articles.heading: ‘I miss old Google’: readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AI
articles.summary: A feature called AI Overviews has been a profound change, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting
articles.content:
Google has put artificial intelligence at the front and center of its search bar. The most-visited site on the internet still shows the same list of links to users, but they have to scroll past a summarized response from an AI chatbot, a feature Google calls AI Overviews. The change to what was once the gateway to the rest of the internet has been profound, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting.
“AI is driving the most significant upgrade of the Google Search experience ever,” wrote Liz Reid, Google’s vice-president of search, last August. In May, the company said more AI is coming.
As people grow accustomed to AI chatbots, they’re spending more time with Google’s and therefore more time on Google.com. Academic studies are finding that people navigate less to sites beyond Google if an AI Overview can give them a good enough answer, even if the bot cites the sites that feed it. Clicks, also known as traffic, are often the most significant way a website earns money from advertising. Media outlets and website owners are enduring a sustained traffic decline. Large US media companies are suing Google, alleging that AI summaries have redirected and reduced traffic to their sites, cutting into their revenue.
Google said it had not seen a decline in aggregate traffic and that such accusations are based on “flawed methodologies”. Reid, the company’s vice-president of search, wrote last year: “Total organic click volume from Google Search to websites has been relatively stable year-over-year.”
The Guardian asked readers whether Google has improved or worsened in the age of AI and how their habits of searching the internet have changed.
‘Google is better now’
Better, mainly because it leads you in your quest rather than you having to search on yourself. I am happy to have the AI lead me to an answer but the mega caution is that Google AI or any of them are not at all trustworthy. I have had it admit that it was lying to me and apologise! Sionn Achog, retired teacher 76, Dublin
I find that AI responses are more informative than previously, which simply referred the user to other relevant websites. Peter Warb, 75, UK
AI has made Google better. I use AI mode for all my searches. Jose Garcia Jr, 40, recovery coach, Dallas, Texas
AI has improved Google search. The analysis and chat functions are so much more useful than a ranked list of websites that still need to be explored by the user. Reviewing a list of websites is still an option but is very time consuming, and frustrating. Alan Caruana, consultant, 62, Malta
Far more better, faster and real. I search now with confidence, complete assurance and a high degree of accuracy. Eleazar Eke, electrical engineer, 67, Onitsha, Nigeria
Much better. It hasn’t changed my behavior, just getting better and more focused results. Catherine Weber, former political analyst, 57, Oregon
It’s made Google search much better, I find that I rarely actually click on the website links any more. I find information I want much faster and have a deeper understanding of any topic as I can ask questions about it and drill into the areas I’m interested in. Mark Johnson, 52, software engineer, London
Greatly improved it by getting at more arcane info regarding subject matter. Juxtaposition has improved with AI and abstruse knowledge of subjects becomes more accessible to layman. Wonderful tool with power to extend mind through sensing connections and very akin to human thinking. Samuel Lieberstein, 90, retired teacher, Cherry Hill, New Jersey
‘Search has gotten worse’
Search has become worse. Google AI obscures sources and tries to claim information it did not create while diverting traffic from the sources it steals from. Sean Peters, document processor, 41, Portland, Oregon
Every time I search I have to scroll down to find an actual real website to find a full article or discussion or to confirm that the AI summary isn’t making things up. Occasionally when I am feeling particularly bitter, I remember to add the ““-ai”” tag to my search. Ewan Herbert, English teacher, 33, Japan
Worse. I have disabled AI overviews using an extension. Chris Gibson, Dundee
Absolutely worse. I want to be able to decide for myself which results are the most useful and relevant, and we’re no longer able to turn off the AI summary results. Jon Wilkinson, personal trainer, 43, Manchester, UK
‘It’s so bad I quit Google’
Google has been enshittified … I do miss old Google Search and I really hope something of equal capabilities eventually comes to replace it.
The search engine I currently use is good for a lot of things, but if I need to look for something in languages other than English, the quality of the results is much lower. Image search is also not as good as that of Google used to be. Sofia, postdoctoral physics researcher, 30, Lausanne, Switzerland
My first stop now is Duck Duck Go, a pale imitation of Google’s search engine at the height of its powers. Unfortunately, the top results often include Grokipedia entries and other garbage. Craig Garrett, book editor, 52, New York City
I have stopped using Google. I now use another search engine with no AI overviews. Guy Arthur Simpson, writer 66, Spain
I’ve made a conscious effort to find a browser which does not lead with the AI results. Mine is now Ecosia. Dan Jennings, IT, 54, Southampton, UK
I do a lot of research for my studies, and the AI features are a nightmare! I’m still scouring for a decent search engine without any of these ‘AI features’, the last thing i want is to accidentally utilise a water-wasting AI behemoth datacentre when I forget that crucial suffix. I’ve even resorted to using my local library’s resource of legal cases for my work, at least it is trustworthy. Catherine O’Leary, student studying law, politics and sociology, 17, Newcastle Upon Tyne
Google has become almost useless, searches I’ve made in the past which yielded specific results, (news articles, local information, historical references) no longer appear. I no longer submit to Google search first, I go directly to Wikipedia as my first source, then to DuckDuckGo, (with AI disabled) then to Reddit and only to Google as a last resort. Pedro Reyes, 61, Galicia, Spain

articles.heading: Technology, Power, and ‘Constitutional Rot’
articles.summary: The federal government increasingly relies on private companies to govern: Palantir for foreign intelligence, Amazon for cloud computing, Starlink for
articles.content:
The federal government increasingly relies on private companies to govern: Palantir for foreign intelligence, Amazon for cloud computing, Starlink for satellite communications, and OpenAI and Anthropic for artificial intelligence. Meanwhile, digital platforms shape who gets heard and how people encounter politics and news.
None of that changes a word of the U.S. Constitution. But it is profoundly changing how the Constitution operates.
That was the sweeping—and sobering—argument Yale Law Professor Jack Balkin brought to Stanford’s 2026 Constitution Day lecture on September 17. Technological change, he argued, is reordering power among branches of government, blurring the line between public and private authority, weakening institutions essential to democratic debate, and accelerating what he calls “constitutional rot.”
“The Constitution on the page may stay exactly the same while the Constitution in practice changes dramatically because of changes in technology,” Balkin said.
Balkin, the Knight Professor of Constitutional Law and the First Amendment at Yale Law School and founder and director of Yale’s Information Society Project, delivered “Technology and Constitutional Rot,” presented by the Stanford Constitutional Law Center.
Michael McConnell, the Richard and Frances Mallery Professor of Law and director of the center, introduced Balkin. Constitution Day, McConnell said, is not simply about venerating a document completed in 1787, but about continuing the argument over what the Constitution means and how it should govern.
A Constitution Under Structural Pressure
Balkin defined “constitutional rot” as the process by which a democratic republic becomes less democratic and less republican: government grows less responsive to popular will, officials less oriented toward the public good, and norms of cooperation and fair play begin to erode.
Its “four horsemen,” he said, are widening wealth inequality, political polarization, loss of trust, and policy disasters that leave citizens viewing the government as incompetent or indifferent.
The United States has experienced such periods before, including the first Gilded Age and the decades preceding the Civil War. Balkin described the present as a “second Gilded Age,” marked by similar forces, including rapid technological disruption, extraordinary concentrations of wealth, bitter political division, and distrust of institutions.
Technology did not create those conditions, he stressed. But it is making them worse.
The Algorithmic State
Balkin calls the social order built around data, platforms, algorithms, robotics, and artificial intelligence the “algorithmic society.” Its governmental counterpart, the “algorithmic state,” increasingly uses prediction, automated decision-making, and AI in policing, immigration, taxation, public benefits, national security, warfare, and other areas.
That shift disproportionately empowers the executive branch, he said. Digital systems enhance what Alexander Hamilton prized in executive government—decision, activity, secrecy, and dispatch—while adding vast new capacities to gather information, predict behavior, and act.
Congress retains its formal powers but lacks comparable technological infrastructure, expertise, and speed. Courts, he said, can act only when disputes reach them, while the opacity and complexity of technological systems make oversight difficult.
When Government Governs by Platform
Major technology companies, Balkin stressed, are no longer simply contractors selling government products. They increasingly provide “the infrastructure through which government itself operates.”
At the same time, platforms act as “special purpose sovereigns,” he said, exercising governing authority of their own by setting rules, excluding users, ranking speakers, structuring markets, and resolving disputes. The result is what he described as “mutual co-optation”: governments seek technological capacity from private firms, while the firms seek contracts, favorable regulation, protection, and influence.
That poses a foundational constitutional problem because many protections depend on the distinction between public and private power. The First Amendment constrains government censorship while protecting private editorial judgment; the Fourth Amendment limits government searches while private companies routinely collect vast amounts of personal data.
“In a world in which we can no longer tell what’s private and what’s public,” Balkin said, “we have enormous tension on the constitutional system.”
When Everything Is ‘Content’
Democracy depends on institutions that produce knowledge, shape public opinion, and enable citizens to evaluate those who govern them, he said. Digital technology has enabled extraordinary freedom of expression while simultaneously weakening institutions—including journalism, universities, and science—that help distinguish knowledge from falsehood. The result is what Balkin called a “politics of attention,” with platforms rewarding engagement, not truth. These forces, he argued, compound constitutional rot. Concentrated wealth magnifies political power, attention-driven systems intensify polarization, opaque algorithms fuel distrust, and weakened knowledge institutions make policy failures harder to prevent and correct.
Can Constitutional Rot Be Reversed?
After joking that he had delivered “a total downer of a talk,” Balkin turned to renewal.
His grounds for optimism were historical. Earlier periods of constitutional rot were followed by sweeping reform: Reconstruction after the Civil War and, after the first Gilded Age, the Progressive Era and New Deal. But “history is not like clockwork,” he cautioned. Technology does not dictate political outcomes; people decide how technologies are designed, regulated, owned, and used.
Because the problems are structural, Balkin argued, the solutions must be as well. He pointed to stronger digital privacy protections, new approaches to civil rights and due process in algorithmic systems, better oversight of government technology procurement, stronger congressional technological capacity, and broad reforms to democratic institutions.
“Technology does not determine our fate,” Balkin concluded. “It changes possibilities for exercising power.” The constitutional challenge, he said, is to discipline those new technologies of power so they serve democratic and republican ends.
About Stanford Law School
Stanford Law School is one of the world’s leading institutions for legal scholarship and education. Its alumni are among the most influential decision makers in law, politics, business, and high technology. Faculty members argue before the Supreme Court, testify before Congress, produce outstanding legal scholarship and empirical analysis, and contribute regularly to the nation’s press as legal and policy experts. Stanford Law School has established a model for legal education that provides rigorous interdisciplinary training, hands-on experience, global perspective and a focus on public service.

articles.article_title: ETSU and Northeast State expand radiologic technology pathway - ETSU News
articles.heading: ETSU and Northeast State expand radiologic technology pathway
articles.summary: ETSU and Northeast State are creating a seamless pathway from an associate degree in radiologic technology to ETSU’s bachelor’s degree program.
articles.content:
East Tennessee State University and Northeast State Community College are expanding educational opportunities for students through a new articulation agreement that creates a direct pathway from Northeast State's Associate of Applied Science in Radiologic Technology to ETSU's Bachelor of Science in Radiologic Science .

Northeast State welcomed 19 students as the first cohort of the Radiologic Technology program in spring 2025. The students completed their two-year associate degrees in spring 2026, becoming the program's first graduates and the first students eligible to continue their education through this pathway to ETSU.

"We are pleased to see the first graduates of Northeast State's Radiologic Technology program have an opportunity to continue their education through this partnership with ETSU," said Dr. Stephanie Barham, Assistant Vice President for Academic Programs, Assessments, and Accreditation at Northeast State Community College. "This agreement reflects the strength of our institutions working together to create meaningful opportunities for students and support the continued development of healthcare professionals in our region."

The agreement also provides flexibility for licensed radiographers who want to advance their education while continuing to work in the field, bolstering the region's healthcare workforce.

"This articulation agreement is an excellent opportunity for licensed radiographers to obtain an advanced degree while working," said Dr. Ester L. Verhovsek-Hughes, chair and professor in the ETSU Department of Allied Health Sciences. "All courses are offered 100% online, allowing students to pursue their degree without the need to attend classes on campus. Advisors work directly with each student to develop a personalized program of study that prepares them for advancement in their field."

By connecting two-year and four-year degree programs, ETSU and Northeast State are helping students build on their existing education and prepare for continued career growth.

Go Beyond

East Tennessee State University was founded in 1911 with a singular mission: to improve the quality of life for people in the region and beyond. Through its world-class health sciences programs and interprofessional approach to health care education, ETSU is a highly respected leader in rural health research and practices. The university also boasts nationally ranked programs in the arts, technology, computing, and media studies. ETSU serves approximately 14,000 students each year and is ranked among the top 10 percent of colleges in the nation for students graduating with the least amount of debt.
