articles.title: Science, technology not contrary to faith, pope says
articles.description: Science, technology not contrary to faith, pope says Catholic Courier
articles.description_html: Science, technology not contrary to faith, pope says  Catholic Courier
articles.article_title: Science, technology not contrary to faith, pope says - Catholic Courier
articles.heading: Science, technology not contrary to faith, pope says
articles.summary: At his Sept. 23 general audience, Pope Leo XIV said that progress in science and technology is not contrary to belief in God.
articles.content:
VATICAN CITY (CNS) — Progress in science and technology is not contrary to belief in God, and Christians should be actively involved in shaping that progress so that it serves human dignity and the common good, Pope Leo XIV said.
At his Sept. 23 general audience, the pope also pointed to Venerable Archbishop Fulton Sheen, who is set to be beatified Sept. 24 in St. Louis, as an example of a Catholic who embraced the technology of his time to spread the Gospel.
Continuing his series on documents of the Second Vatican Council, Pope Leo reflected on the council’s conciliar constitution “Gaudium et Spes,” particularly its teaching on human activity and progress in the world.
Human beings, made in God’s image, are agents of progress
Created in the image and likeness of God, the human being is an agent of progress, the pope said, using freedom and intelligence to increase knowledge and advance society.
Yet as scientific and technological achievements multiplied, he said, some thinkers began portraying God and humanity as “rivals: in order to assert his knowledge, his freedom and his progress, man is thought to have to emancipate himself from God.”
Pope Leo called that view erroneous and quoted the late theologian, Jesuit Father Henri de Lubac, who described it as the “tragedy of atheistic humanism.”
“Ultimately, however, by denying the relationship with God, one also loses the possibility of affirming the transcendent value of the human person,” the pope said.
Quoting the conciliar constitution, he said Christians instead believe “that the triumphs of the human race are a sign of God’s grace and the flowering of His own mysterious design.”
Christians should direct progress toward human flourishing
Human achievement, therefore, should not draw the faithful away from involvement in scientific, technological or social progress, the pope said. Rather, the Gospel calls them to participate in building society while keeping such progress oriented toward human flourishing.
“Let us carry out our daily activities with true charity, offering our work to the Lord both as a means for personal sanctification and as an expression of our desire ever more fully to bring about God’s kingdom, especially through pursuing the common good, caring for the needy and defending human dignity,” he told English-speaking pilgrims.
Humanity’s freedom and activity are not absorbed or nullified by an encounter with God, Pope Leo said. Instead, humanity finds its fullest truth and freedom in Christ.
“From this perspective, an important truth emerges: to encounter God, the human being must not abandon his earthly occupations, but can live his vocation fully, carrying out his daily work well and sanctifying it,” he said.
Christians, he said, should therefore participate fully in society’s progress while reminding others of its “ultimate purpose.”
Pope Leo’s catechesis echoes his recent encyclical “Magnifica Humanitas,” in which he addressed the development of artificial intelligence and stressed that technological advances must remain at the service of human dignity.
Authentic human progress, the pope said at the general audience, “must be inspired and guided by charity” and improve the lives of all people, particularly those who are disadvantaged.
“Dear brothers and sisters, the Second Vatican Council invites us to share the bread of knowledge and know-how, so that every person and every people may develop their potential, and together, with God’s help, we may build a better future,” he said.
Pope points to Sheen as an example
Mentioning the upcoming beatification of Archbishop Sheen in his greeting to English-speaking pilgrims, Pope Leo recalled the American prelate’s innovative use of radio and television for evangelization.
“May the example and intercession of this holy bishop, known for his evangelizing work through the media, inspire many others likewise to find new ways of spreading the Gospel message with joyful enthusiasm,” he said.

articles.title: Richard Childress Racing announces technology and technical-focused leadership appointments ahead of 2027 season
articles.description: Richard Childress Racing announces technology and technical-focused leadership appointments ahead of 2027 season Jayski
articles.description_html: Richard Childress Racing announces technology and technical-focused leadership appointments ahead of 2027 season  Jayski
articles.article_title: Richard Childress Racing announces technology and technical-focused leadership appointments ahead of 2027 season | Jayski
articles.heading: Richard Childress Racing announces technology and technical-focused leadership appointments ahead of 2027 season
articles.summary: Richard Childress Racing announces technology and technical-focused leadership appointments ahead of 2027 season Jayski
articles.content:
Richard Childress Racing announced today two key leadership appointments designed to strengthen the organization’s competition program, accelerate technological innovation and position RCR for long-term success as the company prepares for the 2027 NASCAR season and beyond.
Richard Boswell, who has led Austin Dillon over the past two seasons as crew chief of the No. 3 Chevrolet in the NASCAR Cup Series, will take on a larger role with the race team as Vice President of Competition. Boswell will provide direction across RCR’s competition efforts, with a focus on performance, collaboration with key partner Chevrolet and building a stronger foundation for sustained success on the racetrack.
The son of a late model and Busch Series driver and a former driver himself, Boswell brings more than 15 years of professional motorsports experience to his new role. His career includes time at Hendrick Motorsports, JR Motorsports and Stewart-Haas Racing (SHR), where he helped launch the team’s O’Reilly Auto Parts Series program and oversaw its competition operations. He made his Cup Series crew chief debut at SHR, earning a victory with Chase Briscoe in 2024. Boswell joined RCR in 2025 and led Austin Dillon to a Cup Series win that same year.
Boswell’s leadership style, grounded in accountability and discipline, makes him well suited to lead RCR’s competition efforts. He will finish the current season as crew chief before moving fully into his new role at season’s end.
In addition to strengthening its competition leadership, RCR is expanding its focus on emerging technology with the creation of a Director of Development and Innovation position. Art Trejo has been appointed to the newly created role, where he will lead the company’s efforts to identify, develop and implement emerging technologies. Trejo’s background in military leadership, advanced technology and engineering will strengthen the organization. A 27-year Officer in the United States Navy with degrees from both Princeton University and UCLA, Trejo joins RCR from SpaceX and has extensive experience working in complex, technology-driven environments.
The addition of a dedicated Development and Innovation position represents a continued evolution of RCR’s approach to technology and innovation. The organization has increasingly incorporated advanced technology into its operations, including engineering, manufacturing and competition, while continuing to explore new opportunities and improve performance across the company.
“Everyone at Richard Childress Racing remains relentless in our desire to win and compete at the highest levels of our sport but we know we’re not quite where we need to be,” said Richard Childress, Chairman and CEO of Richard Childress Racing. “We’re announcing these changes now because we want to make sure we have the right people, the right leadership and the right technology in place to compete at the level RCR expects to compete at. Richard Boswell is a talented leader who knows racing, knows how to lead people, and knows what it takes to win. I know he will do a great job taking on a larger role in leading our competition team. Art Trejo brings a completely different set of experiences and a new way of thinking that I believe can help take our racing operations forward. We’re going to keep pushing, keep investing and keep looking for ways to get better.”
For more information, please visit rcrracing.com.
— Richard Childress Racing —

articles.heading: A congressional representative just proposed killing America’s border tower program
articles.summary: The proposed bill comes days after an MIT Technology Review investigation revealed that over 1,050 people have died within the advertised range of surveillance towers.
articles.content:
A congressional representative just proposed killing America’s border tower program
The proposed bill comes days after an MIT Technology Review investigation revealed that over 1,050 people have died within the advertised range of surveillance towers.
Delia Ramirez, a Democratic US representative from Illinois, has announced a plan to introduce new legislation to terminate the surveillance tower program along the US southern border.
The announcement comes just days after publication of an MIT Technology Review investigation, “Dying on Camera,” in which we looked at deaths along the border that took place close to one or more of these towers. MIT Technology Review found that nearly one in four deaths we analyzed between 2015 and early 2026 occurred within their advertised range. We also showed that the Department of Homeland Security does not keep track of these deaths or other metrics on the towers’ success or failure.
Ramirez, who sits on the Homeland Security Committee, cited MIT Technology Review’s reporting that nearly “1,100 people have died within range of a billion-dollar surveillance tower system between 2015 and 2026,” adding, “The towers that we have paid a billion dollars to just don’t work.”
The legislation, the Reimagining Safety Act, was developed in consultation with community groups and local and state representatives. The advocacy organizations Just Futures Law, which focuses on immigrant rights and racial justice, and Mijente, which describes itself as a “vehicle for building independent Latinx political power,” helped shape the calls to terminate the border towers program, following a joint report they put out earlier this year on the technology used by ICE. The legislation is intended to be part of a broader proposal to replace the Department of Homeland Security with a new Department of Community Safety while moving CISA, FEMA, TSA, and customs functions to other existing federal agencies. Her office has yet to release the text of the proposed legislation, saying that it will come in the next few weeks.
There has been growing public support for abolishing ICE in the wake of the second Trump administration’s highly visible enforcement operations across American cities, the buildout of its detention apparatus, and shootings by ICE and CBP agents. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a delivery driver, was shot in the back by an ICE agent just last weekend in Austin, Texas.
But for Ramirez, abolishing just ICE is not enough. At a press conference held in Chicago on Wednesday, Ramirez said, “There’s no question that DHS has to be dismantled. We need to provide them a road map in how we do it,” Ramirez said.
It will not be the first time that a bill to dismantle the Department of Homeland Security has been introduced, but previous proposals have not gone very far. This proposal will also face a steep uphill battle in Congress, where even some Democrats favor reforming rather than outright dismantling the organization. Ramirez, however, sits on both the House committee that oversees the department, and is the ranking member on the Homeland Security Committee’s cybersecurity subcommittee.

articles.article_title: Auto industry leaning into hybrid technology
articles.heading: Auto industry leaning into hybrid technology
articles.summary: Next time you go car shopping, you're going to see a lot more hybrid vehicles than in the past. They're growing in popularity like never before.
articles.content:
Wednesday, September 23, 2026 4:56PM
LOS ANGELES (KABC) -- Next time you go car shopping, you're going to see a lot more hybrid vehicles than in the past. They're growing in popularity like never before.
"People should think of hybrid technology today like they might have thought of fuel injection technology 50 years ago. It's rapidly becoming standard technology," said Karl Brauer, executive analyst at iSeeCars.com.
Obviously, Toyota got a huge head start on everyone else, and many of their models are now hybrid-only, like the best-selling RAV4, Camry and Sienna. But other mainstream brands have really stepped up their hybrid game too. Notably Hyundai, as well as corporate sibling Kia. Across the board, automotive brands are working on adding them.
"There are a lot of automakers scrambling to get hybrids onto the market as quickly as possible, because they see that's where the market really comes together," added Brauer.
Some big names in the automotive space are recovering from missteps with EV investment and development, as things have changed in the marketplace.
"The bets they placed on EVs is costing a lot of car companies a lot of money," Brauer said.
So brands that had shoved hybrids aside are wisely hurrying up to bring them out and catch up to where the market is right now.
The payoff to a hybrid of course is the fuel economy. For example, with the 2026 redesign, Kia added a hybrid version of the Telluride, rated at 32 mpg combined with all-wheel drive or 36 combined with two-wheel drive. Keep in mind, the Telluride is a pretty good-sized SUV with three rows of seats.
"If you're producing three-row SUVs that get 30, 35 miles-plus per gallon, and those are selling extremely well, you're doing a lot better job of reducing the amount of gas that's being burned, and the amount of emissions being created, than if you can hardly get anyone to buy one EV," Brauer said.
If you want an EV, there are plenty of them out there. If you want pure gasoline for your ride, plenty of those are out there too. But increasingly, they're being joined by hybrid technology, which was once seen as only a niche choice.

articles.heading: What is the value of human progress? Pope Leo explores whys behind technology in Sept. 23 general audience
articles.summary: "To encounter God, the human being must not abandon his earthly occupations, but can live his vocation fully, carrying out his daily work well and sanctifying it."
articles.content:
(OSV News) — The following is the full text of Pope Leo XIV’s general audience address given September 23 in St. Peter’s Square.
Brothers and sisters, good morning and welcome!
As we continue our journey through the Pastoral Constitution Gaudium et Spes of the Second Vatican Ecumenical Council, we come to the third chapter of the first part, which bears the intriguing title: “Man’s Activity Throughout the World”. The fundamental question is this: what is the value of human activity in the world, and therefore of technical, social and scientific progress? We may recall that, less than four years after the close of the Council, on the night of July 20-21, 1969, man set foot on the moon for the first time.
Created in the image and likeness of God, the human being is the agent of progress. With freedom and intelligence, he increases his knowledge, thereby advancing society as a whole. We can easily see this by considering the improvements in living conditions over successive generations. Indeed, the document states, “many benefits once looked for, especially from heavenly powers, man has now enterprisingly procured for himself” (no. 33).
For this reason, some thinkers have portrayed scientific and technical progress as something that weakens man’s relationship with God, to the point of making it seem superfluous, or even as antagonistic to the Christian faith. And this interpretation has brought about a change in the way contemporary man views the world, compared with previous ages. Such a prejudice is particularly prevalent in that part of Western culture which has lost its reference to Christian revelation. In post-Christian humanisms, the human being and God are mistakenly presented as rivals: in order to assert his knowledge, his freedom and his progress, man would have to emancipate himself from God. Ultimately, however, by denying the relationship with God, one also loses the possibility of affirming the transcendent value of the human person. This is the “tragedy of atheistic humanism,” well described by a leading theologian of the Second Vatican Council, Henri de Lubac.
The Council wishes to provide a clear answer: Christians, states Gaudium et Spes, “can justly consider that by their labor they are unfolding the Creator’s work, consulting the advantages of their brother men, and are contributing by their personal industry to the realization in history of the divine plan” (no. 34). Indeed, the Constitution continues, “far from thinking that works produced by man’s own talent and energy are in opposition to God’s power, and that the rational creature exists as a kind of rival to the Creator, Christians are convinced that the triumphs of the human race are a sign of God’s grace and the flowering of His own mysterious design” ( ibid.). In essence, God has placed in the hands of men and women a creation that is still in statu viae — that is, on a journey, in the process of growth — so that they may bring it to fulfillment through their wise activity.
Here there is an important reference to the mystery of the Incarnation. Humanity — and with it work, progress and the autonomy of created realities — is not absorbed or nullified by the encounter with God, but rather taken up in its entirety, continuing to be, in Christ, free and active: indeed, it is in him that it finds full truth and freedom. Furthermore, in the Eucharistic celebration, the fruit of human labor, represented by bread and wine, is placed upon the altar every day to be transformed into the Body and Blood of Christ.
From this perspective, an important truth emerges: to encounter God, the human being must not abandon his earthly occupations, but can live his vocation fully, carrying out his daily work well and sanctifying it. Christians, like everyone else, are involved in building the city of man, striving towards the end of all things and the encounter with God, and reminding those with whom they share the adventure of progress, science and life of this ultimate purpose.
Earthly progress must certainly be clearly distinguished from the development of the Kingdom of Christ; however, the Council affirms that “to the extent that the former can contribute to the better ordering of human society, it is of vital concern to the Kingdom of God. … All the good fruits of our nature and enterprise, we will find them again, but freed of stain, burnished and transfigured” (no. 39).
Finally, let us recall that in order to become authentic human progress — that is, progress for the whole person and for all people — technical and scientific progress must be inspired and guided by charity. Only in this way can it always be placed in the service of human dignity and promote the living conditions of all, especially the most disadvantaged.
Dear brothers and sisters, the Second Vatican Council invites us to share the bread of knowledge and know-how, so that every person and every people may develop their potential, and together, with God’s help, we may build a better future.
Appeal for World Day of Migrants and Refugees
Next Sunday, 27 September, marks the World Day of Migrants and Refugees. My thoughts go out to migrants and refugees, especially minors compelled to leave their homeland. Children and teenagers are the most vulnerable, and they often endure unspeakable suffering: violence, torture, exploitation, traumatic conditions, and it is not uncommon for them to lose their lives along migration routes. I appeal to everyone’s sense of responsibility: let us all feel a sense of involvement in the lives of these young people, who must always be protected and supported.
Special greetings to English speakers, American bishop’s beatification noted
I greet all the English-speaking pilgrims and visitors taking part in today’s Audience, particularly the groups from England, Ireland, Denmark, Norway, Malta, Tanzania, Australia, Hong Kong, India, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam and the United States of America. Tomorrow in Saint Louis, Missouri, Venerable Fulton Sheen will be beatified. May the example and intercession of this holy bishop, known for his evangelizing work through the media, inspire many others likewise to find new ways of spreading the Gospel message with joyful enthusiasm. Upon all of you and your families, I invoke the peace and joy of our Lord Jesus Christ. God bless you!
Summary of the Sept. 23, 2026 general audience
Dear brothers and sisters, as we continue our series of catecheses on the Second Vatican Council, today we consider the meaning and value of human activity as presented by the Pastoral Constitution Gaudium et Spes. Revolutionary advances in science and technology in the past century have led some to assume that belief in God is now obsolete, and that true human autonomy can be affirmed only by emancipation from God. The Council Fathers emphasized, on the contrary, that “the achievements of the human race are a sign of God’s greatness and the fulfillment of his mysterious design” (n. 34). Indeed, far from inhibiting believers from being engaged in human activity, the Gospel message compels us to contribute to authentic human flourishing through our involvement in society. Let us carry out our daily activities with true charity, offering our work to the Lord both as a means for personal sanctification and as an expression of our desire ever more fully to bring about God’s kingdom, especially through pursuing the common good, caring for the needy and defending human dignity.

articles.heading: New technology could help farmers keep better tabs on soil health
articles.summary: A group of researchers have developed a low-cost electronic sensor capable of continuously monitoring soil pH.
articles.content:
Listen to this article Voice: Michigan Farm News — Laura
Powered by BeyondWords
At first glance, a farm field doesn’t seem all that complicated. It’s just dirt and crops.
But amongst the landscape lies one of Earth’s most complex ecosystems — a bustling network of microbes, nutrients, roots and chemical reactions that quietly govern the health of every harvest.
For years, understanding what’s happening beneath that surface has been one of agriculture’s biggest challenges. Important soil and plant indicators, like pH, microbial activity and plant physiology, are always changing, yet notoriously difficult to track in real time.
Now, a group of researchers in the Paul M. Rady Department of Mechanical Engineering at CU Boulder have developed a low-cost electronic sensor capable of continuously monitoring soil pH, offering a new window into the hidden world below our feet.
READ NEXT: JOHN DEERE PARTNERS WITH SPECIALTY CROP TECHNOLOGY INCUBATOR FARM RESERVOIR
They believe it’s a step toward a future in which farms can constantly monitor their own soil conditions, helping growers detect changes sooner and respond with more informed decisions.
“In many cases, by the time farmers discover that something is wrong with their soil or plants, the window for effective treatment may have already passed,” said Professor Gregory Whiting, leader of the Boulder Experimental Electronics and Manufacturing Laboratory. “Monitoring these factors continuously can help us better manage agricultural land and secure our food production.”
The study, led by PhD student Juan Cisneros Barba, was recently published in the journal Scientific Reports. It marks the latest breakthrough in a prolific year for Whiting and his team, whose recent discoveries are helping farmers listen to soils, monitor living plants and enable farms of the future to gather important information.
Soil pH: The ‘master variable’
Few measurements carry more weight in agriculture than soil pH. Often called the “master variable,” it influences nearly everything on a farm from nutrient availability to plant growth.
But despite its importance, Whiting says tracking pH comes with challenges.
“Traditional pH sensors are often not very well suited for soil. Think of a small glass bulb that’s fragile and needs to be recalibrated a lot,” said Whiting, who is also affiliated with the Materials Science & Engineering Program.
“The measurement they provide drifts over time and changes for different environments. This requires them to be frequently and manually calibrated, which can be cumbersome.”
Because of this, the group pivoted toward a new kind of electronic sensor that uses a pH-sensitive dye called alizarin to provide more dependable readings.
The device itself isn’t necessarily new. Scientists around the world — including Whiting and his team — have been studying the technology for years. They’ve shown it works in simple settings and can be printed efficiently at low cost.
But a critical question remained: Could they reliably monitor real soil outside the lab for weeks or even months?
To find out, the researchers buried a series of electrochemical sensors in various types of soil. Some featured more organic matter while others were more sandy or muddy, with both compacted and uncompacted soils included to mimic the kinds of changing environmental conditions they would encounter in the field.
They also improved the original sensor, moving to a printed circuit board-based design that was easier to manufacture. By pairing it with an inexpensive, field-deployable readout system, the technology became more practical to distribute and use outdoors.
The results exceeded the team’s expectations. Across multiple soil types, the redesigned sensor delivered reliable, continuous pH measurements for months, while a multi-month outdoor monitoring test in soil showed stable performance without the need for constant recalibration.
For Whiting, it was the strongest evidence yet that these low-cost, battery-powered printed electronics can move beyond the lab and into real agricultural environments.
“It’s really just about usability,” Whiting said. “These things cost close to nothing to make, function with minimal human effort and can be used in various soil types, allowing the technology to actually be useful in farms.”

The device itself isn’t necessarily new. Scientists around the world — including Whiting and his team — have been studying the technology for years. They’ve shown it works in simple settings and can be printed efficiently at low cost.

But a critical question remained: Could they reliably monitor real soil outside the lab for weeks or even months?

To find out, the researchers buried a series of electrochemical sensors in various types of soil. Some featured more organic matter while others were more sandy or muddy, with both compacted and uncompacted soils included to mimic the kinds of changing environmental conditions they would encounter in the field.

They also improved the original sensor, moving to a printed circuit board-based design that was easier to manufacture. By pairing it with an inexpensive, field-deployable readout system, the technology became more practical to distribute and use outdoors.

The results exceeded the team’s expectations. Across multiple soil types, the redesigned sensor delivered reliable, continuous pH measurements for months, while a multi-month outdoor monitoring test in soil showed stable performance without the need for constant recalibration.

For Whiting, it was the strongest evidence yet that these low-cost, battery-powered printed electronics can move beyond the lab and into real agricultural environments.

“It’s really just about usability,” Whiting said. “These things cost close to nothing to make, function with minimal human effort and can be used in various soil types, allowing the technology to actually be useful in farms.”

articles.title: Microsoft strengthens its commitment to the Middle East by investing in technology, digital resilience, and people
articles.description: Microsoft strengthens its commitment to the Middle East by investing in technology, digital resilience, and people The Official Microsoft Blog
articles.description_html: Microsoft strengthens its commitment to the Middle East by investing in technology, digital resilience, and people  The Official Microsoft Blog
articles.article_title: Microsoft strengthens its commitment to the Middle East by investing in technology, digital resilience, and people - Microsoft On the Issues
articles.heading: Microsoft strengthens its commitment to the Middle East by investing in technology, digital resilience, and people
articles.summary: Microsoft has served the Middle East since it began operations in the region in 1991. Since then, we’ve steadily expanded our presence and investments, growing from a local technology provider into a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educational institutions, and civil society organizations. Today, Microsoft is reaffirming that commitment through a new framework focused initially...
articles.content:
Microsoft has served the Middle East since it began operations in the region in 1991. Since then, we’ve steadily expanded our presence and investments, growing from a local technology provider into a long-term partner to governments, businesses, educational institutions, and civil society organizations. Today, Microsoft is reaffirming that commitment through a new framework focused initially on Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.
We are expanding our investments in the Middle East with confidence in the region’s future as it pursues one of the world’s most ambitious AI transformations. We will add to our local partnerships across the region. We will build on the work we have done to stand by these countries’ governments and people through a period of significant challenges. As we look to the future, we will invest further in technology, digital resilience, and the people across the region.
From now until 2030, we will pursue the following initiatives with our partners in the region:
Technology
We will expand cloud and AI infrastructure across the Middle East
Microsoft will continue to invest in cloud and AI infrastructure across the region, expanding capacity, launching new capabilities, and delivering long-term infrastructure commitments. We plan to invest more than $10 billion in capital and operating expenses between now and 2030 in the region.
We will deepen our partnerships through national AI champions
Microsoft will deepen strategic partnerships with governments and national AI champion organizations to translate AI ambition into economic growth, modern public services, and global competitiveness. This builds on work with organizations including HUMAIN, G42, QAI, and the Government of Kuwait, alongside digital-government initiatives such as TAMM in the UAE, SDAIA’s ALLaM in Saudi Arabia, TASMU in Qatar, and Microsoft 365 Copilot adoption across the Government of Kuwait.
These partnerships will support responsible AI adoption, sovereign-ready cloud services, Arabic and multilingual AI, and the use of AI to improve services for citizens and businesses. They will be supported by capabilities including Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield, where relevant and available.
We will invest in subsea and terrestrial connectivity
Digital resilience depends on strong and reliable networks. Protecting subsea and terrestrial connectivity requires sustained cooperation between governments and the private sector, but the foundation of continuity is redundancy. A diverse network of high-capacity routes allows traffic to be rerouted around disruptions, minimizing latency and maintaining critical data flows.
Microsoft has helped expand both the capacity and reliability of digital connectivity across regions through investments in major international subsea cable systems, including SeaMeWe-6, which has landings in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, as well as operating a global network spanning more than 275,000 miles of terrestrial and subsea fiber. During network disruptions, Microsoft has demonstrated the value of redundancy by rerouting traffic through Middle East corridors and maintaining service continuity with minimal impact on customers.
Building on this foundation, Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030. This investment will expand capacity, strengthen regional data flows, and support Microsoft’s growing cloud and AI infrastructure footprint across the region.
We will build AI infrastructure with the planet in mind
As we expand our cloud and AI infrastructure in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, we will do so with a focus on responsible growth. Guided by Microsoft’s global goals to address carbon, water, waste, and ecosystems, we will work with our lessor partners to ensure that the cloud infrastructure supporting our services advances Microsoft’s water-positive ambitions, including by prioritizing zero-water cooling technologies where feasible.
Water resilience is particularly important across the Middle East. Building on Microsoft’s global experience advancing water stewardship through water reuse, replenishment, and innovative water management solutions, we will work with governments and local stakeholders to identify opportunities that advance responsible water stewardship across the region.
As AI accelerates economic opportunity across the Middle East, expanding access to clean energy will be essential to ensuring this growth is sustainable. We will also collaborate with regulators, utilities, and our lessor partners to help create the market conditions needed to expand carbon-free electricity procurement and stimulate new clean energy investment. By combining infrastructure investment with local partnerships and innovation, we aim to support the region’s energy and water priorities while helping build the sustainable foundations needed for long-term AI-led economic growth.
Digital resilience
We will launch a new Middle East digital resilience initiative
Conflict in the Middle East has reinforced the connection between digital resilience and digital sovereignty. Microsoft has worked with customers to support business continuity through resilience options tailored to different operational and regulatory needs. Going forward, Microsoft will make digital resilience a cornerstone of its Middle East strategy, helping organizations strengthen continuity and recovery through digital resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, continuity planning, and enablement programs that help identify vulnerabilities, protect critical data, and build tested recovery capabilities.
We will strengthen data protection, privacy, and business continuity
Microsoft will expand our existing commitments on data-protection sovereignty and business continuity to eligible governments and customers in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. These are designed to give organizations greater confidence in how their data, systems, and operations are protected while maintaining continuity in times of uncertainty. They will be complemented by Microsoft’s growing sovereign-cloud portfolio, including Sovereign Public Cloud and Sovereign Private Cloud capabilities, together with Project Digital Shield and other capabilities that support security, privacy, transparency, and operational resilience.
We will expand and strengthen cybersecurity cooperation
As Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE accelerate their digital transformation, cybersecurity has become a core pillar of national and economic security. As governments, critical infrastructure, and economies become more connected, cyber threats and influence operations can have consequences that extend far beyond physical borders. That’s why we are announcing that we are deepening our partnerships with the cybersecurity authorities in these countries.
A network of dedicated Microsoft cybersecurity champions in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE will help governments translate these resources into action and connect national priorities with expertise across Microsoft. Stronger cybersecurity benefits far more than individual networks. It helps build trust to ensure digital transformation will succeed.
We will advance responsible AI through governance, assurance, and inclusion
Microsoft will work with governments, businesses, researchers, and civil society organizations across the Middle East to help people and institutions benefit from new technology. As AI advances, realizing its full potential will require not only access to powerful technology, but the governance, assurance, and skills required to deploy it confidently and responsibly.
We will help strengthen AI governance capabilities across the region and support practical approaches to testing, evaluating, and assurance systems. We will also expand collaboration with the Responsible AI Future Foundation (RAIFF), co-founded with G42 and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), to support the development and sharing of responsible AI practices and evaluation tools that can be applied across high-impact AI use cases in the Middle East and beyond.
By helping organizations align with emerging international practices, we aim to strengthen confidence in AI systems, support responsible innovation, enhance global competitiveness, and ensure that the Middle East plays an active role in shaping the future of AI.
We will advance AI for Good research and innovation
Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab will continue to support the region through research and partnerships focused on food security, low-resource language development, and climate and disaster resilience. This includes work through initiatives such as the LINGUA program, which supports the development of language technologies for underserved communities.
In partnership with governments, NGOs, nonprofits, and research institutions, the AI for Good Lab will continue developing and scaling AI solutions that address real-world challenges across the Middle East and beyond.
People
We will prepare the next generation for the AI economy
We believe AI should enhance human ambition, strengthen human capability, and help prepare workers to thrive in a changing economy. That is why Microsoft will continue to invest in AI skills, workforce readiness, public-sector capability building, and inclusive talent development across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, building on existing commitments to help skill more than 4.2 million people by 2030.
This work includes training for public-sector leaders, students, and workers; initiatives focused on expanding opportunities for women; and partnerships with educational institutions across the region. This work builds on programs such as Saudi Arabia’s AI Global Leadership Program, AI Skills 4 Women programs in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, and the Women’s Datacenter Academy in Saudi Arabia. Microsoft will also engage with workforce coalitions that can support national talent strategies and policy recommendations.
We will help education communities prepare learners for the AI era
Microsoft is working with governments, educators, institutions, and partners across the Middle East to develop responsible AI principles across primary, secondary, and tertiary education. This includes supporting AI literacy, helping educators integrate AI into teaching and learning, and sharing practical guidance for responsible AI use in educational settings. Across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, we will work with local partners to ensure students and educators can benefit from AI safely, responsibly, and effectively and will engage educators, policymakers, industry leaders, and civil society to support practical approaches to AI implementation that reflect local priorities.
We will help empower workers in the AI economy
We will partner with governments, employers, workers, education providers, and other stakeholders to help people adapt to changing workplace demands. Our focus is on practical skills development, workforce readiness, and leadership development that helps countries build competitive economies and create new opportunities for workers in an AI-enabled future.
We will support local and national AI talent priorities across the Middle East
Microsoft is partnering with governments, academic institutions, and civil society organizations to support national talent priorities by advancing AI skills, leadership development, and workforce readiness programs for public-sector leaders, students, underrepresented talent, and people across the Middle East. The goal is to help countries build globally competitive workforces, accelerate innovation, and unlock new economic opportunities in the AI era.
From ambition to impact
While no one can predict the future, one thing is certain: Microsoft has been part of this region’s journey for more than 35 years, and we are committed to being a partner for the long term. We look forward to continuing to work alongside governments, businesses, educators, and communities to help build that future together.

articles.title: NESCC and ETSU sign radiologic technology pathway agreement
articles.description: NESCC and ETSU sign radiologic technology pathway agreement WJHL
articles.description_html: NESCC and ETSU sign radiologic technology pathway agreement  WJHL
articles.article_title: NESCC and ETSU sign radiologic technology pathway agreement
articles.heading: NESCC and ETSU sign radiologic technology pathway agreement
articles.summary: KINGSPORT, Tenn. (WJHL) — Northeast State Community College (NESCC) and East Tennessee State University (ETSU) have signed an agreement allowing radiologic technology students to seamlessly transfe…
articles.content:
KINGSPORT, Tenn. (WJHL) — Northeast State Community College (NESCC) and East Tennessee State University (ETSU) have signed an agreement allowing radiologic technology students to seamlessly transfer from NESCC to ETSU to complete their bachelor’s degree.
NESCC’s first radiologic technology cohort welcomed 19 students who graduated with their two-year Associate of Applied Science degree in spring 2026. According to NESCC President Jeff McCord, all of those students have jobs and have passed their board exams.
“The job field is wide open again, 100% placement rate, probably before they even graduated. So it’s a great opportunity for students coming out of high school or coming back to school to try a new career. We’re open to all of them.”
McCord said students do not have to use the program immediately.
“They may work for a while and want to advance in their career,” he said. “And so ETSU offers that opportunity to continue their education to continue their progress in their career.”
ETSU President Brian Noland said the pathway program gives working adults a chance to earn an additional degree and certificate.
“The way this is structured, it gives them an opportunity to continue their studies in a technology-oriented format that allows them to earn an additional degree, which allows them to put additional resources on the table for them and for their families,” Noland said.
Click here to learn more about NESCC’s Radiologic Technology program.

articles.title: University showcases role as regional engine on Southeast Kansas Bio-Technology Tour
articles.description: University showcases role as regional engine on Southeast Kansas Bio-Technology Tour Pittsburg State University
articles.description_html: University showcases role as regional engine on Southeast Kansas Bio-Technology Tour  Pittsburg State University
articles.article_title: University showcases role as regional engine  on Southeast Kansas Bio-Technology Tour
articles.heading: University showcases role as regional engine  on Southeast Kansas Bio-Technology Tour
articles.summary: When leaders from the private and public sectors gathered for the Southeast Kansas Bio-Technology Tour, the stop at Pittsburg State University offered a powerful illustration of the university as an economic engine.
articles.content:
Academics
Campus
Research

State and local leaders, economic development professionals, educators, and business representatives got an up-close look at the many ways the university is helping to drive growth.
Attendees saw firsthand how Pitt State supports the region through a workforce pipeline, applied research, STEM education, and collaboration with economic development.
At Tyler Research Center, they learned about the National Institute for Materials Advancement (NIMA) and viewed construction progress on the university's new prove-out facility, then toured the nationally recognized Plastics Engineering Technology program in the Crossland College of Technology.
Together, the three assets create a complete workforce ecosystem: The Plastics Engineering Technology program educates and trains students; NIMA engages those students in cutting-edge research and industry partnerships; and the prove-out facility will provide a place where discoveries can be scaled, tested, and commercialized alongside industry partners.
For Southeast Kansas, that means a stronger pipeline of highly skilled workers, greater support for existing manufacturers, attraction of new technology-based industries, and increased economic competitiveness in advanced materials and manufacturing sectors.
"Pittsburg State University is deeply connected to the future of Southeast Kansas," President Thomas Newsom told attendees. "Our mission is not only to educate students, but to ensure they have opportunities to succeed while meeting the workforce and economic needs of our region."
The university's academic programs provide the foundation for specialized training and research opportunities.
“Our faculty include professors with valuable industry experience, professors who have earned international awards in education, and three who have been recognized among the top 2% of researchers worldwide,” noted College of Arts & Sciences Dean Chris Childers.
In Crossland College of Technology, the tour coincided with the annual Company Days, which annually draws industry representatives from across the country for the chance to connect with prospective hires in Construction Management and Engineering Technology; 2-year Electrical Technology; Environmental and Safety Management; Wood Product Manufacturing; Graphic Communications; Automotive Technology; Diesel & Heavy Equipment; Electronics Engineering Technology; Manufacturing Engineering Technology; Mechanical Engineering Technology; and Plastics Engineering Technology.
Tour attendees also learned about planned program expansions in several STEM programs that will help meet emerging workforce demands — programs like Criminal Justice, which soon will have state-of-the-industry academic space in the new Kansas Bureau of Investigation building being built at the east edge of campus, and Cybersecurity, which will have expanded lab space in the soon-to-be renovated Yates Hall.
The theme of career readiness was reinforced by Lisa Riedle, dean of the Crossland College of Technology.
"The university’s longstanding motto, ‘By Doing Learn,’ together with internships, industry partnerships, advisory boards, and applied learning experiences — that all gives our students incredible real-world experience before they even get to graduation,” Riedle said.
The college also continues to grow transfer pathways through expanded 2+2 agreements with community colleges, creating additional opportunities for students to pursue technical and engineering-related careers close to home.
An expanded footprint for academic programs like Diesel & Heavy Equipment, for which a planned $20 million facility will provide laboratory and training space, will bolster career readiness.
Research is another area in which Pittsburg State is creating measurable economic impact, tour attendees learned.
“We engage students in meaningful research experiences in numerous program areas while supporting industry innovation,” said Associate Vice President for Research and Innovation Ram Gupta.
The university’s annual Research Colloquium now includes participation from university students, area high school students, and regional community colleges. It introduces young scholars to research while creating connections that strengthen the regional talent pipeline.
At NIMA, students work alongside faculty and industry partners on applied research projects that address real-world manufacturing challenges. The work has resulted in publications, patents, grant funding, and innovations that directly benefit business and industry.
The university also was awarded distinctive national recognition from the Carnegie Foundation; it is among just 33 universities to earn dual designation for student access and opportunity in addition to research activity.
Economic development extends beyond research and workforce training.
Wes Streeter, associate vice president for economic and community engagement, which includes the Kansas Small Business Development Center at Pittsburg State, highlighted the SBDC’s role in helping entrepreneurs and small businesses succeed across the region.
This fall, the center relocated to the first floor of the historic Besse Hotel, improving accessibility and visibility for clients from across Southeast Kansas who seek business assistance.
"Pittsburg State's impact extends far beyond the boundaries of campus and far beyond the boundaries of Pittsburg,” he said.
Whether preparing future engineers, supporting advanced manufacturing research, helping small businesses grow, strengthening STEM education, or building partnerships throughout Southeast Kansas, the university is serving as a catalyst for opportunity and economic progress.
For tour participants, the message was clear:
Pittsburg State University is helping to shape the economic future of Southeast Kansas, one partnership, one innovation, and one student at a time.

"Pittsburg State's impact extends far beyond the boundaries of campus and far beyond the boundaries of Pittsburg,” he said.

Whether preparing future engineers, supporting advanced manufacturing research, helping small businesses grow, strengthening STEM education, or building partnerships throughout Southeast Kansas, the university is serving as a catalyst for opportunity and economic progress.

Pittsburg State University is helping to shape the economic future of Southeast Kansas, one partnership, one innovation, and one student at a time.

articles.content:
J.C. Bahr-de Stefano, a venture capitalist in New York, wanted a table at 4 Charles Prime Rib earlier this month. The West Village steakhouse is one of the city’s most covetable tables, with spots there on the reservation platform Resy being snapped up within seconds of their release.
So Stefano turned to Instinct, a personal AI assistant. “I didn’t lay out explicit actions to take,” Stefano said. “I just said, ‘I want you to do this. Go do it,” he said.
The bot went and tried. When it couldn’t come up with a table, he encouraged it to keep going. “I said, ‘You can figure it out. Come on.’ It was like giving it a pep talk,” he said.
Leaving the bot to its work, Stefano turned to getting a reservation somewhere else for himself and his parents. When he tried to log into Resy, he found that he had been locked out.
“I realized after a couple minutes that Instinct might have done something,” he said. Indeed, it had. Given the job of finding a reservation, he said, the AI assistant had been pinging Resy “hundreds of times every hour of the day.”
“Of course I got banned,” he said. “Resy figured it was a bot which is a totally fair response.”
Resy said in a statement to the industry magazine Restaurants Business that it “does not currently permit unapproved third-party bots or agents to independently access or interact with the Resy platform.” Stefano, who has since had his account reinstated, said he learned his lesson. “That was my first time and last time doing that,” he said.
Speak to an agent, or just get your own?
Personal AI agents, like Instinct, are part of an emerging category of apps that act as digital personal assistants. Users provide the app with credentials like email logins and credit card information and then ask the aps to do things for them.
People have used AI assistants to find new apartments and cancel subscriptions, as well as to manage their own calendars and make doctor’s appointments. Instinct recently raised $350 million, and in September, Meta released Muse, its own personal AI agent, which has been downloaded more than 2 million times already.
These AI agents have been developed at a time when airlines, insurance companies and utility providers are making it increasingly difficult to speak to a human in order to solve a problem. After years of yelling “agent” during automated customer service calls in the hopes of reaching a real person, it’s little wonder why people are trying to automate their annoying tasks, even if it means unleashing a new avalanche of bots onto the internet.
Making restaurant reservations on their creator’s behalf is one of the AI assistants’ most visible use cases, especially as diners face the growing headache of navigating different apps and credit card reward tiers just to book a meal. Many popular restaurants have abandoned phone numbers and email addresses in favor of managing everything via their reservation platform of choice.
Apps like Dorsia, which charge a yearly membership fee of up to $25,000, and gray-market reservation marketplaces like AppointmentTrader have created a class system where deep-pocketed diners can cut to the front of the line. Personal AI agents now threaten to make that even worse.
Tables are for people
“We are dehumanizing the last standing experience that is still totally human,” said Roni Mazumdar, the co-owner of several award-winning restaurants including Dhamaka and Semma in New York.
Mazumdar is concerned that if some people are able to walk around with a bot in their pockets that can constantly scrape a website looking for a table, it’ll reinforce a system that is already frustrating restaurant operators where reservations are gobbled up by clout chasers.
“When the entire system is gamed, you create an environment where those who are excited by a place can’t even go, but someone who doesn’t really care gets to say, ‘Yeah, I went there’ for bragging rights. It’s just a lose-lose proposition,” he said.
“For as long as we’ve had hard-to-get-into restaurants, we’ve had people trying to hack the system. These bots are nothing new,” said Ben Leventhal, the founder of the loyalty platform Blackbird and a co-founder of Resy. He said that Resy did what it was supposed to do by enforcing its terms of service, but that the industry will have to adapt and evolve as people use new tools.
Leventhal added that the AI assistants do provide some easier avenues to bad behavior among diners, though, and reservation platforms need to find a way to deal with that. “People want to skip the line, and obviously that’s not going to scale for legitimate platforms,” he said.
Jeremy Mustakas, the COO of Jean-Georges Restaurants in New York, said that AI tools have been helpful in streamlining some of their back-office operations, but that humanity is still at the core of what restaurants do, even if costs some efficiencies. “Not every interaction or task needs to be optimized,” Mustakas said. “Our work requires patience, discretion, even spontaneity. AI can’t read the room the way a great hospitality professional can.”
Rogue reservations
Like other AI systems, these personal agents don’t always behave the way people want them to. Brian Distelburger, a tech entrepreneur, also got banned from Resy for using an overeager agent to look for a table at, yes, 4 Charles Prime Rib. And in August, Jason Yeh, a venture capitalist in Los Angeles, said that he prompted his Instinct bot to look for restaurant reservations for a trip to Tokyo.
“Instinct found an opening for a random restaurant I never suggested, and made a reservation despite the restaurant having a 100% charge cancellation policy,” he posted on X. “Honestly kind of insane how anyone would give them keys to their accounts at large, and they better cover the $200 cancellation fee here.”
His Instinct bot was apologetic in a way familiar to anyone who has used Claude or ChatGPT. “Honest answer: I keep running notes from our conversations so your preferences carry over,” the messages Yeh posted on X read. “The failure was acting on my own notes without verifying them against what you actually said.”
Some tech evangelists have suggested that this is a key step towards an internet that will be all bots, where one person’s personal AI assistant will interact with a reservation platform or restaurant’s bot and hash things out between them or even set up an “auction” to decide who gets the reservation.
Stefano isn’t sold on that approach. “If there are 1,000 agents trying to get one table and it goes to the one that bids the most, to me that feels almost like dystopian capitalism. That’s taking it too far,” he said.
Leventhal said he doesn’t think restaurant operators will want to cede control of who gets to eat at their establishment to bots. “The idea that these systems are going to become obsolete because of an agent-to-agent layer doesn’t take into account the broad context of how the restaurant industry functions,” he said. “I don’t see a world where restaurants get comfortable letting a bunch of bots hash it all out.”
“It takes the magic out of restaurants quite quickly,” said Mazumdar. “I just think people should get a fair shot of going out and dining and having a good time and that it shouldn’t have to feel like a game.”
“We have clear pathways to using the technology to automate the tasks, but they can never automate the humanity,” said Mustakas. “The technology should open doors, but it shouldn’t create a digital velvet rope.”

articles.heading: World Surf League Appoints Hal Oreif as Chief Technology Officer
articles.summary: World Surf League Appoints Hal Oreif as Chief Technology Officer World Surf League
articles.content:
LOS ANGELES, Calif., USA (Wednesday, September 23, 2026) - The World Surf League (WSL) announced the appointment of Hal Oreif as Chief Technology Officer. In this role, Oreif will lead the league's global technology strategy, software engineering, applied science and AI, data architecture, and digital products to enhance fan engagement, athlete performance technology, partner integrations, and live event delivery.
Oreif joins the WSL following a distinguished career leading large-scale engineering, product, and data organizations across top media and technology enterprises. Most recently, he led engineering, data, and machine learning teams across Amazon Ads and Prime Video. Previously, he served as Chief Technology Officer at Warner Bros. and at IAC (the holding company behind brands such as Ticketmaster, Expedia, and Match Group).
"Hal's proven track record of applying advanced technologies, especially artificial intelligence, machine learning, real-time data, and scalable cloud architectures, to live sports and entertainment makes him an outstanding addition to our executive team," said Ryan Crosby, WSL CEO. "His leadership will be instrumental in elevating our fan experience, empowering our athletes, and unlocking new value for our global partners."
"The WSL is uniquely positioned with full ownership of its ecosystem and an authentic digital-first audience," said Oreif. "By harnessing advanced AI, machine learning, and real-time telemetry, we have an incredible opportunity to redefine how people experience competitive surfing by delivering deeper personalization for fans, advanced insights for our surfers, and high-impact digital products for our partners across every touchpoint."
Oreif holds a Bachelor's and Master's in Computer Science, and completed the Executive Management Program at the UCLA Anderson School of Management.

PPG Low Temperature Cure automotive coating technology showcased at SURCAR Asia 2026
SHANGHAI, Sept. 23, 2026 – PPG (NYSE: PPG) today announced that it showcased PPG Low Temperature Cure coating technology at the eighth SURCAR Asia automotive conference, held Sept. 16-17 in Shanghai. The technology offers automakers a path toward more integrated coating processes across multiple substrate types.
Alina Wang, PPG Market Manager, OEM Asia
Metal bodies and plastic components such as bumpers typically require separate paint processes because of differences in heat resistance and curing conditions. PPG Low Temperature Cure coating technology combines coating material design and advanced curing mechanisms to broaden the processing window across metal and plastic substrates, helping enable more integrated body-and-bumper coating processes.
“This technology is about creating greater flexibility in how vehicles are painted,” said Haijiao Wang, PPG strategic marketing manager, topcoat, Asia Pacific, Automotive OEM Coatings, who presented the technology at the SURCAR event. “It streamlines paint operations, delivers consistent color across substrates and enables more integrated manufacturing processes.”
The platform offers two cure options: a stand-alone basecoat that cures at 110°C on its own, and a three-layer system that cures at 90°C together. This gives automakers flexibility to match the technology to different parts and production lines, expand the application of heat-sensitive substrates, and introduce low-temperature curing in phases according to individual production line requirements. The lower cure temperatures also provide a more energy-efficient alternative to standard higher-temperature processes that cure at 140°C.
PPG plans to begin line trials with leading automakers worldwide to further evaluate the technology across different paint processes, production conditions and vehicle platforms, accelerating its progression from technical development toward broader commercial application.
To learn more about PPG Low Temperature Cure technology and other innovations featured at SURCAR Asia 2026, visit www.automotive.ppg.com.

articles.title: AI Isn't the Apocalypse. Technology Analysts Need to Say So
articles.description: AI Isn't the Apocalypse. Technology Analysts Need to Say So TechNewsWorld
articles.description_html: AI Isn't the Apocalypse. Technology Analysts Need to Say So  TechNewsWorld
articles.article_title: AI Isn't the Apocalypse. Technology Analysts Need to Say So
articles.heading: AI Isn't the Apocalypse. Technology Analysts Need to Say So
articles.summary: AI extinction warnings are grabbing headlines, but where's the evidence? Mark Vena challenges the doomsday narrative and calls on technology analysts to bring technical scrutiny to the debate.
articles.content:
The AI debate has developed a strange pattern.
An AI model produces unexpected or potentially scary results, someone predicts the end of humanity, and the conversation jumps straight to whether civilization has only a few years left. Missing somewhere between the demonstration and the obituary is the evidence. We should demand it.
Claims that AI will destroy humanity require a credible explanation of how software could acquire the power to overcome human resistance in the physical world. An alarming prediction, even from an accomplished researcher, doesn’t settle that question.
Longtime technology analysts should lead this discussion. Too often, we leave it to executives with products to sell and politicians who turn uncertainty into campaign material. People who understand how technology reaches the market need to speak up, together, regardless of their political views.
An Extinction Forecast Needs More Than Imagination
Start with an honest boundary. Nobody can prove that every future AI system will be harmless. But fear-mongering about an impending AI-driven extinction event treats speculation as knowledge. The stronger argument is that the evidence doesn’t justify the certainty of the apocalypse narrative.
The International AI Safety Report, published in February and led by AI expert Yoshua Bengio, found that current systems lacked the capabilities needed for the loss-of-control scenarios it examined. The report also warned that relevant abilities were improving. That supports continued testing and safeguards. It doesn’t establish an approaching extinction event.
Even a highly capable model needs a means to act. Producing a plan is different from carrying it out. Software tools can expand its reach, but access to them must come from somewhere. Intelligence doesn’t automatically grant control.
Physical constraints matter too. Computing requires equipment and electricity. Actions outside a computer depend on connections to machines or people. A serious catastrophe argument must explain how those dependencies are acquired and sustained.
These barriers aren’t guarantees. Security can fail, and people can grant dangerous permissions. But each required failure belongs in the argument. Asking for that chain of events is basic analysis.
Industry Leaders Push Back on AI Alarmism
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed back directly. In a July interview, he criticized people who "spend too much time theorizing about these science fiction outcomes." His broader argument was that frightening people away from AI could undermine adoption and American competitiveness.
Central to this is Huang's message that frontier companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic should address risks through their development, engineering, and testing processes — like any product company that ships only high-quality solutions.
The standard should be clear: establish rigorous AI testing procedures and don't release products with known critical bugs. Risk ultimately isn't just with models. It also lies with companies that allow weak internal due diligence across their teams.
Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez has voiced similar objections. Asked in a 2024 interview about public misconceptions, he identified "the fear that certain individuals and organizations espouse about this technology being a terminator, an existential risk."
The disagreement predates today’s models. In 2017, Mark Zuckerberg criticized doomsday rhetoric, saying "It’s really negative, and in some ways, I actually think it is pretty irresponsible." That historical comment shows how long this argument has persisted. It cannot, by itself, settle questions about newer systems.
These executives certainly have commercial interests. Their confidence deserves scrutiny, as do warnings from competing executives. However, their objections challenge the suggestion that everyone who understands AI agrees catastrophe is coming.
Arguments for broadly shared AI benefits also offer an alternative to fatalism. Analysts should test those promises as closely as extinction predictions. Neither becomes evidence because a prominent executive sounds certain.
The Media Must Ask Better Technical Questions
A frightening prediction is easy to package. Explaining its assumptions takes work. When coverage lacks technical depth, a possibility can start to sound like a forecast. Readers may conclude the engineering questions are settled when an article has barely examined them.
Reporters don’t need to build models, but they do need to assess whistleblowers' credibility and potential agendas more carefully. They also need to distinguish controlled-test results from evidence that a system can operate independently in the real world. Editors should demand that distinction before allowing a dramatic claim to carry a story.
Mainstream coverage isn’t uniformly alarmist. Some commentary has challenged extinction forecasts and emphasized product accountability. Other reporting has examined how doomsday speculation can distract from present harms and the people responsible for them.
The problem is coverage that repeats extraordinary claims without examining the steps required to make them possible. Technical fluency should help a newsroom recognize when a compelling story has outrun its evidence.
Data Centers Have Become the Next Target
Anxiety now extends to the infrastructure behind AI. Data centers face growing public opposition, with local construction disputes feeding a broader political backlash. Buildings full of computers are being asked to answer for everything people dislike about the technology industry.
The economic benefits of data centers are already showing up in public accounts. In Loudoun County, Virginia, existing facilities generated $1.2 billion in property tax revenue in fiscal 2026, helping fund local services and ease the burden on other taxpayers.
Across Virginia, an independent legislative study estimated that the industry supported roughly 74,000 direct and indirect jobs and $5.5 billion in annual labor income, with much of that benefit coming from construction. Those paychecks reach electricians and other skilled workers, well beyond Silicon Valley. Contracts can also create electricity savings when large customers pay more than it costs to serve them.
Georgia Power projects approximately $950 million in annual customer savings beginning in 2029 from its large-load growth portfolio, equivalent to about $180 annually for a typical residential customer. Those are projected savings, not reductions already delivered.
Every proposal needs scrutiny, but a debate that counts electricity demand while ignoring wages and tax revenue leaves out a substantial part of the economic picture.
Some objections are practical. Residents deserve answers about electricity bills and water use. Noise matters to neighbors. Developers weaken their case when they dismiss these concerns or substitute vague promises for enforceable commitments.
Still, treating every data center as a step toward human extinction turns planning into a referendum on an imagined apocalypse. Communities need to examine a facility’s actual costs and benefits.
Construction creates work for skilled trades and business for suppliers, while operating facilities can provide technical jobs and local tax revenue. Permanent staffing is smaller, and advocates should say so.
Construction jobs shouldn’t be discounted simply because they involve building infrastructure rather than writing software. Communities should examine tax concessions carefully, but rejecting a project also means giving up potential benefits.
America Cannot Regulate Its Way to Leadership
AI requires computing capacity. Excessive regulation that delays that capacity is likely to weaken America’s competitive position. Blanket restrictions and uncertain approval processes discourage investment without necessarily addressing the risks behind public concern.
Bernie Sanders’ proposal to ban artificial superintelligence and pause advanced AI development until federal safety rules are established risks putting American innovation on Washington’s timetable.
If competing countries continue developing those capabilities, an American "pause" could weaken the U.S. technological lead and create national security disadvantages. Sanders' separate proposed moratorium on new AI data centers could also delay construction jobs and the local tax revenue those facilities can generate.
Prolonged uncertainty can discourage investment and favor large companies with the resources to wait out restrictions, making it harder for smaller competitors to enter the market. Protecting the public requires enforceable safeguards, but broad prohibitions risk sacrificing economic opportunity without securing comparable restraint from America’s rivals.
National security implications also deserve attention. The federal government explicitly connects domestic AI infrastructure with strategic capabilities. The policy implication is straightforward: making responsible construction unnecessarily difficult could undermine the capabilities Washington wants to protect.
America should remember its nuclear experience. Reactor expansion slowed beginning in the 1970s. Regulatory changes and public opposition contributed, alongside rising costs and weaker electricity demand. Blaming regulation alone misreads the history. Ignoring its role is equally misleading.

Yet AI has become a political football in a midterm election year. Complex questions are entering campaigns built around simple messages. Supporting development becomes evidence of recklessness. Supporting safeguards becomes evidence of hostility to progress. Neither accusation evaluates a model or a construction proposal.
Analysts Need to Speak Together
This is where longtime analysts must act. We are often privy to advanced product roadmaps under nondisclosure agreements, and in my experience, thoughtful companies seek feedback on their plans. We don’t have to agree on politics, but we should agree that technical claims must survive technical questioning.
A shared effort could give editors access to specialists and help them publish clear responses when claims outrun the facts. Explain what was tested. Identify what remains unknown. Ask how extinction probabilities were produced before those numbers become campaign slogans.
Authority brings obligations. Analysts should disclose vendor relationships and correct their mistakes. Experience earns attention; it doesn’t excuse weak reasoning. The independence that challenges alarmism must also challenge industry promises.
Nor should we mock worried readers. They hear warnings from respected researchers and assume those warnings mean something. Our responsibility is to explain the disagreement.
Analysts need to defend sensible safeguards while confronting exaggerated claims, across political lines and without waiting for vendor permission. We need to speak collectively and with authority on this topic, showing the evidence behind our conclusions.
Fear shouldn’t drive decisions that America might spend decades trying to reverse.
