The AI debate has developed a strange pattern.

An AI model produces unexpected or potentially scary results, someone predicts the end of humanity, and the conversation jumps straight to whether civilization has only a few years left. Missing somewhere between the demonstration and the obituary is the evidence. We should demand it.

Claims that AI will destroy humanity require a credible explanation of how software could acquire the power to overcome human resistance in the physical world. An alarming prediction, even from an accomplished researcher, doesn’t settle that question.

Longtime technology analysts should lead this discussion. Too often, we leave it to executives with products to sell and politicians who turn uncertainty into campaign material. People who understand how technology reaches the market need to speak up, together, regardless of their political views.

An Extinction Forecast Needs More Than Imagination

Start with an honest boundary. Nobody can prove that every future AI system will be harmless. But fear-mongering about an impending AI-driven extinction event treats speculation as knowledge. The stronger argument is that the evidence doesn’t justify the certainty of the apocalypse narrative.

The International AI Safety Report, published in February and led by AI expert Yoshua Bengio, found that current systems lacked the capabilities needed for the loss-of-control scenarios it examined. The report also warned that relevant abilities were improving. That supports continued testing and safeguards. It doesn’t establish an approaching extinction event.

Even a highly capable model needs a means to act. Producing a plan is different from carrying it out. Software tools can expand its reach, but access to them must come from somewhere. Intelligence doesn’t automatically grant control.

Physical constraints matter too. Computing requires equipment and electricity. Actions outside a computer depend on connections to machines or people. A serious catastrophe argument must explain how those dependencies are acquired and sustained.

These barriers aren’t guarantees. Security can fail, and people can grant dangerous permissions. But each required failure belongs in the argument. Asking for that chain of events is basic analysis.

Industry Leaders Push Back on AI Alarmism

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed back directly. In a July interview, he criticized people who "spend too much time theorizing about these science fiction outcomes." His broader argument was that frightening people away from AI could undermine adoption and American competitiveness.

Central to this is Huang's message that frontier companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic should address risks through their development, engineering, and testing processes — like any product company that ships only high-quality solutions.

The standard should be clear: establish rigorous AI testing procedures and don't release products with known critical bugs. Risk ultimately isn't just with models. It also lies with companies that allow weak internal due diligence across their teams.

Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez has voiced similar objections. Asked in a 2024 interview about public misconceptions, he identified "the fear that certain individuals and organizations espouse about this technology being a terminator, an existential risk."

The disagreement predates today’s models. In 2017, Mark Zuckerberg criticized doomsday rhetoric, saying "It’s really negative, and in some ways, I actually think it is pretty irresponsible." That historical comment shows how long this argument has persisted. It cannot, by itself, settle questions about newer systems.

These executives certainly have commercial interests. Their confidence deserves scrutiny, as do warnings from competing executives. However, their objections challenge the suggestion that everyone who understands AI agrees catastrophe is coming.

Arguments for broadly shared AI benefits also offer an alternative to fatalism. Analysts should test those promises as closely as extinction predictions. Neither becomes evidence because a prominent executive sounds certain.

The Media Must Ask Better Technical Questions

A frightening prediction is easy to package. Explaining its assumptions takes work. When coverage lacks technical depth, a possibility can start to sound like a forecast. Readers may conclude the engineering questions are settled when an article has barely examined them.

Reporters don’t need to build models, but they do need to assess whistleblowers' credibility and potential agendas more carefully. They also need to distinguish controlled-test results from evidence that a system can operate independently in the real world. Editors should demand that distinction before allowing a dramatic claim to carry a story.

Mainstream coverage isn’t uniformly alarmist. Some commentary has challenged extinction forecasts and emphasized product accountability. Other reporting has examined how doomsday speculation can distract from present harms and the people responsible for them.

The problem is coverage that repeats extraordinary claims without examining the steps required to make them possible. Technical fluency should help a newsroom recognize when a compelling story has outrun its evidence.

Data Centers Have Become the Next Target

Anxiety now extends to the infrastructure behind AI. Data centers face growing public opposition, with local construction disputes feeding a broader political backlash. Buildings full of computers are being asked to answer for everything people dislike about the technology industry.

The economic benefits of data centers are already showing up in public accounts. In Loudoun County, Virginia, existing facilities generated $1.2 billion in property tax revenue in fiscal 2026, helping fund local services and ease the burden on other taxpayers.

Across Virginia, an independent legislative study estimated that the industry supported roughly 74,000 direct and indirect jobs and $5.5 billion in annual labor income, with much of that benefit coming from construction. Those paychecks reach electricians and other skilled workers, well beyond Silicon Valley. Contracts can also create electricity savings when large customers pay more than it costs to serve them.

Georgia Power projects approximately $950 million in annual customer savings beginning in 2029 from its large-load growth portfolio, equivalent to about $180 annually for a typical residential customer. Those are projected savings, not reductions already delivered.

Every proposal needs scrutiny, but a debate that counts electricity demand while ignoring wages and tax revenue leaves out a substantial part of the economic picture.

Some objections are practical. Residents deserve answers about electricity bills and water use. Noise matters to neighbors. Developers weaken their case when they dismiss these concerns or substitute vague promises for enforceable commitments.

Still, treating every data center as a step toward human extinction turns planning into a referendum on an imagined apocalypse. Communities need to examine a facility’s actual costs and benefits.

Construction creates work for skilled trades and business for suppliers, while operating facilities can provide technical jobs and local tax revenue. Permanent staffing is smaller, and advocates should say so.

articles.content:
Richard Childress Racing Builds for the Future: Announces Technology and Technical-Focused Leadership Appointments Ahead of 2027 NASCAR Season
By RCR Staff
WELCOME, NC (September 23, 2026) – Richard Childress Racing announced today two key leadership appointments designed to strengthen the organization’s competition program, accelerate technological innovation and position RCR for long-term success as the company prepares for the 2027 NASCAR season and beyond.
Richard Boswell, who has led Austin Dillon over the past two seasons as crew chief of the No. 3 Chevrolet in the NASCAR Cup Series, will take on a larger role with the race team as Vice President of Competition. Boswell will provide direction across RCR’s competition efforts, with a focus on performance, collaboration with key partner Chevrolet and building a stronger foundation for sustained success on the racetrack.
The son of a late model and Busch Series driver and a former driver himself, Boswell brings more than 15 years of professional motorsports experience to his new role. His career includes time at Hendrick Motorsports, JR Motorsports and Stewart-Haas Racing (SHR), where he helped launch the team’s O’Reilly Auto Parts Series program and oversaw its competition operations. He made his Cup Series crew chief debut at SHR, earning a victory with Chase Briscoe in 2024. Boswell joined RCR in 2025 and led Austin Dillon to a Cup Series win that same year.
Boswell’s leadership style, grounded in accountability and discipline, makes him well suited to lead RCR’s competition efforts. He will finish the current season as crew chief before moving fully into his new role at season’s end.
In addition to strengthening its competition leadership, RCR is expanding its focus on emerging technology with the creation of a Director of Development and Innovation position. Art Trejo has been appointed to the newly created role, where he will lead the company’s efforts to identify, develop and implement emerging technologies. Trejo’s background in military leadership, advanced technology and engineering will strengthen the organization. A 27-year Officer in the United States Navy with degrees from both Princeton University and UCLA, Trejo joins RCR from SpaceX and has extensive experience working in complex, technology-driven environments.
The addition of a dedicated Development and Innovation position represents a continued evolution of RCR’s approach to technology and innovation. The organization has increasingly incorporated advanced technology into its operations, including engineering, manufacturing and competition, while continuing to explore new opportunities and improve performance across the company.
“Everyone at Richard Childress Racing remains relentless in our desire to win and compete at the highest levels of our sport but we know we’re not quite where we need to be,” said Richard Childress, Chairman and CEO of Richard Childress Racing. “We’re announcing these changes now because we want to make sure we have the right people, the right leadership and the right technology in place to compete at the level RCR expects to compete at. Richard Boswell is a talented leader who knows racing, knows how to lead people, and knows what it takes to win. I know he will do a great job taking on a larger role in leading our competition team. Art Trejo brings a completely different set of experiences and a new way of thinking that I believe can help take our racing operations forward. We’re going to keep pushing, keep investing and keep looking for ways to get better.”
For more information, please visit rcrracing.com .

Ondas Acquires Three Defense Technology Businesses to Expand Its Integrated Autonomous Defense Systems Platform
Acquisitions add field-deployed and near-term mission-ready capabilities across acoustic intelligence, resilient communications, remote operations and GNSS-denied navigation, strengthening existing Ondas platforms and enabling new integrated solutions and revenue opportunities.
Insignito adds a unique passive acoustic sensing layer to detect, classify, and track drones particularly useful for small FPV drone systems and fiber optic systems that are difficult to detect by traditional methods.
Ottopia Defense combines AI-powered autonomy capabilities and ultra-low-latency teleoperation, and intelligent networking, connecting unmanned maneuvering platforms with human operators and command centers for one-to-many capabilities.
Caribou Labs is a provider of GNSS-denied navigation and resilient communications technology that will add key capabilities and differentiation for Ondas platforms in combat environments.
WEST PALM BEACH, FL / ACCESS Newswire / September 23, 2026 / Ondas Inc. (NASDAQ:ONDS) ("Ondas" or the "Company"), a leading provider of autonomous systems and next-generation defense and security technologies, announced today that it has acquired three defense technology businesses, adding advanced capabilities that enhance the Company's mission capabilities and expand its addressable markets. The acquired businesses bring technologies ranging from systems already deployed in active conflict environments to capabilities positioned for near-term mission integration across Ondas' existing platforms. The acquisitions are designed to strengthen Ondas' existing and future autonomous platforms, accelerate the development of integrated solutions and create new opportunities for growth across the defense and autonomous systems markets.
"These acquisitions reflect our strategy of assembling the critical technologies required to make autonomous systems more capable, resilient and scalable in contested environments," said Eric Brock, Chairman and CEO of Ondas Inc. "Together, these businesses give Ondas more to sell and more ways to win. They add commercial revenue streams we can grow across our customer base, and they strengthen our ability to pursue larger, longer-term customer programs where we deploy and sustain more capable autonomous systems on behalf of the customers we serve."
Insignito - AI-Enabled Acoustic Intelligence for C-UAS.
Insignito's mission-ready technology creates a passive acoustic sensing layer designed to detect, classify, track and localize drones by their acoustic signatures, including small drones, FPV systems, low-altitude threats and autonomous or RF-silent platforms that can challenge traditional radar and radio-frequency detection. Its flagship DUMBO system has been successfully deployed in conflict zones listening to the operating environment rather than transmitting RF or electromagnetic energy, applying real-time signal processing, advanced acoustic modeling, artificial intelligence and proprietary algorithms to identify unmanned aerial vehicle signatures. The technology is designed to complement radar, RF and electro-optical sensors, adding an independent sensing modality to a layered, multi-sensor C-UAS architecture.
Beyond passive detection, Insignito has developed several additional capabilities including WaveGuide, a software-based mission-planning capability that models the acoustic detectability of aerial platforms along planned trajectories; Silent Propellers, which applies acoustic engineering to reduce the noise signature of unmanned aircraft; and Banshee, an acoustic-enabled drone interception technology under development. Collectively, these capabilities span detection, mission planning, signature reduction and interception.
Ottopia Defense - Mission-Critical Communications and Remote Control for Unmanned Systems.
Ottopia Defense ("Ottopia") provides software and communications infrastructure connecting unmanned maneuvering platforms with remote operators and command centers. The technology is designed to maintain the continuous, real-time flow of video, telemetry, mission data and commands in remote, harsh, bandwidth-constrained, degraded and mission-critical environments. Its architecture dynamically manages high-priority operational data across available communications channels, helping preserve the connection between unmanned platforms and human operators when battlefield connectivity is inconsistent or disrupted.
Ottopia's mission-ready platform combines AI-enabled autonomy, ultra-low-latency teleoperation, remote control and resilient communications, enabling operators to supervise multiple unmanned systems, monitor live video and telemetry, and intervene whenever human judgment or direct control is required. Its one-to-many architecture allows a smaller number of operators to manage multiple assets from centralized mission centers or distributed command environments while preserving human oversight and command authority.
Caribou Labs - Resilient Communications for GNSS-denied environments.
Caribou Labs ("Caribou") is a deep-tech, dual-use company specializing in EW environments providing resilient communications and deterministic identification. The company combines domain expertise in RF engineering, sensing and defense systems. Caribou's mission is to deliver GPS-independent positioning timing and visibility when digital infrastructure fails. The company's products are complementary to Ondas' autonomous systems by helping to complete an end-to-end autonomy and resiliency stack that includes connectivity, navigation, identification and regulatory compliance across aerial, ground and command platforms. Caribou's technology is currently deployed in active conflict environments and has a global pipeline of new customer opportunities.
Building an Integrated Technology Stack for Autonomous Defense
Ondas intends to integrate these technologies across its existing portfolio. Insignito adds acoustic sensing that enhances Ondas' current C-UAS solution with an additional FPV drone detection layer. Ottopia provides the resilient connectivity and human command capabilities required for remote operations of unmanned ground vehicles such as Iron Wave. Caribou adds navigation, positioning and communications capabilities for GNSS-denied environments that are required across Ondas' platforms. Combined with Ondas' existing autonomous platforms, sensors, software and mission systems, these capabilities are expected to strengthen an increasingly integrated technology stack spanning detection, connectivity, navigation, autonomy and mission execution. This approach is central to Ondas' Systems-of-Systems strategy: combining differentiated technologies across multiple platforms to enhance existing products, accelerate the development of new solutions and expand the markets and revenue opportunities available to the Company.
Transaction Summary of Strategic Acquisitions
Ondas acquired the businesses for aggregate consideration of $56 million, payable in cash or Ondas common stock. Based on Ondas' forecasts, the purchase price represents less than three times the businesses' expected 2027 revenue. The transactions also include potential earnout consideration of up to $32 million in the aggregate, payable in cash or Ondas common stock upon the achievement of key performance milestones through 2028.
In connection with the acquisitions, the Company approved inducement grants of restricted stock units (RSUs) representing 2,979,063 shares of the Company's common stock and stock options exercisable for 80,000 shares of the Company's common stock with an exercise price of $7.72 per share to a total of 37 newly-hired employees in connection with the acquisitions. The equity awards were granted under the Ondas Inc. 2026 Inducement Plan pursuant to the Nasdaq Rule 5635(c)(4) inducement grant exception as a component of each individual's employment compensation and were granted as an inducement material to his or her acceptance of employment with the Company. RSUs representing (i) 222,727 shares of the Company's common stock vest in eight (8) equal quarterly installments over two years following the closing date, subject to the applicable employee's continued employment with the Company; (ii) 1,866,061 shares of the Company's common stock vest one-third on September 23, 2027 and subsequently in eight equal quarterly installments, subject to the applicable employee's continued employment with the Company; and (iii) 890,275 shares of the Company's common stock vest on the closing date. Stock options representing 80,000 shares of the Company's common stock vest one-third on September 23, 2027 and subsequently in twenty-four equal monthly installments, subject to the applicable employee's continued employment with the Company.
About Ondas Inc.
Ondas Inc. (NASDAQ:ONDS) is a leading provider of autonomous systems, robotics, and mission-critical technologies for defense, homeland security, public safety, critical infrastructure, and industrial markets. The Company develops and deploys integrated unmanned and autonomous platforms across air, ground, and stratospheric environments, including autonomous drone systems, counter-UAS technologies, robotic ground systems, advanced unmanned aircraft and propulsion solutions, demining and engineering systems, and integrated sensing and communications technologies designed to support intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, security, and operational missions in complex environments. Ondas' solutions are deployed globally by government, defense, and commercial customers to protect infrastructure, borders, transportation networks, personnel, and strategic assets.
For additional information on Ondas Inc., visit www.ondas.com.

The company's products are complementary to Ondas' autonomous systems by helping to complete an end-to-end autonomy and resiliency stack that includes connectivity, navigation, identification and regulatory compliance across aerial, ground and command platforms. Caribou's technology is currently deployed in active conflict environments and has a global pipeline of new customer opportunities.

Building an Integrated Technology Stack for Autonomous Defense

Ondas intends to integrate these technologies across its existing portfolio. Insignito adds acoustic sensing that enhances Ondas' current C-UAS solution with an additional FPV drone detection layer. Ottopia provides the resilient connectivity and human command capabilities required for remote operations of unmanned ground vehicles such as Iron Wave. Caribou adds navigation, positioning and communications capabilities for GNSS-denied environments that are required across Ondas' platforms. Combined with Ondas' existing autonomous platforms, sensors, software and mission systems, these capabilities are expected to strengthen an increasingly integrated technology stack spanning detection, connectivity, navigation, autonomy and mission execution. This approach is central to Ondas' Systems-of-Systems strategy: combining differentiated technologies across multiple platforms to enhance existing products, accelerate the development of new solutions and expand the markets and revenue opportunities available to the Company.

Transaction Summary of Strategic Acquisitions

Ondas acquired the businesses for aggregate consideration of $56 million, payable in cash or Ondas common stock. Based on Ondas' forecasts, the purchase price represents less than three times the businesses' expected 2027 revenue. articles.heading: New technology helps Montana crime lab detect drugs at lower concentrations
articles.summary: As part of National Forensic Science Week, new technology is helping scientists at the Montana State Crime Lab detect drugs at lower concentrations than ever be
articles.content:
New technology helps Montana crime lab detect drugs at lower concentrations
NBC Montana Staff — As part of National Forensic Science Week, new technology is helping scientists at the Montana State Crime Lab detect drugs at lower concentrations than ever before.
That can be especially important when dealing with powerful synthetic opioids, where even tiny amounts can have a significant effect.
Inside the Montana State Crime Lab in Missoula, scientists work to determine exactly what is in drug evidence submitted by investigators across the state.
“So in this room, we analyze drugs that are seized from a person, not within their blood or urine or anything like that. This is where we're analyzing powders, tablets ... or liquids that officers find and submit to the crime lab,” Chemistry Supervisor Andrew Wade said.
But what scientists are finding isn't always simple.
In 2025, Montana participated in a nationwide project that examined 100 evidence items submitted to the lab. Scientists found the samples contained, on average, about nine different constituents, including active drugs, cutting agents and other substances.
“We found that the state of Montana, 56% of the drugs that we've received contain more than nine constituents ... We're seeing about nine constituents per actual item received, which is pretty high comparatively to the other ... states that contributed to this,” Wade said.
Sometimes, what's mixed into a drug can make it harder for scientists to find what they're looking for.
“What the problem is is that can block some of the signal from these other drugs,” Wade said.
That's particularly important when scientists are looking for extremely potent substances such as fentanyl analogs.
One way the lab tackles that problem is by extracting some ingredients before analyzing the sample again.
“What we're doing behind us is we extract out the acetaminophen, we extract out mannitol, some sugars, maybe baking soda that drugs are being cut with ... So on top of analyzing the drugs that we received, we then have to go and extract out some of those ingredients that we don't wanna see that could be masking other drugs that are in our cases,” Wade said.
The lab then uses sophisticated instruments to identify the substances.
“Basically here, this is the gas chromatograph and mass spectrometer. This is the gold standard in drug chemistry,” Wade said.
The instrument first separates the different compounds in a sample. The mass spectrometer then creates what amounts to a chemical fingerprint.
“When it hits this mass spectrometer, we hit it with a voltage, 70 volts, and that fragments it in a unique, repeatable way, and that gives us the fingerprint of the drug,” Wade said.
Those fingerprints appear as peaks on a computer screen. Scientists use the position of the peaks and fragmentation patterns to identify what's in a sample.
“Every drug, like for example, methamphetamine and amphetamine, they have a known retention time when we run it ... When it hits this mass spectrometer ... that gives us the fingerprint of the drug,” Wade said.
Another instrument allows scientists to detect substances at even lower concentrations.
“So this is the liquid chromatography mass spectrometer. And basically if the GC is the gold standard, this is the platinum standard,” Wade said.
The LC-MS-MS can detect substances at lower concentrations, which is increasingly important when scientists are looking for powerful fentanyl analogs.
“This instrumentation allows us to lower our limit of detection, meaning we can see things at smaller concentrations,” Wade said.
The technology is also helping Montana identify substances that may be new to the state and, in some cases, new to forensic laboratories across the country.

articles.content:
Are we killing ourselves with technology?
Published 8:07 am Wednesday, September 23, 2026
| Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... |
I am a hypocrite. It’s best to admit that up front, before I get too deep in the weeds in this discussion of technology. I’m writing this on my MacBook after all, having just reread Wendell Berry’s 1987 essay entitled, “Why I Am Not Going to Buy a Computer.”
What makes this even more hypocritical is that just behind me on a bookshelf sits a mint condition Remington Rand Model 5 manual typewriter (circa 1937). Furthermore, there is a stack of yellow legal pads in the cabinets beneath the old manual. I could opt for either for writing instead of the laptop, but I do not.
Berry wrote everything by hand. That’s over 50 books of poetry, essays, novels, and short stories, all written out in longhand and then typed by Berry’s wife Tanya. Berry didn’t want to lose the human touch.
All of this has me pondering how much technology we really need? When do we reach a point of negative return? Personally, I feel that in many ways we’re already past that point.
On the heels of Berry’s death in late August, I decided to start reading his fiction. I’ve devoured his essays and poetry over the years, but have yet to explore his fiction.
However, before beginning my Berry vision quest, I found myself rereading his computer essay in response to another book I’m reading, Paul Kingsnorth’s “Against the Machine: On the Unmaking of Humanity.”
I began the Kingsnorth book in hopes that it would give me a bit of hope, a desire brought on by recent news articles warning of the dangers of artificial intelligence (AI).
AI seems to be everywhere I turn these days and, to be honest, it doesn’t give me a warm, fuzzy feeling. My initial misgivings were over the fact that it seems to have the effect of dumbing us down.
It seems that many students can no longer write their own papers or speeches, and many professionals can no longer complete their own presentations or business analysis without a little (or a lot) of help from ChatGPT or Microsoft Copilot. Are we consistently killing our ability to think for ourselves?
Recent headlines like The Wall Street Journal’s, “Biggest AI Rivals Agree They Need to Slow It Down” have my AI concern radar activated. It seems that Elon Musk, Sam Altman, and Dario Amodei all believe there is a need “to slow development of the technology before their advances create a menace than can’t be controlled.”
I remember watching “Terminator” on the big screen in 1984. Back then, the thought of military superintelligence like “Skynet” becoming self-aware and trying to wipe out humanity seemed like something I would never have to worry about in my lifetime.
It seems that Musk, Altman, and Amodei think otherwise. Amodei’s warning about the risks of AI comes after an Anthropic employee left the company while announcing to the world “that there was a greater than 10% chance that AI systems could destroy civilization within the next decade.” What are we to think?
The “self-awareness” and “self-improvement” capabilities of current AI systems led the CEOs to warn that continued progress could yield systems that “could outrun our ability to understand and control” them. Terminator’s Skynet no longer seems far-fetched.
Berry once wrote, “It is easy for me to imagine that the next great division of the world will be between people who wish to live as creatures and people who wish to live as machines.” I believe he lived to see the beginnings of that reality.
One of the lies of technology has always been, according to Kingsnorth, that it will “save either time or labor” which he argues is seldom (if ever) true. The advancement of technology also seems to always come at price.
Kingsnorth gives email as an example citing that “…we were promised that the advent of email would save us hours of time: no more faxing, or opening and replying to letters! Now we spend, by some estimates, thirty days a year on email alone, and it is increasingly impossible to be out of touch with anyone, anywhere.”
To this I would add our so called “smartphones.” A quick Google search reveals that the average person spends 4 to 5 hours per day on their phone. That adds up to 70 days per year.
Again, I’m a hypocrite in writing this. I use a computer to do the bulk of my writing, and I use a smartphone to check email and social media, to text, and to actually phone others. I’ve even caved to tech in my outdoor pursuits.
For example, I now use cellular game cameras, and while I admit that I get excited when the pictures come to my phone, I also must admit that the cameras have done nothing to make me a better hunter. Arguably, they’ve made me worse, as woodsmanship is an acquired skill, one that, like most skills, improves with practice and time.
Fortunately, I can still claim that I’m very limited in my usage of AI. I use a computer, and search engines, but I don’t use Microsoft Word’s Copilot while writing, and I’ve never used ChatGPT (not even to make a better looking, enhanced photo of myself, which seems to be the trend these days).
I cringe when I see the integration of AI at every turn in the workplace. That reality has even led me to research personal protections against its use. Can I obtain some sort of conscientious objector status against the use of AI?
Pope Leo XIV, while not opposing its use, has insisted that AI must be “regulated and kept subordinate to human dignity.” That seems like a reasonable first step to me, but what are the next steps?
For now, I’ll be right here hypocritically typing away on my computer while pondering just how much technology is too much, both indoors and out. Until next time, here’s to seeing you out there in our great outdoors.

articles.heading: Novai publishes study supporting use of DARC imaging technology to identify patients at risk of central vision loss from macular atrophy
articles.summary: Novai. a medtech company combatting blindness and disability by pioneering early detection and intervention for eye and brain diseases, today announced the publication of a peer-reviewed study in Expert Review of Ophthalmology, which successfully demonstrates its ‘Detection of Apoptosing Retinal Cells’ (DARC) imaging technology as a promising biomarker for identifying patients at high risk of central vision loss caused by macular atrophy (MA).
articles.content:
Novai. a medtech company combatting blindness and disability by pioneering early detection and intervention for eye and brain diseases, today announced the publication of a peer-reviewed study in Expert Review of Ophthalmology, which successfully demonstrates its ‘Detection of Apoptosing Retinal Cells’ (DARC) imaging technology as a promising biomarker for identifying patients at high risk of central vision loss caused by macular atrophy (MA). By revealing disease activity at an earlier stage than currently possible, DARC offers a novel approach to predicting future patterns of atrophy progression, supporting more accurate patient stratification for clinical trials, and earlier initiation of treatment, as appropriate.
Founder and CEO, Novai.
Image Credit: Novai
MA, also known as late dry-AMD or Geographic Atrophy (GA), is the advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) which is a leading cause of irreversible vision loss and blindness worldwide. Characterized by the progressive loss of retinal cells responsible for central vision, a key challenge in MA is that retinal cells can become stressed and begin to die long before structural damage is visible on conventional imaging. This has historically limited the ability to identify patients at greatest risk of vision loss. Novai's DARC imaging technology combines a fluorescently labelled Annexin A5 probe with advanced data science, AI-powered algorithms, and digital image processing, to detect and quantify the number and pattern of distribution of sick, stressed, and apoptotic retinal cells in patients, before structural loss becomes apparent.
The paper, titled ‘Predicting directional macular atrophy progression using angular plot analysis of DARC (apoptosing retinal cells), EZ (ellipsoid zone) loss, EZ–RPE (retinal pigment epithelium) difference, and HRF (hyperreflective foci)’, builds on research carried out at Imperial College London, demonstrating the application of Novai’s DARC retinal imaging technology for the detection of early cellular stress, and predicting the directional expansion of atrophy.
The retrospective exploratory study leveraged data from the Phase 2a DARC trial (ISRCTN10751859). The findings demonstrated that baseline DARC measurements were more strongly associated with the future direction of macular atrophy growth than three established optical coherence tomography (OCT) biomarkers, including ellipsoid zone (EZ) loss, EZ-retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) difference, and hyperreflective foci density. DARC signals were also detected beyond the visible margins of existing atrophy, consistent with the identification of stressed and apoptotic photoreceptors before structural damage becomes visible on OCT. Prospective validation of these findings is ongoing in the DAB trial (ISRCTN22122298).
The finding that DARC could provide a window into active disease, including where that disease activity is occurring, at an earlier stage addresses a major unmet need in geographic atrophy. By identifying ongoing cellular activity before irreversible structural loss becomes established, DARC has the potential to identify patients at greatest risk of progression and central vision loss, when there may still be an opportunity to intervene. This is particularly important given the rapidly expanding pipeline of therapies for geographic atrophy, where improved biomarkers of disease activity could help identify the patients most likely to benefit, support earlier and more appropriate treatment, and provide a means of monitoring biological response. While prospective validation is ongoing, DARC could therefore support better informed clinical decision-making, improve clinical trial stratification and, ultimately, enable more personalized treatment and monitoring strategies aimed at preserving vision.”
Maria Francesca Cordeiro, Professor, Founder and CEO, Novai
Novai will be attending the EURETINA Congress 2026 (1-4 October, Vienna, Austria) and the AAO Annual Meeting 2026 (9-12 October, New Orleans, LA, USA). The team will be available to discuss the DARC platform, current and future clinical applications, and potential research and commercial partnerships.

articles.summary: /PRNewswire/ -- Velo3D, Inc. (Nasdaq: VELO), a metal 3D printing technology company that enables customers to build mission-critical metal parts, today...
articles.content:
Vic Fryzel and Robert Purnell bring complementary expertise in platform performance and manufacturing execution at Forge 1
FREMONT, Calif., Sept. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Velo3D, Inc. (Nasdaq: VELO), a metal 3D printing technology company that enables customers to build mission-critical metal parts, today announced that Vic Fryzel has joined as Executive Vice President, Technology, and Robert Purnell as Senior Director, Operations. Together, they strengthen the technology and operational leadership supporting production at Forge 1, Velo3D's Livermore Production Campus in California.

articles.article_title: Sphere And Disguise Announce Multi-Year Technology Partnership To Advance The Future Of Immersive Live Entertainment
articles.heading: Sphere And Disguise Announce Multi-Year Technology Partnership To Advance The Future Of Immersive Live Entertainment
articles.summary: New York, NY – Sphere Entertainment Co. (NYSE: SPHR) and Disguise, a g | Since Sphere opened in 2023, Disguise has served as a key technology partner supporting Sphere's groundbreaking live residency productions.
articles.content:
New York, NY – Sphere Entertainment Co. (NYSE: SPHR) and Disguise, a global leader in visual technology for live events, location-based entertainment and virtual production, today announced a new multi-year partnership to develop advanced technologies custom-made for Sphere's immersive entertainment venue.
Since Sphere opened in 2023, Disguise has served as a key technology partner supporting the delivery of Sphere's groundbreaking live residency productions and corporate events. For these events, Sphere uses Disguise media servers and software to process, synchronize and play back content in real-time, at a scale unparalleled in live entertainment. Building on that successful collaboration, the companies are expanding their relationship to advance technologies and workflows to accelerate video playback capabilities and help prepare Sphere for the next phase of global growth.
‘Sphere was built to redefine live entertainment, and continuing to push the boundaries of immersive experiences requires technology partners that share our ambition’, said Ryan Dolan, Executive Vice President, Head of Event & Interactive Technology, Sphere. ‘Every artist who has performed at Sphere has benefited from Disguise’s technology, and we’re looking forward to developing future iterations of immersive productions to support our long-term vision of offering these experiences to audiences in new Sphere venues around the world’.
‘We’re honored to have Sphere’s vote of confidence in our technology and are incredibly grateful for the relationship and all the development of the last three years’, says Fernando Küfer, CEO of Disguise. ‘We are excited to now focus on the expansion of Sphere’s video offerings around Disguise’s technology. What motivates us at Disguise is supporting the most incredible entertainment experiences in the world. When an artist imagines something the world has never seen, they should be able to reach for it and know the system can deliver. There's no better partner than Sphere to build that future with and it's a personal joy to work with a team and company like them’.
As part of the collaboration, Sphere will be the first partner to bring Disguise’s next-generation technology to market. The new technology developed through this partnership will enable Sphere to maintain its leadership position in live entertainment while supporting its expansion.
About Sphere Entertainment Co.
Sphere Entertainment Co. is a leader in immersive experiences, technology and media. The Company includes Sphere, an experiential medium powered by advanced technologies. The first Sphere opened in Las Vegas, with plans also announced for Sphere venues in Abu Dhabi and National Harbor. In addition, the Company includes MSG Networks, which operates two regional sports and entertainment networks, MSG Network and MSG Sportsnet, as well as a direct-to-consumer and authenticated streaming product, MSG+, delivering a wide range of live sports content and other programming. More information is available at www.sphereentertainmentco.com.
About Disguise

Disguise is a global technology company driving the next dimension of entertainment. The company's' ecosystem of software, hardware and services powers end-to-end visual experiences across live events, immersive attractions, theme parks, stadiums, virtual production and broadcast. With the technical depth to run the largest and most complex productions in the world, Disguise gives teams the confidence to realise their most ambitious visions.
From Disney to Snapchat, Netflix to ESPN, Bad Bunny to Beyoncé, the Burj Khalifa to the Sydney Opera House, Disguise powers experiences for the biggest entertainment companies, brands, studios and venues in the world, revolutionising every sector of the industry. Find more information at: www.disguise.one

articles.article_title: Georgia Tech students build anti-drone system designed to detect hidden threats
articles.heading: Georgia Tech students build anti-drone system designed to detect hidden threats
articles.summary: Two Georgia Tech students are betting on something new, turning an idea into a defense technology company with help from a university program designed to bring startups to life.
articles.content:
Georgia Tech students build anti-drone system designed to detect hidden threats
Two Georgia Tech students are betting on something new, turning an idea into a defense technology company with help from a university program designed to bring startups to life.
"This is the cradle. We live and die by this box," said Tejas Balaji, the company's co-founder.
After years of dreaming and months of building, the hard work is beginning to pay off for Balaji and fellow Georgia Tech student Maxwell Hadaway. The two founded Sokol Technologies, a company developing anti-drone technology and autonomous defense systems.
The founders say their system uses sound and cameras to detect drones, including those that can evade traditional detection systems such as radar.
Balaji and Hadaway hope to fill a gap by providing military and security personnel with another way to detect drones.
"We are here to fill that puzzle piece," Hadaway said.
Building the technology is only half the challenge. The other half is building the business.
"Nothing worth doing comes without effort," Balaji said.
That is where Georgia Tech's CREATE-X program comes in. The program connects student entrepreneurs with mentors, resources and investors.
"That really helped us address the problems we faced just getting this off the ground," Balaji said.
Those ideas are becoming real companies. Georgia Tech says more than 700 students have created startups through CREATE-X, with a combined valuation of more than $4.5 billion.
Margaret Weniger, the program's director, said the work begins with investing in each entrepreneur.
"For us, it's really about investing in the person," Weniger said. She said the program helps students develop professional and entrepreneurial skills while connecting them with resources to move their startups forward.
For Balaji and Hadaway, the project is about more than making money. They hope their business can save lives.
"It means guys who are out there defending us and our allies have the slightest bit of clarity when there are threats coming in that are today relatively invisible," Balaji said

FAU’s Michael Twardowski, Ph.D., Named Edwin A. Link 
Ocean Technology and Defense Endowed Professor
 | Newswise
articles.heading:
FAU’s Michael Twardowski, Ph.D., Named Edwin A. Link 
Ocean Technology and Defense Endowed Professor
articles.summary: Michael Twardowski, Ph.D., an internationally recognized expert in optical oceanography and marine sensing technologies, has been named the first Edwin A. Link Ocean Technology and Defense Endowed Professor at FAU's Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute.
articles.content:
Newswise — Michael Twardowski, Ph.D., an internationally recognized expert in optical oceanography and marine sensing technologies, has been named the Edwin A. Link Ocean Technology and Defense Endowed Professor at Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute. This first endowed professorship at FAU Harbor Branch was made possible through the generous support of the Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute Foundation, Inc., which has helped advance groundbreaking oceanographic research and education at FAU for decades.
Twardowski is a research professor at FAU Harbor Branch and director of the Center for Marine Applied Technology and Engineering, where he leads multidisciplinary research at the intersection of ocean science, engineering and advanced sensing technologies. For more than 30 years, his work has focused on developing innovative optical technologies and applying them to some of the most challenging problems in marine science, environmental monitoring and national defense.
“Endowed professorships are among the most powerful investments the Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute Foundation can make in the future of ocean science,” said Cara Perry, chair of the Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute Foundation, Inc. Board of Directors and vice president of FAU’s Division of University Communications. “The foundation is proud to recognize and support Dr. Twardowski, whose pioneering research, collaborative approach and commitment to developing advanced technologies embody Harbor Branch’s longstanding legacy of innovation and exploration. His work reflects the same spirit of curiosity and ingenuity that defined Edwin A. Link and continues to inspire Florida Atlantic’s Harbor Branch today.”
The endowed professorship honors Link – inventor, engineer and ocean explorer – whose technological innovations helped lay the foundation for FAU Harbor Branch’s tradition of exploration and discovery. Link is best known for inventing the Link flight simulator, first commercialized in 1929. His invention revolutionized pilot training and was used to train more than 500,000 airmen during World War II. Link ultimately received 27 U.S. patents for his inventions.
Later in life, Link turned his attention from the skies to the depths of the ocean, becoming a pioneer in underwater archaeology, submersibles and marine technology. His engineering expertise and passion for exploration complemented the vision of FAU Harbor Branch’s founder, J. Seward Johnson, Sr., who established the institute in 1971 to advance understanding of the ocean through scientific exploration.
Among Link’s most significant contributions to ocean exploration was the development of advanced submersibles, including the Johnson-Sea-Link. On Jan. 29, 1971, Link and Johnson launched the submersible at the newly established Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute, giving scientists a new capability to explore the deep ocean firsthand.
Link also had a longstanding connection to FAU. In 1965, a grant from the Link Foundation helped FAU establish the nation’s first undergraduate ocean engineering program, reflecting his commitment to advancing ocean science and engineering education.
“I am deeply grateful to the Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute Foundation board for this honor and for its investment in the future of ocean technology at Florida Atlantic,” said Twardowski. “This professorship will help me expand our applied research efforts, strengthen collaborations and develop new technologies that address some of the most pressing challenges facing our oceans. I am especially proud to carry the Link name forward as we continue building on his legacy of innovation that has defined FAU Harbor Branch.”
For more than 30 years, Twardowski has led the development of optical sensing technologies and their application to a wide range of basic and applied research challenges in marine science and national defense. He has authored more than 130 peer-reviewed publications on topics including remote sensing of optical and biogeochemical properties, bioluminescence, holographic imaging microscopy, biological camouflage, underwater imaging and autonomous monitoring.
Twardowski is also a member of the science team for NASA’s PACE mission, where he is working to advance ocean-color algorithms used to better understand ocean ecosystems and biogeochemical processes. A key focus of his research is developing partnerships with defense primes and sensor manufacturers to translate innovative ocean-sensing technologies into real-world applications for marine science and national defense.
The appointment strengthens FAU Harbor Branch’s longstanding tradition of pairing scientific discovery with technological innovation – a heritage that dates to the institute’s founding and the trailblazing work of Johnson and Link.
“Mike Twardowski represents exactly the kind of innovative researcher and scientific leader that an endowed professorship should recognize,” said Gregg Fields, Ph.D., FAU vice president for research. “His research is pushing the boundaries of how we observe and understand the ocean while addressing challenges of critical importance to environmental science, climate research, maritime operations and national security. This endowment recognizes his extraordinary accomplishments and contributions to ocean science. As an R1 research institution, Florida Atlantic is committed to investing in world-class researchers whose discoveries and technologies have the potential to make a meaningful impact far beyond our campuses.”
- FAU -
About Florida Atlantic University:
Florida Atlantic University is one of the nation’s fastest-rising public research universities, serving more than 32,000 students in South Florida. Ranked among the Top 100 Public Universities by U.S. News & World Report, Florida Atlantic is also one of only 13 institutions nationwide to hold Carnegie Foundation designations for R1 research, opportunity and community engagement. Guided by its strategic plan, “2031FAU: Where Tomorrow Begins,” the university is focused on delivering career-ready education and experiential learning, driving scholarly inquiry that creates healthier, safer and more prosperous communities, strengthening institutional excellence, and elevating its impact across South Florida and beyond. Florida Atlantic continues to advance its position as Florida’s first quantum university, integrating research, education and industry partnerships around next-generation computing technologies. Through other signature strengths in neuroscience and healthy aging, environmental, ocean and coastal innovation, and national defense and autonomous systems, Florida Atlantic expands knowledge, fuels economic opportunity and fulfills its mission as South Florida’s hometown university.

articles.title: Tampa company promotes e-recycling and gives old technology a second life
articles.description: Tampa company promotes e-recycling and gives old technology a second life Bay News 9
articles.description_html: Tampa company promotes e-recycling and gives old technology a second life  Bay News 9
articles.article_title: Tampa company promotes e-recycling and gives old technology a second life
articles.heading: Tampa company promotes e-recycling and gives old technology a second life
articles.summary: eSmart Recycling partners with local groups to cut electronic waste by refurbishing old devices.
articles.content:
TAMPA, Fla. — A Tampa-based electronics recycling company is partnering with local organizations to promote September as e-recycling month and encourage people to give old technology a second life.
eSmart Recycling in Tampa accepts a wide range of used electronics and devices, from laptops, monitors and headphones, to toys and household items. Employees sort, test, wipe and break down items so they can be reused, resold or donated.
“Anything with a plug switch or battery, we will take,” said Logan Melton, test bench coordinator at eSmart Recycling.
Melton said computers, tablets and other devices go through a data-wiping process before going on to their second-life.
“They go through this process if it’s for a customer, if it’s for us selling something, if it’s for us giving back to the community, they all need to be wiped,” Melton said.
Tony Selvaggio founded eSmart Recycling in 2014 after moving from Venezuela. He said many people have not learned the effect old electronics can have when they are thrown away instead of recycled.
“I think that most people don’t fully understand the impact that it’s behind old technology because it’s relatively new, so we’re used to hoarding it, and now we’re starting to get to a point where it’s starting to hit our waste streams,” Selvaggio said.
Selvaggio said e-waste can build up in landfills and may contaminate water supplies if it is not handled correctly. He said 80% of technology is thrown away instead of recycled, while the U.S. produces more than 60 million tons of electronics every year.
eSmart Recycling has partnered with Tampa Bay Tech and the Digital Education Foundation to help raise awareness about e-recycling.
“The partnership with the Digital Education Foundation and the partnership with somebody like TBT plays such an important role to create a solution,” Selvaggio said. “Because you can’t tackle the problem on your own.”
The company also connects refurbished technology with local children. Melton said about half of the laptops in good enough condition at the warehouse will end up in the hands of children.
The Digital Education Foundation says roughly 85,000 households in Hillsborough and Pinellas counties do not have internet access, and that donated technology can help close the digital divide.
For more information about e-recycling and how to get rid of old electronics, click here.

articles.heading: Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Micron is enjoying a generational demand wave.
articles.content:
- MU -2.17%

- NVDA -1.63%

Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) has been one of the hottest stocks of 2026, but I think there could be a lot more coming. The reality is that the memory chip market remains one of the hottest areas in the stock market, and until there is relief in memory chip supply, elevated prices will persist. That primes Micron to thrive in one of the biggest, if not the biggest, demand waves in its history.

If you invest $5,000 now, I think it could be worth a lot more just a few years later. But how much? Let's take a look.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Micron is thriving in today's market conditions

The number of data centers being built and the number of chips being placed inside them have made it hard for multiple supply chains to keep up. Memory chips are arguably under the most strain, as every supplier in this industry has far more demand than supply.

Building new chip fabrication facilities isn't an easy task, either. It can take years to build up adequate production facilities, and there's also some hesitation from the chip manufacturers themselves. This demand wave isn't likely to last forever, and if Micron and its peers overbuild, they could find themselves in a precarious position in the future, with too much supply.

Regardless, Micron is building new production facilities, but they won't be active until mid-2027 and into 2028. So it will be some time before there's enough production capacity available to ease the shortage. In fact, Micron's management team estimates that it will be 2028 or later before there is any relief. That means the memory chip prices will stay elevated throughout at least 2027, but what happens beyond that?

Many AI hyperscalers have informed investors that it will be years before the build-out is over, and it could last through at least 2030 . That means there will still be heightened demand, and even if memory chip prices fall, they will likely remain at a level that allows Micron to maintain high profitability. That bodes well for the stock, but where would that price the stock by 2028?

Let's take a look at some Wall Street projections, as those point to massive growth ahead.

Micron is a screaming buy right now

For fiscal year (FY) 2027, ending in September 2027, Wall Street analysts estimate 89% growth to $245 billion in revenue. That would rank Micron among the largest revenue companies on Earth. From an earnings per share (EPS) standpoint, they estimate $156.53, up from the projected $73.46 in FY 2026.

Wall Street analysts have undershot projections relating to the AI build-out for some time, and I'd expect no difference next year. However, I'll use the consensus estimate for this projection, which I believe represents a conservative forecast.

Over the past decade, Micron's valuation has seen a lot of highs and lows due to the cyclical nature of its business. However, the average is right around 22 times earnings.

MU PE Ratio data by YCharts

Using a 20 times earnings valuation to bake in even more conservatism, that would price Micron's stock at $3,130 per share. Micron's stock is currently just over $1,000, so this would represent a triple, turning a $5,000 investment into more than $15,000 by approximately this time next year.

If the demand curve for memory chips stays elevated, I could see the investment being worth more than $20,000 by 2028. That's an incredible return in a relatively short time frame, making Micron one of the best bets investors can make right now.

articles.summary: By Michelle Nichols, John Irish and Courtney Rozen UNITED NATIONS, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Executives from OpenAI, Anthropic and Hugging Face will brief the UN Security Council on Wednesday amid warnings
articles.content:
AI leaders to brief UN amid warnings the technology could slip beyond human control

By Michelle Nichols, John Irish and Courtney Rozen

UNITED NATIONS, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Executives from OpenAI, Anthropic and Hugging Face will brief the UN Security Council on Wednesday amid warnings increasingly powerful AI technologies could soon improve themselves, ‌slip beyond human control and threaten international security.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Hugging Face co-founder ‌Clément Delangue are due to brief the 15-member council during the annual General Assembly gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.

Altman plans to urge world leaders ​to adopt benchmarks for measuring AI capabilities and assessing the safeguards companies put in place as they develop the technology, an OpenAI executive told reporters on Tuesday.

Council members, including leading AI rivals the United States and China, are also set to speak. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot will chair the meeting.

A European diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the main objective of the meeting was to shine a light ‌on the practical risks of AI losing control ⁠in ways that affect international security and the security of individual states.

"These are issues that fall squarely within the Security Council's mandate," the diplomat said. "The key question is whether we could one day face ⁠a situation where algorithms interacting with each other trigger a war. That is really at the heart of the issue."

Ahead of a meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday, the US and China have discussed setting up a notification system ​for ​common goals and common threats that would cover AI-related incidents that rise ​to a national security level.

TRUMP WANTS TO ENCOURAGE AI, ‌NOT REIN IT IN

Trump told world leaders at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday that he "rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control" AI, describing the technology as amazing, but noted that the US would be careful.

"We're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said. "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution."

"We're going to encourage it, not rein it in. We're going to watch it closely ‌through the Department of Justice," he said.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has warned that rapidly ​advancing artificial intelligence poses risks that cannot be ignored, putting him at odds ​with Trump.

Guterres has long pushed for global governance of ​AI and in 2023 created a 39-member advisory body for one year, with members including tech company ‌executives, government officials and academics from countries such as the ​US, Russia and Japan.

The 193-member ​UN General Assembly then created the Independent International Scientific Panel last year. Yoshua Bengio, a Canadian considered one of the "Godfathers of AI" and co-chair of the panel, will also brief the Security Council.

The Security Council met for the first time on ​the risks of AI in 2023, when China ‌said the technology should not become a "runaway horse" and the United States warned against its use to censor or ​repress people. Then-US Secretary of State Antony Blinken chaired a Security Council meeting on AI in 2024.

(Reporting by ​Michelle Nichols, John Irish and Courtney Rozen; Editing by Howard Goller)

articles.title: Europe’s Debate on Cooling Technology Is Heating Up
articles.description: Europe’s Debate on Cooling Technology Is Heating Up Internationale Politik Quarterly
articles.description_html: Europe’s Debate on Cooling Technology Is Heating Up  Internationale Politik Quarterly
articles.article_title: Europe’s Debate on Cooling Technology Is Heating Up
articles.heading: Europe’s Debate on Cooling Technology Is Heating Up
articles.summary: After another temperature record-breaking summer, the need for Europe to introduce air conditioning more widely has become obvious. Luckily, there is a solution with additional benefits.
articles.content:
The headlines have become eerily familiar by now: Come summer, and France breaks a temperature record; then Germany; then United Kingdom; then Spain.
As the world’s fastest warming continent, Europe remains profoundly unprepared for the extreme heat that lies ahead. The scorching sidewalks of Berlin, blistering bus rides of London, and torrid Metro trains of Paris exposed some of these vulnerabilities as infrastructure across the continent has, quite literally, buckled under this summer’s sweltering heat. However, the consequences of extreme temperatures extend well beyond damaged roads and disrupted trains. The scale of health impacts associated with this summer has demonstrated just how dangerous this new era will be.
To address the suffocating heat, air conditioning has emerged as an obvious intervention. Yet, across Europe the technology has become a proxy battle in a much larger climate-policy war. Nowhere is this more evident than in the public exchange between France’s far-right former presidential candidate Marine Le Pen and her hard-left opponent Jean-Luc Mélénchon. Le Pen’s Rassemblement National has adopted an expansive, but vague pro-AC stance. By contrast, Mélénchon, leader of La France Insoumise, has adopted a radically different posture toward the intervention, citing its environmental harm as the reason for his opposition.
It’s a good example of politicians engaging in the wrong debate. The question is not whether Europeans should cool their homes. They will. Instead, it should be what kind of cooling infrastructure needs to be built and whether Europe can use this transition to accelerate the realization of broader decarbonization goals.
The Heat Will Kill You First
Extreme heat is Europe's most lethal climate killer. In Germany, 14,000 heat-related deaths were registered this summer, while Spain and France recorded 7,300 and 4,500 excess deaths respectively. These staggering statistics reveal vast under preparedness across the continent. American environmental journalist Jeff Goodell’s predictions in his 2023 book The Heat Will Kill You First ring eerily true.
Casualties resulting from extreme heat can go far beyond just the impact of higher temperatures on health. For instance, increased aggression caused by soaring temperatures can lead to increases in fatal assault, as well as femicide—mortality incidences not currently captured in excess heat death statistics. Also obscured are the profound neo-natal consequences, with one study linking an additional 1° Celsius increase in temperature (above the 90 percentile) during the week preceding delivery to an increase of approximately four additional stillbirths per 10,000 births.
In addition to fostering violence, heat has also been shown to reduce cognitive functioning in young adults living in non-air-conditioned buildings—a concerning sign in an era of virtual work. There are also implications for those working in an office, suggesting that mild heat can impair team performance. Productivity losses are particularly pronounced in outdoor sectors, such as construction and agriculture, where exposure is prolonged, difficult to avoid, and extremely high risk for workers in the sector.
Most consequently, heat likely affects the long-term accumulation of human capital. Recent evidence has identified significant impacts on educational outcomes with children demonstrating lower learning, reading, pattern recognition, and memory outcomes, as well as even lower test scores on university entrance exams. These consequences can disadvantage already vulnerable children, as low-income families are less likely to have consistent cooling. The cumulative effects of prolonged heat exposure will not be fully realized until this generation of heat-exposed children have come of age.
A Climate Dilemma
While the impacts of heat on human wellbeing are impossible to ignore, there is still a significant cooling gap between the United States and Europe. The Europeans’ resistance to air conditioning sharply contrasts with the acceptance of the Americans, who have, for decades, normalized the presence of AC units in homes. Roughly 90 percent of Americans reported having AC, as compared to 23 percent of Europeans. The dearth in Europe is partly historical, but the climate that European infrastructure was originally built for no longer exists.
Air conditioning offers an obvious form of adaptation, but it also presents a climate dilemma. While AC protects people from rising temperatures, it can contribute to the very emissions that cause them. The true greenhouse gas emissions associated with an AC unit depend on many factors, including the unit type (room air conditioners versus central air conditioners), the product’s energy efficiency, the source of electricity (sustainable or carbon-intensive grid), and the product’s age. As such, AC has the potential to become a “maladaptive” solution in the green transition.
Given the urgency of the heat emergency in Europe, plug-in technologies that can be installed in residential and commercial buildings without significant infrastructure retrofits, tenant disturbances, or permitting processes are crucial. In key buildings, such as hospitals and schools, immediate interventions are necessary to protect those most at risk. Window-mounted or packaged terminal air conditioners—popular in the American HVAC model—are a natural champion in this sense, but their performance is limited and may present long-term barriers to Europe’s climate ambitions. Ultimately, this raises a question for European policymakers: What adaptation technology should governments promote to reduce heat-associated health risks whilst minimizing long-term climate harm?
Two Birds, One Stone
One technology that can simultaneously provide cooling relief and accelerate decarbonization objectives are heat pumps. Heat pumps in window-mounted or packaged terminal configurations are nearing commercial readiness in Europe and are capable of both cooling and heating interiors with higher efficiency than electric resistance heating systems in traditional HVAC designs. Heat pumps maintain interior temperatures by transferring heat from indoors-to-outdoors or vice versa. Heat transfer is inherently more efficient than heat generation via electric resistance, with conservative studies indicating heat pumps consume roughly 64 percent less electricity. Room heat pumps’ higher-efficiency cooling and heating services provide an opportunity to expand Europe’s cooling coverage while also contributing to the decarbonization of building heat.
What’s more, Europe is a frontrunner in heat pump installation, with 7.3 million heat pump units sold across the continent in 2025 alone. Norway is a national leader globally, with over 60 percent of the country’s households equipped with a heat pump, of which 93 percent are air-to-air models—the technology used in window-mounted and packaged terminal devices. Across the Nordics, air-to-air heat pumps account for 21 percent of primary heating in Finland and 11 percent in Sweden. France and Italy led European heat pump sales in 2025, with 528,000 and 423,000 units sold, adding to existing stocks of 7 million and 5 million, respectively. Air-to-air units account for roughly 50-80 percent of installation in southern Europe.
Heat pumps concede nothing on cooling performance while also delivering a low-carbon, highly efficient heating service. The technology’s twin functions provide solutions to Europe’s near-term cooling challenge while contributing to its long-term decarbonization agenda, including the EU’s 2040 fossil fuel boiler phase-out, all without complex retrofits or tenant disruptions. Incentivizing room heat pumps is the kind of efficiency climate policy that is urgently required at this moment.
Policymakers in Brussels have recognized this potential and introduced several incentive packages for heat pump adoption. At the EU level, the Electrification Action Plan targets 4 million heat pump installations per year by 2030, up from 2.4 million in 2025. The plan also calls on member states to bring household electricity-to-gas price ratios down to a maximum of 2.5, which directly impact the operating economics of heat pumps. Member states with the lowest ratios already record three times the heat pump sales of those above 3.0.
Additionally, the EU’s Energy Performance of Buildings Directive has barred member states from offering grants, preferential loans, or reduced tax rates for stand-alone fossil fuel boilers. The resulting policy environment prioritizes electrified heating (and with heat pumps, cooling) as the only subsidized path forward.
At a national level, support differs between heat pump technologies. Most programs were designed to replace fossil-fuel boilers, and therefore assume a machine connected to the building’s water circuit, which lack the installation simplicity of air-to-air room units. Italy provides the most favorable regime for air-to-air, extending both its Ecobonus and Conto Termico 3.0—worth up to 65 percent of system costs—to air-to-air units. France likewise recognizes reversible air-to-air systems under its Certificats d’Économies d’Énergie scheme.
In principle, the technology with the fastest deployment window and the lowest retrofit burden should receive the greatest support. However, significant policy variance at the national level must be addressed to facilitate wider adoption. For instance, Germany’s development bank provides up to 70 percent of costs or €21,000 per dwelling, but air-to-air units are only eligible if they serve as the primary heating system covering at least 65 percent of demand in addition to other performance characteristics. The Netherlands’ ISDE incentive excludes air-to-air systems entirely, as does the United Kingdom’s Boiler Upgrade Scheme.
An Opportunity
In response to the urgent push brought on by this summer’s heat, European policymakers have an opportunity to address an adaptation barrier and mitigation priority in tandem. Roughly three-quarters of European homes do not yet have air conditioning, but as temperatures rise to unbearable levels, that will change.
To prevent the emergence of a negative feedback loop from AC to emissions, to warming, policymakers need to capitalize on this window of opportunity before homes purchase their cooling technology. Strategic subsidies and targeted information campaigns on heat pumps can offer European consumers an alternative to traditional air conditioning, one that simultaneously delivers on long-term climate goals, including decarbonization, sustainable cooling, and the fossil-fuel boiler phase out.
It has become increasingly clear that cooling is not a luxury good, it is a necessary form of adaptation. As each successive summer smashes records, policymakers should support cooling technologies that can simultaneously address human health and climate needs.
Dan Helmeci co-writes IPQ’s Carbon Critical column and is a master’s student at Columbia University.
