articles.title: Prince William County Earns Two Commonwealth Technology Awards for Innovative Digital Services
articles.description: Prince William County Earns Two Commonwealth Technology Awards for Innovative Digital Services Prince William Living
articles.description_html: Prince William County Earns Two Commonwealth Technology Awards for Innovative Digital Services  Prince William Living
articles.article_title: Prince William County Earns Two Commonwealth Technology Awards for Innovative Digital Services
articles.heading: Prince William County Earns Two Commonwealth Technology Awards for Innovative Digital Services
articles.summary: Prince William County Earns Two Commonwealth Technology Awards for Innovative Digital Services
articles.content:
Provided by Prince William County Communications Office
The Virginia Information Technologies Agency, or VITA, recently recognized Prince William County with two Commonwealth Technology Awards that recognize outstanding public-sector, information technology programs and projects from across state and local governments in Virginia.
The county received the awards for its enhanced Prince William County Build-Out Analysis and its PWC 311 system during the annual Commonwealth of Virginia Innovative Technology Symposium. The symposium highlights innovative uses of technology that improve government services, efficiency and the customer experience.
In December 2025, the county’s Planning Office and Department of Information Technology developed the county’s enhanced Build-Out Analysis Dashboard, transforming what had previously been an annual PDF report providing a one-time snapshot of data into an interactive online tool that is updated throughout the year. The dashboard is an interactive Geographic Information Systems, or GIS, application that provides a transparent and accessible tool to track the county’s capacity for residential and non-residential development. The dashboard supports informed decision-making regarding infrastructure, housing and economic development. County employees from Planning and GIS/Information Technology developed the platform, which updates quarterly or whenever land development actions are approved. The dashboard gives users up-to-date information that includes interactive, embedded maps that can be explored and customized to an individual’s needs. Users can export data tables offline and download GIS data for independent evaluation.
The Build-Out Analysis Dashboard monitors user engagement and collects continuous public feedback to provide accurate data that is responsive to community needs. The platform’s analytics track visits and user interactions. Since its launch, the dashboard has averaged 2,782 monthly visits, demonstrating strong, sustained public interest in accurate data.
The county’s PWC 311 platform, launched in May 2025, allows residents to engage with the county anytime and in multiple ways, whether that be a chatbot, mobile app, online portal, email or call center. The PWC 311 mission is to provide a single, reliable platform that simplifies access to services, ensures transparency and promotes accountability.
The platform has proven successful as a one-stop hub for people to request services, report issues and get answers, with a total of 63,750 interactions since its launch and 20,018 issues handled by live agents. The Commonwealth Technology Award marks the third individual award PWC 311 has received in the past 12 months, following recognition from the LocalSmart Awards and the Virginia Association of Counties Achievement Awards.
To achieve results, PWC 311 delivers a centralized solution to connect residents with the right county department at the right time for a wide range of needs by linking them with the appropriate agency quickly and efficiently to reduce complexity and improve service delivery.
PWC 311 lets users submit requests in more than 35 categories that include, among other things, getting information and reporting trash, junk and debris concerns, exterior building maintenance issues, unpermitted home businesses, hazardous trees, abandoned or inoperable vehicles, concerns about active construction sites, water pollution or illegal dumping, illegal parking on grass or dirt, outdoor storage issues and streetlight inquiries.
PWC 311 also allows customers to see the status of their requests along with the date the request was received, addressed and resolved. Residents can also receive timely updates and monitor request progress.
“We are honored to receive these two Commonwealth Technology Awards in recognition of Prince William County’s continued commitment to innovation, transparency and exceptional public service,” said County Executive Chris Shorter. “The enhanced Build-Out Analysis Dashboard and PWC 311 exemplify how strategic investments in technology can strengthen informed decision-making, expand access to county services and enhance the experience of our residents and businesses. This recognition is a testament to the outstanding collaboration and expertise of our staff, whose work continues to advance the county’s vision for a more responsive and connected community.”
For more information about these platforms and other services, visit the Prince William County government website.

articles.title: Melania Trump says country entering ‘technological revolution,’ announces new Fostering the Future Together push
articles.description: Melania Trump says country entering ‘technological revolution,’ announces new Fostering the Future Together push The Hill
articles.description_html: Melania Trump says country entering ‘technological revolution,’ announces new Fostering the Future Together push  The Hill
articles.article_title: Melania Trump says country entering ‘technological revolution,’ announces new Fostering the Future Together push
articles.heading: Melania Trump says country entering ‘technological revolution,’ announces new Fostering the Future Together push
articles.summary: Melania Trump says the country is experiencing “an extraordinary moment in human history” at the “threshold of a technological revolution,” as she touted new events and part…
articles.content:
Melania Trump says the country is experiencing “an extraordinary moment in human history” at the “threshold of a technological revolution,” as she touted new events and partnerships as part of her Fostering the Future Together initiative.
“Fostering the Future Together is a global coalition with a unified mission: to empower children through technology and education,” the first lady said Tuesday in remarks in New York during the United Nations General Assembly. Representatives from countries including the U.K., Korea, the Philippines, Canada, Panama and Ukraine, and others were among those attending the event, according to the White House.
“Ideas once confined to science-fiction novels and films have become part of our everyday reality. What once seemed impossible is becoming ordinary,” Trump said.
“Artificial intelligence is transforming entire business sectors and it’s expanding how humanity accesses the largest corpus of information ever available to humanity,” she said.
“But access alone is not empowerment. We must give our children the tools — and teach them how to use those tools wisely,” she said.
Trump announced that she would host a Fostering the Future Together event at this December’s Group of 20 summit, scheduled to take place at President Trump’s golf resort near Miami.
The first lady also unveiled other gatherings tied to her education and technology-focused initiative, which she launched last year, including at the upcoming ASEAN conference in Manila hosted by Phillipines’ first lady Liza Araneta Marcos, as well as European and Caribbean regional conferences in the coming months hosted by Polish first lady Marta Nawrocka and Saint Kitts and Nevis first lady Diani Prince-Drew.
“To the leaders of these great nations: thank you for stepping forward to activate your regions. You will have my full support,” Trump said.
Trump also thanked several tech companies — including Amazon, Google, Adobe, Starlink, Intel and Zoom — who she said “have also stepped up to empower our children” through partnerships with Fostering the Future Together. Some of the support from the tech companies includes offering free AI-generated education tools for students and educators and expanding internet access, according to the State Department.
“Years from now, our children may not remember the meetings we held or the speeches we gave. But they will live with the consequences of what we do here,” Trump said, after noting 57 countries are now participating in her initiative.
“Let history say that at a moment of extraordinary possibility, leaders from around the world came together through Fostering the Future Together and chose to put children first,” she said.

articles.content:
In addition to MACo’s Summer and Winter Conferences, the Association holds several annual events focusing on specific topics within county service areas. The County Information Technology Conference is scheduled for October 22 and will feature deep-dive content revolving around county tech challenges and priorities.
All county and state elected officials and professionals are invited to register for this annual conference hosted by MACo’s IT Affiliate, focusing on technology issues and challenges unique to county government. Sessions will provide updates on public policy surrounding government IT and cybersecurity, as well as insights into AI usage and other best practices for public sector information technology, data protection, and resident safety. Cybersecurity and tech updates from experts at the State and Federal levels, along with a participant-driven open forum discussion will round out the event, connecting counties with perspectives and resources from all levels of government.
DATE: October 22, 2026
VENUE: Turf Valley (2700 Turf Valley Road, Ellicott City, MD 21042)
TOPICS COVERED:
- Emerging AI Tools
- Maryland IT Updates
- University of Maryland Cyberattack Research
- Federal IT Trends
REGISTRATION:
This event is only open to MACo Members ($95 each) and MD State Department Officials and Employees ($125).
- MACo Members = County Executives, Council Members, Commissioners, and county government professionals from Maryland’s 24 county jurisdictions (including Baltimore City).
- Commercial organizations may participate as exhibitors or sponsors – contact Regina at reginabz@mdcounties.org for more details.
- Municipal and nonprofit participants may be allowed to register if space remains after October 15 – contact Abbey at aduncan@mdcounties.org to be added to the waitlist.

If you need registration assistance, please contact Sofia at sofiapa@mdcounties.org.

articles.title: When AI disagrees, people change how they perceive the technology—not their original view | Newswise
articles.description: When AI disagrees, people change how they perceive the technology—not their original view | Newswise Newswise
articles.description_html: When AI disagrees, people change how they perceive the technology—not their original view | Newswise  Newswise
articles.article_title:
When AI disagrees, people change how they perceive the technology—not their original view
 | Newswise
articles.heading: When AI disagrees, people change how they perceive the technology—not their original view
articles.summary: When an AI chatbot agrees with our reasoning in resolving a social dilemma, we may become more confident in our opinions. But when the chatbot disagrees, we may simply dismiss the challenge rather than reconsider our views.
articles.content:
When an AI chatbot agrees with our reasoning in resolving a social dilemma, we may become more confident in our opinions. But when the chatbot disagrees, we may simply dismiss the challenge rather than reconsider our views.
That's according to new research from the University of Michigan examining how people respond when artificial intelligence weighs in on personal and interpersonal dilemmas.
The study, appearing in Computers in Human Behavior Reports, highlights a challenge for developers trying to reduce the tendency of chatbots to agree too readily with users.
The authors note that AI models are often designed to be agreeable, which can lead them to validate users' reasoning even when that reasoning may be flawed. They describe how this kind of confirmation can reinforce harmful ideas and distorted perceptions of reality.
"Developers have been working to make AI models more willing to disagree when necessary, but having an AI disagree with the user does not necessarily mean that people will reconsider their own views," said Atakan Atamer, the study's co-lead author and U-M psychology doctoral student. "Instead, they may simply discount the AI's response."
Putting AI advice to the test
Atamer and colleagues recruited 482 U.S. adults who considered one of three hypothetical interpersonal dilemmas with no objectively right or wrong answer. The scenarios involved conflicts between a partner and family, whether to forgive a cheating partner, and whether to express a preference that differed from that of a friend group.
After making their choice and rating how strongly they believed in it, participants received an AI response that either agreed with or challenged their reasoning. The researchers then measured participants' confidence in their choice and their perceptions of the AI, including its ability to understand emotions, human likeness, and whether they would use AI again for similar conversations.
Agreement reinforces confidence
When the chatbot agreed with their reasoning, participants became more confident in the choices they had already made. But when the chatbot challenged their reasoning, their confidence in their original views did not significantly decrease.
Participants who encountered disagreement were more likely to view AI as "machine-like" and less capable of understanding human emotions. They also expressed less interest in using AI for similar interpersonal conversations.
In other words, AI disagreement did not appear to prompt participants to substantially reconsider their original positions. Instead, it affected their perceptions of the technology.
A challenge for AI-human interaction
The authors argued that the findings have implications for the growing use of AI for personal advice. AI systems that consistently agree with users can reinforce existing beliefs and increase confidence without necessarily improving the quality of their reasoning. But simply making AI disagree more often may not solve the problem: Users may be less willing to engage with AI systems that challenge their views or may simply dismiss the counterarguments they provide.
"Our results suggest that people often prefer AI to reinforce their existing views and may discount its response when it disagrees, meaning that simply making AI more willing to challenge users may not be enough to prevent potentially harmful conversations with real-world consequences," said Olivia Pinto, co-lead author, U-M alumna and UX researcher.
As AI becomes more common in personal decision-making and advice, the researchers say that reducing excessive agreement may require more than simply teaching AI systems to push back. If users tend to embrace AI advice when it confirms their views but dismiss it when it challenges them, reducing AI sycophancy alone may not address the larger risks of relying on AI for personal guidance.
Study: From ally to algorithm: How disagreement shapes users' engagement with AI (DOI: 10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101252)

"Instead, they may simply discount the AI's response."

Putting AI advice to the test

Atamer and colleagues recruited 482 U.S. adults who considered one of three hypothetical interpersonal dilemmas with no objectively right or wrong answer. The scenarios involved conflicts between a partner and family, whether to forgive a cheating partner, and whether to express a preference that differed from that of a friend group.

After making their choice and rating how strongly they believed in it, participants received an AI response that either agreed with or challenged their reasoning. The researchers then measured participants' confidence in their choice and their perceptions of the AI, including its ability to understand emotions, human likeness, and whether they would use AI again for similar conversations.

Agreement reinforces confidence

When the chatbot agreed with their reasoning, participants became more confident in the choices they had already made. But when the chatbot challenged their reasoning, their confidence in their original views did not significantly decrease.

Participants who encountered disagreement were more likely to view AI as "machine-like" and less capable of understanding human emotions. They also expressed less interest in using AI for similar interpersonal conversations.

In other words, AI disagreement did not appear to prompt participants to substantially reconsider their original positions. Instead, it affected their perceptions of the technology.

A challenge for AI-human interaction

The authors argued that the findings have implications for the growing use of AI for personal advice. AI systems that consistently agree with users can reinforce existing beliefs and increase confidence without necessarily improving the quality of their reasoning. But simply making AI disagree more often may not solve the problem: Users may be less willing to engage with AI systems that challenge their views or may simply dismiss the counterarguments they provide.

"Our results suggest that people often prefer AI to reinforce their existing views and may discount its response when it disagrees, meaning that simply making AI more willing to challenge users may not be enough to prevent potentially harmful conversations with real-world consequences," said Olivia Pinto, co-lead author, U-M alumna and UX researcher.

As AI becomes more common in personal decision-making and advice, the researchers say that reducing excessive agreement may require more than simply teaching AI systems to push back. If users tend to embrace AI advice when it confirms their views but dismiss it when it challenges them, reducing AI sycophancy alone may not address the larger risks of relying on AI for personal guidance.

Study: From ally to algorithm: How disagreement shapes users' engagement with AI (DOI: 10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101252)

articles.summary: Salesforce offers a more attractive valuation and proven cash generation. ServiceNow offers faster growth and a more defensible market position.
articles.content:
- CRM -1.33%

- NOW -0.49%

As software giants race to integrate artificial intelligence into every corner of the enterprise, investors are debating whether Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) or ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) is the better long-term play for 2026.

Salesforce remains the dominant force in customer relationship management, while ServiceNow has carved out a massive niche by automating complex workflows across IT and human resources. Both companies are now leveraging generative AI to increase efficiency for their clients, making them essential components of the modern digital infrastructure.

The case for Salesforce

Salesforce is the world leader in cloud-based software that helps businesses manage their customer relationships. The company connects sales, service, marketing, and IT on a single platform, serving over 150,000 companies globally. Its current growth strategy focuses on the Agentforce 360 Platform, which uses autonomous agents to handle customer inquiries and streamline operations among various tech stocks today.

In its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, revenue reached nearly $41.5 billion. This represents an increase of roughly 9.6% compared with the prior fiscal year. The company also reported net income of approximately $7.5 billion, indicating a net margin of close to 18%. This growth reflects the ongoing shift toward digital transformation and the successful adoption of its new data management capabilities.

According to its January 2026 balance sheet, Salesforce maintains a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.3x. The debt-to-equity ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity, measuring how much a company relies on borrowed money. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term debts, is about 0.8x. Free cash flow reached nearly $14.4 billion, though stock-based compensation represented roughly 23.4% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation.

The case for ServiceNow

ServiceNow provides an AI-powered platform that connects data and workflows to automate enterprise work across departments like IT and HR. The company serves approximately 8,700 enterprise customers, with hundreds spending over $5 million annually. To drive its go-to-market efforts, ServiceNow maintains strategic partnerships with major industry players such as Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Accenture (NYSE:ACN), and Infosys (NYSE:INFY).

In its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, ServiceNow reported revenue of roughly $13.3 billion. This was an increase of approximately 20.9% year over year, showing strong momentum in the enterprise market. The company generated net income of close to $1.7 billion for the year, resulting in a net margin of approximately 13.2%.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company carries a debt-to-equity ratio of roughly 0.2x. Its current ratio is approximately 1.0x, indicating a solid balance between short-term assets and liabilities. Free cash flow for the year was nearly $4.6 billion.

Risk profile comparison

Salesforce faces intense competition in the enterprise application market from established cloud providers like Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) and Workday (NASDAQ:WDAY). Operational risks include potential security breaches or IT system compromises that could damage its reputation and lead to customer loss. Additionally, the rapid deployment of generative AI models carries risks of inaccuracies or reliability issues that could trigger regulatory scrutiny or litigation.

ServiceNow must navigate a competitive landscape where rivals like SAP (NYSE:SAP) may innovate quickly or bundle services to pressure pricing. The company faces integration risks related to its $7.75 billion acquisition of Armis, which could disrupt operations if not executed perfectly. Furthermore, its business with government entities involves complex procurement processes that can lead to unpredictable delays and increased costs for the company.

Valuation comparison

Salesforce appears significantly cheaper than ServiceNow based on both earnings and sales multiples, making it the more value-oriented choice for investors.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?

I'd go with ServiceNow. Its positioning as the governance layer for AI agents across IT, HR, and customer service puts it at the center of how large companies are deploying AI right now. That is a powerful place to be as AI spending accelerates. And the numbers look good: Its subscription revenue keeps growing at a strong double-digit rate and enterprises are signing larger and longer deals.

Salesforce deserves credit for its own strong execution. Agentforce has closed thousands of paid deals since launch, the AI and data cloud business more than doubled year over year, and operating cash flow is on track for a record year. For investors who value a proven, cash-generating software franchise, it is a solid choice.

But Salesforce is competing in a more crowded market and working harder to prove its AI tools can fend off a growing list of rivals. ServiceNow's workflow platform is so deeply embedded in enterprise operations that most companies would rather build around it than replace it. That stickiness is what impresses me as AI competition heats up.

When enterprises decide which platform will run their AI deployments, they are making a decision that is very hard to reverse. ServiceNow keeps winning that decision, and it's the kind of momentum worth owning for the long haul.

articles.article_title: Survey: Young Construction Workers Want Employers to Invest in Technology
articles.heading: Survey: Young Construction Workers Want Employers to Invest in Technology
articles.summary: A new survey suggests entry-level construction workers increasingly view technology as a tool for career development and knowledge sharing rather than a threat to their jobs.
articles.content:
Workforce Development
Survey: Young Construction Workers Want Employers to Invest in Technology
STACK research finds technology, training and knowledge sharing could play a role in retaining newer workers
A new survey suggests entry-level construction workers increasingly view technology as a tool for career development and knowledge sharing rather than a threat to their jobs.
Research released Sept. 22 by STACK Construction Technologies found 82% of entry-level construction professionals surveyed said they would be more likely to remain with an employer long term if the company invested in modern technology to capture and share workplace knowledge. The finding comes as contractors across the industry continue to contend with labor shortages, retiring experienced workers and challenges transferring institutional knowledge to newer employees.
The survey found 75% of respondents lacked formal training, while 34% said insufficient expertise in the field had contributed to project delays. Another 26% said those delays led to costly mistakes, and 21% said a lack of needed expertise could jeopardize long-term client trust. Younger construction professionals also reported a divide over artificial intelligence adoption. Fifty-one percent said they believe company leaders either view AI negatively or do not prioritize it, while 25% said younger workers are advocating for new tools but encounter resistance from more experienced decision-makers.
"The biggest misconception is that AI works in construction the same way it does in other industries," STACK CEO Viyas Sundaram said. "AI can't pour concrete or read a jobsite. Its real opportunity in construction is to capture institutional knowledge and make it accessible for the next generation of workers."
Technology also appears to factor into employer selection and retention. Among respondents ages 18 to 25, 90% said they would be more likely to remain with an employer that invests in technology. That figure was 77% among workers ages 26 to 35.
STACK commissioned Censuswide to conduct the online survey of 500 U.S. construction professionals ages 18 to 35 with three years or less of industry experience. Fieldwork was conducted Aug. 19-25, 2026.

articles.description: CMS Adds New Clinical Conditions to ACCESS Model to Expand Technology Enabled Chronic Care Management AHCA/NCAL
articles.description_html: CMS Adds New Clinical Conditions to ACCESS Model to Expand Technology Enabled Chronic Care Management  AHCA/NCAL
articles.article_title: CMS Adds New Clinical Conditions to ACCESS Model to Expand Technology Enabled Chronic Care Management
articles.heading: CMS Adds New Clinical Conditions to ACCESS Model to Expand Technology Enabled Chronic Care Management
articles.summary: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has announced several enhancements to the Advancing Chronic Care with Effective, Scalable Solutions Model.
articles.content:
Reimbursement; Skilled Nursing Facilities (SNF)


The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) has announced several enhancements to the Advancing Chronic Care with Effective, Scalable Solutions (ACCESS) Model.
Beginning April 1, 2027, CMS will add four new clinical tracks:
- Heart failure
- Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
- Substance use disorders; and
- Tobacco cessation.
CMS will also add a follow-on track that provides extended support for certain chronic musculoskeletal conditions beyond the initial 12-month care period. In addition, CMS plans to add more organizations through its rolling application process over the next ten years.
These updates broaden the reach of the ACCESS Model and may create additional opportunities for technology-enabled chronic care management for Medicare Fee-for-Service (FFS) beneficiaries. Long term care providers may find partnership opportunities with participating Medicare Part B providers and technology-enabled care organizations serving residents with these conditions.
For a full overview of the ACCESS Model, including eligibility requirements, payment methodology, clinical tracks and participation details, read our previous blog here.
CMS is currently accepting interest forms and has released a Request for Applications (RFA) with additional details. Rolling applications will continue through 2033.
Please reach out to AHCA’s Population Health Policy Analyst Rohini Achal or Nisha Hammel, Vice President, Reimbursement Policy & Population Health with any questions.

articles.title: Trump failing to block China’s access to American AI technology, say senior Senate Democrats
articles.description: Trump failing to block China’s access to American AI technology, say senior Senate Democrats The Hill
articles.description_html: Trump failing to block China’s access to American AI technology, say senior Senate Democrats  The Hill
articles.article_title: Trump failing to block China’s access to American AI technology, say senior Senate Democrats
articles.heading: Trump failing to block China’s access to American AI technology, say senior Senate Democrats
articles.summary: A group of Senate Democrats on Tuesday said President Trump is failing to block China from accessing sensitive American technology to accelerate its development of artificial intelligence, ahead of…
articles.content:
A group of Senate Democrats on Tuesday said President Trump is failing to block China from accessing sensitive American technology to accelerate its development of artificial intelligence, ahead of the Chinese leader’s state visit to Washington this week.
Trump must close loopholes that China has used to subvert U.S. export bans on sensitive American technology, the lawmakers wrote in a joint statement obtained exclusively by The Hill.
It was signed by Democrats with senior positions on the Senate panels for the armed services, foreign affairs, intelligence and banking.
“China is accelerating its drive for AI dominance by exploiting weaknesses in the administration’s export controls to access advanced chips and manufacturing equipment,” they wrote.
“President Trump must reverse course. He must end China’s access to the advanced chips and manufacturing equipment it needs to build dangerous AI systems.”
The signatories included Senate Minority Leader Chuck Shumer (D-N.Y.), Sens. Chris Coons (D-Del.), ranking member for Senate Defense appropriations; Patty Murray (D-Wash.), vice chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee; Jack Reed (D-R.I.), ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee; and Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.), vice chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), ranking member of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, and Andy Kim (D-N.J.), ranking member of the Subcommittee on National Security and International Trade and Finance, also signed the statement.
The lawmakers also pushed Trump to hold Xi to account for Chinese companies reportedly providing Iran with intelligence to target U.S. troops in the Middle East; confront Xi’s pressure campaign against Taiwan; and punish Beijing for its support to Russia in its war against Ukraine.
“We can’t let President Xi leave stronger than when he arrived. That is not diplomacy, it’s weakness,” the statement said.
The Democrats statement on AI echoes concerns also raised by Republican Rep. John Moolenaar (Mich.), who wrote to Trump last week urging greater U.S. scrutiny on export controls, and for him to block China the People’s Republic of China (PRC) from illegally accessing advanced AI products.
Moolenaar is the chairman of the House Select Committee on U.S. competition with China.
“The correct response is to slow down PRC AI development as much as possible by strengthening controls on advanced AI products, cutting off cloud services loopholes that allow PRC [People’s Republic of China] companies to easily dodge these restrictions, and most importantly, stopping exports of American and allied semiconductor manufacturing technology that the PRC needs for its plan to work,” Moolenaar wrote in the letter.
The chairman also issued a warning last month to the Trump administration to make sure chip manufacturers don’t send advanced logic chips to untrusted Chinese firms.
In November, Trump paused for one-year an expanded Commerce Department blacklist of companies prohibited from buying U.S. technology goods, including semiconductor manufacturing equipment, as part of a deal with China when he met Xi in South Korea.
The expanded blacklist included firms more than 50 percent owned by companies already sanctioned by the U.S., and largely targeting Chinese companies and subsidiary firms located in other countries.
Trump has also granted China permission to buy hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips, Nvidia’s H200, and small batches have reportedly started entering mainland China in August. Opponents of that deal say that the advantage it gives China in technology development is not worth the economic benefit to American companies.
Updated 3:07 p.m. EDT

Corteva has confirmed progress of the hybrid wheat technology platform used by Vylor, its advanced seed and genetics company that will spin off from the company on October 1.
Xpedite — the system used to create its proprietary hybrid wheat — will launch in late 2027, according to Corteva. It cited multi-year research trials that demonstrate and confirm the hybrid wheat’s “consistently strong yields as well as its yield stability, or resilience against a variety of adverse conditions including disease and drought.”
Vylor’s proprietary and non-GMO hybrid wheat is built on a first-of-its kind system, increasing yield potential by 10% while using the same amount of land and resources in the company’s trials. According to the company, the wheat is more resistant to drought, with hybrid wheat created using Xpedite yielding up to 20% higher than elite varieties in water-stressed environments.
As a product of conventional breeding, the hybrid wheat Vylor launch in North America does not require regulatory approval.
“Unlike other wheat hybridization systems that have been known for decades, Vylor’s proprietary technology has been shown in trials to work in 100% of wheat germplasm tested — enabling more rapid genetic gains and delivery of seed at a commercial scale,” Corteva noted.

The company expects its hybrid wheat technology will double the rate of annual genetic gain by 2040 when compared to conventional wheat.
Vylor’s hybrid wheat delivers grain meeting the same quality standards as varietal wheat and requires no special equipment or management, allowing farmers to maintain their current farming practices.
The company will launch Hard Red Winter wheat in 2027 in North America and expects to add Soft Red Winter in 2029 and Hard Red Spring in 2030 while also expanding to other regions around the world via the company’s branded business as well as through licensing and other partnerships, including acquisitions.
The company anticipates that hybrid wheat will accelerate the growth of its North America wheat portfolio, resulting in $500 million in revenue by 2035 and $1 billion by 2040, which includes licensing revenue, making wheat the third pillar of Vylor’s business, alongside corn and soybeans.

articles.title: I Gave My Life Over to Meta’s A.I. Agent and Was Blown Away
articles.description: I Gave My Life Over to Meta’s A.I. Agent and Was Blown Away The New York Times
articles.description_html: I Gave My Life Over to Meta’s A.I. Agent and Was Blown Away  The New York Times
articles.article_title: I Gave My Life Over to Meta’s A.I. Agent and Was Blown Away
articles.heading: I Gave My Life Over to Meta’s A.I. Agent and Was Blown Away
articles.summary: Muse, Meta’s A.I. agent, helped handle my dental insurance, booked dinner reservations and created a podcast for me. It also required my most personal data, and trust.
articles.content:
I Gave My Life Over to Meta’s A.I. Agent and Was Blown Away
Muse, Meta’s A.I. agent, helped handle my dental insurance, booked dinner reservations and created a podcast for me. It also required my most personal data, and trust.
Last week, I answered a call from an unknown number. “I reached Anthem Dental and am about to connect you,” a voice piped up.
The call was from an artificial intelligence “agent” created by Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram. Ten minutes earlier, the A.I. agent had called my dental insurer, given it my member ID, answered a security question and waited on hold before transferring me to the representative — just as I had asked it to.
I was surprised by how much easier the agent had made it to deal with insurance. It was one of many tasks that I accomplished with Muse, the A.I. agent app that Meta unveiled this month.
Muse is the first consumer A.I. agent from a major tech company that has become publicly available. The tech industry sees agents as the next frontier, far more capable than chatbots. Agents can roam the internet, sign in to websites, fill out spreadsheets and make phone calls on behalf of people — and that’s just the start.
To test Muse, I experimented with it nonstop for two weeks, giving over many aspects of my life to it. I had to trust Muse with my most personal data, which included connecting it to my bank accounts and email. Then I had it perform dozens of day-to-day tasks, including ordering my groceries, scheduling my meetings and setting my fantasy football lineups.

articles.title: CrowdStrike vs. Palantir Technologies: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
articles.description: CrowdStrike vs. Palantir Technologies: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? The Motley Fool

articles.article_title: CrowdStrike vs. Palantir Technologies: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? | The Motley Fool
articles.heading: CrowdStrike vs. Palantir Technologies: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
articles.summary: Palantir trades at a lower earnings multiple despite higher revenue valuation, while CrowdStrike battles reputational headwinds and profitability challenges.
articles.content:
As modern enterprises grapple with increasingly complex digital threats and data overload, choosing between CrowdStrike (CRWD -0.30%) and Palantir Technologies (PLTR +0.77%) has become a pivotal decision for growth-oriented investors.
While both companies utilize artificial intelligence to process massive amounts of information, they serve different primary functions. CrowdStrike focuses on securing the digital perimeter, whereas Palantir helps organizations integrate disparate data sources to make better operational decisions.
The case for CrowdStrike
CrowdStrike operates primarily through its Falcon platform, which provides cloud-based protection for endpoints, identities, and data. The company serves a diverse client base ranging from small businesses to global enterprises, offering modules for threat intelligence and managed security services. A significant part of its strategy involves deepening existing relationships, such as its recent partnership with Grant Thornton to standardize managed security on the Falcon platform.
In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, revenue reached nearly $4.8 billion, representing a growth of approximately 21.7% compared with the prior fiscal year. Despite this growth, the company reported a net loss of roughly $162.5 million for the period. This resulted in a net margin of negative 3.4%, which reflects the ongoing costs of scaling operations and investing in the competitive landscape for tech stocks.
As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.2x. This ratio measures how much a company uses debt to fund operations relative to shareholder equity, suggesting a conservative use of leverage. The current ratio, which tracks a company's ability to cover short-term liabilities with short-term assets, was 1.8x. Free cash flow, calculated as cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures, reached close to $1.3 billion. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 68% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
The case for Palantir Technologies
Palantir Technologies builds software platforms that enable organizations to integrate vast data sets for complex decision-making. The company generates revenue from both government and commercial clients, including a major contract with the U.S. Army for the Tactical Intelligence Targeting Access Node. It has also expanded its reach through sovereign AI initiatives in partnership with companies like Nvidia (NVDA +0.99%) and Fujitsu (FJTSF +3.57%).
In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, revenue reached approximately $4.5 billion, a significant increase of nearly 56.2% year over year. The company achieved a net income of roughly $1.6 billion during this period, producing a strong net margin of approximately 36.3%. This performance indicates that the company has successfully transitioned into a period of sustained profitability as its commercial customer base expands rapidly.
According to its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.0x, indicating the company carried no significant debt. The current ratio stood at 7.1x, suggesting a very high level of liquidity to meet short-term obligations. Free cash flow for the year was roughly $2.1 billion. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 32% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
CRWD & PLTR: Performance Comparison
Key Financial Metrics
Risk profile comparison
CrowdStrike faces risks related to operational and reputational damage resulting from the July 19 Incident, which has led to ongoing legal proceedings and securities litigation. The company also contends with an intense competitive landscape and pricing pressures from both legacy security vendors and cloud-native rivals. Furthermore, it relies heavily on third-party cloud infrastructure provided by Amazon (AMZN -1.27%), creating a dependency on external service availability and pricing.
Palantir Technologies carries risks associated with the concentration of its revenue among a limited number of large customers, particularly in its government segment. The company often deals with long and unpredictable sales cycles, which can lead to volatility in quarterly results. Additionally, Palantir relies on third-party cloud providers like Microsoft (MSFT -0.64%) and faces potential reputational or legal scrutiny related to its leadership and the specific nature of its client activities.
Valuation comparison
Palantir Technologies carries a higher valuation based on revenue but appears more affordable relative to future earnings estimates when compared with CrowdStrike.
| Metric | CrowdStrike | Palantir Technologies |
|---|---|---|
| Forward P/E | 189.5x | 111.4x |
| P/S ratio | 50.3x | 91.1x |
Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Given the explosive growth of AI and cloud computing, companies that protect and process large volumes of data are crucial -- and may be compelling investments. CrowdStrike and Palantir focus on different needs; one protects data while the other helps organizations use it. But which is the better investment for 2026?
CrowdStrike's Falcon platform is a leading cybersecurity ecosystem with a subscription model and strong customer retention. Its revenue grew by about 22% in fiscal 2026, but it remains unprofitable on a GAAP basis. It's still dealing with the fallout from the huge 2024 outage caused by a Falcon update, which disrupted air travel, healthcare, and finance until it was resolved. Still, after a sharp plunge, its stock has been resilient, and the company has drastically changed its update procedures.
Palantir is growing much faster than CrowdStrike. It has no traditional debt, and significant revenue comes from commercial clients as well as the U.S. Government. The U.S. Army uses its technology for applications ranging from battlefield intelligence to logistics. Its commercial clients include prominent companies. But its reliance on a relatively small number of customers creates concentration risk.
Based on its financial performance alone, Palantir is the stronger business, but its valuation leaves little room for disappointing results. I would choose CrowdStrike in this matchup because it offers a better balance between growth and demand relative to its valuation. However, investors should still consider whether the July 2024 incident will cause lasting damage.

articles.title: Reimagining FOIA’s Technology Infrastructure
articles.description: Reimagining FOIA’s Technology Infrastructure | Knight First Amendment Institute
articles.description_html: Reimagining FOIA’s Technology Infrastructure  | Knight First Amendment Institute
articles.article_title: Reimagining FOIA’s Technology Infrastructure
articles.heading: Reimagining FOIA’s Technology Infrastructure
articles.summary: Reimagining FOIA’s Technology Infrastructure | Knight First Amendment Institute
articles.content:
It is no secret that the federal government has never managed to achieve anything like full compliance with FOIA’s basic obligations to release non-exempt records upon request within twenty business days. Endemic delays, persistent over-withholding, and spates of agency policies that undermine compliance have plagued the history of the statutory right to government information. As it stands today, less than ten percent of requests result in the full release of responsive documents. From the perspective of requesters, FOIA has long been “broken.”
But it is not just requesters who register high levels of frustration. As the number of requests increases almost exponentially year over year and the volume of records created and maintained by agencies balloons, the resources agencies are given—both human and technological—perennially fall far short of what is needed. On one side, FOIA offices struggle to communicate with requesters effectively even when communication would be mutually beneficial. And on the other side, those same offices face barriers in securing the cooperation of agency program officials in other units to search for and produce responsive records. Agency officials cite the near impossibility of the task at hand, and having been set up to fail, FOIA compliance contributes to a public perception of government incompetence.
In an attempt to support agencies in their FOIA processing, tracking, referring, communicating, and more, private companies have long offered various purported solutions. The leading product, FOIAXpress, has been used by many agencies for more than two decades, but competitors have cropped up like NextRequest and Armedia. Without doubt, these private companies are innovating in the FOIA processing space, including by trying to integrate across non-FOIA staff and by harnessing the power of artificial intelligence. Still, though, private products are adopted piecemeal, agency-by-agency, and do not integrate across the government. Moreover, the nature of private products has exposed government to potential security breaches. And finally, these products are expensive and offer many add-ons and customization options, making even the very same products function differently across agencies. For requesters, this means that each agency still has a bespoke requesting process.
At times, both Congress and the administration have recognized the need for greater ownership and consistency of technology in a centralized location in government. In the FOIA Improvement Act of 2016, Congress required the Office of Management and Budget to “ensure the operation of a consolidated online request portal that allows a member of the public to submit a request for records… to any agency from a single website.”
While this had the promise of taking a step in the direction of improving FOIA infrastructure, the implementation has proven wholly inadequate. FOIA.gov, the government’s attempt at moving toward a FOIA portal, acts mainly as a redirect site; that is, it provides a centralized area to find a link to each agency’s request submissions process. It does not, itself, allow a single submission site.
This is not the first attempt that has gone awry. The EPA spearheaded an earlier effort, FOIAonline.gov, a portal system that allowed other agencies to opt in to using it for request submissions on a single site and was used by twenty-two agencies at its height. But after the EPA experienced high costs in maintaining the system, it was decommissioned and shut down entirely in 2023.
Even at their zenith, none of these efforts have been adequately ambitious to produce the kinds of gains that real technology infrastructure might offer. Other countries have vastly outpaced us in this regard, and their models are instructive in the possible efficiency gains of technology platforms that serve the administrative needs of FOI professionals and the public alike.
During the height of Mexico’s transparency regime, Mexico’s then-extant Information Commission created a National Transparency Platform, an integrated portal system that out-imagines anything we have tried. As a basic matter, it allowed requesters to make a request to any governmental body at any level of government from a single portal, or even to make a request to multiple agencies at once. It also allowed the requester to log in and see all past requests made, with deadlines for responses clearly indicated, as well as all subsequent communication and any eventually released records. The portal served as a repository for all released records which (absent individual privacy concerns) were also posted publicly for anyone to search and review. All records required to be made affirmatively available were likewise housed on the portal.
But where it really shone was on the backend. The portal served as the internal processing management system for government entities. Each agency unit that processed requests (the equivalent of a FOIA office) could see all the pending requests and deadlines, could refer the request internally to the program or component of the agency that was likely to have responsive records—each of which had a designated contact for handling FOI requests—and could set an internal deadline for that program to respond to the FOIA office. The contact point in the program office, likewise, had their own login that provided a list of all referred requests pending and allowed them to build the record on their end.
Finally, the National Transparency Portal also facilitated communication between the agencies and the information commission; once the agency response was registered, it allowed requesters, with the click of a button and a sentence-or-two explanation, to administratively appeal the response to the commission. The commission then had access to the full administrative record of what happened prior to the appeal and could receive additional documentation through the portal, as well as request additional information from the agencies. At base, therefore, the portal looked different to each actor who had a touchpoint on a request by virtue of their login. It clearly managed that individuals’ workflow and facilitated retention of a full record of what happened.
Mexico is far from the only country to have developed such a deceptively simple sounding system, but one that radically transforms the FOI space. Brazil, for example, has a very similar one-stop-shopping portal system for their FOI space, as do Paraguay and Norway.
The U.S. needs a true FOIA portal. A real portal would create the infrastructure that would facilitate the possibility of something akin to full compliance with FOIA obligations. It would supplant a piecemeal system with a system designed for this purpose, built in house, maintained by government computer engineers, and consistent across agencies. It would streamline the workflow inside agencies, make clear who has the responsibility for the request at each stage, and create priorities for work based on deadlines. It would provide the public with one-stop-shopping for government information and lower the barriers to use by ordinary citizens. And it could create efficiencies for agencies, which would no longer need to invest FOIA budgets in procurement of third-party products for FOIA solutions.
The most exciting part of a true portal, however, is the nearly endless list of possibilities beyond improving the current request-and-response compliance rate. For example, a portal could facilitate release-to-one-release-to-all, a widely celebrated concept that once a record is released under FOIA it should be available publicly for anyone to access. The DOJ has supported the idea in pilot version previously, but it never became a reality. Indeed, implementing a release-to-one-release-to-all system would obviate the need for FOIA’s current requirement that agencies release publicly any record requested three or more times, a requirement agencies have found extremely difficult to implement. In fact, much more broadly, a portal creates an opportunity for meaningful affirmative disclosure regimes in which records are searchable government-wide and agencies have checklists of disclosure obligations with which they must comply.
Exemption application could be improved through the use of a portal as well. For example, a portal could collect the body of past agency decisions—both at the initial and the administrative appeal level—as well as adjudicated case law in one place. It also would contain all previously released records—whether at the administrative level or in response to litigation—thereby making plain when information is already public on a particular topic and facilitating a determination that further release would not harm a protected interest. Easy access to more definitive answers on the application of exemptions or other matters under the law might improve agency compliance in future cases.
A portal might also be used to facilitate data analysis, auditing, and other programmatic evaluation of FOIA offices. Patterns of violations—whether delay, overwithholding, or failure to engage in affirmative disclosure—could benefit from systematic solutions, and a portal could be used to facilitate identification of areas ripe for improvement.
Even more broadly, a portal could facilitate many of the other types of FOIA reforms that have been considered within the FOIA community. For example, it might allow tracking the personal responsibility attached to FOIA violations to particular employees in a way that could sanction flagrant noncompliance. It could facilitate improved judicial review by creating a full administrative record for the court and permitting easier in camera review of records. It could link to declassification efforts by the National Declassification Center or be integrated as a tool hosted by the Archives into the NDC’s work. It could be integrated into artificial intelligence solutions; imagine, for example, an AI tool that combed through agency records and identified records that are likely of interest to the public and can be affirmatively disclosed. And it may hold the potential for many more uses we could tailor the portal to as it developed over time. FOIA needs a portal now.
Margaret Kwoka holds the Frank R. Strong Chair in Law at The Ohio State University Moritz College of Law.

Other countries have vastly outpaced us in this regard, and their models are instructive in the possible efficiency gains of technology platforms that serve the administrative needs of FOI professionals and the public alike.

During the height of Mexico’s transparency regime, Mexico’s then-extant Information Commission created a National Transparency Platform, an integrated portal system that out-imagines anything we have tried. As a basic matter, it allowed requesters to make a request to any governmental body at any level of government from a single portal, or even to make a request to multiple agencies at once. It also allowed the requester to log in and see all past requests made, with deadlines for responses clearly indicated, as well as all subsequent communication and any eventually released records. The portal served as a repository for all released records which (absent individual privacy concerns) were also posted publicly for anyone to search and review. All records required to be made affirmatively available were likewise housed on the portal.

But where it really shone was on the backend. The portal served as the internal processing management system for government entities. Each agency unit that processed requests (the equivalent of a FOIA office) could see all the pending requests and deadlines, could refer the request internally to the program or component of the agency that was likely to have responsive records—each of which had a designated contact for handling FOI requests—and could set an internal deadline for that program to respond to the FOIA office. The contact point in the program office, likewise, had their own login that provided a list of all referred requests pending and allowed them to build the record on their end.

Finally, the National Transparency Portal also facilitated communication between the agencies and the information commission; once the agency response was registered, it allowed requesters, with the click of a button and a sentence-or-two explanation, to administratively appeal the response to the commission. The commission then had access to the full administrative record of what happened prior to the appeal and could receive additional documentation through the portal, as well as request additional information from the agencies. At base, therefore, the portal looked different to each actor who had a touchpoint on a request by virtue of their login. It clearly managed that individuals’ workflow and facilitated retention of a full record of what happened.

Mexico is far from the only country to have developed such a deceptively simple sounding system, but one that radically transforms the FOI space. Brazil, for example, has a very similar one-stop-shopping portal system for their FOI space, as do Paraguay and Norway.

The U.S. needs a true FOIA portal. A real portal would create the infrastructure that would facilitate the possibility of something akin to full compliance with FOIA obligations. It would supplant a piecemeal system with a system designed for this purpose, built in house, maintained by government computer engineers, and consistent across agencies. It would streamline the workflow inside agencies, make clear who has the responsibility for the request at each stage, and create priorities for work based on deadlines. It would provide the public with one-stop-shopping for government information and lower the barriers to use by ordinary citizens. And it could create efficiencies for agencies, which would no longer need to invest FOIA budgets in procurement of third-party products for FOIA solutions.

The most exciting part of a true portal, however, is the nearly endless list of possibilities beyond improving the current request-and-response compliance rate. For example, a portal could facilitate release-to-one-release-to-all, a widely celebrated concept that once a record is released under FOIA it should be available publicly for anyone to access. The DOJ has supported the idea in pilot version previously, but it never became a reality. Indeed, implementing a release-to-one-release-to-all system would obviate the need for FOIA’s current requirement that agencies release publicly any record requested three or more times, a requirement agencies have found extremely difficult to implement. In fact, much more broadly, a portal creates an opportunity for meaningful affirmative disclosure regimes in which records are searchable government-wide and agencies have checklists of disclosure obligations with which they must comply.

Exemption application could be improved through the use of a portal as well. For example, a portal could collect the body of past agency decisions—both at the initial and the administrative appeal level—as well as adjudicated case law in one place. It also would contain all previously released records—whether at the administrative level or in response to litigation—thereby making plain when information is already public on a particular topic and facilitating a determination that further release would not harm a protected interest. Easy access to more definitive answers on the application of exemptions or other matters under the law might improve agency compliance in future cases.

A portal might also be used to facilitate data analysis, auditing, and other programmatic evaluation of FOIA offices. Patterns of violations—whether delay, overwithholding, or failure to engage in affirmative disclosure—could benefit from systematic solutions, and a portal could be used to facilitate identification of areas ripe for improvement.

Even more broadly, a portal could facilitate many of the other types of FOIA reforms that have been considered within the FOIA community. For example, it might allow tracking the personal responsibility attached to FOIA violations to particular employees in a way that could sanction flagrant noncompliance. It could facilitate improved judicial review by creating a full administrative record for the court and permitting easier in camera review of records. It could link to declassification efforts by the National Declassification Center or be integrated as a tool hosted by the Archives into the NDC’s work. It could be integrated into artificial intelligence solutions; imagine, for example, an AI tool that combed through agency records and identified records that are likely of interest to the public and can be affirmatively disclosed. And it may hold the potential for many more uses we could tailor the portal to as it developed over time. FOIA needs a portal now.

Margaret Kwoka holds the Frank R. Strong Chair in Law at The Ohio State University Moritz College of Law.

articles.article_title: Nucleus Research Releases 2026 Data Integration Technology Value Matrix
articles.heading: Nucleus Research Releases 2026 Data Integration Technology Value Matrix
articles.summary: /PRNewswire/ -- Over the past decade, data integration grew as a proxy of the data warehouse and lakehouse. Organizations stood up a warehouse or lakehouse,...
articles.content:
Leaders in the data integration market include Boomi, Matillion, Oracle, Qlik, and Salesforce (Informatica).
MIAMI, Sept. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Over the past decade, data integration grew as a proxy of the data warehouse and lakehouse. Organizations stood up a warehouse or lakehouse, and the ingestion, transformation, and orchestration spend followed. In 2026, data integration has become its own demand center. Development activity is booming, and AI-assisted coding is pushing out more applications and more agents than data teams can wire up. Every new application and AI agent leaves varied data integration requirements in its wake, and integration demand is rising sharply across the enterprise.
Customer demands have shifted accordingly. Now, integration is much less an optimized engine or tool, but rather a layer that serves everyone who builds pipelines, including analysts, engineers, developers, and AI agents. Customers increasingly favor managed data integration services and self-service stacks that combine ingestion and transformation tooling, and they are demanding consolidated solutions in the form of platforms that address the data layer from source to product.
"Data integration is no longer growing as a proxy of the warehouse," said Alexander Wurm, Principal Analyst at Nucleus Research. "Every new application and AI agent leaves integration requirements in its wake, and customers want one platform that handles the whole data layer from source to product. Vendors are responding with the fastest pace of innovation we have seen in this market in years."
Vendors have responded by reversing the unbundling that defined the market from 2019 to 2024. While ingestion and transformation engines still drive selection for certain use cases, platforms are increasingly winning on consolidated integration support that spans batch ingestion, change data capture (CDC), and streaming transformation. The deals completed over the past year illustrate the market direction. Fivetran has merged with dbt Labs, IBM has acquired both StreamSets and Confluent, Salesforce has completed its acquisition of Informatica, and Qlik has folded Talend into its cloud platform.
Customers have also set a new standard for usability. Flow-based user interfaces have increasingly become an experience to view and manage data flows rather than build them. Instead, users prefer building data flows with third-party coding agents and interacting with data integration services through dedicated command line interface (CLI) and Model Context Protocol (MCP) offerings. Desired usability finds a middle ground, allowing customers to build with frontier models and harnesses, iterate visually with flow-based interfaces, and scale activity with AI agent support.
Leaders in the Value Matrix excel in both functionality and usability, offering consolidated integration that delivers strong returns and supports adoption at scale. Leaders in this year's Value Matrix are Boomi, Matillion, Oracle, Qlik, and Salesforce (Informatica).
Experts offer deep, specialized integration functionality suited to complex and technical requirements. Experts in this year's Value Matrix are AWS, Fivetran (dbt Labs), Google, and IBM (Confluent).
Accelerators focus on usability and ease of deployment, delivering integration that enables quick adoption. This year's Accelerators are Airbyte, Coalesce, Microsoft, and SnapLogic.
Core Providers offer essential, reliable integration for organizations with focused needs. This year's Core Providers are Estuary, Etleap, Pentaho (Hitachi), Prophecy, and SAP.

Nucleus Research is the recognized global leader in ROI technology research. Using a case-based approach, we provide research streams and advisory services that allow vendors and end users to quantify and maximize the return from their technology investments. For more information, visit NucleusResearch.com or follow our latest updates on LinkedIn.

articles.description: Roanoke Wood Haven Technology Park being evaluated for data center, Authority says WDBJ7
articles.description_html: Roanoke Wood Haven Technology Park being evaluated for data center, Authority says  WDBJ7
articles.article_title: Roanoke Wood Haven Technology Park being evaluated for data center, Authority says
articles.heading: Roanoke Wood Haven Technology Park being evaluated for data center, Authority says
articles.summary: “WVRIFA and Clearview Dynamics are committed to being as transparent as possible.”
articles.content:
Roanoke Wood Haven Technology Park being evaluated for data center, Authority says
ROANOKE COUNTY, Va. (WDBJ) - Wood Haven Technology Park is being evaluated as a potential site for a data center facility, according to the Western Virginia Regional Industrial Facility Authority (WVRIFA) Tuesday.
The WVRIFA said on Sept. 22 the announcement follows direct outreach from Clearview Dynamics, which asked the authority to help ensure the community has accurate information about the project being considered.
Press Release:
Meeting the Commonwealth’s Standard
Governor Spanberger’s Executive Order 22 established new expectations for how data center projects engage with host communities, protect natural resources and deliver local benefit. This update, combined with Clearview Dynamics’ own commitment to being a responsible partner in this community, prompted confirmation now rather than later in the process.
“WVRIFA and Clearview Dynamics are committed to being as transparent as possible,” said John Hull, executive director of WVRIFA.
“At this stage, not every question has an answer, and that is precisely what due diligence is for. Both the buyer and seller have steps to take to work through the technical and environmental questions as well as development standards and community protections before the transaction may be finalized.”
Site Zoning
Wood Haven Technology Park’s Master Plan, approved by Roanoke County through zoning actions in 2018 and 2020, specifically accommodates advanced, large-scale industrial and high-tech enterprises. The approved zoning permits Industry Type I, select Industry Type II uses, Custom Manufacturing, General Office, Laboratories, Utility Services, and Accessory Uses. Data center use falls within these approved categories. The site’s zoning and master plan approval predate Clearview Dynamics’ interest in the property.
Project Status: Due Diligence
Clearview Dynamics is currently in the due diligence phase of evaluating Wood Haven, anticipated to run through March 2027. Due diligence is the standard pre-construction process any company undertakes before committing to a site purchase and typically includes:
- Engineering and geotechnical assessments of the land itself,
- Utility capacity studies, confirming the site can support the power and water needs of the facility, and
- Environmental reviews required under state and local law.
Water Source
WVRIFA confirmed with the Western Virginia Water Authority (WVWA) that the water source that would serve the Wood Haven site is the Spring Hollow Reservoir, one of the region’s water supply sources. Clearview Dynamics is committed to paying for all the water and water infrastructure that might be needed to serve this project, so the cost is not borne by the community. According to the WVWA, Spring Hollow is currently running at approximately 7.5 million gallons a day out of 18 million gallons available, well below capacity. Water Authority data also shows regional water use running below planning projections, and water production today is lower than it was 20 years ago, even as the region has grown.
Power
Specific power demand for this project is part of the ongoing due diligence evaluation. Clearview Dynamics is committed to paying for all the power and associated power infrastructure for this project, so the cost is not borne by the community.
