articles.content:
- MRVL +1.93%

- CL=F -0.93%

What Happened?

Shares of networking chips designer Marvell Technology (NASDAQ: MRVL) jumped 6.1% in the afternoon session after the company announced it will showcase industry-first 2nm optical interconnect demonstrations for artificial intelligence data center connectivity at the European Conference on Optical Communication 2026.

The highly anticipated product reveal coincided with a powerful sector-wide rally across artificial intelligence chipmakers, driven by converging macroeconomic and geopolitical tailwinds. Semiconductor stocks surged as positive bilateral talks between the U.S. and China helped mitigate investor concerns over potential export controls and international trade barriers. This diplomatic relief, paired with retreating crude oil prices and falling Treasury yields, revitalized broader market risk appetite and provided strong valuation support for capital-intensive hardware producers.

Riding this favorable macro environment, Marvell detailed its next-generation infrastructure showcase in Málaga, Spain, featuring 2nm 400G-per-lane optical PAM4, 800G ZR and ZR+ pluggables, 1.6T ZR technology, and a massive 102.4-terabit co-packaged optics platform designed to scale AI data centers. Adding to the bullish sentiment, Morgan Stanley analyst Joseph Moore raised his price target on Marvell Technology to $268 from $246 ahead of the company's upcoming October 6 Investor Day, explicitly citing the firm's lucrative scale-up connectivity opportunities and its expanding custom silicon partnership with Google.

The shares closed the day at $257.14, up 5.5% from the previous close.

Is now the time to buy Marvell Technology? Access our full analysis report here, it's free .

What Is The Market Telling Us

Marvell Technology's shares are extremely volatile and have had 62 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today's move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

The previous big move we wrote about was 4 days ago when the stock gained 5.4% on the news that Treasury yields retreated below 5% and oil prices declined, sparking a recovery across growth-oriented equities following the Federal Reserve's interest rate increase. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield dropped to 4.949%, alleviating pressure on borrowing costs and valuation multiples per CNBC. Technology and semiconductor stocks had faced sharp selling in the prior session after the Federal Reserve unanimously raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to a target range of 3.75% to 4.00%. Lower yields often provide a tailwind for technology companies, whose high-growth valuations are sensitive to the discount rates applied to projected earnings. Additionally, falling energy prices eased worries regarding persistent inflation, helping major stock indices rebound from their post-announcement declines.

Marvell Technology is up 187% since the beginning of the year, but at $256.26 per share, it is still trading 19% below its 52-week high of $316.43 from June 2026. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of Marvell Technology's shares 5 years ago would now be looking at an investment worth $4,199.

articles.content:
Update to Technology Use for K-2 Students
Summary: Seattle Public Schools is updating how technology is used in kindergarten through second grade classrooms beginning Jan. 4, 2027.
Update to Technology Use in Kindergarten Through Second Grade
Letter to Families
Dear K-2 Families,
Seattle Public Schools is updating how technology is used in kindergarten through second grade classrooms beginning Jan. 4, 2027.
As part of this shift, SPS will move away from the current 1:1 iPad model, in which each kindergarten through second grade student is assigned their own individual iPad for usage at school or home, and transition to a classroom-based approach to technology access in grades K-2. iPads will remain available at school, and teachers will use them intentionally when technology supports instruction, accessibility, assessment, or other approved learning activities.
Students in kindergarten through second grade will have limited daily technology use, generally ranging from 0 to 30 minutes as part of a balanced instructional day. This does not mean students will be required to use technology every day. Some days may include no iPad use when the learning goal is better supported through direct instruction, reading, writing, discussion, manipulatives, movement, or hands-on exploration.
Technology will continue to be one of many tools teachers use to support student learning. Our focus is to ensure technology complements, rather than replaces, the hands-on, social, language-rich, and interpersonal experiences that are especially important during the early elementary years.
District-adopted curriculum and instructional resources include technology components, and students will continue to engage with those tools when they are part of classroom learning. Teachers will use technology intentionally and in developmentally appropriate ways alongside direct instruction and other classroom experiences.
What is changing?
Beginning Jan. 4, 2027, K-2 students will no longer be assigned an individual iPad through the 1:1 device model. Instead, iPads will be shared and managed as classroom resources.
How much technology will students use?
Daily technology use will generally range from 0 to 30 minutes. The amount of time may vary based on the lesson and student needs, and technology will not be required every day.
Will students still use iPads?
Yes. iPads will remain available in classrooms for approved learning activities, assessments, accessibility supports, and other situations in which technology meaningfully supports instruction.
What will learning look like without individual devices?
Students will continue to learn through teacher-led instruction, reading, writing, discussion, small-group work, hands-on activities, manipulatives, movement, creative projects, and exploration. Technology will be used when it adds value to these experiences.
What about district-adopted curriculum?
Students will continue to use the technology components included in district-adopted curriculum and instructional resources when those tools are part of classroom learning.
What about students who need technology for accessibility or other supports?
Technology will remain available when needed for accessibility, assessment, approved instructional activities, or other student supports. Additional implementation guidance will be shared as details are finalized.
This change reflects our continued focus on providing developmentally appropriate learning experiences for our youngest students while ensuring technology remains available when it meaningfully supports learning. Additional details and family resources will be shared before the change takes effect.
If you have questions, please contact Seattle Public Schools using Let’s Talk.
Thank you for your continued support of our students and schools.
Sincerely,
Michael Starosky
Assistant Superintendent of Academics
Seattle Public Schools
Carlos Del Valle
Assistant Superintendent Tech Optimization
Seattle Public Schools
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
Beginning Jan. 4, 2027, Seattle Public Schools will move from a 1:1 iPad model to a classroom-based approach to technology access in kindergarten through second grade. Students will continue to have access to technology at school, but technology use will generally be limited to 0-30 minutes per day and used when it meaningfully supports learning.
Why is SPS making this change?
Seattle Public Schools is committed to providing developmentally appropriate learning experiences for young children. Research and instructional best practices emphasize the importance of balancing technology use with:
- Direct teacher instruction
- Reading and writing
- Small-group learning
- Discussion and conversation
- Play-based learning
- Hands-on exploration
- Movement and social interaction
The goal is for technology to complement learning, not replace these important experiences.
Does this mean students will use technology every day?
No. The 0-30 minute range is not a daily requirement. Some days may include no iPad use if the lesson is better supported through:
- Reading
- Writing
- Discussion
- Manipulatives
- Science exploration
- Art activities
- Movement
- Teacher-led instruction
Technology use will vary based on instructional goals.
What will students do instead of using individual devices?
Students will continue to engage in:
- Teacher-led instruction
- Reading and literacy activities
- Writing and storytelling
- Math lessons and manipulatives
- Science investigations
- Small-group and partner work
- Art and creative projects
- Movement activities
- Social-emotional learning
These experiences will remain the primary ways students learn in K-2 classrooms.
Will students still use district-adopted digital curriculum?
Yes. District-adopted curriculum and instructional resources include technology components, and students will continue to engage with those resources when they are part of classroom learning. Teachers will determine when technology supports the learning objectives of a lesson.
Will students still complete assessments using technology?
Some classroom, district, or state-required assessments may continue to use technology.
Additional assessment guidance will be provided as implementation plans are finalized.
Are changes planned for grades 3-12?
Currently, the announced changes apply to kindergarten through second grade only. If future recommendations affect other grade levels, SPS will communicate those changes separately.
How was this decision made?
The district considered:
- Research on child development
- Instructional best practices
- Feedback from educators
- Student learning needs
- The role of technology in early elementary classrooms
The focus is on creating balanced, engaging, and developmentally appropriate learning experiences for young learners.
Where can families learn more?
Additional information, implementation details, and family resources will be shared before Jan. 4, 2027.
Families will receive updates through:
- SPS communications
- School newsletters
- The SPS website
- Family engagement opportunities
Questions may be directed to:
Key Takeaways
- K-2 students will no longer be assigned individual iPads beginning Jan. 1, 2027.
- iPads will remain available as shared classroom resources.
- Technology use will generally range from 0-30 minutes per day.
- Students will continue to use technology for instruction, assessments, accessibility, and approved learning activities.
- Hands-on, teacher-led learning will remain the primary instructional approach in K-2 classrooms.
- Students with IEPs, 504 Plans, and assistive technology needs will continue to receive required supports and accommodations.

Students in kindergarten through second grade will have limited daily technology use, generally ranging from 0 to 30 minutes as part of a balanced instructional day. This does not mean students will be required to use technology every day. Some days may include no iPad use when the learning goal is better supported through direct instruction, reading, writing, discussion, manipulatives, movement, or hands-on exploration.

Technology will continue to be one of many tools teachers use to support student learning. Our focus is to ensure technology complements, rather than replaces, the hands-on, social, language-rich, and interpersonal experiences that are especially important during the early elementary years.

District-adopted curriculum and instructional resources include technology components, and students will continue to engage with those tools when they are part of classroom learning. Teachers will use technology intentionally and in developmentally appropriate ways alongside direct instruction and other classroom experiences.

What is changing?
Beginning Jan. 4, 2027, K-2 students will no longer be assigned an individual iPad through the 1:1 device model. Instead, iPads will be shared and managed as classroom resources. 

How much technology will students use?
Daily technology use will generally range from 0 to 30 minutes. The amount of time may vary based on the lesson and student needs, and technology will not be required every day. 

Will students still use iPads?
Yes. iPads will remain available in classrooms for approved learning activities, assessments, accessibility supports, and other situations in which technology meaningfully supports instruction. 

What will learning look like without individual devices?
Students will continue to learn through teacher-led instruction, reading, writing, discussion, small-group work, hands-on activities, manipulatives, movement, creative projects, and exploration. Technology will be used when it adds value to these experiences. 

What about district-adopted curriculum?
Students will continue to use the technology components included in district-adopted curriculum and instructional resources when those tools are part of classroom learning. 

What about students who need technology for accessibility or other supports?
Technology will remain available when needed for accessibility, assessment, approved instructional activities, or other student supports. Additional implementation guidance will be shared as details are finalized.

This change reflects our continued focus on providing developmentally appropriate learning experiences for our youngest students while ensuring technology remains available when it meaningfully supports learning. Additional details and family resources will be shared before the change takes effect.

If you have questions, please contact Seattle Public Schools using Let’s Talk.

Thank you for your continued support of our students and schools.

Sincerely,

Michael Starosky 
Assistant Superintendent of Academics 
Seattle Public Schools 

Carlos Del Valle 
Assistant Superintendent Tech Optimization 
Seattle Public Schools

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Beginning Jan. 4, 2027, Seattle Public Schools will move from a 1:1 iPad model to a classroom-based approach to technology access in kindergarten through second grade. Students will continue to have access to technology at school, but technology use will generally be limited to 0-30 minutes per day and used when it meaningfully supports learning.

Why is SPS making this change?

Seattle Public Schools is committed to providing developmentally appropriate learning experiences for young children. Research and instructional best practices emphasize the importance of balancing technology use with:

  • Direct teacher instruction
  • Reading and writing
  • Small-group learning
  • Discussion and conversation
  • Play-based learning
  • Hands-on exploration
  • Movement and social interaction

The goal is for technology to complement learning, not replace these important experiences.

Does this mean students will use technology every day?

No. The 0-30 minute range is not a daily requirement. Some days may include no iPad use if the lesson is better supported through:

  • Reading
  • Writing
  • Discussion
  • Manipulatives
  • Science exploration
  • Art activities
  • Movement
  • Teacher-led instruction

Technology use will vary based on instructional goals.

What will students do instead of using individual devices?

Students will continue to engage in:

  • Teacher-led instruction
  • Reading and literacy activities
  • Writing and storytelling
  • Math lessons and manipulatives
  • Science investigations
  • Small-group and partner work
  • Art and creative projects
  • Movement activities
  • Social-emotional learning

These experiences will remain the primary ways students learn in K-2 classrooms.

Will students still use district-adopted digital curriculum?

Yes. District-adopted curriculum and instructional resources include technology components, and students will continue to engage with those resources when they are part of classroom learning. Teachers will determine when technology supports the learning objectives of a lesson.

Will students still complete assessments using technology?

Some classroom, district, or state-required assessments may continue to use technology.

Additional assessment guidance will be provided as implementation plans are finalized.

Are changes planned for grades 3-12?

Currently, the announced changes apply to kindergarten through second grade only. If future recommendations affect other grade levels, SPS will communicate those changes separately.

How was this decision made?

The district considered:

  • Research on child development
  • Instructional best practices
  • Feedback from educators
  • Student learning needs
  • The role of technology in early elementary classrooms

The focus is on creating balanced, engaging, and developmentally appropriate learning experiences for young learners.

Where can families learn more?

Additional information, implementation details, and family resources will be shared before Jan. 4, 2027.

Families will receive updates through:

  • SPS communications
  • School newsletters
  • The SPS website
  • Family engagement opportunities

Questions may be directed to:

Key Takeaways

  • K-2 students will no longer be assigned individual iPads beginning Jan. 1, 2027.
  • iPads will remain available as shared classroom resources.
  • Technology use will generally range from 0-30 minutes per day.
  • Students will continue to use technology for instruction, assessments, accessibility, and approved learning activities.
  • Hands-on, teacher-led learning will remain the primary instructional approach in K-2 classrooms.
  • Students with IEPs, 504 Plans, and assistive technology needs will continue to receive required supports and accommodations.

articles.summary: Healthy Living and Technology Made Simple: Is AI a Friend or Foe? City of Aiken, SC (.gov)
articles.content:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
Healthy Living and Technology Made Simple: Is AI a Friend or Foe?
Thursday, October 22, 2026
9:00 a.m. – 12:00 p.m.
Aiken, SC – The City of Aiken Department of Parks, Recreation and Tourism, in conjunction with the Senior Commission, will host a free event, “Healthy Living and Technology Made Simple: Is AI a Friend or Foe?” on Thursday, October 22, 2026, at 9:00 a.m. at Lessie B. Price Senior & Youth Center, 841 Edgefield Avenue NW. The mission of the Senior Commission is to facilitate educational programming to advance the well-being of seniors (age 50 and above) in Aiken.
The program is free and designed to introduce older adults to the practical ways artificial intelligence (AI) can make everyday life easier, healthier, and more manageable—while also helping participants understand the potential risks of using this rapidly evolving technology. AI can save time, organize information, and provide helpful ideas; it can also make mistakes and should not be relied upon for critical decisions without verification. The Senior Commission hopes the program will leave participants feeling more confident, informed, and empowered to use technology rather than intimidated by it.
“Artificial intelligence is becoming part of our everyday lives, whether we realize it or not,” says Aimee Hanna, Chair of the Aiken Senior Commission. “Our goal is not to make everyone a technology expert. It is to show seniors how AI can be a useful tool for everyday situations while teaching them how to recognize when information may be inaccurate, misleading, or unsafe.”
The panelists and presenters include Mr. Cliff Etheridge, President of BIT Services; Ms. Alyce Frank, Director of Case Management at Aiken Regional Medical Center; and Ms. Paige Romanowski, health coach and founder of Bodyrite Training. Their presentations will emphasize practical, real-world examples relevant to older adults, covering topics such as Medical Information, Scam Prevention, Healthy Meal Planning, Exercise and Wellness, Effective Email and Letter Writing, and Travel Planning.
A variety of local businesses and organizations that serve our senior community are sponsoring and supporting the event.
Thank you to our sponsors: Family Pharmacy, Hospital Auxiliary of Aiken County, Holy Family Hospice and Palliative Care, Meals on Wheels, MDVIP, Nuclear Care Partners, Overflow Foundation, SC Hearing Associates, Sertoma International, Shadow Oaks Assisted Living, Shellhouse Funeral Home / Shellhouse-Rivers Funeral Home, and The Herlong Financial Group.
Register online at coa.page/pfaa or in person at Lessie B. Price Aiken Senior & Youth Center, Smith-Hazel Recreation Center, or Odell Weeks Activities Center. A light breakfast with coffee will be served to registered participants.
For more information, call 803-642-7600 and press 3. Stay up to date by following us on Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter (@aikenparksrec) or by downloading the Aiken Explorer app. For weather alerts, text AIKENRAINALERT to 91896
The City of Aiken Department of Parks, Recreation, and Tourism invites people of all ability levels to enjoy programs, parks, and facilities. Individuals needing special assistance to participate should notify PRT Administrative Office 48 hours in advance.

articles.title: Ottawa County unveils new technology giving real-time info to deputies during emergencies
articles.description: Ottawa County unveils new technology giving real-time info to deputies during emergencies wwmt.com
articles.description_html: Ottawa County unveils new technology giving real-time info to deputies during emergencies  wwmt.com
articles.article_title: Ottawa County unveils new technology giving real-time info to deputies during emergencies
articles.heading: Ottawa County unveils new technology giving real-time info to deputies during emergencies
articles.summary: The Ottawa County Sheriff’s Office is unveiling a new system, providing first responders with real-time information, no matter where or what the threat is.
articles.content:
Ottawa County unveils new technology giving real-time info to deputies during emergencies
HOLLAND, Mich. — The Ottawa County Sheriff’s Office is unveiling a new system that will provide first responders with real-time information, no matter where or what the threat is.
Known as ‘Project B.E.A.C.O.N.’ (Business, Education, Agriculture, & Community Operational Network), the initiative is designed to establish a Real-Time Information Center for first responders through the use of drones and live feeds.
“One of the things that responding deputies need more than anything is accurate information and details,” Ottawa County Sheriff Eric DeBoer said. “If we can get eyes on scene that much quicker before our deputies, it's just that many more lives that we could save.”
Over the last decade, the sheriff's office has responded to hundreds of water rescues. Each one is a race against the clock, and some end in a family’s worst nightmare.
“Nine years ago last week, we got the phone call no parent ever wants to receive,” Jon Marcus, a father, told News Channel 3.
Marcus’s son, Nate, died after being found unresponsive on a beach. Nate had graduated from college just four months earlier and was working part time for his uncle's boat business at the time.
“Nine years later, we still ask ourselves these questions,” Marcus said. “Could today's technology have directed the first responders to the scene more quickly, giving them a better chance to save our son?”
The sheriff’s office is now hoping to bridge that gap by bringing this new technology into law enforcement.
If there is an incident where the drone would be an asset, a button is pressed. The drone, capable of both thermal and optical video recordings, takes off automatically and heads toward the emergency.
“With any rescue, there's two parts. There's finding the victim, and then there's rescuing the victim,” DeBoer said. “This hastens that first process, and possibly even a second.”
In the case of a lost swimmer, the drone locates the person and drops a floatation device, all while streaming live video to first responders.
This technology has the ability to reduce the average response time of over 10 minutes down to two.
“Think about what those minutes could mean to someone struggling in the water,” Congresswoman Hillary Scholten said. “If we can use drones and other emerging technology to locate someone faster, get critical information to rescuers sooner, and help first responders make better decisions before they even arrive on the scene, it will make the difference between life and death.”
The network’s usefulness goes far beyond the beach, said DeBoer, spanning into farms and schools.
In the instance of a hazmat chemical spill, a drone will deploy within seconds to provide continuous high-definition and thermal overwatch, allowing hazmat specialists to assess chemical dispersion, verify vapor trails, and direct evacuation perimeters safely before first responders enter hazardous contamination zones.
“We have a lot of chemicals out there on a lot of our farms,” DeBoer said. “Anytime we can put a robot into something that might be hazardous instead of the deputy, I don't have to worry about having our deputies injured.”
In cases of an active threat at local schools, emergency dispatchers and analysts can immediately access permission-based, real-time camera feeds.
“In the event of an incident that occurred there, all the cameras that are in the system will pop up,” said DeBoer. “You'll hear dispatch being able to recount things firsthand as they happen. So our deputies have that information as they go.”
The scenarios mentioned above are just the beginning of how this technology could help, according to DeBoer, but before it ever comes into the community, funding must be secured.
The department has a current goal of $3 million for 10 years, and is actively seeking technology partnerships, corporate sponsorships, and grant collaborations to support capital equipment procurement, sensor integration, and operational sustainment for the center.
To contact the sheriff’s office, click here.

articles.title: News - From Lab to Launch — NPS Accelerates Technology Transition
articles.description: News - From Lab to Launch — NPS Accelerates Technology Transition DVIDS
articles.description_html: News - From Lab to Launch — NPS Accelerates Technology Transition  DVIDS
articles.article_title: From Lab to Launch — NPS Accelerates Technology Transition
articles.heading: From Lab to Launch — NPS Accelerates Technology Transition
articles.summary: Innovation at the Naval Postgraduate School (NPS) does not end when a research project is completed or a patent is awarded. Transforming an idea from a creative spark in the lab into a game-changing capability in the hands of a warfighter requires a seamless transition between academia, military and industry.
articles.content:
Innovation at the Naval Postgraduate School (NPS) does not end when a research project is completed or a patent is awarded. Transforming an idea from a creative spark in the lab into a game-changing capability in the hands of a warfighter requires a seamless transition between academia, military and industry.
NPS excels at this.
Through its Emerging Technology and Innovation Office (ETIO), part of the Office of Research and Innovation (ORI), NPS serves as a bridge between government research and private sector innovation, helping identify pathways for technologies developed by faculty and students to mature into products and services with military and commercial value.
By working closely with the institution’s Partnership Intermediary Agreement (PIA) organizations — including Fleetwerx, the Naval Postgraduate School Foundation and TechLink — NPS connects researchers with entrepreneurs, investors and companies interested in developing new capabilities.
This technology transfer is a critical component of the Department of the Navy innovation ecosystem. It enables federal laboratories and research institutions to collaborate with industry through agreements that allow for the exchange of expertise, testing opportunities and intellectual property.
"We engage with non-federal entities to promote technologies that have been developed at our labs,” said Agata Maslowska, NPS technology transfer lead. “The goal is to improve technologies that we developed, or evaluate commercial technologies that already exist, and determine how they can be scaled to meet military needs.”
ETIO facilitates several mechanisms that help bridge the gap between research and operational application. While Cooperative Research and Development Agreements, or CRADAs, provide a framework for the execution of research between NPS and non-federal entities, the institution has developed critical mechanisms with its PIA partners to ensure key innovations don’t just stay in the lab.
“Part of the question is, how do we actually get technology into the hands of the warfighter?” said Kaitie Penry, Director of Emerging Technology and Innovation within ORI. “There are several different pathways, and technology transfer helps enable that transition.”
One pathway involves licensing NPS-developed intellectual property to companies that can further develop, manufacture and ultimately deliver products back to government customers. In addition, with the help of its PIA partners, ETIO facilitates more direct engagement with potential partners who can help mature research into market-ready solutions.
To support that effort, NPS launched a series of “From Lab to Launch” Reverse Pitch events, the next of which is BlueTech Nexus, slated for Sept. 22 at Hopkins Marine Station in Monterey.
This reverse pitch event will convene strategic investors, maritime technology companies, defense integrators and Navy stakeholders to preview a select portfolio of NPS patented technologies available for licensing, with a focus on autonomy, AI, sensing and maritime systems.
BlueTech Nexus will also feature a new collaboration with California State University Monterey Bay (CSUMB). Students in a business-oriented commercialization course are helping transform technical research into market-focused presentations designed to resonate with investors and technology companies.
Unlike traditional pitch events where startups seek investment, NPS researchers present technologies directly to industry representatives, venture capital firms and prospective commercialization partners at these “From Lab to Launch” events.
And these efforts have proven successful. NPS’ first reverse pitch event back in 2025 resulted in one of the largest licensing returns in school history, demonstrating the value of connecting innovators directly with the commercial marketplace.
“The highlight was a piece of technology where the co-inventor was a student,” Penry said. “It really shows why NPS can make a difference when you have the warfighter in the room doing the research and developing the technology.”
That combination of student operational experience and faculty defense expertise remains one of NPS’ greatest strengths. Military students arrive on campus directly from operational assignments and bring firsthand knowledge of challenges confronting the fleet and joint force. Working alongside faculty researchers, they help develop practical solutions shaped by real-world requirements.
“Our students come from the fleet,” Maslowska said. “They know what is needed to improve operations, and their input is incredibly valuable.”
Many NPS inventions include student co-inventors, underscoring the institution's unique role in combining education, research and operational relevance.
“It reinforces the credibility of the research and education conducted here at NPS,” Penry said. “The more our technologies are wanted out in the community, the more it shows that what we are doing here has an impact on national security.”
One of the most significant recent opportunities for expanding technology transition has been the U.S. Department of War’s Defense Patent Holiday initiative. The program allows companies to obtain Commercial Evaluation Licenses (CELs) for no fee, giving them an opportunity to evaluate patented government technologies before committing to full licensing agreements.
The initiative lowers barriers for industry to explore federal innovations while creating new pathways for technology transition, commercialization and eventual fielding.
To date, 25 Defense Patent Holiday CELs have been executed across the military services, and 14 of them are from Navy organizations. Of those, impressively, 10 originate from NPS technologies. Those licenses represent companies across the defense, aerospace, space systems, communications, advanced technology and energy sectors.
While some defense laboratories have participated selectively, NPS embraced the initiative as an opportunity to increase visibility for its research portfolio and accelerate transition opportunities.
“It’s a lot of work, but it’s worth the investment,” Maslowska said. “We’ve already seen tremendous interest in our technologies.” That interest is reflected in the technologies attracting the greatest commercial attention.
The clear leader is NPS’ Mixed Reality technology portfolio, which has generated four executed CELs and another currently in process. Originally developed to support training and quality assurance applications, the technology is drawing interest for defense readiness, aviation flight training, workflow guidance, logistics operations, manufacturing training and human-machine teaming applications.
“What is fascinating is how many different applications companies see in the same technology,” Maslowska said. “There are so many different ways they want to utilize it.”
The second most sought-after technology is NPS’ Phase Change Composite thermal management technology, which currently has two executed CELs and two more pending. Potential applications include spacecraft thermal management, thermal energy storage, expeditionary power systems, off-grid energy generation, disaster response support and infrastructure temperature regulation.
Another emerging technology attracting significant attention is the Extended Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) Network, an artificial intelligence and machine learning capability developed at NPS. The technology has already generated one executed CEL and two additional licenses in process. Companies are exploring applications ranging from hyperspectral imagery analysis and automatic target recognition to anomaly detection, healthcare analytics, energy exploration and mining operations.
Taken together, current licensing activity indicates concentrated demand in four major areas: immersive training and mixed reality, thermal management and energy storage, artificial intelligence for sensing and analytics, and space and remote-sensing technologies.
The growing interest demonstrates the broader relevance of research conducted at NPS, where technologies designed to solve military challenges often possess significant commercial potential as well.
“NPS and other DON laboratories are vital for fostering innovation that can develop capabilities for military needs,” said Dr. Maddie Mettler, technology manager with TechLink. “To move those innovations to market, we need to bring industry partners to the table.”
“The tech transfer ecosystem empowers industry partners to harness the research investment DON labs like NPS have made to increase the speed at which technology can be delivered to the warfighter and adapted for civilian use,” she continued. “Events like BlueTech Nexus and new initiatives such as the Defense Patent Holiday are bringing technology transfer to the forefront in the DON.”
As NPS’ ETIO continues to create opportunities for the rapid transition of NPS-developed technologies, such as the upcoming BlueTech Nexus, the institution is expanding the network needed to transition promising technologies beyond the research stage. “The opportunity right now is to make those technologies matter,” Maslowska said. “To make them into something that both the U.S. economy and the warfighter can benefit from.”
By connecting military operators, faculty researchers, industry partners and investors, NPS is helping accelerate the innovation process and shorten the distance between discovery and deployment.
In doing so, the university is demonstrating that the true measure of innovation is not simply a patent on the wall, but a capability delivered to those who need it most.
NPS, located in Monterey, California, provides warfighting-focused graduate education, including classified studies and interdisciplinary research, to advance the operational effectiveness, technological leadership and warfighting advantage of the naval service. Established in 1909, NPS offers master’s, doctoral and distance-learning certificate programs to U.S. Department of War military and civilian students, as well as to international partners, to develop warfighters and leaders who can think critically, solve complex operational problems and deliver mission-ready solutions through advanced education and research.

articles.content_html:
Innovation at the Naval Postgraduate School (NPS) does not end when a research project is completed or a patent is awarded. Transforming an idea from a creative spark in the lab into a game-changing capability in the hands of a warfighter requires a seamless transition between academia, military and industry.

NPS excels at this.

Through its Emerging Technology and Innovation Office (ETIO), part of the Office of Research and Innovation (ORI), NPS serves as a bridge between government research and private sector innovation, helping identify pathways for technologies developed by faculty and students to mature into products and services with military and commercial value.

By working closely with the institution’s Partnership Intermediary Agreement (PIA) organizations — including Fleetwerx, the Naval Postgraduate School Foundation and TechLink — NPS connects researchers with entrepreneurs, investors and companies interested in developing new capabilities.

This technology transfer is a critical component of the Department of the Navy innovation ecosystem. It enables federal laboratories and research institutions to collaborate with industry through agreements that allow for the exchange of expertise, testing opportunities and intellectual property.

"We engage with non-federal entities to promote technologies that have been developed at our labs,” said Agata Maslowska, NPS technology transfer lead. “The goal is to improve technologies that we developed, or evaluate commercial technologies that already exist, and determine how they can be scaled to meet military needs.”

ETIO facilitates several mechanisms that help bridge the gap between research and operational application. While Cooperative Research and Development Agreements, or CRADAs, provide a framework for the execution of research between NPS and non-federal entities, the institution has developed critical mechanisms with its PIA partners to ensure key innovations don’t just stay in the lab.

“Part of the question is, how do we actually get technology into the hands of the warfighter?” said Kaitie Penry, Director of Emerging Technology and Innovation within ORI. “There are several different pathways, and technology transfer helps enable that transition.”

One pathway involves licensing NPS-developed intellectual property to companies that can further develop, manufacture and ultimately deliver products back to government customers. In addition, with the help of its PIA partners, ETIO facilitates more direct engagement with potential partners who can help mature research into market-ready solutions.

To support that effort, NPS launched a series of “From Lab to Launch” Reverse Pitch events, the next of which is BlueTech Nexus, slated for Sept. 22 at Hopkins Marine Station in Monterey.

This reverse pitch event will convene strategic investors, maritime technology companies, defense integrators and Navy stakeholders to preview a select portfolio of NPS patented technologies available for licensing, with a focus on autonomy, AI, sensing and maritime systems.

BlueTech Nexus will also feature a new collaboration with California State University Monterey Bay (CSUMB). Students in a business-oriented commercialization course are helping transform technical research into market-focused presentations designed to resonate with investors and technology companies.

Unlike traditional pitch events where startups seek investment, NPS researchers present technologies directly to industry representatives, venture capital firms and prospective commercialization partners at these “From Lab to Launch” events.

And these efforts have proven successful. NPS’ first reverse pitch event back in 2025 resulted in one of the largest licensing returns in school history, demonstrating the value of connecting innovators directly with the commercial marketplace.

“The highlight was a piece of technology where the co-inventor was a student,” Penry said. “It really shows why NPS can make a difference when you have the warfighter in the room doing the research and developing the technology.”

That combination of student operational experience and faculty defense expertise remains one of NPS’ greatest strengths. Military students arrive on campus directly from operational assignments and bring firsthand knowledge of challenges confronting the fleet and joint force. Working alongside faculty researchers, they help develop practical solutions shaped by real-world requirements.

“Our students come from the fleet,” Maslowska said. “They know what is needed to improve operations, and their input is incredibly valuable.”

Many NPS inventions include student co-inventors, underscoring the institution's unique role in combining education, research and operational relevance.

“It reinforces the credibility of the research and education conducted here at NPS,” Penry said. “The more our technologies are wanted out in the community, the more it shows that what we are doing here has an impact on national security.”

One of the most significant recent opportunities for expanding technology transition has been the U.S. Department of War’s Defense Patent Holiday initiative. The program allows companies to obtain Commercial Evaluation Licenses (CELs) for no fee, giving them an opportunity to evaluate patented government technologies before committing to full licensing agreements.

The initiative lowers barriers for industry to explore federal innovations while creating new pathways for technology transition, commercialization and eventual fielding.

To date, 25 Defense Patent Holiday CELs have been executed across the military services, and 14 of them are from Navy organizations. Of those, impressively, 10 originate from NPS technologies. Those licenses represent companies across the defense, aerospace, space systems, communications, advanced technology and energy sectors.

While some defense laboratories have participated selectively, NPS embraced the initiative as an opportunity to increase visibility for its research portfolio and accelerate transition opportunities.

“It’s a lot of work, but it’s worth the investment,” Maslowska said. “We’ve already seen tremendous interest in our technologies.” That interest is reflected in the technologies attracting the greatest commercial attention.

The clear leader is NPS’ Mixed Reality technology portfolio, which has generated four executed CELs and another currently in process. Originally developed to support training and quality assurance applications, the technology is drawing interest for defense readiness, aviation flight training, workflow guidance, logistics operations, manufacturing training and human-machine teaming applications.

“What is fascinating is how many different applications companies see in the same technology,” Maslowska said. “There are so many different ways they want to utilize it.”

The second most sought-after technology is NPS’ Phase Change Composite thermal management technology, which currently has two executed CELs and two more pending. Potential applications include spacecraft thermal management, thermal energy storage, expeditionary power systems, off-grid energy generation, disaster response support and infrastructure temperature regulation.

Another emerging technology attracting significant attention is the Extended Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) Network, an artificial intelligence and machine learning capability developed at NPS. The technology has already generated one executed CEL and two additional licenses in process. Companies are exploring applications ranging from hyperspectral imagery analysis and automatic target recognition to anomaly detection, healthcare analytics, energy exploration and mining operations.

Taken together, current licensing activity indicates concentrated demand in four major areas: immersive training and mixed reality, thermal management and energy storage, artificial intelligence for sensing and analytics, and space and remote-sensing technologies.

The growing interest demonstrates the broader relevance of research conducted at NPS, where technologies designed to solve military challenges often possess significant commercial potential as well.

“NPS and other DON laboratories are vital for fostering innovation that can develop capabilities for military needs,” said Dr. Maddie Mettler, technology manager with TechLink. “To move those innovations to market, we need to bring industry partners to the table.”

“The tech transfer ecosystem empowers industry partners to harness the research investment DON labs like NPS have made to increase the speed at which technology can be delivered to the warfighter and adapted for civilian use,” she continued. “Events like BlueTech Nexus and new initiatives such as the Defense Patent Holiday are bringing technology transfer to the forefront in the DON.”

As NPS’ ETIO continues to create opportunities for the rapid transition of NPS-developed technologies, such as the upcoming BlueTech Nexus, the institution is expanding the network needed to transition promising technologies beyond the research stage. “The opportunity right now is to make those technologies matter,” Maslowska said. “To make them into something that both the U.S. economy and the warfighter can benefit from.”

By connecting military operators, faculty researchers, industry partners and investors, NPS is helping accelerate the innovation process and shorten the distance between discovery and deployment.

In doing so, the university is demonstrating that the true measure of innovation is not simply a patent on the wall, but a capability delivered to those who need it most.

NPS, located in Monterey, California, provides warfighting-focused graduate education, including classified studies and interdisciplinary research, to advance the operational effectiveness, technological leadership and warfighting advantage of the naval service. Established in 1909, NPS offers master’s, doctoral and distance-learning certificate programs to U.S. Department of War military and civilian students, as well as to international partners, to develop warfighters and leaders who can think critically, solve complex operational problems and deliver mission-ready solutions through advanced education and research.

articles.title: Intel's CEO Just Gave Micron Technology Investors Great News
articles.description: Intel's CEO Just Gave Micron Technology Investors Great News The Motley Fool
articles.description_html: Intel's CEO Just Gave Micron Technology Investors Great News  The Motley Fool
articles.article_title: Intel's CEO Just Gave Micron Technology Investors Great News | The Motley Fool
articles.heading: Intel's CEO Just Gave Micron Technology Investors Great News
articles.summary: Memory prices could continue to rise next year.
articles.content:
Investors can sometimes get great news from unexpected places. While investors typically focus on a company's earnings reports and press releases when assessing a stock's potential, it's also worth paying close attention to what others in the industry are saying.
Micron Technology (MU +2.77%) is a great example of a company where it's arguably more important to determine what lies ahead amid the memory shortage than anything else; investors know the current results are going to be strong. The big question is: how long is the shortage going to drag on? Management will likely have a rosy forecast, but when others in the industry also have a promising outlook, that can be the confirmation investors need to remain bullish on the stock.
Last week, Micron investors received terrific news from Intel (INTC +12.14%) CEO Lip-Bu Tan, who expects the memory shortage to be even worse next year.
Image source: Getty Images.
Memory prices could continue rising
Many CEOs have been complaining about rising memory prices impacting their products. According to Tan, who says he correctly predicted this year's bottleneck, "next year is going to be even worse."
For Micron investors, this is great news, as it means prices may remain elevated and continue rising into next year. That's likely to result in stronger sales and earnings, potentially setting up an even stronger year for Micron in 2027.
Currently, the stock is trading at an incredibly low forward price-to-earnings multiple of less than seven. That's based on analyst expectations and hinges on the assumption that demand will remain insatiable and that Micron's profits will continue to soar. Many investors, however, have remained cautious because demand for memory and storage products has historically been cyclical, with the fear that if a slowdown comes, these types of stocks could crash.
NASDAQ: MU
Key Data Points
Is Micron's stock a slam-dunk buy right now?
News of the memory shortage potentially getting worse next year is great for Micron investors, but it also isn't exactly a new development. There have been reports that the memory shortage might span multiple years, and thus, this might not have a game-changing impact on the tech stock.
Micron's stock has soared more than 260% this year, yet its valuation still doesn't look expensive given how well the business has been performing. But while it has the potential to rise further due to strong earnings, investors should be careful not to buy and forget about Micron's stock, as things can change quickly in the tech sector. Despite its low valuation, this can still be a risky and volatile holding.

articles.heading: DXC Technology announces Americas market president
articles.summary: Ashburn-based DXC Technology named Jonathan Nikols president of the Americas, overseeing sales across North, Central and South America.
articles.content:
Nikols has more than 25 years of experience leading tech sales teams
Beth JoJack //September 21, 2026//
Fortune 500 global IT services and consulting company DXC Technology, based in Ashburn, announced Friday it’d appointed Jonathan Nikols as president of the Americas market.
In the role, Nikols will oversee sales across North America, Central America and South America. He will report to DXC Technology President Paul Taylor.
Rick Ruiz, who provided interim leadership for the Americas, will continue as senior leader of DXC’s U.S. public sector and Canada territories. He will report to Nikols.
“The Americas is central to DXC’s growth opportunity, and Jonathan brings the sales leadership, customer focus and operating discipline we need,” Taylor said in a statement. “His experience building large-scale technology sales organizations will help us improve execution, deepen customer relationships, strengthen pipeline management and help customers put AI to work to deliver measurable business outcomes.”
With more than a quarter-century of experience leading technology sales teams, Nikols most recently served as chief revenue officer at South Carolina-based Mobile Communications America, a provider of voice, data and security solutions. There, he was responsible for bookings across the company’s public safety and enterprise customer portfolio. Nikols also previously served as senior vice president of global enterprise sales at Verizon Business and held leadership positions at HP, Polycom and NCR.
Nikols, who earned a bachelor’s degree in business from Illinois State University, is a four-time Technology & Services Industry Association Star Award winner.
DXC has about 130,000 employees in 70 countries. It reported $12.64 billion in fiscal 2026 revenue, down 1.8% year-over-year.

articles.title: Pittsburgh has cataloged its surveillance technology. Experts say there's more work to do
articles.description: Pittsburgh has cataloged its surveillance technology. Experts say there's more work to do 90.5 WESA
articles.description_html: Pittsburgh has cataloged its surveillance technology. Experts say there's more work to do  90.5 WESA
articles.article_title: Pittsburgh has cataloged its surveillance technology. Experts say there's more work to do
articles.heading: Pittsburgh has cataloged its surveillance technology. Experts say there's more work to do
articles.summary: Councilors invited a panel of experts to speak following the release earlier this month of a report inventorying surveillance technologies used by the city.
articles.content:
Pittsburgh city government has plenty more to learn when it comes to regulating surveillance technology, according to a panel of national experts who testified before City Council on Monday.
Councilors invited the experts to speak following the release earlier this month of a report inventorying surveillance technologies used by the city. The report detailed tech from drones to automated red-light enforcement cameras to license plate readers and gunshot detection technology. It explained what each initiative is used for, by whom, and how much each initiative costs.
Experts at the meeting said the report was a good first step, but could go further in providing more info.
“I think gathering additional information about the type of data collected, how long it is stored, the conditions for access, and extending this to many Pittsburgh independent authorities who also have considerable infrastructure for surveillance would be a good next step in understanding the privacy and surveillance impact of technology in the city of Pittsburgh, and determining whether further restrictions are needed to ensure that these technologies are not misused or abused,” said Lorrie Cranor, a Carnegie Mellon University professor who focuses on tech privacy and security.
Councilor Deb Gross, who sponsored legislation calling for the report earlier this year, told WESA the city has “some catching up to do” when it comes to surveillance policy.
“We've been very busy policymaking, but this is a policy area I think that we haven't updated for a while,” Gross said.
“There are civil rights obligations, privacy obligations that the city really needs to ensure are protected,” she explained. “We need to really do a lot of learning to understand the technologies and also understand their impacts.”
Clarence Okoh, National Director of Civil Rights and Technology at the advocacy organization TechTonic Justice, described to Council a number of instances in which surveillance technology had crossed lines in other cities. He cited an incident last year in Maryland, in which police handcuffed a 16-year-old after an AI weapon detection system misidentified a bag of Doritos as a gun.
“AI-powered state surveillance represents one of the most urgent civil and human rights crises of our time,” he said. “The array of surveillance technologies held by local law enforcement and other public agencies often more closely resemble a military arsenal than tools of a democratic government.”
He encouraged legislators to be proactive in making policies about surveillance, and to consider creating an “AI Bill of Rights” to ensure people’s rights are protected before adopting new tech.
“Local governments must be more than passive consumers of powerful technologies,” he said. “You must take on the urgent task of defending our collective rights against mass surveillance, systemic discrimination, and automated inequality.”
Mike Siegel, a city councilor from Austin, TexasX, emphasized the importance of keeping an eye on surveillance policy. Austin cancelled its contracts with automated license plate reader companies Flock and Axon last year.
“These are definitely issues of national concern,” he said. “They're issues of constitutional rights, issues of fundamental liberty.”
He cited his city’s Transparent and Responsible Use of Surveillance Technology (TRUST) Act, which examines surveillance technology before it is acquired.
“The idea is that before any tool is acquired, whether it's purchased or received for free under some grant program, that there be a surveillance impact report that really gets into what this tool will use,” he said. “What type of data is collected? Where is the data held? What are the guardrails on access to that data?”
Councilor Erika Strassburger said she wanted to make sure that conversations about surveillance policy don’t impede all possible uses of the technology. She hopes to define appropriate versus inappropriate uses of surveillance in the future.
“That's what I really wanna try to get to in the future with this discussion, is the differentiation, but also the overarching framework for the way that we make decisions and the way that we can scaffold this decision-making for our various departments in government, so that we're not inadvertently signing up for something that we're not intending to,” she said.
Gross said she wants to ensure current pressing issues of AI, data centers, and surveillance technology are talked about in the same conversation. She says she and other members of council have received questions from constituents on all three topics.
She looks forward to gathering further information on city surveillance technologies, and examining what other cities have done on surveillance regulation.
“We always look at our kind of benchmark cities and other cities that are leading the way, and then we have to kind of take their legislation and see what is applicable or allowable under Pennsylvania statute or under our specific Class 2 powers,” she said. “So that's the work in front of us.”
City Council plans to schedule a public hearing in the coming weeks to discuss the surveillance technology inventory and allow residents to weigh in on uses of the technology.

articles.summary: Marvell Takes Aim at AI Data Centers With New 2nm Optical Technology
articles.content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.
Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL) shares gained 4% Monday after the chipmaker detailed a set of 2-nanometer optical connectivity demonstrations aimed at AI data centers.
The company plans to present the technology during ECOC 2026, a major European optical communications conference. The demonstrations cover several configurations designed for higher-speed links inside and between data center facilities.
- Warning! GuruFocus has detected 3 Warning Sign with MRVL.
- Is MRVL fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.
Marvell will show 400G-per-lane optical PAM4 using its 2nm process, along with an 800G ZR/ZR+ pluggable solution that includes MACsec security. PAM4 is an optical signaling method used to transmit more data through each lane.
The portfolio also includes demonstrations of 1.6T ZR and O-band coherent-lite technology. Marvell said the solutions are intended to support the increasing bandwidth requirements of AI infrastructure.
The company's ECOC lineup comes as data center operators seek faster optical connections while managing power consumption and network security. The technologies will be displayed at the event in Malaga, Spain, which runs through Sept. 24. The demonstrations reflect Marvell's focus on optical components as AI workloads place additional demands on data center networking capacity, speed and efficiency.

articles.description: Search Launches for Permanent Chief Information Officer Dartmouth

articles.article_title: Search Launches for Permanent Chief Information Officer | Dartmouth
articles.heading: Search Launches for Permanent Chief Information Officer | Dartmouth
articles.summary: Search Launches for Permanent Chief Information Officer Dartmouth
articles.content:
Dartmouth has launched a search for the next vice president and chief information officer to lead Information, Technology and Consulting.
The CIO will oversee enterprise technology, cybersecurity, research computing, enterprise systems, and business transformation while providing strategic guidance on technology governance, resource allocation, operational resilience, and emerging technologies.
ITC serves as Dartmouth’s central home for enterprise technology, infrastructure, and digital services across campus. The CIO’s leadership is particularly instrumental in providing vision, direction, and management for ITC, working in close partnership with academic and administrative units, faculty, and the broader Dartmouth community to advance the institution’s technology strategy and support its teaching, research, and operational needs.
“As we begin the search for our next vice president and chief information officer, we are eager to hear your perspectives on the qualities, priorities, and opportunities that should guide this important appointment,” said Provost Santiago Schnell, who invites members of the Dartmouth community to provide their input by Sept. 30 on what factors should guide the appointment.
Thomas DeChiaro, who has been serving as interim CIO since May 2025, will continue serving in that role until the position is filled.
The search committee will be chaired by Erin DeSilva, senior associate provost for learning innovation. In addition to DeSilva, the committee includes:
- Libby Barlow, senior associate provost for institutional research and effectiveness
- Daniel Chamberlain, associate dean of libraries, research and digital strategies
- Zoya Chhabra, chief of staff to the president
- Scott Frew, chief financial officer
- Nick Jacobson, associate professor of biomedical data science and psychiatry, Geisel School of Medicine

ITC serves as Dartmouth’s central home for enterprise technology, infrastructure, and digital services across campus. Thomas DeChiaro, who has been serving as interim CIO since May 2025, will continue serving in that role until the position is filled.

articles.description_html: Teaching and Learning with Technology Impact Award seeks 2027 nominees  The Pennsylvania State University
articles.article_title: Teaching and Learning with Technology Impact Award seeks 2027 nominees | Penn State University
articles.heading: Teaching and Learning with Technology Impact Award seeks 2027 nominees
articles.summary: Teaching and Learning with Technology supports and celebrates Penn State technology-forward faculty with the 2027 Impact Award, now in its 10th year and with an increased monetary prize. Nominations for the award are now being accepted.
articles.content:
UNIVERSITY PARK, Pa. — Teaching and Learning with Technology, part of Penn State University Libraries, supports and celebrates Penn State technology-forward faculty with the 2027 Teaching and Learning with Technology Impact Award, now in its 10th year and with an increased monetary prize. Nominations for the award are now being accepted.
Given annually, the award celebrates the accomplishments of a faculty member whose work transforms education through the use of technology, over an extended period of time, and influences more than one specific academic area. The award seeks to recognize an individual Penn State faculty member who has a demonstrated history of developing projects, courses, collaborations or scholarship with innovative educational or instructional technology. Of particular interest are projects that have the potential to significantly improve teaching, learning and scholarship at Penn State and beyond.
Nominations for the 2027 Teaching and Learning with Technology Impact Award are open through Friday, Oct. 16. All full-time Penn State faculty — tenure track or non-tenure track, term or no term and teaching faculty — are eligible for nomination. University faculty, staff and students should submit award nominations. Self-nominations also are welcome and encouraged. The Teaching and Learning with Technology Impact Award is a recognized undergraduate teaching award and includes a $5,000 cash award, a commemorative medal and additional support to increase the reach and impact of the recipient’s work.
Lee Ahern, an associate professor of advertising/public relations in the Donald P. Bellisario College of Communications, is the recipient of the 2026 Teaching and Learning with Technology Impact Award.
More information and prior years’ recipients can be viewed on the Teaching and Learning with Technology Impact Award’s webpage. Questions about the award or process may be directed to tltaward@psu.edu.

articles.title: Opinion: Can you turn it off? The new test of tech sovereignty
articles.description: Opinion: Can you turn it off? The new test of tech sovereignty Fierce Network
articles.description_html: Opinion: Can you turn it off? The new test of tech sovereignty  Fierce Network
articles.article_title: Opinion: Can you turn it off? The new test of tech sovereignty
articles.heading: Opinion: Can you turn it off? The new test of tech sovereignty
articles.summary: FNTV’s Sovereignty Spectrum assesses whether technology suppliers give customers meaningful control ov | FNTV's Stephen Saunders argues that tech sovereignty comes down to whether customers can keep operating without their supplier, and ranks vendors from Red Hat to Palantir on how well they pass that test.
articles.content:
- FNTV’s Sovereignty Spectrum assesses whether technology suppliers give customers meaningful control over their critical infrastructure, data and operational systems
- Sovereignty is about control, not just data location
- The real test is whether customers can operate independently
Technology lock-in is hardly new. IBM built powerful proprietary ecosystems half a century ago. Escaping could mean replacing hardware, rewriting applications and retraining workforces. But the principal penalty was economic.
Today’s most important tech platforms occupy an entirely different position. They hold data, identities and encryption keys. They enforce policy, interpret events, coordinate infrastructure and increasingly use AI to recommend or initiate decisions. They are becoming the operational nervous system through which an institution perceives, decides, acts — and ultimately succeeds or fails.

That makes sovereignty more than vendor lock-in.


If replacing a supplier costs $100 million, you have a commercial dependency. If a supplier, foreign government, sanction, license withdrawal or political decision can materially impair your ability to operate, you have a sovereignty problem. An organization can own its data and still lose meaningful control of the systems that interpret it and determine what happens next.
This is what I mean by Operational Sovereignty: meaningful control over increasingly autonomous systems. In a recent conversation, Versa Networks CEO Kelly Ahuja captured why data residency alone is not enough: “Maybe the data plane is ... localized, but the control and management or operations may not be.”
To help carriers, enterprises and industries understand their sovereignty dependency/independency, FNTV has developed the Sovereignty Spectrum (see figure). It measures customer authority, substitutability, portability, survivability and decision independence. Paradoxically, the better the product, the deeper the dependency: customers build more of themselves around it. That requires either exceptional trust in the provider — or a meticulously designed exit strategy.

When the supplier has a worldview
There is another factor in the sovereignty calculation: institutional alignment.
Most technology companies lobby governments. That does not necessarily make them politically aligned. Nokia states in its Code of Conduct that it is “independent of any political affiliations” and does not participate in the political or electoral process through donations to political groups, while still advocating its interests with governments.
Ericsson similarly embeds this principle in its Code of Business Ethics and Group Policy on Government and Policy Advocacy, stating that it does not contribute directly or indirectly to political parties or individual politicians, while permitting transparent policy advocacy.
In other words, political non-alignment is not merely a posture for these companies; it is embedded in their formal corporate governance.
These companies have commercial interests and policy positions, but they are primarily infrastructure suppliers, rather than ideological actors.
Palantir is different by its own description. Its 2025 annual report says it generally will not work with customers or governments whose positions conflict with its mission to support “Western liberal democracy [sic] and its strategic allies.” That is an explicit corporate worldview.
Palantir’s influence also extends beyond its own platform: it has formal partnerships with several companies elsewhere on the spectrum, including Oracle, Microsoft, Google, AWS, Snowflake, SAP and Cisco, allowing its decision and AI layer to become embedded across a much broader technology stack.
Oracle also warrants closer scrutiny than a conventional “neutral vendor” label. Its support for Israel goes beyond public statements. Oracle donated about $2 million in military equipment to elite IDF units operating in Gaza, including telescopic sights and protective equipment. Safra Catz also said the company had provided technology to Israel’s war effort that she described as “really profoundly scary.” Larry Ellison’s position is similarly explicit: in 2017 he donated $16.6 million to Friends of the Israel Defense Forces, then the largest single gift in the organization’s history. Taken together, Oracle’s political alignment is expressed through rhetoric, material support and technological support.
With companies like Palantir and Oracle, political neutrality cannot simply be assumed. When a vendor controls databases, identity, security, cloud infrastructure, workflow or AI decision systems, the customer has to ask what happens if the supplier’s strategic or political interests diverge from its own.
The Sovereignty Spectrum
The spectrum is not a product-quality ranking. Companies within each band are alphabetical and are not individually ranked.

Ties that bind
Level 1 — Sovereignty benchmark: Red Hat
Red Hat remains the benchmark because open-source foundations, portable skills and broad deployment choice provide unusually strong credible exit.
Level 2 — European control and high-assurance operations: OVHcloud · Thales
OVHcloud and Thales combine European control with regional or high-assurance operations, although customers still consume provider-operated or partner-dependent technology.
Level 3 — Operator-controlled infrastructure: Ericsson · Nokia
Ericsson and Nokia sit relatively high because operators can run their standards-based infrastructure locally for decades. Much of the underlying technology is built around open industry standards, but the vendors’ own software, management systems and integrated platforms remain proprietary. Switching is expensive, yet customers generally retain operational authority — and the trust between operator and supplier is often built over decades.
Level 4 — Local control over hyperscaler technology: T-Systems
T-Systems can add a locally accountable control layer over hyperscaler technology.
Level 5 — Customer-operated, open and multivendor: Arista · HPE · Juniper
Arista, HPE and Juniper preserve considerable customer operation and interoperability.
Level 6 — Strong control, deeper platform dependence: Broadcom/VMware · Cisco · Nutanix · Palo Alto Networks
Broadcom/VMware, Cisco, Nutanix and Palo Alto Networks provide strong customer control but can create deeper platform dependence as management, virtualization and security become control planes.

Level 7 — Local operation with geopolitical or institutional exposure: Huawei · Orange Business · SAP
Huawei can provide a highly complete locally operated stack, while creating political, legal or supply-chain exposure in some jurisdictions. Orange Business and SAP can support local control, although SAP shows how dependency becomes institutional when software is embedded in core business processes. Orange’s Philippe Ensarguet, VP cloud and software engineering and Orange Fellow, described the cumulative danger of adding specialist dependencies bluntly: “Every time we onboard a new partner ... basically we are digging the hole in which we will fall.”
Level 8 — Narrower proprietary control planes: Cloudflare · Lumen
Cloudflare and Lumen occupy narrower control planes than hyperscalers, limiting the potential blast radius of dependence while remaining proprietary platforms.
Level 9 — Open formats and cross-cloud deployment: Databricks
Databricks benefits from open formats and cross-cloud deployment, improving portability even though its higher-level services remain proprietary.
Level 10 — Proprietary global cloud platforms: AWS · Google · Microsoft*
AWS, Google and Microsoft have invested heavily in sovereign-cloud controls, but customers still depend on proprietary global platforms, whose development and many essential operational mechanisms remain outside customer control. Increasingly close ties to Palantir amplify concerns.
Level 11 — Cross-cloud reach with data gravity: Snowflake*
Snowflake improves cloud and location choice while retaining substantial data gravity and switching friction.
Level 12 — Deep institutional platform dependence: Oracle* · ServiceNow
Oracle offers strong dedicated and isolated deployment options, but its databases, applications and cloud services can span several institutional layers. ServiceNow can become embedded in the workflows through which institutions operate, making exit a reconstruction of processes rather than a simple software migration.

Level 13 — Institutional decision dependence: Palantir
Palantir is on the lowest rung because its technology sits at the point where data becomes perception, decision and action. That is why continuity is the ultimate sovereignty test. As European Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen put it: “We have to be able always to continue our operations in all circumstances.”
* indicates a verified formal relationship or partnership with Palantir
A practical way to test any supplier is to turn the sovereignty argument into six operational questions:
Stephen M. Saunders MBE is a communications analyst and USPTO-registered inventor examining how digital infrastructure — 5G, cloud and AI — is reshaping industry, power and society, as well as underpinning the emerging, ubiquitous global digital economy. As anchor of FNTV and a longtime industry insider, he focuses less on growth narratives and more on execution, risk and how hyperscale technology is distorting markets, governance and society at scale.
