articles.title: We needed the Driver’s Privacy Protection Act. Technology found a way around it.
articles.description: We needed the Driver’s Privacy Protection Act. Technology found a way around it. The Hill
articles.description_html: We needed the Driver’s Privacy Protection Act. Technology found a way around it.  The Hill
articles.article_title: We needed the Driver’s Privacy Protection Act. Technology found a way around it.
articles.heading: We needed the Driver’s Privacy Protection Act. Technology found a way around it.
articles.summary: As advancements in technology allow private companies like Flock Safety to bypass the Driver’s Privacy Protection Act of 1994, experts argue that current privacy laws must be updated to regul…
articles.content:
In 1989, actress Rebecca Schaeffer was murdered by a stalker who obtained her home address through California motor-vehicle records. Her death became one of the most prominent examples of the privacy and safety dangers created by the widespread availability of personal information held by state motor-vehicle departments.
Congress responded by passing the Driver’s Privacy Protection Act in 1994.
The principle was straightforward: Just because the government possesses personal information about drivers does not mean that information should be freely disclosed, sold or redistributed. The law restricts the disclosure and resale of personal information contained in state motor-vehicle records while allowing exceptions for legitimate purposes, including law enforcement and public safety.
But there is an important irony in the history of the law. Congress was responding, in part, to a technological problem. Advances in technology at the time had made state motor-vehicle records increasingly accessible, and existing laws had failed to keep pace.
More than 30 years later, technology has advanced again. Companies such as Flock Safety can collect license-plate information independently of state motor-vehicle databases. Flock’s own policies say its license-plate-reader system collects license-plate images, vehicle characteristics, dates, times and camera locations. It does not need a DMV database to observe a vehicle.
That distinction matters. The Driver’s Privacy Protection Act regulates personal information contained in state motor-vehicle records. It does not, on its face, regulate every piece of vehicle information that a private company can independently observe on a public road.
But it raises a larger question: What happens when technology allows private companies to create information that can be used for many of the same identification and tracking purposes without ever obtaining the underlying government record?
Imagine driving down a public road and passing an automated camera. The camera records your license plate, the time you passed and the camera’s location. One observation may seem insignificant. But repeated observations can create something much more revealing: a record of where a particular vehicle has been and when.
The government did not give a private company your DMV record. A company can create a different database around the same identifying marker: your license plate.
That may place the information outside the Driver’s Privacy Protection Act’s specific restrictions. But it does not eliminate the privacy concern that motivated Congress in the first place.
There is a legitimate argument for automated license-plate readers. Law enforcement can use them to locate stolen vehicles, investigate crimes and respond to public-safety threats. Those are legitimate government interests, and privacy protections should not make it impossible for police to do their jobs.
But public safety should not automatically become a blank check for surveillance.
The more important questions are what happens after a vehicle is recorded. How long is the information retained? Who can access it? With whom can it be shared? Can information collected for one purpose later be used for another?
Flock has recently taken steps to address some of these concerns. On Aug. 13, the company announced that it was reducing its recommended default retention period for license-plate-reader data from 30 days to seven days. Flock also announced additional safeguards, including mandatory misuse detection for customers and other access and accountability measures.
That change deserves recognition. Seven days is substantially less than 30 days, and Flock says the system automatically deletes data on a rolling schedule. But seven days is a recommended default, not a universal limit. The actual retention period can vary according to a customer’s contract and applicable state or local law.
That distinction illustrates why this issue should not be framed as a choice between public safety and privacy. There is a fundamental difference between an officer seeing a vehicle on a public road and a searchable database containing repeated observations of that vehicle.
One is an observation. The other can become a history.
The Driver’s Privacy Protection Act was never a declaration that Americans have an absolute right to anonymity on public roads. It was a recognition that information capable of identifying and locating people can be dangerous when it is collected, distributed and used without meaningful limits.
Today, technology has created another path to information about our movements. The government no longer has to hand over the record, because a camera can create one.
That does not mean automated license-plate readers should be banned. It means our privacy laws need to address the technology we actually have, rather than the technology we had in 1994.
Americans should not have to choose between public safety and personal privacy when reasonable rules can protect both. The Driver’s Privacy Protection Act was written for the technology of 1994. Our privacy laws need to catch up with the technology of 2026.
Shaun M. Simmons is a security professional with more than two decades of experience spanning public safety in the private, state, and federal security sectors. He is currently an independent security contractor and grassroots political organizer in Canyon County, Idaho.

articles.title: Carter Stubbs named Institute auditor
articles.description: Carter Stubbs named Institute auditor MIT News
articles.description_html: Carter Stubbs named Institute auditor  MIT News
articles.source: MIT News | Massachusetts Institute of Technology
articles.article_title: Carter Stubbs named Institute auditor
articles.heading: Carter Stubbs named Institute auditor
articles.summary: New Institute Auditor Carter Stubbs brings deep knowledge of MIT audit program to the role, overseeing comprehensive financial, operational, compliance, and technology reviews across the Institute.
articles.content:
Carter Stubbs has been appointed MIT’s Institute auditor, effective Nov. 2.
Stubbs, who currently serves as audit assistant director for IT Audit and Advisory Services, has been a member of the MIT community for more than 11 years and brings deep institutional knowledge, highly salient management experience, and a forward-looking vision to the role. Stubbs will succeed Michael Moody, who has served as Institute auditor for 12 years and will retire from MIT in October.
Executive Vice President and Treasurer Glen Shor announced the news today in a letter to MIT’s Academic Council.
“Carter stood out in a competitive field of candidates thanks to his impressive audit and IT expertise, collaborative leadership style, and robust understanding of MIT’s complex operations,” Shor says. “He has earned the trust and admiration of colleagues inside and outside the division and is well-positioned to write its next chapter.”
As Institute auditor, Stubbs will lead a team of internal auditors responsible for independently evaluating MIT’s academic, research, and administrative processes, including operations at Lincoln Laboratory. He will oversee a comprehensive, risk-based audit and advisory program spanning financial, operational, compliance, and technology reviews across the Institute.
The MIT Audit Division maintains a dual reporting structure to ensure its independence. Stubbs and the audit team work for the MIT Corporation Risk and Audit Committee, but receive administrative support from the MIT Office of the Executive Vice President and Treasurer.
“Carter’s strong technical command of IT auditing and hands-on experience auditing and advising on major systems implementations will be especially valuable as the Institute continues to advance its business and digital transformation roadmap,” says Pat Callahan, the chair of the Risk and Audit Committee. “The committee will be well-served by his experience with our current audit program, his demonstrated leadership and sound judgment, and his wide-ranging knowledge of the Institute.”
Stubbs joined MIT in 2015 as a senior auditor of information technology, steadily assuming increasing responsibility for information technology, data analytics, and advisory services. He now leads those functions for the Audit Division and serves on the division’s management team. Working closely with the Institute auditor, Stubbs shapes annual risk assessment work, audit planning, and broader division strategy while managing the oversight of complex engagements; contributing to quality assurance and advancing the division’s capabilities; and proactively responding to emerging institutional needs. Stubbs collaborates with leaders from across MIT’s academic, research, administrative, and technology units, including Lincoln Laboratory, and facilitates communications with Institute governance.
During his time at MIT, Stubbs has built an extensive network of partners and developed a multifaceted understanding of the Institute’s operating model, higher education and research risks, and the leadership judgment necessary to navigate complex institutional matters. He has helped steer cross-Institute efforts involving research data management, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and digital transformation. A graduate of the 2025 MIT Leader to Leader program, Stubbs served as an advisor to the MIT Working Group on Artificial Intelligence in Administration and Operations and is a member of the MIT Data Incident Response Team.
“I am honored to serve as MIT’s next Institute auditor,” says Stubbs. “The Audit Division plays an essential role in advancing the Institute’s mission of education and research through independent insight, trusted partnership, and thoughtful perspective on risk. I look forward to building on the division’s strong foundation and helping the Institute navigate an increasingly complex regulatory and risk environment.”
Prior to joining MIT, Stubbs held audit roles at Clean Harbors Environmental Services, Denbury Resources, and PricewaterhouseCoopers, where he developed broad expertise in IT and business process controls across multiple industries. He holds certifications as both a certified internal auditor and certified information systems auditor and earned a BBA in information and operations management from Texas A&M University.

articles.article_title: Police hold first community listening session on technology Thursday
articles.heading: Police hold first community listening session on technology Thursday
articles.summary: The Sept. 24 and Oct. 7 sessions are the first public forums since council asked the department to answer questions about its Flock license plate reader program
articles.content:
The Sept. 24 and Oct. 7 sessions are the first public forums since council asked the department to answer questions about its Flock license plate reader program

ALEXANDRIA, Va. — The Alexandria Police Department will hold the first of two community listening sessions on its use of technology Thursday, as residents continue to press the city to end its contract with Flock Safety.

The sessions run from 6:30 to 7:30 p.m. Thursday, Sept. 24, at the James M. Duncan Jr. Branch Library, and 6:30 to 7:30 p.m. Wednesday, Oct. 7, at Patrick Henry Recreation Center. APD's announcement describes them broadly, as a chance to learn about the technology the department uses, ask questions, share concerns and give feedback "to help inform future decisions."

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Police Dept, Alexandria, VA (@alexandriavapd)

A post shared by Police Dept, Alexandria, VA (@alexandriavapd)

The city's written answers to council tie the sessions to the license plate reader program. Asked how APD would engage the community as the city transitions away from Flock, the department named the same two dates and said the locations were chosen to reach residents on the east and west sides of the city.

Mayor Alyia Gaskins asked at council's Sept. 8 meeting that community meetings on the technology be held on their own rather than folded into other gatherings.

Where technology fits in the chief's plan

The sessions follow through on a commitment in the Public Safety Plan McGuire presented to council in June. The plan organizes the department's priorities around five pillars spelling GREAT — Geographical Policing and Accountability, Relationships, Evidence-Based Strategies and Enforcement, Assessment, and Technology. The technology pillar covers real-time emergency information, expanded crime-analysis tools and planning for the costs and staffing new technology requires, and pledges community education and feedback before major technology decisions.

McGuire has pushed technology since his first public safety update to council in March, when he described it as a force multiplier for a department facing hiring and retention pressures and asked for deeper investment, including in drones and real-time information. At a community meeting on the plan in July, he put it more plainly: the department cannot be everywhere at once.

The license plate reader debate has since become the first major test of that pledge.

What has come out since Sept. 8

The department posted answers to council's questions Sept. 18. Among them: the Flock contract runs through April 2027 and can be ended at any time, an outside audit by Ohio State criminologist Robin Engel is expected to begin by Oct. 1, and APD has cut off access to its cameras for 12 Virginia agencies with immigration enforcement agreements.

Police Chief Tarrick McGuire has since confirmed that decision and asked a city commission to help set the rules for what replaces Flock.

The program dominated open public comment at council's Sept. 19 public hearing, where about a dozen speakers addressed surveillance, most calling for the city to end its contracts with license plate reader companies. Two Alexandria City High School seniors spoke about camera placement in their neighborhoods. Other speakers raised pedestrian safety near schools.

When one speaker called for removing speed and red-light cameras as well if they feed the same network, a police official told council those cameras are not integrated into license plate reader databases and that the data does not overlap. Gaskins asked that the clarification be circulated to council and posted publicly.

The department's answers and dashboard are posted on the city's website .

No Virginia agency deputized to enforce immigration law on patrol can search Alexandria's cameras anymore

Alexandria City Council will decide how long police keep license plate data, APD says

Four police agencies, one state law, four different sets of rules for license plate cameras

Gaskins: 'I do not think there's a role for Flock in this community'

Police won't publish Flock camera locations and have no plans to shorten data retention

Alexandria's Flock page now lists the 161 Virginia agencies that can search its cameras

Gaskins says Alexandria police won't share license plate data in immigration cases

articles.heading: City of Wilmington names Jennifer Clift as information technology director
articles.summary: WILMINGTON — The City of Wilmington has promoted Jennifer Clift to Information Technology Director. Clift, who has served as Interim IT Director for the past several months, brings nearly 18 years of…
articles.content:
WILMINGTON — The City of Wilmington has promoted Jennifer Clift to Information Technology Director. Clift, who has served as Interim IT Director for the past several months, brings nearly 18 years of service with the City and more than 30 years of experience in information technology and public-sector technology leadership.
As IT Director, Clift will oversee the City’s information technology operations and continue leading efforts to provide secure, reliable, and user-focused technology solutions across the organization. Her focus will include ensuring that the City’s technology services evolve to meet the needs of the organization and the community.
“I’ve had the pleasure to work with Jen over the past 14 months, and her genuine desire to find solutions and help others is the exact leadership needed for this vital role,” City Manager Becky Hawke said in a press release. “When combined with her deep knowledge of the City and strong technical expertise, she’s well prepared to build on the great work already underway in her department.”
Clift joined the city as a senior systems analyst, supporting applications across multiple departments and helping modernize core systems. She was promoted to assistant IT director 10 years ago and has since played a key role in advancing the city’s technology services, with a focus on customer service, organizational transparency, and making technology more accessible and approachable for employees.
Before joining the city, Clift worked at Brown University, where she contributed to large-scale academic and administrative technology initiatives. She relocated from Rhode Island to Wilmington 20 years ago.
Clift holds the Certified Government Chief Information Officer credential, a Lean Six Sigma Green Belt, and a Prosci Change Management certification. She is also a Fellow of the UNC School of Government’s Leading for Results program.

articles.title: NIH makes major investments to advance human-based research infrastructure and technologies
articles.description: NIH makes major investments to advance human-based research infrastructure and technologies National Institutes of Health (NIH) | (.gov)
articles.description_html: NIH makes major investments to advance human-based research infrastructure and technologies  National Institutes of Health (NIH) | (.gov)
articles.article_title: NIH makes major investments to advance human-based research infrastructure and technologies
articles.heading: NIH makes major investments to advance human-based research infrastructure and technologies
articles.summary: Projects spanning the nation will accelerate scientific discovery, reduce reliance on animals.
articles.content:
NIH makes major investments to advance human-based research infrastructure and technologies
Monday, September 21, 2026
NIH makes major investments to advance human-based research infrastructure and technologies
Projects spanning the nation will accelerate scientific discovery, reduce reliance on animals.
The National Institutes of Health (NIH) is making its biggest push yet to move biomedical research beyond animal model use, unveiling five major initiatives that could reshape how new drugs and treatments are developed and evaluated. Together, the efforts signal a significant investment into human-based technologies as the future of preclinical science, aiming to make research faster, more predictive, and more directly relevant to human health.
Efforts include more than $88 million in funding for biomedical infrastructure projects nationwide; a new challenge offering over $7 million in awards to demonstrate how quantum-enabled approaches can improve detection and measurement in lab-based New Approach Methodologies (NAMs); a state-of-the-art laboratory at the NIH Clinical Center that will integrate standardized human organoid models, robotics, AI, and advanced data capabilities to enable experiments on reproducible human biological systems; an initiative to recruit grant reviewers who are experts in human-based science; and a new request for information from the scientific community to assess the feasibility of an annual public report tracking the number of vertebrate animals used in NIH-funded research.
“NIH is building the scientific infrastructure needed to develop, validate, and scale technologies that better reflect human biology,” said NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya, M.D., Ph.D. “Our goal is to give researchers better tools to understand human disease and translate discoveries into treatments that improve patients’ lives.”
Part of NIH’s Biomedical Research Facilities Program, 10 construction projects totaling $88 million, located across the nation, will spur the advancement of NAMs and enable investigation into a host of major health issues facing Americans, including chronic disease, environmental health, rare childhood diseases, cancer research, obesity and metabolic dysfunctions. Traditionally, many awards in this program have supported the construction and renovation of research infrastructure focused on further development of animal models for research. While animal models are still an important tool for human biomedical discovery, NIH’s goal is to reduce the use of animals whenever feasible.
These new awards also reflect NIH’s commitment to a broad geographical distribution of taxpayer funds, with awardees representing nine states from coast to coast. Several of the grants are to institutions in NIH Institutional Development Award (IDeA) States, with a focus on building research capacity in areas that traditionally lag peer states in health care technology, services, or research resources and where these lags may adversely affect the health status of the local population in the future.
“We are at a unique moment in biomedical research, with new tools and technologies giving us an unprecedented opportunity to advance research methodologies that more closely reflect human biology,” said Nicole Kleinstreuer, Ph.D., NIH Deputy Director for Program Coordination, Planning, and Strategic Initiatives. “But realizing that opportunity requires a strong foundation and a research enterprise with the capacity to innovate across the country. These new awards will help build that foundation by expanding access to resources, expertise and infrastructure, ensuring that scientists with transformative ideas will advance the next generation of biomedical research.”
The Quantum-Enabled Approaches for Predictive Preclinical NAMs for Toxicity and Safety (Qu-SAFE) Challenge seeks proof-of-concept and prototype sensing systems that use quantum technology, either alone or combined with classical methods, to improve how researchers detect and measure biological signals in lab-based NAMs systems used for drug safety and toxicity evaluation. This includes tools such as organ-on-a-chip devices that generate human-relevant data without relying on animal models. The challenge’s goal is to unlock new kinds of biological data and signals that can’t currently be measured, making these preclinical models better at predicting real-world drug safety and effectiveness. Top submissions will earn portions of prizes totaling over $7 million.
NIH will also establish a Bio Genesis Autonomous Human Biology Laboratory within the NIH Clinical Center, aligned with the NIH Standardized Organoid Modeling (SOM) Center, to integrate standardized human organoid models, robotics, AI, and advanced data capabilities into a closed-loop experimental platform to enable clinically driven questions to be tested in reproducible human biological systems. These new lab systems will generate data that continuously informs the next experiment and accelerates translation while reducing reliance on animal models.
Two final efforts include a newly issued request for information (RFI) to seek input from domestic and foreign NIH-funded institutions on the reporting of laboratory animal numbers, and a push to recruit reviewers with expertise in human-based science. For the first, NIH’s Office of Laboratory Animal Welfare (OLAW) is gathering input on feasibility, current capabilities, expected benefits, and expected burdens associated with yearly reporting of the number of live, vertebrate animals in NIH-funded labs. This effort would increase transparency regarding animal use and would assist the agency in measuring the progress of its work to reduce the use of animals in NIH-supported research. For the second, NIH recognizes that the agency needs robust expertise to help review the many new facets of science presented by human-based approaches. Building up this expertise in the peer review process will help ensure relevant experts are included in the evaluation of these new technologies and projects and help facilitate the shift of research from animal-based methods to human-based science. Experts in human-based science are encouraged to express their interest here.
About the National Institutes of Health (NIH): NIH, the nation's medical research agency, includes 27 Institutes and Centers and is a component of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. NIH is the primary federal agency conducting and supporting basic, clinical, and translational medical research, and is investigating the causes, treatments, and cures for both common and rare diseases. For more information about NIH and its programs, visit www.nih.gov.
NIH…Turning Discovery Into Health®

NIH will also establish a Bio Genesis Autonomous Human Biology Laboratory within the NIH Clinical Center, aligned with the NIH Standardized Organoid Modeling (SOM) Center, to integrate standardized human organoid models, robotics, AI, and advanced data capabilities into a closed-loop experimental platform to enable clinically driven questions to be tested in reproducible human biological systems. These new lab systems will generate data that continuously informs the next experiment and accelerates translation while reducing reliance on animal models.

Two final efforts include a newly issued request for information (RFI) to seek input from domestic and foreign NIH-funded institutions on the reporting of laboratory animal numbers, and a push to recruit reviewers with expertise in human-based science. For the first, NIH’s Office of Laboratory Animal Welfare (OLAW) is gathering input on feasibility, current capabilities, expected benefits, and expected burdens associated with yearly reporting of the number of live, vertebrate animals in NIH-funded labs. This effort would increase transparency regarding animal use and would assist the agency in measuring the progress of its work to reduce the use of animals in NIH-supported research. For the second, NIH recognizes that the agency needs robust expertise to help review the many new facets of science presented by human-based approaches. Building up this expertise in the peer review process will help ensure relevant experts are included in the evaluation of these new technologies and projects and help facilitate the shift of research from animal-based methods to human-based science. Experts in human-based science are encouraged to express their interest here.

NIH is the primary federal agency conducting and supporting basic, clinical, and translational medical research, and is investigating the causes, treatments, and cures for both common and rare diseases. For more information about NIH and its programs, visit www.nih.gov.

articles.heading: Michael Luca Named Director of Carnegie Mellon University’s Block Center for Technology and Society
articles.summary: Michael Luca, Professor of Economics, Technology, and Policy at Carnegie Mellon University, has been appointed to lead the university-wide Block Center for Technology and Society.
articles.content:
Michael Luca Named Director of Carnegie Mellon University’s Block Center for Technology and Society
Media Inquiries
Michael Luca, Professor of Economics, Technology, and Policy at Carnegie Mellon University, has been appointed to lead the university-wide Block Center for Technology and Society.
Luca will also serve as the Trustees Professor of Technology and Society. As director, he will lead the center’s efforts to assess how emerging technologies are reshaping society and how decisions being made now by business leaders, policymakers and technologists can shape what happens next.
As advances in AI, robotics and digital technologies reshape how we work, communicate and live, the Block Center brings together researchers across Carnegie Mellon with policymakers, business leaders and the public to connect evidence to real-world decisions.
“Mike is an exceptional scholar and leader who brings a rare combination of rigorous research and a clear understanding of how research can inform the choices leaders are making right now,” said Kirsten Martin(opens in new window), H. John Heinz III Dean of Heinz College.
Luca’s work focuses on the interplay among technology, human behavior and business and policy decisions, examining how those forces shape market and societal outcomes.
“Technological innovation can boost productivity, improve health and address societal challenges,” Luca said. “At the same time, the impact of technology depends on how it is developed, implemented and governed.” Luca emphasizes the need for a proactive approach to assessing technological change and anticipating and mitigating its risks, noting the need to “understand where technology can create value, who benefits and what challenges need to be addressed along the way.”
Founded in 2019 through the generosity of Carnegie Mellon alumnus Keith Block and his wife, Suzanne Kelley, the Block Center was created around a simple premise: technological progress should work for the benefit of society. Its work supports interdisciplinary research and connects academic inquiry to questions facing companies, policymakers, technology users and the public.
“Suzanne and I established the Block Center to help ensure that technology changes the world for the better. This founding premise still guides everything the center does,” said Keith Block, founder and CEO of Smith Point Capital. “We’re proud to see the Block Center enter this next chapter under Mike’s leadership.”
Carnegie Mellon offers a distinctive environment for that work: researchers developing new technologies work alongside scholars studying how those technologies affect people, markets, institutions and culture. The university has a long history of technological innovation in areas such as artificial intelligence, robotics, computer science, information systems and human-computer interaction, complemented by strengths in economics, psychology, public policy, design and the arts. Heinz College, where Luca will be based, has long operated at that intersection, integrating people, policy and technology.
“The Block Center plays an essential role in ensuring that technological progress is informed by a deep understanding of its implications for people and society,” said Theresa Mayer(opens in new window), Carnegie Mellon’s vice president for research. “By bringing together expertise across technology, policy, economics and the social sciences, the center helps turn rigorous research into practical guidance for leaders navigating rapid technological change. Luca’s leadership will expand the reach and impact of this important work.”
Luca’s own research illustrates this approach. He and his coauthors have documented discrimination and racial disparities in online marketplaces such as Airbnb and studied how design choices could enable or mitigate them. The research helped spur changes in platform design and in how discrimination was measured on major platforms.
The same emphasis on connecting evidence to real-world decisions has shaped Luca’s work beyond academic journals. He has served in advisory roles with organizations including the OECD, the National Association for Business Economics, the Behavioural Insights Team, and CNBC’s Technology Executive Council. He has also written dozens of articles for broader audiences, including in The Wall Street Journal and Harvard Business Review.
“Research has a role to play throughout technological change whether in developing new technologies, measuring their effects, anticipating emerging challenges, or evaluating business and policy responses,” Luca said.
Among Luca’s first initiatives as director are two new cross-university programs launching this academic year. The Block Public Engagement Fellowship will support Carnegie Mellon faculty in bringing research and evidence into broader public conversations. The Block Student Fellowship on AI and Society will enable students from across the university to develop practical, interdisciplinary projects focused on the societal impact of AI.
The center will also expand opportunities for researchers to engage with policymakers, companies and civil society on emerging questions about technology and society.

articles.article_title: Chulalongkorn University and AIST Sign MoU on Quantum Technology
articles.heading: Chulalongkorn University and AIST Sign MoU on Quantum Technology
articles.summary: Thailand’s Chulalongkorn University and AIST sign an MoU to expand quantum technology research, training and ecosystem development.
articles.content:
Insider Brief
- Chulalongkorn University and Japan’s AIST, through G-QuAT, signed a five-year MoU to expand cooperation in quantum technology between Thailand and Japan.
- The agreement covers joint research, researcher exchanges, academic events and activities focused on quantum computing applications, human resource development and ecosystem building.
- Chulalongkorn will coordinate the collaboration through Siam Quantum Square, while AIST will provide access to its quantum computing infrastructure and related technologies.
PRESS RELEASE — Chulalongkorn University and the National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST) in Japan, through the Global Research and Development Center for Business by Quantum-AI Technology (G-QuAT), signed a memorandum of understanding to drive collaboration in quantum technology and the development of quantum ecosystems between Thailand and Japan. Prof. Dr. Pranut Potiyaraj, Dean of the Faculty of Science, Chulalongkorn University, and Dr. Masahiro Horibe, Deputy Director of G-QuAT acting on behalf of G-QuAT Director, Dr. Kazuya Masu, signed the MoU. The signing, which took place on July 24, 2026, at Room 105, Maha Chulalongkorn Building, was attended by representatives from the government sector, the industry sector, and academic institutions from both countries.
This MOU marks an important step towards establishing long-term cooperation in quantum technology with the aim of promoting research, human resource development, and the application of quantum computing technology for the benefit of industry and society, as well as strengthening the international quantum ecosystem between Thailand and Japan.
Under this collaboration, the two institutions will jointly organize activities including seminars and academic conferences, exchanges of scientists and researchers, and joint research projects on areas of mutual interest. Chulalongkorn University will coordinate the collaboration through Siam Quantum Square (SQ²), while AIST will carry out its activities through the Corporate Planning and Management Headquarters. The MOU will remain in effect for a period of five years.
According to Prof. Dr. Pranut Potiyaraj, Dean of the Faculty of Science, Chulalongkorn University, “The collaboration between Chulalongkorn University and G-QuAT, AIST, is an important milestone in the development of quantum science and technology in Thailand, an area that is currently advancing rapidly around the world. Although Thailand entered the scene later than many other countries, building collaborative networks with a world-class partner like Japan will enable Thailand to learn and develop more rapidly in terms of knowledge, technology, and the quantum ecosystem that Japan has firmly established. Japan’s experience and development approaches will serve as an important model that Thailand can adapt to enhance the country’s capabilities in the future.”
“This collaboration is aligned with the vision of the Faculty of Science and Chulalongkorn University to promote quantum technology as one of the country’s key technologies. One of the most urgent priorities for Thailand is the development of a skilled workforce, as the current number of qualified personnel remains insufficient to meet the demands of the research and industrial sectors. The Faculty of Science is therefore in the process of developing quantum-related curricula and will take advantage of its collaboration with AIST as a key mechanism to accelerate the development of skilled professionals, thereby supporting the tangible growth of quantum technology in Thailand,” Prof. Dr. Pranut added.
Dr. Masahiro Horibe, Deputy Director of G-QuAT, AIST, made the observation that “Cross-border collaboration plays a vital role in accelerating the application of quantum technology in industry and society. We are confident that the collaboration between AIST and Chulalongkorn University will help generate tangible outcomes and expand opportunities for innovation in both countries.”
“Thailand has long been an important partner to Japan in terms of the economy, investment, and industry, with numerous Japanese companies operating businesses and manufacturing bases in Thailand. At the same time, the role of quantum technology will be more important in the development of industries and businesses in the future. AIST therefore places great importance on building partnerships with leading Thai universities such as Chulalongkorn University to jointly advance research, promote human resource development, and provide Thai researchers with opportunities to access Japan’s quantum computing infrastructure and advanced technologies. This will contribute to strengthening Thailand’s quantum capabilities in the long run,” Dr. Horibe added.
Dr. Horibe concluded, “The next five years will be a crucial period for building the global quantum technology market and industrial ecosystem. Thailand has the potential to become a hub for quantum technology in Southeast Asia, with the strength of its industrial sector and supply chains. AIST therefore expects this collaboration to contribute to the development of a quantum ecosystem, the growth of new industries and markets, and the establishment of collaborative networks connecting the academic, research, and business sectors of both countries. These efforts will help drive the practical adoption of quantum technology and generate economic impact in the future.”
The signing ceremony was followed by a panel discussion on the topic “Opportunities for Thailand–Japan Collaboration in Quantum Computing and Quantum Technologies” with the purpose of exchanging perspectives on quantum technology collaboration, the development of manpower, and industrial applications of the technology. The panelists included:
- Dr. Masahiro Horibe, G-QuAT, AIST (Japan)
- Dr. Naoki Mitsumoto, DENSO Corporation
- Dr. Masao Kondo, Fujitsu Limited
- Dr. Warit Asavanant, Optical Quantum Computer (OptQC)
- Dr. Jirawat Tangpanitanon, Quantum Technology Foundation (Thailand) Co., Ltd. (QTFT)
- Assoc. Prof. Dr. Worawat Meevasana, Quantum Technology Research Initiative (QTRic)
- Asst. Prof. Dr. Salinporn Kittiwatanakul, Siam Quantum Square (SQ2), Chulalongkorn University
The section was moderated by Dr. Kamonluk Suksen.
The event received excellent support from key organizations within Thailand’s science, research, and innovation ecosystem, including the National Higher Education, Science, Research, and Innovation Policy Council (NXPO), the Thailand Science Research and Innovation (TSRI), the National Science and Technology Development Agency (NSTDA), and the National Institute of Metrology (Thailand), reflecting the significance of the collaboration in advancing Thailand’s efforts to become part of the global quantum technology ecosystem.

articles.heading: Amazon invests another $1.9 billion in the Delivery Service Partner program, launching new safety initiatives and AI-powered technology
articles.summary: Amazon has invested $21.7 billion to support DSPs and their Delivery Associates throughout the eight-year program history.
articles.content:
Key takeaways
- Amazon is investing $1.9 billion in the DSP program in 2027, helping DSPs increase DA pay to a national average of nearly $24/hour.
- Safety investments and DSP leadership are delivering results, with serious crashes down more than 23%.
- AI-powered tools like Wellspring and Smart Delivery Glasses are making deliveries faster and more accurate.
- Amazon is committing $70 million over the next five years towards community impact initiatives led by DSP owners.
Every year, we bring thousands of Delivery Service Partner (DSP) owners from across the U.S. and Canada together in Las Vegas for Ignite Live, our annual conference to share what’s next for the program and celebrate everything this community has accomplished. It’s one of my favorite moments of the year, and I’m always proud to see so many entrepreneurs who have built their own businesses through this program come together in one place.
This year at Ignite Live, we shared updates about how we’re continuing to invest in DSP owners and their teams. Here are a few of the things I’m most excited about.
Safety is always our top priority
Our overarching goal has always been to build the safest delivery network in the world. Since 2022, we’ve invested more than $543 million in safety initiatives, programs, and technology for DSP owners and their teams. Combined with the strong safety leadership of DSP owners themselves, those investments are delivering real results: serious vehicle crashes dropped more than 23% across our network last year.
We’re continuing that progress with new safety technology designed to give DSP’s Delivery Associates (DA) more visibility on the road. For example, we’re rolling out new surround-view cameras that identify vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians from all directions and notify DAs. By the end of this year, the technology will be installed in 50% of Rivian electric delivery vehicles across the network.
We’re also launching additional dynamic hazard alerts in the Amazon Delivery App, so DAs get real-time notifications about accidents, road closures, and construction ahead on their route. In addition, navigation will now automatically adjust routes during inclement weather or when hazards are detected, without the DA having to take any action.
Thanks to Netradyne’s in-vehicle safety cameras, DSP owners have real-time safety technology that help protect their DAs on the road. Now, we're using more advanced AI techniques to identify driving trends that are more likely to lead to accidents and surfacing these insights to DSPs so that owners can provide early coaching for their teams. These efforts, combined with DSP owners’ safety-first leadership, are what’s driving continued safety gains across our network.
Investing in DSP owners and their teams
This year, we're investing an additional $1.9 billion in the DSP program, including support for DSP owners' ability to attract and retain talent. We anticipate that over the past three years these investments will have helped DSP owners increase driver pay by an average of 16% nationwide, with national average earnings rising by roughly another $1 to nearly $24 per hour. The increased rates we pay DSPs will continue to support them in recruiting and retaining high-performing teams, which is essential for building sustainable delivery businesses. Specifics will vary by DSP and geography, as each DSP determines how best to invest in their business and teams. All DSPs provide healthcare coverage and paid time off for their full-time DAs, and many also offer 401(k) plans, tuition reimbursement and other benefits. These are decisions DSP owners make as employers, and our investments are designed to help support those efforts.
AI and technology that learns from every delivery
We continue to utilize technology, in the form of hardware and AI-backed software systems, to help DSP owners run stronger operations and improve the daily delivery experience for DAs.
Our generative AI mapping technology, known as Wellspring, keeps getting smarter with every delivery. It learns from each trip to a location and builds an increasingly accurate model of the physical world over time. Since 2024, we’ve identified 202 million parking locations, mapped 2.8 million building entrances, and cataloged 85,000 mailrooms and lockers. For DSP owners, this technology helps their DAs more efficiently and accurately deliver to customers.
We’re also investing in AI-based routing technology that dynamically adjusts for real-world conditions, accounting for considerations such as reduced visibility after sunset, or the extra time a downtown delivery might need to find parking during busy lunch hours.
We’re also investing in AI-based routing technology that dynamically adjusts for real-world conditions, accounting for considerations such as reduced visibility after sunset, or the extra time a downtown delivery might need to find parking during busy lunch hours.
Last year, we introduced Amazon Smart Delivery Glasses, AI-powered wearable technology designed with input from hundreds of DAs. The glasses use computer vision to display real-time navigation suggestions and delivery details directly in a DA's line of sight, creating a hands-free experience that helps them stay focused on their surroundings rather than looking down at a phone. In addition to adding new features, such as an LED headlamp, hands-free scanning, and proactive address verification, we will continue to scale out the deployment and expect to have more than 20,000 devices in the field by the end of 2027.
How DSP owners are giving back—and our commitment to go further together
DSP owners consistently go beyond delivery—donating school supplies, supporting local hospitals, and stepping up during disaster relief. To help scale that impact, we’re committing $70 million over the next five years toward community initiatives led by DSPs and supported by Amazon.
A key piece of that commitment is Amazon Local Good, which turns the Last Mile delivery network into a community logistics engine that helps nonprofits get donated goods to people who need them, at no cost to the nonprofit. In 2025 alone, DSPs partnering with Amazon Local Good completed 4,800 routes, distributing over 8 million essential items and over 4 million meals. With this latest investment, we expect to transport and deliver over 150 million essential items, including meals, reaching thousands of community members every day over the next five years.
A focus on community can also be seen in the ongoing Together We Give Back to School campaign, where DSP owners are rallying to support more than 100,000 students and 1,000 teachers by donating over one million school supply items. Those numbers speak for themselves and reflect the commitment of DSP owners across the network.
Eight years of building together
Eight years in, the DSP program has grown into something bigger than a delivery network. It’s thousands of small businesses creating real economic opportunities in their communities while raising the bar on safety and delivery quality every year.
Every day, I see firsthand the dedication of our DSP partners and their DAs, who consistently step up to take care of customers across the country. They deliver more than packages—they deliver smiles to Amazon customers. The success of the DSP program reflects what happens when small businesses are given real opportunities and genuine support. To all the DSPs in our network and your teams, thank you for everything you do for Amazon customers and our communities.

- Amazon raises minimum starting pay for full-time core operations employees to $20/hour, with average pay reaching nearly $24/hour
- Prime Big Deal Days 2026: Early deals you can shop right now
- Amazon is giving every US employee a discount on groceries

Microchip Technology Completes Acquisition of Hailo
Adds AI accelerators and vision processors to existing product portfolio
CHANDLER, Ariz., Sept. 21, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Microchip Technology Incorporated (Nasdaq: MCHP), a broadline supplier of semiconductors committed to making innovative design easier through total system solutions, today announced that it has completed its acquisition of Hailo, a provider of accelerated edge AI processors, vision processors, robotics processors and AI software technologies. The acquisition advances Microchip's strategy to enable intelligent, connected systems at the edge and expands its ability to deliver complete solutions for Edge AI, machine vision, robotics and Physical AI applications. The terms of the transaction were not disclosed, and the transaction is not expected to have a material impact on Microchip's financial results.
As artificial intelligence rapidly moves from experimentation to deployment, developers increasingly require solutions that combine AI acceleration, embedded processing, connectivity, security, power efficiency and long-term product support. By bringing together Microchip's broad embedded systems portfolio with Hailo's AI and vision technologies, Microchip has broadened its ability to help customers move more quickly from prototype to production.
"AI is becoming a foundational capability across embedded systems, from industrial automation and robotics to intelligent transportation, smart infrastructure and advanced vision applications," said Steve Sanghi, Chief Executive Officer and Chair of the Board of Microchip Technology. "Hailo strengthens our ability to deliver complete, production-ready platforms that enable customers to deploy intelligent systems at scale. This acquisition expands our product offerings in one of the most important technology transitions in the embedded industry."
The addition of the Hailo product portfolio expands Microchip's Edge AI offerings with proven AI accelerators and vision processors supporting computer vision, transformer-based models, multimodal workloads and advanced video analytics. With this acquisition, Microchip’s portfolio will enable customers to develop intelligent edge systems ranging from low-power smart cameras to high-performance robotics, autonomous machines and next-generation Physical AI platforms.
"The completion of this acquisition is an important enhancement to Microchip's Edge AI strategy," said Mark Reiten, Senior Corporate Vice President of Microchip's Intelligent Compute Business Unit. "Hailo brings industry-leading edge AI acceleration, vision processing expertise and a vibrant developer ecosystem. Combined with Microchip's embedded processing, FPGA, connectivity, security, analog and power solutions, we can deliver a broader and more complete platform for customers building intelligent edge systems."
Hailo brings an established ecosystem that includes more than 100 customers, an active developer community exceeding 10,000 users and broad engagement across open-source and AI development platforms. Microchip’s strategy is to continue investing in software tools, development environments and next-generation technologies that simplify AI adoption and accelerate deployment into production applications.
"Joining Microchip opens exciting opportunities for our customers, partners and developer community," said Orr Danon, founder and Chief Executive Officer of Hailo. "Microchip's global reach, customer relationships and embedded systems expertise provide a powerful platform for expanding access to advanced Edge AI and vision technologies. As part of Microchip, we are well positioned to accelerate innovation and help customers bring intelligent systems to market faster."
Microchip plans to continue supporting Hailo's existing product portfolio, software environment and customer engagements while driving future innovation across AI acceleration, vision processing and intelligent edge computing. Customers will be able to benefit from expanded access to Microchip's worldwide sales organization, technical support resources and broad portfolio of embedded solutions.

articles.heading: Can Investing in Marvell Technology Stock Double Your Money?
authors: David Jagielski, CPA, The Motley Fool
articles.summary: If Jensen Huang is right, then Marvell could not only double but soar to around five times its current value.
articles.content:
Can Investing in Marvell Technology Stock Double Your Money?
Earlier this year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said that Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL) could be the next trillion-dollar company. If that's true, then there could be significant upside for the chipmaker, whose valuation is around $220 billion right now.
Given the promising outlook from Huang and Marvell posting strong growth in recent numbers, is investing in the business likely to double your money in the near term?
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Image source: Getty Images.
Marvell's stock is up big this year, but the market has been cautious of late
Since the start of 2026, Marvell's stock has risen nearly 190%, as of the end of last week. It's been on a tremendous run driven not only by Huang's praise for the business but also by its solid quarterly results.
However, in recent months, the stock has traded sideways, and it's currently down about 26% from its 52-week high. There's been some apprehension of late, likely due to Marvell's high valuation. The stock is trading at more than 80 times its trailing earnings, a steep multiple that reflects high expectations for future growth.
The market may simply be reluctant to pay an even higher multiple for the stock. While Marvell may one day be a trillion-dollar company, when that day comes is anyone's guess. The company does have plenty of potential upside given the growth in artificial intelligence and the ongoing need for chips, but with it reporting 37% revenue growth in its most recent quarter, that may simply not be enough to send the stock soaring a whole lot higher, at least, not in the short term.
The stock could double again, but investors shouldn't expect it to happen soon
Marvell's stock has already more than doubled this year, but how soon it can double from here is a big question mark. I don't doubt that it will double in value and one day reach a valuation of more than $400 billion, but it may take several years for that to happen.
Its current valuation already prices in rosy growth prospects and strong numbers. For it to rise quickly again, Marvell would effectively have to perform even better and give investors reason to be more bullish about its business than they already are today.
This can be a good growth stock to hold for the long haul, and it may very well double yet again, but this time around, it could take a whole lot longer to do so.
Should you buy stock in Marvell Technology right now?
Before you buy stock in Marvell Technology, consider this:
The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and Marvell Technology wasn't one of them. The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years.
Consider when Netflix made this list on December 17, 2004... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $387,158!* Or when Nvidia made this list on April 15, 2005... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $1,365,749!*
Now, it's worth noting Stock Advisor's total average return is 932% — a market-crushing outperformance compared to 211% for the S&P 500. Don't miss the latest top 10 list, available with Stock Advisor, and join an investing community built by individual investors for individual investors.
*Stock Advisor returns as of September 21, 2026.
