articles.heading: HVRSD Plans Screen-Time Limits as Parents Push for More Intentional Technology Use
articles.summary: As a group of Hopewell Valley parents pushes for a more intentional approach to technology in schools, the Hopewell Valley Regional School District is
articles.content:
As a group of Hopewell Valley parents pushes for a more intentional approach to technology in schools, the Hopewell Valley Regional School District is preparing to track student screen time, establish limits on its use and bring more parents into discussions about digital learning and artificial intelligence.
Superintendent Rosetta Treece used a significant portion of her report at the Sept. 14 Board of Education meeting to address the growing community conversation, outlining steps the district has already taken to limit technology and protect face-to-face learning, as well as changes still in the works.
The presentation came before public comment, when parents and students involved with the effort laid out their concerns and read from a petition that had gathered more than 100 signatures in its first few days.
The discussion continued after public comment, with board members weighing how quickly the district should move and Treece making several specific commitments.
“We will have screen time limits set before this year is out,” Treece said. “We will be able to drill down and see what kids are doing and for how long before this year is out.”
She said the district is also examining additional controls around AI.
District says work has been underway
Treece began her presentation by acknowledging the renewed community interest while emphasizing that questions about technology, social media and student well-being have been part of district conversations for years.
She pointed to earlier parent involvement in the district’s Digital Wellness Committee, the “Wait Until 8th” effort encouraging families to delay smartphones, community forums, work with Common Sense Media and tech-free activities in the schools.
“We are already having those shared conversations, and I’m always open to more because we always, always, always can do better,” Treece said.
She said the district plans to revamp its Digital Wellness Committee and recruit new members, providing another avenue for parents to participate.
Treece also described a broader philosophy in which technology should be used when it adds to instruction rather than simply replacing work that could be done another way. The presentation characterized HVRSD’s approach as “human-centered, evidence-based, and future-ready,” centered on the question, “What best supports learning?”
Students still need to learn to use technology because it is embedded in testing, higher education and the workplace, Treece said, but it should not replace skills they need to develop themselves.
“Our job is to make sure that kids can think critically, analyze, and synthesize, that they can communicate with their words and collaborate effectively, not through a device,” Treece said.
Bell-to-bell cellphone restrictions already in place
The broader discussion comes as HVRSD implements a bell-to-bell cellphone policy this school year, prohibiting students from accessing personal internet-enabled devices during the school day. New Jersey now requires public school districts to have such policies beginning this school year.
Treece said HVRSD had already been moving toward tighter cellphone restrictions before the state requirement. Timberlane Middle School is now in its fourth year using Yondr pouches, meaning this year’s high school freshmen and sophomores had already spent their middle school years under cellphone restrictions.
At Hopewell Valley Central High School, students now place their phones in signal-blocking pouches during the school day. Treece said implementation has gone smoothly, with students complying and spending more time interacting with one another during lunch.
“They’re playing games again. The hacky sack is back,” Treece said. “They’re actually looking at each other’s faces and talking.”
The cellphone restrictions are one piece of the district’s broader effort to put boundaries around technology use. The newer questions raised at the meeting centered largely on school-issued devices, screen time and AI.
Screen-time tracking and summer Chromebooks
Among the most concrete changes is an effort to use the district’s existing technology platform to determine how much time individual students spend on school-issued devices and what they are doing during that time.
Treece said the district is close to being able to categorize use “down to the child” and establish guidelines that would allow administrators to intervene when screen use becomes excessive, whether it is happening independently or as part of classroom instruction. The district’s Education and Social-Emotional Learning Committee is targeting the spring for an initial report on the data, board member Alex Reznik said later in the meeting.
Treece also announced that the district plans to collect student Chromebooks at the end of the school year rather than routinely leaving them with students throughout the summer.
She said administrators currently receive alerts during nights, weekends and summer when students use district devices to search for or write concerning material, requiring staff to follow up.
“These are really meant to be educational tools that can assist, but it shouldn’t be — we don’t want to give kids an opportunity to just have screen time all the time,” Treece said.
There could be exceptions for students who need devices for Advanced Placement summer work or as part of an Individualized Education Program, she said.
Parents ask district to go further
The parent effort came into fuller view during public comment.
Kristin Broderick of Hopewell Township, speaking about EcoPTO’s “more green time, less screen time” work, said the group appreciated steps the district had already taken and wasn’t approaching the issue from a place of blame.
She urged district officials to listen with “really open ears,” arguing that the technology landscape has changed rapidly.
“We really value all that you’ve done,” Broderick said, adding that “there’s so much more that’s happening in 2026” and that parents wanted to continue working with the district.
Kayla McLaughlin, a Bear Tavern parent who identified herself as a member of Schools Beyond Screens’ Hopewell Valley chapter, said she believed the district was already thinking seriously about technology and AI but called for a broader systems-level approach.
“The adoption of technology has outpaced our ability to evaluate its effectiveness,” McLaughlin said.
She asked the board to consider additional districtwide technology norms and create a working group of educators, parents, community members, students and experts.
“This isn’t one group’s job,” she said. “It’s not the district’s alone. It’s not teachers alone. It’s not parents alone. It’s not students alone. All of us together have to do this, or it does not happen.”
Gabe Dominguez, an EcoPTO co-president and member of its Beyond Screens Circle, introduced the petition, saying it had collected more than 100 signatures in several days.
Dominguez characterized the effort as an attempt to encourage the direction the district had already begun taking.
“We’re here to put wind in your sails to take the next step,” he said.
The petition calls for an “analog-first” approach summarized as “screens down, pencils up,” with digital devices used when a learning objective specifically requires them. It also asks the district to measure time spent on school-issued devices and make that information available to parents, establish daily limits on certain types of screen use, end routine take-home Chromebook use and form a working group within 60 days.
Julie Cesari, a Bear Tavern parent, said she appreciated the principles Treece described but believed there remained a disconnect between the administration’s goals and what students sometimes experience in classrooms.
“We need to do more, and we need to do it now,” she said.
Board joins the discussion
The conversation continued as board members responded to the parents and Treece’s presentation.
Board President Anita Williams Galiano cautioned that reducing technology can affect students differently.
She noted that school-issued computers have helped students who may not have extensive educational support at home and that technology can also serve as an essential communication or learning tool for some students with disabilities.
“We are responsible for every single one of our children,” Williams Galiano said, adding that the district should reconsider its technology strategy without losing sight of students “on the margins” who may depend on those tools.
Board member Mark Peters pushed for a more formal plan, suggesting the district establish a working group or use an existing committee to create a strategic roadmap with goals and dates.
Peters also raised the issue of adults modeling the behavior expected of students.
“I find it challenging when an 18-year-old that’s a senior at the high school watches a 26-year-old teacher on their phone, and they’re being told they can’t be on their phone,” he said.
He encouraged the administration and board to bring community volunteers into the process and establish concrete milestones for reducing screen use where appropriate.
Treece responded that parents from the group were already being invited to participate in the district’s existing AI task force and that new volunteers would be sought for the Digital Wellness Committee.
Peters pressed for dates and measurable goals, prompting Treece to make the commitment that screen-time limits and more detailed monitoring would be in place before the end of the school year.
AI without replacing thinking
Artificial intelligence was another recurring piece of the discussion.
One of Treece’s presentation slides carried the heading, “AI: Explore Carefully. Protect Thinking,” and stated that the district could not prepare students “by pretending AI does not exist.”
Treece said HVRSD has guidelines governing AI and a task force of teachers and administrators exploring its use. At the same time, she said AI should not replace reading, writing, analysis, problem-solving or students’ ability to explain and defend their own ideas.
She offered her own presentation as an example. Treece said she researched and developed the content herself before using AI to help with its visual presentation.
“I put all of the content into that, and then it made it pretty,” she said.
Even then, she said she had to review and change the results because the AI altered some of her language.
“Teaching kids how to use it so that they’re more efficient at work, yes,” Treece said. “Having it do your work for you, no.”
Treece said the district intends to bring community members into both its AI and digital wellness work while continuing to evaluate where technology supports learning — and where it gets in the way.

“I find it challenging when an 18-year-old that’s a senior at the high school watches a 26-year-old teacher on their phone, and they’re being told they can’t be on their phone,” he said.

He encouraged the administration and board to bring community volunteers into the process and establish concrete milestones for reducing screen use where appropriate.

Treece responded that parents from the group were already being invited to participate in the district’s existing AI task force and that new volunteers would be sought for the Digital Wellness Committee.

Peters pressed for dates and measurable goals, prompting Treece to make the commitment that screen-time limits and more detailed monitoring would be in place before the end of the school year.

AI without replacing thinking

Artificial intelligence was another recurring piece of the discussion.

One of Treece’s presentation slides carried the heading, “AI: Explore Carefully. Protect Thinking,” and stated that the district could not prepare students “by pretending AI does not exist.”

Treece said HVRSD has guidelines governing AI and a task force of teachers and administrators exploring its use. At the same time, she said AI should not replace reading, writing, analysis, problem-solving or students’ ability to explain and defend their own ideas.

She offered her own presentation as an example. Treece said she researched and developed the content herself before using AI to help with its visual presentation.

“I put all of the content into that, and then it made it pretty,” she said.

Even then, she said she had to review and change the results because the AI altered some of her language.

“Teaching kids how to use it so that they’re more efficient at work, yes,” Treece said. “Having it do your work for you, no.”

Treece said the district intends to bring community members into both its AI and digital wellness work while continuing to evaluate where technology supports learning — and where it gets in the way.

Purchase of Shares by CFO Vlad Prantsevich
Solidion Technologies also announced today that its CFO Vlad Prantsevich has increased his holdings with the purchase of 1,030 shares at $7.13 per share, bringing his total holding to 3,455 shares, which is 0.04% of issued share capital.

Solidion Technologies also announced today that its Board Member Karin-Joyce Tjon has increased her holdings with the purchase of 5,000 shares at $7.20 per share, bringing her total holding to 17,853 shares, which is 0.20% of issued share capital.

articles.title: Can the US win the AI cold war with China?
articles.description: Can the US win the AI cold war with China? Al Jazeera

articles.article_title: Can the US win the AI cold war with China?
articles.heading: Can the US win the AI cold war with China?
articles.summary: US attempts to slow down Chinese progress on AI through economic restrictions could backfire.
articles.content:
Can the US win the AI cold war with China?
US attempts to slow down Chinese progress on AI through economic restrictions could backfire.
The success of China’s cheap AI technology has clearly worried American AI companies. Industry leaders have openly called on the US government to take action on competition from the Chinese AI industry.
Washington has already imposed various restrictions on the sale of chips to China. Last year, it launched the Pax Silica initiative, aimed at securing supply chains for AI technology that exclude Beijing; 23 states have since joined, along with the European Union. There is now pressure from the US AI industry to ban or restrict Chinese AI models.
It increasingly appears that the two great powers are on the verge of an AI cold war, each building its own camp and bidding to set the rules of the AI era. The question now is: Having declared this war, can the US win it?
The limits of export controls
At present, the US and its allies hold the upper hand in several key areas of AI development. China’s frontier AI models remain heavily dependent on imports, chief among them chips, chip-designing software, and chipmaking equipment.
As a result, US export controls hinder China’s ability to keep pace with the latest AI technologies; they drive up costs and undermine investor confidence. They will, however, not hold China’s AI development back forever.
It is important to remember AI development is by no means a single contest over chips; human capital, financial capital, market size, regulatory agility, and industry adoption matter just as much. In response to US export controls, China is not only investing in domestic alternatives but also improving AI model architecture, optimising AI training and inference efficiency, and squeezing more out of the chips it already has.
While trying to catch up with development in chips, China is seeking various loopholes in US export controls to circumvent the restrictions. In June, the US government curbed the ability of Chinese companies to buy advanced US chips via overseas subsidiaries. This loophole was closed, but new ones will emerge.
Whether the US can contain China’s advancement in AI also hinges on the willingness of its allies to cooperate. Advanced chips are not made in a single country. Instead, their supply chain spans multiple political entities, bringing together US design, Dutch and Japanese equipment, and Taiwanese manufacturing.
This dependence means that US export controls, if pushed too far, revised too often, or kept in place for too long, could backfire. US allies, unhappy that Washington keeps offloading steep commercial costs onto them for the sake of its own national security, may well develop policy fatigue and begin actively investing in alternative supply chains to bypass US technology and regulations altogether.
Christophe Fouquet, CEO of the Dutch chipmaking equipment giant ASML, has questioned restricting sales of the most advanced chipmaking equipment to China – under US pressure – would even work or would only push it to redouble its efforts to develop its own.
Doubts about the current US strategy have been voiced even within the US AI industry. US chip giant Nvidia, for example, is against the chip export restrictions, as China is a major market for the company. CEO Jensen Huang has called export controls a “failure” that has cost US companies billions.
Moreover, Chinese open-source AI models have become indispensable to the US tech industry. This year, nearly 200 US startups sent letters to the Trump administration arguing that banning access to advanced Chinese AI models – which tend to be open-source – rather than regulating it would cripple US startups and leave the US market in the hands of a few AI giants. As with all monopolies, the result would be stifled innovation, a diminished US lead in AI, and higher prices for US consumers.
Beijing’s rare earth card
In the AI cold war, China is not just playing catch-up. It is also wielding significant leverage over the US.
Rare earths, which are key to chipmaking, are probably Beijing’s strongest card. The country not only holds the world’s largest reserves of rare earths but dominates their mining and processing. It alone accounts for 91 percent of global rare earths separation and refining production.
Washington is well aware of this. Last year, in response to the renewed trade war, Beijing flexed its rare earths muscle by banning the export of heavy rare earths to the US, which dealt a heavy blow to US manufacturing. It forced Washington to call a quick truce – one that saw Beijing suspend the ban for a year.
Since then, the US has redoubled its efforts to wean itself off Chinese rare earths – to no avail. Not only are Chinese clay deposits – from which rare earth-bearing ores are extracted – more economical than those found in the US or its allies, but China has also mastered the ability to process those ores into rare earths, a capability long spurned by the West because of the pollution it generates.
Although the technology is hardly rocket science, the US and its allies lack the human capital and technology to catch up quickly. China has tens of thousands of experienced engineers working on rare earths processing; in the West, there are just a handful of such experts.
In light of this, should the US escalate its measures against China, it would itself be hit with embargoes and tariffs – measures that would also hinder its own AI development.
Worse still for Washington, rare earths are also used in weapons ranging from F-35 fighter jets to anti-ballistic missile defence systems. Given that fighting between the US and Iran could flare up again at any moment – and that the US army has nearly drained its interceptor stockpiles in the previous round – Washington cannot afford to enter the next round unprepared.
As much as the US would like to restrict China’s AI advance, doing so could be too costly for its own industry. Despite efforts to decouple, “Chimerica” – a term coined to describe the economic symbiosis between the two – is here to stay. The sooner Washington realises that the US needs China as much as China needs the US, the better – not just for both countries, but for the whole world, which could otherwise be caught in the crossfire when these two superpowers duel.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Disney appoints first-ever chief technology officer
articles.description: Disney appoints first-ever chief technology officer blooloop

articles.article_title: Disney appoints first-ever chief technology officer
articles.heading: Disney appoints first-ever chief technology officer
articles.summary: Media giant to focus on technology across segments
articles.content:
Disney has appointed Karandeep Anand as its first-ever chief technology officer as the company expands its focus on technology as a key growth driver.
Anand, who will also serve as the company's senior executive vice president, will oversee enterprise technology, infrastructure, data and AI platforms, product, and engineering across Disney’s segment technology teams.
"I’ve admired Disney my entire life for how it blends unforgettable storytelling with the latest technology to constantly push the boundaries of what entertainment can be," said Anand.
Karandeep Anand will serve as Disney's chief technology officer and senior executive vice presidentDisney
"I’m honored to join a team with such extraordinary creative talent, and I look forward to building on the company’s impressive technology capabilities to help Disney connect fans worldwide with its beloved stories and characters in new and innovative ways."
Anand, who most recently served as CEO of generative AI chatbot service Character.AI, will report to Disney's CEO Josh D'Amaro.
"Karandeep brings a rare mix of experience across infrastructure, consumer technology and AI, and will be a vital addition to Disney’s senior leadership team as we further our three priorities: great storytelling as our North Star, technology in service of creativity, and operating as One Disney," said D’Amaro.
"He is an expert builder and strategist, technical and product-minded, with sharp instincts for what fans actually want," D'Amaro added.
Disney expands tech push
"He also has real enthusiasm and respect for Disney, a clear sense of where technology and creativity meet, and shares our belief that technology creates the most value when it helps people do their best work.”
Before working at Character.AI, Anand was president and chief product officer of financial technology company Brex. He also served in leadership roles at Meta's Facebook and Microsoft.
Alongside Anand’s appointment, several members of Character.AI’s technical team are expected to join Disney.
His appointment also comes as Walt Disney World prepares to beta test a new AI-powered booking experience designed to help guests plan their Disney vacations.

articles.title: Las Cruces adds privacy rules to Flock camera contract
articles.description: Las Cruces adds privacy rules to Flock camera contract Las Cruces Sun-News
articles.description_html: Las Cruces adds privacy rules to Flock camera contract  Las Cruces Sun-News
articles.article_title: Las Cruces adds privacy rules to Flock camera contract
articles.heading: Las Cruces adds privacy rules to Flock camera contract
articles.summary: Las Cruces added restrictions to its Flock contract, but officials are pushing for broader surveillance oversight.
articles.content:
Las Cruces adds privacy rules to Flock camera contract
- Las Cruces has added new restrictions to its Flock Safety camera contract, including a ban on using data for AI training.
- A new public portal shows how police use the automated license plate readers, but councilors say it is not comprehensive enough.
- Councilor Michael Harris is proposing a broader surveillance ordinance to cover all technologies, not just license plate readers.
- Councilor Johana Bencomo expressed concern about how the parent company, Flock, protects data from vulnerable communities.
New restrictions were added to Las Cruces' Flock Safety contract, including a ban on using the data to train artificial intelligence systems, Las Cruces District 3 City Councilor Michael Harris said.
The changes also require the city to be notified of requests to disclose data collected through the system, Harris said.
In comments to the Las Cruces Sun-News, Harris said a broader approach is needed to require public input and Las Cruces City Council approval for surveillance technology beyond a new Flock transparency portal published by the city.
The Las Cruces Police Department announced the portal Sept. 15. The portal shows how law enforcement uses automated license plate readers and provides information about camera usage and searches.
While the portal is welcome, it covers only license plate readers, leaving other technologies, including drones and live-view cameras, outside its scope, Harris said.
A surveillance technology ordinance he is proposing would require privacy rules, data retention limits, safeguards against misuse, cost benefit reviews, transparency reports and public comment before council approval of new systems or continued use of existing ones, Harris said.
Systems should also undergo reviews every couple of years, or sooner after major software changes, because their capabilities can expand over time, Harris said.
“There should be a process to review approvals of systems every couple of years, or more often if there are substantial software changes, so the community can decide rather than have invasive features forced by companies,” Harris said.
Las Cruces District 4 City Councilor Johana Bencomo said the portal doesn't address concerns about how police collect and share data.
During a training session several weeks ago Bencomo and Harris learned how police use the Flock system, conduct audits and share data with other agencies, Bencomo told the Las Cruces Sun-News.
Flock cameras photograph the rear of vehicles, not drivers. The system does not use facial detection or provide live video, Bencomo said.
Out of state agencies granted access must sign an affidavit agreeing to follow New Mexico protections related to immigration, cannabis use and reproductive health care, Bencomo said.
Although she trusts LCPD’s internal safeguards, she remains concerned about the parent company and whether it protects vulnerable communities, Bencomo said.
“I continue to believe that the data most protected is the data not collected,” Bencomo said.
The portal should identify which agencies provide network data to LCPD, show the number of vehicles detected during the previous 30 days, offer a downloadable public search audit and link to the department’s license plate reader policy, Bencomo said.
Broader oversight should address surveillance across technologies and vendors, Harris said.
“Instead of playing whack a mole with every technology or vendor, Las Cruces should be ahead of the curve with a robust policy for protecting our community’s safety and privacy,” Harris said.
Andrea Marvez is the public safety reporter for the Las Cruces Sun-News. Reach her by email at amarvezsarquis@gannett.com or by phone at 575-541-5406. For more local news follow her on Instagram at @andreamarvez and on Facebook at @AndreaMarvez.

New restrictions were added to Las Cruces' Flock Safety contract, including a ban on using the data to train artificial intelligence systems, Las Cruces District 3 City Councilor Michael Harris said.

The changes also require the city to be notified of requests to disclose data collected through the system, Harris said.

In comments to the Las Cruces Sun-News, Harris said a broader approach is needed to require public input and Las Cruces City Council approval for surveillance technology beyond a new Flock transparency portal published by the city.

The Las Cruces Police Department announced the portal Sept. 15. The portal shows how law enforcement uses automated license plate readers and provides information about camera usage and searches.

While the portal is welcome, it covers only license plate readers, leaving other technologies, including drones and live-view cameras, outside its scope, Harris said.

A surveillance technology ordinance he is proposing would require privacy rules, data retention limits, safeguards against misuse, cost benefit reviews, transparency reports and public comment before council approval of new systems or continued use of existing ones, Harris said.

Systems should also undergo reviews every couple of years, or sooner after major software changes, because their capabilities can expand over time, Harris said.

“There should be a process to review approvals of systems every couple of years, or more often if there are substantial software changes, so the community can decide rather than have invasive features forced by companies,” Harris said.

Las Cruces District 4 City Councilor Johana Bencomo said the portal doesn't address concerns about how police collect and share data.

During a training session several weeks ago Bencomo and Harris learned how police use the Flock system, conduct audits and share data with other agencies, Bencomo told the Las Cruces Sun-News.

Flock cameras photograph the rear of vehicles, not drivers. The system does not use facial detection or provide live video, Bencomo said.

Out of state agencies granted access must sign an affidavit agreeing to follow New Mexico protections related to immigration, cannabis use and reproductive health care, Bencomo said.

Although she trusts LCPD’s internal safeguards, she remains concerned about the parent company and whether it protects vulnerable communities, Bencomo said.

“I continue to believe that the data most protected is the data not collected,” Bencomo said.

The portal should identify which agencies provide network data to LCPD, show the number of vehicles detected during the previous 30 days, offer a downloadable public search audit and link to the department’s license plate reader policy, Bencomo said.

Broader oversight should address surveillance across technologies and vendors, Harris said.

“Instead of playing whack a mole with every technology or vendor, Las Cruces should be ahead of the curve with a robust policy for protecting our community’s safety and privacy,” Harris said.

Andrea Marvez is the public safety reporter for the Las Cruces Sun-News. Reach her by email at amarvezsarquis@gannett.com or by phone at 575-541-5406. For more local news follow her on Instagram at @andreamarvez and on Facebook at @AndreaMarvez.

articles.heading: GlobalFoundries Finalizes $375M CHIPS Award for Quantum Technology R&D
articles.summary: GlobalFoundries and U.S. Commerce finalize a $375M CHIPS award for quantum R&D and domestic semiconductor manufacturing capabilities.
articles.content:
- September 21, 2026

- Capital Markets , National , Quantum Business

Insider Brief

- GlobalFoundries and the U.S. Department of Commerce finalized a $375 million CHIPS R&D award to support the company’s Quantum Technology Solutions business.

- The five-year award is tied to milestones and is intended to expand U.S.-based quantum semiconductor R&D and manufacturing capabilities.

- GF is focusing its quantum roadmap on cryogenic CMOS, advanced packaging and heterogeneous integration, alongside a separate $300 million silicon photonics R&D letter of intent.

PRESS RELEASE — GlobalFoundries (Nasdaq: GFS) (GF) today announced it has finalized a definitive agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce ’s CHIPS Research and Development Office for a $375 million award for research and development to accelerate the company’s Quantum Technology Solutions (QTS) business, designed to help scale domestic quantum semiconductor manufacturing and strengthen the United States’ leadership in quantum technologies.

The agreement advances the goal of establishing a secure, U.S.-based ecosystem for the development and manufacturing of quantum chips. Through Quantum Technology Solutions, GF is accelerating R&D and expanding access to advanced manufacturing capabilities and enabling quantum computing companies to move from research and prototyping toward commercial-scale production. Under the agreement, GF is eligible to receive up to $375 million in funding over a five-year period tied to the achievement of specified milestones.

“This is another important milestone for Quantum Technology Solutions and our efforts to build a scalable domestic quantum manufacturing ecosystem,” said Nicholas Sergeant, vice president and general manager of Quantum Technology Solutions at GlobalFoundries . “Since launching, we have expanded engagement with customers and ecosystem partners who are leveraging GF’s R&D and manufacturing expertise to address some of the industry’s most challenging scaling requirements. We’re grateful for the Department of Commerce ’s support as we continue building the foundation for a secure, domestic quantum manufacturing ecosystem.”

GF has continued to advance its quantum technology roadmap and deepen collaborations across the quantum ecosystem. The company’s efforts are focused on enabling the transition from research-driven innovation to scalable manufacturing through differentiated capabilities in cryogenic CMOS technologies, advanced packaging and heterogeneous integration, helping position GF as a foundry partner of choice for emerging quantum applications.

The completion of the agreement reflects continued progress toward establishing a robust U.S. quantum supply chain and expands GF’s broader efforts to advance critical semiconductor technologies. GF has also recently announced it has entered into a $300 million letter of intent with the Department ’s CHIPS Research and Development Office to accelerate R&D in silicon photonics. GF’s initiatives in quantum computing and next-generation optical connectivity are two technologies expected to be foundational to future AI infrastructure and advanced computing systems. GF is focused on continuing to strengthen its position as a trusted manufacturing partner for emerging technology innovators through investments in research.

articles.title: SK hynix Hosts ‘2026 Global Forum,’ Sharing Its Technology Vision and Future Strategy for the AI Era
articles.description: SK hynix Hosts ‘2026 Global Forum,’ Sharing Its Technology Vision and Future Strategy for the AI Era news.skhynix.com
articles.description_html: SK hynix Hosts ‘2026 Global Forum,’ Sharing Its Technology Vision and Future Strategy for the AI Era  news.skhynix.com
articles.article_title: SK hynix Hosts ‘2026 Global Forum,’ Sharing Its Technology Vision and Future Strategy for the AI Era | SK hynix Newsroom
articles.heading: SK hynix Hosts ‘2026 Global Forum,’ Sharing Its Technology Vision and Future Strategy for the AI Era
articles.summary: On the 18th (local time), SK hynix hosted its ‘2026 Global Forum’ at the Marriott Hotel in Santa Clara, California, US. SK hynix has held the forum every year since 2012 to introduce its technology vision and growth direction to
articles.content:
On the 18th (local time), SK hynix hosted its ‘2026 Global Forum’ at the Marriott Hotel in Santa Clara, California, US. SK hynix has held the forum every year since 2012 to introduce its technology vision and growth direction to global talent.
This year’s forum was attended by active professionals working at the forefront of the global AI and semiconductor fields, along with researchers from leading US universities, who saw firsthand the future blueprint SK hynix is drawing. From SK hynix, a large group of key executives — including CEO Kwak Noh-Jung and Ahn Hyun, President and Chief Development Officer — and working-level executives from each technology field also attended, engaging closely with the global talent set to lead technological innovation in the AI era.
Under the slogan ‘Share the Vision, Shape the Future, Together,’ the forum featured a General Session and Topic Round Table Sessions. The program focused on sharing
SK hynix’s technological capabilities, development roadmap, AI industry forecasts, and response strategies. To foster deeper discussions, a panel discussion was newly added to the General Session, and the Topic Round Table Sessions were structured as small-group seminars.
The forum opened with a keynote by CEO Kwak Noh-Jung, the first speaker of the General Session. CEO Kwak highlighted the technological leadership of SK hynix at the heart of the AI industry, as well as its elevated standing in the global semiconductor ecosystem – where the company is expanding its influence by growing production bases like the Yongin Cluster and the Indiana Fab, and establishing a new Global AI R&D Center in the US.
“Without memory, the AI industry cannot exist,” he said. “Just as we set a new milestone with HBM, we will continue to open up new possibilities for AI through the next-generation memory we are now preparing.” He added, “As the AI industry continues to grow, demand for AI memory will remain high. Keeping pace with this trend, we will solidify our current technological edge and overwhelming market dominance through our new global production hubs and R&D foundations.”
In the panel discussion that followed, deeper technological discussions took place, under the theme ‘At the Inflection Point of Technology, Opening the Next Chapter of Memory.’ Professor Sangwoo Jeon of UC Irvine served as moderator, with panelists Vice President Hyungsoo Kim, head of the DRAM Design department; Vice President Jaewon Lee, head of the AI Interface department; Vice President Kangwook Lee, head of the Package Development department; and Vice President Hoshik Kim, head of the Memory Systems Research department.
The panelists observed that the rapid advancement of AI is bringing a crucial turning point for the memory industry. Whereas individual technical fields previously focused on improving their own performance, connecting different technologies and finding solutions from a total system perspective will become far more critical moving forward.
The conversation also turned to the capabilities required for future engineers amid this technological change. Panelists predicted that it will become increasingly important for engineers to have deep domain expertise with understanding of adjacent technologies, and collaborate effectively with experts across various fields to solve problems together.
The final speaker of the General Session was Vice President Bogun Jin, head of the Corporate Culture division. Under the theme ‘Corporate Culture: The Source of SK hynix’s Technological Competitiveness,’ Jin introduced the company’s talent-centered philosophy and explained in detail the distinctive corporate culture that its management and employees are building together. “The strength that has allowed SK hynix to lead the AI memory market lies in an organizational culture that is both flexible and horizontal,” Jin stressed. “The one-team culture that brings together each individual’s capabilities to generate greater synergy, along with a culture that continually challenges itself to try new approaches, is likewise the foundation of our technological competitiveness.”
In the thematic round table sessions that followed, participants were first divided into active professionals and academic researchers, and then further grouped into four areas — Silicon Design, Process & Device, Advanced Package, and AI System. Across a total of eight sessions, small-group seminars were held together with SK hynix’s working-level executives. In the seminars for active professionals, participants actively exchanged views on current issues in memory technology in the AI era and on the direction of its future development. In the seminars for academic researchers, in-depth discussions were held on each researcher’s own field of semiconductor research.
On one side of the venue, an exhibition space was also set up to showcase SK hynix’s product portfolio and flagship technologies. The company displayed its flagship products leading the current AI ecosystem, such as HBM, as well as its next-generation memory solutions. This year’s forum also introduced a new space displaying research papers by SK hynix scholarship recipients published in top global academic conferences and journals.
This Global Forum was a meaningful occasion for SK hynix to share its technology vision and global growth strategy directly with the experts leading today’s AI industry and the global talent who will shape the future technology paradigm. Going forward, SK hynix will continue to engage actively with experts in the semiconductor and AI fields and to advance its technological innovation.

articles.title: Nvidia boss says there is ‘0% chance’ AI destroys the world by 2030
articles.description: Nvidia boss says there is ‘0% chance’ AI destroys the world by 2030 The Guardian
articles.description_html: Nvidia boss says there is ‘0% chance’ AI destroys the world by 2030  The Guardian
articles.article_title: Nvidia boss says there is ‘0% chance’ AI destroys the world by 2030
articles.heading: Nvidia boss says there is ‘0% chance’ AI destroys the world by 2030
articles.summary: Jensen Huang dismisses warnings from former Anthropic researcher and others as ‘doomsday narratives’
articles.content:
The boss of the chipmaker Nvidia has said AI will not develop to a point that will lead to the extinction of the human race within a few years, rejecting such assertions as overblown “doomsday narratives”.
Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the $5tn AI chipmaker, said the claims made on social media by the former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon that AI could become “superhuman” and kill off humanity within the decade were “irresponsible”.
“2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that’s going to be the end of the world,” Huang said in an interview with CBS News. “Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible.”
Coxon’s remarks, which were backed by two other researchers at the maker of the AI system Claude, prompted an international debate about the dangers and lack of oversight of AI as companies race to develop ever more powerful models.
US lawmakers have criticised AI companies over the risks and Anthropic published a threat intelligence report detailing how criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have tried to use its powerful AI models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and spy on dissidents.
Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, Sam Altman, the boss of the ChatGPT maker OpenAI, and Elon Musk have called for development of the technology to be slowed down.
However, Donald Trump has dismissed anxiety over the AI development as a “hoax” and a “conspiracy”, adding that a slowdown could give China the edge.
On Sunday, Scott Bessent, the US Treasury secretary, said the US and China had agreed to set up an AI dialogue mechanism to alert each other to help contain the technology’s potential dangers.
Huang said predictions of an extinction-level event caused by AI were “not grounded in science”.
Huang also claimed AI companies’ recent calls for national and international safety regulation aim to duck existing laws that would hold them to account.
Citing recent cases where AI companies including Anthropic and OpenAI triggered cybersecurity incidents during testing, he said there were plenty of laws to tackle the problems.
“You have cybersecurity unauthorised entry laws, you have damage liabilities … if your product does harm, if your product doesn’t perform as you promised, and if you entered into contracts with companies for service level agreements, there are plenty of laws associated with that. My point is, apply those first. And don’t let this doomsday narrative cause somebody to relieve them of the laws that currently exist.”
He continued: “Now, go and read between the lines. They’re actually not asking for more laws. They’re asking to be relieved of the laws we do have. And I think that’s a problem.”
On Monday the the Tony Blair Institute (TBI) thinktank published a paper arguing that countries risk “profound and compounding disadvantage” if they fail to embrace AI and fall behind other nations.
However, it also warned that the institutions meant to support the choices leaders would have to make were not equipped to do so.
“The previous [industrial] revolution transformed our world over generations, AI will do so within a decade,” said Tony Blair in a foreword to the paper. “New capabilities are emerging at an extraordinary pace, with profound implications for economies, education, science, labour markets, public services and national security. But the risks are equally profound and growing, and so too is public concern.
“Today’s political leaders… must make hard choices that will signficantly alter their countries’ trajectories. However, the institutions of the modern state meant to support political leaders in making these choices are simply not equipped for what is coming.”

articles.article_title: KMS Technology Introduces Troy Cantrell as Field CTO to Advance Enterprise Execution
articles.heading: Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: ATLANTA, September 21, 2026--KMS Technology names Troy Cantrell, a 25-year enterprise technology leader, as Field CTO to advance its Enterprise Execution strategy.
articles.content:
- NOW -2.17%

Cantrell will work with enterprise leaders and KMS delivery teams on Enterprise Execution: the discipline of turning AI-native intent into validated, production-ready outcomes

ATLANTA, September 21, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )-- KMS Technology , a global, AI-native technology services company, introduced Troy Cantrell as its Field Chief Technology Officer. In this role, Cantrell will work directly with enterprise leaders and KMS global delivery teams to advance the company's Enterprise Execution strategy: turning AI-native ideas into validated, production-grade business outcomes.

Cantrell brings 25 years of enterprise technology leadership spanning large-scale ERP programs, ServiceNow implementations, and AI and innovation initiatives. Throughout his career, he has focused on a consistent challenge: accountability for what happens after go-live.

"Across every major technology shift, the hardest work begins after the system goes live," Cantrell said. "With ERP, the question was whether the business could operate successfully once the implementation team left. With ServiceNow, it was whether people trusted the workflows enough to run their operations through them. AI is the latest and highest-stakes version of that challenge. Someone has to own whether AI actually works in production, under real conditions — not just in a demo."

Marvell to Showcase Industry-First 2nm Optical Technology Demos for AI Data Center Infrastructure at ECOC 2026
- First 2nm demos: Demonstrations of first 2nm 400G/lane optical PAM4, first 2nm 800G ZR/ZR+ pluggable with MACsec and first 2nm 1.6T ZR and O-band coherent-lite technologies.
- Enabling AI infrastructure scaling: Marvell advanced optical and silicon design leverages leading-edge process nodes to deliver the improvements in performance, bandwidth density and power critical to scaling AI infrastructure efficiently.
- Innovation on display at ECOC: Marvell to showcase the breadth of its comprehensive AI infrastructure portfolio through 38 advanced technology demos. These include the Marvell 102.4T co-packaged optics (CPO) platform, alongside additional demos developed with its partner ecosystem.
SANTA CLARA, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Marvell Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MRVL), a leader in data infrastructure semiconductor solutions, today announced industry-first 2nm optical interconnect demonstrations that advance the next generation of AI data center connectivity. The technologies will be showcased at the European Conference on Optical Communication (ECOC) 2026, September 20–24, 2026, in Málaga, Spain, underscoring how Marvell continually delivers new waves of advanced connectivity solutions to scale AI infrastructure.
As AI data center architectures scale from 1.6T to 3.2T and beyond, operators require faster, lower-power and more secure optical interconnects to serve AI scale-up, scale-out and scale-across domains. Increasing bandwidth density while reducing power per bit has become critical to scaling AI infrastructure efficiently.
Building upon a multi-generational history of industry firsts—including the first 5nm 200G/lane 1.6T Marvell® Nova DSPs in 2023, the 3nm 1.6T Ara platform in 2024 and the 2nm 800G Libra DSPs announced earlier this year—today Marvell is extending its portfolio of industry-leading 2nm connectivity solutions, including optical PAM4, coherent-lite PAM4/IMDD and ZR/ZR+ coherent solutions in the 2nm node. These technologies are optimized to enable ultra-high-speed interconnects that deliver faster communication between XPUs, CPUs, accelerators, and memory resources and improve energy efficiency to help data center operators manage the ever-increasing power demands of large AI deployments.
At ECOC 2026 Marvell will highlight:
- First 2nm 400G/lane optical PAM4 demonstration: Highlighting the company’s multi-generational PAM4 leadership, the technology provides low-power, ultra-high-speed optical connections to help scale AI infrastructure, enabling the transition to 3.2T data center connectivity.
- First live demonstration of 2nm 800G ZR/ZR+ with MACsec: Powered by the Marvell Libra 2nm coherent DSP, the 800G ZR/ZR+ OSFP pluggable integrates media access control security (MACsec), expanding the company’s extensive coherent DSP and Marvell COLORZ® pluggable portfolios, delivering efficient, high-performance and secure optical transmission for hyperscale AI and cloud data center networks worldwide.
- First 2nm 1.6T ZR and coherent-lite O-band demonstrations: The 1.6T ZR and 1.6T coherent-lite demonstrations are powered by next-generation Marvell DSPs announced earlier this year, optimized to deliver high-bandwidth connectivity within and between data center facilities and paving the way for 3.2T connectivity.
- Advanced CPO technology for next-generation AI fabrics: The Marvell CPO platform integrates optics directly with AI accelerators and switch silicon, as per-lane speeds and multi-rack AI pods push past copper’s reach limits. Demonstrated at 102.4 Tbps with 200G-per-lane silicon photonics, the platform delivers the bandwidth density and power efficiency needed to scale AI fabrics.
“AI data center operators need optical interconnect technologies that deliver higher bandwidth, lower power and greater security across every part of the network,” said Xi Wang, senior vice president and general manager, Connectivity Business Unit at Marvell. “These ECOC demonstrations highlight how Marvell continually pushes the envelope of what is possible in optical technology to help hyperscaler and cloud data center customers achieve new levels of performance, efficiency and scalability to drive new waves of innovation.”
Marvell Executive Presentations and Booth Demos at ECOC 2026
Marvell executives will also participate in presentations and panels on optical connectivity for next-generation AI data center infrastructure. This includes a fireside chat on new and emerging optical technologies with Senior Vice President and General Manager of the Connectivity Business Group Xi Wang, and sessions by several other Marvell experts. A full lineup of Marvell speaking sessions is available here.
In addition to industry-first 2nm demonstrations, Marvell will also showcase solutions across its AI infrastructure portfolio at ECOC (Booth # 2002), from 224G SerDes and 1.6T optics to coherent interconnects and optical memory fabrics.
To learn more or experience the technology demonstrations at ECOC 2026, contact your Marvell sales representative.
About Marvell
To deliver the data infrastructure technology that connects the world, we’re building solutions on the most powerful foundation: our partnerships with our customers. Trusted by the world’s leading technology companies for over 30 years, we move, store, process and secure the world’s data with semiconductor solutions designed for our customers’ current needs and future ambitions. Through a process of deep collaboration and transparency, we’re ultimately changing the way tomorrow’s enterprise, cloud and carrier architectures transform—for the better.

articles.title: ‘As dangerous as smoking’: Parents push districts, legislators to curb technology in education
articles.description: ‘As dangerous as smoking’: Parents push districts, legislators to curb technology in education NonDoc Media
articles.description_html: ‘As dangerous as smoking’: Parents push districts, legislators to curb technology in education  NonDoc Media
articles.article_title: ‘As dangerous as smoking’: Parents push districts, legislators to curb technology in education
articles.heading: ‘As dangerous as smoking’: Parents push districts, legislators to curb technology in education
articles.summary: Some parents are pushing Oklahoma school districts and legislators to evaluate the use of technology in education as concerns mount.
articles.content:
On the back of new warnings and a growing body of research, some parents want their local school district — and the Oklahoma Legislature — to set stricter limits on the use of technology in education, teeing it up as a leading topic of conversation among teachers, lawmakers and families.
Some legislators — who tried and failed to set a one-hour limit for elementary students last session — and education leaders emphasize the need to balance technology’s benefits and risks in classrooms. Former Secretary of Education Dan Hamlin said in a July interview that overuse of tablets, laptops and other tools has caught his attention.
“I have seen a lot of schools using the [tools] much more than what even the company has recommended. (…) And oftentimes, the research says even less than what the company is suggesting, when we have the research available,” said Hamlin, who departed the governor’s Cabinet and the University of Oklahoma for a job in Texas last month. “We have kind of sent out some guidance to some districts, and — I do not want to hit anyone on the way out the door — we have been working with folks to curtail that.”
Hamlin did not elaborate on which districts received guidance about reducing screen time.
Around the state, districts use technology in education for a variety of reasons, from supplementing instruction to administering assessments and even taking “brain breaks.” However, Oklahoma State Department of Education spokesperson Brenna Long said the agency does not distribute formal screen time guidance.
In the absence of state-level recommendations, some parents are pushing policymakers to create limits.
“They are saying it is as dangerous as smoking,” said Stillwater Public Schools parent Ryan Hendrix. “I do not blame the schools. I do not blame the teachers. I do not blame parents for going along with it. I feel like [the education technology industry] in general has misled the positive outcomes of the technology itself. But we need to wake up and realize that pen and paper is the better form of education.”
Hendrix is working with fellow Stillwater parent Emily Graham to seek changes through their group, Schools Beyond Screens, and they are not alone. Anonymized survey results in the district show other parents want to see action. The survey received about two dozen responses from Stillwater parents, many of whom indicated they would be interested in opting their student out of technology use in the classroom. Respondents shared a variety of concerns, including screen addiction and distraction from learning.
“My children each began public school with a passion for books and reading. Each year they fall further away from written literature. They have less patience for reading. Their attention spans are shorter, and they become obsessed with using tablets or Chromebooks,” one respondent wrote.
On Aug. 27, the group hosted a forum in Stillwater that featured several speakers, including SPS Superintendent Tyler Bridges. Graham said roughly 50 people attended.
“There were great questions from the audience which mainly focused on how [education technology] is used in Stillwater schools, how the district ensures data privacy and learning efficacy, what role the [technology] has in the classroom and what the outcome of tech use has been,” Graham said.
After the forum, Bridges told the Stillwater News Press that one of the platforms used by the district can measure individual screen time. Bridges said the district hopes “to be able to provide those reports to parents on a weekly or monthly basis.”
About 50 miles south in Edmond, a local attorney is advocating for changes to Edmond Public Schools’ technology policy.
During the district’s Aug. 3 board meeting, Katie Ogden Smith asked leaders to “thoughtfully reassess the role that technology plays in our classrooms.” She said new research suggests that technology can produce “harmful consequences for students.”
“Central to these concerns is that technology changes not just how students access information, but how they think. Screen-based learning tends to fragment attention. It prioritizes speed over depth and reduces opportunities for sustained focus. These are not minor side effects. These are the very things that education is meant to cultivate,” Ogden Smith said. “There is also increasing evidence that heavy reliance on screens contributes to rising levels of anxiety, distraction and social disconnection among students. Executive function — the very basis of cognitive memory — inhibition control and cognitive flexibility suffer.”
During an interview, Ogden Smith said a growing body of research should enable action.
“There is actual causation,” she said. “There is enough evidence to say that there is a causal link between the introduction of these educational technology programs and the introduction of Chromebooks and iPads to these declining test scores.”
Just outside of Edmond in Oakdale, attorney Lindsey Sherwood is working with Distraction-Free Schools, a national group with chapters in dozens of states pushing “legislative action and policy changes to address the overuse of smartphones, social media, and digital products in our nation’s schools.”
Sherwood said her child’s experience with technology in school inspired her to act. She said the use of technology forced adjustments to her parenting.
“Early on, when my son, my older son, started first grade, I think it was, he started talking about the iPad, and it was what we would talk about when he came home. It was what he would talk about as his favorite part of the school,” Sherwood said. “What we have observed over the years is that we have had to take a more intentional approach.”
Sherwood said she opted her eldest son out of technology use in class.
“That was kind of what started this grassroots effort that we have been working on for about a year and a half now,” Sherwood said, noting that she also has concerns about data privacy. “I mean, the breach of privacy is enormous, and it is so significant and problematic.”
In August, NBC News published a story about Amira, a literacy screen that is used in Oklahoma and nationwide. The outlet reported that privacy issues have become a growing concern among parents whose children use the platform at school.
‘Digital tools clash with the way human beings are built to learn’
Armed with a warning from the U.S. Surgeon General’s Office and a recently published book, parents are advocating for change around the country.

Horvath said technology can be beneficial for “intelligent tutoring systems” and “interventions for learning disorders.”

Fellow tech giant Microsoft recently announced that it will adopt guardrails and privacy standards for Microsoft AI tools used in schools.
In Philadelphia, parents are suing a school district in federal court after the district repealed an opt-out policy.
Sen. Ally Seifried (R-Claremore) met with Sherwood and seemed to agree with her assessment.

While he won’t be at the Oklahoma State Capitol in the spring, Hamlin expressed a need to correct course.

SANTA CLARA, Calif., September 21, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )-- Marvell Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MRVL), a leader in data infrastructure semiconductor solutions, today announced industry-first 2nm optical interconnect demonstrations that advance the next generation of AI data center connectivity. The technologies will be showcased at the European Conference on Optical Communication (ECOC) 2026, September 20–24, 2026, in Málaga, Spain, underscoring how Marvell continually delivers new waves of advanced connectivity solutions to scale AI infrastructure.

As AI data center architectures scale from 1.6T to 3.2T and beyond, operators require faster, lower-power and more secure optical interconnects to serve AI scale-up, scale-out and scale-across domains. Increasing bandwidth density while reducing power per bit has become critical to scaling AI infrastructure efficiently.

Building upon a multi-generational history of industry firsts—including the first 5nm 200G/lane 1.6T Marvell® Nova DSPs in 2023, the 3nm 1.6T Ara platform in 2024 and the 2nm 800G Libra DSPs announced earlier this year—today Marvell is extending its portfolio of industry-leading 2nm connectivity solutions, including optical PAM4, coherent-lite PAM4/IMDD and ZR/ZR+ coherent solutions in the 2nm node. These technologies are optimized to enable ultra-high-speed interconnects that deliver faster communication between XPUs, CPUs, accelerators, and memory resources and improve energy efficiency to help data center operators manage the ever-increasing power demands of large AI deployments.

At ECOC 2026 Marvell will highlight:

- First 2nm 400G/lane optical PAM4 demonstration: Highlighting the company's multi-generational PAM4 leadership, the technology provides low-power, ultra-high-speed optical connections to help scale AI infrastructure, enabling the transition to 3.2T data center connectivity.

First 2nm 400G/lane optical PAM4 demonstration: Highlighting the company's multi-generational PAM4 leadership, the technology provides low-power, ultra-high-speed optical connections to help scale AI infrastructure, enabling the transition to 3.2T data center connectivity.

- First live demonstration of 2nm 800G ZR/ZR+ with MACsec: Powered by the Marvell Libra 2nm coherent DSP , the 800G ZR/ZR+ OSFP pluggable integrates media access control security (MACsec), expanding the company's extensive coherent DSP and Marvell COLORZ® pluggable portfolios, delivering efficient, high-performance and secure optical transmission for hyperscale AI and cloud data center networks worldwide.

- First 2nm 1.6T ZR and coherent-lite O-band demonstrations: The 1.6T ZR and 1.6T coherent-lite demonstrations are powered by next-generation Marvell DSPs announced earlier this year , optimized to deliver high-bandwidth connectivity within and between data center facilities and paving the way for 3.2T connectivity.

- Advanced CPO technology for next-generation AI fabrics : The Marvell CPO platform integrates optics directly with AI accelerators and switch silicon, as per-lane speeds and multi-rack AI pods push past copper's reach limits. Demonstrated at 102.4 Tbps with 200G-per-lane silicon photonics, the platform delivers the bandwidth density and power efficiency needed to scale AI fabrics.

Demonstrated at 102.4 Tbps with 200G-per-lane silicon photonics, the platform delivers the bandwidth density and power efficiency needed to scale AI fabrics.

"AI data center operators need optical interconnect technologies that deliver higher bandwidth, lower power and greater security across every part of the network," said Xi Wang, senior vice president and general manager, Connectivity Business Unit at Marvell. "These ECOC demonstrations highlight how Marvell continually pushes the envelope of what is possible in optical technology to help hyperscaler and cloud data center customers achieve new levels of performance, efficiency and scalability to drive new waves of innovation."

Marvell Executive Presentations and Booth Demos at ECOC 2026

Marvell executives will also participate in presentations and panels on optical connectivity for next-generation AI data center infrastructure. This includes a fireside chat on new and emerging optical technologies with Senior Vice President and General Manager of the Connectivity Business Group Xi Wang, and sessions by several other Marvell experts. A full lineup of Marvell speaking sessions is available here .

Marvell to Showcase Industry-First 2nm Optical Technology Demos for AI Data Center Infrastructure at ECOC 2026

Business Wire
Sun, September 20, 2026 at 10:00 PM MST 5 min read
  • MRVL
    +1.45%

  • First 2nm demos: Demonstrations of first 2nm 400G/lane optical PAM4, first 2nm 800G ZR/ZR+ pluggable with MACsec and first 2nm 1.6T ZR and O-band coherent-lite technologies.

  • Enabling AI infrastructure scaling: Marvell advanced optical and silicon design leverages leading-edge process nodes to deliver the improvements in performance, bandwidth density and power critical to scaling AI infrastructure efficiently.

  • Innovation on display at ECOC: Marvell to showcase the breadth of its comprehensive AI infrastructure portfolio through 38 advanced technology demos. These include the Marvell 102.4T co-packaged optics (CPO) platform, alongside additional demos developed with its partner ecosystem.

SANTA CLARA, Calif., September 21, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Marvell Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MRVL), a leader in data infrastructure semiconductor solutions, today announced industry-first 2nm optical interconnect demonstrations that advance the next generation of AI data center connectivity. The technologies will be showcased at the European Conference on Optical Communication (ECOC) 2026, September 20–24, 2026, in Málaga, Spain, underscoring how Marvell continually delivers new waves of advanced connectivity solutions to scale AI infrastructure.

As AI data center architectures scale from 1.6T to 3.2T and beyond, operators require faster, lower-power and more secure optical interconnects to serve AI scale-up, scale-out and scale-across domains. Increasing bandwidth density while reducing power per bit has become critical to scaling AI infrastructure efficiently.

Building upon a multi-generational history of industry firsts—including the first 5nm 200G/lane 1.6T Marvell® Nova DSPs in 2023, the 3nm 1.6T Ara platform in 2024 and the 2nm 800G Libra DSPs announced earlier this year—today Marvell is extending its portfolio of industry-leading 2nm connectivity solutions, including optical PAM4, coherent-lite PAM4/IMDD and ZR/ZR+ coherent solutions in the 2nm node. These technologies are optimized to enable ultra-high-speed interconnects that deliver faster communication between XPUs, CPUs, accelerators, and memory resources and improve energy efficiency to help data center operators manage the ever-increasing power demands of large AI deployments.

At ECOC 2026 Marvell will highlight:

  • First 2nm 400G/lane optical PAM4 demonstration: Highlighting the company's multi-generational PAM4 leadership, the technology provides low-power, ultra-high-speed optical connections to help scale AI infrastructure, enabling the transition to 3.2T data center connectivity.

  • First live demonstration of 2nm 800G ZR/ZR+ with MACsec: Powered by the Marvell Libra 2nm coherent DSP, the 800G ZR/ZR+ OSFP pluggable integrates media access control security (MACsec), expanding the company's extensive coherent DSP and Marvell COLORZ® pluggable portfolios, delivering efficient, high-performance and secure optical transmission for hyperscale AI and cloud data center networks worldwide.

  • First 2nm 1.6T ZR and coherent-lite O-band demonstrations: The 1.6T ZR and 1.6T coherent-lite demonstrations are powered by next-generation Marvell DSPs announced earlier this year, optimized to deliver high-bandwidth connectivity within and between data center facilities and paving the way for 3.2T connectivity.

  • Advanced CPO technology for next-generation AI fabrics: The Marvell CPO platform integrates optics directly with AI accelerators and switch silicon, as per-lane speeds and multi-rack AI pods push past copper's reach limits. Demonstrated at 102.4 Tbps with 200G-per-lane silicon photonics, the platform delivers the bandwidth density and power efficiency needed to scale AI fabrics.

"AI data center operators need optical interconnect technologies that deliver higher bandwidth, lower power and greater security across every part of the network," said Xi Wang, senior vice president and general manager, Connectivity Business Unit at Marvell. "These ECOC demonstrations highlight how Marvell continually pushes the envelope of what is possible in optical technology to help hyperscaler and cloud data center customers achieve new levels of performance, efficiency and scalability to drive new waves of innovation."

Marvell Executive Presentations and Booth Demos at ECOC 2026

Marvell executives will also participate in presentations and panels on optical connectivity for next-generation AI data center infrastructure. This includes a fireside chat on new and emerging optical technologies with Senior Vice President and General Manager of the Connectivity Business Group Xi Wang, and sessions by several other Marvell experts. A full lineup of Marvell speaking sessions is available here.

In addition to industry-first 2nm demonstrations, Marvell will also showcase solutions across its AI infrastructure portfolio at ECOC (Booth # 2002), from 224G SerDes and 1.6T optics to coherent interconnects and optical memory fabrics.

To learn more or experience the technology demonstrations at ECOC 2026, contact your Marvell sales representative.

Through a process of deep collaboration and transparency, we're ultimately changing the way tomorrow's enterprise, cloud and carrier architectures transform—for the better.
