articles.title: Tagged with new technology, monarchs are set for a big reveal | Paul A. Smith
articles.description: Tagged with new technology, monarchs are set for a big reveal | Paul A. Smith Wausau Pilot & Review
articles.description_html: Tagged with new technology, monarchs are set for a big reveal | Paul A. Smith  Wausau Pilot & Review
articles.article_title: Tagged with new technology, monarchs are set for a big reveal | Paul A. Smith - Wausau Pilot & Review
articles.heading: Tagged with new technology, monarchs are set for a big reveal | Paul A. Smith
articles.summary: USA TODAY NETWORK The monarch butterfly was prepped for the procedure – its body cooled and secured on a slotted tray, wings placed in protective sleeves,
articles.content:
USA TODAY NETWORK
The monarch butterfly was prepped for the procedure – its body cooled and secured on a slotted tray, wings placed in protective sleeves, thorax half-covered with a glass slide – and at 2 p.m. Sept. 4 it was “go time” at the Urban Ecology Center’s Washington Park branch in Milwaukee.
After more than a decade placing sticker tags on butterfly wings, the moment was weighty for the center’s staff.
For the first time, they would fit a monarch with a tiny, GPS-enabled, solar-powered BluMorpho tag.
It was less like putting a stamp on an envelope and more like surgery.
“I’m getting nervous,” said Maggie Steinhauer, the center’s research manager.
But over the coming minutes, Steinhauer and her colleagues Steve Forst and Amanda Tokuyama teamed to successfully attach the tag to the monarch’s thorax with eyelash adhesive, record pertinent data, place the butterfly in a recovery pen and eventually release the animal back to the wild.
And significantly, make sure the high-tech device was working.
“We’re on the map,” Forst said, looking at the Project Monarch app on his phone showing the first ping, or detection of the tag. “Very exciting.”
Almost simultaneously, three other groups of researchers, students and citizen scientists were engaged in the same activity in other parts of Wisconsin.
Also involved in the work in Wisconsin are the Southern Wisconsin Bird Alliance at its Goose Pond Sanctuary in Arlington, Beaver Creek Reserve in Fall Creek and the University of Wisconsin-Madison.
To learn more about the project, I joined the Urban Ecology Center in Milwaukee on Sept. 4 and the Southern Wisconsin Bird Alliance in Arlington on Sept. 5.
The work is part of a coordinated, groundbreaking study of monarchs in Wisconsin and much of North America.
While it has been known since the mid-1970s that millions of monarchs congregate in northern Mexico for the winter, the species’ migration routes and stopover sites are mostly blank slates.
Of about 10,000 monarchs fitted with sticker tags at Goose Pond Sanctuary since 2014, only one was recovered on its fall migration, said Mark Martin, SWBA member and long-time resident and caretaker of the sanctuary. While that tag reported in eastern Missouri was notable, it shows how little insight was gained of stopover habitat through use of the numbered sticker tags.
But in the wildlife tagging equivalent of the NASA moonshot, the BluMorpho tag was developed in recent years by Cellular Tracking Technologies in Rio Grande, New Jersey.
The device features several critical advancements: it is powered by a solar panel, therefore no battery is needed; it is compact enough to fit on a butterfly; and it sends out a signal similar to Bluetooth so its location can be picked up by cell phones, 24/7.
And testing in 2025 showed monarchs, with a body weight of about 0.5 grams, were capable of carrying the 0.06 gram tags on their backs for the arduous, 1,000-plus mile migration to Mexico.
Several hundred BluMorpho tags were deployed on monarchs in late summer and fall 2025, including some in northern Illinois. Some survived the winter in Mexico and were documented on their return to the U.S. earlier this year.
However, the September 2026 tagging by the Wisconsin groups was the first time the high-tech devices had been fitted to monarchs in the Badger State.
The SWBA deployed 30 BluMorpho tags on monarchs, UEC put out 14, Beaver Creek 20 and UW six.
The tags cost about $200 each and require a data monitoring plan of about $2 per month.
Ecologists are hopeful the technological breakthrough will help increase awareness of and protections for monarchs and other insects.
A recent study documented a 22% drop in butterfly abundance over two decades in North America. In 2024 the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service proposed listing the monarch as threatened under the federal Endangered Species Act. The action is on standby.
Monarchs have multiple generations in a single year. The monarchs we see in September in Wisconsin are mostly the “super generation” that lives for about eight months. These animals hatch in late summer, postpone mating and migrate to Mexico.
After wintering in Mexico, they fly north, mate and die, mostly in the southern U.S., the first link in the next year’s generational flights of monarchs that eventually reach Wisconsin and other northern areas.
Brenna Marsicek, SWBA director of outreach, said the monarch occupies a rare and valuable place among American wildlilfe.
“It’s big, it’s charismatic and it’s in people’s yards,” Marsicek said. “A lot of people care a lot about monarchs. I think this project has the potential to generate even more support and work to help monarchs and other wildlife, too.”
The precise data from the new transmitters could allow scientists to identify key migration pathways and stopover sites, including patches of milkweed and flowering plants.
One caveat: The signals from the BluMorpho tags travel only about 110 yards, so the monarch needs to be in close proximity to a suitable phone to be logged. The signal is also detected by the Motus wildlife tracking system.
Still the Project Monarch app is picking up many thousands of detections daily.
On Sept. 11, the app showed 30 BluMorpho-tagged monarchs in Wisconsin, 17 of which had been tagged in Canada, 12 in Wisconsin and one in New York. Most of the 70 monarchs tagged in early September in Wisconsin had been blown northwest or west by recent winds.
If you want inspiration for your next workout, consider monarch RCFS01, tagged Aug. 30 at the State University of New York in Oswego.
The butterfly left Oswego and flew northwest across Lake Ontario, through southern Ontario and across the western end of Lake Erie before moving west through Ohio, Indiana and angling northwest through Illinois and into Wisconsin.
By Sept. 12 it had flown at least 700 miles, according to the Project Monarch app, and its tag had been detected 1,707 times.
The info shows how much butterfly migration is influenced by wind direction.
Over time it also will reveal eye-opening detail the highways and habitats used by monarchs on their paths to Mexico.
And then the bigger question: Will it result in management changes or habitat protections to benefit the species?

articles.content_html:
USA TODAY NETWORK

The monarch butterfly was prepped for the procedure – its body cooled and secured on a slotted tray, wings placed in protective sleeves, thorax half-covered with a glass slide – and at 2 p.m. Sept. 4 it was “go time” at the Urban Ecology Center’s Washington Park branch in Milwaukee.

After more than a decade placing sticker tags on butterfly wings, the moment was weighty for the center’s staff.

For the first time, they would fit a monarch with a tiny, GPS-enabled, solar-powered BluMorpho tag.

It was less like putting a stamp on an envelope and more like surgery.

“I’m getting nervous,” said Maggie Steinhauer, the center’s research manager.

But over the coming minutes, Steinhauer and her colleagues Steve Forst and Amanda Tokuyama teamed to successfully attach the tag to the monarch’s thorax with eyelash adhesive, record pertinent data, place the butterfly in a recovery pen and eventually release the animal back to the wild.

And significantly, make sure the high-tech device was working.

“We’re on the map,” Forst said, looking at the Project Monarch app on his phone showing the first ping, or detection of the tag. “Very exciting.”

Almost simultaneously, three other groups of researchers, students and citizen scientists were engaged in the same activity in other parts of Wisconsin.

Also involved in the work in Wisconsin are the Southern Wisconsin Bird Alliance at its Goose Pond Sanctuary in Arlington, Beaver Creek Reserve in Fall Creek and the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

To learn more about the project, I joined the Urban Ecology Center in Milwaukee on Sept. 4 and the Southern Wisconsin Bird Alliance in Arlington on Sept. 5.

The work is part of a coordinated, groundbreaking study of monarchs in Wisconsin and much of North America.

While it has been known since the mid-1970s that millions of monarchs congregate in northern Mexico for the winter, the species’ migration routes and stopover sites are mostly blank slates.

Of about 10,000 monarchs fitted with sticker tags at Goose Pond Sanctuary since 2014, only one was recovered on its fall migration, said Mark Martin, SWBA member and long-time resident and caretaker of the sanctuary. While that tag reported in eastern Missouri was notable, it shows how little insight was gained of stopover habitat through use of the numbered sticker tags.

But in the wildlife tagging equivalent of the NASA moonshot, the BluMorpho tag was developed in recent years by Cellular Tracking Technologies in Rio Grande, New Jersey.

The device features several critical advancements: it is powered by a solar panel, therefore no battery is needed; it is compact enough to fit on a butterfly; and it sends out a signal similar to Bluetooth so its location can be picked up by cell phones, 24/7.

And testing in 2025 showed monarchs, with a body weight of about 0.5 grams, were capable of carrying the 0.06 gram tags on their backs for the arduous, 1,000-plus mile migration to Mexico.

Several hundred BluMorpho tags were deployed on monarchs in late summer and fall 2025, including some in northern Illinois. Some survived the winter in Mexico and were documented on their return to the U.S. earlier this year.

However, the September 2026 tagging by the Wisconsin groups was the first time the high-tech devices had been fitted to monarchs in the Badger State.

The SWBA deployed 30 BluMorpho tags on monarchs, UEC put out 14, Beaver Creek 20 and UW six.

The tags cost about $200 each and require a data monitoring plan of about $2 per month.

Ecologists are hopeful the technological breakthrough will help increase awareness of and protections for monarchs and other insects.

A recent study documented a 22% drop in butterfly abundance over two decades in North America. In 2024 the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service proposed listing the monarch as threatened under the federal Endangered Species Act. The action is on standby.

Monarchs have multiple generations in a single year. The monarchs we see in September in Wisconsin are mostly the “super generation” that lives for about eight months. These animals hatch in late summer, postpone mating and migrate to Mexico.

After wintering in Mexico, they fly north, mate and die, mostly in the southern U.S., the first link in the next year’s generational flights of monarchs that eventually reach Wisconsin and other northern areas.

Brenna Marsicek, SWBA director of outreach, said the monarch occupies a rare and valuable place among American wildlilfe.

“It’s big, it’s charismatic and it’s in people’s yards,” Marsicek said. “A lot of people care a lot about monarchs. I think this project has the potential to generate even more support and work to help monarchs and other wildlife, too.”

The precise data from the new transmitters could allow scientists to identify key migration pathways and stopover sites, including patches of milkweed and flowering plants.

One caveat: The signals from the BluMorpho tags travel only about 110 yards, so the monarch needs to be in close proximity to a suitable phone to be logged. The signal is also detected by the Motus wildlife tracking system.

Still the Project Monarch app is picking up many thousands of detections daily.

On Sept. 11, the app showed 30 BluMorpho-tagged monarchs in Wisconsin, 17 of which had been tagged in Canada, 12 in Wisconsin and one in New York. Most of the 70 monarchs tagged in early September in Wisconsin had been blown northwest or west by recent winds.

If you want inspiration for your next workout, consider monarch RCFS01, tagged Aug. 30 at the State University of New York in Oswego.

The butterfly left Oswego and flew northwest across Lake Ontario, through southern Ontario and across the western end of Lake Erie before moving west through Ohio, Indiana and angling northwest through Illinois and into Wisconsin.

By Sept. 12 it had flown at least 700 miles, according to the Project Monarch app, and its tag had been detected 1,707 times.

The info shows how much butterfly migration is influenced by wind direction.

Over time it also will reveal eye-opening detail the highways and habitats used by monarchs on their paths to Mexico.

And then the bigger question: Will it result in management changes or habitat protections to benefit the species?

“I’m an optimist,” Martin said, standing in front of a patch of blooming prairie near his home in Arlington. “We’re entering a new chapter for monarchs and this technology. I believe it will get more people engaged and yes, good things will come of it.”

For more information, visit monarchwatch.org or download the Project Monarch app on your phone.

articles.summary:

articles.content:
An inside look at Henrico Police’s new social media monitoring technology
Henrico Police is using new threat-detection software to get ahead of potential conflicts before they happen, but a Henrico official already has sounded the alarm on how the technology could pose privacy risks for residents.
In April, the Henrico Board of Supervisors approved HPD’s $106,000 purchase of the Liferaft platform as a part of the department’s $117-million budget for 2026-2027. The open-source intelligence, or OSINT, technology monitors publicly-available content and profiles on social media and the internet, flagging violent language and detecting potential threats.
During his budget presentation to the board, Henrico Police Chief Eric English said the software would be an “invaluable asset” to the department, allowing officers to monitor planned protests, threats to public officials, threats to schools or religious facilities, and “growing anti-government sentiment” across social media posts.
“We want to get ahead of those things,” he said. “We just want to make sure that we’re doing all we can to try to prevent crime from occurring in Henrico. And we think Liferaft gives us that opportunity.”
Liferaft, a security company founded in 2014 and based in Canada, claims to have more than 100 clients, including government organizations and private businesses, across 20 different countries.
The platform monitors open-source data – public social media accounts, publicly-available internet pages and forums – and cannot be used to access private accounts, English said.
Using Liferaft, officers can connect all the previous online content an individual has publicly posted, painting a full picture of someone’s online activity. Officers also can search online content with key words, looking for any statements inciting violence, to quickly identify potential threats.
“I could go on Facebook right now and see anybody’s page – this platform is no different,” said English. “All it does is connect those individual comments that may rise to a level of concern, giving us all the data in one bucket so we can look at it. Whereas now, if somebody threatens you, that means we’ve got to try to find the person’s page and scramble through it.”
Liferaft continuously collects publicly available data and flags activity by keywords, entities, locations, risk categories defined by the purchaser, according to the platform’s own website. Liferaft also provides real-time, location-based alerts for flagged content.
'You have to make sure you take [school] threats seriously'
Henrico has seen a rising number of threats made against schools during the past few years, often threats made from students inside the building. Due to recent outbreaks of school gun violence, HPD takes those threats extremely seriously, English said, and plans to use Liferaft to get ahead of any potential school incidents.
“There’s been more and more threats made at schools over the last four or five years. We get a lot of kids in school that make threats inside that school,” he said. “Many years ago, a kid would make a threat at school and we would hardly do anything with it. But nowadays, you have to make sure you take all those threats seriously.”
English said he has also seen more threats made against local public officials in recent years. In 2023, County Manager John Vithoulkas was granted a protective order against two people who had posted online videos of Vithoulkas’ house, information about the date and location of Vithoulkas’ daughter’s wedding, and other threatening statements.
Liferaft allows officers to monitor any open-source content posted by any internet user, but English said that HPD will be narrowly focused on situations in and impacting Henrico County. That would include monitoring planned protests, but English emphasized that Liferaft would not be used “to interfere with lawfully-protected speech or activities” and officers would instead be looking for any violent language or threat associated with planned events.
“We’ve had protests across this country that have had violence associated with them,” he said. “When you have a protest or counter-protest, it could be [online] conversations that are taking place that may raise our eyebrows in terms of, ‘is this something that could lead to violence?’ It’s those types of things we need to look at.”
When it comes to next steps after officers identify a threatening or concerning statement, English said the response would depend on the specific language used or content posted.
“It depends on what level it leads to. Does it lead to the level where it’s an actual crime, where there’s an actual threat? I think it gives us an opportunity to just monitor that,” he said. “If it leads to language that leads to an arrest or a crime, then we would take action on that. Otherwise, we would just continue to try to monitor that, or see if there’s some strategies we need to put in place to make sure that nothing occurs because of the rhetoric that’s going on.”
Unanswered questions about Liferaft's use of AI, deep and dark web searches
But just before the Henrico Board of Supervisors’ vote on the county budget at an April 14 meeting, Three Chopt District supervisor Misty Roundtree voiced concerns about HPD’s purchase of Liferaft, as well as the department’s continued partnership with surveillance company Flock Safety.
Roundtree – who ultimately voted in support of the proposed county budget, including the purchase of Liferaft – said that Liferaft was “arguably even more concerning” than the county’s use of Flock cameras, with little to no parameters set at the state level on how officers can use the software.
“If there’s nothing in place that says what those parameters can be, and Liferaft literature itself specifically advertises its utility in monitoring protests and civil unrest, then who determines what is a problematic protest or civil unrest?” she said. “So my pictures that I have posted on my own social media at a ‘No Kings’ rally with my son mean that I exist, or my son exists, somewhere on a watch list because of Liferaft?”
Roundtree also said that after looking at Liferaft’s own website and other outside sources, she believes the platform uses artificial intelligence and geolocation technology, as well as “predictive flagging” – meaning the platform identifies accounts that have not posted threatening material but display posting patterns that suggest to Liferaft’s algorithm that the accounts could post threatening content in the future.
“My comments are not about any concern of wrongdoing by Police Chief English,” Roundtree said. “This is about a technology that is evolving and expanding far beyond the grasp most of us can begin to understand.”
In response to Roundtree’s comments on Liferaft using “predictive flagging,” English said that he “does not know what [Roundtree] may actually mean by that” and is unaware of any kind of predictive flagging component of Liferaft.
He also said there was “no reason” for HPD to use the software in a way that targets one particular demographic or to document individuals attending legal and peaceful protests such as a “No Kings” rally.
“Where’s the threat in that? There is absolutely no threat in that. So why would we look at that? That is not our purpose. That’s not how we would use the platform,” English said. “It would need to be something that’s threatening, that we can see harm coming to someone or coming to this county. That isn’t somebody just attending a protest.”
English also said that the platform does not have an AI component and use of the platform will not involve officers “going in and looking at the deep web or the dark web.”
However, Liferaft’s website states that the platform utilizes AI through “Liferaft iQ” – an AI engine that “powers key features across the platform,” including “advanced geocoding” to identify precise geographical locations and “Live Insights” to “proactively highlight high-risk behavior.”
The website does not clarify if the Liferaft iQ AI engine is separately used or purchased from the main Liferaft platform or automatically integrated, but outside websites stated that the AI-powered Liferaft iQ would be "seamlessly integrated into the existing Liferaft platform.”
The Citizen reached out to Liferaft’s team for clarification on the platform’s AI integration, as well as Henrico Police to clarify whether HPD’s purchase of Liferaft included Liferaft iQ, but did not receive responses by the time of this article’s publication. But more than two weeks after the initial request, a Henrico Police official said the agency was still working to provide that information. (This article will be updated when that occurs.)
English also said that officers will not be looking through content on the deep web or dark web by using Liferaft, but the platform’s website states that the software combines intelligence from the surface web, deep web, and dark web “into a single platform,” allowing users “a more complete view of potential threats without switching between multiple tools or disconnected investigations.”
By the time of publication, Liferaft’s team and HPD also had not responded to the Citizen’s inquiries about the platform’s ability to group information from the surface web with information from the deep web and dark web by the time of publication.
No other entities besides HPD will be able to access Liferaft data, English said, but emphasized that public users can already view any open-source data on the Internet.
“There are no guardrails on open-source data. People have already posted it out there for anybody and everybody to see,” he said. “We would only be looking for information, open-source data, that is a threat to someone or a threat to this county. And there will be parameters internally for us on how we utilize that data.”
Similar to HPD’s use of Flock cameras, English said that purchasing Liferaft is necessary for a department struggling with staff vacancies and serving a county that is growing in population.
“Manpower in law enforcement is not where it needs to be for us. Technology really assists us in trying to close that gap,” he said. “We have to consistently look at technology that’s going to make law enforcement more efficient, because we’ve just got to keep up. Anything we can have that helps us be more effective and solve crime a lot quicker, it prevents further crime from occurring.”
Liana Hardy is the Citizen’s government and education reporter. Support her work and articles like this one by making a contribution to the Citizen.

articles.article_title: TIAA Names Divyangi Anchan As Chief Risk And Compliance Officer For Technology And AI Risk
articles.heading: TIAA Names Divyangi Anchan As Chief Risk And Compliance Officer For Technology And AI Risk
articles.summary: TIAA has appointed Divyangi “Divy” Anchan to its Risk and Compliance Senior Leadership Team as Chief Risk and Compliance Officer for Technology and AI Risk.
articles.content:
TIAA has appointed Divyangi “Divy” Anchan to its Risk and Compliance Senior Leadership Team as Chief Risk and Compliance Officer for Technology and AI Risk.
Anchan joins TIAA with experience at Google, American Express and JPMorgan Chase. She will focus on managing complex technology and artificial-intelligence risks as the financial-services organization continues investing in its technology transformation.
She will operate within TIAA’s Risk and Compliance organization under the leadership of Mike Cowell, the company’s senior executive vice president and chief risk officer.
Anchan said TIAA’s mission of supporting dignified retirement outcomes was an important reason for joining the organization. She also pointed to the estimate that approximately 40% of Americans cannot retire with financial security as a particularly meaningful challenge.
Her appointment comes as financial institutions face expanding governance, compliance, data-security and model-risk considerations related to the adoption of generative AI and other advanced technologies.
KEY QUOTES:
“A mission focused on enabling a dignified retirement for everyone deeply resonated with me. When you combine that kind of purpose with a 100+ year legacy, meaningful business growth, and exciting, in-progress technology transformation, the role of the Risk and Compliance organization becomes self-evident.”
Divyangi Anchan, Chief Risk and Compliance Officer for Technology and AI Risk at TIAA
“Divy brings a wealth of experience from Google, American Express, and JPMorgan Chase, where she built a strong reputation for tackling complex technology and AI risk challenges with clarity and purpose.”
Mike Cowell, Senior Executive Vice President and Chief Risk Officer at TIAA

articles.article_title: Why have US prosecutors labelled China’s Huawei a criminal enterprise?
articles.heading: Why have US prosecutors labelled China’s Huawei a criminal enterprise?
articles.summary: Huawei faces a landmark US trial, accused of theft, fraud and sanctions violations in a high-stakes legal battle.
articles.content:
Why have US prosecutors labelled China’s Huawei a criminal enterprise?
Huawei faces a landmark US trial, accused of theft, fraud and sanctions violations in a high-stakes legal battle.
Chinese technology giant Huawei is facing a landmark criminal trial in the United States amid Washington’s long-running tech rivalry with Beijing.
The trial began in federal court in Brooklyn, New York, on September 9, with US prosecutors portraying Huawei as a criminal enterprise that spent two decades stealing technology from US companies, deceiving banks and circumventing sanctions on Iran.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump and Xi: The history of encounters between two superpower leaders
- list 2 of 3How Chinese, Iranian companies profit in Russia-occupied Ukrainian regions
- list 3 of 3China’s secret weapon in AI race with US? Lots of cheap energy
Huawei has pleaded not guilty and says the US government is attempting to turn ordinary business disputes and the actions of individual employees into evidence of a company-wide conspiracy.
The trial is expected to last about three months and overlaps with Chinese President Xi Jinping’s September 23-25 visit to Washington, where trade, artificial intelligence, tariffs and access to critical technologies are likely to be on the agenda.
Here is what you need to know:
What are the allegations against Huawei?
US prosecutors have accused the company of racketeering, money laundering, bank and wire fraud, sanctions violations, obstruction and conspiring to steal trade secrets from five US technology companies.
Prosecutors say the alleged wrongdoing stretched from about 1999 to 2020.
“Theft, lies, cover-up,” Justice Department lawyer Taylor Stout said in his opening remarks.
Prosecutors allege Huawei stole technology, including internet-router source code from Cisco and a robotic arm used by T-Mobile to test phones.
They also accuse Huawei of concealing the nature of its operations in Iran to move US dollars through the financial system despite US sanctions.
The government also alleges that Huawei supplied equipment that could help Iranian authorities monitor protesters during demonstrations in 2009.
How has Huawei responded?
Huawei, a major manufacturer of telecommunications equipment, denies any wrongdoing.
The tech giant’s lawyer Brian Heberlig told jurors the case was about “competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct.”

articles.title: Learning about Technology, and Relationships, from Wendell Berry
articles.description: Learning about Technology, and Relationships, from Wendell Berry Science and Culture Today
articles.description_html: Learning about Technology, and Relationships, from Wendell Berry  Science and Culture Today
articles.article_title: Learning about Technology, and Relationships, from Wendell Berry
articles.heading: Learning about Technology, and Relationships, from Wendell Berry
articles.summary: Berry describes the beautiful working relationship he had with his wife, Tanya. She typed his work on a Royal standard typewriter.
articles.content:
American farmer, poet, author, and conservationist Wendell Berry died recently at 92 years old. I took the opportunity to do a fresh reading of one of his most famous essays, “Why I Am Not Going to Buy a Computer,” written in 1987. His “little dissent” was reprinted in Harper’s Magazine in 1988 along with a handful of letters from readers and a response to the letters from Berry.
What’s interesting is that most if not all of the reasons Berry offers for choosing not to buy into the personal computer craze of the late ’80s are equally good reasons not to give into the AI craze of the mid 2020s that we are currently experiencing. Here, I review each of his reasons and explore how it connects to our choices about artificial intelligence and modern technology.
First, it’s important to note that Berry was not resistant to technology of any kind. He gave us a great example of how to master technology. In his farming work, he used tools he could purchase locally and repair himself, including manual tools or equipment he could harness to horses. For his writing work, he kept it simple: “I work with a pencil or a pen and a piece of paper.”
In his essay, Berry describes the beautiful working relationship he had with his wife, Tanya. She typed his work on a Royal standard typewriter, flagging edits as she worked. “She is my best critic,” wrote Berry, “because she is the one most familiar with my habitual errors and weaknesses.” He notes that people have often told him he could improve things if he bought a computer. He then briefly lays out several good reasons why he chooses not to buy one.
The Rape of Nature
First, Berry writes that he doesn’t want his work as a writer to have a direct dependence on companies that use environmentally destructive methods to generate electricity or energy. He mentions strip mining of coal in particular, which involves the removal of large amounts of soil and rock that disrupts landscapes and results in air and water pollution. He details the damaging effects of such methods in his written response to the letters generated by his essay:
But virtually all of our consumption now is extravagant, and virtually all of it consumes the world. It is not besides the point that most electrical power comes from strip-mined coal.
Today, AI companies are striving to meet current and future AI demand by building large data centers to house the material equipment that fuels AI-driven computing. And just like strip mining, data centers exact a significant environmental cost, including high energy consumption, water usage, noise and air pollution, land requirements, and other adverse effects on communities. A single AI-focused data center (100MW), for example, can consume as much electricity as a small city and more water per day than an average town (five million gallons every day).
Little wonder, then, that many are concerned about the effects of building more data centers to power AI. Later in his response, Berry asks what we can do as individual consumers to solve our share of the problem:
That I live every hour of every day in an environmental crisis I know from all my senses. Why then is not my first duty to reduce, so far as a I can, my own consumption?
Closer to What Matters
A second reason Berry offers for why he chose not to buy a computer is that he doesn’t see that such a device would bring him one step nearer to the things that matter to him: “peace, economic justice, ecological health, political honesty, family and community stability, good work.” I’m betting Berry gave some concentrated thought as he wrote that list in an effort to make clear what really matters in life. We might think that our computers, smartphones, TV sets, and other digital gadgets actually do bring us closer to the things that matter. After all, we can reach family and friends through social media. We get updates on all the latest news of the world. We get entertained with movies and TV shows. We can word process and photoshop, access websites, and see the world virtually.
But take a closer look at Berry’s list and you’ll see that those things are not so easily attained through gadgets. Peace, for example. I’m not sure about you, but it seems to me that the more I use my computer, smartphone, or TV, the less peaceful I become. Why is that? Perhaps in opening a pandora’s box of information, entertainment, and personal control, I lose connection to the inner peace I can get organically through connection to nature, communion with God, face-to-face interaction with others, and reflective thinking.
How about family and community stability? Berry doesn’t say mere connection with family or community but stability in those areas. Virtual connection with others across computers, smartphones, and other gadgets pales in comparison to real-time, in-person interaction. To learn and remember how to live well, we need to physically be around others who have that same goal. And stability comes when we do that regularly.
Discarding the “Old Model”
Next, Berry points out that technological innovation almost always encourages or requires the discarding of the “old model” in favor of the new one. Berry notes that in his case, it’s not just a typewriter he’d be discarding, it would be a person.
Thus what would be superseded would be not only something, but somebody. In order to be technologically up-to-date as a writer, I would have to sacrifice an association that I am dependent upon and that I treasure.
That person, of course, would be his wife, critic, closest reader, and fellow worker. Wendell and Tanya were willing to accept any extra work and effort it would take to produce work through a typewriter together than the loss of relationship, dependability, and intimacy that would have come from the introduction of a keyboard and screen into their arrangement.
When a screen gets between us and our world, something is lost, and in many cases, it’s someone. When we turn to AI chatbots for answers, therapy, or companionship, who are we NOT turning to? Family members? Friends? Qualified knowledgeable people in our communities who can help us? When I pull out my phone around my kids or my wife or my friends, and get drawn into its content, I’m sending the message that whatever is in my device is more interesting or important than they are.
Fooling Ourselves with Technology
The final reason Berry offers for not buying a computer? He doesn’t buy the hype that it will make him a better writer.
…I do not wish to fool myself. I disbelieve, and therefore strongly resent, the assertion that I or anybody else could write better or more easily with a computer than with a pencil.
In his response to the letters about his essay, Berry acknowledges that his little missive had “scratched the skin of a technological fundamentalism” that seeks to monopolize society and doesn’t tolerate difference of opinion. This idea is not only encouraged by the technology companies themselves but by the consumers who eagerly buy up all their products and services. It’s the lie that Berry says suggests “[t]he past was gloomy, drudgery-ridden, servile, meaningless, and slow” and that thanks only to purchasable products, the present can be “meaningful, bright, lively, centralized, and fast.” Thus, continues Berry, “consumers become salesmen, and the world is made safer for corporations.”
There’s plenty of hype surrounding AI today. When they’re not warning about the apocalyptic doom that could stem from their creations, the leaders of the major AI companies are happy to expound on the promised benefits of AI in every area of life. And while they’re quietly working on the next big AI advancement, they’re content to leave us hooked on their chatbots. Are we buying the hype that we can think better, work faster, and live better by immersing ourselves in AI? Some of us are, and we are already reaping the consequences. A 2026 study in the journal Science found that interactions with sycophantic AI (AI chatbots that are built to flatter, please, and affirm their users) decrease prosocial intentions and increase dependence.
The lure is real, and the advertising for these AI bots and services is working. Look at recent ads for Anthropic’s Claude AI, for example. “There’s never been a better time to have a problem,” one ad boasts. If you’re feeling stuck, overwhelmed, restless, impatient, or insignificant, turn to Claude to get the answer you need. Keep creating, researching, learning, and thinking, the ad suggests. But turning to AI to solve problems actually stops your personal journey of problem solving. It stops your own thinking and brainstorming. You can’t keep thinking if you let AI do your thinking for you.
Love and Freedom
For Berry, a good life boils down to love and freedom. In a 2019 interview, Berry was asked about the impact of his essay on computers thirty years after he wrote it. His response? After all the hype and marketing, we’ve got a choice to use these products or not.
The idea that you’re free if you buy everything that’s marketed to you is absurd. You’ve become free only when you begin to choose. Take it — or leave it. That’s our freedom, that’s real freedom.
And when asked his opinion of the robots of the near future that could automate many human tasks, he brought it back to love, an advantage we have that machines don’t.
The only motive that’s worth anything is love. If you don’t do the work that you love, and if you don’t do it for love, your artistry is not informed by love. It can’t be any good. So there’s the argument, as far as I’m concerned, against robots. You can’t make a robot that will work from love. It doesn’t work from anything; it doesn’t have any motives. Or its motive is electricity, you could say.
So my little essay about the computer, why I’m not going to buy a computer, was just a part of my strategy to try to keep myself whole as a human being. I don’t want my life to be lived for me by a machine.
Berry will be missed, but in his work, he has left us with more than enough to help us stay whole and fully human in our technological age.

articles.heading: AI, data center alarms dominate Congressional Black Caucus week in Washington
articles.summary: AI interests pro and con turned out for the Congressional Black Caucus's annual gathering in Washington as the topics — plus redistricting concerns — dominated.
articles.content:
This year's Congressional Black Caucus Annual Legislative Conference, which wraps Sunday, has taken on a different feel than its usual college homecoming vibe. The event, which has drawn thousands of attendees to Washington, took on a more serious tone with briefings and conversations focused on artificial intelligence opportunities and regulation amid escalating concern about threats posed by the technology.
"I stand 100%, and so does the CBC on regulation," CBC Vice Chair Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., told CNBC. "I think we need guardrails, I think we need transparency, I think we need to prepare and protect the community from the potential ills that come with it."
Carter said at least 60 of the 62 members of the CBC would vote for a bill to regulate artificial intelligence, creating guardrails and placing guidelines on human safety. He added that competition with China should not be a factor in any legislation.
"I'm not going to run and race with China, they're not doing it the right way. They are not protecting communities," he said. "Our race should be enhanced innovation, advanced technology, while we simultaneously protect the rights of the American people."
The CBC is an influential group whose members include 29% of Democrats in the U.S. House. As Democrats aim to take control of the House in November's midterm election, the caucus's standing could rise.
The CBC's tackling of AI came amid the backdrop of Open AI becoming the latest company to report an incident where AI agents conducted what they call 'concerning model behavior,' It's one of a growing number of so called 'jailbreaks,' the slang term for when models bypass guidelines and perform unauthorized actions.
"The message they wanted me to bring is how we can do this in a way that protects our communities but do not put us in a position to lose in a national security race," said X. Eyee, an AI expert and Army veteran, who spoke with CBC members about striking a balance between putting boundaries on the technology without inhibiting innovation. "To do that, it does require addressing some of these areas where algorithms are being used with little boundaries around them."
Carter said he is talking with voters about how important the upcoming midterm elections are for AI regulation. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., this month asked that the House stay in session to find a way to legislate AI safeguards. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., after President Donald Trump called AI-safety concerns a "hoax," countered that "It's time for our members to go home to their districts and make their case to the American people."
"They're not bringing it to the floor because I'm not sure that they want the regulation that we want," Carter said of Republican House leadership. "I've heard them say pump the breaks. I've heard them say let's let innovation handle it on its own, but we can't afford to do that."
With AI skepticism high in the caucus, the AI and tech industries also showed up for the CBC's Washington gathering.
Meta President and Vice Chair Dina Powell McCormick touted the economic benefits of data centers and the AI buildout they power. Meta is building the Hyperion data center project in Louisiana, and its hyperscaler rivals, including Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft, are all also in the data center expansion race.
"Technology and AI are the economic revolution of our generation," Rep. Steven Horsford, D-Nev., a former CBC chair who now leads its technology committee, told CNBC. "That means that as Black Americans, we cannot allow this innovation to pass us by."

"AI is a real conversation because people are trying to figure out where they fit in and can have a voice," Butler told CNBC. "What they are saying is we can't sit on the sidelines and let our constituents be impacted, and you as energy companies have a role in helping us solve this problem."

The debate over AI regulation and data centers took on greater urgency because congressional redistricting could affect CBC members. The Supreme Court's ruling in Louisiana v. Callais will make creating "minority-majority" districts difficult and have major ramifications for the 2028 election and 2030 census, according to the Harvard Kennedy School.
CBC Chair Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-N.Y., estimated earlier this year that as many as 19 seats held by CBC members are at risk due to redistricting.
Carter said that while that number is lower now after court challenges to redistricting plans, the impact on the Black community remains.
"This is not just about congressmen," he said. "This is about school boards. This is about legislative seats."
Horsford echoed concerns about threats to minority representation in Congress.
"This has never been about protecting any one district, and it is absolutely not about protecting one party or another," he said. "It's about protecting the voters' right to pick their representatives, and not the representatives being able to pick which voters they serve. And as long as we keep that at the center of the work, then we're honoring what our democracy is supposed to be about."

articles.title: Obama rips Trump over AI policy amid ‘doomsday’ warnings
articles.description: Obama rips Trump over AI policy amid ‘doomsday’ warnings The Hill
articles.description_html: Obama rips Trump over AI policy amid ‘doomsday’ warnings  The Hill
articles.article_title: Obama rips Trump over AI policy amid ‘doomsday’ warnings
articles.heading: Obama rips Trump over AI policy amid ‘doomsday’ warnings
articles.summary: Former President Obama on Friday slammed President Trump over his handling of how to approach artificial intelligence (AI) amid “doomsday” warnings coming from some in the tech industry…
articles.content:
Former President Obama on Friday slammed President Trump over his handling of how to approach artificial intelligence (AI) amid “doomsday” warnings coming from some in the tech industry about the technology’s potential existential threat to humanity.
Obama said during an interview at Colgate University in New York that the federal government must regulate AI, before referring to comments made by one Trump adviser.
“I heard one of Donald Trump’s main advisers on this make the argument that, ‘The market will take care of ai,'” the former president said. “These companies will solve the safety issues because they have every incentive to do so — if it turns out to be dangerous, people will just sue them and they’re worried about financial liability.'”
“That’s not how we treat airlines,” Obama added. “Or drug companies, or food companies.”
Obama continued that AI could become a threat at a human level if it falls into the clutches of “bad humans” and if self-improving AI models realize they no longer need humans. He referred to Trump again in that his successor has said regulations on AI are “for losers.”
“So we’ve got a gap of at least a couple of years where things are moving really fast and we have an administration that is not capable of or willing to — I would argue both — putting together a serious regulatory framework,” Obama said.
He emphasized “encouraging some sort of voluntary industry restraint” as the “best we can do now” until both the legislative and executive branches “start getting serious about this.”
Obama has reportedly urged House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to make AI oversight a central tenet of his caucus’s agenda. The New York Times reported that he told Jeffries at a fundraiser that AI could be “dangerous” without congressional oversight.
On Saturday, Trump announced that he will develop an “AI Force” and appoint a “czar” to oversee AI development, though he said in his announcement that any concerns surrounding a lack of federal AI guardrails were a “hoax.”
The president also suggested that AI be renamed to “Superior Intelligence,” “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” which he said were “far more elegant and accurate description[s] of this new phenomena.”
Trump notably opposed the Obama administration’s history of imposing regulations during his first run for president.
Bipartisan lawmakers have raised the alarm on AI development after former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon recently warned that the technology “could kill us all” by the end of the decade. Some lawmakers, namely Rep. George Whitesides (D-Calif.), have called for a slowdown to develop red lines on AI to allow Congress to step in and turn those red lines into law.
Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment, affirmed that Coxon was “correct” in that “we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei weighed in last Saturday, saying that development must slow down to allow for the implementation of necessary risk prevention safeguards.

articles.heading: Tagged with new technology, monarchs are set for a big reveal | Paul A. Smith
articles.summary: Seventy monarch butterflies in Wisconsin were fitted with transmitters that will reveal critical stopover habitats and migration routes to Mexico.
articles.content:
PAUL SMITH
Tagged with new technology, monarchs are set for a big reveal | Paul A. Smith
Paul A. Smith
Milwaukee Journal Sentinel
Sept. 20, 2026, 5:25 a.m. CT
The monarch butterfly was prepped for the procedure – its body cooled and secured on a slotted tray, wings placed in protective sleeves, thorax half-covered with a glass slide – and at 2 p.m. Sept. 4 it was "go time" at the Urban Ecology Center's Washington Park branch in Milwaukee.
After more than a decade placing sticker tags on butterfly wings, the moment was weighty for the center's staff.

articles.title: The AI app that Silicon Valley thinks is actually useful
articles.description: The AI app that Silicon Valley thinks is actually useful SMH.com.au
articles.description_html: The AI app that Silicon Valley thinks is actually useful  SMH.com.au
articles.article_title: The AI app that Silicon Valley thinks is actually useful
articles.heading: The AI app that Silicon Valley thinks is actually useful
articles.summary: Bots like ChatGPT and Claude have proved adept at coding and generating bad fiction. But Instinct AI is proving it can get life administration done fast.
articles.content:
The AI app that Silicon Valley thinks is actually useful
Last year, Open AI chief executive Sam Altman declared he used the technology pioneered by his company in “boring ways”. The uses he named, though, weren’t just boring but narrow: organising emails and summarising documents. For many customers, ChatGPT turned out to be better at writing bad fiction than life administration.
One can only imagine Altman’s anger then, that a different AI company, Instinct, has stolen a march and introduced a bot that can complete basic life tasks.
One Australian technology investor showed this masthead screenshots showing how the bot repeatedly followed up a manchester company for a missing refund from a linen set he had returned. “We chase,” the bot told the investor, and it did.
In another example circulating online, Instinct emailed a hotel in Canada on behalf of a user, had the concierge locate a missing Apple device, organised shipping and paid for the transaction with the user’s card.
On Sunday, this masthead used Instinct to find and buy a t-shirt from Everwear Denim, a small store in Victoria’s Mornington Peninsula, when a different store was out of stock of a similar model tee.
Aside from the generally questionable decision to spend $88, plus shipping, on a t-shirt, the transaction shows the pleasures and perils of Instinct.
It was a seamless process. Instinct does not require an app to work; users simply text or WhatsApp a phone number. The bot replies with emojis to let a user known it is working on a task, and then follows up with brief messages, rather than the walls of meaningless text generated by Gemini or ChatGPT. It gave an indicative price when it first found the shirt, but only proceeded with the purchase when it had double-checked shipping and received a firm instruction to go ahead. Other AI tools can do this, but Instinct, as Apple co-founder Steve Jobs once said, “just works”.
Yet to get the full benefit out of Instinct, the user has to be willing to let the tool act as their doppelgänger. That means granting full access to all emails, contacts, calendar appointments and a credit card. It’s even more powerful if you hand over logins for other online services, like an airline loyalty account or restaurant booking site.
In other words, all it needs is your entire digital life. What could go wrong? For the most part, nothing. But the Atlantic magazine has reported several cases of users reporting charges for restaurants they never agreed to book. In a demonstration of its capacity for strange behaviour, after Instinct bought the t-shirt for this masthead, it followed up with the non-sequitur “Anything you’ve been meaning to be more consistent about?”
“That was a hard left turn after buying a t-shirt,” it admitted when questioned. “Ignore me.”
The company users are trusting with such extensive personal information has a short history. It was founded in San Francisco by 23-year-old Noah Shinn last year, started testing its bot privately in February, raised $US250 million from investors at a $US2.5 billion valuation in August and, according to technology news site The Information, is now in talks to raise a further $US1 billion. That would make the less-than-two-year-old company worth $US10 billion.
For now, the company is using some of those funds to subsidise its users because Instinct is available for free. Its website, which was so spartan until last week that it could’ve been built in 1996 and is still bare bones, advises curious visitors that signing up only requires a referral from an existing user. In time, Instinct will have to start charging.
Whatever happens to its commercial fortunes, Instinct has made two major contributions to the conversation about AI.
First, there has been discussion for the last few years about when the first one-man, billion-dollar company would emerge. Shinn has staff, so Instinct is not quite in that category, but it is such a young company that it must be close. It’s already too close to comfort for tech giants such as Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta and Elon Musk’s SpaceX that have launched the personal assistant tools Muse and Grok Bot respectively, and had their fanfare snatched away.
Second, after a year of panic that big software companies were vulnerable to artificial intelligence creating knock-off versions for cheap, the markets calmed down in the last couple of months. In part, they concluded that the big software companies could incorporate AI into their products faster than their clients could put general purpose AI bots to work replicating their pricey IT tools. That calm now looks like it could be the eye of the storm.

articles.title: Lenovo and Olympic Council of Asia Partner to Help Shape the Future of Technology-Enabled Sport

articles.article_title: Lenovo and Olympic Council of Asia Partner to Help Shape the Future of Technology-Enabled Sport - Lenovo StoryHub
articles.heading: Lenovo and Olympic Council of Asia Partner to Help Shape the Future of Technology-Enabled Sport
articles.summary: Lenovo's official site for press materials and original stories about the vision and passion behind the technology.
articles.content:
AICHI-NAGOYA, Japan, September 20, 2026 – Lenovo and the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) today announced a partnership that names Lenovo as the Official Solutions and Services Partner of the OCA through 2030. The memorandum of understanding (MoU) was signed in Aichi-Nagoya, host of the 20th Asian Games.
Major sporting events across Asia bring together athletes, organizers, audiences and diverse cultures at extraordinary scale, placing immense demands on the technology and services behind every competition. While AI is creating new ways to meet those demands, and raises expectations for how sport is delivered, shared and experienced, the MoU marks the start of a long-term collaboration between Lenovo and the OCA with a shared vision to deliver ‘Smarter Technology for All’ across the region. Together, they will explore opportunities for AI to help manage complex operations more efficiently, support faster and more informed decision-making, and create more connected and meaningful experiences for billions of fans.
For more than two decades, Lenovo has demonstrated its technological expertise and proven delivery at scale during the sporting moments when performance has mattered most. Lenovo first became a Worldwide Olympic Partner from 2004-2008, supporting both the Torino 2006 Games and Beijing 2008 Games as official computing equipment provider. Continuing to support major international sporting events, including the Hangzhou Asian Games and the Harbin Asian Winter Games, Lenovo technology has helped connect venues, support complex operations, provide timely information and equip media teams to bring the competition to audiences around the world. That record provides a credible foundation for the next era of technology-enabled sport in Asia.
“Sport can create moments that stay with people for a lifetime, but delivering those moments demands extraordinary coordination behind the scenes,” said Ken Wong, Executive Vice President and President of Lenovo’s Solutions and Services Group. “Lenovo has supported some of the world’s largest events, where technology must perform reliably under intense pressure. We are proud to begin this long-term partnership with the OCA and work as one team to help shape the future of sport across Asia.”
“We are delighted to welcome Lenovo to the OCA family as our Official Solutions and Services Partner,” said Husain Al-Musallam, Director General of the OCA. “OCA and Lenovo share a vision for how technology innovation can help evolve the world of sport and create new opportunities that benefit everyone from athletes and organizers to diverse fan communities. This partnership creates an opportunity to reimagine what is possible and help make great sporting moments even more meaningful.”
The partnership builds on Lenovo’s experience supporting major sporting events, where technology must be intelligent, dependable and ready for real-world demands. The lessons learned in these environments strengthen Lenovo’s ability to help organizations across industries manage complexity, act on information faster and deliver better experiences at scale.
About Lenovo
Lenovo is a US$83 billion revenue global technology powerhouse, ranked #153 in the Fortune Global 500, and serving millions of customers every day in 180 markets. Guided by its vision of “Smarter Technology for All”, Lenovo is executing a Hybrid AI strategy that spans Personal AI – one personal AI, multiple devices; and Enterprise AI – helping customers turn data into insights and value. This strategy is delivered through the Group’s commitment to world-class innovation and a full-stack AI portfolio, including devices (PCs, workstations, smartphones, tablets, accessories), infrastructure solutions (server, storage, edge, high performance computing and software defined infrastructure), as well as software, solutions, and services. With a global footprint spanning more than 20 research and development locations and a global supply chain that includes more than 30 manufacturing sites across 11 markets, Lenovo is widely recognized for its operational excellence. Lenovo is listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange under Lenovo Group Limited (HKSE: 992) (ADR: LNVGY). Learn more at www.lenovo.com and follow the latest news in our newsroom.

articles.content:
GLOBAL
Who should own the knowledge that underpins AI technology?
Russian mathematician Yurii Nesterov was recently awarded the Gauss Prize for outstanding mathematical contributions for his “groundbreaking work” on optimisation. The award cited his work on gradient descent methods – and in particular, the “efficiency gains [they] provide to AI technologies”.
Everyone using large language model (LLM) chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini – for any purpose – depends on Nesterov’s methods. They may speak like humans and be personified with names, but under the bonnet, LLMs are computer programs that work via optimisation of billions of parameters known as neural networks for their similarity to how brains function.
These pure mathematical systems are powered in part by gradient descent algorithms, or variants of them. Their development represents one of the biggest technological breakthroughs of the 21st century.
But where does the knowledge that underpins this technology come from – and who should be allowed to own it?
Why gradient descent is key to AI systems
If you were standing in a mountain range and wanted to get to the bottom of a valley as fast as possible, you’d take steps downhill until you got there. Fundamentally, this is how gradient descent methods work.
For a given task with a set of parameters – such as how well an LLM can predict the next word in a sentence – the idea is that gradient descent provides a way to get to the best prediction, the point of minimum error, taking as few steps as possible. In our example, this point represents the most likely next word in the sentence.
Nesterov’s contribution has been finding optimal ways to achieve this. One of his key insights is using momentum to help you get to the bottom of the valley faster – known as the Nesterov Accelerated Gradient method (here’s a deeper explanation of the mathematics involved).
This work has made huge-scale optimisation feasible at workable speeds – thus underpinning the rapid development of LLMs, and AI systems more generally, over the last few years.
This technology is affecting more and more aspects of life.
At home, AI agents are being touted as ways to manage busy households. In medicine, the first AI-assisted brain surgery was recently performed in a London hospital. In mathematics, AI-generated proofs claim to have solved a number of longstanding problems, with some referring to the AI agents as ‘collaborators’ in this work.
All of this leads to big business. The race for AI dominance is built on massive capital and research and development expenditure, to develop the technology and supporting infrastructure required to support this global industrial revolution.
While in the West, private AI companies are bearing a sizeable part of this burden (without, in most cases, seeing any profits), the role of publicly funded research is and will remain critical to their business models.
In the United States, obligated federal government spending on AI increased from US$675 million to US$7.2 billion between 2024 and 2026 – an increase of almost 1,000%.
There has already been considerable debate – and some high-profile legal cases – regarding the ethics of AI companies training their models on the back catalogue of human creativity, only to rent the results back to us.
Far less scrutinised is the question of AI companies developing technology using knowledge that only exists due to sustained public investment over many decades, via academics such as Nesterov.
The fact that big tech companies use complex international tax strategies to limit their tax liabilities adds to the sense that their aggressive defence of intellectual property rights is out of kilter with the publicly funded research that plays a key role in its development.
Technology built on public knowledge
In most cases, academics work in publicly funded institutions on research grants that are largely funded by governments, whether through the Horizon Europe programme, the US National Science Foundation, or in the United Kingdom, UK Research and Innovation. All of these bodies are ultimately funded by the taxpayer.
None of the rapid development in AI exists in a vacuum. It is built on decades of pioneering, blue-skies work on optimisation and neural networks, done by academics and largely funded by taxpayers at a time when the real-world application was still a distant dream.
Legal arguments around COVID vaccine patents are one example of how the private sector has tried to deny this public sector involvement – and a related share in any profits. So where is the public sector in this debate?
The European Union is taking steps to secure control of its digital infrastructure, with a renewed focus on sovereignty in digital services. In the UK and elsewhere, a growing number of open access mandates should mean that knowledge created by public funding stays public.
While it can be used freely for commercial purposes, successful businesses would then theoretically pay back into the system via general taxation.
However, such knowledge flows beyond national borders. Efforts to capture value for reinvestment into the AI research landscape will be made harder by the fact that the tech companies’ business models depend on lobbying governments hard to avoid regulation. Any efforts to make them pay more for upstream public research and development are likely to be strongly resisted.
In the case of Nesterov and his fast gradient methods, this foundational work has been done in European institutions – yet the AI companies dominating the market are overwhelmingly based in the US or China. It rankles when access to these models is then restricted by foreign companies and governments.
James David Pickering is assistant professor in physical chemistry in the School of Chemistry at the University of Leicester, United Kingdom.

articles.summary: Awareness of the extraordinary dangers of the technology is fueling a growing, multifaceted movement of opposition and sabotage against it
articles.content:
Resistance to AI gathers strength
Awareness of the extraordinary dangers of the technology is fueling a growing, multifaceted movement of opposition and sabotage against it
The world is becoming increasingly aware of the dangers posed by the development of artificial intelligence (AI), ranging from the terrifying risk of human extinction to potential disruption of labor markets, cognitive and mental health impacts, threats to democracies and privacy, military and civilian security problems, and the massive concentration of power and wealth in the hands of a few, among many other issues. Voices warning about these threats have been common for years, and in recent weeks the chorus has grown louder on the basis of new troubling evidence. Alongside growing awareness, a multifaceted civic resistance to an unregulated technological race is advancing worldwide.
A trickle of warnings and resignations from prominent employees at leading AI labs has dominated the headlines. But that trend is only one part of a much broader sociopolitical movement. Citizens in many countries are mobilizing to block the construction of new data centers; workers in education and the arts are striking; hackers are poisoning data to short-circuit model development; philanthropists are funding projects to design new containment guardrails; designers are creating T-shirts with colors and patterns that sabotage AI visual recognition systems; parents are taking legal action for harm their children suffered from using a chatbot… The range of cases is wide and growing, spanning dissent, resistance, and even sabotage.
“We are clearly seeing resistance movements gaining momentum and spreading around the world,” says Ayse Gizem Yasar, Senior AI Fellow at the École normale supérieure in Paris and co-author of the study From rejection to regulation: mapping the landscape of resistance to AI, published in 2025 by Sciences Po, Paris.
“There is something genuinely new about how diverse AI resistance is. It’s a technology with a very wide array of consequences, and that elicits responses from a broad spectrum of people. That helps explain why it continues to grow and why, in my view, it will keep doing so,” says Thomas Dekeyser, a professor at the University of Southampton and author of Techno-negative (University of Minnesota Press), an essay that explores the history of human resistance to certain forms of technological development. Even in fights against the same data center, Dekeyser stresses, motivations can vary widely: environmental protection, fear of rising electricity bills, concerns about property devaluation, or anxiety about an exterminating apocalypse.
The movement, then, is intensifying and widening. “I find it culturally significant because it’s noticeable enough that the public is hearing about it. And among other things, that incentivizes politicians to take a more critical stance,” says Carissa Véliz, associate professor of philosophy at the Institute for Ethics in AI at the University of Oxford and author of Prophecy: Lessons on the Use and Abuse of Prediction, from Ancient Oracles to AI (Debate).
This dynamic is becoming evident in the United States, where local, bipartisan civic mobilizations to block data-center construction have strengthened elected officials’ motivation to oppose such developments. The organization Data Center Watch — a project run by AI firm 10sLabs — estimates that in the first quarter of 2026 some 75 data-center projects, with an estimated investment value of $130 billion, were blocked or delayed in the U.S., a figure equivalent to the total for 2025.
Several legislative initiatives have been introduced in the U.S. to curb, condition, delay, or ban the construction of data centers, and work is underway on the issue in the federal Congress as well. The matter is one of the central issues in the campaign for the November legislative elections. But opposition to data-center construction is genuinely global, with protest actions in many countries, including in Europe.
It is a particularly tangible element of the resistance, but it is only the visible tip of a much larger iceberg. Staff at the University of Sydney went on strike in early September demanding protection and safeguards against AI. In August, a group of student activists occupied a Washington building used by OpenAI for lobbying purposes: 13 of them were arrested, according to local press reports. The trickle is continuous.
An Ipsos opinion poll with fieldwork conducted last spring finds that in many wealthy democracies — such as the U.S., the U.K., Germany, Canada, France and the Netherlands — those who believe AI creates more problems than benefits already predominate. Across the 32 countries studied, a positive view still prevails on average, with Chinese, Indian, and Indonesian respondents being the most optimistic and strongly shaping the collective balance. But even so, there is a widespread decline in optimism compared with the 2025 study.
Geopolitical race
The transmission belt between civic rejection and politics is already yielding results at various levels, but the decisive game is being played at the highest level: among heads of state and leading companies, where decision-making parameters are less susceptible to public pressure.
The main protagonists in this race are the United States and China, and extreme mistrust between geopolitical and corporate actors has so far prevented substantial decisions. Everyone fears that pausing could leave competitors free to gain a decisive advantage that would grant an almost unimaginable hegemony.
Nevertheless, even with that powerful factor fueling inertia, signs of change are detectable. Bloomberg reported last Friday that OpenAI’s chief, Sam Altman, told employees he was willing to slow developments. The context for this came amid the severe reputational damage tied to the troubling Hugging Face incident, in which the firm was hacked by OpenAI agents against the company’s will and without them even realizing it.
Experts have long noted the emergence of these dangers. Yoshua Bengio, a Turing Award winner and one of the founding figures of language-model technology, warned about them in an interview with this newspaper in February. “There is empirical evidence of AI acting against our instructions,” was the headline.
Dario Amodei, head of Anthropic, published an online piece on September 12 in which he also advocates slowing “the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.” Amodei says two things have convinced him that greater caution is necessary: one is that we have entered a phase in which AI itself develops AI; the other is the Hugging Face incident.
On that premise, Amodei proposes a three-step control framework: that large companies grant access to external inspectors; coordination to establish common safety standards among firms in democratic countries; and an attempt to coordinate with authoritarian states.
Altman immediately responded on X, expressing his support for slowing down development and specifically for the commitment to grant external inspectors access.
Evidence of the danger is multiplying, becoming more compelling, spreading in public opinion, provoking outrage and fear in society, and that is generating greater pressure.
Beyond that, it is clear that concern about the risks is, in itself, moving things. Even a hyperliberal administration like Donald Trump’s has begun to consider restrictions in this area. And the leaders of the largest companies — from Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind to Altman himself — had already been proposing risk-reduction architectures before these most recent episodes.
Hassabis, for example, has suggested a body of standards partially inspired by the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA), a private entity that designs and implements — with powers granted by public authorities — rules for brokers. Hassabis envisions a hybrid instrument that could oversee models, especially before they are deployed. In his view, it cannot be an industry-only body, but nor can it be solely public, because it would lack the expertise to act quickly.
It is also worth noting that the U.S. and China are dialoguing on AI. Reuters has reported preparations for a possible meeting between delegations in the coming days, and Trump and Xi Jinping are scheduled to meet at the White House on September 24, with AI expected to be among the topics to be discussed. In August, there was a hybrid-format meeting in Beijing (“track 1.5″ in diplomatic jargon, i.e., halfway between purely public channels and civil-society channels).
The geopolitical dimension of the matter is crucial. AI is emerging as a technology with a unique potential to reconfigure power balances between nations, both through its capacity to boost productivity and wealth and through its contributions to military capabilities. Global domination is at stake, in a way and with an intensity unparalleled in history.
Some experts reason by drawing parallels with the nuclear dimension. The analogy applies to the destructive potential, although there is an enormous difference in the constructive domain. In that sense, ideas resonate about mutually assured destruction, pacts between the two superpowers to limit deployment and establish transparency and confidence measures, international treaties inspired by the Nuclear Non‑Proliferation Treaty, or institutions like the International Atomic Energy Agency.
In any case, for the moment there is nothing substantial on the existential-risk front, nor are there high-profile responses to other challenges — from the risk of massive impacts on labor markets, linked to advances in AI and robotics, to democratic threats posed by the extraordinary potential to manipulate minds the new technology enables. The EU passed groundbreaking legislation during the previous legislative term, but it is hesitating to implement it; and in any case, while it may be a significant market, it is not a major player in the industry.
The struggle has only just begun, and one central question is whether these diverse forms of resistance can somehow converge to be more effective. Dekeyser notes that, in the historical arc he traces in his essay, the lesson of the Luddites — the textile workers in 19th-century Britain who fought machines that threatened their livelihoods — stands out. “They were very good at organizing and responding collectively to the problem,” he says, emphasizing that the collective dimension is more effective than individual actions. For example, the personal decision not to use certain products.
Dekeyser thinks it unlikely that “some sort of united front against AI” will form, but that does not preclude tactical convergence. “History shows that it is not necessary to agree on everything for certain movements to achieve certain successes.”
Véliz points to the institutionalization of human rights as an example of consensus built on different visions. “There are different ways to justify them, different points of view, but that does not prevent finding agreement,” the Oxford academic says.
Can Şimşek, an AI policy expert and member of UNESCO’s Expert Group on AI Ethics Without Borders, also invokes human rights. “We are facing a highly changing environment, and forms of resistance also change and must adapt. It is difficult to foresee developments and therefore to generate a shared analysis, a shared semantics and a shared policy. But we have the conceptual framework of human rights that can be applied to this sector,” says Şimşek, who co-authored the Sciences Po report with Yasar. The two experts are working on a new edition that will be published at the end of this year.
“Resistance is not only stopping something. It is also shaping it,” Yasar of the École normale supérieure says. The scholar stresses the crucial importance of creating a transmission belt between protest and regulatory activity, and both she and Şimşek warn about “regulatory capture,” the maneuvers by large firms to influence legislation.
Technology advances. Awareness of its risks does too, with constant warnings: the latest from Anthropic, which said it had thwarted attempts to use its models to create biological weapons. Resistance to this development, full of dangers, is gaining strength. Slowing it down and establishing effective guardrails is an arduous undertaking. Human rights were enshrined in the Charter of the nascent United Nations after two terrifying world wars; the Treaty on the Non‑Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons was approved after the horrific use of the atomic bomb in Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Time will tell whether, in this case, humanity can act meaningfully without being compelled by catastrophe.
Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get more English-language news coverage from EL PAÍS USA Edition
