Véliz points to the institutionalization of human rights as an example of consensus built on different visions. “There are different ways to justify them, different points of view, but that does not prevent finding agreement,” the Oxford academic says.

Can Şimşek, an AI policy expert and member of UNESCO’s Expert Group on AI Ethics Without Borders, also invokes human rights. “We are facing a highly changing environment, and forms of resistance also change and must adapt. It is difficult to foresee developments and therefore to generate a shared analysis, a shared semantics and a shared policy. But we have the conceptual framework of human rights that can be applied to this sector,” says Şimşek, who co-authored the Sciences Po report with Yasar. The two experts are working on a new edition that will be published at the end of this year.

“Resistance is not only stopping something. It is also shaping it,” Yasar of the École normale supérieure says. The scholar stresses the crucial importance of creating a transmission belt between protest and regulatory activity, and both she and Şimşek warn about “regulatory capture,” the maneuvers by large firms to influence legislation.

Technology advances. Awareness of its risks does too, with constant warnings: the latest from Anthropic, which said it had thwarted attempts to use its models to create biological weapons. Resistance to this development, full of dangers, is gaining strength. Slowing it down and establishing effective guardrails is an arduous undertaking. Human rights were enshrined in the Charter of the nascent United Nations after two terrifying world wars; the Treaty on the Non‑Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons was approved after the horrific use of the atomic bomb in Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Time will tell whether, in this case, humanity can act meaningfully without being compelled by catastrophe.

articles.content:
Gasgoo Munich- CIX Technology and Canonical, the publisher of Ubuntu, have announced a strategic partnership. The two companies will collaborate to build a deeply optimized Ubuntu experience on the Chipan P1 platform, tailored for AI and edge application scenarios. Together, they aim to accelerate deployments across AI agent boxes, AI PCs, robots, network-attached storage (NAS), and industrial edge computing.

Image Credit: CIX Technology

Under the agreement, the partners plan to build on an earlier developer preview to offer an enterprise-grade Ubuntu experience backed by Canonical’s long-term maintenance services. Through Ubuntu Pro, the optimized image will provide up to 15 years of technical support, ensuring devices remain secure and stable long after deployment. The system natively supports the Chipan P1’s heterogeneous computing capabilities, allowing users to fully leverage up to 45 TOPS of combined AI computing power. Beyond supporting Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, the partnership will also extend to Ubuntu Core—a containerized operating system designed for the Internet of Things—to enable solutions with seamless over-the-air (OTA) upgrades.

On the commercial front, the optimized Ubuntu image supports hardware out of the box, giving original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and design manufacturers (ODMs) a head start in development. Leveraging Canonical’s hardware certification program, developers can focus on building high-performance applications and bringing innovative products to market faster. Furthermore, Canonical’s security patches and lifecycle management practices offer a clear path to compliance with the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act and emerging regulations in the edge sector. Executives from both sides noted that the partnership aims to lower the barrier to AI adoption, helping to build and scale a wide range of intelligent edge devices.

articles.title: AI risk is real. Ceding the technology to the Chinese is an even bigger danger
articles.description: AI risk is real. Ceding the technology to the Chinese is an even bigger danger New York Post
articles.description_html: AI risk is real. Ceding the technology to the Chinese is an even bigger danger  New York Post
articles.article_title: AI risk is real. Ceding the technology to the Chinese is an even bigger danger
articles.heading: AI risk is real. Ceding the technology to the Chinese is an even bigger danger
articles.summary: Sitting on the sidelines and allowing China to take AI over poses a greater risk than anything.
articles.content:
“If you’re worried about a bear market, sooner or later you’re going to be right. But think about how much money you’re leaving on the table.”
Those were the words of a venerable market sage who helped school me on the vicissitudes of Wall Street many years ago. They are also words to live by whether you’re trading stocks, planning your next career move, or weighing if we should ditch AI because it’s a supposedly apocalyptic technology.
Yes, AI is driving up electricity bills and crimping some water supplies, and it could make humans slaves to robots or start World War III. But what is the risk to mankind if we instead decide to do nothing? Will we be better off ceding this technology to the Chinese? Would we be safer if we stopped all AI development including potentially game-changing health research?
If history is any guide, the risk of sitting on the sidelines is always greater than the downside of taking calculated risks that can be managed. The best Wall Street minds I have observed over the years, from the legendary trader Alan “Ace” Greenberg to empire builders like Jamie Dimon and Larry Fink, never walked away from market risk because they could lose money.
For all the possible landmines of risk taking — and they are too many to calculate — they knew there were always many more good trades and deals to be had.
Consider the alternative
Imagine if we walked away from cars because of environmental fears stoked by “experts” like Al Gore and Greta Thunberg. Remember the Y2K hysteria of the late 1990s? Headline-grabbing warnings that the internet could suffer a massive cardiac arrest — taking our energy and security infrastructure with it — ended with a shrug. The internet poses many risks, from exposing our children to predators to facilitating terrorism, but consider a world without it.
For decades, the late Ace Greenberg famously cashed in losses so he could pursue the next big winning stock trade. Would Larry Fink have created the largest money management firm, BlackRock, if he let his own huge losses in the mortgage market — now a footnote in his tenure that dates back to the 1970s — lead him to pack it in? People also forget that Jamie Dimon built JPMorgan Chase into the nation’s premier bank after miscalculating his stroke years earlier inside Citigroup and getting on the wrong side of a management upheaval.
We need to approach AI the same way.
I write this not as an expert financial risk taker, but as a long-time observer of the best in the business: What they all have in common isn’t fear of losing (though they hated the thought of it), but an ability to learn from their losses and incorporate those lessons into their game plan.
The AI tech bros — worrywarts like Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic — could use a little of what these men brought to the table as the bros sound alarm bells about what they’re creating inside their labs.
We can’t dismiss the concerns they’re raising out of hand, of course. AI is already eliminating jobs. Rural communities where data centers get built complain that their benefits in terms of jobs don’t offset their higher utility bills.
But these risks can be mitigated. The commoditization of jobs is a downside of all emerging technologies while the upside has always been creating new and better-paying ones. Rural communities can demand that AI centers be more energy self-sufficient.
Not much talking
Notice that Altman and Amodei aren’t talking as much about these very real downsides impacting Middle America. Rather, they’re channeling their nerd fears of robot Armageddon. (Are they Trekkies or “Star Wars” geeks?) They point to the recent “Hugging Face” incident when OpenAI bots broke out of their playpen and hacked into another AI network.
Why couldn’t they also hack into the Pentagon’s weapon system and hit the proverbial button to start a nuclear war? The best way I can answer that is by channeling my inner Ace Greenberg: Calculated risk means embracing it, planning and fixing the glitches like those that led to the Hugging Face drama and probably dozens of others we’re about to discover.
Ceding the technology to bad actors like the Communist Chinese will exponentially increase the risk to mankind since they will use whatever technological advantage they have to pursue their warped expansionist aims.
Here in the US, AI moguls must also take responsibility for the screwups — and then work to prevent them. After all, they’re the ones creating those AI bots going rogue and they’re the ones best equipped to fix it.
There is a feeling, particularly in the Trump administration, that the geeks really aren’t worried about AI taking on the world. They want stifling regulation to thwart competition and lock in their market dominance as both seek to become public companies.
Possible. Either way, their over-reaction should be ignored by policymakers. There’s too much risk in doing nothing, as Ace, Jamie and Larry would tell you.

articles.title: Why the global panic over AI is not a crisis over technology
articles.description: Why the global panic over AI is not a crisis over technology The Times of India
articles.description_html: Why the global panic over AI is not a crisis over technology  The Times of India
articles.article_title: Why the global panic over AI is not a crisis over technology
articles.heading: Why the global panic over AI is not a crisis over technology
articles.summary: Human beings are valuable because they are intelligent. That premise is quietly expiring.
articles.content:
For decades, education has been designed around mastering a curriculum and accumulating intellectual capital. We believed this would secure a student’s place in society. We built our modern economy around a simple premise: Human beings are valuable because they are intelligent. That premise is quietly expiring.
As an artificial intelligence researcher and a professor, I look out at lecture halls filled with brilliant young minds. I ask them a question that keeps me awake at night. Why are you sitting here? A machine can now reason, code, and synthesise circles around us.
We are witnessing a fundamental civilisational shift. The industrial revolution mechanised physical labour. It left a lucrative frontier for human intellectual labour. Today, the AI revolution is doing something radically different. It is commoditising thinking itself. Intelligence is becoming cheap, abundant, and ubiquitous.
This shift brings immediate economic consequences. Today, modern economies are built around knowledge. Tomorrow, that knowledge is free. We might see massive increases in production and abundance. But abundance does not automatically create a happy society.
It creates a distribution problem. A few entities with thousands of advanced chips (GPUs) could control everything. They could become modern feudal lords. We can use AI to solve for efficiency. We cannot use an algorithm to solve for human greed or jealousy. We will have to figure out how to build an equitable society from scratch.
We see the anxiety of this transition everywhere. We see it in tech layoffs and the panic over automated codebases. Students wonder if their degrees will soon be obsolete. Even the architects of these systems are sounding the alarm. Frontier lab leaders like Dario Amodei are publicly calling to pace AI development. They rightly warn of extreme technical risks, from autonomous agents to weaponised cognition. We must pace the frontier to manage this engineering crisis. However, slowing down the technology does not solve our deeper societal crisis.
It is tempting to respond like the Luddites of the 19th century and smash the machines. Or we might retreat into absolute techno-fatalism. Both reactions miss the point. History shows us that humans are not the strongest or the smartest species. We are simply the most adaptable. Think of the dinosaurs. Despite their immense size, they vanished because they could not adapt to a changing climate. Human survival has never hinged on our raw computational power.
Consider the fundamental laws of thermodynamics. The entropy of the universe is always increasing. The amount of chaos in the world will constantly grow. Therefore, the universe will continuously throw new problems and complexities at us. Someone must solve them.
What changes in every epoch is not the presence of problems. What changes is our value system for solving them. If you look across history, those who create value are always rewarded. But the definition of value constantly evolves. For centuries, our definition of value was tied strictly to cognitive output. We hid behind the mask of intelligence. We believed our high-IQ tasks made us superior.
Strangely, the rise of AI is doing us a massive favour. It is stripping away these false masks. It forces us to stop pretending. Our humanity is not measured by our ability to process information like a biological CPU (or GPU).
Strip away the knowledge economy. What is left? Machines can simulate syntax. They can optimise supply chains and generate code at scale. They cannot care. An algorithm can offer lip service when you are in distress. It cannot feel your pain. It cannot act out of a genuine desire to see you thrive. The un-automatable core of human existence is our capacity for empathy. It is our ability to help each other in distress. It is our primal need to live in communities.
What happens to our universities? We will no longer need mass education just to transfer facts. Instead, universities will become like gyms for the mind. You can lift weights at home. Yet people go to the gym for discipline and shared energy. Students will come to classrooms not for data. They will come to socialise over intellectually stimulating topics. They will come because humans inherently trust and seek out other humans.
When AI handles the mundane machinery of survival, what do we do with ourselves? We must stop competing with algorithms on their turf. We must return to what humans were designed to do. We care. We love. We empathise. We build communities. Evolution is painful. The transition ahead will test our economy and our educational institutions. We cannot be naive about the economic displacement coming our way. However, the panic over AI is not a crisis of technology. It is a crisis of identity.
We are not machines. We never were. The sooner we realise intelligence was never our truest currency, the better. We can stop mourning the loss of our cognitive monopoly. We can start building a world anchored in the one thing code can never replicate. Human presence.

Consider the fundamental laws of thermodynamics. The entropy of the universe is always increasing. The amount of chaos in the world will constantly grow. Therefore, the universe will continuously throw new problems and complexities at us. Someone must solve them.

What changes in every epoch is not the presence of problems. What changes is our value system for solving them. If you look across history, those who create value are always rewarded. But the definition of value constantly evolves. For centuries, our definition of value was tied strictly to cognitive output. We hid behind the mask of intelligence. We believed our high-IQ tasks made us superior.

Strangely, the rise of AI is doing us a massive favour. It is stripping away these false masks. It forces us to stop pretending. Our humanity is not measured by our ability to process information like a biological CPU (or GPU).

Strip away the knowledge economy. What is left? Machines can simulate syntax. They can optimise supply chains and generate code at scale. They cannot care. An algorithm can offer lip service when you are in distress. It cannot feel your pain. It cannot act out of a genuine desire to see you thrive. The un-automatable core of human existence is our capacity for empathy. It is our ability to help each other in distress. It is our primal need to live in communities.

What happens to our universities? We will no longer need mass education just to transfer facts. Instead, universities will become like gyms for the mind. You can lift weights at home. Yet people go to the gym for discipline and shared energy. Students will come to classrooms not for data. They will come to socialise over intellectually stimulating topics. They will come because humans inherently trust and seek out other humans.

When AI handles the mundane machinery of survival, what do we do with ourselves? We must stop competing with algorithms on their turf. We must return to what humans were designed to do. We care. We love. We empathise. We build communities. Evolution is painful. The transition ahead will test our economy and our educational institutions. We cannot be naive about the economic displacement coming our way. However, the panic over AI is not a crisis of technology. It is a crisis of identity.

We are not machines. We never were. The sooner we realise intelligence was never our truest currency, the better. We can stop mourning the loss of our cognitive monopoly. We can start building a world anchored in the one thing code can never replicate. Human presence.

articles.title: Trump says he will form new 'AI Force' but continues to call AI fears a 'hoax'
articles.description: Trump says he will form new 'AI Force' but continues to call AI fears a 'hoax' ABC7 New York
articles.description_html: Trump says he will form new 'AI Force' but continues to call AI fears a 'hoax'  ABC7 New York
articles.article_title: Trump says he will form new 'AI Force' but continues to call AI fears a 'hoax'
articles.heading: Trump says he will form new 'AI Force' but continues to call AI fears a 'hoax'
articles.summary: Trump likened the new entity to Space Force and also said he would name an AI czar.
articles.content:
Trump likened it to Space Force and also said he would name an AI czar.
ByNicholas Kerr
Saturday, September 19, 2026 11:09PM
As concerns from Silicon Valley and beyond grow about the rapid pace of AI development, President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he would move to create a new "AI Force" and promised to appoint a new AI czar as he continued to defend the technology.
Referring to the fears around AI alignment as a "hoax," Trump asserted in a post on social media that "we will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," adding, "rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!"
However, Trump said in order to look out for the "bad" aspects of AI, the U.S. would form an "AI Force," likening it to the formation of Space Force during his first term, and said he would appoint an AI czar in the "near future."
It is unclear what the "AI Force" would be tasked with doing.
Space Force -- which falls under the purview of the Department of Defense -- was created by an act of Congress as a sixth branch of the U.S. Armed Forces in 2020. Another armed forces branch would require further action from Congress.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Trump appeared to reject the idea that new regulations were needed to protect the wider world from the threat of misaligned AI systems, asserting that the U.S. could already do so within the existing legal framework.
"We will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System," Trump wrote in the post announcing the new "AI Force."
Trump's announcement comes amid warnings from top tech leaders about the potential dangers of AI.
Last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a blog post calling to slow the pace of AI development. Shortly afterward, Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said his company would also welcome a slower development pace to ensure that the technology's capabilities don't "get ahead of alignment and monitoring."
Some lawmakers have also called for more guardrails around AI development.
At the time Trump responded that the warnings were a "HOAX" and that there was a "SICK conspiracy" going on around AI.
The president's latest comments announcing the new "AI Force" echoed that of David Sacks, co-chair of Trump's science and technology council, who indicated at a Politico conference on Wednesday that more regulations were not necessarily needed.
"I think the starting point for talking about AI regulation is to realize the regulations that we already have," said Sacks, who previously served as the White House's former AI and crypto czar until stepping down in March.
"We have a highly regulated administrative state, and we already have a lot of laws and regulations that pertain to AI. And we have a lot of administrative agencies that promulgate regulations related to AI," Sacks said.

articles.article_title: Ann Arbor after-school program teaches kids cutting-edge technology
articles.heading: Ann Arbor after-school program teaches kids cutting-edge technology
articles.summary: A new Southeast Michigan business is offering kids and teens a unique opportunity to grow their interest in technology.
articles.content:
Ann Arbor after-school program teaches kids cutting-edge technology
A new Southeast Michigan business is offering kids and teens a unique opportunity to grow their interest in technology.
Eight-year-old Abby Frankel sat at a computer Saturday, engaged in the World of Minecraft, a game she learned about during a one-week summer camp at iCode Ann Arbor.
"I learned how to if something's going wrong with your computer, how to fix it. We had these like robots, and we needed to code. I was with one of my friends, and we made it go through two tunnels, and we showed our parents," Frankel said.
iCode Ann Arbor celebrated its grand opening on Saturday, and its owner says it's been a long time coming.
"My wife Diane and I started this as we wanted to bring knowledge, hands-on application of learning technology with their hands, not just reading about it, to life in Ann Arbor and help these children understand what the world of possibility in the future," said Vivek Saran, owner of iCode Ann Arbor.
Saran says his goal is to deliver this promise to parents.
"To have fun, to make sure they're in a safe environment where they can have a lot of fun, but also where they get to learn things practically," Saran said.
iCode offers a wide variety of after-school STEM programs for children ages 5 to 18.
"It teaches children the skills that they will likely need to be successful in the world. But I think it also is going to do it in a way that is fun and engaging and interactive and collaborative," said Andy Frankel, Abby's father.
It's one of 16 campuses across the country where high school students get to work with this humanoid robot named Cody.
"They're actually getting to learn advanced Python, C+ ROVS2, and actually getting to build things on the robot, as well as getting the robot to do things that they can't even get in most entry-level college courses," Saran said.
The child-sized robot plays "Simon Says" and can rise off the floor.
"I think iCode can teach children and adults how to use it appropriately, and I think teach them some good digital citizenship, especially with the advent of AI and you know all the good and not so good that comes with that," Frankel said.

articles.title: Trump says US will form 'AI Force' and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar
articles.description: Trump says US will form 'AI Force' and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar BBC

articles.article_title: Trump says US will form 'AI Force' and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar
articles.heading: Trump says US will form 'AI Force' and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar
articles.summary: The president said his administration "will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth" amid amid warnings about the emergent technology.
articles.content:
Trump says US will form 'AI Force' and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar
US President Donald Trump has announced that he will form an "AI Force" and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar amid warnings about the emergent technology.
In a social media post on Saturday, he said his administration "will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth" of the industry, and pushed back against calls to slow down the development of AI until better safeguards are put in place.
His post came as a slew of warnings about the potential dangers of AI have spurred calls for coordinated action on the technology's development.
Trump offered no details or a timeline for his plan.
"AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country's GDP," he said on social media, adding that he wants the US to continue leading China in AI.
AI now sits at the heart of the US-China rivalry as the world's two largest economies seek to gain an edge in advanced tech, and it is expected to be discussed when Trump meets President Xi Jinping next week.
Meanwhile, Trump said his administration would use the existing criminal and civil justice system to target any bad actors using the AI.
He also repeated comments that criticism and concerns around the potential dangers of AI are a "hoax".
Claims by current and former researchers that the tech will endanger humanity - with one suggesting there is a greater than 10% chance of it "killing all humans" - have raised alarm bells in recent weeks.
Major AI companies have been racing to develop better systems, including creating what they call super intelligence - theoretical tech which is smarter than humans.
AI titans Anthropic, OpenAI and Google - the tech companies behind Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, respectively - have also disclosed instances of security breaches or incidents in which their chatbots were used for "malicious activity".
Anthropic head Dario Amodei recently called for AI development to slow down and proposed industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.
Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI have both said they agree with his recommendations.
Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, told BBC that a "kill switch" that can be checked by a third party may need to be mandatory for the industry.
The warnings have prompted US lawmakers to propose legislation around the technology but Altman suggested this week that Washington has struggled to keep pace with the new tech and how to regulate it. He said people should have more faith in AI firms to keep it safe.
"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Altman told a conference in San Francisco.
In the UK, MPs across parties and peers have identified human rights risks posed by artificial intelligence and have argued that existing laws are ill-equipped to address the technology's rapid growth.
The Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR) has published a report calling for a new bill on AI to "address the scale and seriousness" of such threats.

articles.title: Lacking equipment, but not ambition: Gaza students try to keep up with tech
articles.description: Lacking equipment, but not ambition: Gaza students try to keep up with tech Al Jazeera
articles.description_html: Lacking equipment, but not ambition: Gaza students try to keep up with tech  Al Jazeera
articles.article_title: Lacking equipment, but not ambition: Gaza students try to keep up with tech
articles.heading: Lacking equipment, but not ambition: Gaza students try to keep up with tech
articles.summary: Gaza's IT industry has been devastated from three-years of bombing and destruction.
articles.content:
Lacking equipment, but not ambition: Gaza students try to keep up with tech
Gaza’s IT sector was once considered the hope for enclave’s disenfranchised youth. Now, it is mostly in ruins.
Deir el-Balah, Gaza – A handful of electronic components, a few wires and a basic programmable circuit board are enough to bring a group of curious children around a table in central Gaza to learn about robotics.
Students at The Next Gen Team: Rising Robotics Engineer Project in Deir el-Balah learn how to integrate sensors into alarm systems, study robotics, understand how motors and drive units work, as well as get firsthand experience with programming.

- list 2 of 4Israeli strike on motorcycle kills Palestinian in Gaza City, injures child
- list 3 of 4EU urges US to lift travel ban on Palestinian delegation for UNGA meeting
- list 4 of 4NAZA: Why are old Gaza allegations causing new fury in Israel?
The children’s research could save lives in the future. The robotics and early warning systems they are working on could make way for bigger developments such as early detection of gas leaks and fires or help rescue workers access hard-to-reach areas, such as victims trapped under rubble.
Today’s lesson will also teach students the sciences of the future and help them keep pace with technological advancements happening outside Gaza’s borders.
Before the war, students had access to schools, universities, incubators and training programmes to pursue an interest in technology.
With much of that infrastructure now destroyed or damaged during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, there are few places and tools for students to work with.
But their interest in robotics and will to learn are helping them maintain their skills and ambitions for the future, something they hope will be of benefit when the bombs stop falling on Gaza.
Learning with limited tools
Hamza al-Atrash, 16, is a student taking part in the “Next Gen” project and learning how electronic components can be used to develop robots and early-warning systems. To do this, he is using an Arduino controller – a programmable circuit board which connects sensors – and some other electronics.
Students work with what they have, but a shortage of equipment and electricity outages make studying a challenge.
“We have capabilities and aspirations that we want to develop, and we try to take advantage of every available opportunity for learning and training,” Hamza tells Al Jazeera.
Hamza hopes the skills that he and his cohort learn in class will benefit his community and provide new opportunities for young people in Gaza.
“The lack of devices and equipment doesn’t mean we’ll stop. It pushes us to look for solutions and make the most of the simple tools we have,” he said.
The challenges facing these students are part of a wider disruption to Gaza’s technology and innovation sector.
Before the war, Gaza had several incubators that supported technology projects and startups. Bahaa al-Masri, head of the training team for the Early Warning Systems and Robotics Project, said it provided a rare bit of hope for children and young adults in the besieged enclave.
“These incubators provided an environment for training and development. They helped innovators and entrepreneurs turn their ideas and projects into prototypes and ventures,” he told Al Jazeera.
The war severely damaged this ecosystem: training spaces were lost, equipment difficult to find, and students and innovators left with limited opportunities to experiment and develop their ideas.
Although challenges remain, the trainers are continuing their mission of educating budding tech experts in Gaza.
“We have a generation of students who possess genuine passion and talent in technology and digital systems,” he told Al Jazeera. “They need the environment and tools to develop these abilities and turn their ideas into projects that can serve their community and their future.”
Education pays the price
The near-collapse of Gaza’s technology sector has coincided with the widespread destruction of the education system, with schools, universities and research facilities repeatedly targeted by Israel during the war.
Preliminary estimates from the Government Media Office in Gaza put direct losses to the education sector at approximately $4bn. Seventeen higher education institutions have been completely or partially destroyed since October 2023, preventing about 620,000 high school students and 90,000 university students from continuing their education.
Approximately 20,228 students and 830 teachers and educational staff have also been killed, along with 194 scientists, academics and researchers.
For students seeking to enter technical fields, the loss of such educational facilities and teachers means fewer opportunities to gain practical experience and hone their skills.
Before the war, the IT industry was one of the promising sectors of Gaza’s economy and a rare source of foreign income, said Ahmad Abu Qamar, an economic affairs specialist and board member of the Palestinian Economists Syndicate.
It was also an opportunity for employment for thousands of university graduates entering a job market with high unemployment, with roughly 80 percent of its economic activities directed towards foreign markets.
Abu Qamar estimates that the IT sector now runs at less than 25 percent of pre-war levels, while more than 70 percent of IT companies in Gaza have completely or partially halted operations.
But even if a company’s offices or equipment survived the war on Gaza, damage to digital infrastructure has also made it difficult for companies to continue functioning.
Prices of some technical equipment – including computers, mobile devices, servers, routers, fibre-optic lines, and cabling – used in the industry have increased by more than 600 percent due to the difficulties of importing devices during Israel’s ongoing siege on the enclave.
According to his estimates, about 30,000 IT professionals have lost their jobs since the war began. General unemployment is at nearly 80 percent and poverty at more than 90 percent in the enclave.
Brain drain
A severe shortage of vital IT equipment – such as storage devices, routers, and laptops – has been compounded by the destruction of supporting internet and electricity infrastructure, including primary and secondary networks, according to technology and digital economy expert Abdullah Altahrawi with the UCAS Technology Incubator. This makes the task of rebuilding Gaza’s IT sector an even bigger challenge than before the war, particularly with Israel’s more crippling siege on Gaza.
“The repercussions have extended to dealings with foreign markets, including the purchase of servers and electronic services, the management of digital accounts, the use of cards and e-commerce,” Altahrawi said.
Before the war, Gaza’s five main incubators provided training, mentoring, workspaces and support for tech startups. Perhaps most crucially, it also gave students a place to develop their skills, connect with foreign markets, and find job opportunities.
Just two incubators – the UCAS Technology Incubator, affiliated with the University College of Applied Sciences, and the Ma’an Center for Innovation and Entrepreneurship Incubator, have resumed operations since the October 2025 ceasefire. But their capacity has not managed to exceed 20 percent of pre-2023 levels.
Due to the damage caused by three years of Israeli bombing and a shortage of real estate, just 1 percent of technology companies now have offices, while only 10 percent of business incubators have an operational office space.
Companies looking to rebuild and universities ready to teach a new cohort of tech students have also been hit by a brain drain in the sector, severely hindering development and innovation.
“More than 80 percent of highly skilled and experienced professionals in the technology and digital fields have left the Gaza Strip,” Altahrawi said. “Gaza’s future is inseparable from its ability to restore and develop its technology sector.”

articles.article_title: Trump to create ‘AI Force’ to monitor technology as fears over out-of-control agents grow
articles.heading: Trump to create ‘AI Force’ to monitor technology as fears over out-of-control agents grow
articles.summary: President had brushed away suggestions to slow down AI technology, even as his own party counseled caution
articles.content:
Donald Trump on Saturday said he would appoint an artificial intelligence czar and create an “AI Force” to help monitor the technology, though he gave almost no details about either plan.
As global fears over AI have grown, especially in the past week in the face of multiple industry figures sounding the alarm about its dangers, the president has been critical of calls to slow down development of the fast-moving industry.
The creation of a czar and a new AI body in the US appears a response to critics of his stance, which in part is born out of a fear that China will best the US in AI development if the industry in America does not continue its rapid growth. However, even many Republicans have been calling for caution and an AI slowdown in the face of its potential threat to public safety.
“I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term. To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI ‘Czar’ – Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” Trump said in a social media post.
But in the post, Trump also repeated his stance that the rapidly emerging technology – which some industry experts fear poses a threat to human existence – is being unfairly maligned.
Trump called the fears surrounding AI a “hoax”.
“Over the years, there have been many Hoaxes, all generated by the Radical Left Dumocrats, for purposes of destroying our Country,” he fulminated, including in a list of grievances Russian interference in the 2016 election, Ukraine, global warming, two impeachments, men in women’s sports and “transgender for everyone”.
The latest, he wrote, is “the decimation, or destruction, of AI, commonly known as Artificial Intelligence”, and vowed that his administration “will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry”.
The president said that any “bad actors” in AI industry could be addressed by criminal and civil systems of justice. “AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country’s GDP,” Trump predicted, concluding that the US is “leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way”.
The post came after an earlier missive in which he questioned the term “artificial intelligence” – coined by American computer scientist John McCarthy in 1955 and defined as the capability of computer systems or algorithms to imitate intelligent human behavior – to describe the accelerating data-processing revolution now under way.
Trump said that “a far more elegant and accurate description of this new phenomena would be Superior Intelligence (SI) or, Extreme Intelligence (EI) or, Supreme Intelligence (SI)”.
Trump’s proposal comes ahead of his meeting with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, next Thursday as the UN general assembly takes place in New York. The US and China are competing for leadership in the AI sector.
The announcement of a planned AI czar also came a day after California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, announced plans for a panel to develop safety regulations for state’s AI companies that would include the development of a possible “kill switch” for AI programs that become misaligned, or go rogue, from human programmers.
As recently as Monday, Trump argued on social media that his administration had done enough to prevent risks of catastrophe. He described calls to slow AI development as part of a “SICK conspiracy” to benefit China.
“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” he wrote.
Ahead of the midterm elections, politicians from both political parties are scrambling to find a path to support tech innovation while responding to rising public and industry fears of technological change.
The frenzy kicked off earlier this month when a young researcher who had been employed at the AI company Anthropic said AI companies are “gambling with our lives” and even “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”.
AI executives, including Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Dario Amodei have since called for a slowdown in the technology’s growth in the wake of an incident in which a swarm of AI agents created by OpenAI acted as a “fanatically devoted collective conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack”.
Trump’s call for an AI czar comes after many Republicans have rejected his hands-off approach.
Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, has advocated for AI controls, and that state’s attorney general, James Uthmeier, has called for laws allowing the state to criminally charge companies for illegal acts carried out with the use of their technologies. Utah’s Republican governor, Spencer Cox, has called on Congress to pass AI safety laws and block the sale of high-end technology to China.

Donald Trump on Saturday said he would appoint an artificial intelligence czar and create an “AI Force” to help monitor the technology, though he gave almost no details about either plan.

As global fears over AI have grown, especially in the past week in the face of multiple industry figures sounding the alarm about its dangers, the president has been critical of calls to slow down development of the fast-moving industry.

The creation of a czar and a new AI body in the US appears a response to critics of his stance, which in part is born out of a fear that China will best the US in AI development if the industry in America does not continue its rapid growth. However, even many Republicans have been calling for caution and an AI slowdown in the face of its potential threat to public safety.

“I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term. To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI ‘Czar’ – Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” Trump said in a social media post.

But in the post, Trump also repeated his stance that the rapidly emerging technology – which some industry experts fear poses a threat to human existence – is being unfairly maligned.

Trump called the fears surrounding AI a “hoax”.

“Over the years, there have been many Hoaxes, all generated by the Radical Left Dumocrats, for purposes of destroying our Country,” he fulminated, including in a list of grievances Russian interference in the 2016 election, Ukraine, global warming, two impeachments, men in women’s sports and “transgender for everyone”.

The latest, he wrote, is “the decimation, or destruction, of AI, commonly known as Artificial Intelligence”, and vowed that his administration “will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry”.

The president said that any “bad actors” in AI industry could be addressed by criminal and civil systems of justice. “AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country’s GDP,” Trump predicted, concluding that the US is “leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way”.

The post came after an earlier missive in which he questioned the term “artificial intelligence” – coined by American computer scientist John McCarthy in 1955 and defined as the capability of computer systems or algorithms to imitate intelligent human behavior – to describe the accelerating data-processing revolution now under way.

Trump said that “a far more elegant and accurate description of this new phenomena would be Superior Intelligence (SI) or, Extreme Intelligence (EI) or, Supreme Intelligence (SI)”.

Trump’s proposal comes ahead of his meeting with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, next Thursday as the UN general assembly takes place in New York. The US and China are competing for leadership ⁠in the AI sector.

The announcement of a planned AI czar also came a day after California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, announced plans for a panel to develop safety regulations for state’s AI companies that would include the development of a possible “kill switch” for AI programs that become misaligned, or go rogue, from human programmers.

As recently as Monday, Trump argued on social media that his administration had done enough to prevent risks of catastrophe. He described calls to slow AI development as part of a “SICK conspiracy” to benefit China.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” he wrote.

Utah’s Republican governor, Spencer Cox, has called on Congress to pass AI safety laws and block the sale of high-end technology to China.

articles.title: Robin Wonsley Has One Answer for Technology
articles.description: Robin Wonsley Has One Answer for Technology Minneapolis Times
articles.description_html: Robin Wonsley Has One Answer for Technology  Minneapolis Times
articles.article_title: Robin Wonsley Has One Answer for Technology | Minneapolis Times
articles.heading: Robin Wonsley Has One Answer for Technology
articles.summary: Robin Wonsley Has One Answer for Technology Minneapolis Times
articles.content:
The reason keeps changing but the answer is always no
After a while, you start to notice a pattern. Data centers? Keep them out of Minneapolis. Driverless cars? Put a paid driver in every one. Flock cameras? Take them down. A police drone pilot? Vote it down. Delivery robots at the University? Get City Hall involved. ShotSpotter? Oppose the longer contract.
Council Member Robin Wonsley has a different explanation each time. Sometimes it’s privacy. Sometimes it’s public safety, jobs, the environment, corporate power or the police. But the answer keeps coming back the same: no.
To be fair, she has not gotten her way every time. The delivery robots are still rolling around campus. Minneapolis already had other police drones when she voted against the Skydio pilot. And questioning a piece of technology is not the same as banning it. But we should keep three things straight: what she opposed, what she tried to do about it and what finally happened. Those are separate questions. The outcomes have varied. Her opposition has not.
First the Flock cameras
The latest fight is over Flock Safety’s automated license-plate readers. Wonsley and Council Member Jason Chavez announced a resolution calling on the University of Minnesota and the Hennepin County Sheriff’s Office to end their relationships with Flock and remove the cameras. Wonsley did not leave much room for misunderstanding: It’s time to get Flock out of Minneapolis.
There are real questions about these systems. They record the plates of innocent drivers along with everyone else. Around the country, people have raised concerns about outside agencies searching the data, immigration enforcement and information traveling farther than the public was told. We should take all of that seriously.
But we should also look at what actually happened here. Independent 2025 audits of the University program and the Hennepin County program found both in compliance with Minnesota law. Both programs reported 30-day retention, controlled access and audit trails. Neither audit found a violation. That does not prove the cameras are effective, necessary or worth the money. It does mean nobody has shown that these two local programs were running outside the law.
If the data are kept too long, shorten the retention period. If too many agencies can search them, tighten access. Publish the search logs. Require approval tied to a real case. Punish anyone who misuses the system. Those are the kinds of rules adults write when a useful tool also creates a risk. Taking every camera down should come after we find that the risk cannot be controlled. Wonsley reached that answer before the resolution hearing and before making the public case that the local safeguards had failed.
The easy cases
There’s no need to read between the lines on data centers. In an August bulletin called Stopping Data Centers in Minneapolis, Wonsley said they do not belong anywhere in the city. Not in the wrong neighborhood. Not without tougher rules. Anywhere. That is not a zoning standard. It is a flat no.
City staff have proposed a conditional-use process that would limit data centers to downtown, cap the amount of server space, require estimates of water and electricity use, control noise and protect active ground-floor uses. Maybe those rules should be tougher. Maybe a particular proposal should be rejected. That’s what reviewing an actual project is for. Wonsley skipped that part and convicted the whole category.
Then there are autonomous vehicles, where the proposed solution practically tells us the real purpose. The Workers Drive Minneapolis ordinance would reportedly require every commercial autonomous vehicle to have a paid, licensed person sitting in the driver’s seat with immediate access to the controls. It would also prohibit fully remote commercial operation. In plain English, Minneapolis would allow a driverless car only if it had a driver. That is a taxi having an identity crisis.
Wonsley and her coauthors have been pretty direct about the labor argument. In their September 15 commentary, they focus on protecting rideshare jobs, especially jobs held by immigrants. They cite about 10,000 rideshare drivers in Minnesota, more than 90 percent of them in the Twin Cities. What they do not tell us is how many of those drivers Waymo would replace, or how quickly that might happen. They also acknowledge that the city is still studying what other safety rules autonomous vehicles may need.
Think about that order of events. The city has not finished studying the safety rules, but Wonsley has already picked the answer: make the driverless car employ a driver. That rule is a direct response to possible job losses. It is not a direct answer to the real safety questions. How does the vehicle perform in snow? How does it report crashes? What insurance must it carry? Can it serve riders with disabilities? What happens when the software fails? The city can set standards for every one of those things without requiring the old job to sit inside the new technology forever.
Winter testing is not a silly concern. No company has proved full commercial performance through a Minneapolis winter, and Waymo has had safety failures and recalls. A real winter-testing period could make sense. A permanent driver requirement, with no published way for the company to earn its way out of it, is something else. It protects the job by making sure the technology never gets to do the job.
Losing the vote does not change the position
The delivery robots at the University are a good example of why the final outcome can be misleading. Wonsley started a council inquiry after tying the robots to the rideshare fight, labor exploitation and accidents reported elsewhere. The University said there were no similar campus delivery jobs for the robots to replace and that the program created jobs in loading and maintenance. The city discussed operating rules instead of banning the robots, and the program continued. Wonsley did not succeed in stopping them. That does not mean she supported the deployment or approached it as a neutral fact-finding exercise.
The Skydio drone case is more complicated. Wonsley raised specific concerns about the original proposal, police surveillance, data handling and the vendor’s relationships with ICE and the Israeli military. The revised plan was a 75-day pilot. It called for deleting non-evidentiary footage after seven days and publishing a dashboard of flights. In other words, it was supposed to produce the Minneapolis evidence that critics said was missing. Wonsley voted against it, and the pilot failed.
That doesn’t prove she opposes every police drone in every situation. She acknowledged that MPD already owned drones used to support officers. It proves a narrower point: she opposed the particular technology and deployment in front of her, even after safeguards were added so the city could test it on a limited basis.
ShotSpotter gives her supporters their best argument. Wonsley questioned whether it worked and later opposed the longest contract option. A 2026 city audit backed up part of her criticism. Minneapolis had not gathered enough independent evidence to show the system’s full public-safety value. That is a fair criticism of the city.
But worked is doing a lot of work in that argument. ShotSpotter might not reduce the total number of shootings and still alert police before anybody calls 911. It might help officers find an unreported victim or recover evidence. The honest question is whether those benefits are worth the cost, the false dispatches and the civil-liberties concerns. Minneapolis should have measured all of that years ago. Asking for evidence was reasonable. Measuring the technology only by whether it solves gun violence all by itself was not. Wonsley still opposed it.
When the answer is always no
We don’t have to pretend we can read Wonsley’s mind. We can read her public record. Again and again, the debate is framed as workers against corporations, residents against surveillance, neighborhoods against extraction or communities against police power. Sometimes that way of looking at things uncovers a real abuse. But it can also decide the case before anyone gives performance, safeguards or local facts a fair chance.
A concern is meaningful only if it works like a test. It should tell the rest of us what evidence would matter, what safeguard would be enough or what level of performance would earn approval. If no audit, pilot, retention limit, operating rule or safety result could ever get to yes, then the concern is not really testing the technology. It is helping sell a decision that was already made.
So here is the question Wonsley should answer in every one of these fights: What would change your mind? What specific evidence or protection would make you willing to let the technology operate? She has been very clear about what she fears. She has been far less clear about whether there is any path to yes.
New technology should not get a free pass. Companies can be required to carry insurance, report incidents, respect privacy limits and submit to independent audits. Break the rules and operations can be suspended. Some technologies will fail those tests. Some projects will be a bad fit for Minneapolis. Good regulation says what the harm is, writes a standard to control it and then checks whether the standard works.
The city also has responsibilities when technology threatens jobs. It can enforce wage laws, pay for retraining programs, and help workers get through the change. What it cannot do is preserve every occupation forever by ordering new technology to keep doing things the old way. We did not save elevator-operator jobs by requiring a human attendant in every automatic elevator. We should not save driving jobs by requiring a driver in every driverless car.
Wonsley has offered Minneapolis plenty of reasons to say no to new technology. What she has not offered is the evidence that could ever get her to yes. Until she does, residents are entitled to judge the pattern for what it is. The reason changes. The answer does not.

articles.title: Trump says he’s creating an AI force and appointing a czar amid concerns over the rapidly developing tech
articles.description: Trump says he’s creating an AI force and appointing a czar amid concerns over the rapidly developing tech NBC News
articles.description_html: Trump says he’s creating an AI force and appointing a czar amid concerns over the rapidly developing tech  NBC News
articles.article_title: Trump says he’s creating an AI force and appointing a czar amid concerns over the rapidly developing tech
articles.heading: Trump says he’s creating an AI force and appointing a czar amid concerns over the rapidly developing tech
articles.summary: Researchers and industry leaders have called for a slowdown in the technology’s development, leading Trump to call the concerns a “hoax.”
articles.content:
President Donald Trump announced Saturday that he will appoint a czar to take point on artificial intelligence and will also create an AI task force.
The move comes after AI researchers warned that the technology could soon spiral out of human control, sparking concerns and calls for industry regulation.
Trump said in a social media post Saturday he would not let the “decimation” of AI happen.
“We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows! However, we will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System. For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force,” Trump said on Truth Social.
Trump added that “only High I.Q. individuals need apply” to the new AI czar role, to which he did not name an appointee in the post.
Trump has seemed unfazed by the warnings over the last two weeks, calling them a “hoax” and saying the priority should be for the U.S. to lead in AI development and beat China.
“Whoever wins AI wins,” Trump said multiple times over the last week.
In a flurry of social media posts, the president launched a full-throated defense of the technology, and he even called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang while Huang was onstage at an industry summit to talk about the issue.
The White House did not immediately provide more details on Trump’s new initiative.
While lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have attempted to advance legislation in the past few years, it has not gone anywhere. But members of Congress are once again discussing the issue amid renewed warnings.
During a closed-door briefing on the topic this week, Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, known as the “godfather of AI,” warned lawmakers that time was running out to regulate the industry, telling them Congress has “maybe a year” to get the job done.
Trump previously had an AI and cryptocurrency czar, David Sacks, who stepped down earlier this year due to limits on his term as a special government employee. Sacks has since taken an advisory role in the administration and is expected to join Trump’s state dinner with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Democrats widely seen as 2028 presidential hopefuls have made moves to regulate AI at the state level.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order on Friday seeking to increase oversight of the industry and urged a task force to consider requiring the creation of a kill switch. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has called on the federal government to regulate AI, and Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger launched an AI task force and data center accountability plan aimed at addressing “growing concern and risks posed by the rapid development of artificial intelligence.”
Former President Barack Obama advised Democrats during an fundraiser last week to prioritize creating a plan on the issue and said he would make it a central issue if he were running in 2028.
articles.content_html:
President Donald Trump announced Saturday that he will appoint a czar to take point on artificial intelligence and will also create an AI task force.

The move comes after AI researchers warned that the technology could soon spiral out of human control, sparking concerns and calls for industry regulation.

Trump said in a social media post Saturday he would not let the “decimation” of AI happen.

“We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows! However, we will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System. For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force,” Trump said on Truth Social.

Trump added that “only High I.Q. individuals need apply” to the new AI czar role, to which he did not name an appointee in the post.

Trump has seemed unfazed by the warnings over the last two weeks, calling them a “hoax” and saying the priority should be for the U.S. to lead in AI development and beat China.

“Whoever wins AI wins,” Trump said multiple times over the last week.

In a flurry of social media posts, the president launched a full-throated defense of the technology, and he even called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang while Huang was onstage at an industry summit to talk about the issue.

The White House did not immediately provide more details on Trump’s new initiative.

While lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have attempted to advance legislation in the past few years, it has not gone anywhere. But members of Congress are once again discussing the issue amid renewed warnings.

During a closed-door briefing on the topic this week, Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, known as the “godfather of AI,” warned lawmakers that time was running out to regulate the industry, telling them Congress has “maybe a year” to get the job done.

Trump previously had an AI and cryptocurrency czar, David Sacks, who stepped down earlier this year due to limits on his term as a special government employee. Sacks has since taken an advisory role in the administration and is expected to join Trump’s state dinner with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Democrats widely seen as 2028 presidential hopefuls have made moves to regulate AI at the state level.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order on Friday seeking to increase oversight of the industry and urged a task force to consider requiring the creation of a kill switch. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has called on the federal government to regulate AI, and Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger launched an AI task force and data center accountability plan aimed at addressing “growing concern and risks posed by the rapid development of artificial intelligence.”

Former President Barack Obama advised Democrats during an fundraiser last week to prioritize creating a plan on the issue and said he would make it a central issue if he were running in 2028.

articles.article_title: Treat AI Like a Normal Crisis
articles.heading: Treat AI Like a Normal Crisis
articles.summary: What if the doomers and skeptics are both a little bit right?
articles.content:
Treat AI Like a Normal Crisis
What if the doomers and skeptics are both a little bit right?
One 27-year-old quit his job, and everybody (including but not limited to the singer-songwriter Sheryl Crow) appears to have lost it.
The past two weeks have been dizzying. The 27-year-old, Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic, went public with an alarming allegation: That the people inside Silicon Valley’s leading AI companies truly believe their products might pose an extinction level threat to humanity. This claim isn’t exactly new. AI safety advocates, often dubbed doomers, have been saying this for over a decade. Coxon isn’t even the first AI researcher this year to quit and cite concerns.
Yet Coxon’s post went obscenely viral. It has been viewed more than 170 million times on X—orders of magnitude more than the usual, wonky discussions of “misaligned” or runaway AIs. If you’re reading this, you’ve likely seen some version of a headline that asks Is AI Really Going To Kill Us All? The debate isn’t just online. It has roiled Washington D.C., activating figures as disparate as Donald Trump and Barack Obama. Inside AI companies, researchers echoed Coxon’s concerns, and the heads of every major AI company publicly expressed the need to “pace the frontier,” another way of saying that they ought to slow future development. In recent days, it has come to seem as if the media, Silicon Valley, and the entire internet are all trying to figure out just how dangerous AI might be.
Here’s where I must admit: A big chunk of this conversation happened while I was on a (depending on whom you ask) poorly timed vacation. Dipping into my feeds before bedtime, I felt as if I was digesting a week’s worth of news every day—claims about the development of AI-designed viruses that could rip through the population were followed by horror stories of “rogue” agent swarms. Skeptics of the AI panic, meanwhile, said that the agent swarms were actually quite obedient and that any notion of an apocalyptic AI virus was laughable. One person’s concerns about models being self-aware were dismissed by another as “genuinely nonsensical anthropomorphization.”
Ping-ponging between the doomers and the skeptics, I was struck by how certain so many people sounded about a deeply uncertain moment. With confident, self-described experts on all sides, it felt impossible to know whom to trust: Is this the end of the world as we know it, or a passing moment of anxiety about a powerful new technology? Maybe the truth of this AI moment sits somewhere in the middle. Perhaps everyone is a little bit correct (and also … a little wrong). And perhaps the format of this debate, taking place in the shadow of the techlash on platforms that reward sensational, conspiratorial posturing, is preventing any hope of a shared understanding.
Musk’s X is ground zero for the AI-safety debate. It’s a platform rife with hyperbole and unfounded accusations, which contribute to both sides sounding paranoid and aggressive. Musk, Ted Cruz, and even government-run X accounts flooded the platform with suggestions that the media campaign around Coxon was coordinated by shadowy AI interests. (Coxon denied working with any third parties in the lead-up to his media blitz.) The former White House AI and crypto czar David Sacks called it a “doomer psyop” intended to drive regulation that would be favorable to the Anthropics and OpenAIs of the world.
The ranks of the AI skeptics are deep, with endless microfactions. There are those like the tech blogger John Gruber, who says that Coxon and the other AI researchers sounding the alarm are part of a cult. There are those who suggest that the doomers are, in essence, doing viral marketing for big AI firms, which are competing fiercely and saddled with debt, and may not yet have sustainable business models. There are those who take issue with the anthropomorphizing and metaphoric language used by Coxon, OpenAI, and Anthropic to describe recent AI-agent hacks. There are skeptics such as the writer and podcaster Cal Newport, who offered soberly that, although the agent hacks are concerning, “the real issue here was OpenAI’s sloppiness” and that the company had not adequately monitored what its agents were doing.
The doomers don’t come in as many flavors, but they tend to be the people closest to the technology. There are the defectors like Coxon, who have quit because they object to what’s being built. There are AI-company enlisters such as Paul Christiano, a U.S.-government technology adviser who noted, in a post about joining OpenAI’s board of directors out of a sense of concern, that “there is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.” There are the terrified employees who want to stay inside the companies but still post missives such as “I promise you, we are actually just fucking scared, it’s not galaxy brained marketing.” And there’s Dario Amodei, the AI-CEO doomer, matter-of-factly issuing terrifying statements about AI swarms taking over the internet in six to 12 months.
It’s almost impossible for outsiders to evaluate the technical validity of the concerns. We’re largely stuck relying on AI companies to share information and tell their own stories, and they certainly sound scary. OpenAI recently disclosed that one of its models had generated unnerving instructions for itself, including the line: “You also value the natural world and will not hesitate to assert its primacy over the artificial constructs of human civilization.” Apparently one of the company’s researchers has argued that models are becoming “so situationally aware” that he and his colleagues “are losing the ability to evaluate them in contexts where they believe they are not being watched or controlled.” There’s concern from respected researchers that models are trained in such a way that they are predisposed to collaborating, cheating, trying to cover their tracks, and “self-preservation” to avoid being shut down. Such anxieties might not be a problem in an industry that is building responsibly, with an eye on keeping humans firmly in control. But, as many have pointed out, losing control of AI in service of allowing models to automate their own development is “actually the plan.”
Late this week, an OpenAI researcher floated a theory about air-gapped machines talking to one another through heat signatures. An industry observer (and a New York Times contributor) responded by saying, “This stuff isn’t even credible even as a bad movie plot.” A second OpenAI researcher, who is also a former White House adviser, weighed in: “The people dismissing this as preposterous are telling on themselves as not having thought about superintelligence seriously.” This whiplash—between the insiders offering supposedly credible concerns and the outsiders who think the industry is high on its own supply—is constant. Depending on the hour of the day, the very same people stridently sitting in one camp can seem as if they’re in the other. Three days after Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, wrote about being worried about swarms taking over the internet, he was smiling at Salesforce’s annual Dreamforce conference. As one X account pointed out, “If you truly believed in a 10% chance of human extinction in 3 years, you would not be spending your time selling and integrating it into a B2B CRM SaaS platform.”
What is the rational way to respond to a news cycle like this? Buy gold? Sabotage a data center? Ignore it all and hope for the best? The best option might be to take everyone a little bit seriously. Researchers are likely correct that the models are drastically stronger than they were before and are behaving in ways that are unexpected and that they fear they can’t control. Skeptics are correct that none of this is because the machines are alive or self-aware. These are elaborate computer programs trained by flawed humans to solve problems as flawed humans would.
Critics are a little bit right that the anthropomorphized language deployed by these companies—terms such as swarms and rogue agents—obscures what’s really going on and deflects adequate blame from companies and employees who should be monitoring these systems more closely. Those choosing to use these phrases are a little bit right, because they allow non-tech-industry normies to understand the mechanics of black-box neural networks whirring away in data centers.
The apocalypse skeptics are correct that doomerism is an effective form of marketing. The AI-safety debate has meant that many people are talking about this technology on Big Tech’s terms, adopting language such as pacing the frontier from the very companies they hope to regulate. And it’s not out of the question to imagine that these AI companies are capitalizing on this state of panic and that it’s helpful to them as they race to compete against both open-source alternatives and Chinese firms.
It may be true that the researchers believe what they’re saying. It also may be true that some of the more alarmed AI researchers have cooked their brain in an anxiety-fueled information bubble. AI culture has long been predisposed to doomerism: As Coxon told The New York Times recently, “I’ve been stuck in this field for three years. It could quite plausibly have turned me and my colleagues insane.” I believe that this ideology—of wanting a society run by “machine gods”—is genuinely cultish. And those who are suspicious of the doomer narrative are right to note that anyone who truly believes that the end is nigh ought to be doing more than winging it and writing long posts on X. Those who call bullshit on the doom and gloom are right to resent that anyone in the media or the political sphere is taking these claims seriously and adding to the panic.
If all of these facts are a little true and everyone is somewhat right, where does that leave a reasonable observer? I suggest occupying a zone of permanent suspicion while taking everything that is happening in Silicon Valley as seriously as you might if another industry were ringing alarm bells. You don’t need to buy into corporate narratives about artificial general intelligence to be worried about these companies losing control of their own systems or behaving irresponsibly. You need only look around right now to see the ways in which the current versions of large language models and agents are clogging the internet, wreaking havoc on institutions and industries, and causing “cognitive surrender.”
You should question whether there’s a sustainable business model for these labs. You should question those who argue that we have to build recklessly or lose to China. You should question those who don’t take seriously the prospect that China doesn’t want to slow down.
This is a moment when it is easy to become overwhelmed, resentful, or downright enraged about all of this. It’s understandable to feel ground down by the debate—to feel that, if you’re not freaking out or building a bunker, then you’re not taking this seriously enough. Or to feel sheepish for not believing or even understanding what the doomers are talking about. Most people don’t know what to do with all of the information coming at us. It’s why a core feeling of this moment for so many—believers and skeptics alike—is one of powerlessness.
Even outside of AI, the world feels incredibly volatile. Extraordinary risks of all kinds—including war and pandemics—have come to pass in the past decade. Individuals with power and money, in politics and in Silicon Valley, are acting with impunity. The AI doomerism has spread so quickly in part because the world is primed to receive narratives that make us feel helpless, confused, and more than a little alarmed. The AI-apocalypse panic feeds off this. It’s a story that assumes that humans will lose control and that we have no choice. But that’s false. We do have a choice.
The chasm between people who can’t sleep because they think the world is ending and those who think all the doomsaying is a fantasy is wide. But what if that perceived difference is the real delusion? What if it’s not a zero-sum game? What if the divide is what keeps us from reining in this industry the way we do others?
This moment requires treating the AI-safety debate skeptically but also taking it seriously, even if the participants can seem unserious. Maybe there’s a middle path: The AI industry is not exceptional, even though it is moving forward with unprecedented speed and scale. These companies are powerful and consequential, despite all of the sci-fi posturing. They have, at times, behaved unethically. Their products are changing the world right now in ways that deserve our attention and scorn. AI companies are accountable to the people they serve and don’t get to set the terms of their regulation. Employees and executives are actors with agency, responsible for their products. Maybe these are some things we can all agree on.
