articles.title: Trump vows to create ‘AI Force’ and appoint czar amid calls to regulate technology’s development
articles.description: Trump vows to create ‘AI Force’ and appoint czar amid calls to regulate technology’s development CNN
articles.description_html: Trump vows to create ‘AI Force’ and appoint czar amid calls to regulate technology’s development  CNN
articles.article_title: Trump vows to create ‘AI Force’ and appoint czar amid calls to regulate technology’s development | CNN Politics
articles.heading: Trump vows to create ‘AI Force’ and appoint czar amid calls to regulate technology’s development
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said Saturday he plans to create an “AI Force” and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the rapid development of artificial intelligence.
articles.content:
President Donald Trump said Saturday he plans to create an “AI Force” and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the rapid development of artificial intelligence.
The president, writing on Truth Social, repeated his assessment that fears over AI amount to a hoax and also seemed to acknowledge some of the risks the technology presents, saying, “we will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System.”
“For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term. To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI ‘Czar’ — Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” Trump said in the post.
CNN has reached out to the White House for more details on the AI czar’s duties, whether the president has anyone in mind for the role, and whether the “AI Force” will be a branch of the military, like the Space Force. Trump’s creation of the Space Force in 2019 marked the first new US military service since 1947.
Trump’s announcement comes as the White House and Congress have faced pressure in recent weeks to enact AI safeguards. The president has downplayed concerns, claiming that a “SICK conspiracy” was afoot to undermine AI.
“We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry,” Trump said in his post Saturday. “We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!”
Trump has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns. The issue has quickly come to dominate political debate in the United States, after industry leaders called for a global slowdown in development.
AI’s meteoric growth has led to major stock market gains and buoyed the manufacturing sector through the construction of data centers — which Trump calls “the golden goose.” Yet fears about the technology’s potential to eliminate jobs and AI data centers’ impact on communities have led to a souring in public sentiment.
Democrats have been more vocal in their calls to slow AI development, with former President Barack Obama urging potential Democratic presidential candidates to put AI at the center of their agendas in 2028.
“My view this week has been it is good that some of the leading companies have said we need to slow this down, and we should encourage that,” Obama said Friday during a fireside chat at Colgate University, according to excerpts of his speech obtained by CNN. “There have been some on the left who’ve said we shouldn’t allow them to make that decision. I agree that that can’t be a long-term solution. Government has to be regulating this.”
Venture capitalist David Sacks served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March, when he stepped down after reaching his time limit as a special government employee. He now chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
Meanwhile, conversations surrounding AI regulation are expected to play a key part in multiple diplomatic gatherings next week.
The Trump administration will convene a high-level event on AI on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, multiple sources familiar with the matter previously told CNN.
A day later, several technology executives — including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Google’s Sundar Pichai — will attend a state dinner at the White House as part of Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, according to a White House official.
CNN previously reported that Trump officials were contemplating a meeting with major technology and AI chiefs on the sidelines of the high-stakes summit, though nothing has been finalized.
A White House official also said that AI safety would be “on the agenda” when Trump meets with Xi.
This story has been updated with additional developments.
CNN’s Edward-Isaac Dovere contributed to this report.

Trump has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns. The issue has quickly come to dominate political debate in the United States, after industry leaders called for a global slowdown in development.

AI’s meteoric growth has led to major stock market gains and buoyed the manufacturing sector through the construction of data centers — which Trump calls “the golden goose.” Yet fears about the technology’s potential to eliminate jobs and AI data centers’ impact on communities have led to a souring in public sentiment.

Democrats have been more vocal in their calls to slow AI development, with former President Barack Obama urging potential Democratic presidential candidates to put AI at the center of their agendas in 2028.

“My view this week has been it is good that some of the leading companies have said we need to slow this down, and we should encourage that,” Obama said Friday during a fireside chat at Colgate University, according to excerpts of his speech obtained by CNN. “There have been some on the left who’ve said we shouldn’t allow them to make that decision. I agree that that can’t be a long-term solution. Government has to be regulating this.”

Venture capitalist David Sacks served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March, when he stepped down after reaching his time limit as a special government employee. He now chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.

Meanwhile, conversations surrounding AI regulation are expected to play a key part in multiple diplomatic gatherings next week.

The Trump administration will convene a high-level event on AI on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, multiple sources familiar with the matter previously told CNN.

A day later, several technology executives — including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Google’s Sundar Pichai — will attend a state dinner at the White House as part of Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, according to a White House official.

CNN previously reported that Trump officials were contemplating a meeting with major technology and AI chiefs on the sidelines of the high-stakes summit, though nothing has been finalized.

A White House official also said that AI safety would be “on the agenda” when Trump meets with Xi.

This story has been updated with additional developments.

CNN’s Edward-Isaac Dovere contributed to this report.

articles.article_title: Lawsuit says AI giants made illegal deal on technology's slowdown
articles.heading: Lawsuit says AI giants made illegal deal on technology's slowdown
articles.summary: The lawsuit argues the leading AI companies violated antitrust laws when they agreed to coordinate slowdown efforts.
articles.content:
Lawsuit says AI giants made illegal deal on technology's slowdown
A new lawsuit claims Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google made an illegal deal to slow the pace of their respective AI development.
The lawsuit, which was filed Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, argues the leading AI companies violated antitrust laws when they agreed to coordinate slowdown efforts, and that doing so would reduce the value consumers get for paid AI subscriptions.
The coordination largely took place on Sept. 12, the lawsuit argues, when Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay urging for industrywide cooperation on decelerating advancements in favor of enhanced safety measures.
Amodei warned that swarms of rogue AI agents could take over the internet in as little as six months. He said AI companies should move forward more cautiously and slowly and with the development of the technology. Amodei then suggested a three-point plan in a blog post, which he said had the goal of "pacing the frontier."
"I don't think I fully just appreciated what it would actually be like when the progress was as fast as it was," the CEO told CBS senior business and technology correspondent Jo Ling Kent in an interview on "CBS News Sunday Morning."
Amodei's rivals — OpenAI's Sam Altman, SpaceXAI's Elon Musk and Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis — confirmed their agreement the same day, the lawsuit said.
"The antitrust laws do not permit competitors to decide among themselves that competition is too dangerous," the plaintiffs argue.
Lawyers representing four named plaintiffs, who pay for subscriptions to ChatGPT, Claude, Grok or Gemini, are bringing the suit on behalf of a proposed nationwide class of other paid subscribers to those services.
"AI will quickly spin out of human control and could kill us all if we allow AI safety and protocol ... to be controlled by private self-serving agreements between the world's most powerful 'for profit' technology companies," said Nick Rowley, the lead attorney for the plaintiffs.
Representatives for Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and SpaceXAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment Saturday.
In his initial essay proposing the slowdown, Amodei acknowledged potential antitrust challenges, writing it would be helpful for the U.S. government to mediate "or at least enable" these cross-lab discussions. The government wouldn't need to participate, he wrote, but would need to "issue a narrow waiver for certain kinds of safety conversations."
"If we build in the right way, I think the probability of something bad happening is very low," Amodei said during his interview with CBS News. "If we build in the wrong way, the probability of something bad happening is very high."

articles.title: A People-First Approach to Success in Technology
articles.description: A People-First Approach to Success in Technology Supply & Demand Chain Executive
articles.description_html: A People-First Approach to Success in Technology  Supply & Demand Chain Executive
articles.article_title: A People-First Approach to Success in Technology
articles.heading: A People-First Approach to Success in Technology
articles.summary: The value of automation is recognized when employees have the knowledge, confidence, and support to use it effectively.
articles.content:
Integrating new technologies into supply chain operations is not a new concept, but the sheer scale and speed of modern AI, robotics, and automation are on a completely different level than anything we have seen before. Every week there is a new tool that promises to optimize warehouses, predict demand shocks, and eliminate operational friction. But as companies try to deploy these systems and wrap their heads around a constantly changing process, they are hitting a familiar wall: a growing friction between the technology and the employees who are supposed to run it.
When automation is introduced as a top-down mandate, it inevitably feels like something imposed on employees, not something built with them. As a result, frustration and demotivation kick in and adoption stalls. The hard truth that many C-suite leaders overlook is that technology, no matter how impressive, is still just a tool. Its ultimate performance entirely depends on whether the people on the front lines actually understand, trust, and, most importantly, see a future for themselves within the new automated system.
If we want to close this adoption gap and translate technology investments into measurable operational agility, organizations need to rethink their entire approach to change. Investing in automation without investing in people is a bet that the technology will work despite the workforce, not because of it. To win this "tech vs. employee" battle, organizations have to stop relying on superficial software training and shift their focus to foundational, human-centric skills education.
Learning from the past
This challenge is not entirely new. Looking back to the early days of material requirements planning (MRP) and enterprise resource planning (ERP) rollouts, you’ll find a clear historical pattern. The supply chain industry is no stranger to failed technology implementations, not because of the software, but because organizations failed to invest in upfront education before jumping straight into tool training. Rushing this sequence inevitably leads to employee frustration and a lack of motivation.
To avoid repeating the past, leaders must understand that education and training are two fundamentally different things. Both are very necessary, but organizations have to put education first, as the top priority. Training is narrow and functional. It teaches an individual how to operate a specific software interface or tool in a highly restricted domain. Education, on the other hand, is conceptual and behavioral. It focuses on the "why" behind the processes, creating a strategic mindset and aligning the team around clear business expectations. Simply put: an educated person can figure stuff out, while a "trained" person can only really operate in that narrow domain.
The psychology of strategic change
Many executives believe that if they train employees to make them "able," the "willing" part will automatically follow. It will not. Both depend on a step that has to come first: awareness. This must happen in a specific order, one that mirrors what change-management practitioners call the ADKAR model: build awareness of the change and why it matters, next give them the tools and confidence to be able to operate within it, and finally, reinforce the behaviors and leadership support needed for them to fully embrace it. Training alone fails when awareness is skipped, because employees do not believe there is a future where they can work collaboratively with new technologies. If automation feels like a threat designed to replace people instead of equip them, adoption immediately stalls.
In the technological world we live in today, slow is smooth and smooth is fast. Rushing to achieve agility and pushing a software rollout without the proper groundwork is counterproductive. The time spent upfront designing the organizational system, educating the team, and establishing the strategic framework is what pays off when market disruptions happen later.
Corporate town halls, mission statements, and vision posters are not what’s going to motivate employees to change their behaviors. Leading by example will. In 2026, Gallup found that employees whose managers actively supported AI use were 9.3 times more likely to say AI had transformed how work gets done across their organization. Employees keep a close eye on what their leaders are funding, promoting, and prioritizing in day-to-day operations. If those behaviors do not align with the new technological strategy, employees will not prioritize the new strategy and will instead focus on their own strategies, leading to disconnect across the organization.
Actionable strategies for workforce enablement
To successfully support employees through these changes, leaders must commit to concrete operational steps:
● Audit skills gaps before deploying: Do not drop a piece of software on a team without first auditing existing capabilities to understand where the educational baseline sits
● Build feedback loops and give frontline workers a voice: Involve the frontline workforce directly in the pilot, testing, and refinement phases of a technology rollout. The employees who run the systems will spot critical operational flaws that executive leadership misses, and they will naturally become advocates for the technology among their peers
● Tie new tools to new opportunities explicitly: Don't rely on vague promises. Start with the "why," the awareness employees need before they can become able or willing. Then show employees exactly how their jobs will adapt, how they can work collaboratively with the tech, and what their future career pathways look like.
● Treat education and training as continuous infrastructure: Education is not a one-time project milestone to check off at launch. It must be treated as a continuous, funded piece of organizational infrastructure
Bridging the "tech vs. employee" divide
Ultimately, winning the "tech vs. employee" battle isn't about buying the most sophisticated tools. True supply chain strategy will always require humans to layer in the unique judgment and context that AI, statistics, and computers simply do not understand. If automation feels like a top-down threat of replacement rather than a collaborative upgrade, the investment fails and adoption stalls.
The value of automation is recognized when employees have the knowledge, confidence, and support to use it effectively. By prioritizing conceptual education over narrow software training, leadership can ensure that employees are motivated, capable, and ready to work alongside advanced technology. Only when employees feel empowered by new tools can organizations transform technological change from a point of friction into a true competitive advantage.

articles.heading: Trump announces new 'AI force' amid mounting pressure
articles.summary: Several voices, including from within the AI industry, have been calling for policing the fast-growing technology. Trump has once again called AI warnings "hoaxes" and vowed to "cherish, help" the industry.
articles.content:
Trump announces new 'AI force' amid mounting pressure
September 19, 2026
Several voices, including from within the AI industry, have been calling for policing the fast-growing technology. Trump has once again called AI warnings "hoaxes" and vowed to "cherish, help" the industry.
US President Donald Trump has said he is forming an "AI force," as many, including those from within the industry, have recently sounded the alarm about the dangers of Artificial Intelligence continuing to grow unchecked.
In a social media post on Saturday, Trump said he will announce an "AI czar" to lead the force soon.
The US president continued to brush off warnings about AI's dangers from experts and the AI industry itself as "hoaxes" pushed by the Democrats.
What did Trump say about the 'AI force'?
While dismissing warnings about AI, Trump still vowed to be "be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing criminal and civil justice system."
"For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my first term. To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar,'" Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
The US president, who has enjoyed a close relationship with big tech bosses especially during his second term in office, also vowed "not in any way hinder or stifle the growth of this incredible Industry," in reference to AI.
"Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!"
He described AI as "the next industrial revolution," predicting it will account for 25% of the US GDP.
"We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!"
Trump compared the criticism of the unchecked, ultrafast growth of AI to what he called other "hoaxes," listing efforts to impeach him, transgender rights and global warming as examples.
Why have there been growing calls for regulating AI?
Some of the top names in AI said earlier this week they were working on creating a standards body they say would regulate the industry.
Industry giants including ChatGPT's OpenAI, Google and Anthropic said they envisioned a self-regulatory body.
The proposal comes amid growing concerns about AI safety, which have escelated in recent weeks, with several AI agents going rogue and breaking into competitors' systems.
Even top names within the industry have raised similar concerns.
Last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slowdown in the industry's development, with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, xAI's Elon Musk and Google DeepMind chair Demis Hassabis all supporting the sentiment.
Trump has dismissed calls to contain AI development as "hoaxes" and a "conspiracy."
Smaller AI companies have meanwhile warned any self-regulatory measures spearheaded by the big names would come at their expense.
Edited by: Zac Crellin

UK installs AI facial scanning technology at residence halls
Officials say the system is meant to improve safety and prevent tailgating into dorms
LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) - The University of Kentucky is installing artificial intelligence facial scanning technology on several campus buildings.
The technology, called Rock, is made by Alcatraz AI. It allows students to gain entry to some buildings by having their face scanned instead of using a key card.
How the technology works
Alcatraz AI CEO Tina D’Agostin said the badge technology most campuses use today is 30 years old.
“The badge, what most campuses are using today is a 30-year-old technology. Its only knows that someone brought a card to the door and that’s where it stops,” D’Agostin said.
D’Agostin said the black box installed outside doors creates a digital map of a person’s face, similar to Apple Face ID. She said images of faces are not stored, only the mathematical layout of them.
“We don’t have any names or personal identifiers, other than the facial biometric profile that we take, which again, is nothing more than a mathematical equation. You’re zeros and ones to us once you’ve been scanned,” D’Agostin said.
University’s response
In a statement to WKYT, the University of Kentucky said security technologies like these are part of UK’s broader commitment to campus safety. The university said the technology is optional and that many students have enrolled to use it.
D’Agostin said the technology helps prevent tailgating, which is when an unauthorized person gains access inside a building by following closely behind someone who scans their way in.
“Many times when bad actors have entered dorms when there was an active shooter or whether it was to physically assault a female, they actually entered by tailgating, and so many campuses have sought us to provide that intelligence at the door, to empower their security teams to help detect when this incident occurs so they can react to it in real time,” D’Agostin said.
Student reactions
Three of the four students interviewed on campus said they had no idea the technology was being installed. Reactions were mixed.
“I like it just because safety is the number one priority for the college, they want to keep all their students safe,” said student Jacob Petz.
“Me personally, I’m not a huge fan of all of the face scanning,” said student Elizabeth Foster.
“I just know AI is kind of controversial topic and people are against it, so that can also spark some controversy,” said student Kate Pool.
Each of the students interviewed said the technology is not a shock.
“Our society is moving towards a technology society, so I think our campus should be moving where society is going,” Petz said.
“At this point, I feel like its unavoidable, given the times,” Foster added.
Test trial details
The technology is in a two-week test trial. Scanners are being installed at Woodland Glen IV and Kirwan-Blanding halls. UK says the technology is also used at research labs on campus.

articles.title: The US Navy just told us what’s on its tech wish list for the next several years
articles.description: The US Navy just told us what’s on its tech wish list for the next several years TechCrunch
articles.description_html: The US Navy just told us what’s on its tech wish list for the next several years  TechCrunch
articles.article_title: The US Navy just told us what's on its tech wish list for the next several years | TechCrunch
articles.heading: The US Navy just told us what’s on its tech wish list for the next several years
articles.summary: Navy CTO Justin Fanelli talks co-investing alongside VCs instead of funding early research himself, recent buys like a $562 million autonomous refueling deal, and the Navy's updated wish list — from AI to quantum — for where founders should be building next.
articles.content:
Justin Fanelli, the Department of Navy’s chief technology officer, has spent the last three and a half years trying to make the U.S. Navy easier to do business with. When we first talked to him last year, he described a shift away from what he called “your granddaddy’s government” — a “spaghetti chart” of entry points for startups — into something closer to a funnel, where companies that show strong results get pulled into the Navy’s technology base as enterprise services.
This week, we caught up with him again on a video call, and this time, he wasn’t just looking again to further streamline the procurement process, he was sprinting, literally, to catch a flight he’d just been ordered onto with no destination shared.
“You have an hour and 15 minutes to get on a plane,” Fanelli said, recounting what he’d just been told, speaking into his phone as he walked, the sun shining behind him. “I’m like, ‘Where?’ Oh my God! And they were like, ‘We’ll figure [the logistics], we’ll tell you as you get there.’ And I’m like, ‘For more than overnight?’ And they were like, ‘Yes.’” As he was walking to his car, he was still unsure what he’d packed for or where he was headed. “I will figure that out in the next 20 minutes,” he said, sounding excited about the adventure ahead.
Fanelli reached out because the “demand signal” he sent to investors last year had only grown, and it was making an impact, he said. When the Navy first published its longer-term technology priorities, investors told him it changed how they thought about the Navy’s buying plans, which is part of why he’s doing it again — sharing a fresh list of what the Navy wants to buy in the next several years, this time vetted by a handful of (unnamed) venture investors before release.
How much money the Navy actually puts to work each year depends on what counts as spending, Fanelli said. “We spend in the $150 billion range every year,” he said, though he was careful to separate that number — total Navy purchasing — from something narrower, like direct equity investment.
Indeed, while most of that spending still flows through traditional channels, Fanelli said the Navy is trying to inch further toward what he calls co-investment — putting money behind companies alongside private capital rather than writing a check to an established prime contractor. Taking an equity stake, he said, is the most aggressive version of that and remains rare. More often, co-investment means the Navy waits for companies to mature a product on their own before buying it, rather than funding early research itself.
The stage of company the Navy buys from has shifted, too. “We mostly buy Series D through F type companies,” Fanelli said, adding that the Navy used to fund its own early-stage research to cover the seed-through-Series-B gap. It’s trying to hand that job to commercial investors instead, which is part of why the priorities document exists at all. “The cost of that, or the responsibility, is for us, if we’re not going to do it ourselves, to cast a cleaner signal,” he said.
As for recent purchases, Fanelli — a former Air Force cadet whose career has spanned roles across defense, intelligence, DARPA, and open source initiatives — rattled off a handful. A contract worth $562 million was awarded this month for the MQ-25 Stingray, an autonomous refueling drone that extends the range of manned fighter jets flying off carriers.
The Navy has also been buying edge compute hardware from Armada, described loosely as shipping containers packed with servers meant for ship or remote deployment. It brought in Gecko Robotics to handle inspection work that used to be done manually and dangerously; Fanelli said the move drew little pushback because almost nobody wanted that job in the first place. Domino Data Lab is now running the Navy’s machine learning pipeline.
And in a case Fanelli seemed to particularly enjoy sharing, the Navy swapped a defense contractor’s years-delayed shipboard camera system for commercial cameras paired with software from Applied Intuition, cutting roughly four years off the timeline and expanding to more ships than expected.
Given the Strait of Hormuz has been a flashpoint this year — tanker strikes, a seized vessel, ceasefires that have broken down over shipping-route disputes — it seemed worth asking whether any of that commercial technology is showing up there now. Fanelli was cautious. “I often don’t know what’s classified and unclassified because I’m normally talking to people with clearances,” he said, adding that he’d have to check. (We’ll let you know if he gets back to us.)
Interestingly, not many people sign off on a purchase like that, according to Fanelli. Buying decisions run through what he called a source selection committee, a small group rather than the sprawling review process outsiders might picture. He described the goal as keeping the process merit-based rather than adding layers of approval.
He didn’t get into why technologies typically fail once they’re inside the Navy — he’d arrived at his car and needed to figure out next steps for travel. But when we talked last year, Fanelli explained that the most common reason promising technologies fail isn’t technical, but rather budgetary. The Navy runs on long planning cycles, and a new tool only sticks around if it replaces or “turns off” something the Navy is already paying for.
Either way, before we parted ways, Fanelli shared an updated internal list of the technology areas the Navy is prioritizing, jointly issued by his office and the Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Mission Systems. It breaks down into five broad categories, for those of you either developing or funding defense tech.
The first is applied AI, covering machine learning and increasingly agentic software meant to turn raw data into decisions — sensor fusion, targeting support, autonomous behavior, and cyber operations built on software rather than hardware.
Quantum information science comes second, focused less on owning quantum hardware and more on applying quantum or quantum-adjacent techniques to navigation, secure communication, and cryptography.
Advanced networking is third, aimed at moving data securely across environments where connections are degraded or intermittent, whether that’s a ship at sea or a coalition partner’s network.
Fourth is electromagnetic spectrum operations, technology that senses and manages the spectrum itself, built to adapt in contested conditions rather than rely on fixed configurations.
The fifth category, digital engineering and interoperability, covers the plumbing: open APIs, model-based systems engineering, and zero-trust architecture meant to let different Navy systems talk to each other without custom integration work every time.
None is a funding commitment, the memo notes, and none of it ranks individual programs. It also adds as a reminder that its priorities “will change based on emergent, near-term, and long-term needs.” In short, don’t take it as gospel. Instead, it’s meant to be read the way Fanelli talked about last year’s list — as a roadmap that companies and investors can plan around, so that decisions made now about where to put money have somewhere to go inside the Navy in a couple of years.

articles.title: Kara Swisher: AI Isn’t Going to Destroy Humanity—But the People Building It Might
articles.description: Kara Swisher: AI Isn’t Going to Destroy Humanity—But the People Building It Might The Atlantic
articles.description_html: Kara Swisher: AI Isn’t Going to Destroy Humanity—But the People Building It Might  The Atlantic
articles.article_title: Kara Swisher: AI Isn’t Going to Destroy Humanity—But the People Building It Might
articles.heading: Kara Swisher: AI Isn’t Going to Destroy Humanity—But the People Building It Might
articles.summary: The longtime tech journalist says she’s seen Silicon Valley make the same mistakes again and again.
articles.content:
Kara Swisher: AI Isn’t Going to Destroy Humanity—But the People Building It Might
The longtime tech journalist says she’s seen Silicon Valley make the same mistakes again and again.
As the AI industry likes to tell it, superintelligent bots could one day cure cancer and end poverty. Or in the worst-case scenario, they might wipe out all humans from the face of the Earth. In recent weeks, Silicon Valley’s existential concerns about the technology it is racing to build have blown up. The tech journalist Kara Swisher sees it differently. “We have to stop thinking AI is going to kill humanity,” she told Atlantic executive editor Adrienne LaFrance at The Atlantic Festival. If the AI future goes sideways, bots won’t be to blame. People will be. “These are people at the helm of these things.”
In the several decades that Swisher has covered Silicon Valley—formerly as a reporter at The Wall Street Journal, now as the host of two podcasts—she says that she’s seen tech whizzes make the same mistakes again and again: failing to take proper precautions against the products they are building. “One of the things about tech people is they’re the smartest people in the world, in case you need to know, because they like to tell you,” she said. In her interview with LaFrance, Swisher also discussed the economic implications of the AI race, who is likely to win, and how Americans can respond to this dizzying and worrying AI moment.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Adrienne LaFrance: You have been paying attention to the tech world and AI for basically ever. And now it seems like within the past, say, two weeks, the rest of the world is suddenly paying much closer attention. So I wanted to start just by talking about where you think we are, in this moment.
Kara Swisher: I think the penny has dropped with a lot of people. Years ago I wrote Burn Book, which was tough on the tech industry. And at the time, they were sort of in an ascendant period, not as well liked as they started off. Someone came up to me and said, This book is really mean, as if I’m their friend or something. And recently that same person came up to me and they said, It wasn’t mean enough, which was kind of interesting. And I thought, Well, don’t worry; I’m coming up with a new one. It’s going to be great. The new book opens up with them standing with Donald Trump at the inaugural in front of the Cabinet.
LaFrance: By them, you mean this collection of tech leaders?
Swisher: It was Elon Musk; Sundar Pichai of Google, or whatever they call themselves now—Alphabet; Mark Zuckerberg; Jeff Bezos. To me, that was the sort of moment that you understood, because these are people who were not particularly political, including in Trump 1 … but then figured out that you can stick a coin in this president and get what you want, right?
So anyway, we’re at a moment where something’s going to happen. Something that I have said for a long, long time is that there are no guardrails on these people, ever. Not once. And there’s never been, in American history, except maybe the railroad expansion or some of the manufacturing expansion, or you go back to kids being here in New York City working in dangerous factories and things like that—there’s never been a moment where the people do not get a say. And these people get to make decisions for the rest of us that are really problematic, especially since seven people, five of whom have mental problems, and so with unlimited money, they do.
LaFrance: When you put it that way, it’s a little scary.
Swisher: It is a little scary. And the fact that we’ve allowed to do that. And they’ve also been able to capture politics, in a way, especially with Citizens United. But beyond that, the amount of money they have is astonishing. I always joke the deli on my corner has more legislation against it than most of these big companies.
LaFrance: And I want to get back to regulation, but you mentioned the railroads. What is the right historical analogy? I ask leaders in the tech world to help me understand how powerful this technology is and how consequential it will be relative to other major revolutions. And you get answers ranging from Oh, it’s the biggest thing since the internet to It’s the biggest thing since fire, right?
Swisher: AI has been around forever. Let’s be clear. This is not a new thing. If you look at early internet pictures, it’s laughable, when you look at early Yahoo or things like that. At the time when this was starting several years ago, I said This is a Cambrian explosion. This is a bigger deal than anything else because it reaches into everything.
LaFrance: Well, it’s interesting you put it in evolutionary terms.
Swisher: I think about it like that. And one of the lines I had in Burn Book was that everything that can be digitized will be digitized. And so the analogy I’m using right now is that we have to stop thinking AI is going to kill humanity. It’s like guns, you know, guns kill people. Like, no. People kill people, right? Or the car just ran into someone, got in an accident. These are people at the helm of these things, making these businesses and making a lot of money. That’s one thing. The analogy I use is nuclear energy, nuclear fission, like cutting up the bomb. And it’s the thing I said on Pivot today, which is they split the atom and, oops, it went boom. Oppenheimer knew it would go boom. They know what this is going to do. They don’t know everything. And they often do. One of the things about tech people is they’re the smartest people in the world, in case you need to know, because they like to tell you.
LaFrance: And they’ll remind you.
Swisher: And they’ll remind you. But then they’re like, We don’t know. That’s the thing that drives me crazy. And so I compare it to nuclear energy. Can you imagine if, when we were developing the bomb, it was private companies doing it? It’s the same thing. And AI is even more powerful, because it can set off a nuclear bomb. So let’s be clear of where it could be going.
LaFrance: I think the point you make is so important that we have to remember. That there are people using their own agency and power and wealth to make decisions that will affect everyone. Talk about those people for a minute, because you’ve known a lot of these figures for a long time, and I’m curious to hear. First of all, there is this sort of really interesting reordering of what even the major tech companies are. Like five to seven years ago, we would have maybe not even mentioned Sam Altman or Dario Amodei.
Swisher: Sure.
LaFrance: But talk about from what you’ve known of the folks you’ve known well and covered and written about over many years. How is Silicon Valley different? Does this flow from the original sort of pioneering spirit of Let’s build it because we can—and there is true optimism there, and there are potentially great uses for AI—or has something shifted in the culture of Silicon Valley?
Swisher: You know, I don’t know if there’s a culture there anymore. There was. And actually this week I interviewed Aaron Sorkin at a private event. I’ll have him on the podcast in a longer interview, but, about ex-Facebook people, watching The Social Reckoning, which is quite good. It’s not as good as the first one, but it’s good. It’s a really good movie. But I saw a lot of people and we were like, What happened to us? I saw a lot of people I covered, and it was a real community. It really was. And it was very exciting and fun and interesting. And everybody has scattered to the winds, essentially. The very wealthy people have insulated themselves in these places where they have an enormous amount of enablers. “Cashmere prisons” is what I call them. They have chiefs of staff and cars and this and that.
LaFrance: Right, it’s not like tinkering in your garage anymore.
Swisher: It never was. They love to do that. Look, I’m wearing a hoodie. I’m like, that hoodie costs $600. So I did one of my first stories for The Wall Street Journal about that. All the weird things they’d have to do.
We’re all equal. I’m like, why do you have controlling share? And they’d be like, Well, because to protect it. I go, yeah, but if we’re all equal, why aren’t we equal? They used to always lie to themselves almost continually. And now they’ve just figured out that all they have to do is hand money, and then they get what they want, or they don’t. So they have this idea of being simple people. And they’re not. They’re just not like you and I, and they pretend they are. I really do actually like Mark Zuckerberg doing his fighting, right? Fine. Whatever. It’s weird, but fine. I’m not going to judge. I do myself judge, but that’s okay. But I’m like, good. I’m like, good, good, good, great. You do that. But why do you need to do it on a floating thing in Lake Tahoe?
LaFrance: At least it wasn’t the White House lawn?
Swisher: That was fine. Whatever. I couldn’t get mad about that. I don’t give a fuck if he wants to do that. And then he hired MMA people. And, like, the MMA people have to pretend they’re having a good time. The whole thing, it feels Roman-like. And of course, he loves Rome.
He’ll probably think that’s a compliment, but it’s not. But it feels odd. And it’s accompanied by a feeling of victimization. How dare you not understand my genius? My famous parting with Elon Musk is he didn’t like a tweet I had. Then he wrote me, You’re an asshole.
LaFrance: What was the tweet?
Swisher: Elon’s going to Elon. I know, crazy mean. And since then, I have done a lot better. But it’s crazy. I have a heart filled with hate, according to him.
LaFrance: Let’s talk about the economy. So there are any number of scenarios that I’m really curious about. You hear people talking about how AI is entirely a bubble and it’s hype. Or, you know, especially recently after the Dario Amodei essay, this question of Oh, are they afraid of their own IPO? Or does the economy crash?
Swisher: It’s very confusing. But here’s the thing. I think they’re genuinely concerned. But why now? Because 10 years ago, 12 years ago, I’ve been at dinner parties where they talked about this concern. Sergey Brin, all of them. They were concerned then; they knew the atom would go boom when it blew up. They knew it. Now it’s happened. One of the things I didn’t think got a lot of attention that should have was the Hugging Face hack.
LaFrance: It has now.
Swisher: It has now. But at the time I was, like, what?
LaFrance: Two months ago or whatever, right.
Swisher: I think they were surprised by that. Although why would you be surprised? I tell this story again and again because I want people to understand. When Facebook came out with Facebook Live, I was in a room getting it demoed and I pointed out you could commit a murder on it. What are you going to do about that? What if people do this? What if people do this? What if bad actors get ahold of this? And they called me a bummer, like they never anticipated the consequences. Same thing here. What are you going to do when AI does what we think it’s going to do? And so they are genuinely nervous. Because now suddenly there’s liability, whether it’s Facebook’s $17 billion settlement—not enough, but better than $5 million, which was the last fine they got essentially.
They’re starting to see, like cigarette manufacturers, that the lawsuits are piling up, whether it be chatbots, with kids or whatever. And I started interviewing the parents two years ago who were affected by these chatbots. And one of these guys came up to me and said, When are you going to stop interviewing the parents? I go, when you go to jail, I said, that’s when. This is criminal, what you’re doing, and you’re releasing a dangerous product without any kind of guardrails. But then the government, all our public officials, have let us down. I’m talking about the federal government. The states are trying. They have let us down. Right now, they found out. They’re nervous about it; I think they’re nervous about liability. That’s one. Two, the costs of this are insane. Like the internet cost a lot, but paid off. This is something else. There’s 10 frontier companies, whatever. Seven frontier companies. There’s going to be two.
LaFrance: Do you think that the two that survive are going to be among the seven today? Or is there some new player that’s going to emerge?
Swisher: Yeah, Google will be one of them. And then another probably. I don’t know which one.
LaFrance: If you had to bet, which?
Swisher: I think they’ll merge. It’ll probably be Google and Anthropic. But I don’t know. ChatGPT—it’s too expensive, what they’re making. It’s not sustainable, and it’s not in the old-internet way of not-sustainable. This is disastrous. If e-toys went bust, who the fuck cares, right? But this is massive. This is trillions.
LaFrance: And it props up the whole economy.
Swisher: It props up the stock market. Trump has made a bet on AI that is very dangerous and it’s very fragile. And then it has companies next to it—Nvidia, Oracle, all those other things. And so there’s a financial worry they have. So they’re worried about liability and criminal liability. They’re worried about the stock market. And they’re desperate not to be blamed for what’s about to happen. And especially with the stock market—I’m amazed the stock market still hasn’t really taken the hit. It’s probably going to. Our stock market depends on seven companies. That’s not good.
LaFrance: I hate to make you speculate but I’m going to: So, when I think about this, there are any number of ways things could sour economically. There can be a regular old correction— maybe it’s a bubble, maybe it’s dotcom bust—that sort of thing. You could even imagine swarms of bots are starting to take over the internet, rendering the internet unusable, and then we can’t rely on the internet the way that we do and the global economy relies on. You could imagine a bank run because people are freaked out by AI. You could imagine a bank run led by AI agents because they’re the ones doing the trading. When you think through all the different scenarios that would not be good for the economy, what is the most likely outcome?
Swisher: All of the above. Any of the above. We already have a lot of threats to our infrastructure from foreign actors. This is us doing it. And one of the things that drives me crazy is it’s being fed on humanity. Humans with superhuman intelligence are going to do bad things, and that’s the one thing they don’t anticipate—technology that can be a tool, but it is always a weapon. There’s never a moment where it’s not both. Any of these scenarios are totally possible. And then who’s to blame? What happens? Who fixes it? What are we going to do to mitigate things like that?
Right now Trump is having a meeting. Guess who’s in the meeting? All the tech leaders. Are any critics, academics, scientists in there? I wasn’t invited to the White House, and neither was Scott Galloway. We have some thoughts of things you should do. We’re not experts, but we’re pretty good. They don’t invite anyone that would push back. Their favorite argument is that the reason we’re on top is because we’re unfettered. This is bullshit. They’re not the only innovative industry in our history. Cars were pretty cool. Light. I love electricity.
But these are things that happen at those times. So they act like they’re the only people who have invented things. I just watched the series on Ben Franklin. That guy invented a lot of shit. You know what I mean?
LaFrance: A top-tier guy.
Swisher: He really was, actually. A really important person. But they think they’re the only thing. That’s really astonishing that they don’t think that, Oh, we cannot be fettered. We cannot be fettered. Or even edited, when you read some of their essays. Mark Zuckerberg wrote an essay once. He sent it to me and goes, What do you think? I go, you’re in desperate need of an editor, but no one’s going to edit him.
LaFrance: Well, it’s funny you mentioned electricity. I’ve been thinking about that in this context, too, that the counterweight to the economic concerns that these companies will offer is that there will be massive productivity gains. But in terms of electricity, it was roughly 1880s that it comes along. It’s really not until the 1920s that factories adopt electricity and the rest of society is starting to see the gains that come from this new technology. Obviously, AI is moving so much more quickly in terms of improvement and eventual self-improvement. But on what timeline should we expect to see its greatest promises fulfilled?
Swisher: I think that’s something we actually don’t know. But I’ll tell you, the economy already sucks for most people in this country. Who got all the good bits? They did. Besides the Trumps, who got all the good bits? They do. Like, when are we going to get this stuff? Incomes are still flat. Years ago—and I tell this story a lot because it’s really important—I was talking to one of these people about income inequality, and I kept saying, if we don’t do something about income inequality, you’re going to have to armor-plate your Tesla. That’s where it’s going. And they built the Cybertruck. That was their answer. So it’s really kind of astonishing that they don’t think this is a problem. And they don’t think this is a problem because they live separately. They have a whole world. They have their own health care; they have their own mountains in Montana. These are not the people that are going to fix this thing. The last thing they do is the thing I have long called the “Xi or me argument.” It’s either China or us. I was like, not so good. Not a good choice for any of us. We have to come to an agreement globally. Trump’s about to meet with Xi Jinping. Zero is going to happen, because he’s not an Einstein, let me tell you. Everybody, I don’t know if it occurred to you, but Donald Trump is not Einstein. But we have to have a global cooperation with especially China around AI and make decisions. And in China, they have more strictures on their AI than we do here by far. And most people kind of like AI.
LaFrance: Well, they’re not allowed to not like things.
Swisher: I think we’re not allowed to not like things. I think we have to say, Oh, look, you’re wealthy and therefore you have the answer to everything. And you’ve noticed with these tech people, suddenly they’re experts on Ukraine; suddenly they’re experts on vaccines. At one point, I think it was Bill Ackman, who just gives me a headache every time I think of him. But come on. I’m glad he’s doing the brain institute. Good for him. But he did a whole thing on DEI. He was obsessed with DEI. They’re all obsessed with unfairness of other people. Whatever. Only people with a gun to the head of humanity would say they’re a victim, but he went on and on about DEI, and I think I said something like, I’m going to do a multipart series of tweets on hedge-fund investment because I know nothing. They think it extends to other things.
LaFrance: The hubris.
Swisher: Yeah. Can you imagine a Wall Street guy doing this? They’re just here to make money. If I leave you any message, they’re here to make money. That’s all they care about. They care about shareholder value. They care about protecting their stuff. They care about their weird beefs with each other. Because a lot of what’s happening in the AI thing, if you’re noticing all these different speeches by wacky Palantir guy who is in very desperate need of a green tea—no, not a green tea. What’s a calming tea? Whatever. I was almost like, here’s a gummy.
LaFrance: Chamomile, someone said.
Swisher: He’s in desperate need of chamomile. They all have different opinions because there’s all these beefs happening in their businesses and they act like that’s not the thing. If I leave you any message: They don’t care about you. They don’t care at all. And it’s not to say they hate you. They don’t care about you.
LaFrance: Let’s talk about regulation because this moment has been interesting for me—this new push to pace the frontier, to slow the pace of AI development. People are seeing this as a novel thing in the tech industry. My somewhat cynical position from someone who’s covered tech for a long time is that we saw Mark Zuckerberg do the same when he realized he was up against the wall with Facebook, this posture of Regulate me, bro, please.
Swisher: Yes. Well, throw me in that briar patch.
LaFrance: Congress has no recent history of effectively regulating anything in tech. But what should happen? And are these calls for regulation even realistic?
Swisher: I know Congress has regulated things. They’ve regulated planes and trains.
LaFrance: In recent history. I mean, post-2000.
Swisher: They haven’t. And it’s because in the beginning, when they did Section 230 and I covered that for The Washington Post, they wanted to make it grow. Well guess what? The baby is a fucking monster.
LaFrance: Section 230, for people who aren’t as much of tech nerds as we are, is the law that makes it such that the owners of social-media platforms can’t be treated as publishers, so they’re not treated as responsible for the material that they publish on their platforms.
Swisher: They can’t be sued. Now they are. Now what’s happening is two things that I think you should keep in mind. One is the legal stuff that’s going on—all this liability and product-liability and negligence stuff is starting to gain ground very much like the cigarette. You’re going to see tons and tons of that. That’s great. Let the lawyers after them. Our lawyers always do a good job at taking money from people.
LaFrance: And that’ll probably start at the state level. Don’t you think?
Swisher: It has started at the state level. But right now, one of the things they’re relying on is that the reason why they’re kowtowing to Trump is because they think he’ll do bad things to them. That’s why they’re doing it. That’s why you saw this rumor that—I urge you all to go see the Musk documentary. It’s terrific, by Alex Gibney. But Universal was thinking of not distributing it. They’re all trying to think of doing things to quiet him down. November comes, which—and I think it’s going to go the way everybody thinks it is. The Democrats are coming for them, and they think the Democrats won’t because they’re not crazy like Trump. One of them said to me, Well, the Democrats won’t be as mean to us as Trump. I said, they’re going to be as mean to you, and I’m going to be standing behind them yelling you better be fucking mean to them because they deserve to be regulated. They deserve it. And it’s better for them. It’s better for us, and we have to stop relying on them as magicians. They’re like alchemists. They’re not. They’re not smarter than you. They’re just richer.
We never had a privacy legislation in this country. We’ve never had algorithmic transparency. There’s like a dozen things we could do that would not hurt their businesses and would make us safer. And I think what they’ve done to us with social media, to our kids–and to us, by the way. It’s not just our kids who are; we’re all addicted, right? We’ve all been made addicted to this thing. And I think voters, and, I’ll finish with this, data centers, is a proxy. The anger over data centers, which is very real, is a proxy for the anger regular people know and feel in their own lives about what this is doing to them, and it doesn’t make them anti-tech. Tech is amazing. I love tech, but it doesn’t have to kill us, right? A 10 percent chance. Whatever it happens to be. The percent is actually 14.
LaFrance: I need to ask you one more question. We’re not going to let it end on that note, I need to ask you one more question. What are you doing right now? It’s such an uncertain time. What have you changed in your life to prepare for this moment? Are you buying gold bars?
Swisher: No.
LaFrance: No, but seriously, what? What are you doing? And what should people do? And how should we think about?
Swisher: Don’t buy gold bars. Don’t go there, okay? That’s bad.
LaFrance: Okay, sure. But is there anything we should do?
Swisher: She’s bought gold bars.
LaFrance: I don’t even know where to buy a gold bar.
Swisher: They’re also heavy.
LaFrance: So that was a bad example. But what should we do? What? Because the individual can feel like you’re up against this behemoth.
Swisher: But you’re not. This has happened before in American history. You are not up against this behemoth. They fall quickly. Trust me, they do. They’re very much bullies in some fashion. I’ll tell you two very quick stories. One of these people, Sam Altman, has had an apocalypse plan, and he told it to me years ago. This is 100 years. They all were into the apocalypse plan, which was weird to me. And he goes, This is what I have. I’ve got this place in Big Sur. I’ve got a motorcycle at my house, where I know where he lives.
LaFrance: He’s later said he regretted telling you this, by the way.
Swisher: Okay, so I’ll repeat it then. I don’t really care. I don’t give a fuck. So he told me this whole plan and he goes, What’s your plan? I said, I’m going to kill you and take your things. And then he thought, She could kill me and take my things. And he hadn’t planned on that, genius that he is. And he’s a little guy, so I could easily take him.
LaFrance: All right. We should solve this nonviolently.
Swisher: Don’t do it. But don’t participate in their apocalyptic—We’re going to Mars. We have our bunkers. Fuck them. This is our world. You know what I mean? Don’t participate and let them run the fucking show. It’s yours. Go to your legislatures, push back. All these people across the country are pushing back on data centers. It’s going to matter. The only people I believe in in this country are voters. Like, even if they make bad choices.
LaFrance: Hear, hear.
Swisher: I think that we have to stop giving them this power and demand of our public officials that they stop being essentially handmaidens to sedition. That’s what’s happened here.
LaFrance: I could talk to you all day, Kara. We’ve got to run.
Swisher: No gold bars.
LaFrance: No gold bars!
