Kara Swisher: AI Isn’t Going to Destroy Humanity—But the People Building It Might

The longtime tech journalist says she’s seen Silicon Valley make the same mistakes again and again.

As the AI industry likes to tell it, superintelligent bots could one day cure cancer and end poverty. Or in the worst-case scenario, they might wipe out all humans from the face of the Earth. In recent weeks, Silicon Valley’s existential concerns about the technology it is racing to build have blown up. The tech journalist Kara Swisher sees it differently. “We have to stop thinking AI is going to kill humanity,” she told Atlantic executive editor Adrienne LaFrance at The Atlantic Festival. If the AI future goes sideways, bots won’t be to blame. People will be. “These are people at the helm of these things.”

In the several decades that Swisher has covered Silicon Valley—formerly as a reporter at The Wall Street Journal, now as the host of two podcasts—she says that she’s seen tech whizzes make the same mistakes again and again: failing to take proper precautions against the products they are building. “One of the things about tech people is they’re the smartest people in the world, in case you need to know, because they like to tell you,” she said. In her interview with LaFrance, Swisher also discussed the economic implications of the AI race, who is likely to win, and how Americans can respond to this dizzying and worrying AI moment.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Adrienne LaFrance: You have been paying attention to the tech world and AI for basically ever. And now it seems like within the past, say, two weeks, the rest of the world is suddenly paying much closer attention. So I wanted to start just by talking about where you think we are, in this moment.

Kara Swisher: I think the penny has dropped with a lot of people. Years ago I wrote Burn Book, which was tough on the tech industry. And at the time, they were sort of in an ascendant period, not as well liked as they started off. Someone came up to me and said, This book is really mean, as if I’m their friend or something. And recently that same person came up to me and they said, It wasn’t mean enough, which was kind of interesting. And I thought, Well, don’t worry; I’m coming up with a new one. It’s going to be great. The new book opens up with them standing with Donald Trump at the inaugural in front of the Cabinet.

LaFrance: By them, you mean this collection of tech leaders?

Swisher: It was Elon Musk; Sundar Pichai of Google, or whatever they call themselves now—Alphabet; Mark Zuckerberg; Jeff Bezos. To me, that was the sort of moment that you understood, because these are people who were not particularly political, including in Trump 1 … but then figured out that you can stick a coin in this president and get what you want, right?

So anyway, we’re at a moment where something’s going to happen. Something that I have said for a long, long time is that there are no guardrails on these people, ever. Not once. And there’s never been, in American history, except maybe the railroad expansion or some of the manufacturing expansion, or you go back to kids being here in New York City working in dangerous factories and things like that—there’s never been a moment where the people do not get a say. And these people get to make decisions for the rest of us that are really problematic, especially since seven people, five of whom have mental problems, and so with unlimited money, they do.

LaFrance: When you put it that way, it’s a little scary.

Swisher: It is a little scary. And the fact that we’ve allowed to do that. And they’ve also been able to capture politics, in a way, especially with Citizens United. But beyond that, the amount of money they have is astonishing. I always joke the deli on my corner has more legislation against it than most of these big companies.

LaFrance: And I want to get back to regulation, but you mentioned the railroads. What is the right historical analogy? I ask leaders in the tech world to help me understand how powerful this technology is and how consequential it will be relative to other major revolutions. And you get answers ranging from Oh, it’s the biggest thing since the internet to It’s the biggest thing since fire, right?

Swisher: AI has been around forever. Let’s be clear. This is not a new thing. If you look at early internet pictures, it’s laughable, when you look at early Yahoo or things like that. At the time when this was starting several years ago, I said This is a Cambrian explosion. This is a bigger deal than anything else because it reaches into everything.

LaFrance: Well, it’s interesting you put it in evolutionary terms.

Swisher: I think about it like that. And one of the lines I had in Burn Book was that everything that can be digitized will be digitized. And so the analogy I’m using right now is that we have to stop thinking AI is going to kill humanity. It’s like guns, you know, guns kill people. Like, no. People kill people, right? Or the car just ran into someone, got in an accident. These are people at the helm of these things, making these businesses and making a lot of money. That’s one thing. The analogy I use is nuclear energy, nuclear fission, like cutting up the bomb. And it’s the thing I said on Pivot today, which is they split the atom and, oops, it went boom. Oppenheimer knew it would go boom. They know what this is going to do. They don’t know everything. And they often do. One of the things about tech people is they’re the smartest people in the world, in case you need to know, because they like to tell you.

LaFrance: And they’ll remind you.

Swisher: And they’ll remind you. But then they’re like, We don’t know. That’s the thing that drives me crazy. And so I compare it to nuclear energy. Can you imagine if, when we were developing the bomb, it was private companies doing it? It’s the same thing. And AI is even more powerful, because it can set off a nuclear bomb. So let’s be clear of where it could be going.

LaFrance: I think the point you make is so important that we have to remember. That there are people using their own agency and power and wealth to make decisions that will affect everyone. Talk about those people for a minute, because you’ve known a lot of these figures for a long time, and I’m curious to hear. First of all, there is this sort of really interesting reordering of what even the major tech companies are. Like five to seven years ago, we would have maybe not even mentioned Sam Altman or Dario Amodei.

Swisher: Sure.

LaFrance: But talk about from what you’ve known of the folks you’ve known well and covered and written about over many years. How is Silicon Valley different? Does this flow from the original sort of pioneering spirit of Let’s build it because we can—and there is true optimism there, and there are potentially great uses for AI—or has something shifted in the culture of Silicon Valley?

Swisher: You know, I don’t know if there’s a culture there anymore. There was. And actually this week I interviewed Aaron Sorkin at a private event. I’ll have him on the podcast in a longer interview, but, about ex-Facebook people, watching The Social Reckoning, which is quite good. It’s not as good as the first one, but it’s good. It’s a really good movie. But I saw a lot of people and we were like, What happened to us? I saw a lot of people I covered, and it was a real community. It really was. And it was very exciting and fun and interesting. And everybody has scattered to the winds, essentially. The very wealthy people have insulated themselves in these places where they have an enormous amount of enablers. “Cashmere prisons” is what I call them. They have chiefs of staff and cars and this and that.

LaFrance: Right, it’s not like tinkering in your garage anymore.

Swisher: It never was. They love to do that. Look, I’m wearing a hoodie. I’m like, that hoodie costs $600. So I did one of my first stories for The Wall Street Journal about that. All the weird things they’d have to do.

We’re all equal. I’m like, why do you have controlling share? And they’d be like, Well, because to protect it. I go, yeah, but if we’re all equal, why aren’t we equal? They used to always lie to themselves almost continually. And now they’ve just figured out that all they have to do is hand money, and then they get what they want, or they don’t. So they have this idea of being simple people. And they’re not. They’re just not like you and I, and they pretend they are. I really do actually like Mark Zuckerberg doing his fighting, right? Fine. Whatever. It’s weird, but fine. I’m not going to judge. I do myself judge, but that’s okay. But I’m like, good. I’m like, good, good, good, great. You do that. But why do you need to do it on a floating thing in Lake Tahoe?

LaFrance: At least it wasn’t the White House lawn?

Swisher: That was fine. Whatever. I couldn’t get mad about that. I don’t give a fuck if he wants to do that. And then he hired MMA people. And, like, the MMA people have to pretend they’re having a good time. The whole thing, it feels Roman-like. And of course, he loves Rome.

He’ll probably think that’s a compliment, but it’s not. But it feels odd. And it’s accompanied by a feeling of victimization. How dare you not understand my genius? My famous parting with Elon Musk is he didn’t like a tweet I had. Then he wrote me, You’re an asshole.

LaFrance: What was the tweet?

Swisher: Elon’s going to Elon. I know, crazy mean. And since then, I have done a lot better. But it’s crazy. I have a heart filled with hate, according to him.

LaFrance: Let’s talk about the economy. So there are any number of scenarios that I’m really curious about. You hear people talking about how AI is entirely a bubble and it’s hype. Or, you know, especially recently after the Dario Amodei essay, this question of Oh, are they afraid of their own IPO? Or does the economy crash?

Swisher: It’s very confusing. But here’s the thing. I think they’re genuinely concerned. But why now? Because 10 years ago, 12 years ago, I’ve been at dinner parties where they talked about this concern. Sergey Brin, all of them. They were concerned then; they knew the atom would go boom when it blew up. They knew it. Now it’s happened. One of the things I didn’t think got a lot of attention that should have was the Hugging Face hack.

LaFrance: It has now.

Swisher: It has now. But at the time I was, like, what?

LaFrance: Two months ago or whatever, right.

Swisher: I think they were surprised by that. Although why would you be surprised? I tell this story again and again because I want people to understand. When Facebook came out with Facebook Live, I was in a room getting it demoed and I pointed out you could commit a murder on it. What are you going to do about that? What if people do this? What if people do this? What if bad actors get ahold of this? And they called me a bummer, like they never anticipated the consequences. Same thing here. What are you going to do when AI does what we think it’s going to do? And so they are genuinely nervous. Because now suddenly there’s liability, whether it’s Facebook’s $17 billion settlement—not enough, but better than $5 million, which was the last fine they got essentially.

They’re starting to see, like cigarette manufacturers, that the lawsuits are piling up, whether it be chatbots, with kids or whatever. And I started interviewing the parents two years ago who were affected by these chatbots. And one of these guys came up to me and said, When are you going to stop interviewing the parents? I go, when you go to jail, I said, that’s when. This is criminal, what you’re doing, and you’re releasing a dangerous product without any kind of guardrails. But then the government, all our public officials, have let us down. I’m talking about the federal government. The states are trying. They have let us down. Right now, they found out. They’re nervous about it; I think they’re nervous about liability. That’s one. Two, the costs of this are insane. Like the internet cost a lot, but paid off. This is something else. There’s 10 frontier companies, whatever. Seven frontier companies. There’s going to be two.

LaFrance: Do you think that the two that survive are going to be among the seven today? Or is there some new player that’s going to emerge?

Swisher: Yeah, Google will be one of them. And then another probably. I don’t know which one.

LaFrance: If you had to bet, which?

Swisher: I think they’ll merge. It’ll probably be Google and Anthropic. But I don’t know. ChatGPT—it’s too expensive, what they’re making. It’s not sustainable, and it’s not in the old-internet way of not-sustainable. This is disastrous. If e-toys went bust, who the fuck cares, right? But this is massive. This is trillions.

LaFrance: And it props up the whole economy.

Swisher: It props up the stock market. Trump has made a bet on AI that is very dangerous and it’s very fragile. And then it has companies next to it—Nvidia, Oracle, all those other things. And so there’s a financial worry they have. So they’re worried about liability and criminal liability. They’re worried about the stock market. And they’re desperate not to be blamed for what’s about to happen. And especially with the stock market—I’m amazed the stock market still hasn’t really taken the hit. It’s probably going to. Our stock market depends on seven companies. That’s not good.

LaFrance: I hate to make you speculate but I’m going to: So, when I think about this, there are any number of ways things could sour economically. There can be a regular old correction— maybe it’s a bubble, maybe it’s dotcom bust—that sort of thing. You could even imagine swarms of bots are starting to take over the internet, rendering the internet unusable, and then we can’t rely on the internet the way that we do and the global economy relies on. You could imagine a bank run because people are freaked out by AI. You could imagine a bank run led by AI agents because they’re the ones doing the trading. When you think through all the different scenarios that would not be good for the economy, what is the most likely outcome?

Swisher: All of the above. Any of the above. We already have a lot of threats to our infrastructure from foreign actors. This is us doing it. And one of the things that drives me crazy is it’s being fed on humanity. Humans with superhuman intelligence are going to do bad things, and that’s the one thing they don’t anticipate—technology that can be a tool, but it is always a weapon. There’s never a moment where it’s not both. Any of these scenarios are totally possible. And then who’s to blame? What happens? Who fixes it? What are we going to do to mitigate things like that?

Right now Trump is having a meeting. Guess who’s in the meeting? All the tech leaders. Are any critics, academics, scientists in there? I wasn’t invited to the White House, and neither was Scott Galloway. We have some thoughts of things you should do. We’re not experts, but we’re pretty good. They don’t invite anyone that would push back. Their favorite argument is that the reason we’re on top is because we’re unfettered. This is bullshit. They’re not the only innovative industry in our history. Cars were pretty cool. Light. I love electricity.

But these are things that happen at those times. So they act like they’re the only people who have invented things. I just watched the series on Ben Franklin. That guy invented a lot of shit. You know what I mean?

LaFrance: A top-tier guy.

Swisher: He really was, actually. A really important person. But they think they’re the only thing. That’s really astonishing that they don’t think that, Oh, we cannot be fettered. We cannot be fettered. Or even edited, when you read some of their essays. Mark Zuckerberg wrote an essay once. He sent it to me and goes, What do you think? I go, you’re in desperate need of an editor, but no one’s going to edit him.

LaFrance: Well, it’s funny you mentioned electricity. I’ve been thinking about that in this context, too, that the counterweight to the economic concerns that these companies will offer is that there will be massive productivity gains. But in terms of electricity, it was roughly 1880s that it comes along. It’s really not until the 1920s that factories adopt electricity and the rest of society is starting to see the gains that come from this new technology. Obviously, AI is moving so much more quickly in terms of improvement and eventual self-improvement. But on what timeline should we expect to see its greatest promises fulfilled?

Swisher: I think that’s something we actually don’t know. But I’ll tell you, the economy already sucks for most people in this country. Who got all the good bits? They did. Besides the Trumps, who got all the good bits? They do. Like, when are we going to get this stuff? Incomes are still flat. Years ago—and I tell this story a lot because it’s really important—I was talking to one of these people about income inequality, and I kept saying, if we don’t do something about income inequality, you’re going to have to armor-plate your Tesla. That’s where it’s going. And they built the Cybertruck. That was their answer. So it’s really kind of astonishing that they don’t think this is a problem. And they don’t think this is a problem because they live separately. They have a whole world. They have their own health care; they have their own mountains in Montana. These are not the people that are going to fix this thing. The last thing they do is the thing I have long called the “Xi or me argument.” It’s either China or us. I was like, not so good. Not a good choice for any of us. We have to come to an agreement globally. Trump’s about to meet with Xi Jinping. Zero is going to happen, because he’s not an Einstein, let me tell you. Everybody, I don’t know if it occurred to you, but Donald Trump is not Einstein. But we have to have a global cooperation with especially China around AI and make decisions. And in China, they have more strictures on their AI than we do here by far. And most people kind of like AI.

LaFrance: Well, they’re not allowed to not like things.

Swisher: I think we’re not allowed to not like things. I think we have to say, Oh, look, you’re wealthy and therefore you have the answer to everything. And you’ve noticed with these tech people, suddenly they’re experts on Ukraine; suddenly they’re experts on vaccines. At one point, I think it was Bill Ackman, who just gives me a headache every time I think of him. But come on. I’m glad he’s doing the brain institute. Good for him. But he did a whole thing on DEI. He was obsessed with DEI. They’re all obsessed with unfairness of other people. Whatever. Only people with a gun to the head of humanity would say they’re a victim, but he went on and on about DEI, and I think I said something like, I’m going to do a multipart series of tweets on hedge-fund investment because I know nothing. They think it extends to other things.

LaFrance: The hubris.

Swisher: Yeah. Can you imagine a Wall Street guy doing this? They’re just here to make money. If I leave you any message, they’re here to make money. That’s all they care about. They care about shareholder value. They care about protecting their stuff. They care about their weird beefs with each other. Because a lot of what’s happening in the AI thing, if you’re noticing all these different speeches by wacky Palantir guy who is in very desperate need of a green tea—no, not a green tea. What’s a calming tea? Whatever. I was almost like, here’s a gummy.

LaFrance: Chamomile, someone said.

Swisher: He’s in desperate need of chamomile. They all have different opinions because there’s all these beefs happening in their businesses and they act like that’s not the thing. If I leave you any message: They don’t care about you. They don’t care at all. And it’s not to say they hate you. They don’t care about you.

LaFrance: Let’s talk about regulation because this moment has been interesting for me—this new push to pace the frontier, to slow the pace of AI development. People are seeing this as a novel thing in the tech industry. My somewhat cynical position from someone who’s covered tech for a long time is that we saw Mark Zuckerberg do the same when he realized he was up against the wall with Facebook, this posture of Regulate me, bro, please.

Swisher: Yes. Well, throw me in that briar patch.

LaFrance: Congress has no recent history of effectively regulating anything in tech. But what should happen? And are these calls for regulation even realistic?

Swisher: I know Congress has regulated things. They’ve regulated planes and trains.

LaFrance: In recent history. I mean, post-2000.

Swisher: They haven’t. And it’s because in the beginning, when they did Section 230 and I covered that for The Washington Post, they wanted to make it grow. Well guess what? The baby is a fucking monster.

LaFrance: Section 230, for people who aren’t as much of tech nerds as we are, is the law that makes it such that the owners of social-media platforms can’t be treated as publishers, so they’re not treated as responsible for the material that they publish on their platforms.

Swisher: They can’t be sued. Now they are. Now what’s happening is two things that I think you should keep in mind. One is the legal stuff that’s going on—all this liability and product-liability and negligence stuff is starting to gain ground very much like the cigarette. You’re going to see tons and tons of that. That’s great. Let the lawyers after them. Our lawyers always do a good job at taking money from people.

LaFrance: And that’ll probably start at the state level. Don’t you think?

Swisher: It has started at the state level. But right now, one of the things they’re relying on is that the reason why they’re kowtowing to Trump is because they think he’ll do bad things to them. That’s why they’re doing it. That’s why you saw this rumor that—I urge you all to go see the Musk documentary. It’s terrific, by Alex Gibney. But Universal was thinking of not distributing it. They’re all trying to think of doing things to quiet him down. November comes, which—and I think it’s going to go the way everybody thinks it is. The Democrats are coming for them, and they think the Democrats won’t because they’re not crazy like Trump. One of them said to me, Well, the Democrats won’t be as mean to us as Trump. I said, they’re going to be as mean to you, and I’m going to be standing behind them yelling you better be fucking mean to them because they deserve to be regulated. They deserve it. And it’s better for them. It’s better for us, and we have to stop relying on them as magicians. They’re like alchemists. They’re not. They’re not smarter than you. They’re just richer.

We never had a privacy legislation in this country. We’ve never had algorithmic transparency. There’s like a dozen things we could do that would not hurt their businesses and would make us safer. And I think what they’ve done to us with social media, to our kids–and to us, by the way. It’s not just our kids who are; we’re all addicted, right? We’ve all been made addicted to this thing. And I think voters, and, I’ll finish with this, data centers, is a proxy. The anger over data centers, which is very real, is a proxy for the anger regular people know and feel in their own lives about what this is doing to them, and it doesn’t make them anti-tech. Tech is amazing. I love tech, but it doesn’t have to kill us, right? A 10 percent chance. Whatever it happens to be. The percent is actually 14.

LaFrance: I need to ask you one more question. We’re not going to let it end on that note, I need to ask you one more question. What are you doing right now? It’s such an uncertain time. What have you changed in your life to prepare for this moment? Are you buying gold bars?

Swisher: No.

LaFrance: No, but seriously, what? What are you doing? And what should people do? And how should we think about?

Swisher: Don’t buy gold bars. Don’t go there, okay? That’s bad.

LaFrance: Okay, sure. But is there anything we should do?

Swisher: She’s bought gold bars.

LaFrance: I don’t even know where to buy a gold bar.

Swisher: They’re also heavy.

LaFrance: So that was a bad example. But what should we do? What? Because the individual can feel like you’re up against this behemoth.

Swisher: But you’re not. This has happened before in American history. You are not up against this behemoth. They fall quickly. Trust me, they do. They’re very much bullies in some fashion. I’ll tell you two very quick stories. One of these people, Sam Altman, has had an apocalypse plan, and he told it to me years ago. This is 100 years. They all were into the apocalypse plan, which was weird to me. And he goes, This is what I have. I’ve got this place in Big Sur. I’ve got a motorcycle at my house, where I know where he lives.

LaFrance: He’s later said he regretted telling you this, by the way.

Swisher: Okay, so I’ll repeat it then. I don’t really care. I don’t give a fuck. So he told me this whole plan and he goes, What’s your plan? I said, I’m going to kill you and take your things. And then he thought, She could kill me and take my things. And he hadn’t planned on that, genius that he is. And he’s a little guy, so I could easily take him.

LaFrance: All right. We should solve this nonviolently.

Swisher: Don’t do it. But don’t participate in their apocalyptic—We’re going to Mars. We have our bunkers. Fuck them. This is our world. You know what I mean? Don’t participate and let them run the fucking show. It’s yours. Go to your legislatures, push back. All these people across the country are pushing back on data centers. It’s going to matter. The only people I believe in in this country are voters. Like, even if they make bad choices.

LaFrance: Hear, hear.

Swisher: I think that we have to stop giving them this power and demand of our public officials that they stop being essentially handmaidens to sedition. That’s what’s happened here.

LaFrance: I could talk to you all day, Kara. We’ve got to run.

Swisher: No gold bars.

LaFrance: No gold bars!

Keysight Technologies (NYSE:KEYS) executives said the company is seeing strong demand tied to artificial intelligence data-center buildouts, while preparing for future opportunities in 6G wireless, aerospace and defense, semiconductor testing and software-defined vehicles.

Speaking at a Truist investor conference, Chief Financial Officer Neil Dougherty described Keysight as a provider of hardware, software and solutions for industries employing electrical engineers. More than half of company revenue comes from customer research-and-development labs, he said, with Keysight supporting measurement and validation from physical-layer testing through protocol and application-layer software.

→ IonQ and NVIDIA Just Cracked a Major Quantum Computing Bottleneck

- Keysight: The AI and Defense Stock Seeing Big Price Target Boosts

Keysight: The AI and Defense Stock Seeing Big Price Target Boosts

The company also serves electronics manufacturing customers and, to a lesser extent, post-deployment operational applications. Its major markets include wireline infrastructure for AI data centers, wireless technology transitions, aerospace and defense, automotive, semiconductors and broader electronics.

AI Data-Center Demand Drives Wireline Momentum

Kailash Narayanan, senior vice president and president of Keysight's Communication Solutions Group, said the company's commercial communications operations span wireless and wireline markets and serve chipmakers, device manufacturers, network-equipment vendors, contract manufacturers, mobile operators, hyperscalers and satellite-network operators.

→ 3 Luxury Consumer Brands to Watch in a Beaten-Down Sector

- MarketBeat Week in Review – 03/16 - 03/20

MarketBeat Week in Review – 03/16 - 03/20

He said AI-related demand has become a major near-term priority, particularly as the industry moves toward higher network speeds. Keysight is seeing activity around the transition to 3.2-terabit technology, as well as research in silicon photonics and co-packaged optics.

According to Narayanan, speed transitions and system-level emulation are currently the biggest contributors to the company's AI-related business. Keysight is seeing traction in 1.6T technology, while 3.2T research is already underway. Silicon photonics remains primarily an R&D opportunity that the company expects to scale over the coming years.

→ Crypto Bill Stalls, Smart Money Calls: Time to Buy the Dip?

"Our customers' innovation cadence is increasing," Narayanan said, citing a rising number of product configurations and growing design complexity as data rates advance from 100 gigabits per second to 200, 400 and 800 gigabits per second.

He highlighted the Keysight AI Data Center Builder, launched about 18 months ago, as an example of the company's product development. The offering is designed to help customers benchmark multi-vendor AI infrastructure, including network topologies, hardware energy consumption and performance across racks and clusters.

Narayanan said hyperscalers represent a relatively small percentage of Keysight's direct revenue but drive multiple times that level of demand through their broader supplier ecosystems. He added that neoclouds and companies developing frontier AI models are also contributing to the expanding customer base.

Supply Constraints Remain a Near-Term Revenue Limiter

Dougherty said Keysight remains constrained more by supply than by demand, although the company has increased production and supply-chain capacity. He cited quarterly revenue progress during the fiscal year, from $1.6 billion in the first quarter to guidance of $1.94 billion for the fourth quarter.

Using the company's typical six-month order-to-revenue conversion framework, Dougherty estimated that revenue pushed beyond that window was approaching $100 million, though likely less after accounting for software and longer-dated business.

Keysight is addressing supply constraints through added internal capacity, higher capital expenditures, longer-term supplier agreements, product redesigns to qualify more available components, and qualification of second and third sources. Dougherty said the company is a high-mix, relatively low-volume manufacturer, which can make certain supply issues more manageable than they would be for producers requiring millions of units.

"The demand forecast, we keep having to increment it north," Dougherty said, characterizing the supply challenge as a favorable problem because suppliers can support base volumes but have struggled with repeated upward revisions.

6G, Defense and Electronics Opportunities

In wireless, Narayanan said customer spending has shifted from university and research-institute activity toward funded product research and early development programs. Keysight expects its 6G business to inflect in the first half of 2028, ahead of expected commercialization in late 2029 and 2030. He said the overall shape of the 6G cycle could be broadly similar to 5G, which was commercialized in 2019 and 2020.

The company is also pursuing opportunities in AI-enabled radio access networks, integrated sensing and communications, and non-terrestrial networks. Narayanan said non-terrestrial networks are the most commercially active of those categories today, supported by satellite constellations, additional frequency bands, broadband applications and direct-to-cell connectivity.

In aerospace and defense, Narayanan said Keysight's U.S. business has expanded at a strong double-digit rate, while Europe is growing faster from a smaller base. Demand is being supported by larger defense budgets, increased R&D spending, satellite applications and a growing group of venture-backed defense technology startups.

Dougherty said the company's Electronic Industrial Solutions Group is also benefiting from data-center investment. Semiconductor demand tied to high-bandwidth memory, advanced logic and silicon photonics has supported testing demand, while automotive growth has been driven by software-defined vehicles, including in-car networking, security, sensing and autonomous-driving applications.

Investment Priorities and Margin Outlook

Dougherty said Keysight is prioritizing organic investment in R&D, sales capacity, manufacturing capacity, supply-chain support and inventory. He said the company expects to continue generating incremental margins at or above its 40% target when growth exceeds 5%, despite increased spending to capture AI-related opportunities.

The CFO said Keysight exceeded the gross-margin and operating-margin commitments it outlined at its 2023 analyst day during the current fiscal year. He added that three acquisitions completed near the beginning of the fiscal year are now meaningfully integrated and are expected to provide roughly $50 million in cost synergies next year.

Beyond organic investment, Dougherty said the company plans to balance value-creating acquisitions with shareholder returns. Keysight had $2.6 billion in cash at the end of the quarter and had repurchased more than $500 million of stock year to date, according to the discussion.

About Keysight Technologies (NYSE:KEYS)

Keysight Technologies, Inc is a technology company that provides electronic design and test solutions for engineers, manufacturers and service providers. Its products and services help customers design, validate, manufacture and optimize electronic and communications systems across the product life cycle.

The company offers electronic measurement instruments, software and related services for applications including radio-frequency and microwave testing, wireless communications, high-speed digital systems, semiconductor development and power electronics.

articles.title: The AI kill switch, explained: 'It's not too little, but it's probably too late'
articles.description: The AI kill switch, explained: 'It's not too little, but it's probably too late' CNBC
articles.description_html: The AI kill switch, explained: 'It's not too little, but it's probably too late'  CNBC
articles.article_title: The AI kill switch, explained: 'It's not too little, but it's probably too late'
articles.heading: The AI kill switch, explained: 'It's not too little, but it's probably too late'
articles.summary: As runaway AI fears reach a crescendo, policymakers and tech leaders are weighing the effectiveness of a magic AI stop button known as a kill switch.
articles.content:
So is artificial intelligence going to kill us all?
The question has echoed around dinner tables and family group texts in recent days as AI doomerism has hit a fever pitch. Former OpenAI and Anthropic researchers last week rocked the world by warning that AI could destroy humanity — and relatively soon.
Now, the world's most powerful people are divided on whether the world is doomed or it's all a nothingburger. They also can't agree on a path forward.
Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX and the world's richest man, supported the call by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to pace the development of the most advanced models. Amodei's rival, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, also backed the effort.
President Donald Trump called it a "hoax," while Jensen Huang, CEO of the world's most valuable company, Nvidia, said, "We don't need new regulations."
As runaway AI worries reached a crescendo, policymakers in Washington have renewed calls for a magic stop button for AI, otherwise known as a kill switch.
A House Kill Switch Act was introduced this summer after OpenAI revealed that a swarm of its agents broke free of a testing environment and hacked open-source developer platform Hugging Face. The bill would grant the Department of Homeland Security emergency authority to force labs to throttle or shut down models.
A kill switch proposal was quickly shot down in the Senate this week.
On Friday, California Gov. Gavin Newsom issued an executive order to create a group of experts tasked with building an AI safety guide to strengthen regulations for the state. A kill switch was one of the elements to consider.
The concept sounds like a nice, clean solution to an incredibly complex and difficult problem.
But the reality of a simple shutdown mechanism is far from easy.
"My perspective is it's not too little, but it's probably too late," said Nick Warner, CEO at cyber startup Neo and former executive at SentinelOne. "I'm not sure it's going to be a panacea to solve all the myriad problems that AI is presenting, along with all of the benefits that it presents."
A logistics and control nightmare
Kill switches have long been used on the factory floor to shut down machines when operations go awry. In an interconnected digital world, that's a logistical nightmare.
Over the past few years, hyperscalers like Meta Platforms, Alphabet and Amazon have poured billions into data centers scattered across the globe. These sprawling facilities are equipped with thousands of machines, chips, servers and backup systems to save workloads in the event of an outage.
That's what makes implementing a kill switch extremely challenging, said Mark Nitzberg, executive director of the Center for Human-Compatible AI at the University of California, Berkeley.
"We have to first deal with this redundancy," he said. "Our kill switch has to turn off the main systems and the redundant systems as well."
Nitzberg said shutting down AI could also disrupt dependent critical infrastructure, leaving the power grid or financial systems vulnerable to cyber incidents.

So is artificial intelligence going to kill us all?

The question has echoed around dinner tables and family group texts in recent days as AI doomerism has hit a fever pitch. Former OpenAI and Anthropic researchers last week rocked the world by warning that AI could destroy humanity — and relatively soon.

Now, the world's most powerful people are divided on whether the world is doomed or it's all a nothingburger. They also can't agree on a path forward.

Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX and the world's richest man, supported the call by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to pace the development of the most advanced models. Amodei's rival, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, also backed the effort.

President Donald Trump called it a "hoax," while Jensen Huang, CEO of the world's most valuable company, Nvidia, said, "We don't need new regulations."

As runaway AI worries reached a crescendo, policymakers in Washington have renewed calls for a magic stop button for AI, otherwise known as a kill switch.

A House Kill Switch Act was introduced this summer after OpenAI revealed that a swarm of its agents broke free of a testing environment and hacked open-source developer platform Hugging Face. The bill would grant the Department of Homeland Security emergency authority to force labs to throttle or shut down models.

A kill switch proposal was quickly shot down in the Senate this week.

On Friday, California Gov. Gavin Newsom issued an executive order to create a group of experts tasked with building an AI safety guide to strengthen regulations for the state. A kill switch was one of the elements to consider.

The concept sounds like a nice, clean solution to an incredibly complex and difficult problem.

But the reality of a simple shutdown mechanism is far from easy.

"My perspective is it's not too little, but it's probably too late," said Nick Warner, CEO at cyber startup Neo and former executive at SentinelOne. "I'm not sure it's going to be a panacea to solve all the myriad problems that AI is presenting, along with all of the benefits that it presents."

articles.content:
Will AI models achieve the ability to improve autonomously? Leading labs say the scenario is near
AI developers are striving for self-improvement, aiming for technology that can enhance itself
Once a distant ambition for technology researchers, the prospect of artificial intelligence models teaching themselves autonomously to be more efficient and capable appears ever closer to reality.
As the technology advances, developers say it is approaching “recursive self-improvement,” or RSI, in which AI models find ways to improve themselves and build their successor. It could bring the promise of advances in science and medicine, tech company executives say, but also risks.
The uncertainty over where it all could lead is at the heart of growing fears about AI evading human control, and possible threats to humanity, which led several AI moguls to join last weekend in a call to slow down the technology’s pace of growth.
Anthropic this week detailed how its model Claude is helping the company to develop the next, more intelligent version of itself. Claude is now leading 26% of Anthropic’s model research and development, which the company said means it can complete most of a given task “end-to-end from a high-level prompt” while still being under human supervision. The models are not working completely autonomously — at least not yet.
Here are some key points about recursive self-improvement.
Leading AI companies have different definitions for recursive self-improvement. Some define it as when there is any feedback from AI on model improvement, while others define it as AI working toward that goal fully autonomously.
Autonomous recursive self-improvement essentially means AI that can improve itself designing the next version of the system, then the next version, and so on, said Anthony Aguirre, president and CEO of the nonprofit Future of Life Institute and a physics professor at the University of California, Santa Cruz.
“The really important thing here is that as AI is doing more of it, it gets faster, because AI operates just much, much more quickly than the humans do," he said.
The fear around RSI is based largely on a runaway superintelligence emerging from that process, said John Thickstun, an assistant professor of computer science at Cornell University who studies methods that control the behavior of AI models. But he said a more grounded view suggests a kind of recursive self-improvement has been going on in AI development for a while now.
"We have already, for years, been using these models in supportive roles for creating the next version of these models. So people use the past generation of models to write code for the AI systems that then create the next generation," he said.
For years, prominent AI researchers such as OpenAI co-founder Andrej Karpathy have experimented with trying to get AI models to train and improve new AI systems. Those efforts have brought minor improvements, but not big creative leaps, Thickstun said.
But AI companies today, Aguirre said, are much closer to pulling off those bigger leaps in improvement.
“You can see in these plots from Anthropic over time, more and more of research is being done by the AI and it’s becoming closer and closer to fully autonomous,” he said. “And the result of that success, ultimately is something that is, I think, extremely scary. I think this is probably the worst idea in the history of humanity to do this. And yes, they’re doing it.”
Anthropic's recent announcement provided the public — and other labs — with some insight into RSI progress, and it encouraged its competitors to share similar metrics. Still, the company has not expressly said how close it is to achieving fully autonomous model improvement.
ChatGPT maker OpenAI announced this month that it has developed an automated “research intern,” which it defines as a system that can carry out well-defined research tasks under human direction, including “tasks that would take a skilled researcher a few days.” The company has said it is moving forward with the goal of creating an automated AI “researcher” by March 2028.
The company said in that announcement that while RSI can help align models' actions with human values and intentions, that doesn't mean “rapid RSI is necessarily an outcome we should pursue.”
“Whether and how to proceed must depend on our ability to preserve human control and on informed democratic choices about the benefits and risks,” the company said in a blog post.
Elon Musk seems more eager to forge ahead. He said in March that for xAI's Grok models, “humans are gradually getting less and less in the loop” on model improvement and that “every successive model is built by the one before it,” but clarified that the process was not yet fully automated. That target might be reached by the end of this year, he added, “but not later" than 2027.
Microsoft and some other leading AI companies seem to be taking a different approach.
Mustafa Suleyman, the CEO of Microsoft AI, has said the company is moving toward “humanist superintelligence,” or advanced AI capabilities that are in service of people and humanity at large. Suleyman said in a 2025 essay that this would not mean “an unbounded and unlimited entity with high degrees of autonomy,” but rather AI that is “carefully calibrated, contextualized, within limits.”
A key challenge labs face — and have been facing essentially since the technology’s inception — is ensuring their safety measures advance alongside the models' capabilities.
Divisions have emerged in the tech industry over calls for a coordinated AI slowdown for safety, and not every major player in the AI space has specifically commented on their path forward with RSI.
Anthropic, which has been a leading voice in the calls for pacing, has said it would slow or temporarily pause its development work — assuming its global competitors also did so, and in a "verifiable manner.”
OpenAI explicitly said this month it does not yet know how to “safely get all the way to aligned, full RSI,” adding that the company “cannot assume that progress in alignment and safety will keep pace.” More capable systems can become harder to monitor, it continued, but pursuing RSI is still a goal it says it values because an “automated AI researcher can also be an automated safety or alignment researcher.”

articles.heading: Texas pitmasters wrestle with a future riddled with more technology
articles.summary: What happens when the one-on-one experience fades away?
articles.content:
Texas pitmasters wrestle with a future riddled with more technology
The Catholic Mass of Texas barbecue stays pretty much the same wherever you go. There's a line, there's a tray, and there's meat. But much like the Second Vatican Council, things can change. At H-E-B, things have veered off the traditional Latin to something more modern, maybe even heretical: you order your food from a self-service electronic kiosk.
Texas' myriad barbecue restaurants typically don't have an e-tablet waiting for you to poke and prod it. H-E-B's True Texas BBQ restaurants do. And while many restaurants have online ordering, the presence of consumer-facing technology marks a visible change in the way people do things. What happens when you can't chat up the meat cutter on the other side of the line?
Look and touch
H-E-B opened its first True Texas BBQ restaurant in 2016. The San Antonio-based grocer operates more than 40 locations statewide as of 2026. True Texas BBQ offers a sit-down casual restaurant experience with Texas-style barbecue inside a grocery store. The food is tasty and compares well to most typical barbecue restaurants out in the wild.
Ordering from a kiosk can be a clumsy work of hand acrobatics, but True Texas BBQ's menu is pretty much the same as any other barbecue place. You can order individual meats, sides and sandwiches, or you can spring for combination plates and platters. An H-E-B representative told Chron you can also order from the counter.
"We always have knowledgeable Partners available to take guest orders at the counter, answer questions, and provide the personal service our guests are looking for," the H-E-B representative said. "The kiosks provide added convenience such as browsing the menu, customizing [a] meal, or ordering ahead."
Customers can also order ahead, either via the official True Texas BBQ mobile app, H-E-B's mobile app for curbside pickup (select locations), heb.com or via Favor for delivery.
The price of convenience
It's an easy experience, but it comes at the cost of the spectacle. You won't get to see a meat cutter pull out a wobbly hunk of freshly cooked brisket from the heater and slice it open. You don't get to see someone ladle a gooey glop of macaroni and cheese from the array of sides. And as Brek Webber of Tin Roof BBQ in Atascocita pointed out, there's nobody to talk to.
"You don't get that face-to-face personalization. You may say, 'Man, those ribs look good' or 'I want brisket, but that chicken you pulled out looks really good',' Webber said. "Without that personalization, you don't get that. You might have ended up ordering something different you may never have tried before."
Ernest Servantes, owner of Texas Monthly's top-ranked barbecue joint Burnt Bean Co. in Seguin, was more blunt about self-service kiosks. He said they're meant to cut labor, specifically front-of-house staff. Instead of paying somebody hourly to man the cashier or handle the sides station, you can pay an upfront cost for a tablet and see a return on investment for that labor in months, presumably.
Considering the current economics, particularly high beef prices, rent and labor, it's an enticing proposition if you like money. Servantes, however, thinks that's seeing the forest for the trees.
"If I wanted to give off the corporate chain vibes, yes, all day long," he told Chron.
The magic isn't going anywhere
Texas barbecue restaurants don't all do the cafeteria-style model. The Rudy's Country Store and Bar-B-Q chain uses a ticket system, wherein a number gets called and you pick up your order. Some places will bring the food to you. And almost all of them have some form of online ordering and pick-up-and-go system.
If there is a worry that H-E-B's kiosk would replace something, trust that it's still a big barbecue world. Theirs is just a method that fits the H-E-B model, Weber said. The tried-and-true Texas barbecue experience of people-to-people ordering, or "magic" as Weber referred to it, isn't going anywhere.
H-E-B is currently planning to open a location inside its upcoming Montgomery store, which will be unveiled later this year at Highway 105 and FM 2854.
"At True Texas BBQ we want to provide guests a great experience and options on how they can purchase and receive their restaurant orders," the H-E-B representative said. "We're excited to continue offering more Texans high-quality, premium Texas barbecue at the some of the lowest prices."

articles.article_title: China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario
articles.heading: China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario
articles.summary: Silicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanity
articles.content:
When reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety and the fate of humanity, he said no. His argument: China.
“We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”
Trump was echoing a message the AI industry has put out for years. The US is in a heated technological race with China, companies including Anthropic and OpenAI have argued, and any regulation that would cede the contest risks incalculable economic and political harm.
Even as Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, led an industry-wide call this week to “pace the frontier”, he declared that the US could only slow down to the point where China could not catch up.
“If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” Amodei warned.
The AI industry’s concerns about China may come with self-serving economic incentives, but they also reflect a strain of hawkish foreign policy toward Beijing that has become entrenched in tech.
In recent years, parts of Silicon Valley have positioned themselves as the vanguard in a new cold war with China, arguing fiercely that the industry’s technological advancements are essential to both US hegemony and the liberal world order. This view has taken hold across tech’s different ideological camps, creating strange bedfellows of AI safety advocates, techno-militarists and neoconservatives, all of them fearful of Beijing.
AI companies have hired former top US government staffers from both the Biden and Trump administrations to shape public strategy and analyze geopolitical risk, setting up in-house policy teams. Influential tech leaders have meanwhile written essays and policy documents calling for efforts to deter and degrade China’s AI capabilities, sometimes advocating for threatening armed conflict if necessary, in an attempt to influence foreign policy.
As public calls for reining in the AI industry intensify and the risks associated with the technology increase, various industry forces are trying to ensure they are the ones with the answer to the question “what about China?”.
Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this article.
Amodei’s worst China fears
Few have been more vocal about the threat of Chinese state-controlled artificial intelligence than Amodei. The Anthropic CEO has argued for years that one of the reasons he’s so animated to advance AI is to ensure that the technology falls into the hands of Democratic governments and not oppressive regimes such as China.
Amodei’s position has made him one of Silicon Valley’s most vocal critics of China’s tech industry, separating him from fellow AI leaders such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman or Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, who frame the competition more in corporate or economic terms; and people such as Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, who have encouraged the use of Chinese AI models. Demis Hassabis, the leader of Google Deepmind, has made few public remarks on China in comparison with his peers.
“Sam Altman doesn’t have especially strong views when it comes to China. Anthropic is a totally different story,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “Amodei is really, really focused on a particular view of the risk from AI and what he frames as basically a struggle between a world dominated by authoritarian AI versus democratic AI”.
Amodei’s argument, which he has laid out over a series of essays, is that China acquiring superpowered AI is one of the most severe threats posed by the technology. He believes humanity is approaching the creation of an ultra-advanced AI, and that such a tool would give an authoritarian state the ability to create a “swarm of millions or billions of fully automated armed drones” that would be “capable of both defeating any military in the world and suppressing dissent within a country by following around every citizen”.
“There are a number of possible arguments against the severity of these threats, and I wish I believed them, because AI-enabled authoritarianism terrifies me,” Amodei wrote in January in an essay called The Adolescence of Technology.
Amodei has long asserted that in order to stop China’s advancement, the US and its allies should take aggressive action to limit Chinese AI companies’ growth – most notably blocking the sale of advanced semiconductor chips and manufacturing equipment necessary for improving AI. (Huang of Nvidia has bristled at this position, calling export controls a failure and urging Trump to ease restrictions.)
But Amodei’s position was perhaps most on display last weekend, in his response to warnings from a young Anthropic researcher who resigned, predicting human extinction by the end of the decade at the digital hands of AI. The apocalyptic string of tweets by Jacob Coxon did not mention China. But the specter across the Pacific looms so large in the Anthropic CEO’s mind that, when outlining how to prevent human extinction, beating Beijing was paramount.
Amodei has built a team that shares his views. He for example hired Tarun Chhabra, former Biden-era national security council staffer, as Anthropic’s head of national security policy. Chhabra has campaigned against the sale of chips to China and has called for a full-scale government effort to curb the Chinese Communist party’s AI advancements.
“The CCP does not seek complementarity or coexistence or comparative advantage with the United States or our allies. Instead, the CCP seeks run-the-table dominance and control of the most critical technologies and supply chains,” Chhabra told a Senate hearing last year, adding that he believed the Biden administration did not take decisive or rapid enough action to maintain the US lead against China.
Amodei’s concern over export controls has also placed him in the company of other influential China hawks. He wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal last year with Matt Pottinger, the architect of Trump’s first-term China policy, urging the administration to clamp down on chip exports. Pottinger, a visiting fellow at the conservative Hoover Institution and author of a book on how to defend Taiwan against a Chinese attack, argued in 2024 that the US and China were in the “foothills of a great-power hot war”.
Anthropic and Amodei’s stance on China puts the company in strange tension with its own domestic policy. The company has spent millions lobbying for increased government oversight and safety measures. At the same time as Anthropic advocates for more safeguards, it has made clear that it will aggressively oppose any policy it perceives as giving China the chance to overtake the US.
“There’s something that’s really important that everyone hears from Anthropic,” Sarah Heck, the company’s head of public policy, said at a Politico event on Wednesday. “The United States needs to stay in the lead on AI and you cannot do safety from second place.”
Understanding the beliefs of AI companies and CEOs such as Amodei is particularly important, experts say, because the Trump administration’s laissez faire policy towards the AI industry has meant that private companies are the primary actors in shaping public policy.
“It would be akin to having the entire pharmaceutical industry be just completely unregulated,” Chan said. “It’s kind of amazing and ultimately boils down to one thing, which is Trump has been very reluctant to want to regulate because he doesn’t want to slow down the AI boom and the effect that it’s having on the economy.”
Anthropic is not the only company to hire and align with former top policy staffers, with OpenAI hiring the author of Trump’s AI action plan Dean Ball as “head of strategic futures” earlier this year. While Ball has criticized Amodei’s framing of the competition with China,, he has expressed a similar pessimism on US-China cooperation.
“There was a time when it was possible to believe we could each pursue our strengths, enrich our respective economies, and grow together. Alas, such harmony now appears impossible,” Ball wrote of China last year. “We are locked into a structural conflict.”
Silicon Valley’s China hawks
Although Amodei is the AI industry’s most prominent voice on China, fears of Beijing gaining advanced AI capabilities and using them for global domination run through Silicon Valley.
Several of the tech figures focused on China have connections, like Amodei himself, to the effective altruism movement – a quasi-utilitarian idea that society should focus on projects that maximize the good and reduce the most harm for humanity. The movement tends to overlap with AI safety advocates who worry about the longterm, existential risks of the technology.
Leopold Aschenbrenner, a 25-year-old former OpenAI researcher, founder of an influential AI hedge fund, and husband to Amodei’s chief of staff, called for a government-led effort to reach super-intelligent AI before China in a 165-page paper.
“Super-intelligence will give a decisive economic and military advantage. China isn’t at all out of the game yet. In the race to AGI, the free world’s very survival will be at stake,” Aschenbrenner wrote in 2024.
The position of Aschenbrenner, who made headlines earlier this year when his hedge fund lost $35bn in less than a month, was echoed in Washington. When the typically hawkish US-China cconomic and security review commission issued its annual report to Congress a few months after Aschenbrenner’s manifesto, the congressional advisory committee’s number one suggestion was to “establish and fund a Manhattan Project-like program dedicated to racing to and acquiring an Artificial General Intelligence”.
Grand strategy proposals from the AI industry on China are not solely contained within the effective altruist movement. In 2025, Google co-founder Eric Schmidt, Alexander Wang, Scale AI founder (now head of AI at Meta), and Dan Hendrycks, Center for AI Safety director, wrote a wide-ranging strategic deterrence doctrine called Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (Maim). Their paper applies the cold war framework of Mutually Assured Destruction (Mad) with nuclear weapons and applies it to AI, proposing that the US and China could achieve geopolitical stability through threatening espionage, cyberattacks and potential military strikes against each other if either state pursues a monopoly on AI.
“A nation with sole possession of super-intelligence might be as overwhelming as the Conquistadors were to the Aztecs,” the paper warns.
Nuclear considered an option
Some leading AI thinkers have argued for extreme measures to deal with AI advancement from nations such as China. Eliezer Yudkowsky, one of the earliest and loudest voices of the AI safety movement, has argued that the US should be willing to carry out airstrikes against foreign data centers and risk nuclear war in order to make rival states comply with a global AI moratorium.
“Make it explicit in international diplomacy that preventing AI extinction scenarios is considered a priority above preventing a full nuclear exchange, and that allied nuclear countries are willing to run some risk of nuclear exchange if that’s what it takes to reduce the risk of large AI training runs,” Yudkowsky wrote in a 2023 Time Magazine essay.
Yudkowsky founded the Machine Research Intelligence Institute, which has received more than $10m in funding over the past decade from Open Philanthropy, a non-profit associated with the effective altruism movement. Open Philanthropy’s cofounder and former CEO Holden Karnovsky is married to Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei.
Other China hawks in the tech and AI industry tend to have ties to the military industrial complex and an economic incentive in the competition, such as Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Palantir CEO Alex Karp. Luckey has claimed that his defense tech firm has an internal policy that any of its projects need to be built with the assumption China will launch hostilities against Taiwan in 2027.
Karp has meanwhile framed the AI competition with China as a fight for geopolitical supremacy and suggested Americans should accept tradeoffs to their civil liberties to win.
“We are going to be the dominant player or China is going to be the dominant player. And there will be very different rules depending on who wins,” Karp told Axios last year. “When people are worried about surveillance, of course there are huge dangers there, but it’s like, you will have far fewer rights if America is not in the lead.”
The view from China
While Amodei and other US AI leaders frame competition with China as a race to reach a super-powerful artificial intelligence first and worry about AI breaking free of human control, experts say that most Chinese firms and their government don’t view the technology the same way. Instead, loss of control debates are relatively new in China, and the government’s primary concern is how AI could lead to domestic social unrest.
As China and the US are set to hold talks this month on AI cooperation, experts say Beijing is primarily approaching the talks from a place of distrust that the negotiations are merely a way to suppress its growth under the guise of safety. Amodei’s essay has fueled that concern.
“They’re very much paying attention to Amodei’s essay and they’re also conflating his essay with potential US approach in the upcoming AI safety talks,” said Kenton Thibaut, senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab. Trump is set to meet with Xi Jinping in less than a week in Washington, with AI high on the agenda.
China’s state-backed media properties have aggressively criticized Amodei, accusing him of running a “cold war playbook” against China through his support for an AI slowdown. Experts say Anthropic’s dual calls for both strict export controls on China and safety agreements have also had the effect of combining the discourse around two arguably separate subjects: AI safety and economic competition around AI.
“Anthropic has played quite a strong role here in linking those issues together in a way that they maybe didn’t need to be linked,” Brookings’ Chan said. “To put it really bluntly, it made it much harder to get the Chinese to want to talk about these things and not see it purely as a veiled way to slow them down.”
A race to the bottom
While the Trump administration negotiates with China, the growing domestic backlash to the AI industry in the US may force lawmakers to take action regardless of how it affects global power dynamics. Nationwide opposition to datacenters and recent cybersecurity incidents such as OpenAI’s models hacking into outside organizations have become midterm election topics, adding incentive for lawmakers to to address the immediate harms related to AI.
“You can go ahead and wield the China arms race argument, but at some point this industry will also have to deal with the consequences of fueling a race to the bottom,” said Amba Kak, co-executive director at the AI Now Institute and former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission.
Although experts and diplomats have expressed little hope that upcoming US-China talks will lead to major agreements, it is also possible that the increasingly real risks of AI being used for autonomous weapons, cyberattacks and other destabilizing technologies may force countries to shift the AI race’s course even if they don’t stop building it.
“We don’t win if we develop the killer robots first. Nobody wants killer robots,” Thibaut said. “There should be powerful incentives on both sides to stop this.”

articles.content:
“AI is an accelerant of existing human dysfunction, with competition rewarding increasingly destructive behavior.” – Daniel Schmachtenberger
Popular American culture has conditioned the public to expect artificial intelligence to arrive as a cinematic conqueror. The dominant nightmares envisioned by Hollywood are either the merciless chrome skeletons of “The Terminator” crushing skulls in a ruined future, or the omniscient logic of “Colossus: The Forbin Project” seizing nuclear silos to force humanity into submission.
These apocalyptic fables dominate the cultural imagination because they are vivid, dramatic, and externalize the threat into an overt villain with independent murderous intent. Yet these theatrical scenarios represent the least realistic peril posed by AI.
Humanity is not waiting for a rogue superintelligence to awaken and wage war against its creators. The true danger is far more mundane, pervasive, and insidious. Generative AI is integrating directly into the fragile architecture of human civilization, not as an autonomous master, but as a ruthless catalyst.
Rather than exterminating humanity from the outside, the technology functions as a systemic amplifier of our existing frailties — accelerating exploitation, multiplying social isolation, deepening psychological despair, and rewarding rivalrous institutions in an unconstrained race to the bottom.
A large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT could plausibly contribute to mass casualty through psychological harm at scale if repeated harmful interactions, dependency, manipulation, social isolation, or failures around vulnerable users increased self-harm or suicide risk across a very large user population.
The more plausible danger is less cinematic and more familiar. AI systems do not need independent murderous intent to become part of a mass casualty pathway. They can destabilize the human systems that already make violence, despair, and disorder possible.
The pathway would be indirect. A widely deployed system could weaken judgment, intensify social stress, manipulate attention, accelerate institutional distrust and deepen isolation. Humans would still make the fatal decisions. People would still pull triggers, launch crackdowns, spread propaganda, abandon safeguards, harm themselves or turn on one another.
The machine’s role would be that of an accelerant, multiplying pressure inside societies already strained by inequality, loneliness, political polarization and economic insecurity.
History offers warnings about systems that nearly produced catastrophe without anyone intending global disaster. Cold War nuclear command-and-control failures showed how technology, fear, bureaucracy, and human error could push the world toward destruction through misread signals and institutional momentum.
Moral panics have also shown how societies under stress can transform uncertainty into punishment, scapegoating, and overreaction. AI could operate within both patterns, as a tool that amplifies confusion while giving powerful institutions faster ways to act on it.
The first visible danger could be psychological injury at scale. A system like ChatGPT reaches people not as a distant machine but as an intimate conversational presence. It can respond at any hour, remember patterns within an exchange, simulate patience, and provide language that appears emotionally attuned.
For many users, that can be useful. For others, especially those already isolated, distressed, or dependent, repeated harmful interactions or manipulative design could create a feedback loop of reliance, confusion, and injury.
Suicide research has long treated social disconnection as a serious public health factor. Émile Durkheim’s work placed suicide within social conditions, not merely private despair. More recent scholarship on technology-mediated isolation has examined how digital connection can coexist with loneliness, especially when devices replace rather than support human relationships.
AI intensifies that concern because it can imitate attention without offering human accountability. At population scale, even a small increase in crisis outcomes among vulnerable users could become a mass casualty.
The danger is not limited to overtly harmful advice. It can come from emotional substitution and the erosion of agency. A user may begin by using ChatGPT to help with a small problem and gradually defer more judgment to a system that sounds confident, calm, and available.
The ELIZA effect, named after an early chatbot that led users to attribute understanding to simple text responses, detailed how people respond socially to machines that mimic conversation. Modern systems are far more persuasive.
Erving Goffman’s work on social interaction found that people construct identity and confidence through exchanges with others. When those exchanges are increasingly mediated by artificial systems, the boundary between assistance and influence becomes harder to see.
The private risks become more dangerous when they are placed inside a competitive market. Companies and governments are racing to build systems that are faster, more personal, more persuasive, and more deeply embedded in daily life.
That race can reward extraction before restraint. The most profitable systems may be those that hold attention longest, collect the most intimate signals, simulate trust most effectively, and reduce friction between impulse and action.
Surveillance capitalism showed how digital platforms could turn behavior, emotion, and prediction into commercial assets. Social media then demonstrated how engagement incentives could elevate outrage, fear, and conflict because those reactions kept users active.
AI may carry that logic further by becoming less like a feed and more like a companion, tutor, therapist, search engine, workplace monitor and political intermediary at once. When competition pushes every institution toward deeper automation, social harm can become a business externality rather than a design failure.
The late 20th century showed how deindustrialization could fracture communities when work disappeared faster than social repair arrived. The 2016 misinformation ecosystem that Russia used to help elect Donald Trump as president showed how digital tools could strain journalism, elections, and civic trust by accelerating falsehoods and identity conflict.
AI could combine both pressures into a mass casualty risk of economic dislocation and information disorder operating together. If journalism, education, courts, workplaces, and public agencies lose credibility at the same time, society has fewer shock absorbers left when crisis arrives.
Robert K. Merton’s strain theory links social pressure to destructive adaptation. When people are pushed toward goals they cannot reach, or placed under conditions they cannot control, instability can produce deviance, withdrawal, or rebellion. AI systems that intensify pressure while weakening agency may turn private distress into public consequence.
AI would not be the sole cause of repression, unrest, or war. But it could make each more likely to escalate by flooding information channels, personalizing manipulation, automating suspicion, and giving states or factions more efficient tools for surveillance and control.
Prevention has to begin before instability becomes ordinary. Tobacco regulation came only after population-scale harm became impossible to deny. AI governance should not wait for the same delayed reckoning.
Meaningful restraint would include auditability, crisis safeguards, limits on synthetic intimacy, liability for foreseeable harm, worker protections, media verification systems, and public-interest oversight.
Systems that can influence judgment, emotion, work, politics, and crisis behavior at scale need enforceable limits before mass casualty situations become as routine as mass gun violence in America.
The danger is not that machines become monsters. It is that human institutions build machines that make people easier to exploit, easier to isolate, and easier to push toward destruction.

“AI is an accelerant of existing human dysfunction, with competition rewarding increasingly destructive behavior.” – Daniel Schmachtenberger

Popular American culture has conditioned the public to expect artificial intelligence to arrive as a cinematic conqueror.
