articles.summary: Analyzing Germany's F127 frigate program, this article examines why relying heavily on U.S. Aegis technology may undermine national sovereignty and defense readiness.
articles.content:
Analyzing Germany’s F127 frigate program, this article by German defense media hartpunkt examines why relying heavily on the U.S. Aegis technology and ecosystem may undermine national sovereignty and defense readiness.
By Lars Hoffman / hartpunkt
The German Navy’s future F127 class air defense frigates are intended not only for area air defense, but also for the even more demanding Ballistic Missile Defence (BMD) mission. To achieve this, current plans are to equip them with Aegis—arguably the most advanced Western combat management system for BMD—along with U.S.-manufactured sensors and effectors. In doing so, the Bundeswehr (German military) is closely aligning its configuration with the U.S. Navy’s Aegis “Program of Record.” For instance, the SPY-6 radar was selected over the alternative SPY-7 radar. This decision has been justified on the grounds that it is the only way to close the existing capability gap “at short notice,” as no capable European alternative is available, with the first ship scheduled to enter service around the middle of the coming decade.
The adoption of U.S. standards and the BMD capability also impacts structural requirements and is expected to cost several billion euros per ship. This has been criticized by some politicians as being too expensive, and the project currently appears to be under review.
Despite all the criticism regarding costs—though a cruiser-sized ship with the required capabilities is simply not cheap—it is easily overlooked that a comprehensive focus on the described U.S. of-the-shelf purchase brings a number of disadvantages that are likely to be just as politically difficult to communicate.
For example, purchasing technology selected and used by the U.S. Navy creates a high and potentially decades-long dependency on decisions made across the Atlantic. In case of doubt, the U.S. Navy dictates how the program proceeds, what modifications are made to the systems, and which weapons are to be integrated.
Choosing a purely U.S. configuration comes at a time when the United States is presenting itself as significantly more unpredictable, both politically and economically, than in past decades. Switzerland’s order for Patriot air defense systems serves as a good example here. After the administration under President Joe Biden had already ordered a reprioritization of the ordered PAC-3 guided missiles, the Trump administration last year summarily postponed the delivery of all five Swiss systems so that other countries could be prioritized.
While the Bundeswehr is currently benefiting from this decision because it can use the Swiss Patriots to replace contributions sent to Ukraine, it could soon find itself among the disadvantaged parties of such reprioritizations. Incidentally, Switzerland now anticipates a delay of at least six years. Thus, the argument that capability gaps can only be closed quickly using U.S. systems remains more of a hypothesis than a fact.
To the surprise of most experts, the USA has also expended such massive quantities of interceptor missiles of all classes in the ongoing, lingering Iran war that stockpiles have now dwindled dangerously. In the coming years, in accordance with the “America First” policy, the U.S. armed forces will presumably be supplied first, while allied users of U.S. systems can only hope to be considered in a timely manner. What it means to be unable to produce interceptor missiles oneself and to depend on foreign deliveries can currently be observed in Ukraine, as well as in some Gulf states.
At the same time, national technological sovereignty has recently gained significantly in importance across all military fields. In addition to the risk of systems malfunctioning or supply chains breaking down, uncertainty regarding the cohesion of NATO is likely to play a role. While the recent summit of the defense community did not lead to the feared fracture, no one can predict whether this will remain the case. Washington’s repeatedly demonstrated ambitions to annex Greenland are unlikely to have contributed to reassurance.
It is therefore only sensible that the German Ministry of Defense is striving for the greatest possible national sovereignty in strategic key technologies currently under development, such as deep strike, access to space, or military clouds.
However, Ballistic Missile Defence and air defense in general should also be considered among these key technologies. The threat from ballistic missiles has been growing for years due to the proliferation of technology; even the Houthi rebels in Yemen apparently possess medium-range capable ballistic missiles.
Germany would therefore be well-advised to build up its own capabilities here regarding software, sensors, and effectors—potentially in cooperation with partners who already possess relevant expertise and where Berlin is not automatically relegated to the children’s table due to an excessive power asymmetry.
For instance, Israel has demonstrated that, despite enormous domestic burdens and the constant Iranian threat, it was able to provide the Federal Republic with a means for territorial missile defense in record time with the Arrow-3 system.
The timing for domestic developments is currently as favorable as rarely before. Funds are still available, the programming of fire control software has been greatly simplified thanks to the maturity of artificial intelligence, and Germany is likely to have access to data crucial for air defense through its support for Ukraine. Furthermore, numerous projects surrounding the military use of space are being launched, which will likewise provide added value for air defense.
Moreover, combat management software and certain sensors from domestic development—or at least without “black boxes”—would in the future enable the integration of European guided missiles currently under development, such as those designed to counter hypersonic weapons. By contrast, insiders doubt that this will be possible within a U.S. Navy Program of Record.
If the current approach is maintained, in a worst-case scenario this could mean that German air defense frigates might no longer be usable after expending their missiles if U.S. deliveries fail to materialize, while European missiles would be available but non-integrable.
Added to this is the economic aspect: purchasing U.S. systems generates billions of euros in value creation in the United States, not at home. At the same time, Germany remains technologically left behind in the high-end sector of air defense.
The example of IRIS-T SLM shows that things can be done differently. This air defense system is being deployed so successfully in Ukraine that it has already been ordered by numerous armed forces worldwide, and a second production line is reportedly even being established. Manufacturing in Germany creates high-quality jobs and channels tax revenues into the state treasury, amortizing government R&D funds that flowed into component parts of IRIS-T. Moreover, manufacturer Diehl is likely earning the necessary funds from the venture to invest in its own research and development.
If, despite these arguments favoring a domestic development approach, there is a fear of alienating the U.S. or doubts about domestic capabilities, an intermediate solution might be conceivable: four instead of eight frigates could be procured with the planned U.S. BMD configuration, while four others could initially be equipped with technology from Germany and partner countries for area air defense to replace the aging F124s at the beginning of the coming decade. The issue of BMD could then be addressed during the first modernization of those frigates.
One advantage of such a solution would be that part of the sensor suite for these ships is already available. Specifically, the TRS-4D long-range radars produced by Hensoldt for the F124 appear ready for deployment.
This article by Lars Hoffman was originally published in German language at hartpunkt.de. It has been translated and republished with authorization.

articles.article_title: Europe does not want to depend on foreign technology in the new digital order
articles.heading: Europe does not want to depend on foreign technology in the new digital order
articles.summary: Brussels wants to build its own capabilities in semiconductors, cloud computing and artificial intelligence as it seeks greater technological sovereignty from the US and China
articles.content:
Europe does not want to depend on foreign technology in the new digital order
Brussels wants to build its own capabilities in semiconductors, cloud computing and artificial intelligence as it seeks greater technological sovereignty from the US and China
For years, Europe grew used to a contradiction that it is only now beginning to see as a risk: being one of the world’s foremost regulatory powers in the digital sphere while remaining dependent on others for much of the technology those rules were designed to govern. Over the past decade, Brussels has assembled an extensive legislative arsenal aimed at curbing the power of big tech, from the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) to the Digital Markets Act, the Digital Services Act and the AI Act. Yet while Europe was writing rules, the United States and China were building companies, data centers, chips, cloud platforms and artificial-intelligence models on a scale that no European firm has managed to match.
Artificial intelligence has blown that contradiction wide open. Technology is no longer merely a question of business competitiveness; it has become a matter of power. Cloud services, data centers, semiconductors, networks, software and computing capacity have become strategic infrastructure. Those who control them do not simply provide services; they can influence the decision-making of those who depend on them.
The scale of Europe’s dependence is captured by one particularly striking figure: 92% of Western data is stored on U.S.-owned infrastructure, according to an Oliver Wyman analysis of European digital sovereignty. The problem, therefore, is not simply that Europe uses applications or services developed elsewhere. A critical share of the information on which the Western economy runs is housed in infrastructure that Europe does not control.
The European Commission itself offers another measure of that dependence: the EU relies on non-EU countries for more than 80% of its digital products, services, infrastructure and intellectual property, according to data compiled by EU institutions and cited by the European Parliament in its January 2026 resolution on technological sovereignty. The figure helps explain why Brussels no longer sees technological dependence as merely a business issue, but increasingly as a strategic challenge.
The European Commission has accepted that diagnosis and is trying to change the model. The goal is not to push U.S. companies out of the European market or to build a digital fortress isolated from the United States and China. Instead, the idea gaining ground in Brussels is that Europe should have enough homegrown alternatives to be able to choose, negotiate and, if necessary, do without a foreign supplier in technologies it considers critical.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen summed it up on June 3, 2026, when she unveiled the European Technology Sovereignty Package: “We cannot afford to depend on others for the technologies that keep our hospitals running, our energy grids stable and our services secure.” She added: “This is about protecting our citizens, defending our interests and making our own choices.”
The package presented by Brussels on June 3 is the clearest expression yet of that shift. The Commission has put forward two new legislative proposals, the Chips Act 2.0 and the Cloud and AI Development Act, known as CADA, alongside a European open-source strategy and a roadmap for digitalization and artificial intelligence in the energy sector.
These measures have not yet become law. They are legislative proposals that must still make their way through the EU’s policymaking process. But they offer a clear indication of the direction Brussels wants European technology policy to take.
The picture is even more striking in the cloud-computing market. AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, the three major U.S. hyperscalers, account for roughly 70% of the European cloud-infrastructure market, while European providers hold only about 15%.
In 2017, European cloud providers controlled around 29% of the market. Five years later, their share had fallen to 15%, where it has since remained largely stagnant.
A hyperscaler is a technology giant that operates vast networks of data centers and provides computing power, storage and digital services on demand to other companies. Its influence also stems from the ecosystems it has built. A company may start by using a provider’s storage services and end up relying on the same vendor for databases, development tools, cybersecurity, data analytics and artificial intelligence.
That is where the concept of vendor lock-in comes into play: the phenomenon whereby customers become effectively tied to a particular technology platform. The more dependent a company becomes on a single provider, the more difficult and costly it is to switch. Europe has spent several years trying to tackle this problem through regulation. The Data Act, which began to apply in September 2025, includes measures designed to make it easier for customers to change providers of data-processing services, including cloud and edge-computing services. The regulation seeks to improve interoperability and portability while reducing the technical and financial barriers that make leaving a platform difficult.
The next step is the Digital Markets Act. In June 2026, the European Commission informed Amazon and Microsoft of its preliminary view that AWS and Azure should be designated as “gatekeepers” under the legislation. Brussels argues that the two companies are the EU’s leading cloud providers, with entrenched market positions, high switching costs and strong lock-in effects. The decision is not yet final, but it would extend the EU’s approach to regulating large digital platforms into the heart of cloud infrastructure. For Brussels, the cloud is no longer merely a market for IT services; it has become a strategic infrastructure.
The reason is artificial intelligence. Advanced AI models require enormous amounts of computing power. Training and running them depend on specialized processors, data centers, storage systems, high-speed networks and vast quantities of energy. AI is turning data centers into the factories that will produce much of the digital economy of the future.
The CADA project
That is why the Commission has designed the Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA). The proposal aims to at least triple the European Union’s data-center capacity over the next five to seven years, speed up and simplify permitting procedures for new facilities, improve access to energy, land, water and financing, and ensure sufficient computing capacity to support the expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud services. It also introduces a common European framework for assessing cloud and AI sovereignty and would allow public authorities to use that framework when making procurement decisions.
The most innovative aspect of CADA is precisely its definition of sovereignty. Brussels wants to move beyond the idea that a cloud service is sovereign simply because the data are physically stored within the European Union. The proposed framework establishes four levels of sovereignty. The first requires that data be processed and stored on infrastructure located in the EU. The second adds independence from third countries and transparency regarding the software supply chain. The third requires that the provider be owned and controlled from within the EU. The fourth, and highest, level demands full transparency and control over the software supply chain, as well as freedom from interference by third countries.
The distinction matters because a server may be located in Madrid while control remains in Seattle. That is precisely the concern that Sebastián Muriel, Telefónica’s chief digital officer, has brought into the European debate. In an article published in the business daily Cinco Días on May 23, titled Europe, Wake Up: Digital Sovereignty Cannot Be Built by Signing Lease Agreements, he argued that “believing sovereignty consists merely of hosting data on European soil is clearly insufficient.”

articles.summary: Skimmer fraud costs Americans more than $1 billion a year, and thieves now use both physical devices on card readers and RFID technology that can steal card information from a few inches away, including in checkout lines.
articles.content:
Card skimming scams evolve as technology advances, experts say
JEFFERSON COUNTY, Ala. (WBRC) - Scammers are finding new ways to steal card information as technology changes, according to cybersecurity and consumer protection experts. Skimming once meant a hidden device on a gas pump or card reader. Now, a scammer could steal card information without touching it.
Skimmers steal card numbers
UAB cybersecurity expert Dr. Ragib Hasan said scammers use small skimming devices to steal card numbers.
“They can then use that to make fake fraudulent transactions using your credit card number or they can even clone your card,” Hasan said.
On Wednesday, Cosmin Vaduva and Elena Caldarareasa were charged with planting skimmers at three Jefferson County businesses. Investigators arrested the pair in Mississippi with skimmers, fake cards and more than $10,000 in cash.
The FBI says skimmer fraud now costs Americans more than a billion dollars a year.
Hasan said the scam has changed as card technology has improved. Years ago, when magnetic stripes were the main form of payment, skimming was widespread and easy to pull off. He said he was once a victim himself, after a waiter at a Las Vegas restaurant used a skimmer to steal and clone his card.
Chip technology made cards harder to clone, Hasan said, which led scammers to develop insert-style skimmers that steal data as a chip card is pushed into a reader. He said the technology to build these devices has become widely available on underground markets, making the scam accessible even to petty criminals — not just organized, tech-savvy operations.
“There’s a whole underworld market for that,” Hasan said. “So these days, a lot of the regular criminals... are also using these skimmers.”
A safer way to pay
Better Business Bureau President Carl Bates said there is a safer way to pay.
“Tap if you can versus sticking it in and pulling it out or sliding it. Always tap,” Bates said.
But Bates said tapping to pay also carries risks.
“A guy behind you can be using his phone... and be skimming cards out of your purse or out of my wallet just in line at Walmart. And then you walk out and you don’t even know that your card’s been stolen,” Bates said.
Bates said this kind of theft can happen anywhere people are standing close together — at the grocery store, the airport, even in a TSA line.
RFID skimming targets tap-to-pay chips
This method is called RFID skimming, which targets the same chip that allows tap-to-pay transactions.
“If you just tap it close to a credit card reader with a NFC or near field communications enabled, then that can also take payment from you. Now, scammers have noticed this also, and they take advantage of standing very close to you,” Hasan said.
Digital wallets on phones offer a defense, using face or fingerprint scans so scammers cannot access a card without approval. RFID-blocking cards or sleeves also help.
“This will stop anybody from being able to attack any of my cards in my wallet or in your purse,” Bates said.
Bates said digital wallets like Apple Pay or Samsung Pay are not vulnerable to RFID skimming the way physical cards are, since they require active approval through a password, fingerprint or facial scan. He said protecting that phone password matters too — a weak or easily guessed passcode can undo the added security of a digital wallet.
Inspect devices before use
Hasan said to look closely at a card reader before inserting or swiping a card.
“If the payment slot looks like it’s out of place, it looks like something that doesn’t match the rest of the device, then likely it’s a skimmer... If it feels loose, don’t use it,” Hasan said.
Hasan said scammers also sometimes install hidden cameras near keypads to record PIN numbers as they’re entered. He recommends covering the keypad with your hand while entering a PIN, even if no camera is visible.
Bates said the Better Business Bureau gives away RFID-blocking sleeves for free. They can also be purchased online or on amazon for a few dollars.
What to do if you’re a victim
Hasan and Bates both said catching fraud quickly is critical. Warning signs include unfamiliar charges on a card statement — often small “test” charges scammers make before attempting larger purchases — or a fraud alert from a bank or credit card company.
Hasan recommends:
- Contacting the credit card company immediately to report fraud and freeze the card
- Setting up real-time transaction alerts, especially for card-not-present purchases
- Using a credit card rather than a debit card when possible, since credit card companies are required to investigate disputes and typically reverse fraudulent charges quickly. Debit card fraud is harder to recover because the money is withdrawn directly from a bank account.
Bates said consumers should always call their financial institution directly to verify any fraud alert, rather than trusting a call or text that claims to be from the bank — a common tactic scammers use to obtain PIN numbers after already stealing account information.
Protect your passwords, too
Bates said password security plays a major role in preventing fraud, especially as more people store payment methods, driver’s licenses and even passports on their phones.
He said scammers can often guess passwords built around personal information — a pet’s name, a car, a birthday — because so much of that information is publicly available on social media.
“How many people use the same password on their phone that they used for their PIN number?” Bates said. “You don’t want anything that’s connected with your personal information and your password.”
Bates recommends passwords with at least 12 characters that combine unrelated words and random numbers — nothing tied to a birthday, hometown, family member or pet. He also recommends enabling two-factor authentication whenever it’s available.
Bates said card and identity fraud is increasingly run by organized crime operations based overseas, not individual scammers.
“This is not two guys in their basement doing this,” Bates said. “It is organized crime from across the world... large operations, hundreds of people sitting in rooms working on decoding information to see if they can crack people’s passwords.”
Bottom line
Both experts said the safest approach is a layered one: use tap-to-pay or a digital wallet when possible, protect phones and accounts with strong passwords and biometric locks, inspect card readers before use, and monitor accounts closely for suspicious activity.
“It’s like an arms race between the scammers and the good guys,” Hasan said. “Scammers are always coming up with new ways to scam, and that’s why the good guys... are trying to develop technology to protect against that.”

“It’s like an arms race between the scammers and the good guys,” Hasan said. “Scammers are always coming up with new ways to scam, and that’s why the good guys... are trying to develop technology to protect against that.”

articles.content:
UN Crime Congress: Technology is transforming crime – and the response to it
Sitting in her Vienna office ahead of a pivotal UN gathering in Abu Dhabi, Monica Juma is focused on a simple reality: crime has evolved faster than many of the institutions designed to combat it.
Criminal networks now move money, goods and information across borders at lightning speed, exploiting everything from new technologies to global instability. Yet the same tools that help drive illicit activity could also transform the fight against it.
Technology, while creating what Ms. Juma describes as “an ecosystem of criminal profiteering with a very far-reaching footprint”, can also enable faster, smarter and more coordinated responses to threats that increasingly touch every corner of the world.
Those challenges – from cyber-enabled crime to trafficking and online scams – will be at the centre of discussions in Abu Dhabi at the 15th UN Crime Congress; the world's largest gathering focused on crime prevention and criminal justice.
As the newly appointed Executive Director of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), Ms. Juma is preparing to attend the event for the first time in her current role.
We sat down with her to discuss the criminal threats reshaping the world and the opportunities for governments and institutions to respond more effectively.
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity
UN News: The UN Crime Congress convenes every five years, and provides a platform where the world converges to ask the question: how has crime changed?
Ms. Juma: The defining factor today is, of course, technology. Five years ago, technology was evolving very differently. Now, it is enabling a multitude of crimes across various sectors. What we are seeing is a convergence of crime types that is creating an ecosystem of criminal profiteering with a very far-reaching footprint across the world.
With technology, millions of people can become targets within a fraction of a second. There is no need for intermediaries, or to cross borders.
Caption: UNODC Executive Director Monica Juma during an interview with UN News and UNIS Vienna. (Credit: UNIS Vienna/Laura Skocek)
UN News: How can the Crime Congress help ensure that justice and law enforcement systems in developing countries are not left behind amid a widening global digital gap?
Ms. Juma: Technology, in fact, is not leaving anyone behind. Countries that are considered very advanced in terms of technology, are as vulnerable as the weakest ones. Organized criminals have no border inhibitions.
Traffickers no longer just depend on people carrying people across borders in boats. They are now also using technology and disinformation to create fake jobs, and sometimes even ending up in legitimate business supply chains, including banking services.
This is exactly why the UN Crime Congress platform is so important. That is the value of the UN. We have the capacity to bring everyone to the table, and that is what we will see in Abu Dhabi. There will be representation from everywhere in the world.
At UNODC, we are increasingly creating platforms for interface across borders and sectors; for example: investigators, prosecutors, police enforcement officials, judicial officials, now even investigative journalists.
The purpose is to create a convergence of competencies that can be quickly used to convey information, evidence, or suspicions to somebody who can act on it almost immediately.
We are encouraging countries to cooperate more, including in the areas of intelligence sharing and forensic analysis among others, but the ability to translate that cooperation has not been fully enabled so far on the Member State side. Doing so requires the right policies, relationships, and mechanisms.
UN News: Why is the UN Cybercrime Convention so important?
Ms. Juma: The United Nations Convention against Cybercrime was adopted unanimously by the General Assembly in 2024, and we have more than 80 signatories already. The Convention provides a full toolkit that facilitates cooperation among countries and creates similar standards that will enable faster and more agile responses to common threats.
We are calling on and encouraging countries to ratify it so that it can enter into force, because, until that happens, its full utilization would be limited.
Now, ratification is a domestic legislative process, but a lot of countries that I have personally spoken to have indicated that that process is ongoing. We hope that it can enter into force soon.
UN News: Hundreds of thousands of victims of trafficking are forced to commit cybercrimes in ever-expanding, large-scale scam centres. How can the Crime Congress address their plight?
Ms. Juma: First of all, these scam centres are really a global crisis. Our last report on scam centres in Southeast Asia indicated that victims came from more than 80 nationalities around the world. This is a global situation that is expanding exponentially. These scam centres are a real pandemic if you think about it.
Many times, they manifest as genuine opportunities for young people who are curious – who want to work and experience the world. It is very important that they are conceived as victims rather than culprits, and that we identify the real perpetrators of the crime. It is the people that are deceiving them, recruiting them, and misleading them.
It is also important to protect the victim’s rights and support them through rehabilitation and treatment. Some of them have been through very traumatic experiences, including torture and abuse, and these experiences will stay with them for a very long time. For our part, UNODC has been supporting capacity building within criminal justice systems to effectively handle victims and vulnerable groups.
UN News: What can be done to ensure that the Crime Congress delivers real solutions at a time of increasing geopolitical polarisation and global tensions?
Ms. Juma: It is true that the world is in a very concerning situation, but it is also true that the threat of crime is something that people feel every day across the world.
It is impossible to create any level of productivity or sustainability if you are experiencing insecurity at a personal, local, or community level – which is what drugs and crime is doing. It affects people at every level, and that reality makes it easier to cooperate and look for solutions.
And so, we have a situation where there is a convergence, both at the level of the threat, and the desire to look for solutions. As we come to Abu Dhabi, there is no debate whether this is important or not.
We hope that we can take the solutions presented in Kyoto (the venue of the 2021 UN Crime Congress) to now look at the current threats that are being accelerated by new intervening variables such as technology.
We look to the role of technology in aiding us to respond in an agile and more effective manner, so that we can restore safer environments, secure communities, and hopefully achieve better prosperity for the world.

Micron Technology designs and produces memory and storage hardware used in everything from smartphones and PCs to data centers, so long running tightness in DRAM and NAND supply directly touches the products it sells into these markets. As one of the larger US based chip manufacturers by scale, with a reported market value of about $1.1 trillion, its comments on supply conditions can influence how investors think about capacity planning across the wider semiconductor sector.

Does the team leading Micron Technology have what it takes? See our full breakdown of the management team's track record and compensation.

What extended shortages and rising prices signal for the Micron Technology Narrative

For Micron Technology, management warning that tight memory supply and higher pricing could run through 2027 directly reinforces the Narrative catalyst built on multi year AI demand, constrained capacity and a richer product mix. It leans into the thesis that advanced DRAM, HBM and high capacity DDR5 aimed at AI data centers can support stronger earnings quality than past commodity cycles. It also increases the pressure on the risk side of that story, since a sector that already needs heavy investment and faces worker shortages now has to execute large US and Japan fab build outs without letting cost or timing slip.

See how these catalysts shape Micron Technology's path to a $1,507 fair value .

The clearest test of this read will be how Micron's long term customer agreements and utilization plans look through 2027, especially whether the company keeps reporting high take or pay coverage across its AI oriented memory output as new fabs and its 512GB DDR5 modules move toward volume production in the second half of 2027.

articles.content:
City of Ontario
The City of Ontario is located approximately 35 miles east of downtown Los Angeles, with direct access to the I-10, I-210, and I-15 freeways. Over 130 years of success have paved the way for this growing community to be the Premier Community of the Inland Empire.
The Deputy Information Technology Director is a key member of the IT Agency’s leadership team, overseeing day-to-day operations and service delivery across Operations, Systems, Applications, and Information Security. This is an exciting opportunity to support a sophisticated technology environment that includes major City construction projects and extensive public safety operations, as well as help position Ontario for the next generation of municipal technology. Ontario seeks an accomplished, people-focused technology leader with strong communication and relationship-building skills and a commitment to exceptional customer service.
Competitive candidates will offer at least six years of progressively responsible IT experience in a governmental agency, including two years in a managerial capacity. Bachelor’s degree is strongly preferred.
Salary range $162,698 – $216,486 DOQE, with competitive benefits. For brochure and to apply visit www.tbcrecruiting.com. Recruitment closes Sunday, October 18, 2026.

articles.title: UNMC demonstrates telehealth, VR technology to help close rural care gaps
articles.description: UNMC demonstrates telehealth, VR technology to help close rural care gaps WOWT
articles.description_html: UNMC demonstrates telehealth, VR technology to help close rural care gaps  WOWT
articles.article_title: UNMC demonstrates telehealth, VR technology to help close rural care gaps
articles.heading: UNMC demonstrates telehealth, VR technology to help close rural care gaps
articles.summary: Medical professionals gathered at the University of Nebraska Medical Center Friday for a conference focused on treating stroke patients, where educators demonstrated technology they believe could eventually help close gaps in rural care.
articles.content:
UNMC demonstrates telehealth, VR technology to help close rural care gaps
Medical professionals gathered at a UNMC conference to see technology aimed at improving stroke treatment and rural access to care
OMAHA, Neb. (WOWT) - Medical professionals gathered at the University of Nebraska Medical Center Friday for a conference focused on treating stroke patients, where educators demonstrated technology they believe could eventually help close gaps in rural care.
Holobox connects patient to specialist
Cheyanne Wood, of Curtis, Nebraska, suffered a stroke last November at age 31.
“I was in inpatient rehab for 19 days. And then I spent seven months in outpatient physical therapy,” Wood said.
First Alert 6 spoke with Wood in Omaha as she was projected from Kearney using a holobox, a freestanding, life-sized cabinet that projects a 3D person.
Every two weeks, Wood travels three and a half hours to Lincoln to see her neuro-ophthalmologist. She said advances in telehealth have helped with communication about her recovery at home.
“I can sit in my bed and talk to her over a computer screen and then have her send me exercises and then I print those off. I’m able to access those immediately. It’s, it’s astronomical and just unbelievable at, at best,” Wood said.
UNMC says distance is one of the biggest challenges for rural residents seeking care.
“So there’s not a whole lot in the middle. And rural communities don’t have access to all the things that we do in the metro area. You know, there’s not a physical therapist on every three blocks. And transportation can be an issue,” said Nichole Cooks, stroke coordinator, UNMC.
VR training technology on display
Instructors with iExcel, a program at UNMC, showed off VR training technology currently being used at the university. The technology is designed for students to interact with 3D models of anatomical concepts, like arteries.
“The importance of 3D technology is that it helps people simplify complex anatomical concepts and medical concepts. So, being able to see different anatomical elements in 3D just reinforces those spatial relationships and how things relate to each other, versus it being in 2D on a textbook or on a PowerPoint,” said Dheeraj Varandan, technical director, iExcel.
Varandan said the technology also allows students to simulate scenarios, including communicating with patients, before encountering them in practice.
“The concept of simulation is brought to immersive reality, lets us create these scenarios ahead of time and train people, you know, being able to communicate with the patient, how that might turn out, just really simulate those scenarios in immersive reality,” Varandan said.
The hope is to eventually get more professionals to adopt these advances to better serve metro and rural Nebraskans.
Wood told First Alert 6 she is continuing her home exercises and recently graduated from physical therapy. She said she is grateful for the hope advances in telehealth have given her in her recovery.

articles.title: Plasma Technology Could Help Plant-Based Packaging Replace Plastic
articles.description: Plasma Technology Could Help Plant-Based Packaging Replace Plastic cnr.ncsu.edu

articles.article_title: Plasma Technology Could Help Plant-Based Packaging Replace Plastic
articles.heading: Plasma Technology Could Help Plant-Based Packaging Replace Plastic
articles.summary: Researchers have found that using advanced plasma technology to apply layered, protective coatings to the surface of cellulose-based films can improve their water resistance, opening new possibilities for plant-based packaging.
articles.content:
A new study has found a sustainable and scalable way to improve the durability of plant-based packaging; it’s a discovery that researchers say could help curb the environmental footprint of plastic.
In the study, researchers used advanced plasma technology to apply layered, protective coatings to the surface of cellulosic nanofibril (CNF) films, with the goal of reducing water absorption and improving moisture resistance.
They found that one of the plasma-treated coatings reduced liquid water absorption in CNF films to less than 1%, while another weakened the film’s moisture barrier and allowed more water vapor to pass through.
According to the researchers, the results show that the plasma technology — dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma — can be used to precisely control how CNF films interact with moisture, opening new possibilities for plant-based packaging.
“This research provides a practical strategy for turning natural plant and tree fibers into functional, water-resistant packaging. It moves society one step closer to replacing everyday plastic wraps with truly renewable, biodegradable materials,” said one of the study’s lead authors Nathalie Lavoine, an associate professor in the Department of Forest Biomaterials at North Carolina State University.
CNF films are derived from renewable biomass such as wood pulp. They are completely biodegradable and provide strong barriers against oxygen and grease, offering a more sustainable alternative for additives, coatings and films in packaging products.
Many conventional packaging products such as potato chip bags, candy wrappers and squeeze pouches are made by fusing multiple layers of petroleum-based plastics with materials like aluminum foil or paper.
Because the layers are difficult to separate, standard recycling facilities often cannot process this type of packaging. As a result, it may end up in landfills, where it can eventually break down into microplastics that can contaminate soil and water.
Widespread industrial adoption of more sustainable alternatives like CNF films remains limited in part because of their poor moisture barrier performance. Because cellulose naturally attracts water, the films rapidly absorb moisture from the environment.
Moisture absorption can compromise the structural integrity of CNF films, causing them to lose strength and experience a significant reduction in gas barrier performance. In packaging, this can compromise product protection and shorten shelf life.
If CNF films were used in a potato chip bag and that bag were exposed to high humidity, for example, moisture could permeate the film and reach the chips. This could cause the chips to lose their crispness and become stale. For some foods, moisture can promote the development of bacteria, resulting in foodborne illness.
Plasma treatment helps address these problems by modifying the surface of CNF films to block water, while preserving the original mechanical performance and structural integrity of the cellulose.
Lavoine said one of the primary advantages of plasma treatment is that the technology itself is more sustainable than traditional chemical coating processes that use large amounts of water, generate high heat and produce toxic waste.
The technology is also scalable, according to Lavoine. In fact, the technology is already used in the packaging industry, meaning the DBD plasma treatment process can be seamlessly integrated into existing manufacturing lines.
Still, Lavoine said that she and her collaborators must address several key challenges before DBD plasma treatment can reach real-world production. That includes refining the process so that it doesn’t allow water vapor to leak through.
While that permeability can be useful for tailoring CNF films for medical products such as breathable wound dressings, it would need to be minimized for packaging applications where moisture resistance is essential.
Lavoine said additional testing and optimization are also needed to assess coating speeds, energy use and physical durability, ensuring the material can withstand real-world handling while remaining economically viable and environmentally and socially safe.
The paper “Surface modification of cellulose nanofibril films via organosilicon deposition using dielectric barrier discharge plasma (DBD) plasma for packaging applications,” is published in the journal Applied Surface Science. Co-authors include Mirela A. Artner of NC State University, Lucia Švandová of Masaryk University, and Jacopo Profili of the University of Quebec in Rimouski.
This research was supported in part by the College of Natural Resources at NC State University, the 2022-23 NC State Internationalization Seed Grant, the Mitacs Globalink Research Award (#IT35099) and the intramural research program of the U.S. Department of Agriculture, National Institute of Food and Agriculture, McIntire-Stennis, grant number NI22MSCFRXXXG054.

Note to editors: The study abstract follows.
“Surface modification of cellulose nanofibril films via organosilicon deposition using dielectric barrier discharge plasma (DBD) plasma for packaging applications”
Authors: Mirela A. Artner and Nathalie Lavoine, NC State University; Lucia Švandová, Masaryk University; and Jacopo Profili, University of Quebec in Rimouski
Published: September 8, Applied Surface Science
DOI: 10.1016/j.apsusc.2026.168134
Abstract: Films made of cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs) are promising sustainable alternatives to petroleum-based plastic packaging due to their gas and grease barrier properties, high strength-to-flexibility ratio, tunable transparency, and biodegradability. However, cellulose’s hygroscopic nature limits its direct use in food packaging. Here, we exploit dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma to tune the surface properties of CNF films and improve their water/moisture barrier performance. Two strategies were tested: (i) static-mode deposition of organosilicon fragments using 2,4,6,8-tetramethylcyclotetrasiloxane (TMCTS) as precursor, and (ii) formation of multilayers with varied surface chemistries by adjusting the plasma carrier gas and organosilicon fragment chemistry. Strategy (i) identified process parameters enabling uniform deposition of hydrophobic TMCTS fragments on CNF film surfaces. Strategy (ii) extended this by creating a multilayer structure combining tailored inorganic (hydrophilic) and organic (hydrophobic) layers, which substantially reduced water absorption and improved protection relative to untreated films. These results demonstrate that optimizing plasma gas composition, treatment time, and application mode (static vs. dynamic) allows controlled deposition of chemical moieties, enabling CNF films with tunable water and water–vapor barrier properties suited to diverse food-packaging requirements. Plasma treatment thus offers a sustainable, scalable route to enhance CNF film performance and expand their use in packaging applications.

articles.title: Man sentenced for raping college student in the Bronx in 2001 thanks to DNA technology advancements
articles.description: Man sentenced for raping college student in the Bronx in 2001 thanks to DNA technology advancements ABC7 New York
articles.description_html: Man sentenced for raping college student in the Bronx in 2001 thanks to DNA technology advancements  ABC7 New York
articles.article_title: Man sentenced for raping college student in 2001 thanks to DNA technology advancements
articles.heading: Man sentenced for raping college student in 2001 thanks to DNA technology advancements
articles.summary: The suspect was tied to both the 2001 rape of a 21-year-old woman in the Bronx and a May 2000 rape of a 27-year-old woman in Manhattan by the cutting edge technology.
articles.content:
Friday, September 18, 2026 8:32PM
MELROSE, Bronx (WABC) -- Jancys Santiago was sentenced to 25 years behind bars for raping a college student in 2001, in the state's first rape case to be indicted based on genealogy from DNA database.
He will also serve five years post-release supervision and will be required to register as a sex offender.
Santiago was tied to both the 2001 rape of a 21-year-old woman in the Bronx and a May 2000 rape of a 27-year-old woman in Manhattan by the cutting edge technology. He was convicted in the Bronx case in June.
"This decision was more than 20 years in the making," Bronx District Attorney Darcel Clark said.
He was living in Groveland, Florida, when he was arrested, and extradited to New York to face charges in both cases.
In the Bronx case, Santiago allegedly broke into a 21-year-old neighbor's apartment while she was sleeping in Dec. 2001. He covered his victim's face, bound her with a wire hanger, and raped her.
"She survived and she is here with us today," Clark said.
Katy Vicchitto faced Santiago in court on Friday.
"My experience as a survivor of a sexual assault affects every aspect of my life," she said. "It is like a filter that every new physical and social experience goes through."
Investigators had no way of knowing that they were looking for the victim's neighbor in her rape.
The victim's rape kit generated a donor profile that eventually matched the donor profile from Santiago's Manhattan rape case, entered in 2005 and logged into the system as "John Doe."
"Unfortunately, at the time the DNA profile could not be linked to a specifical individual and the identity of the assailant remained unknown for many decades. Over time, technology advanced," Clark said.
In 2022, the Bronx District Attorney's Office received a three-year $500,000 grant from the Justice Department's Bureau of Justice Assistance to reexamine this and other cold cases.
"This process led investigators to only one man. Jancys Santiago," Clark said.
Santiago was sentenced last December to 20 years in prison, then five years of post-release supervision, in the Manhattan case.
Vicchitto met the victim of that case, Sarah Clark, for the first time.
"This process has been very difficult, but today's sentence validates forensic science and the power of reporting and advocacy," Vicchitto said.
The two survivors, tied together by trauma, were united finally by justice and closure.
"I hope this is only the beginning. One down. Hopefully thousands more to go," Clark said.

articles.heading: Beyond Bottled Water: EPA Showcases Technology That Provides Safe Drinking Water to Disaster-Hit Areas
articles.summary: EPA Region 7 held a demonstration event featuring the Region’s Water-on-Wheels Mobile Emergency Water Treatment System (WOW Cart) at Clinton State Park in Lawrence, Kansas.
articles.content:
Beyond Bottled Water: EPA Showcases Technology That Provides Safe Drinking Water to Disaster-Hit Areas
September marks National Preparedness Month
LENEXA, KAN. (SEPT. 18, 2026) – Today, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Region 7 held a demonstration event featuring the Region’s Water-on-Wheels Mobile Emergency Water Treatment System (WOW Cart) at Clinton State Park in Lawrence, Kansas. The event — held during National Preparedness Month — included federal partners, local public health leaders, and water-focused non-profits.
EPA Region 7 Administrator Jim Macy and U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Region 7 Administrator Jay Van Der Werff gave remarks on the importance of emergency response and federal partnership.
“The best emergency responses start with thoughtful preparation,” said EPA Regional Administrator Macy. “Together with our partners, we will continue to support solutions that increase community resiliency in the face of disaster, including technology like the Water-on-Wheels Mobile Emergency Water Treatment System that we highlighted today.”
“Today’s demonstration reinforces that resilient water infrastructure and strong state and local preparedness are essential before disaster strikes,” said FEMA Regional Administrator Van Der Werff. “Events like this help local and state partners assess capabilities, strengthen coordination, and better understand when and what kind of additional support may be needed or available to protect the Water Systems Community Lifeline.”
EPA Region 7, the Kansas Rural Water Association, and WaterStep staffed booths throughout the day to provide information on water sampling and testing, WOW Cart technology, and technical assistance. The EPA Region 7 Mobile Command Post and Mobile Drinking Water Lab, which are routinely deployed in response to environmental emergencies, were also on display.
Following an emergency event, communities need access to clean water not only for drinking, but also for cooking, cleaning, and medical triage. The WOW Cart is a versatile water treatment system that is about the size of a shopping cart and can produce up to 10,000 gallons of treated water per day. WOW Carts can replace or supplement the need for bottled water following disasters.

Since 2020, WOW Carts have been used in tornado, hurricane, and flood responses both nationally and internationally. The WOW Cart was developed through an EPA partnership with WaterStep.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence is center stage in NC at the 2026 Cybersecurity conference at Duke University
articles.description: Artificial Intelligence is center stage in NC at the 2026 Cybersecurity conference at Duke University ABC11 News
articles.description_html: Artificial Intelligence is center stage in NC at the 2026 Cybersecurity conference at Duke University  ABC11 News
articles.article_title: Cybersecurity at Duke conference focuses on challenges of AI, emerging technology
articles.heading: Cybersecurity at Duke conference focuses on challenges of AI, emerging technology
articles.summary: The 2026 Cybersecurity at Duke conference featured lawmakers, intelligence experts, tech leaders, professors and students.
articles.content:
WTVD
Friday, September 18, 2026 8:16PM
DURHAM, N.C. (WTVD) -- Artificial intelligence and its impact on cybersecurity were the focus Friday as Duke University hosted its third annual "Cybersecurity at Duke" conference.
Lawmakers, intelligence experts, technology leaders, professors and students gathered at Duke's Penn Pavilion to discuss emerging technological challenges and the implications for cybersecurity and geopolitics.
The event included remarks from NSA Deputy Director Tim Kosiba, as well as Congresswomen Deborah Ross and Valerie Foushee.
Panelists discussed how to balance the potential risks of AI with the need for the United States to remain competitive in emerging technologies and use those technologies for national defense.
Art Ehuan, executive director of Duke's cybersecurity program, said addressing the challenges posed by AI will require cooperation across sectors.
"The problems we're going to see with AI, and in particular, genetic AI, is they're going to require a whole-of-government, whole-of-society approach. Academia has to work with government, with corporations, and vice versa. There is no there's no conceivable way that any one organization can do this on their own," Ehuan said.
Kosiba said technological advances alone will not determine which organizations succeed in the next era of intelligence.
"But I can tell you that the next era of intelligence will not belong to organizations that simply have the most technology. As technology alone does not create a sustainable advantage. People do," Kosiba said.
Experts at the conference said AI is likely to be one of the most transformative technologies for cybersecurity, while emphasizing the need for safeguards as the technology develops.
SEE ALSO | New warnings about the risks of AI to humanity revive a long-running debate
The two-day conference is bringing together members of government, academia and the technology sector to discuss cybersecurity and emerging technologies.

articles.description: The Rise of Parasite Authors The Atlantic
articles.description_html: The Rise of Parasite Authors  The Atlantic
articles.article_title: The Rise of Parasite Authors
articles.heading: The Rise of Parasite Authors
articles.summary: First, AI stole their books. Now it’s stealing their readers.
articles.content:
Editor’s note: This work is part of AI Watchdog, The Atlantic’s ongoing investigation into the generative-AI industry.
Earlier this summer, Tamra Westberry received a Facebook notification that made her heart sink. A fellow author had taken to social media to endorse Westberry’s latest book, Project Erebus, after reading about it in a weekly roundup of the latest paranormal-romance releases. Independent authors like Westberry, who is based in Texas and has published dozens of books under the pen name Tara West, usually welcome an encouraging word and a bit of cross-promotion. But Westberry was dismayed. She had never heard of a book called Project Erebus. And she certainly wasn’t its author.
She looked up her author profile on Amazon, and there it was: Project Erebus, a book that featured character names she’d previously used, with a cover echoing that of her recent work. Translations were available in German, French, Italian, and Spanish. The book was a complete mystery to her, but after she read its sample pages, she suspected it was made by someone who’d used AI tools. (I ran the book’s cover and promotional blurb through Pangram, which suggested that they were completely AI-generated.)
Westberry emailed Amazon and requested that the company delink the unaffiliated books from her profile. Amazon removed the books from the platform within a week or so—but not before some of her fans purchased them, read them, and left reviews. “No real detail, characters remain undeveloped. I almost felt I was reading an essay written by a school child,” one disappointed reader wrote in a two-star review for Project Erebus on Goodreads, a literary social network owned by Amazon that had also attributed the book to West.
Across categories—fantasy, horror, even coloring books—writers say they’re seeing AI-generated listings crop up on their Amazon author pages. Some of these works are in entirely different genres from their usual work—such as a children’s series misattributed to a writer of steamy love stories—whereas others echo the subject matter or jacket designs of preexisting books. One writer reported someone sneaking in a fake edition under the listing of their real book. Because Amazon often sends out emails notifying author-page followers about new listings, these titles are able to leech a writer’s fan base, make ill-gotten revenue, and confuse readers.
AI companies pirated millions of books to train today’s most popular models, as The Atlantic has previously reported. Those models are now being used to churn out books in a matter of minutes and place them alongside books that represent years of hard work. In some cases, people go beyond mass-producing second-rate content or publishing copycats of new releases, using the names of established authors on parasitic works that feed off preexisting brands. Writers feel that they have little recourse regarding what AI models ingest, or spit out. “It’s deeply unsettling, after I spent years crafting stories and building my brand, that some no-talent grifter can bottom-feed off my fan base with AI slop,” Westberry, who’s written more than 50 books that were included in a data set used by the likes of OpenAI, Meta, and Anthropic, told me.
The parasite-creator problem is pervasive. Professors have found AI-generated academic papers published under their names; recent reporting suggests that sneaking AI-generated songs onto artists’ streaming profiles is a relatively simple move. The issue has also become endemic to Amazon, the world’s largest online book retailer, which sells hundreds of millions of books annually in the U.S. alone. The platform groups works with the same byline under a unified profile thanks to a largely automatic system. Authors say that Amazon has failed to make a concerted effort to address the phenomenon, and that the onus falls on them to monitor their pages, in a crazy-making game of whack-a-mole.
An Amazon spokesperson told me that the company does take measures to prevent, detect, and remove content that violates its guidelines, but it did not provide more details about how these systems work. “We are committed to a bookstore that readers love and publishers and authors trust, and work directly with authors to address any issues or errors affecting their accounts,” the spokesperson said.
To some degree, Amazon’s parasite-author problem predates the widespread advent of AI. A decade ago, Stephen King publicly urged the site to stop associating his own works with those of Stephen R. King., another horror author whose name was confusing fans. Such instances, however, were few and far between because of the time and effort it required to publish a title. For many writers of genre fiction, which relies on high output and familiar tropes, staying afloat means playing a volume game, releasing numerous books a year to make a living. In some cases, parasite titles can even latch on to real ones. This past July, Noelle W. Ihli published The Last to Drown, a successful thriller that’s listed at $16 for a paperback on Amazon. A romance author who writes under the name Olivia Sinclair (and who asked to keep her legal name private for work and family reasons) previously got Amazon to remove a number of suspected AI books from her profile and thought the problem had been solved until six children’s books about the adventures of cartoon turtles and foxes were listed on her page in July and August. The books, all of which contained summaries flagged as 100 percent AI-written by Pangram, were delinked from her profile earlier this month, shortly after I notified Amazon of the listings. They still remain online with Sinclair listed as the author, however, in addition to at least two seemingly duplicate copies with yet another author name.
The process of removing these works appears to be primarily complaint-driven: When Amazon does act, it does so reactively, instead of preemptively, according to Ross, the Alliance of Independent Authors’ founder. “Verified authorship at upload would end most of this overnight,” she said. Amazon did not provide a response when asked why it doesn’t verify profile identities across the board. Meanwhile, authors feel largely powerless. For self-published writers in particular, selling books on Amazon is a key aspect of their livelihood. “It’s such a catch-22,” Anna Blakely, a writer who has also run into seemingly AI-generated books on her profile. (Blakely is a pen name; I agreed to withhold the author's real name to protect her privacy.) She predicts that roughly 90 percent of her income comes from sales on the platform. “There’s really no other viable option.”
Other platforms claim to be taking a proactive approach to tackling their own versions of parasite authors. Last year, Spotify announced plans to crack down on songs—AI-generated or otherwise—erroneously appearing on artists’ profiles. The company said it would invest more in its response process for content mismatches, in addition to introducing a new impersonation policy and more recently unveiling a feature for artists to review new music on their profiles. But even these efforts appear to be ineffective: A recent 404 Media report demonstrated how AI-generated songs can still be easily uploaded to real artists’ profiles on streaming services including Spotify and Amazon Music.
Keeping an eye on this flood takes up valuable time and effort that authors could have otherwise put toward writing real books. It also adds insult to injury for writers whose books helped refine the AI tools being used to rip off their work. “It’s a devaluing of words, a devaluing of ideas, a devaluing of the accomplishment and the excitement of literature,” said Ben H. Winters, another author who has found what appears to be AI-generated work released under his name on Amazon. Like the rest of the writers I spoke with, his work surfaced in The Atlantic’s searchable database of copyrighted content that trained AI models. “They’ve assimilated all of this stuff, and now they’re spitting it back at us.”

articles.summary: One of the military's primary engine providers is also undertaking a transition at the very top, among other key promotions and hires to note.
articles.content:
Tech, growth and sales leadership moves across the market
One of the military's primary engine providers is also undertaking a transition at the very top, among other key promotions and hires to note.
Aerospace Corp.
Debra Emmons has moved up to senior vice president of the civil systems group following four years as chief technology officer at the nonprofit organization, which she first joined in 2003.
Emmons succeeds Jim Myers, who retired from Aerospace in August after five years there. Emmons’ career in space includes satellite-focused roles at Hughes Space and Communications.
Aerospace also promoted Kristin St. Peter to senior vice president, general counsel and secretary in a move to take effect Jan. 2. Aerospace operates a federally-funded research-and-development center focused on national security space.
AttainX
Peta Leonard has joined the software application development provider as vice president of artificial intelligence, a role she brings two decades of experience to.
“Peta will help shape and advance our AI vision and strategy, working closely with our teams, customers, and leadership to identify where AI can create real, measurable impact,” AttainX said in a LinkedIn post on the hire.
Leonard most recently worked as a vice president at TSPi.
Aurex
Bob Jurenko has joined the space- and missile defense-focused company as vice president of business development, a role he brings two decades of experience to.
Jurenko will oversee Aurex’s efforts to expand its opportunity set, add new customers and shape other initiatives around products and capabilities.
He most recently worked as director of hypersonic and strategic defense programs at Firefly Aerospace.
DMI
Bharat Soni has joined the technology solutions provider as vice president and general manager for its federal services unit, a role he brings three decades of experience to.
Soni will oversee DMI’s push for growth across the federal mission space, a strategy that includes generative artificial intelligence.
He most recently worked as senior director of strategic solutions at C3 AI. His career also includes roles at Guidehouse and Accenture Federal Services.
DLH
Brooke Pierce has joined the technology solutions provider as president of its health segment, a role she brings two decades of experience to.
DLH’s health business includes work in technology, scientific research, data analytics, artificial intelligence and mission support services.
Pierce most recently worked as a vice president at Leidos, where she spent seven years altogether. Her career also includes roles at Cotiviti and ARDX.
Draganfly Defense USA
AJ Pasagian has joined the drone systems and solution provider’s U.S. defense subsidiary as president, a role he brings 35 years of Marine Corps service experience to.
Pasagian’s career includes an assignment as commanding general for Marine Corps Systems Command, where he led a team of 2,400 personnel and was its acquisition decision authority.
“AJ joins Draganfly at an important time as we continue to expand our U.S. defense operations and respond to growing demand for trusted, North American-developed unmanned systems,” Draganfly said in a LinkedIn post on his new role.
Herrick Technology Laboratories
Tom Cece has moved up to vice president of engineering at this maker of software-defined radios, which he first joined in 2016.
“Tom will lead our engineering department, where he will accelerate innovation and spearhead the development of advanced hardware and software architectures designed to protect our warfighters and give our defense and government partners a definitive edge in contested spectrum environments,” HTL said in a LinkedIn post on his new role.
HTL credits Cece with helping advance its product lines that include the radios, as well as direction-finding antennas and other communication solutions.
Horizon3
Chad Keefer has joined the cybersecurity company as vice president of federal sales, a role he brings 24 years of industry experience to.
Keefer will lead Horizon3’s go-to-market strategy centered around its autonomous penetration testing platform, which is designed to help operators find security issues and close attack paths.
He most recently worked as head of U.S. federal at Infoblox. His career also includes roles at Appian and Forescout Technologies.
Lentech
Ryan Rohr has joined the employee-owned contractor as chief growth officer, a role he brings 19 years of experience to.
Rohr will oversee Lentech’s overall efforts to advance its market position, expand customer relationships and increase partnerships. Lentech announced the hire of Rohr six months after Rose Allen joined the company as CEO.
He most recently worked as chief strategy officer at Thomson Reuters Special Services, the global tech company’s subsidiary for the U.S. government market.
Reconview
Gary Noel has joined the mobile surveillance solutions provider as vice president of federal and international sales after eight years at Lockheed Martin.
“Gary will drive Reconview’s growth across federal government initiatives and lead our international sales strategy, bringing our advanced AI-powered security and surveillance solutions to global partners and public-sector clients,” Reconview said in a LinkedIn post on his new role.
Noel’s tenure at Lockheed included separate stints as manager of international government affairs and business development, plus chief of staff for international business development.
RTX
Jill Albertelli will move up to president of the company’s Pratt & Whitney engine manufacturing segment on Jan. 1, when she will succeed the retiring Shane Eddy.
Albertelli has been with Pratt & Whitney for three decades and currently works as president of the military engine business. Her career has included roles involving engineering, manufacturing, supply chain, quality, commercial programs, sales and strategy.
Eddy has worked at Pratt & Whitney for four decades and will support the company as an adviser between Jan. 1 and March, when he will retire.
Sabel Systems
Mini Polaski has joined this provider of engineering services as senior vice president and general manager for its aerospace digital acceleration business unit, a role she brings two decades of experience to.
Polaski will lead Sabel’s efforts to scale across the Air Force market and build on its portfolio of product lifecycle management support.
Polaski most recently spent five years at Leidos as chief engineer. Her career also includes roles at Northrop Grumman and Boeing.
Sabel has also hired Alexis Wenzel as vice president of business development for the Air Force account. She most recently was a BD director at BAE Systems Inc. and before that held a similar role at ICF.
Scope Infotech
Kathryn Wetherby has joined the software engineering services provider as chief strategy officer, a role she brings 25 years of health technology experience to.
Wetherby will work with Scope Infotech CEO Riyaz Momin on efforts related to the company’s market position, operational maturity and growth planning.
Wetherby most recently spent 10 years at the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, including as acting director of its marketplace IT group.
Significance Inc.
Brad Zwirschitz has joined the professional services provider as chief growth officer, a role involving revenue growth and market expansion initiatives.
Zwirschitz will oversee Significance’s functions in business development, capture strategy, partnerships and go-to-market efforts. He most recently worked as president of Main Sail.
Mary Ahern Snyder started Significance in 2014 and has led it ever since as president and CEO.
T-Mobile
Stacy Schwartz has joined the wireless carrier as vice president of its government business, a role she brings three decades of experience.
Schwartz’s career includes 25 years at AT&T, where she was a vice president in its public sector unit. She has also led the public sector unit at RingCentral.
George Fischer, an executive vice president at T-Mobile’s business group, announced the hire of Schwartz in a LinkedIn post.
American Systems
Christopher “Chris” Carson has joined the board of directors as an independent member at the employee-owned contractor, where he will also chair its audit and finance committee.
Carson moves into the seat formerly held by Barry Broadus, who was a member for nine years. Broadus is the former ICF chief financial officer who retired in the spring after four years in that role.
Carson is a four-decade market veteran helped found the government practices at Argy and then at BDO, which acquired Argy in 2012. He is also a former chief financial officer for Ultra Safe Nuclear Corp.
Riverside Research
David Deptula and Stacey Dixon have joined the board of trustees at the nonprofit science firm, which announced its hire of new CEO Tom Lash earlier this month.
Deptula is a retired Air Force lieutenant general who retired in 2010 after a 34-year career in service that culminated with four years as deputy chief of staff for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.
Dixon is a former principal deputy director of national intelligence, the second-highest ranking official in the intelligence community. She also served in leadership roles at the Intelligence Advanced Research Projects Activity and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency.

Eddy has worked at Pratt & Whitney for four decades and will support the company as an adviser between Jan. 1 and March, when he will retire.

Sabel Systems

Mini Polaski has joined this provider of engineering services as senior vice president and general manager for its aerospace digital acceleration business unit, a role she brings two decades of experience to.

Polaski will lead Sabel’s efforts to scale across the Air Force market and build on its portfolio of product lifecycle management support.

Polaski most recently spent five years at Leidos as chief engineer. Her career also includes roles at Northrop Grumman and Boeing.

Sabel has also hired Alexis Wenzel as vice president of business development for the Air Force account. She most recently was a BD director at BAE Systems Inc. and before that held a similar role at ICF.

Scope Infotech

Kathryn Wetherby has joined the software engineering services provider as chief strategy officer, a role she brings 25 years of health technology experience to.

Wetherby will work with Scope Infotech CEO Riyaz Momin on efforts related to the company’s market position, operational maturity and growth planning.

Wetherby most recently spent 10 years at the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, including as acting director of its marketplace IT group.

Significance Inc.

Brad Zwirschitz has joined the professional services provider as chief growth officer, a role involving revenue growth and market expansion initiatives.

Zwirschitz will oversee Significance’s functions in business development, capture strategy, partnerships and go-to-market efforts. He most recently worked as president of Main Sail.

Mary Ahern Snyder started Significance in 2014 and has led it ever since as president and CEO.

T-Mobile

Stacy Schwartz has joined the wireless carrier as vice president of its government business, a role she brings three decades of experience.

Schwartz’s career includes 25 years at AT&T, where she was a vice president in its public sector unit. She has also led the public sector unit at RingCentral.

George Fischer, an executive vice president at T-Mobile’s business group, announced the hire of Schwartz in a LinkedIn post.

American Systems

Christopher “Chris” Carson has joined the board of directors as an independent member at the employee-owned contractor, where he will also chair its audit and finance committee.

Carson moves into the seat formerly held by Barry Broadus, who was a member for nine years. Broadus is the former ICF chief financial officer who retired in the spring after four years in that role.

Carson is a four-decade market veteran helped found the government practices at Argy and then at BDO, which acquired Argy in 2012. He is also a former chief financial officer for Ultra Safe Nuclear Corp.

Riverside Research

David Deptula and Stacey Dixon have joined the board of trustees at the nonprofit science firm, which announced its hire of new CEO Tom Lash earlier this month.

Deptula is a retired Air Force lieutenant general who retired in 2010 after a 34-year career in service that culminated with four years as deputy chief of staff for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.

Dixon is a former principal deputy director of national intelligence, the second-highest ranking official in the intelligence community. She also served in leadership roles at the Intelligence Advanced Research Projects Activity and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency.

articles.article_title: K-Love Names Dee Sethmajhi as Chief Technology Officer - Radio World
articles.heading: K-Love Names Dee Sethmajhi as Chief Technology Officer
articles.summary: K-Love has announced the appointment of Debashree “Dee” Sethmajhi as the ministry’s chief technology officer.
articles.content:
K-Love has announced the appointment of Debashree “Dee” Sethmajhi as the organization’s chief technology officer.
Effective Sept. 21, Sethmajhi will lead technology strategy across broadcast infrastructure, engineering, digital products, data and cybersecurity for the ministry that includes the K-Love and Air 1 networks, according to a release.
Sethmajhi succeeds Ed Rice, who was K-Love’s chief technology officer up until this past March.
She will report to CEO Tom Stultz.
“Dee brings a rare combination to this role: deep technical capability, an entrepreneurial spirit and a genuine heart for ministry,” Stultz said in making the announcement.
Sethmajhi’s appointment comes during a period of technical transformation for the ministry. K-Love completed its migration from satellite to IP-based program delivery earlier this year, a story Radio World will feature later this fall.
In the release, K-Love said it continues to expand its broadcast footprint toward a presence in every top 50 U.S. market. Currently, the ministry serves listeners through approximately 1,100 U.S. signals.
Sethmajhi brings approximately 15 years of experience in technology, including time at Oracle, where she held product strategy roles focused on global cloud platforms and enterprise systems. She later co-founded The Stability App, an AI-powered digital health platform she designed and built as its chief technology officer.
Through Every Nation Churches & Ministries, she has served on mission teams across Africa, Europe and South America, working with university students and local church leaders.
