The team also installed a pair of cameras over the entire setup that provides a birds-eye view of the tabletop experiment. Finally, they developed a “software stack,” or a set of programs that enables the robot to navigate through every step of setting up and continuously tuning an experiment. These steps include recognizing a specific component, knowing how to safely approach and pick it up, where to move it, and how to avoid collisions with other parts of the experiment along the way.

Finally, they designed a simple virtual user interface to allow an experimenter to remotely direct the robot. For instance, when a user drags the icon for a mirror from one spot to another, and clicks a button to confirm, the robot responds by picking up the actual mirror and placing it down at the corresponding location on the table.

As a demonstration, they directed the robot to assemble various components into a laser cavity. A laser cavity consists of two mirrors arranged on either side of a crystal. When a beam of light is shone into the setup, it pings back and forth between the two mirrors. With each pass, the light also passes through the crystal, which amplifies the light’s intensity, to a point that whatever light escapes, is intense enough to form a laser.

“We wanted to pick a demonstration in optics that’s reasonably challenging,” says co-lead author Seou Choi, a graduate student in electrical engineering and computer science. “This is not something a new trainee could do in an afternoon. It requires a lot of alignment and component experience.”

In the end, the robot successfully built a functional laser cavity by autonomously carrying out 50 maneuvers, all within 30 minutes. When the researchers introduced physical disturbances to the setup, such as randomly moving a component on the table, the system automatically readjusted components to maintain the laser’s intensity.

“Even tiny vibrations or temperature changes can degrade an optics experiment,” Vaidya says. “An autonomous lab could continuously monitor its own performance and repair the alignment before valuable data is lost.”

The researchers envision that robotic labs like theirs could be paired with a nearby library of physical components that another robot could fetch and deliver to a tabletop robot to arrange into an experiment. Such a system could work to build and run experiments, then break them down and set up new ones on demand, or continuously run an experiment that requires active 24/7 monitoring.

“A system like this could help industry test prototypes faster, for everything from cameras and displays to solar cells and AR/VR goggles,” Vaidya says.

For their part, the researchers are applying the new robot lab to test promising carbon-capture materials. By shining light with specific properties at these materials, they can get information about how a material absorbs carbon dioxide.

“Experimental optics is the backbone of many important fields,” Vaidya says. “Our work takes the first step toward optical labs that can operate faster, more reliably, and without manual intervention in a domain that demands extreme precision and diversity of experimental setups.”

Self-Recovery of Precision Optical Systems”

articles.summary: A bacterial infection is wiping out Florida's citrus trees. Growers hope a rootstock developed with gene-editing technology could keep the disease at bay.
articles.content:
Environment Story Of The Day NPR hide caption

Environment

Environment

By

Catherine Welch

Could genetically modified trees protect Florida's citrus industry?

- Download

- Embed < iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5966501/nx-s1-9929215" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">

- Transcript

Guy Davies, an inspector for the Florida Division of Plant Industry, checks an orange tree for the insect Asian citrus psyllid that carries the bacterium causing disease, "citrus greening," from tree to tree on May 13, 2013, in Fort Pierce, Florida. Joe Raedle/Getty Images hide caption

Citrus growers in Florida are planting new trees that have been modified using gene-editing technology to ward against the lethal citrus greening disease.

Growers have tried everything from tents to sprays to protect citrus trees from the bacterial infection, which has killed off many of Florida's citrus trees and led to a massive decline in the amount of citrus the state produces. Now growers are waiting to see if the genetic modifications, which the Environmental Protection Agency approved earlier this year, will keep the trees alive.

Citrus greening arrived in Florida in 2005. The disease is spread by a tiny winged insect called an Asian citrus psyllid. It attacks the trees' immune system, so they can't fight the infection. Once infected, a tree produces bitter, discolored fruit and usually dies a few years later. There's no cure.

Ron English's family ran a citrus business in Valrico, Fla., for generations until greening wiped it out, forcing them to close in 2015.

"We had some of the best looking groves around, and all the time and effort that we had spent, you just see it diminish right before you," English said.

In the late 1990s, before citrus greening arrived in Florida, growers were shipping out around 300 million boxes of fruit each season, said Matt Joyner, CEO of Florida Citrus Mutual, a trade association that represents citrus growers. By comparison, they shipped a little more than 15 million boxes during this year's season, which ended in June, he said.

Soilcea, a Tampa-based company, used CRISPR gene-editing technology to design a rootstock that resists greening. Known as CarriCea T1, it keeps a tree's immune system working, allowing growers to rely less on insecticides.

Focusing on the rootstock to fight the bacteria is key, said Soilcea CEO Yianni Lagos. He explained that although the first sign that a tree is infected is yellowing leaves, "before you even have symptoms, half the root system is already dead."

Lagos is now waiting to see what happens when the rootstock is grafted onto trees and planted.

Ron English shows off citrus trees planted with the CarriCea T1 rootstock at Soilcea's test field in Thonotosassa, Fla. Catherine Welch hide caption

In a SoilCea test field, the results so far are promising. Trees with the CarriCea T1 rootstock are taller and greener.

English cares for the dozens of trees in the test field that have the modified rootstock. They were planted last summer next to trees without it.

"That's the CarriCea rootstock — see how big the leaves have filled out," English said, pointing to a tree with the modification.

The smaller tree next to it does not have the CarriCea T1 rootstock. It's smaller with yellower leaves.

"See the discoloration, that's the disease already working through the tree," he said.

The real test for the CarriCea T1 tree will be the fruit, which takes years to show up — not only how it grows, but also how it tastes.

"The data suggests it's gonna work, but until you have a 10-year-old tree, you don't know how the tree is going to perform," Lagos said.

articles.title: Bethany Children's Health Center to feature assistive technology, adapted sports at resource fair
articles.description: Bethany Children's Health Center to feature assistive technology, adapted sports at resource fair kgou.org
articles.description_html: Bethany Children's Health Center to feature assistive technology, adapted sports at resource fair  kgou.org
articles.article_title: Bethany Children's Health Center to feature assistive technology, adapted sports at resource fair
articles.heading: Bethany Children's Health Center to feature assistive technology, adapted sports at resource fair
articles.summary: The free event was born out of a desire to meet the needs of children with physical and intellectual disabilities and their families.
articles.content:
Bethany Children's Health Center is hosting its third "All Abilities Resource Fair" from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m. on Saturday.
The free event was born out of a desire to meet the needs of children with physical and intellectual disabilities and their families. The health center wanted to help them access hands-on experiences with equipment and assistive technology, and learn how their children can participate in adapted sports.
“Care is beyond just a diagnosis or a treatment. It impacts their whole life – so their daily living tasks, their mobility, their participation in social aspects,” said Darcey Riemer, a physical therapist assistant and assistive technology professional. “So these tools can help them improve their quality of life and independence.”
The fair will feature positioning and mobility equipment, including wheelchairs, gate trainers, adaptive strollers and bathing equipment. Stephanie Delk, a physical therapist assistant and assistive technology equipment technician, said participants can see how they work and practice folding them down.
Delk said something as simple as bathing their child can seem daunting for these families. This equipment helps make ordinary tasks more manageable.
She added that the event is casual, and nothing will be available for purchase.
“I think having all the equipment in one place for people is a huge opportunity,” Delk said.
The fair will highlight adapted sports with Oklahoma Youth Parasports athletes. Wheelchair tune-ups and tours of the health center’s Smart Home will also be available. The space shows how homes can integrate technology to support safe and independent living.
The Saturday event isn’t just for families who have children with disabilities. Bethany Children’s is also inviting pediatric therapists, special education teachers and other professionals who support children with disabilities.
“I hope that people walk away with more confidence in their abilities to care for their kids and to give their kids more independence in life,” Delk said. “Just because our kids have something like a disability that might hold them back – I don't want it to hold them back. I want them to see that assistive technology is for everyone.”
Interested Oklahomans can register online.

articles.title: How technology can help shape the future of mental health treatment
articles.description: How technology can help shape the future of mental health treatment wellcome.org
articles.description_html: How technology can help shape the future of mental health treatment  wellcome.org
articles.article_title: How technology can help shape the future of mental health treatment | Wellcome
articles.heading: How technology can help shape the future of mental health treatment
articles.summary: Explore how digital mental health technologies could expand access to safe, effective and personalised treatment, and the research Wellcome supports.
articles.content:
How technology can help shape the future of mental health treatment
Technology is embedded in almost every aspect of our lives, including how we look after our mental health. People are increasingly turning to digital tools for support, from mental health apps to AI-powered chatbots, however, in healthcare settings, digital tools remain relatively uncommon. They have the potential to expand access to support, personalise treatment and help shape the future of mental healthcare.
Technology is now embedded in almost every aspect of our lives, including how we look after our mental health. Around the world, people are increasingly turning to digital tools for support, from mental health apps to AI-powered chatbots. Emerging evidence suggests many people are already using large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT to discuss their mental health concerns.
Yet digital mental health technologies remain relatively uncommon in healthcare settings compared with established treatments such as talking therapies and medicines. When people hear the term, they may think of wellness apps offering meditation exercises or online mood tracking. In reality, digital mental health interventions are part of a diverse and rapidly evolving field that includes tools designed to prevent, diagnose, monitor and treat mental health conditions. They have the potential to expand access to support, personalise treatment and help shape the future of mental healthcare. Better mental health care means having more useful options. Digital approaches can sit alongside medicines, therapy and other forms of support, giving people and services greater choice in how care is delivered.
What is the problem we are trying to solve?
More than one billion people worldwide live with a mental health condition, yet access to effective support remains a major global challenge: the global median number of mental health workers is just 13 per 100,000 people. In England, at the end of June 2026, more than 2.37m people had an open referral with mental health services, and patient experience has declined in recent years.
The scale of unmet need can seem overwhelming. But technology offers an opportunity to find new ways to provide effective mental health support to people who are not well-served by existing services.
At Wellcome, we want to move beyond recognising the scale of the problem to championing using technology for the things it excels at: more personalised, flexible, scalable and easily accessible care. We are interested in how technology can help people access effective care in ways that work for them.
We want to address two key challenges. First, how can we develop effective interventions that can reach far more people than traditional models of care alone? Second, how can we generate the practical evidence that health systems need to confidently adopt and integrate new innovations into routine care?
What are digital interventions and how can they help?
Digital mental health technologies, often called digital interventions, can support the prevention, assessment, treatment and ongoing management of mental health conditions. Incorporating digital interventions into mental health care gives people more choice over how, when and where they access support.
For some people, digital support may be easier to access than traditional services. It can help overcome barriers related to distance, cost, stigma and mobility, while offering more flexible and personalised ways to engage with care. Someone might complete a course of therapy from home, use an app between appointments to practise techniques they learned in therapy or track how they are feeling throughout the week to share with their clinician, and help guide treatment decisions.
Digital mental health technologies take many forms, including:
- internet and app-delivered therapy, such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)
- structured therapeutic programmes delivered online or via mobile app
- wearables: devices that monitor physiological and behavioural signals that may be relevant to mental health
- internet and app-based interventions to support mental health that can be used independently or alongside support from a healthcare professional
- AI-enabled tools such as chatbots trained to have conversations about mental health and deliver dialogue-based interventions
- teletherapy platforms: virtual video or text-based sessions connecting people with trained clinicians
The important question is whether these options help people get effective support when they need it. Digital interventions will not replace mental health professionals entirely or solve every challenge facing mental health services. However, they could become an important part of the future mental health toolkit, helping more people access effective support while offering new ways to personalise care and expanding the options people have for treatment.
What is needed to realise the full potential of digital mental health technology?
Realising the full potential of digital mental health technologies will require more than supporting the development of innovative new treatments. While research and innovation in this field are advancing rapidly, many promising interventions never reach the people who could benefit from them. To translate innovation into real-world impact, governments, health services, researchers, funders and companies must work together to design solutions that meet people's needs, build robust evidence that they are effective and safe and create pathways for implementation at scale.
Three factors will be particularly important:
Embedding lived experience
Like any mental health intervention, digital tools are best and most effective when they are developed with the people they are intended to support. Involving people with lived experience throughout design, development, evaluation and implementation can help ensure interventions meet real needs effectively and are accessible, engaging and culturally relevant. It can also help address barriers related to stigma, language, disability and differing levels of digital confidence, increasing the likelihood that innovations will be adopted and used in practice.
For example, SloMo is a blended therapy for people living with psychosis that combines traditional in-person sessions with a mobile app that supports people between therapy sessions. It was created by lived experience experts, clinical researchers, clinical psychologists, designers and software developers. Its innovative design, based on bubbles, was created by lived experience experts and helps slow down thinking to support better wellbeing and reduce paranoia.
Amy Grant
Experiencing paranoia is like a beehive. Busy, noisy, unwanted thoughts racing around. Some paranoid thoughts are common and most people will experience them at some point. Like, "everyone is watching me". But sometimes they can become overwhelming. Constantly buzzing around in your head. At times the worries can feel silly, childish or embarrassing, but in the moment the evidence is too compelling to ignore. This was my experience. I'm Amy, resident zine maker and lived experience researcher. I'm part of a team who are trying to help people overcome these types of worries with a new therapy called SloMo.
Amy Hardy
I've always been very passionate about working in mental health. I think the mind is fascinating and particularly in terms of psychosis. People with psychosis were more likely to have experienced trauma and are more likely to drop out of therapy. The challenge was how do we create a therapy that is more appealing and easier to use that would improve access, experience and outcomes.
Chris
My contribution to this project stems from me suffering with paranoia, anxiety and feeling overwhelmed. Whether it's on the bus or in the queue in the supermarket, or just in a local park.
Amy Hardy
Paranoia is one of the most common difficulties in psychosis. Our ability to go on our gut instincts to make snap decisions. And that's really important because we need to be able to do that to function in life. But if we rely on that too much, it can cause problems. What we set out to do was to try and develop a digitally supported therapy, synchronised with a mobile app for paranoia in psychosis. To support people to learn to slow down their thinking.
Chris
The challenge was for all of us to agree that the app is going to be designed in a way that's going to be suitable for everyone.
Amy Hardy
Wellcome have supported this work. And what they allowed us to do was to put together an interdisciplinary team.
Anna Wojdecka
The key challenge of the project was finding the right analogy that will allow us to visualise thoughts. People who experienced such an emotional distress were finding it very difficult to think with abstract concepts, such as thoughts, while they were experiencing distress.
Chris
We didn't want it to look too dull, but we didn't want it to look too flashy either. If the app was a bit too tricky or flashy to use, that could heighten the anxiety.
Anna Wojdecka
To our surprise, it turned out that the analogy of thoughts as bubbles really resonated with people.
Amy Grant
Just like how speech bubbles let you see what a comic character might be thinking. SloMo uses bubbles to help you write out and see your own thoughts. It gives you a new perspective. You start to ask yourself different questions like, "why did I think that?"
Chris
The bubble's perfect and it can spin as well. If your thoughts are really running, you can slow down the bubble.
Amy Grant
When I did SloMo therapy, writing in the bubbles helped me to slow down and process the situations I'm in. Because I was thinking more consciously.
Amy Hardy
We found that SloMo reduced paranoia, but importantly, we also found that it improved people's confidence, wellbeing, and quality of life. Encouragingly, we found that SloMo was equally effective regardless of people's backgrounds.
Anna Wojdecka
They felt heard. They started going out of the home, something that was really out of reach for them before. Yeah, it was very powerful to hear that.
Amy Grant
The number one thing SloMo has done for me is build confidence. From that, other areas in my life have improved, such as my relationships, socialising, and pursuing other goals. I hope SloMo will reach the people who usually slip through the net and give them the confidence to achieve what they want in life.
Amy Hardy
Digital health has significant potential to revolutionise mental health care. So we're really encouraged and we're very keen to move into scaling up SloMo across other NHS trusts in the UK.
Chris
I'm definitely proud, 100%. I personally do see the difference it can and will make.
Collaborating across sectors
Companies play an important role in helping promising interventions reach people. They bring expertise in user experience design, marketing, sustainable business planning and scaling digital services, helping to bridge the gap between research and real-world impact. Partnerships between researchers, people with lived experience, health services and companies can help bridge the gap between promising research and care, ensuring evidence-based interventions are sustainable and supporting their delivery at scale.
For example, Wellcome’s funding call brought research and lived experience expertise together with companies and not-for-profits to fund treatments of anxiety, depression and psychosis that had a clear route to scale-up.
Considering underserved groups
People should be able to trust that digital care is safe, effective and designed around their needs. That means considering who may be unintentionally excluded, protecting people's data and making sure people can access human support when they need it.
For example, Wysa, a chatbot-based mobile app that uses principles from cognitive behavioural therapy, is already being used in some UK services. Wellcome is funding research with Wysa to adapt it for adolescent girls in rural India, a group with extremely limited access to mental health treatments, focusing on designing for shared devices, unstable or low bandwidth internet connections and cultural barriers to care. The team will then evaluate its effectiveness, helping generate the evidence needed to understand where and for whom such tools can be most beneficial.
What is Wellcome doing?
Wellcome is championing the development of safe and inclusive digital mental health technologies that can expand access to support, improve treatment and strengthen mental health systems, as well as supporting the generation of evidence of how well they work and who they work best for. We believe these innovations could play an important role in shaping the future of mental health care.
We have brought together multidisciplinary partners to help promising digital tools and treatments reach more people with mental health problems.
Led by Prof Cathy Creswell, the University of Oxford is adapting and evaluating Online Support and Intervention in collaboration with Koa Health. Online Support and Intervention is a therapist-guided, parent-led platform for treating anxiety in children aged 5 to 12, already in use in the UK, and will be tested across diverse settings including the Philippines, Chile and Thailand.
Led by Chaitali Sinha, Wysa Ltd is adapting and evaluating its AI-enabled chatbot-based mental health app to improve access to effective support for adolescent girls experiencing symptoms of anxiety or depression in rural India.
Led by Prof Dixon Chibanda, the University of Zimbabwe in collaboration with Inuka is testing a chat-based platform that enables lay health workers to deliver problem-solving and behavioural support to people experiencing depression in Zimbabwe.
Led by Dr Matteo Cella, King’s College London with HelloSelf is developing and testing an AI-enabled chatbot to support the delivery of CIRCuiTS, a digital version of cognitive remediation for young people experiencing psychosis and depression.
Led by Prof Mario Alvarez-Jimenez, the University of Melbourne with Orygen is developing and evaluating MOST-Nexus, an AI-enabled digital mental health platform that provides personalised, adaptive support for young people across multiple continents.

Incorporating digital interventions into mental health care gives people more choice over how, when and where they access support.

For some people, digital support may be easier to access than traditional services. It can help overcome barriers related to distance, cost, stigma and mobility, while offering more flexible and personalised ways to engage with care. Someone might complete a course of therapy from home, use an app between appointments to practise techniques they learned in therapy or track how they are feeling throughout the week to share with their clinician, and help guide treatment decisions.

Digital mental health technologies take many forms, including:

  • internet and app-delivered therapy, such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)
  • structured therapeutic programmes delivered online or via mobile app
  • wearables: devices that monitor physiological and behavioural signals that may be relevant to mental health
  • internet and app-based interventions to support mental health that can be used independently or alongside support from a healthcare professional
  • AI-enabled tools such as chatbots trained to have conversations about mental health and deliver dialogue-based interventions
  • teletherapy platforms: virtual video or text-based sessions connecting people with trained clinicians

The important question is whether these options help people get effective support when they need it. Digital interventions will not replace mental health professionals entirely or solve every challenge facing mental health services. However, they could become an important part of the future mental health toolkit, helping more people access effective support while offering new ways to personalise care and expanding the options people have for treatment.

Qi Yang / Getty Images

What is needed to realise the full potential of digital mental health technology?

Realising the full potential of digital mental health technologies will require more than supporting the development of innovative new treatments. While research and innovation in this field are advancing rapidly, many promising interventions never reach the people who could benefit from them. To translate innovation into real-world impact, governments, health services, researchers, funders and companies must work together to design solutions that meet people's needs, build robust evidence that they are effective and safe and create pathways for implementation at scale.

Three factors will be particularly important:

Embedding lived experience

Like any mental health intervention, digital tools are best and most effective when they are developed with the people they are intended to support. Involving people with lived experience throughout design, development, evaluation and implementation can help ensure interventions meet real needs effectively and are accessible, engaging and culturally relevant. It can also help address barriers related to stigma, language, disability and differing levels of digital confidence, increasing the likelihood that innovations will be adopted and used in practice.

For example, SloMo is a blended therapy for people living with psychosis that combines traditional in-person sessions with a mobile app that supports people between therapy sessions. It was created by lived experience experts, clinical researchers, clinical psychologists, designers and software developers. Its innovative design, based on bubbles, was created by lived experience experts and helps slow down thinking to support better wellbeing and reduce paranoia.

Pressing play on the video above will set a third-party cookie. Please read our cookie policy for more information.

“I just want it to help other people as much as it has me.” – Lived experience experts and researchers talk about developing the SloMo app.

Amy Grant
Experiencing paranoia is like a beehive. Busy, noisy, unwanted thoughts racing around. Some paranoid thoughts are common and most people will experience them at some point. Like, "everyone is watching me". But sometimes they can become overwhelming. Constantly buzzing around in your head. At times the worries can feel silly, childish or embarrassing, but in the moment the evidence is too compelling to ignore. This was my experience. I'm Amy, resident zine maker and lived experience researcher. I'm part of a team who are trying to help people overcome these types of worries with a new therapy called SloMo.

Amy Hardy
I've always been very passionate about working in mental health. I think the mind is fascinating and particularly in terms of psychosis. People with psychosis were more likely to have experienced trauma and are more likely to drop out of therapy. The challenge was how do we create a therapy that is more appealing and easier to use that would improve access, experience and outcomes.

Chris
My contribution to this project stems from me suffering with paranoia, anxiety and feeling overwhelmed. Whether it's on the bus or in the queue in the supermarket, or just in a local park.

Amy Hardy
Paranoia is one of the most common difficulties in psychosis. Our ability to go on our gut instincts to make snap decisions. And that's really important because we need to be able to do that to function in life. But if we rely on that too much, it can cause problems. What we set out to do was to try and develop a digitally supported therapy, synchronised with a mobile app for paranoia in psychosis. To support people to learn to slow down their thinking.

Chris
The challenge was for all of us to agree that the app is going to be designed in a way that's going to be suitable for everyone.

Amy Hardy
Wellcome have supported this work. And what they allowed us to do was to put together an interdisciplinary team.

Anna Wojdecka
The key challenge of the project was finding the right analogy that will allow us to visualise thoughts. People who experienced such an emotional distress were finding it very difficult to think with abstract concepts, such as thoughts, while they were experiencing distress.

Chris
We didn't want it to look too dull, but we didn't want it to look too flashy either. If the app was a bit too tricky or flashy to use, that could heighten the anxiety.

Anna Wojdecka
To our surprise, it turned out that the analogy of thoughts as bubbles really resonated with people.

Amy Grant
Just like how speech bubbles let you see what a comic character might be thinking. SloMo uses bubbles to help you write out and see your own thoughts. It gives you a new perspective. You start to ask yourself different questions like, "why did I think that?"

Chris
The bubble's perfect and it can spin as well. If your thoughts are really running, you can slow down the bubble.

Amy Grant
When I did SloMo therapy, writing in the bubbles helped me to slow down and process the situations I'm in. Because I was thinking more consciously.

Amy Hardy
We found that SloMo reduced paranoia, but importantly, we also found that it improved people's confidence, wellbeing, and quality of life. Encouragingly, we found that SloMo was equally effective regardless of people's backgrounds.

Anna Wojdecka
They felt heard. They started going out of the home, something that was really out of reach for them before. Yeah, it was very powerful to hear that.

Amy Grant
The number one thing SloMo has done for me is build confidence. From that, other areas in my life have improved, such as my relationships, socialising, and pursuing other goals. I hope SloMo will reach the people who usually slip through the net and give them the confidence to achieve what they want in life.

Amy Hardy
Digital health has significant potential to revolutionise mental health care. So we're really encouraged and we're very keen to move into scaling up SloMo across other NHS trusts in the UK.

Chris
I'm definitely proud, 100%. I personally do see the difference it can and will make.

Collaborating across sectors

Companies play an important role in helping promising interventions reach people. They bring expertise in user experience design, marketing, sustainable business planning and scaling digital services, helping to bridge the gap between research and real-world impact. Partnerships between researchers, people with lived experience, health services and companies can help bridge the gap between promising research and care, ensuring evidence-based interventions are sustainable and supporting their delivery at scale.

For example, Wellcome’s funding call brought research and lived experience expertise together with companies and not-for-profits to fund treatments of anxiety, depression and psychosis that had a clear route to scale-up.

Considering underserved groups

People should be able to trust that digital care is safe, effective and designed around their needs. That means considering who may be unintentionally excluded, protecting people's data and making sure people can access human support when they need it.

For example, Wysa, a chatbot-based mobile app that uses principles from cognitive behavioural therapy, is already being used in some UK services. Wellcome is funding research with Wysa to adapt it for adolescent girls in rural India, a group with extremely limited access to mental health treatments, focusing on designing for shared devices, unstable or low bandwidth internet connections and cultural barriers to care. The team will then evaluate its effectiveness, helping generate the evidence needed to understand where and for whom such tools can be most beneficial.

What is Wellcome doing?

Wellcome is championing the development of safe and inclusive digital mental health technologies that can expand access to support, improve treatment and strengthen mental health systems, as well as supporting the generation of evidence of how well they work and who they work best for. We believe these innovations could play an important role in shaping the future of mental health care.

We have brought together multidisciplinary partners to help promising digital tools and treatments reach more people with mental health problems.

Led by Prof Cathy Creswell, the University of Oxford is adapting and evaluating Online Support and Intervention in collaboration with Koa Health. Online Support and Intervention is a therapist-guided, parent-led platform for treating anxiety in children aged 5 to 12, already in use in the UK, and will be tested across diverse settings including the Philippines, Chile and Thailand.

Led by Chaitali Sinha, Wysa Ltd is adapting and evaluating its AI-enabled chatbot-based mental health app to improve access to effective support for adolescent girls experiencing symptoms of anxiety or depression in rural India.

Led by Prof Dixon Chibanda, the University of Zimbabwe in collaboration with Inuka is testing a chat-based platform that enables lay health workers to deliver problem-solving and behavioural support to people experiencing depression in Zimbabwe.

Led by Dr Matteo Cella, King’s College London with HelloSelf is developing and testing an AI-enabled chatbot to support the delivery of CIRCuiTS, a digital version of cognitive remediation for young people experiencing psychosis and depression.

Led by Prof Mario Alvarez-Jimenez, the University of Melbourne with Orygen is developing and evaluating MOST-Nexus, an AI-enabled digital mental health platform that provides personalised, adaptive support for young people across multiple continents.

articles.content:
Pearson Acquires Assessment Technology Provider, ITS
Strengthens global assessment and verification capabilities with proven technology and talent
LONDON, Sept. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Pearson (FTSE: PSON.L), the world's lifelong learning company, today announced it has acquired ITS, a Baltimore, Maryland-based assessment technology company specializing in the management, delivery and reporting of assessment programs. The acquisition strengthens Pearson's core assessment and verification capabilities with proven technology and talent; expanding growth opportunities in professional assessment and related markets worldwide.
ITS's enterprise offerings complement Pearson's existing strengths and broaden the range of assessment services available to customers, including remote testing and proctoring, performance-based assessment, and continuous certification.
Following the acquisition, ITS will become part of Pearson Professional Assessments, building on an existing and successful longstanding commercial relationship between ITS and Pearson.
Art Valentine, president of Assessment & Qualifications at Pearson said, "Organizations are turning to Pearson for assessment and verification they can trust. We know ITS well and value the proven technology, deep industry knowledge, and dedicated team they bring. This acquisition strengthens Pearson's role as verified skills and assessment infrastructure and supports our long-term assessment strategy."
Pat Ward, president of ITS said, "Joining Pearson is a natural next step for a partnership that has driven innovation in professional assessment since 2009. It has been an amazing journey as ITS has grown from a startup to hosting some of the world's largest and most prestigious tests. Pearson and ITS share the same values, a vision for how AI can improve assessment, and commitment to protecting the integrity and quality of assessment for customers. I'm excited about what we achieve together."
About Pearson
At Pearson, our purpose is simple: to help people realize the life they imagine through learning. We believe that every learning opportunity is a chance for a personal breakthrough. That's why our c. 18,000 Pearson employees are committed to creating vibrant and enriching learning experiences designed for real-life impact. We are the world's lifelong learning company, serving customers in nearly 200 countries with digital content, assessments, qualifications, and data. For us, learning isn't just what we do. It's who we are. Visit us at plc.pearson.com
About ITS
Internet Testing Systems (ITS) is a leader in assessment technology, helping testing and certification organizations build, deliver, and evolve their assessment programs. With decades of experience and a comprehensive suite of solutions spanning the assessment lifecycle, ITS combines proven technology with deep industry expertise to support secure test delivery, practice and preparation, certification maintenance, remote proctoring, test development, and AI-powered assessment. ITS partners with organizations around the world to solve complex assessment challenges, modernize programs, and create better experiences for candidates and professionals. Learn more at testsys.com.

The last week or so has seen disturbing claims about the capacity of superintelligent AI to destroy the planet . It has also seen warnings coming from figures within the industry itself, including Anthropic’s report that criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have attempted to use its models to “design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and surveil dissidents” and Elon Musk’s claim it could be “ more dangerous than nukes ”.

Our reporting team has been trying to make sense of the scale of these claims. Is the great AI freakout justified? They will be here from 3pm BST (4pm CEST, 10am EDT) to try and answer any questions you might have.

Aisha Down is the Guardian’s global technology reporter, Dan Milmo is our global technology editor and Blake Montgomery is tech editor for Guardian US and author of the TechScape newsletter ( sign up to that here ).

articles.article_title: Tuopu Group Partners With Ensuring Technology to Accelerate Embodied AI Deployment
articles.heading: Tuopu Group Partners With Ensuring Technology to Accelerate Embodied AI Deployment
articles.summary: body { font-size: 16px; line-height: 34px; ...
articles.content:
Gasgoo Munich- Ensuring Technology and Tuopu Group have recently signed a strategic partnership agreement. The two companies will launch comprehensive cooperation around the "perception-to-action" capabilities of embodied intelligence, aiming to unlock core tactile sensing technologies for dexterous hands and accelerate large-scale commercial deployment.

Tuopu Group took a strategic stake in Ensuring Technology back in August. This latest agreement marks a shift from financial ties to deep industrial synergy, signaling a new phase in their collaboration.

Image Source: Ensuring Technology

Ensuring Technology specializes in the tactile infrastructure required for embodied intelligence. By focusing on contact perception and tactile data during robot-physical world interactions, the company has built a comprehensive hardware-software ecosystem. This spans tactile sensors, data acquisition, and compute-integrated hardware alongside software architectures.

The company's proprietary multi-dimensional tactile technology is designed to be high-density, lightweight, and capable of sensing multiple types of force while integrating sensing with computation. The system captures data on normal force, tangential force, and contact variations, finding applications in dexterous hands, humanoid robots, electronic skin, and data collection for embodied intelligence.

Yuansheng has established a complete technology chain linking tactile sensors, data, and intelligence through to mass manufacturing. Notably, its tactile sensors have achieved automotive-grade reliability in volume production and are now in the phase of designated batch delivery to prominent domestic and international clients in dexterous hands, robotics, and data collection.

Tuopu Group, for its part, has been aggressively expanding into embodied intelligence. The company established a dedicated Robot Actuator Business Unit—complete with an independent management structure and specialized team—to drive this initiative. Tuopu has already moved into core hardware areas including dexterous hands, joint actuators, motor controls, and precision structural components, positioning itself as one of the few domestic players capable of high-volume production for robotic parts.

articles.title: Soldiers and students study drone technology together
articles.description: Soldiers and students study drone technology together BBC
articles.description_html: Soldiers and students study drone technology together  BBC
articles.article_title: Soldiers and students study drone technology in Hereford together
articles.heading: Soldiers start new training to 'adapt to current drone threats'
articles.summary: The new degree in Hereford combines drone technology, robotics and engineering skills.
articles.content:
Soldiers start new training to 'adapt to current drone threats'
Soldiers are swapping military life for university study as part of a new degree designed to prepare the next generation of drone and robotics engineers.
The Autonomous Robotics programme has been developed in partnership with the Army, with military personnel studying alongside civilian students on two and three-year engineering degrees.
The course is being delivered by the New Model Institute for Technology and Engineering (NMITE), a specialist engineering higher education institution in Hereford.
For some of the soldiers taking part, the move from active service to academic life represents a dramatic change of pace.
Thirty-one-year-old Sgt Callum Dervey joined the Army at 18 after leaving school with what he describes as "a few GCSEs".
Now, after 13 years of military service, he has returned to education.
"I'm now back in a cohort of people who are much younger than myself," he said.
"Coming back into an academic setting is certainly already starting to feel challenging, but I'm sure it's going to get easier."
Focusing on autonomous systems, robotics and drone technology, organisers say the course aims to meet growing demand for expertise in emerging technologies.
Military personnel on the programme are taking three-year secondments from active service and are expected to take the skills they develop back into the Army.
Dervey said the Army was looking to increase its engineering expertise and adapt to emerging threats.
"It's so we can adapt rapidly in line with what the current threats are," he said.
"The skills and experience we get from working with academia, industry partners and end users can be taken back and taught to the field Army, which will be crucial in the future."
NMITE president and chief executive James Newby said the degree had been conceived with defence and security in mind, but its applications extended well beyond the military.
"They'll be learning about autonomous systems and robotics and control and mechatronics and systems thinking," he said.
"Those are hugely important skills in manufacturing, agriculture and humanitarian work."
Student Matthew Ryall, who has enrolled on the three-year MEng course, said discussions with lecturers had opened his eyes to the range of careers available.
"It's expanded so much that it could be anything, whether it's manufacturing, defence, whether it's in the air, on the ground or underwater as well," he said.

articles.article_title: Fueling a return journey from Mars
articles.heading: Fueling a return journey from Mars
articles.summary: MIT PhD candidate Lanie McKinney is developing technologies that could help humans explore Mars and return safely home. She is interested in using the resources already available on the planet to provide life support as well as propellant for the return journey.
articles.content:
When Lanie McKinney was 3 years old, her parents stopped at a massive meteor crater during a road trip through the U.S. Southwest. As they prepared to leave, McKinney began to protest.
“I want to wait here for the next one,” she told them.
She didn’t yet understand that another meteor wasn’t likely to land in exactly the same spot. But the story, which her parents still tell, captures a fascination that has remained with McKinney throughout her life.
“I just always remember being captivated by space and what is out there,” she says.
Today, McKinney is entering her fifth year as a PhD candidate at MIT, where she works in the Aerospace Plasma Group with Esther and Harold E. Edgerton Associate Professor Carmen Guerra-Garcia. McKinney’s research focuses on developing technologies that could help humans explore Mars.
One of the challenges of sending humans to the Red Planet is figuring out how to supply them once they arrive — including how to enable their journey back home. Rather than transporting everything from Earth, McKinney is interested in using the resources already available on the planet, a concept known as in-situ resource utilization, or ISRU.
“If we don’t build gas stations on Mars, it will be very difficult to get humans back to Earth,” she says. “We’re going to need some way to produce the propellant on site.”
McKinney’s research uses cold plasma to convert carbon dioxide, which is abundant in the martian atmosphere, into oxygen and carbon monoxide, a technology that could eventually be used to produce life support and propellant on Mars.
An Oklahoma native, McKinney earned her bachelor’s at the University of Tulsa, where she studied physics and applied mathematics. She had initially expected to pursue astrophysics, but a summer research internship at the University of Colorado at Boulder introduced her to plasma physics through a project involving dusty plasmas in the lunar environment.
“I thought it was an incredibly interesting problem,” she says.
At MIT, McKinney has developed a small reactor that can convert carbon dioxide into oxygen and other products. The challenge now is separating out the oxygen before it recombines.
“We can actually perform the conversion step really well,” she says. “But what happens in a plasma is we convert it, and then we get a mixture that needs to be separated.”
Her current work pairs the plasma reactor with an oxygen-selective membrane designed to extract oxygen rapidly. The integration process isn’t well-understood, leaving McKinney and her colleagues with questions about how the reactive plasma environment will affect the membrane.
“We are not entirely sure what we will see,” she says.
For McKinney, the possibility of connecting laboratory experiments to future human missions is what makes the work particularly rewarding.
“I get to work in a really cool lab and develop exciting experiments,” she says. “I get ownership over an entire experimental system, and then I get to connect that to performance requirements for a future Mars system. That’s just the dream.”
That same philosophy has shaped McKinney’s work beyond her thesis. Through MIT’s Space Resources Workshop, she has participated in NASA competitions focused on sustaining humans in space. Her first competition involved designing a self-sustaining Mars mission for 10 years.
“I had no clue what was going on,” she says. “I didn’t know anything about space systems. So, my mentality was, let me jump in and learn.”
She later co-led MIT’s CERBERUZ team for NASA’s LunaRecycle Challenge, which asked teams to develop ways to recycle waste on missions to the moon and deep space. The MIT team recently won first prize in Phase 2, receiving $775,000 in awards for a system that grinds mixed trash into powder that can be reused via injection molding to make spare parts and 3D-printing filament.
Another project McKinney enjoyed brought together engineers and architects through MAS.S66/4.154/16.89 (Space Architecture) to tackle a different problem: how to protect lunar habitats from radiation using only resources available on the moon. The students’ solution was to produce cast bricks from lunar regolith that could be stacked without mortar or another binder. For McKinney, the project demonstrated the value of bringing together people with different expertise.
“The kinds of innovative solutions that can be discovered when you work on a team that brings together different expertise and experiences was one of the project’s major takeaways,” she says.
The experience reflects a broader lesson McKinney has taken from MIT: Research may involve focused individual work, but solving the problems of human space exploration will require collaborations across disciplines.
“I feel like I have learned so much from being a part of these different teams,” she says.
McKinney sees that collaboration as essential to the future she hopes to help build. Reaching the Moon and Mars is only the first step: “What comes next is building up a permanent presence so that we can do amazing science and be really effective at exploration,” she says.
McKinney’s fascination with exploration extends beyond her research. She is an avid hiker and mountaineer, having grown up hiking with her family in the Rockies. She recently completed a mountaineering course in Alaska and summited Mount Baker in the Cascade Range. She sees a connection between those adventures and the curiosity that first drew her to space.
“I love to explore and go on adventures,” she says. “And space is the ultimate thing you could explore.”
That curiosity has also shaped how McKinney approaches her work. When she arrived at MIT from the University of Tulsa, she initially felt intimidated.
“I thought that it was a fluke that I’d gotten in,” she says. “I was very nervous that I was not going to measure up to the environment.”
Over time, she learned to approach unfamiliar problems by asking questions and committing fully to whatever interested her.
“If something interests you, try it and go all in,” she says.

Marvell is only one way to get exposure to the build out of AI data centers and cloud infrastructure, so it is worth scanning 89 AI infrastructure stocks .

Marvell Technology sells semiconductor solutions that move and process data across data centers and networks worldwide, making high speed optical links and secure transaction processing core to how it competes in the broader chip industry.

3 things going right for Marvell Technology that this headline doesn't cover.

How does the GlobalFoundries deal change Marvell Technology's AI data center position?

The expanded GlobalFoundries agreement gives Marvell more assured capacity for SiGe chips used in pluggable optics, NPO and CPO, all critical to high bandwidth AI data centers. This helps reduce supply bottleneck risk for its optical portfolio and tightens an existing manufacturing relationship that already spans more than a decade.

What does the Azure Payment HSM v2 launch mean for Marvell's business model?

By combining LiquidSecurity hardware with Utimaco software and Microsoft Azure, Marvell shifts part of its security hardware footprint into a cloud delivered, usage based service. That positions the company closer to recurring payment workloads for banks and processors, rather than relying only on traditional on premises HSM hardware sales.

What should investors watch next to judge whether these partnerships are gaining traction?

The first checkpoint is the Azure Payment HSM v2 public preview that begins on 17 September 2026 in Western U.S. and Western Europe. From here, investors can watch for any disclosed customer adoption metrics or expansion of availability regions, along with Marvell's capacity plans for higher speed SiGe optical products beyond the current 200G per lane benchmark.

articles.heading: AI transformation is '10% technology, 90% people'
articles.summary: NobleOak's Cathy Doyle and Databricks' Rochana Golani explain why closing the skills gap matters more than choosing the right AI tool
articles.content:
NobleOak's Cathy Doyle and Databricks' Rochana Golani explain why closing the skills gap matters more than choosing the right AI tool
Two senior figures driving artificial intelligence (AI) adoption inside their organisations have reached the same conclusion from opposite sides of the boardroom table: the technology is ready, but the workforce is not.
In separate interviews with HRD, Cathy Doyle, chief people and culture officer at Sydney-based life insurer NobleOak, and Rochana Golani, vice president (VP) of learning and enablement at data and AI company Databricks in California, both argued that AI transformation is fundamentally a talent problem dressed up as a technology one.
"It's not a technology problem, it's a talent problem," Golani said. "Every organisation that I talk to keeps bringing this up: 10% technology, 90% people."
The chief people officer as 'utility player'
For Doyle, that shift is reshaping her own job description. As NobleOak's chief people and culture officer, she now oversees the insurer's people function alongside its use of artificial intelligence and AI agents. "I look after all of our people and AI agents – I look after AI as well as technology, as well as people and strategic projects," she said.
She sees that dual mandate becoming the norm rather than the exception. "No longer can you just be one hat to wear in an organisation," Doyle said, describing the kind of multi-skilled executive she calls a "utility player" – someone equally credible on commercial strategy and technical capability. Chief people officers (CPOs) who can't demonstrate both, she argued, risk being sidelined as businesses reorganise around AI.
That doesn't mean every CPO needs to become a data scientist, Doyle was quick to add. "I'm not a cyber specialist, but I know I need a head of cyber," she said. "You've just got to go back to your disciplines, what environment am I working in, and therefore what do I need to cover, and then what skill sets do I need to go get."
Why managers, not executives, decide if transformation sticks
Golani's view from inside a fast-growing technology company points to a similar conclusion, delivered from a different altitude in the organisation chart: leadership commitment matters, but the real transformation happens, or stalls, with frontline managers.
"Managers to me is where this work starts and how we drive that transformation," she said. "I think of managers as the biggest change agents that do this well." She argued that manager expectations need to shift toward active role-modelling of AI use, coaching teams through the change rather than simply mandating it from above.
That philosophy has shaped how Databricks talks to its own customers about workforce change. Rather than hiring in new AI-fluent talent, Golani said the more successful organisations she works with retrain their existing people.
She pointed to National Australia Bank (NAB), which she said is running am AI bootcamp, as an example of upskilling at scale rather than a hiring spree.
Golani also drew a distinction between organisations merely "scaling" old habits with new tools and the smaller group genuinely reinventing how they work. "A very large percentage of people today are what we call 'scaling' – they're doing the things that they used to do, they're just doing it with AI," she said.
Genuine reinvention, that is creating new revenue streams from AI rather than just accelerating existing processes, is rarer: "it's less than 5% of companies that are able to do this," she estimated.
Curiosity over budget
Doyle's own experience underlines how deliberately some organisations are investing in AI literacy at the top. She described taking NobleOak's CEO and a small executive group to Silicon Valley for an intensive AI immersion.
"The CEO and five of us, we went and did an AI course, we went to Silicon Valley to find out what Silicon Valley thought of AI, and went to Google," she said, adding the group also completed "an AI for executives course" and a design session at Stanford University.
That trip left her candid about the gap between markets. "We're way behind in Australia compared to what's happening in Silicon Valley," Doyle said, pointing partly to a cultural reluctance to share knowledge.
"Here we keep secrets in Australia," she said, contrasting it with what she saw at Google: "if you don't share your code and you're not being open, then you're not being a Google citizen."
For HR leaders without an executive travel budget, though, Doyle argued the barrier to entry is lower than it looks. "I would say you don't need a big budget, but you do need a level of curiosity and time," she said, pointing to free vendor workshops, professional-body sessions and simple hands-on experimentation as accessible starting points.
Both leaders were careful to frame AI as augmenting judgment rather than replacing it. "It is just an assistant, it's a coworker," Golani said. "But the human is the ultimate owner, and also the critical thinker – the person who actually has the judgment to understand what is good work from not."
That tension – between AI as collaborator and the anxiety it can generate on the shop floor – echoes recent reporting on staff resistance to poorly explained AI rollouts, and feeds into the wider debate over whether AI could eventually replace entire job categories, rather than simply reshape them.
For both Doyle and Golani, the answer to that anxiety isn't a better tool – it's a better-prepared workforce.

articles.heading: Advances in Technology
articles.summary: Q&A with Dr. Shlomo Argamon, Associate Provost for AI
articles.content:
Advances in Technology
Q&A with Dr. Shlomo Argamon, Associate Provost for AI
News headlines are blaring about AI: its benefits, its dangers and its impact on culture, education, the workplace and society as a whole. Dr. Shlomo Argamon, Touro’s resident AI expert, shares his thoughts and insights on what everyone needs to know about AI and how Touro has incorporated AI into curriculum across all programs to prepare students for the new world they will enter.
What AI skills should today’s college students, specifically those in nontechnical fields, master before graduating?
College students in all fields need to master AI literacy, including ethical considerations. They also need to know how to collaborate with technical professionals. They need to understand basic AI concepts and terminology, and how to use AI tools effectively. This includes recognizing and addressing AI biases and understanding common risks associated with AI. Additionally, students should learn to use AI-powered software relevant to their field and be capable of collaborating with technical professionals to use AI effectively in their work.
How are you teaching AI skills across the Touro system? What is your goal?
AI@Touro is working to integrate AI education across all disciplines to prepare students for AI-driven careers. Touro now offers multiple new AI courses for students, including a new Master of Science in Artificial Intelligence Systems and an Advanced Certificate in Applied AI through the Graduate School of Technology. AI is also being integrated into existing courses across disciplines, including in the general education curriculum. The goals are to prepare students for working with AI, foster innovation and critical thinking, and ensure they can handle AI-related risks ethically and effectively. An essential component of our strategy is working with all of our faculty and administrators, training them in AI through a variety of bootcamps and workshops, and building a sense of collective teamwork around AI initiatives.
Will AI make certain jobs unnecessary? In what fields might that happen?
AI is more likely to transform jobs rather than eliminate them, with significant effects in some areas like manufacturing and transportation. While AI will not destroy jobs overall, it will change the nature of many roles. People who can effectively use AI will tend to replace those who cannot, leading to a shift in the job market. We are likely to see an increasing shift towards jobs that emphasize human interaction, such as in the service sector. Fields like manufacturing, where automation and robotics can handle repetitive tasks, and transportation, where self-driving vehicles could revolutionize trucking and logistics, are likely to see the most disruption.
How are professionals currently using AI in medicine and finance to benefit patients and clients?
AI enhances healthcare and financial services through advanced data analysis and AI-based automation. In medicine, AI assists in medical imaging analysis, supports radiologists, accelerates drug discovery, personalizes behavioral medicine with wearable technology, provides early-stage virtual health assistants for patients and improves surgical outcomes through robotics. It also streamlines administrative tasks, freeing up healthcare professionals to spend more time on patients. In finance, AI-driven algorithms optimize investment strategies, detect fraud, improve customer service with chatbots, automate routine tasks, analyze financial documents and provide predictive analytics for market trends.
Will colleges and universities need to incorporate AI into training for all disciplines? What about high schools?
Incorporating AI into education, starting at the high school level, is essential to prepare students for the future economy and society. Colleges and universities need to integrate AI education into various subjects to ensure students are ready to address AI use effectively in their careers. High schools should introduce basic AI concepts to create informed citizens and consumers. Vocational training should also include specific AI applications relevant to fields like manufacturing, construction and agriculture.
Does AI have biases in terms of race, gender or religion? What kind of impact does that have on the results people get when using AI?
AI systems work by incorporating large amounts of public or private information into a large language model (LLM). AI is “trained” by the data it incorporates from these sources. AI systems amplify biases in their training data, leading to potentially discriminatory outcomes. Biases in AI stem from the training data, which often reflects societal biases. If not properly managed, this can result in discriminatory outcomes in areas like hiring, lending and law enforcement. Mitigating these biases involves using diverse datasets and bias detection tools and adjusting how the tools are used to support human decision-making. While bias can never be entirely removed, it must be continuously monitored and addressed to minimize its impact.

articles.title: Orcutt school board Area 5 candidates talk technology, school safety, trustee compensation
articles.description: Orcutt school board Area 5 candidates talk technology, school safety, trustee compensation santamariatimes.com
articles.description_html: Orcutt school board Area 5 candidates talk technology, school safety, trustee compensation  santamariatimes.com
articles.article_title: Orcutt school board Area 5 candidates talk technology, school safety, trustee compensation
articles.heading: Orcutt school board Area 5 candidates talk technology, school safety, trustee compensation
articles.summary: Three candidates are competing for the Area 5 seat on the Orcutt Union School District board of trustees in the Nov. 3 election, with incumbent Shaun Henderson facing challengers David
articles.content:
Three candidates are competing for the Area 5 seat on the Orcutt Union School District board of trustees, with incumbent Shaun Henderson facing challengers David Morgan and Whitney May in the Nov. 3 election.
The candidates discussed quetions regarding cellphone and artificial intelligence policies, school facilities and safety, and trustee compensation, and their responses included different views on classroom technology and trustee pay, while all three emphasized student safety, transparency and community input.
On technology, Henderson said the district’s “off and away” cellphone policy was developed after a committee of administrators, teachers, parents and students studied cellphone use during the 2024-25 school year. The committee surveyed students, parents and staff before recommending that students keep cellphones in their backpacks and away from classroom workspaces.
Henderson said teachers have reported the policy has improved classroom focus and increased group discussions. The district also is reducing the use of school-issued devices, he said, with technology intended for assignments where it provides a particular benefit rather than being the default for every assignment.
The district is using artificial intelligence through MagicSchool, which Henderson described as a tool that can help teachers develop lessons and provide individualized support. He said the district is focused on teaching students to use AI responsibly while protecting student information.
“We want to make sure everyone understands how to use AI in a kind and thoughtful way,” Henderson said.
May said she was encouraged by the district’s efforts to reduce technology use but remains concerned about the amount of classroom work being done on electronic devices, particularly in math. She said watching her daughter try to learn math on a Chromebook was frustrating, and that students need opportunities to learn without relying too heavily on screens.
“I think my bigger concern is with technology being used ... too much in different subjects, especially for math,” May said.
May said students need to “really cement those facts,” and said she believes traditional learning methods can provide a different type of engagement.
Morgan said the board should determine whether technology is helping students by consulting teachers, parents and students and looking at measures such as test scores. He said test scores are not a complete measure of education but can provide useful information.
“You can seek input from parents as well,” Morgan said. “You know, it's a conversation that everybody at the table needs to be invited to and participate in.”
Morgan said students should be asked about how classroom technology affects their learning, but said younger students may not be able to explain their experiences as clearly as older students.
“A five-year-old may not be able to articulate that, but a high school senior certainly should be able to,” he said.
Facilities and safety also were central to the candidates’ responses, with each emphasizing different areas for attention.
Henderson said safety is his top priority and cited the district’s single points of entry, fencing around schools, annual safety plans and additional vice principals. He also pointed to emergency-response systems, and said he supports eventually adding a safety administrator who would rotate between Orcutt Junior High School, Lakeview Junior High School and Orcutt Academy High School.
“Every child, teacher, and staff member deserves to feel physically and emotionally safe,” Henderson said.
Henderson said the district continues to monitor student behavior and suspension trends and is reviewing ways to improve safety and security. He also cited the district’s cameras, emergency communication systems and software designed to monitor social media for potential threats.
Sign up to receive headlines in your inbox!
May said she believes the district has made progress on campus security but wants more attention paid to general building maintenance. She cited roofs and problems caused by heavy rain as examples of projects that need attention.
“I think there are definitely areas that need to be brought up to speed in that,” May said.
May said she has been frustrated when her children have experienced canceled or shortened school days because of rain. She said the district should consider how quickly needed projects can be completed while minimizing disruption to students and instruction.
Morgan said facilities should be prioritized based on the severity of a problem and its effect on students’ ability to learn.
He said classrooms need to be safe and habitable, while cafeteria and office facilities also need to adequately support their functions.
Trustee compensation was another point of difference among the candidates.
May said she was disappointed by the board’s decision to increase its compensation and believes the amount is too high given other needs in the district. She said she does not plan to accept the stipend or health insurance benefits if elected. If she were to receive the stipend, she said she would donate it to the district’s PTAs.
“For me personally, I am not planning on taking the stipend or the health insurance,” May said.
Morgan also said he would not accept trustee compensation if elected. He said discussions about board compensation should be disclosed publicly before a vote and that the reasons for any change should be explained to the community.
“Any discussions about board compensation should be published well in advance of the vote, and any justification for doing so should be clearly articulated to the public,” Morgan said.
Henderson said the compensation change was made under state law and that the district updated its policy after the law changed. He said board agendas, policy updates and meeting minutes are publicly posted. He also said trustees do not receive free health benefits, noting that family coverage would cost at least $800 for the lowest option.
The candidates cited different reasons for seeking the Area 5 seat.
May said she wants greater representation for parents of elementary school students and has heard concerns from families about student behavior and school safety. She has three children in district schools and said her experience as a parent has given her perspective on how the district has changed since the COVID-19 pandemic.
Morgan said his focus would be accountability and transparency, including hearing directly from teachers and classified employees about district operations. He said he has contacted both district unions and received an endorsement from the Orcutt Educators Association.
Henderson, who is seeking a third term after eight years on the board, pointed to his experience in management, human resources, financial and operational management, as well as his more than 33 years living in the area. His three children attended Orcutt Union School District schools, and he said he completed the Masters in Governance Program after joining the board.
Mark Steller and Melanie Waffle are running unopposed in Areas 3 and 4, respectively.

articles.title: City of Raleigh Uses Drones, AI Technology to Create Digital Twin
articles.description: City of Raleigh Uses Drones, AI Technology to Create Digital Twin Dronelife
articles.description_html: City of Raleigh Uses Drones, AI Technology to Create Digital Twin  Dronelife
articles.article_title: City of Raleigh Uses Drones, AI Technology to Create Digital Twin
articles.heading: City of Raleigh Uses Drones, AI Technology to Create Digital Twin
articles.summary: Raleigh deploys drones and AI to build a city digital twin for traffic planning, tree preservation, and community storytelling.
articles.content:
The city of Raleigh, North Carolina is deploying drones and artificial-intelligence (AI)-enabled tools to create a virtual version of itself to meet the urban challenges of today and to help chart the future of the fast-growing metropolis.
Long recognized as the hub of the state’s high-tech Research Triangle region, Raleigh has worked with tech industry partners Esri, NVIDIA and Microsoft to create a digital twin of the city, to help deal with challenges such as traffic management and urban development planning.
“We do a citizen survey every two years and ask citizens all sorts of questions about their priorities and concerns. Development and traffic come up as the top two pretty regularly,” Jim Alberque, the city’s geographic information system (GIS) and emerging technology manager, said in an interview.
“I think the benefit of the digital twin, what it’s given the city in our ability to communicate with our community, is that we don’t have to tell you the story, we can show you the story of the city,” Alberque said.
Drone Data Powers Planning for Parks, Events, and Tree Preservation
One of the city’s most recent uses of the drone-captured data was to aid in the development of Gipson Play Plaza, an 18.5-acre major recreational and community gathering destination located within the 300-acre Dorothea Dix Park.
“We did flights of that to be able to get generate 3D mesh and (orthographic images), to be able to show what that park was like, to be able to communicate that and tell that story,” said Jeff Dawson, the city’s technology and analytics manager.
He added that city officials are exploring how to leverage the digital-twin technology for use in event planning, to ensure that the physical space selected at a given site is adequate to accommodate the event’s needs without having to rely on estimates or saying “we probably have space for a tent there.”
Another application of the technology helps the city’s facility planners to site the construction of future buildings in such a way that the greatest number of stately trees are preserved. “Trees are very big in Raleigh; the ‘City of Oaks,'” Dawson said.
Working on the cutting edge of technology, Raleigh is also starting to incorporate other types of data-collection devices that it currently employs, to contribute to the construction of a virtual clone of the entire city. “We’re to take some of our traditional (Internet of Things) devices, so sensors that we have out in the community — whether that be cameras or things that are in motion, so scooters or vehicles — and starting to incorporate those into this digital twin to get a much more high-fidelity view,” he said.
Early Adopter of Drones
The city of Raleigh was an early adopter of drone technology, with the Parks Department starting its first drone program in 2018. The information technology (IT) department began its own drone program about two years ago.
Dawson said the city has taken a decentralized approach in its drone usage.
“We have drones in IT, in Raleigh Parks and Raleigh Water, and then the police department has a large fleet of drones,” he said. “They’re more on their own, because of the law enforcement nature of it, it’s a little bit different from how the rest of us are operating.”
To create the digital twin project, the city basically relies on four drones, three U.S.-made Freefly Astros and one Mavic product. Dawson said that about two years ago, faced with the possibility of federal bans on the use of Chinese-made drones, Raleigh officials made the decision to gradually replace its existing drone fleet with NDAA-compliant products such as the Astro.
“It was an end-of-life thing. We were looking for something that was Blue Listed and that’s when we came across the Astro and started heading down that route, and then adopted them across the board,” he said.
Novel Use of AI Technology
Alberque said the city, with its roots in the tech-savvy Research Triangle, also was among the first communities in the country to fully embrace the use of AI technology.
“We use standard operations to capture imagery. We then take that imagery and use Esri technology to create derivative products,” he said. Those derivative products might be orthophotos or 3D meshes. “So, obviously there’s a bunch of AI on board.”
When the city first launched the digital-twin project, city leaders decided that, as one of the fastest-growing cities in the country, the earliest use of the technology should be centered around modeling the future urban form of the city.
“What does the city look like today? What is it going to look like tomorrow? And what might it look like in a year?” Alberque asked.
As the digital twin project evolved, city leaders found additional uses for the technology, such as micro-weather modeling. “We’re working with a firm around doing some micro-weather modeling that takes into effect climate data, wind patterns, those sorts of things, but also using the urban-built environment to model ventilation corridors and wind patterns,” he said.
But perhaps the most innovative use to which the city has put the technology is in using the digital twin to help illustrate the story of Raleigh.
“We found that it’s a really valuable tool to do storytelling,” Alberque said. “We’re leveraging GIS as a platform for our digital twin. We can then incorporate other data and use that as a platform for storytelling, whether that be around some environmental-modeling things or some operational things related to our transit service.”
