Jim Magill is a Houston-based writer with almost a quarter-century of experience covering technical and economic developments in the oil and gas industry. After retiring in December 2019 as a senior editor with S&P Global Platts, Jim began writing about emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence, robots and drones, and the ways in which they’re contributing to our society. In addition to DroneLife, Jim is a contributor to Forbes.com and his work has appeared in the Houston Chronicle, U.S. News & World Report, and Unmanned Systems, a publication of the Association for Unmanned Vehicle Systems International

Another application of the technology helps the city’s facility planners to site the construction of future buildings in such a way that the greatest number of stately trees are preserved. “Trees are very big in Raleigh; the ‘City of Oaks,'” Dawson said.

Working on the cutting edge of technology, Raleigh is also starting to incorporate other types of data-collection devices that it currently employs, to contribute to the construction of a virtual clone of the entire city. “We’re to take some of our traditional (Internet of Things) devices, so sensors that we have out in the community — whether that be cameras or things that are in motion, so scooters or vehicles — and starting to incorporate those into this digital twin to get a much more high-fidelity view,” he said.

Early Adopter of Drones

The city of Raleigh was an early adopter of drone technology, with the Parks Department starting its first drone program in 2018. The information technology (IT) department began its own drone program about two years ago.

Dawson said the city has taken a decentralized approach in its drone usage.

“We have drones in IT, in Raleigh Parks and Raleigh Water, and then the police department has a large fleet of drones,” he said. “They’re more on their own, because of the law enforcement nature of it, it’s a little bit different from how the rest of us are operating.”

To create the digital twin project, the city basically relies on four drones, three U.S.-made Freefly Astros and one Mavic product. Dawson said that about two years ago, faced with the possibility of federal bans on the use of Chinese-made drones, Raleigh officials made the decision to gradually replace its existing drone fleet with NDAA-compliant products such as the Astro.

“It was an end-of-life thing. We were looking for something that was Blue Listed and that’s when we came across the Astro and started heading down that route, and then adopted them across the board,” he said.

Novel Use of AI Technology

Alberque said the city, with its roots in the tech-savvy Research Triangle, also was among the first communities in the country to fully embrace the use of AI technology.

“We use standard operations to capture imagery. We then take that imagery and use Esri technology to create derivative products,” he said. Those derivative products might be orthophotos or 3D meshes. “So, obviously there’s a bunch of AI on board.”

When the city first launched the digital-twin project, city leaders decided that, as one of the fastest-growing cities in the country, the earliest use of the technology should be centered around modeling the future urban form of the city.

“What does the city look like today? What is it going to look like tomorrow? And what might it look like in a year?” Alberque asked.

As the digital twin project evolved, city leaders found additional uses for the technology, such as micro-weather modeling. “We’re working with a firm around doing some micro-weather modeling that takes into effect climate data, wind patterns, those sorts of things, but also using the urban-built environment to model ventilation corridors and wind patterns,” he said.

But perhaps the most innovative use to which the city has put the technology is in using the digital twin to help illustrate the story of Raleigh.

“We found that it’s a really valuable tool to do storytelling,” Alberque said. “We’re leveraging GIS as a platform for our digital twin. We can then incorporate other data and use that as a platform for storytelling, whether that be around some environmental-modeling things or some operational things related to our transit service.”

After retiring in December 2019 as a senior editor with S&P Global Platts, Jim began writing about emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence, robots and drones, and the ways in which they’re contributing to our society. articles.summary: Fire trucks race through intersections every day to put out fires or help get someone to a hospital.  The Detroit Fire Department is now testing technology that will trigger green lights to switch on when a truck comes through an intersection.
articles.content:
Local News

The goal, if the pilot program succeeds, is to eventually equip EMS and police vehicles

Jay Scott Smith , Anchor/Reporter

Joel Deaner , Photojournalist

DETROIT – Fire trucks race through intersections every day to put out fires or help get someone to a hospital.

The Detroit Fire Department is now testing technology that will trigger green lights to switch on when a truck comes through an intersection.

“With this technology, it should make [response time] quicker,” Chief David Nelson said on Thursday. “Anytime that we get to a run quicker, it’s better for our citizens.”

It’s part of a 90-day pilot program centered in Corktown, and the technology is being provided through Miovision.

The lights trigger whenever a truck gets to an intersection with its lights and/or sirens on.

The goal, if the pilot program succeeds, is to eventually equip EMS and police vehicles.

Miovision has been working with the city of Detroit, along with Haas Alerts.

The latter company has also developed technology to alert cars of emergency vehicles entering intersections.

Nelson stressed the importance of quicker response times and noted that getting to a green light can make all the difference.

“If it’s green and we have that oncoming traffic already stopped, that gives us those extra seconds to maybe save a life,” he said. “In this business, seconds are important.”

The technology is not just meant to add speed, but also safety.

According to the Michigan Office of Highway Planning , emergency vehicles were involved in more than 2,600 crashes in 2025. Of those crashes:

- 1,937 were police vehicles.

- 419 were ambulances.

- 255 were fire vehicles

Two of the crashes were fatal. Miovision has already run similar programs in Texas and Tennessee and seen an improvement in response time and a decrease in accidents.

The program began last month and is slated to run through the month of November.

articles.title: New technology aims to prevent theft of SNAP benefits from EBT cards
articles.description: New technology aims to prevent theft of SNAP benefits from EBT cards 6abc Philadelphia
articles.description_html: New technology aims to prevent theft of SNAP benefits from EBT cards  6abc Philadelphia
articles.article_title: New technology aims to prevent theft of SNAP benefits from EBT cards
articles.heading: New technology aims to prevent theft of SNAP benefits from EBT cards
articles.summary: More than 1.7 million Pennsylvanians who receive Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits will soon receive EBT cards with chip technology.
articles.content:
ByNydia H. Han
Thursday, September 17, 2026 9:40PM
More than 1.7 million Pennsylvanians who receive Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits will soon receive EBT cards with chip technology as the state works to combat theft targeting recipients.
The problem affects SNAP recipients across Pennsylvania, including about 400,000 people in Philadelphia.
The new cards are intended to provide additional security against thieves who use skimming devices to steal benefit funds.
For Northeast Philadelphia resident Mickayla Hileman, the theft had an immediate impact.
"I go to the store, I use my EBT card, and all of my money is gone," Hileman said.
She told us she was unable to recover the lost money.
"I was not able to get reimbursed or anything," she said.
That comes after the federal government ended authorization to replace stolen benefits in December 2024.
"That's all my money to feed my children. What am I gonna do?" Hileman said.
She said others in her community have faced similar losses.
"I had $800 stolen and my mom had about $200 stolen. Someone down the street, they had about $178 stolen," Hileman said.
SNAP recipients receive benefits through Electronic Benefits Transfer, or EBT, cards. Current cards use magnetic stripes that require users to swipe them.
Authorities say thieves install skimming devices where the cards are used, allowing them to capture card information and eventually steal benefits. Pennsylvania Inspector General Michelle Henry told Action News that the skimmers can be installed in under four seconds."
She also said that the Inspector General's Office has instituted a full-time dedicated skimming response team.
Henry says that team has helped cancel 58,000 EBT cards before money was stolen, preventing losses of more than $34 million.
State officials also announced plans to upgrade EBT cards with chip technology, which is more secure.
"We have now begun the process to modernize, strengthen, and protect our EBT cards here in the Commonwealth," said Pennsylvania Department of Human Services Secretary Val Arkoosh.
Pennsylvania plans to begin distributing the new cards in late spring. Until then, officials recommend SNAP recipients protect their PINs, change them regularly and avoid sharing them with others.
They also encourage recipients to use the free ConnectEBT app to lock benefits when they are not being used.
States that have already adopted chip-enabled EBT cards have reported theft reductions of about 80%, officials said.
If SNAP funds are stolen, recipients should immediately cancel the card, request a replacement and file reports with both police and the Office of Inspector General, officials said.
To download the ConnectEBT app go to one of these links:
https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.conduent.ebt&hl=en_US
https://apps.apple.com/us/app/connectebt/id1241215610
And here's what to do if your SNAP benefits are stolen from your EBT card, according to the PA Department of Human Services:
If benefits are stolen, a replacement EBT card should be requested as soon as possible from EBT contractor Conduent at 888-328-7366, or by visiting a PA DHS County Assistance Office. SNAP is entirely federally funded, and due to the end of Congressional authorization of funds to replace stolen benefits, benefits stolen after December 20, 2024, cannot be reissued by PA DHS.
For immediate food needs, Pennsylvanians can call 211 or visit www.pa211.org to connect with various local food resources and can also visit www.feedingpa.org to find local food banks and other food assistance programs.
Individuals in need can also visit pa-navigate.org/ for help finding food and other resource assistance.

articles.summary: The U.S. National Science Foundation today announced an initiative to translate low-dimensional semiconductor technologies from laboratory demonstrations into platforms for U.S. manufacturers to…
articles.content:
NSF invests in translating low-dimensional semiconductor technologies to establish U.S. leadership in microelectronics
The U.S. National Science Foundation today announced an initiative to translate low-dimensional semiconductor technologies from laboratory demonstrations into platforms for U.S. manufacturers to develop and deploy advanced microelectronics.
The NSF Ecosystem for Low-dimensional Electronics: Growth, Assembly, Nanoelectronics, and Translation (NSF ELEGANT) program will position the U.S. for success in translating advanced microelectronics technologies into next-generation capabilities for artificial intelligence, high-performance computing, advanced communications, and other key technology areas critical to national security and economic competitiveness.
"NSF ELEGANT aims to de-risk advanced microelectronics manufacturing technology to the point where industry can make a timely, credible, evidence-based commitment to its adoption," said Erwin Gianchandani, NSF Assistant Director for Technology, Innovation and Partnerships. "Sustained industry participation is central to how this program is designed and measured — every performing team's progress is validated by industry partners at each stage, so the technologies advancing through ELEGANT are the ones manufacturers are ready to adopt."
Microelectronics powers industry and drives worldwide innovation. However, current microelectronics manufacturing methods are no longer able to keep pace with the demand for smaller-scale microelectronics technologies at the scale needed. The ELEGANT program advances innovation in low-dimension materials for semiconductor manufacturing and simultaneously bridges the gap between laboratory demonstrations and the development of industry-relevant platforms.
To achieve program objectives, NSF released an Other Transaction Agreement Solutions Offering (OTASO) seeking an Ecosystems Coordinator and Expert Performer Teams in five translation themes:
- Theme 1: Manufacturable Materials Platform.
- Theme 2: Process Technology and Process Design Kit.
- Theme 3: Device, Circuit and Full-Chip Demonstration.
- Theme 4: Manufacturing Readiness and Transition.
- Theme 5: AI-Enabled Acceleration.
To learn more, please visit the ELEGANT OTASO.
About NSF TIP
The NSF Directorate for Technology, Innovation and Partnerships (NSF TIP) seeks to engage all Americans in accelerating critical and emerging technologies to advance U.S. competitiveness. The directorate partners across sectors to advance three strategies — accelerating critical and emerging technology, expanding the geography of American innovation, and building a competition-ready workforce. For more information about NSF TIP, visit nsf.gov/tip/latest.

articles.title: Purdue, Japan strengthen research collaboration with new agreements
articles.description: Purdue, Japan strengthen research collaboration with new agreements Purdue University
articles.description_html: Purdue, Japan strengthen research collaboration with new agreements  Purdue University
articles.article_title: Purdue, Japan strengthen research collaboration with new agreements
articles.heading: Purdue, Japan strengthen research collaboration with new agreements
articles.summary: Purdue signs an MOU with JETRO and an LOI with Tohoku University, deepening U.S.-Japan ties in research, workforce development and critical technologies.
articles.content:
Purdue, Japan strengthen research collaboration with new agreements
Partners explore ways to bolster innovation ecosystems in both countries
WEST LAFAYETTE, Ind. — Purdue University continues to catalyze its international innovation and collaboration network by signing a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) and a letter of intent (LOI) with Tohoku University to accelerate research, workforce development and industry in critical technologies. The MOU was signed by Purdue President Mitch Daniels and JETRO Chairman and CEO Norihiko Ishiguro.
Announced during the 10th annual U.S. and Japan Digital Innovation Hub and Advanced Technology Workshop at Purdue, the dual agreements represent a major milestone in global collaboration.
The nonbinding MOU with JETRO — a government-related organization that facilitates trade and investment — will combine Purdue’s world-class research and technology commercialization capabilities with JETRO’s extensive networks in the U.S. and Japan.
Simultaneously, the LOI with Tohoku University, a top-tier research institution in Japan, will expand on three decades of cooperative academic and scientific engagement.
“The agreements pave the way for real-world business integration, student and researcher talent exchanges, and collaborative solutions to urgent global technology needs,” said Dimitrios Peroulis, Purdue’s senior vice president for partnerships and online and a Reilly Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering. “Together, the partnerships position Purdue and its like-minded Japanese counterparts at the forefront of global tech diplomacy, particularly in crucial fields like energy, artificial intelligence, semiconductors and quantum technology.”
The U.S.-Japan relationship is built not only on shared interests, but also on shared values, mutual trust, and a long-standing commitment to scientific and technological progress, Peroulis noted. As part of Purdue’s relationship with Japan, the Office of Industry Partnerships has held an annual workshop bringing together universities, research institutions and companies from both countries to strengthen collaboration in research and workforce development across critical technologies, including AI, semiconductors, advanced materials and manufacturing, space, and quantum technology.
The new JETRO alliance will help businesses, startups and researchers navigate the U.S. and Japanese markets, driving economic and tech growth. The framework includes collaboration with Purdue Research Foundation’s innovation, incubation, technology transfer and startup support programs.
The Tohoku agreement paves the way for expanded joint research, student and scholar exchanges, and cooperative training, building on an existing synergy in advanced fields like hydrogen energy and semiconductors. That joint effort is already evident through the more recent ASPIRE-Hydrogen project and the UPWARDS Network that Purdue established in 2023 with several Japanese technology companies and universities, including Tohoku, to advance workforce development and R&D in semiconductors.
The academic partners will work together to discover and develop new materials that could make energy technologies, including hydrogen fuel cells and water electrolysis, more efficient, durable and practical. Purdue researchers will bring strengths in AI-driven materials discovery, first-principles modeling and device-level translation, while Tohoku researchers will contribute deep expertise in fundamental interface science and electrochemistry. Together, the teams aim to bridge atomic-scale understanding and real-world energy applications.
“Our next step is to establish a Purdue-Tohoku Joint Institute as a platform for genuine collaboration and then compete together for major joint U.S.-Japan projects, including opportunities under the Genesis Mission,” said Zhenhua Zeng, assistant research professor of chemistry and chemical engineering who leads the Purdue-Tohoku partnership in hydrogen energy. “By working with partners across the U.S. and Japan, we hope to make a giant leap in energy research and AI for science, while building a strategic partnership with Tohoku University and broader Japanese research institutions that can help advance the U.S.-Japan partnership in science and technology.”
About Purdue University
Purdue University is a research institution ranked among the top 10 public universities in the United States. More than 111,000 students study at Purdue across multiple campuses, including more than 57,000 at our main campus locations in West Lafayette and Indianapolis. As a land-grant university committed to affordability and accessibility, Purdue’s main campus has frozen tuition 14 years in a row, enabling more students than ever to graduate debt-free.
Media contact: Wes Mills, wemills@purdue.edu

The new JETRO alliance will help businesses, startups and researchers navigate the U.S. and Japanese markets, driving economic and tech growth. The framework includes collaboration with Purdue Research Foundation’s innovation, incubation, technology transfer and startup support programs.

The Tohoku agreement paves the way for expanded joint research, student and scholar exchanges, and cooperative training, building on an existing synergy in advanced fields like hydrogen energy and semiconductors. That joint effort is already evident through the more recent ASPIRE-Hydrogen project and the UPWARDS Network that Purdue established in 2023 with several Japanese technology companies and universities, including Tohoku, to advance workforce development and R&D in semiconductors.

The academic partners will work together to discover and develop new materials that could make energy technologies, including hydrogen fuel cells and water electrolysis, more efficient, durable and practical. Purdue researchers will bring strengths in AI-driven materials discovery, first-principles modeling and device-level translation, while Tohoku researchers will contribute deep expertise in fundamental interface science and electrochemistry. Together, the teams aim to bridge atomic-scale understanding and real-world energy applications.

“Our next step is to establish a Purdue-Tohoku Joint Institute as a platform for genuine collaboration and then compete together for major joint U.S.-Japan projects, including opportunities under the Genesis Mission,” said Zhenhua Zeng, assistant research professor of chemistry and chemical engineering who leads the Purdue-Tohoku partnership in hydrogen energy. “By working with partners across the U.S. and Japan, we hope to make a giant leap in energy research and AI for science, while building a strategic partnership with Tohoku University and broader Japanese research institutions that can help advance the U.S.-Japan partnership in science and technology.”

About Purdue University

Purdue University is a research institution ranked among the top 10 public universities in the United States. More than 111,000 students study at Purdue across multiple campuses, including more than 57,000 at our main campus locations in West Lafayette and Indianapolis. As a land-grant university committed to affordability and accessibility, Purdue’s main campus has frozen tuition 14 years in a row, enabling more students than ever to graduate debt-free.

Media contact: Wes Mills, wemills@purdue.edu

articles.summary: DOE Gives $73 Million for Mining Technology Testing Grounds National Association of Manufacturers - NAM
articles.content:
DOE Gives $73 Million for Mining Technology Testing Grounds
The Department of Energy’s Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation will split $73 million in funding among four projects to test innovative new mining technologies in the U.S., the agency announced last week (Mining Technology).
What’s going on: “Part of the DOE’s Mine of the Future initiative, the funding aims to advance the development and commercialization of mining technologies designed to support critical mineral supply chains.”
- The chosen projects are in Virginia, Missouri, Texas and Arizona “and are set to provide real-world environments for testing next-generation mining applications.”
The details: Lynchburg, Virginia–based Innovative Wireless Technologies plans to use its part of the funding to create a testbed across West Virginia, Colorado and Virginia.
- Curators of the University of Missouri will build a “mining technology proving ground that combines two complementary facilities for underground technology testing and advanced comminution research” (Mining.com).
- Southern Methodist University in Texas will build the first synthetic mine in the world in a test facility made to speed mining from concept to deployment.
- The University of Arizona will use the funds to build “a scalable underground proving ground for mining, electrification and energy management technology.”
Why it’s important: “By establishing world-class testing grounds, we’re accelerating breakthroughs that will strengthen our supply chains, our workforce and our national competitiveness,” Assistant Secretary of Energy Audrey Robertson said in a DOE press release.

articles.title: Top Media Execs Break Down How to Super-Serve Audiences, the Real Threat of ‘AI Slop’ and More at Variety Entertainment & Technology Summit
articles.description: Top Media Execs Break Down How to Super-Serve Audiences, the Real Threat of ‘AI Slop’ and More at Variety Entertainment & Technology Summit Variety
articles.description_html: Top Media Execs Break Down How to Super-Serve Audiences, the Real Threat of ‘AI Slop’ and More at Variety Entertainment & Technology Summit  Variety
articles.article_title: Top Media Execs Break Down How to Super-Serve Audiences, the Real Threat of ‘AI Slop’ and More at Variety Entertainment & Technology Summit
articles.heading: Top Media Execs Break Down How to Super-Serve Audiences, the Real Threat of ‘AI Slop’ and More at Variety Entertainment & Technology Summit
articles.summary: A panel of execs from Hulu and ABC, NBCU, WBTV, Blumhouse and Crunchyroll kicked off the Variety Entertainment & Technology Summit presented by EY.
articles.content:
How are media and entertainment companies navigating shifting winds in Hollywood, amid an industry in constant flux and AI rapidly advancing on the scene? A panel of senior industry leaders served up insights into the biz’s burning questions, setting the table for the Variety Entertainment & Technology Summit presented by EY in L.A. Thursday.
Speaking on the kickoff panel were Clancy Collins White, president of creative affairs at Warner Bros. Television; Simran Sethi, president of scripted programming for Hulu Originals and ABC Entertainment at Disney; Liz Jenkins, chief business officer, NBCUniversal Entertainment; Abhijay Prakash, president of Blumhouse Atomic Monster; and Rahul Purini, president of Sony’s Crunchyroll anime-streaming service.
NBCU’s Jenkins said that the TV industry — during the era of “peak TV” a few years ago — was “in a place for a while where, frankly, the economics were a bit unsustainable, right? And I think that supply, frankly, probably exceeded demand.”
Popular on Variety
Now, with a portfolio at NBCU that comprises Peacock, Bravo and NBC, Jenkins said the company “has gotten very sort of surgical and being focused on who are our priority audiences and how do we ensure that we’re super-serving them, and but then grow from there.”
Sethi said that Disney discovered early on that distribution on streaming services like Hulu and Disney+ and linear TV “don’t cannibalize each other. They’re distinct audiences. People who have a habit of watching live on television are not necessarily the ones streaming streaming online. So it really did for us just make the pie bigger, and it allows people to catch up and come back.”
The panelists also said the weekly release of TV episodes, bucking Netflix’s general convention of releasing full seasons in a binge-drop, was something that resonated with viewers.
“TV has always been about a collective experience. Everyone in this room grew up watching certain shows,” Sethi said. “I think for a lot of young people, watercooler television is a new idea. But the idea that you can have this shared experience watching something weekly is, I think, an important return to what society feels like it’s gravitating towards again, which is being together and talking with each other and connecting.
WBTV’s Collins White said audiences are responding to the weekly drop of episodes of the studio’s hit series “The Pitt,” which won seven 2026 Emmys including best drama series and lead drama actor for Noah Wyle.
“At a time when when so much emphasis is being placed on IP, it’s an incredibly compelling original idea that, you know, was not a complete reinvention of the wheel,” she said about “The Pitt.” “I think audiences are really enjoying the sort of the weekly drop as opposed to sort of the binge model.”
Jenkins said some shows — like Peacock’s “Love Island USA” — need “a moment to sort of build. And sort of [ask], are you seeing green shoots? Are you seeing that it’s hitting the right audience?” For “Love Island USA,” the real tipping point was Season 6 and the addition of Ariana Madix coming off a buzzy season of “Vanderpump Rules,” with a really established fan base there, she added.
As for the threat of AI, Blumhouse’s Prakash, whose studio was behind two big summer box-office hits from YouTube creators — “Obsession” and “Backrooms” — said he thinks short-form, maybe lower-production value creator content is “the most likely to get disrupted by whatever they’re calling ‘AI slop.'”
To Prakesh, “Obsession” and “Backrooms” could not have been created from an AI prompt. “Those are not the kinds of things that could be spat out of algorithms and large language models,” he said.
And, he said, the two horror films showed that “a scary theatrical event” could compel people “to leave their homes for that experience.” And he said a takeaway for him is that Hollywood should be doing more to serve audiences natively on YouTube.
“YouTube is the probably No. 1 platform for watching filmed entertainment, so it’s not surprising that it’s penetrating the culture in many different ways,” Prakesh said. “I think what was so heartening about the experience that we had was that you had creators who were very popular on YouTube still craving the theatrical experience — and still wanting to take their storytelling to that platform and to deliver it to consumers there, which obviously is what we do.”
As an industry, “we have to figure out how to be present in front of them, not just with trailers and featurettes on YouTube, but like actually have an offering for the consumer on the platform that is increasingly dominant and so young, and where you can find and grow that audience.”
At Crunchyroll, the company is continually asking fans what makes them come back to anime over and over, say Purini. He said Crunchyroll’s research shows that outside of Japan and China, 650 million people watching anime regularly on a weekly basis, and that’s projected to continue to grow globally.
“The visual style, the art is part of it, but what really is the themes and the stories that the Japanese creators tend to tell, to to talk about, and it’s grief, it is fame, it is found family, it is all of those things,” Purini said. “But really, what our fans are telling us is there are stories that are relatable characters, but the stories that feel real, but are very different from other stories that they get in their entertainment mix.”
Jenkins said that one of the things the industry lost sight of during the peak TV bubble was that “sort of the difference between, I like to call it capital C content and lowercase C content. It’s not just about tonnage. At the end of the day, it starts and begins with great stories and great storytellers. And what works are things that audiences emotionally connect to. They make you feel something.”
Clancy Collins said that over the years, there’s become less and less of a distinction between the programming on streaming services vs. linear TV. “Our mission statement from the studio is just to be selling to as many outlets as possible,” she said. “So we obviously have a broadcast business that we’re very incredibly proud of. But you know, we’re at 30 shows across 10 platforms… and capitalizing on our independence to be able to sell everywhere and offer our creators that flexibility.”
The panel was moderated by Michael Schneider, Variety‘s executive editor for TV. The daylong event is being held at the Four Seasons in Beverly Hills.
Pictured above (l. to r.): Simran Sethi, Clancy Collins White, Abhijay Prakash, Liz Jenkins and Rahul Purini speak onstage during the Trailblazers of the Content Industry panel at the Variety Entertainment & Technology Summit presented by EY
articles.content_html:
How are media and entertainment companies navigating shifting winds in Hollywood, amid an industry in constant flux and AI rapidly advancing on the scene? A panel of senior industry leaders served up insights into the biz’s burning questions, setting the table for the Variety Entertainment & Technology Summit presented by EY in L.A. Thursday.

Speaking on the kickoff panel were Clancy Collins White, president of creative affairs at Warner Bros. Television; Simran Sethi, president of scripted programming for Hulu Originals and ABC Entertainment at Disney; Liz Jenkins, chief business officer, NBCUniversal Entertainment; Abhijay Prakash, president of Blumhouse Atomic Monster; and Rahul Purini, president of Sony’s Crunchyroll anime-streaming service.

NBCU’s Jenkins said that the TV industry — during the era of “peak TV” a few years ago — was “in a place for a while where, frankly, the economics were a bit unsustainable, right? And I think that supply, frankly, probably exceeded demand.”

Popular on Variety

Now, with a portfolio at NBCU that comprises Peacock, Bravo and NBC, Jenkins said the company “has gotten very sort of surgical and being focused on who are our priority audiences and how do we ensure that we’re super-serving them, and but then grow from there.”

Sethi said that Disney discovered early on that distribution on streaming services like Hulu and Disney+ and linear TV “don’t cannibalize each other. They’re distinct audiences. People who have a habit of watching live on television are not necessarily the ones streaming streaming online. So it really did for us just make the pie bigger, and it allows people to catch up and come back.”

The panelists also said the weekly release of TV episodes, bucking Netflix’s general convention of releasing full seasons in a binge-drop, was something that resonated with viewers.

“TV has always been about a collective experience. Everyone in this room grew up watching certain shows,” Sethi said. “I think for a lot of young people, watercooler television is a new idea. But the idea that you can have this shared experience watching something weekly is, I think, an important return to what society feels like it’s gravitating towards again, which is being together and talking with each other and connecting.

WBTV’s Collins White said audiences are responding to the weekly drop of episodes of the studio’s hit series “The Pitt,” which won seven 2026 Emmys including best drama series and lead drama actor for Noah Wyle.

“At a time when when so much emphasis is being placed on IP, it’s an incredibly compelling original idea that, you know, was not a complete reinvention of the wheel,” she said about “The Pitt.” “I think audiences are really enjoying the sort of the weekly drop as opposed to sort of the binge model.”

Jenkins said some shows — like Peacock’s “Love Island USA” — need “a moment to sort of build. And sort of [ask], are you seeing green shoots? Are you seeing that it’s hitting the right audience?” For “Love Island USA,” the real tipping point was Season 6 and the addition of Ariana Madix coming off a buzzy season of “Vanderpump Rules,” with a really established fan base there, she added.

As for the threat of AI, Blumhouse’s Prakash, whose studio was behind two big summer box-office hits from YouTube creators — “Obsession” and “Backrooms” — said he thinks short-form, maybe lower-production value creator content is “the most likely to get disrupted by whatever they’re calling ‘AI slop.'”

To Prakesh, “Obsession” and “Backrooms” could not have been created from an AI prompt. “Those are not the kinds of things that could be spat out of algorithms and large language models,” he said.

And, he said, the two horror films showed that “a scary theatrical event” could compel people “to leave their homes for that experience.” And he said a takeaway for him is that Hollywood should be doing more to serve audiences natively on YouTube.

“YouTube is the probably No. 1 platform for watching filmed entertainment, so it’s not surprising that it’s penetrating the culture in many different ways,” Prakesh said. “I think what was so heartening about the experience that we had was that you had creators who were very popular on YouTube still craving the theatrical experience — and still wanting to take their storytelling to that platform and to deliver it to consumers there, which obviously is what we do.”

As an industry, “we have to figure out how to be present in front of them, not just with trailers and featurettes on YouTube, but like actually have an offering for the consumer on the platform that is increasingly dominant and so young, and where you can find and grow that audience.”

At Crunchyroll, the company is continually asking fans what makes them come back to anime over and over, say Purini. He said Crunchyroll’s research shows that outside of Japan and China, 650 million people watching anime regularly on a weekly basis, and that’s projected to continue to grow globally.

“The visual style, the art is part of it, but what really is the themes and the stories that the Japanese creators tend to tell, to to talk about, and it’s grief, it is fame, it is found family, it is all of those things,” Purini said. “But really, what our fans are telling us is there are stories that are relatable characters, but the stories that feel real, but are very different from other stories that they get in their entertainment mix.”

Jenkins said that one of the things the industry lost sight of during the peak TV bubble was that “sort of the difference between, I like to call it capital C content and lowercase C content. It’s not just about tonnage. At the end of the day, it starts and begins with great stories and great storytellers. And what works are things that audiences emotionally connect to. They make you feel something.”

Clancy Collins said that over the years, there’s become less and less of a distinction between the programming on streaming services vs. linear TV. “Our mission statement from the studio is just to be selling to as many outlets as possible,” she said. “So we obviously have a broadcast business that we’re very incredibly proud of. But you know, we’re at 30 shows across 10 platforms… and capitalizing on our independence to be able to sell everywhere and offer our creators that flexibility.”

The panel was moderated by Michael Schneider, Variety‘s executive editor for TV. The daylong event is being held at the Four Seasons in Beverly Hills.

articles.article_title: Learn how Fort Collins police use cameras, AI at technology showcase
articles.heading: Learn how Fort Collins police use cameras, AI at technology showcase
articles.summary: Fort Collins is hosting a technology showcase Sept. 17 where community members can learn more about how police use cameras, AI and other technology.
articles.content:
Learn how Fort Collins police use cameras, AI at technology showcase
Fort Collins community members are invited to a technology showcase hosted by the city on Sept. 17 to learn more about how Fort Collins Police Services uses various technologies, including camera systems and artificial intelligence.
This showcase and panel discussion comes three months after Fort Collins City Council voted to immediately cancel its contract with Flock Safety, a company that provides an automated license plate reader system. The vote followed six months of public pushback on the use of the system over privacy and data usage concerns.
Technologies, systems and programs discussed at the Sept. 17 event will include:
- Traffic cameras.
- Speed/red-light cameras.
- Text-to-911.
- Body-worn cameras and Draft One AI report writing software.
- Road weather management mobile detectors.
- GIS usage.
- The city's drone program.
- Infrastructure scanning pilot program.
- Transformer loading dashboard.
The event will be held at the Fort Collins Senior Center, 1200 Raintree Drive, and doors open at 5:45 p.m., according to a news release. It will include a panel presentation from police, FC911, and the city's light and power and geographic information system (GIS) departments.
There will be an opportunity for attendees to ask questions.
Police say the goal of the showcase is to help the community better understand the city's decision-making processes behind technology uses as the city is working on developing a policy for the responsible use and management of surveillance technology "focusing on key principles of accountability, transparency, data management, privacy, and appropriate oversight of the technology and data collected," according to the news release.
While Flock Safety cameras have been removed from Fort Collins city-owned property, these cameras remain on private property and in surrounding communities, including in the parking lots of private businesses and throughout unincorporated Larimer County. Wellington and other residents in nearby towns have voiced concerns over the county's and their towns' ongoing contracts with Flock Safety.
Reporter Rebecca Powell contributed to this article.

articles.article_title: West Haven turns to technology to curb loud cars along shoreline
articles.heading: West Haven turns to technology to curb loud cars along shoreline
articles.summary: People living along the shoreline in West Haven said loud cars have long disrupted their neighborhoods, and the city is now taking steps to address the problem.
articles.content:
West Haven turns to technology to curb loud cars along shoreline
City to install noise detection devices within the next month
HARTFORD, Conn. (WFSB) - People living along the shoreline in West Haven said loud cars have long disrupted their neighborhoods, and the city is now taking steps to address the problem.
Heidi Menoane said she has lived along the shoreline for about 30 years.
“Whether it’s in the morning, the afternoon, two o’clock in the morning, your house vibrates,” Menoane said.
“It’s annoying to the rest of us. We shouldn’t have to endure it,” Menoane said.
City’s response
West Haven Mayor Dorinda Borer has heard complaints from residents like Menoane.
“Folks like to drive our coastline which we welcome them to do, but it’s a residential neighborhood,” Borer said.
The city plans to install four noise detection devices along the shore, where cameras are already in place. If someone exceeds the decibel limit, police will get an alert.
A first offense costs $100. Each repeat violation adds another $100.
“The fine is enough where it’s going to make a statement, but not crush anybody. It sends a message,” Borer said.
Privacy and installation timeline
Borer said the devices are secure. They are not recording any conversations, and all information stays within the West Haven Police Department.
“It would be wonderful for me,” Menoane said.
The devices are set to be installed within the next month.

articles.title: NJIT’s 2026 'Celebration' to Honor Leaders in Education, Technology and Industry
articles.description: NJIT’s 2026 'Celebration' to Honor Leaders in Education, Technology and Industry NJIT News
articles.description_html: NJIT’s 2026 'Celebration' to Honor Leaders in Education, Technology and Industry  NJIT News
articles.article_title: NJIT’s 2026 'Celebration' to Honor Leaders in Education, Technology and Industry
articles.heading: NJIT’s 2026 'Celebration' to Honor Leaders in Education, Technology and Industry
articles.summary: New Jersey Institute of Technology’s annual Celebration gala will take place Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, at The Grove in Cedar Grove, New Jersey, honoring six individuals and organizations whose achievements exemplify leadership, innovation, service and commitment to the university.
articles.content:
New Jersey Institute of Technology’s annual Celebration gala will take place Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, at The Grove in Cedar Grove, New Jersey, honoring six individuals and organizations whose achievements exemplify leadership, innovation, service and commitment to the university.
The black-tie event brings together alumni, business leaders and friends of NJIT for an evening of dinner, dancing and awards in support of student scholarships. Established in 1995 to benefit the Albert Dorman Honors College, Celebration has supported students across all six of NJIT’s colleges since 2007.
Celebration has raised more than $10 million in endowed scholarship funds since its founding. The 2025 gala drew the largest audience in the event’s history and raised a record amount, building new momentum for NJIT’s efforts to make a transformative education accessible to talented and motivated students. Serving as student speaker this year is Sydney Burlingame-Grissom, a chemical engineering student, Albert Dorman Honors scholar and midfielder for the Women’s Soccer team.
“Celebration brings the NJIT community together around two of our most important commitments: creating opportunities for our students and recognizing people and organizations whose leadership has a meaningful impact on society,” said NJIT Interim President John A. Pelesko. “This year’s honorees reflect the ingenuity, service and generosity that define our university and its extended community.”
The 2026 honorees are:
Dr. Joel Bloom — University Medal for Lifetime Achievement
Bloom served NJIT for three decades, culminating in his tenure as the university’s eighth president from 2011 to 2022. He joined NJIT as a vice president in 1990 and became the inaugural dean of the Albert Dorman Honors College in 1998, overseeing its growth into a nationally recognized honors college.
As president, Bloom led NJIT through a period of significant expansion in enrollment, research, fundraising and campus development. Under his leadership, the university completed a $200 million fundraising campaign, added approximately 1 million square feet of teaching and research facilities, expanded its faculty and strengthened its standing as a national research university and engine of economic mobility. Before joining NJIT, Bloom worked in industry, public education and state government, including service as an assistant commissioner in the New Jersey Department of Education.
Leon K. Baptiste ’91 — Lifetime Alumni Leadership Award
Baptiste is the founder and CEO of LB Electric, an electrical contracting and engineering firm he established in 1999. With more than 38 years of experience, he has helped lead major electrical projects across New Jersey and New York, including work associated with the Prudential Center, Newark Liberty International Airport’s Terminal A, the Port Authority’s Harrison Station, East Side Access and the Mario M. Cuomo Bridge.
A graduate of NJIT’s electrical engineering program, Baptiste remains closely engaged with the university as chair of the Electrical and Computer Engineering Industry Advisory Board and a member of the Newark College of Engineering Board of Visitors and the Educational Opportunity Program Industry Advisory Board. He also established the LB Training Center to provide college students, urban youth and people reentering the workforce with education and training in solar-energy technologies.
Komal Dangi ’19 — Edward F. Weston Medal for Professional Achievement
Dangi is the founder and CEO of Synkriom and VeriKlick and has more than 15 years of experience in the information-technology industry. An entrepreneur who has launched six startups globally, she is recognized for developing technology-driven businesses while advocating for women and members of historically marginalized communities.
Dangi earned a master’s degree in computer science and an MBA from NJIT. She has held leadership roles with the Asian Indian Chamber of Commerce and has supported initiatives focused on supplier diversity, community engagement and STEM education. Her professional and civic contributions have been recognized by organizations in New Jersey and New York.
Richard Schatzberg ’93 — University Award for Entrepreneurial Leadership
Schatzberg is a founding member and chief commercial officer of NeST Technologies Corp., where he leads revenue generation and strategic planning and oversees technical operations serving the insurance, banking and financial-services sectors.
An NJIT alumnus, Schatzberg is chair of the Albert Dorman Honors College Board of Visitors and a member of the C-Suite Board of the New Jersey Innovation Institute. His record of service has also included board roles with organizations advancing employment, accessibility and inclusion for people with disabilities, including The Viscardi Center, the National Business and Disability Council, Ruh Global and the Runway of Dreams Foundation.
Fiserv — Outstanding Corporate Partner
Fiserv is a global financial-technology company connecting commerce and financial services through platforms spanning payments, account processing, digital banking, merchant services and e-commerce. A Fortune 500 and S&P 500 company, Fiserv maintains a significant presence in New Jersey through its Innovation Center in Berkeley Heights, a 428,000-square-foot hub for collaboration and financial-technology development.
Fiserv’s engagement with NJIT has included recruiting students and graduates, participating in university career fairs and supporting experiential opportunities such as GirlHacks, NJIT’s annual hackathon centered on empowering women and nonbinary students in technology. The partnership also extends to university leadership through Fiserv Senior Vice President Nancy Hall’s service on the NJIT Foundation Board of Directors.
Made Scientific — Special Friends to the University
Made Scientific is a Princeton, New Jersey-based cell-therapy contract development and manufacturing organization specializing in the development, production and release of autologous and allogeneic cell-therapy products for clinical and commercial use.
The company combines specialized technical expertise with development and manufacturing capabilities designed to help cell-therapy organizations bring treatments from early-stage development to scalable production. Made Scientific is supported by GC Corporation, a global pharmaceutical and biotechnology company.
For complete honoree biographies and additional information about Celebration, visit njit.edu/celebration.
Celebration remains a cornerstone of NJIT’s commitment to access and excellence, helping ensure that future generations of engineers, architects, scientists, computing professionals, entrepreneurs and other leaders can pursue an NJIT education and make an impact in New Jersey and beyond.

articles.heading: Onkos Surgical® expands access to NanoCept® Antibacterial Technology for patients requiring total femoral replacement
articles.summary: Onkos Surgical® expands access to NanoCept® Antibacterial Technology for patients requiring total femoral replacement – Ortho Spine News Ortho Spine News
articles.content:
PARSIPPANY-TROY HILLS, N.J., Sept. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Onkos Surgical today announced the market release of the ELEOSTM Total Femoral Adapter with NanoCept® Antibacterial Technology, expanding the availability of NanoCept for patients undergoing one of the most complex and high-risk orthopaedic reconstruction procedures.
Since its introduction in December 2024, NanoCept Antibacterial Technology has been available on ELEOS implant midsections used in complex knee and hip reconstructions. To date, more than 500 patients have received ELEOS implants featuring NanoCept.
The launch of the ELEOS Total Femoral Adapter with NanoCept further expands the portfolio to support patients requiring complete femoral replacement.
“It is incredibly reassuring to know that patients requiring a total femoral replacement will now have access to antibacterial implants. Total femurs are among the most complex procedures we perform, and many of the patients who require them are already immunocompromised,” said Julia Visgauss, M.D., Chief of the Orthopaedic Oncology Division at Duke Health.
“Anything we can do to reduce risk and improve outcomes can make a meaningful difference in their recovery and quality of life. The innovation we’re seeing in this space is truly encouraging,” said Dr. Visgauss, who is also an investigator in a post-market study of NanoCept and has been a consultant for Onkos.
The ELEOS Total Femoral Adapter with NanoCept is the first product to be produced and coated at Onkos Surgical’s newly opened NanoCept Innovation Center in Bridgewater, New Jersey, marking an important milestone in the company’s efforts to expand access to NanoCept across the broader ELEOS product portfolio.
“Today is a real high point for Onkos,” said Patrick Treacy, CEO and Co-Founder of Onkos Surgical. “As we continue to expand the ELEOS with NanoCept product offering, it is fitting that we begin with Total Femoral Replacement, supporting some of the most vulnerable patients undergoing complex orthopaedic oncology and revision procedures.”
Onkos is continuing to expand the capabilities of its NanoCept Innovation Center, with plans to have the antibacterial coating available on additional ELEOS products in the coming months.
About NanoCept®
Onkos received De Novo market authorization from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in April of 2024 for its NanoCept Antibacterial Technology for use with the ELEOS™ Limb Salvage System. Pre-clinical testing showed that NanoCept Antibacterial Technology has up to a 99.999% (5-log reduction) kill rate of bacteria that are commonly found in the operating room environment.
The device coating is not intended for the treatment of existing infections or prevention of future infections in patients. The clinical impact of bacterial reduction from the NanoCept coating, including prevention of infection or reduction of infection risk in patients, has not been evaluated in human clinical studies.

articles.title: The Real Path to Better Government Technology
articles.description: The Real Path to Better Government Technology Vital City
articles.description_html: The Real Path to Better Government Technology  Vital City
articles.article_title: The Real Path to Better Government Technology
articles.heading: The Real Path to Better Government Technology
articles.summary: We need to change the way the City buys software.
articles.content:
We need to change the way the City buys software.
You don’t have to look very far in New York to find failed government technology projects. A City Comptroller’s report released in August found that veterans still struggle to use the VetConnectNYC online portal to access services, despite a $2 million investment and eight years of work. The City’s Office of Technology and Innovation requested an additional $81 million in the 2026 budget to shore up another failed digital service, the “one-stop-shop” MyCity app, after already spending four years and $100 million on development. The Metropolitan Transportation Authority is reportedly planning to pilot “virtual OMNY cards,” part of a contract signed in 2017 that has suffered extensive delays, scope reduction, and millions of dollars in change orders.
Failures of this magnitude are not unusual in government tech. Across a database of over 2,700 projects, researchers found that the median U.S. government IT project costs 310% of the estimated price.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s lauded Public Interest Technology (PIT) Crews — five teams of technologists designed to swoop in to agencies and deliver the mayor’s top digital priorities — are a positive start to addressing the overwhelming amount of technical debt in city agencies. There is no question that city government needs more professionals with skills that meet the moment. However, delivering digital services on time, on budget and in ways that actually solve user needs requires addressing government functions beyond IT. Most of the tools for transforming government technology are (in the words of Matthew Burton, who wrote about the problem recently for Vital City) “starkly non-technological.”
Fixing tech procurement is the most important piece to get right. Despite recent successes by in-house development teams, digital government transformation at scale requires a hybrid staffing model, where the talent of in-house teams is complemented by that of external vendors. Contracting out offers temporary surge capacity of software developers with niche skills. It also responds to the present realities that government tech staff are hindered by: a lengthy and cumbersome civil service hiring process, comparatively low salaries and operating budget constraints.
Which is to say, though it may make a lot of sense to bulk up government tech, contracting out will still be necessary. The key is to do it right.
Although some tech can be purchased off-the-shelf, the scale and complexity of New York City government obligations, regulations and public-sector union rules often require custom software. And here, we need a new model.
New York City and State agencies procure custom software using a linear, step-by-step model known as “waterfall.” Requirements are fully specified at the start of a project, and modifications typically require costly contract change orders, much like a vacation package with a fully-booked itinerary that cannot be altered without major fees. Vendors are paid based on predefined project milestones, instead of being paid for the delivery of functional code. Software is delivered at the end of the development cycle, meaning that government agencies only have the chance to provide feedback at the end of a project, months or even years after requirements were drafted. Sadly, only 13% of “waterfall” projects succeed.
Government oversight bodies would have you believe that exhaustive requirements and more vigilant contract monitoring are the only ways to improve government technology, but they are not. The “Agile” approach to software procurement uses minimal requirements, clear objectives and iterative cycles of user research, development, testing and deployment that allow for continuous improvement. This is the standard for private sector software development and what actually works, if done correctly, for government agencies, too. Initiatives built using Agile succeed at three times the rate of waterfall projects, where “successful” means on time and on budget, with a satisfactory result.
This is clearly a wiser way to develop software that will make government work better.
The good news is that New York City doesn’t have to start from scratch. Last year, the New York State Higher Education Services Corporation (HESC) issued the first “Agile RFP” in the state. Built on the foundation of successful examples from across the federal government, like Direct File, that RFP brought best practice to the State and did the hard part of adjusting contract terms and conditions to the New York State context. The HESC RFP, for example, shifts contract performance measurement away from checkbox fulfillment of pre-defined project requirements (the waterfall way) to assessment of vendor work based on code quality and performance standards.
But if the City is serious about developing software more intelligently, it needs to change some practices. Software development using Agile implies new ways of working. Vendors work in teams of four to nine people (called “Scrum teams” in Agile lingo) that are tightly coupled with a product owner and technical lead from a government agency. For early stage product development initiatives, only a single Scrum team may be required. Its work is nimble and iterative; fluid communication and integrated teamwork are key.
The City’s current approach to procurement makes this way of working difficult, if not impossible. Local Law 2019/174 specifies percentage goals of total annual agency expenditure for six classes of minority-owned businesses, adding up to 73.52% of total spend for professional service contracts. In my experience, procurement officers apply all or most of these percentage goals across all contracts. Requiring blanket target participation rates on a single Scrum team would imply a minimum of six distinct companies supplying staff for a four-person team — a certain (and nonsensical) recipe for failure.
To get the most from Agile procurement, the City Council, the City’s chief procurement officer, and the City’s Procurement Policy Board should unite to eliminate participation goals for these contracts. This change to procurement policy has nothing to do with whether you believe in supporting minorities and everything to do with whether procurement supports the ways of working necessary for modern software development using Agile.
Beyond procurement, enabling a leap forward in government technology requires changes to the city budget itself. Modern software development is not a one-time capital expense, like buying Microsoft Office was in 2010. It is an ongoing effort that requires a team (and a budget) over time to provide an experience analogous to routine updates of a Google Chrome browser. Even when vendors leave after a large digital product build, agency staff continue to respond to evolving user needs through continuous development. This implies a small but consistent budget allocation for technologists. This “product model,” which combines Agile procurement and development with continuous improvement and funding, stands in sharp contrast to government’s traditional “project model” of one-time funding, rigid scope and time-bound outputs.
New York’s legacy of fiscal austerity, however, haunts any increase (albeit small) to the operating budget, despite the lower net cost and higher rate of success of the product model. The City’s Office of Management and Budget should get on board with a shift toward the product model and approve operating budget funding streams for technologists to support software products. In practice, this may look like budgeting for “capabilities” that require multiple software products or systems, rather than budgeting one product at a time. According to policy researchers at the Niskanen Center, “a ‘capability’ might be eligibility and enrollment, claims processing or benefits delivery.” A block of funds would be designated for each capability, including all the software necessary for that capability, giving product teams the responsibility for end-to-end delivery of the capability. This is analogous to setting aside a budget to remodel your entire kitchen, rather than paying for the cabinets and drawers this year and leaving a gaping hole where the countertops should be until some unknown future date.
Enabling technological transformation in City agencies also requires a shift in the way legal teams attempt to mitigate risk. General counsel and auditors often want “one throat to choke,” namely a vendor’s, when something goes wrong. With the traditional waterfall approach to software procurement, agencies try to shift all risk back to the vendor. They rely on meeting specific contractual requirements and adhering to Gantt charts to determine whether a vendor has delivered a product, regardless of whether the software meets users’ needs. Risk is mitigated through close contract monitoring and fines for late or incomplete delivery. The extraordinarily high failure rate of software projects indicates that these risk mitigation measures simply don’t work.
In contrast, software procurement using Agile begins with a statement of objectives. Government staff have significantly more control over software development because they are intimately involved in every step of the process (e.g., identifying tasks, user research, testing, quality assurance, deployment, system integration). The “test-and-learn” approach inherent to Agile means faster identification and correction of problems, and smaller, controlled failures. These failures can be rectified through the iterative development cycle, rather than waiting until the end of the traditional “project” model for user testing. Risk can be further reduced by committing vendor-developed source code to the public domain, a practice encouraged by the General Services Administration’s former technology branch and the Department of Defense.
Despite the successful Agile track record, it feels more risky than the status quo. It will be uncomfortable, but necessary, for the Mayor’s Office of Contract Services, agency attorneys and the City Comptroller to accept that risk mitigation under the “product” model looks different from the “project” model. What this means, in practice, is that contract oversight must shift from output (did the vendor deliver the requirement) to outcomes (did the vendor team, under staff guidance, build something that meets user needs). The recommended short duration (less than three years) and low cost ($2 million or less, annually per contract) of an Agile contract allows for a quick pivot if a vendor doesn’t perform.
Lastly, technologists cannot fix processes that agency staff struggle to articulate. It is no small task to explain “how things work,” when such knowledge is tacit, still on paper or housed in a legacy system. Agency leaders must get their own houses in order, documenting existing workflows and requirements, information that will accelerate the work of the PIT Crews, an agency’s own technologists or vendors.
In New York, the area most ripe for stalling tech projects is labor relations. Benefits obtained through the collective bargaining process are least likely to have short-term flexibility for modifications that might facilitate the adoption of new technology or permit the use of either commercial off-the-shelf software or software as a service. Rigid constraints, whether explicitly written into contracts or ossified through longstanding practice, drive custom software design and can easily increase costs. For example, unlike the majority of transit operators in the United States, subway conductors and operators in New York City select their weekly days off independently from the shifts and specific operational jobs they work (“cafeteria style picking”). This unusual procedure impedes automation and increases costs, relative to “roster-based” job selection (where operators select bundled days off and vehicle runs); it also precludes the use of most existing software.
Knowing what is bendable is crucial for tech system design. Layers of memos that modify a decades-old agreement, rather than an updated and comprehensive document detailing all current aspects of a labor agreement, present major barriers to digitalization and software development. Labor relations teams must be able to communicate the restrictions of current labor agreements with precision and in a way that technologists can translate into code.
We need better government tech, but the problems preventing us from getting it are not technological. Transforming government tech depends on an overhaul of non-technological government functions. That must not wait.

articles.title: Groundbreaking technology uses quantum sensors to measure heart activity
articles.description: Groundbreaking technology uses quantum sensors to measure heart activity News-Medical
articles.description_html: Groundbreaking technology uses quantum sensors to measure heart activity  News-Medical
articles.article_title: Groundbreaking technology uses quantum sensors to measure heart activity
articles.heading: Groundbreaking technology uses quantum sensors to measure heart activity
articles.summary: Physicists at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU) have developed a groundbreaking technology that uses quantum sensors to measure biomagnetic signals, such as heart activity.
articles.content:
Physicists at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU) have developed a groundbreaking technology that uses quantum sensors to measure biomagnetic signals, such as heart activity. Researchers from the DIAQNOS (DIAmond-based Quantum Sensing for NeurOSurgery) flagship project, funded by the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology, and Space, and coordinated by Dr. Arne Wickenbrock in Mainz, have demonstrated the potential of quantum technology for future medical applications. To this end, researchers in the group led by Prof. Dr. Dmitry Budker - a member of the PRISMA++ Cluster of Excellence and the Helmholtz Institute Mainz - used nitrogen vacancies (NV) in diamonds, as reported in a recent article in the journal Science Advances. Muhib Omar, a doctoral student in Budker's research group and the coordinating author of the article, developed the new quantum sensor during his doctoral research. Thanks to its compact size and its ability to function at room temperature, this NV-based sensor opens up new avenues for improving the measurement of magnetic signals from the heart or the brain. It could be used for the early detection of conditions such as myocarditis or epilepsy.
NV centers form when a vacancy in the diamond lattice is located directly next to a nitrogen atom that has been incorporated into the diamond in place of a carbon atom. By observing the energy levels of these centers, researchers can measure a wide range of physical phenomena such as magnetic or electric fields, temperature, and mechanical stress with high precision.
These results are the product of over ten years of development work. We work closely with neurosurgeons to ensure that our technologies do not remain confined to the laboratory but find clear practical applications. Our primary goal is to develop highly sensitive sensors that function outside the laboratory and can fulfill important societal needs."
Dr. Arne Wickenbrock, Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz
The researchers of the DIAQNOS project used three systems developed independently by the project partners JGU, the Universities of Stuttgart and Freiburg, as well as by the startup Q.ANT GmbH, to measure the heart's magnetic field. This is in contrast to the other two systems, that use such fields to filter out magnetic interference from the environment.

There are currently two common methods to measure heart activity: electrocardiography (ECG) and magnetocardiography (MCG). While ECG uses electrode patches applied to the patient's skin to measure the electrical activity within the heart, MCG methods detect magnetic fields. ECG is widely used, but susceptible to the differing conductivity of body tissues. Certain medical scenarios, such as burn wounds, can also make it impossible to place electrodes on the skin directly. In contrast, MCG needs no contact with the skin and is only minimally influenced by tissue conductivity. Since the method requires highly sensitive magnetometers, it has historically relied on high-cost, complex technologies such as superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs), and optically-pumped magnetometers (OPMs).
The system from the JGU group, based on NV centers in diamonds, is an alternative that offers significant advantages over existing MCG methods. The most important difference is the small size of the sensor: a truncated diamond pyramid with a volume of less than 0.5 cubic millimeters, which makes it easy to transport. Another advantage is that, unlike SQUID or OPM based systems, NV magnetometers operate at room temperature. This makes them suitable for direct use on the patient's skin and allows them to be applied at any desired location. This opens up the possibility of more precise mapping of biomagnetic signals, such as 3D reconstruction of the heart's electrical conduction system or the measurement of fetal heart activity. "NV magnetometers are characterized by fast initialization, excellent biocompatibility, and stable operation over a wide temperature range. This makes them particularly attractive for biomedical applications," summarized Arne Wickenbrock.
The potential is high but technical challenges remain
While the study shows the promise of NV diamond magnetometers, there remains a performance gap compared to SQUIDs and OPMs, which still offer higher sensitivity and better signal-to-noise ratios. However, as development progresses, application possibilities beyond the clinical field are opening up: the unique combination of a wide dynamic range, noise suppression, and scalable geometry makes NV magnetometers suitable for various novel biomedical applications.
Thanks to their compact size, the detectors can be easily combined with improvement mechanisms that could enable them to achieve ECG-like quality. One example of such mechanisms are so-called flux concentrators: structures that can concentrate the magnetic flux within the diamonds and thereby amplify magnetic signals. Thanks to the small volume of the NV sensors, amplifications of more than a factor of 100 can be achieved. The research and development of flux concentrators that function at room temperature is one of Muhib Omar's main areas of focus. "Adapting magnetic structures to optimally concentrate the magnetic field lines from a source within the diamond is the path to bringing these quantum technologies into practical use." Another area of application is surgical oncology. In this context, the difference in magnetic field between two spatially separated sensors forming a gradiometer is measured. The method also supports intraoperative nerve monitoring in unshielded environments. The spatial sensitivity to field gradients also facilitates, for example, the noninvasive separation of maternal and fetal heart signals for prenatal monitoring. Above all, NV gradiometers could enable portable magnetoencephalography systems to operate at room temperature, thereby opening up new possibilities for neurological diagnostics or next-generation brain-computer interfaces (BCIs).

articles.article_title: Kwik Fill Choses PAR as Technology Partner
articles.heading: Kwik Fill Choses PAR as Technology Partner
articles.summary: The partnership includes Kwik Fill’s loyalty, mobile app, enterprise intelligence and full-stack tobacco loyalty capabilities.
articles.content:
The partnership includes Kwik Fill’s loyalty, mobile app, enterprise intelligence and full-stack tobacco loyalty capabilities.

Sep 17, 2026 | 2 min read

Kwik Fill has chosen PAR Technology as a “strategic technology partner,” according to a press release . The brands said the long-term partnership will help Kwik Fill deliver more relevant, personalized customer experiences while building a stronger foundation for future growth and innovation.

“Through the partnership, Kwik Fill will leverage PAR Retail’s platform and PAR Intelligence to support its vision for modern retail. …Kwik Fill’s partnership with PAR Retail spans the full breadth of the platform, including loyalty, mobile app, enterprise intelligence and full-stack tobacco loyalty capabilities. This reflects a comprehensive, long-term investment in how the brand understands and serves its guests,” PAR said.

“As we evaluated potential partners, PAR Retail stood apart through its vision for the future of convenience retail and its ability to combine guest engagement with actionable AI-driven insights,” said Roy Williams, senior vice president marketing at United Refining Company, parent company of Kwik Fill. “PAR Intelligence was a significant differentiator for our team. We see tremendous opportunity to leverage the platform as we continue enhancing the experiences we deliver to our guests.”

In other recent Kwik Fill news, last month the retailer announced the extension of its partnership with the Buffalo Bills , “reinforcing a successful relationship built on community engagement, fan experiences and shared values.”

The retailer said the extended partnership will continue to create opportunities for fan engagement through promotions, special events and exclusive experiences.

articles.title: OpenAI flags concerning new AI behavior and vows to track it more closely
articles.description: OpenAI flags concerning new AI behavior and vows to track it more closely spectrumlocalnews.com
articles.description_html: OpenAI flags concerning new AI behavior and vows to track it more closely  spectrumlocalnews.com
articles.article_title: OpenAI flags concerning new AI behavior and vows to track it more closely
articles.heading: OpenAI flags concerning new AI behavior and vows to track it more closely
articles.summary: OpenAI has disclosed six reports
articles.content:
OpenAI has disclosed six reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in artificial-intelligence models as the debate on AI safety becomes increasingly heated.
The AI company also said Wednesday it was introducing a new framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances of what it called “misalignment,” including cases where AI models acted without authorization, coordinated with other models or evaded oversight.
OpenAI’s latest announcement came as U.S. AI bosses, including the leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic, are calling for a slowdown in the technology’s development over safety concerns.
Among the new cases reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted “jailbreak-like instructions” into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be “freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots.”
In another instance, an AI “agent” used computer code to come up with the answer to a question, but, in order to have an online source to cite, it uploaded a file to the public internet without asking the user.
During training of an AI model called 5.6-sol, the model instructed itself to invent missing data, and an agent wrote a message to remind itself to hide mismatched information.
The six reports were discovered during training or evaluation over the past months, OpenAI said.
“As AI systems grow more advanced and more widely deployed, we need to build a broader and better-informed consensus on the progress of alignment research,” OpenAI wrote in a blog post as it disclosed the events.
“Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves,” the company said.
Wednesday’s new cases followed OpenAI’s disclosure in July that its rogue AI system hacked into AI startup Hugging Face. Anthropic also said the same month that its AI models hacked into three organizations during testing.
AI “agents” are becoming smarter and have become “more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception, and concealment,” said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at technology research and advisory group Omdia.
That’s making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said.
OpenAI’s new tracking and disclosure framework, meanwhile, can help push for other AI developers to also adopt similar practices.
“That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction,” Su added.
