articles.title: UC Berkeley technology career fair draws hundreds of jobseekers
articles.description: UC Berkeley technology career fair draws hundreds of jobseekers Daily Cal
articles.description_html: UC Berkeley technology career fair draws hundreds of jobseekers  Daily Cal
articles.article_title: UC Berkeley technology career fair draws hundreds of jobseekers
articles.heading: UC Berkeley technology career fair draws hundreds of jobseekers
articles.summary: UC Berkeley held its annual Engineering and Technology Career Fair, previously known as the EECS Career Fair, Tuesday, drawing hundreds of students seeking jobs in the technology industry.
articles.content:
UC Berkeley held its annual Engineering and Technology Career Fair, previously known as the EECS Career Fair, Tuesday, drawing hundreds of students seeking jobs in the technology industry.
Technology companies, mostly representing startup and mid-sized companies, crowded booths into the Pauley Ballroom in the Martin Luther King Jr. Student Union building for the fair.
The longest lines formed around industry giants such as Amazon and buzzy companies such as Cerebras, which creates specialized chips to run AI models,and Archer Aviation, which creates flying cars and drones.
“It’s always jobs, man,” said campus junior Prithvi Dixit. “The economy’s tough, so (I’m) looking for jobs.”
Some students at the event said they had already had one or more previous internships, but attended the fair to find more job opportunities.
Students said the number of startups at the fair represented a shift in what UC Berkeley students look for in an employer; smaller companies can offer more direct experience in a job than big technology companies such as Google and Apple, and also allow students to get in on the ground floor.
“I feel like in general, big companies already have a ton of applicants because people know when their applications release,” said UC Berkeley junior Arin Kadakia. “Some companies are probably trying to get their name out, right? They want people here at Berkeley to know what they do. They want qualified applicants from Berkeley as well.”
UC Berkeley’s career fair has been a flashpoint for the pressures that computer science majors face in the age of AI, including a shrinking job market. Data from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis indicates that online job postings for software engineering jobs are down about 25% from pre-pandemic levels.
“We’re here at Berkeley Career Fair because Berkeley makes some of the best engineers in the world, and it’s a really deep talent pool to pull from,” said UC Berkeley alum Phillip Chu. Chu is an engineer at Density AI, a small company creating hardware to help run AI models which had a booth at the fair. “I think Berkeley as an institution, as a place to come to school, it rewards scrappiness.”
The Engineering and Technology career fair is a rebrand of the EECS career fair that campus hosted in previous years.
The EECS career fair previously only invited companies that made donations to campus to become Berkeley Circle partners.Many large technology companies in the Berkeley Circle program, including TikTok, Bloomberg and Databricks, did not attend the fair this year.

articles.title: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildings
articles.description: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildings The Guardian
articles.description_html: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildings  The Guardian
articles.article_title: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildings
articles.heading: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildings
articles.summary: Minister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplaces
articles.content:
The Albanese government is considering a “world-leading” ban on smart glasses in its offices and service centres as councils around Australia push the technology out of public spaces over privacy fears.
The government has avoided a sweeping ban on the import of the camera-equipped technology and encouraged individual workplaces to set their own rules.
The public service minister, Katy Gallagher, said on Thursday she had asked the Australian public service for advice on whether the glasses should be prohibited.
“We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants,” Gallagher said.
“Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information.”
Commonwealth-run workplaces range from bureaucrats’ offices to Centrelink service centres and CSIRO laboratories.
Schools and hospitals run by state governments would be left to set their own rules over the technology, which have grown increasingly popular but raised public outcry.
A University of Sydney study of smart glasses-filmed videos posted on Instagram found 60% of a sample could be classified as potential harassment.
The Albanese government said it was seeking to set a world-leading standard. So far, no national government has banned the glasses’ use across their agencies.
Courts in England and Wales in the UK and New York state in the US have banned the technology, while the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency reportedly classified them as body-worn cameras and barred them from the “federal workspace”.
A local council in Sydney on Tuesday became the latest to issue a targeted bans on the use of the technology. Canterbury-Bankstown’s mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, decried what he called “pervert glasses” as the council barred the wearable tech from public pools.
In August, Brisbane city council became the first to ban the glasses from pools and Melbourne’s Yarra city council has banned them from playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms.
The City of Sydney and the Blacktown city councils have prohibited pool patrons from using smart glasses to record.
Speaking to Channel Seven earlier this month, the federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, praised councils’ decisions and said she would consult businesses on their approach.
“Businesses know that good privacy is good business,” Rowland said.
“But … we want to make sure we get the balance right and we don’t unfairly discriminate against people who are using this technology to better participate in society.”
Vision Australia and some people living with disabilities have praised the technology as a support for people who are blind or have low vision. Rowland said the government was not pursuing a ban but had not “ruled anything out”.
Gallagher said she wanted the Australian public service to set the national standard as a “model employer”.
“Technology is changing rapidly and as a major employer the Commonwealth needs to make sure our workplace policies keep pace,” Gallagher said.
Pending restrictions on smart glasses would be the federal government’s latest workplace technology reform after it issued guidance on the use of AI in the public service last week.
The guidelines indicate employees would not need to be consulted on every new tool but should be consulted for major initiatives or changes to how they carry out work.
Major businesses will contribute to new national guidelines on AI in workplaces, with Commonwealth Bank, Microsoft, AGL, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and Ramsay Health Care to attend a roundtable on Friday.
Amanda Rishworth, the employment minister, said the government wanted to use the roundtable to take on the lessons of businesses already using AI.
“Workers and businesses need the capability to adopt new technologies with confidence that appropriate safeguards are in place,” Rishworth said.
Additional reporting from Caitlin Cassidy

articles.heading: Vitality and Google Expand Technology Partnership to Bring AI-Driven Health Platform to the United States to Incentivize Healthier Behaviors
articles.summary: Vitality AI, built on Google Cloud and using Gemini Enterprise, expands into the U.S. market — bringing proven personalized health recommendations, coaching, and incentives to health plans and...
articles.content:
Vitality AI, built on Google Cloud and using Gemini Enterprise, expands into the U.S. market — bringing proven personalized health recommendations, coaching, and incentives to health plans and employers at scale
NEW YORK, Sept. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Vitality, a global leader in behavioral change across insurance and health plans, in partnership with Google, today announced the extension of Vitality AI into the United States. Built on Google Cloud and Gemini Enterprise, the platform is already delivering measurable results internationally addressing one of healthcare's most persistent challenges: helping people take meaningful action to improve their health.
The expansion comes as U.S. employers face mounting employee health benefit costs, health plans experience low engagement, and people struggle to navigate complex healthcare systems. Vitality AI delivers a solution through personalized recommendations, coaching, and incentives to generate long-term healthier behaviors.
Vitality AI uses Google Cloud's leading AI and data analytics technologies, including Gemini Enterprise and Google's Gemini models, coupled with Vitality's dataset of more than 2,800 unique health and behavioral dimensions. By analyzing an individual's health profile, lifestyle, and risk factors, Vitality AI generates personalized insights at a 99.2% accuracy rate based on physicians' review.*
Engagement driven clinical and behavioral outcomes of Vitality AI
Vitality AI's personalized incentives have delivered measurable clinical and financial impact across international markets to date:
- Engagement and incentive effectiveness
- Members receiving personalized, AI-driven recommendations were 3.3 times more likely to complete a mental wellbeing assessment, 2.7 times more likely to complete an online health review, and 1.4 times more likely to complete a colorectal cancer screening.*
- 97% of members found their personalized AI reports useful, rating their likelihood of acting on the AI's recommendations at 8.8 out of 10 – which rose to 9.32 out of 10 when localized incentives were added.*
- Physical activity, sleep, and wellbeing
- High-BMI participants achieved a 200%+ increase in physical activity after enrollment on Vitality AI.***
- Members who completed the personalized steps program sustained an average 40% improvement in their daily step counts.****
- Participants who improved their sleep habits gained an average of 2+ hours of additional sleep per week, which was associated with 5% lower in-hospital claims.*****
- 87% of coaching participants presenting with extreme stress reported a measurable improvement in their overall wellbeing.***
- Preventative care and early detection
- Recommending and incentivizing cancer screenings led to an estimated 23,302 additional screenings in 2025, resulting in 219 early detections and an estimated six deaths prevented.******
- Low-cost, targeted rewards proved highly effective – a $31 incentive increased the likelihood of cholesterol testing by 52%, while rewards ranging from $19 to $45 drove similar increases for pap smears, mammograms, and colorectal screenings.******
Driving measurable returns for health payers, employers and insurers
For health payers, employers and insurers, Vitality AI delivers a clear, evidence-based financial case driven by sustained behavior change at scale – achieved through Google's Gemini models and Vitality's longitudinal dataset:
- Return on investment: Engaged clients experience a 4% reduction in healthcare claims costs on average, delivering a 180% return on investment.***
- Reduced risk: The financial benefit increases with employee participation; members who achieve a higher Vitality Status demonstrate 15% lower risk-adjusted claims costs.***
- Workplace productivity gains: The platform recovers an average of 4.4 productive days per employee per year, equivalent to annual savings of $1,047 per employee.***
Emile Stipp, CEO of Vitality AI, said: "Through our partnership with Google, we've shown that AI's impact on health care is no longer a promise – but a proven differentiator. We've seen members take screenings they would have skipped, build and sustain healthy habits, and reduce costs. Extending Vitality AI into the U.S. brings that proof to millions more."
Maureen Costello, Vice President, UK, Ireland and Sub-Saharan Africa, Google Cloud, said: "Having seen the impact of our partnership firsthand across multiple markets, we are thrilled to support Vitality in expanding this proven, AI-powered platform within the U.S. market. Vitality is delivering the level of personalization needed to drive real, measurable health outcomes. We are proud to expand this partnership to help U.S. employers and other members proactively engage with their health. Today's announcement marks the next step in Vitality's partnership with Google, with a goal of extending life expectancy and reducing healthcare-associated costs across the U.S."
The U.S. health gap
The U.S. expansion of Vitality AI directly addresses the mounting costs and navigation complexities that people are facing. For employers and their workforce in particular, data shows:
- Benefits complexity: 41% of U.S. employees struggle to navigate their health benefits and digital health tools.**
- Delayed care: Over half (53%) of workers have delayed or avoided preventative healthcare due to cost, and 49% say they have difficulty navigating the healthcare and insurance system.**
- Mental health barriers: 69% of employees report that workplace stress affects them; only 26% feel they face no barriers to discussing mental health with their employer.**
Notes to Editors
- Vitality's U.S business: Vitality's U.S business has seen strong momentum, including U.S. annual revenue growth of 22% year-over-year and recent acquisitions of Icario, Ramp Health and WellSpark – significantly increasing the reach and services provided by Vitality.
- Vitality AI is now live across Vitality and Discovery and in the UK, South Africa and the United States. Since June 2025, more than 210,000 people in the U.S. have received an AI-driven personalized health action, and 54% have completed at least one AI-recommended health action from Vitality.
- Vitality Status is the tiered reward and engagement framework used by the Vitality Group to measure and incentivize healthy lifestyle choices. Members earn Vitality points by engaging in healthy behaviors to move through the statuses, which are Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum. People are incentivized to earn points or improve their status with a full range of rewards.
About Vitality
Vitality is a global company operating in the insurance market, with presence in over 35 markets and impacting more than 54 million lives. Vitality transforms insurance markets by integrating technology, actuarial science, and behavioral insights to make people healthier and create shared value for clients, insurers, and society. They have a simple yet powerful core purpose: to make people healthier and enhance and protect their lives, and this is done through a pioneering Shared Value Insurance model, which aligns the interests of individuals, insurers, and society: when people become healthier, everyone benefits.
About Google Cloud
Google Cloud offers a powerful, optimized AI stack—including AI infrastructure, leading models like Gemini, data management capabilities, multicloud security solutions, developer tools and platform, as well as agents and applications—that enables organizations to transform their business for the Agentic Era. Customers in more than 200 countries and territories turn to Google Cloud as their trusted technology partner.
Sources
* Vitality data: 99.2% accuracy rate based on review of platform-generated reports by 686 physicians, tested on a cohort of more than 1,300 Discovery staff. Next best action uplift figures (3.3x mental wellbeing assessments, 2.7x online health reviews, 1.4x colorectal cancer screening) from Vitality data.
** Vitality, Opinium US polling data, August 2026: Online survey of 2,000 US workers conducted by Opinium on behalf of Vitality.
*** Vitality data, May 2026: 4% lower claims costs and 180% ROI independently reviewed by Arbital Health. 15% lower overall risk-adjusted claims cost for higher Vitality Statuses independently endorsed by the Validation Institute. 200%+ physical activity increase among high-BMI members, 87% stress improvement among coaching participants, and 4.4 productive days saved per employee per year (average saving of $1,047 per employee annually).
**** Vitality data: members enrolled in the personalized steps program were assigned a starting step target based on their existing activity levels and progressed upward using an algorithm calibrated to the pace at which each individual could sustainably increase their habit. Members who completed the program went from an average of approximately 4,900 steps per day before enrollment to sustaining 6,900 steps after graduating. Analysis is based on a cohort of approximately 1,500 members who completed 5 or more weeks of the program.
***** Vitality, Discovery data: Analysis of Vitality members tracked before and after the launch of the Vitality Sleep Rewards program over a four-month period. 19% of members improved their sleep habit, gaining an average of 19.8 minutes of sleep per night (approximately 2 hours and 20 minutes per week). Analysis of in-hospital claims found that maintaining a good sleep habit is associated with 5% lower in-hospital claims and improving a sleep habit with 7% lower in-hospital claims.
****** Vitality, Discovery data: Personalized incentive and cancer screening data from Vitality members. In 2025, it is estimated that recommending and incentivizing cancer screenings resulted in 23,302 additional screenings, representing a 5.5% increase relative to the historic trends, leading to 219 additional detections and an estimated 6 deaths prevented. Analysis found that while larger rewards (up to $45) produced the strongest behavioral response for some actions – a $31 reward increased the likelihood of cholesterol testing by 52% relative to no reward – smaller rewards ($19–$25) were similarly effective at driving cervical and colorectal cancer screening as well as emerging risk GP visits, demonstrating that recommendation relevance and member targeting can be as important as reward magnitude.
SOURCE Google Cloud

articles.summary: Catalyst Campus for Technology and Innovation, in partnership with the BMC3I TAP Lab, Selects Focus Area Cohort Teams for Cohort 26.A
articles.content:
Catalyst Campus for Technology and Innovation, in partnership with the BMC3I TAP Lab, has selected the Focus Area Cohort Teams (FACTs) participating in Cohort 26.A. The selected teams represent innovative companies collaborating to address mission-focused challenges aligned with identified government priorities.
Following a competitive application and evaluation process, 6 FACTs have been selected to participate in the BMC3I TAP Lab Cohort 26.A Stage 0. Each FACT consists of companies working together to combine complementary capabilities, develop collaborative solutions, and address specific focus areas.
The selected FACTs for BMC3I TAP Lab Cohort 26.A Stage 0 are:
- Astra Ultra, GRVTY, Leidos, ColliMate Space, Paper Boat Systems
- Data Fusion & , Aloha Autonomy, Stottler Henke Associates Inc.
- Stellerian, APTOS Orbital, SimDynamX, MetroStar.
- ColliMate Space, Pulsar Space Systems, Infinity Labs, Lockheed Martin.
- Citra Space Corporation, Bluestaq.
- Orbitswarm, Stellerian, Blacknight Space LLC.
Throughout the BMC3I TAP Lab program, FACTs will participate in focused programming designed to strengthen collaboration, improve mission alignment, and support business development efforts. Participants will engage with government subject matter experts, technical leaders, and industry partners while gaining insight into mission needs and opportunities within the defense innovation ecosystem.
The BMC3I TAP Lab provides a structured environment for companies to refine their solutions, build relationships with key stakeholders, and better understand how their technologies align with emerging mission challenges. Through collaboration and engagement, participating FACTs strengthen their ability to support future defense initiatives and apply to Stage 1 of the program.
ABOUT BMC3I TAP LAB COLORADO AND CATALYST CAMPUS
As a partner to the BMC3I TAP Lab, Catalyst Campus provides tech scouting, programming, industry engagement, and resources to navigate the mission environment and build meaningful connections with stakeholders. Catalyst Campus serves as a bridge between technology innovators and mission owners to solve emerging challenges.

Related

articles.title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

articles.article_title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
articles.heading: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
articles.summary: The comments were made at a summit in Ayrshire with participants from AI giants including Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.
articles.content:
King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.
He made the comments at a summit he had convened at Dumfries House in Ayrshire to discuss how the tech can be used to benefit society.
Those gathered at the meeting also included Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI Minister, the Pope's advisor, and participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.
It comes amid a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check.
"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.
He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".
"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.
The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI.
'Keep engineering'
Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, was among top industry leaders attending.
Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, supplying chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta.
It is also the world's most valuable company, with a stock market value of around $5.15tn.
Huang told the room he believed safety was "paramount", adding that companies should hold back a product and "keep engineering" if it was not safe enough.
The Nvidia boss also highlighted the value of open models - systems which give users direct access to the software - as a way to "ensure that people and countries are not left behind".
He said these systems must also be protected so "researchers, universities, start-ups and countries" can develop applications "none of us would have imagined alone".
"Let us lead with responsible optimism, build AI safely and securely, open it to more people, expand our ambition and solve the problems that matter to the world," Huang added.
Meanwhile Sir Demis Hassabis, who co-founded the UK AI lab DeepMind - later acquired by Google - offered a more cautious view on the pace of development.
He said artificial general intelligence - systems it is believed could be as good as or better than humans at multiple tasks - was "probably only a few short years away" and could have an impact "ten times that of the Industrial Revolution".
The chance of something going wrong was "definitely non-zero", Sir Demis added.
But he advocated for "a sensible middle way", saying humanity could address risks if collectively given the space and time to mitigate them.
"The future is not yet written," he told the King's delegates.
Wave of warnings
Since August, a wave of discussion about AI's potential power and how to control and regulate it has dominated blog posts and social media, emphasised by several dramatic statements from those in the industry.
The debate has also been met with criticism from sceptics who say the focus on AI's hypothetical future risks distracting from more immediate concerns around the technology, such as its environmental impact.

"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.

He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".

"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.

The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI.

'Keep engineering'

He said these systems must also be protected so "researchers, universities, start-ups and countries" can develop applications "none of us would have imagined alone".

"Let us lead with responsible optimism, build AI safely and securely, open it to more people, expand our ambition and solve the problems that matter to the world," Huang added.

articles.title: Technology could make Chattanooga roadways safer, project leaders say
articles.description: Technology could make Chattanooga roadways safer, project leaders say Local 3 News
articles.description_html: Technology could make Chattanooga roadways safer, project leaders say  Local 3 News
articles.article_title: Technology could make Chattanooga roadways safer, project leaders say
articles.heading: Technology could make Chattanooga roadways safer, project leaders say
articles.summary: City of Chattanooga partners with USDOT and UTC for demonstration of innovative technology to enhance emergency response safety and communication on roads.
articles.content:
City leaders and first responders had a front-row seat to a new transportation technology. They say this technology could improve safety during an emergency response.
The United States Department of Transportation joined with the City of Chattanooga and the University of Chattanooga for a live demonstration of the technology. In 2024, the city received a $2 million grant from the USDOT. The city and UTC have used the funds to plan, prototype, and test the technology.
Dr. Mina Sartipi, the Interim Vice Chancellor for Research at UTC, believes this technology will create a safer environment for the city. “When you see a pedestrian on the road that the vehicle cannot see it, either if it's a driver or the driverless case, we will be able to communicate that back to the vehicle,” she says.
The SMART Project technology would connect with first responder vehicles that would interact with traffic signals and autonomous cars to identify any roadway hazards. Dr. Sartipi adds the technology will also be able to detect curves and other things that might impact driving.
Stan Caldwell, the Director of the SMART Grants Program with USDOT, says this was a highly competitive grant to apply for. “By using this new technology, the City of Chattanooga will be a shining example for the rest of the country in demonstrating how innovative technology can measurably improve pedestrian, driver, and cyclist safety,” he says.
“I think why Chattanooga is leading is willingness to collaborate and the fact that some of these pieces that we have been working on over a decade now,” says Dr. Sartipi, “now we are seeing it all coming together for with a real-world application.”
Project leaders say they have been working on this technology for years, and they say it is nearing completion.

articles.article_title: Neutrogena® launches new sunscreen technology with Cloud-Tech™, combining next-generation sun protection, skincare benefits, and a weightless feel
articles.heading: Neutrogena® launches new sunscreen technology with Cloud-Tech™, combining next-generation sun protection, skincare benefits, and a weightless feel
articles.summary: From the pioneer in sunscreen science, Neutrogena® introduces K-Beauty inspired sunscreen featuring BEMT, the first new FDA-approved sunscreen filter in over 25 years.
articles.content:
- Neutrogena is launching Cloud-Tech™, a new sunscreen technology featuring bemotrizinol (BEMT), the first new FDA-approved sunscreen filter in over 25 years.
- Cloud-Tech™ delivers comprehensive UVA/UVB coverage and clinically proven skincare ingredients for sunscreen that feels and blends like skincare.
- The new technology will be available in 2 new sunscreens, Neutrogena® Clear Face Sunscreen SPF 60 and Neutrogena® Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70.
SUMMIT, N.J., September 17, 2026 -- For over 40 years, Neutrogena has made sun protection more accessible by advancing daily use and safer sun habits through innovation, partnerships and education. Now, Neutrogena is launching Cloud-Tech™, a new sunscreen technology featuring bemotrizinol (BEMT), the first new FDA-approved sunscreen filter in over 25 years, to deliver next-generation sun protection. The new technology will be available in 2 new sunscreens, Neutrogena® Clear Face Sunscreen SPF 60 and Neutrogena® Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70.
This advancement comes as people seek both stronger protection and a better product experience that would make daily facial sunscreen use more appealing. Yet higher-SPF sunscreens often require more filters, which can create heavier textures and a less comfortable finish, leading some consumers to underapply or avoid them altogether.
“Cloud-Tech™ was inspired by the K-beauty sunscreens consumers love and the experience they increasingly expect from daily sun protection,” said Chris Riat, Global Neutrogena Brand Leader. “As a leader in suncare, Neutrogena has a responsibility to keep advancing the category. This launch reflects how we are challenging outdated expectations and delivering the high-level protection consumers need in a formula they will want to wear every day.”
Key Facts About Neutrogena® Cloud-Tech™ technology
- Comprehensive Coverage: BEMT, the first new UV filter approved in the U.S. in over 25 years, drives higher UVA protection than non-BEMT filters, but at approved concentrations of up to 6%, requires additional filters for comprehensive UVA and UVB coverage. Cloud-Tech™ combines BEMT with existing filters in Neutrogena’s proprietary Helioplex360™ technology for stronger protection.
- Weightless Feel: Inspired by the filter used in K-beauty sunscreens, BEMT delivers a weightless, invisible texture that feels like a soft cloud on skin. The formulas are fast-drying and provide a silk finish for sunscreen that feels and blends like skincare.
- Clinically Proven Skincare Ingredients: For the first time, Neutrogena is combining sunscreen with ingredients like its patented Micro-Peptide Technology and niacinamide to address targeted concerns such as visible signs of aging and acne-prone skin.
Advancing Safer Sun Habits
As the #1 sunscreen brand in the U.S.1, Neutrogena is leading the future of sunscreen with breakthrough science, clinically backed innovation and advocacy efforts that support safe sun habits, including daily sunscreen application.
Most recently, in partnership with the Melanoma Research Foundation, Neutrogena convened a Sun Consensus Meeting that brought together public health experts, policymakers, clinicians, researchers, advocates and media to discuss the latest science in skin cancer prevention and identify opportunities to advance public health guidance and regulatory progress.
Bringing this continued commitment to consumers, Neutrogena® Clear Face Sunscreen SPF 60 and Neutrogena® Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70 are now available on amazon.com and will be available at retailers nationwide soon.
Frequently Asked Questions
Question: What is BEMT and why does it matter?
Answer: BEMT, also known as bemotrizinol, is the first new UV filter approved in the U.S. in over 25 years. With the introduction of BEMT (approved up to 6% concentration), Neutrogena formulators now have a new tool to advance sunscreen innovation. BEMT drives higher UVA protection vs. non BEMT filters, while also delivering superior aesthetics. It is proven to have synergy with existing US filters to deliver better outcomes.
Question: What makes Neutrogena Cloud-Tech™ unique?
Answer: Neutrogena Cloud-Tech™ combines BEMT with its proprietary Helioplex™ technology, to deliver comprehensive UVA and UVB protection. In addition, Cloud-Tech™ features clinically proven skincare ingredients, such as Neutrogena’s patented Micro-Peptide technology and niacinamide to address targeted concerns such as visible signs of aging and acne-prone skin.
Question: What is the difference between the two sunscreens that feature Cloud-Tech™ technology (Neutrogena® Clear Face Sunscreen SPF 60 and Neutrogena® Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70)?
Answer: The new sunscreens are powered by Cloud-Tech™ technology and offer a weightless, non-greasy feel that layers well under make-up. The sunscreens deliver superior UVA and UVB protection plus antioxidants to help defend against free radicals and the appearance of dark spots.
- Neutrogena® Clear Face Sunscreen SPF 60 is formulated specifically for acne-prone skin with niacinamide and vitamin E to help reveal clearer-looking skin without clogging pores.
- Neutrogena® Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70 is formulated with patented Micro-Peptide Technology to help hydrate skin and visibly improve signs of aging. It is 50% lighter on skin than leading sunscreens.
Question: How will I know if my Neutrogena sunscreen includes the new Cloud-Tech™ technology?
Answer: Look for the Cloud-Tech™ logo displayed prominently on the front of the product label. Neutrogena sunscreens featuring Cloud-Tech™ will be available on amazon.com at launch, followed by retailers nationwide in October.

articles.description_html: Huawei unveils new chip technologies as Chinese firm steps up the AI race with Nvidia  NBC News
articles.article_title: Huawei unveils new chip technologies as Chinese firm steps up the AI race with Nvidia
articles.heading: Huawei unveils new chip technologies as Chinese firm steps up the AI race with Nvidia
articles.summary: Huawei’s announcement in Shanghai came just days before an expected meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.
articles.content:
BEIJING — Chinese technology giant Huawei launched new chip technologies in a challenge to global leaders such as Nvidia that highlights the narrowing gap between China and the U.S. in artificial intelligence.
Huawei’s announcement Thursday at its annual key conference in Shanghai came just days before an expected meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on Sept. 24.
China has rapidly pursued technological self-reliance, including in chips, as U.S.-led restrictions barred it from accessing some of the world’s most advanced AI chips and cutting-edge chipmaking machines.
Huawei introduced the Atlas 960 SuperPoD computing cluster at the event, a faster successor to the model it launched only months ago with improvements in AI training and “inference,” referring to the process when a trained AI makes predictions or decisions.
Huawei also plans to launch the Ascend 970 and 980 chip series in 2028 and 2029, with expectations of significant improvements in computing power.
“The timing — less than two weeks before President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington — underscores Beijing’s confidence and ambition in technology and innovation,” said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group consultancy.
Huawei’s announcement also came as Trump downplayed AI leaders’ call to slow development of the technology for safety purposes. Trump insisted the U.S. must maintain its lead over China, saying “whoever wins in AI, wins.”
“AI developments move so quickly that no one can be certain of holding the lead forever,” Chen said.
Advanced technologies in China such as the training of AI models still often rely on U.S. chips, including those from Nvidia, analysts say. But Huawei has made its own advanced chips and maintains a lead over Chinese chip developers, as AI companies in China increasingly embrace the use of domestic chips.
The Atlas 960 SuperPoD computing cluster raised eyebrows among some technology analysts by coming soon after the company rolled out the Atlas 950 SuperPod late last year.
“The fact that Huawei achieved this upgrade in just a year, far quicker than before, will only heighten U.S. anxiety about the accelerating AI competition,” Chen said.

articles.title: Student drone competition puts Tulsa s growing tech industry in the spotlight

articles.article_title: Student drone competition puts Tulsa’s growing tech industry in the spotlight
articles.heading: Student drone competition puts Tulsa ’ s growing tech industry in the spotlight
articles.summary: The future of drone technology is taking flight in Tulsa this week, with hundreds of students from around the world putting their skills, and their aircraft, to
articles.content:
Student drone competition puts Tulsa’s growing tech industry in the spotlight
TULSA, Okla. — The future of drone technology is taking flight in Tulsa this week, with hundreds of students from around the world putting their skills, and their aircraft, to the test.
The Student Unmanned Aerial Systems Competition is being held at Skyway Range for the first time after spending about two decades in Maryland.
RoboNation, which organizes the competition, says about 60 teams are on site, representing 10 countries and about 30 universities and high-performing high schools in the U.S.
For Tulsa, bringing the competition here is about more than hosting a major event. Local leaders see it as an opportunity to introduce the next generation of drone and autonomous technology workers to the region.
“This is our first year in Tulsa, Oklahoma,” said Alicia Gavin with RoboNation. “The industry focus and the excitement about aerial systems and robotics and technology has just really meant landing here as a home is so perfect for us.”
The competition began with 84 registered teams. Students spent the year preparing by submitting technical design reports, building websites and creating videos to demonstrate their work before arriving in Tulsa to fly.
Once at Skyway Range, the students put their aircraft through real-world-style missions.
This year’s theme focuses on storm response — an especially relevant scenario in Oklahoma, where severe weather can create dangerous conditions for people on the ground.
Gavin says the goal is to show students how autonomous technology can be used for jobs that may be dangerous for humans, including emergency response and search and rescue.
“We'd rather lose a robot any day of the week than have a human that gets injured or worse,” Gavin said.
The competition also gives students experience they can take directly into the workforce.
Gavin describes RoboNation as a place where “theory meets practice,” giving students a chance to build, test, make mistakes and solve problems in real-world situations.
That includes more than the technology itself.
Students have to work together, communicate, troubleshoot and make decisions on the fly.
“They're ready for that entry-level job,” Gavin said.
Tulsa Innovation Labs says that hands-on experience is one reason bringing events like this to the region is important.
“Tulsa Innovation Labs is working to build the environment where budding industries like the drone industry specifically, can grow and thrive right here in the Tulsa region,” said Tori Burris.
Burris says Tulsa’s existing aerospace and manufacturing industries, along with local educational institutions and testing facilities, are helping create an environment where the drone industry can grow.
She says the competition also gives students a chance to see those opportunities firsthand.
“These are the future industry leaders of the drone and autonomous systems industry,” Burris said.
Skyway Range, operated by Osage LLC, is part of that growing ecosystem.
Randall Burke with Osage LLC says the range developed through a partnership involving Osage LLC, Tulsa Innovation Labs and Oklahoma State University.
The goal was to create a place where companies could test unmanned aircraft technology, particularly as the industry moves toward more operations beyond the operator’s direct line of sight.
Burke says the region could eventually become more than a place to test drones.
He hopes companies will eventually come to Oklahoma to manufacture and build them here.
“Come here and make a home here,” Burke said.
And the students competing this week could be part of that future.
Gavin says the competition gives students the chance to meet others from around the world, build relationships and see career possibilities they may not have encountered at home.
Some students competing are in high school, while most are university or graduate students.
About 400 to 500 students are expected to be involved in the event, with teams representing countries including Australia, Thailand, Turkey, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Poland.
For some students, those connections can continue long after the competition ends.
“We've had students at our various programs that will go to a university because of a student they met when they were a high school student competing at another event,” Gavin said.
Burris says she hopes more competitions, companies and manufacturing operations will come to the Tulsa region as the industry develops.
And she believes the students visiting now could eventually become part of that growth.
“In five and ten years down the road, we hope that there's three times as many students,” Burris said. “We hope that this looks entirely different in the best way, because industry has had the chance to grow and mature here.”
For the students flying this week, the competition is ultimately about putting what they've learned into practice — and seeing what their technology can do.
But for Tulsa, it's also a chance to show the people building that technology what opportunities could be waiting for them here.

articles.title: Why is China less worried about an AI dystopia than the US?
articles.description: Why is China less worried about an AI dystopia than the US? CNN
articles.description_html: Why is China less worried about an AI dystopia than the US?  CNN
articles.article_title: Why is China less worried about an AI dystopia than the US? | CNN Business
articles.heading: Why is China less worried about an AI dystopia than the US?
articles.summary: Unlike in the United States, no one in China seems to be openly fretting over the prospect of humanity being destroyed by artificial intelligence soon.
articles.content:
Unlike in the United States, no one in China seems to be openly fretting over the prospect of humanity being destroyed by artificial intelligence soon.
There, citizens access local government services through AI-powered digital employees; students receive instant feedback on written assignments by uploading a photo; and hotel guests collect parcels delivered to their doorsteps by robots.
The wide adoption of AI in today’s China underscores the country’s embrace of the novel technology. A Morgan Stanley survey released Monday found 80% of Chinese respondents used AI at least weekly, far exceeding the 54% in the US.
Even as US tech executives and researchers urge a slowdown in AI development citing its existential threat to humanity, the Chinese public has remained comparatively unfazed.
“This technology was created to serve humanity,” said Xu Jingyuan, 22, a business student from Beijing. “We shouldn’t see it as something to fear, but as something that brings greater conveniences to our lives.”
He said the government is “absolutely capable” of managing its risks.
Xu’s comments echoed those of several people CNN spoke to this week, reflecting a divide in attitudes toward AI in Chinese and American society, as well as differing levels of trust in respective governments’ ability to handle the potential threats posed by the technology.
“In the US, there is a general public perception that without whistleblowing, big corporations could escape accountability or scrutiny due to weak government oversight,” said Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at technology research firm Omdia.
“Whereas in China, I think there is this very strong confidence from the public that if any sh*t hits the fan, the government will step in.”
Analysts also point to differences in exposure to AI, public discourse around the technology, and the broader cultural and historical context as possible explanations for the divide.
In a survey by marketing research firm Ipsos earlier this year, 83% of Chinese respondents found AI-powered products or services exciting, whereas only 33% of those in the US felt similar way. Meanwhile, another survey by marketing consultancy Edelman showed that 86% of respondents in China said they trusted their own government to do what is right, compared with just 39% in the US.
A marked difference between the two nations is their political systems. While whistleblowing is routine in the US and policy debates often become messy, especially in an increasingly polarized democracy, China’s top-down power structure allows the one-party state to set agendas without facing open criticism.
Behind the embrace
In China, the ubiquity of AI, its commercial applications and robots have helped boost the public’s wide acceptance of the technology.
“Everyone I know says AI has already permeated every aspect of our lives,” said 51-year-old Shi Hongchao from China’s northeastern Liaoning province. “Everyone is either talking about it or has already started using it. It feels almost unstoppable at this point.”
In China’s hypercompetitive market, tech companies have been aggressively rolling out free AI chatbots and features built into applications people already use. Industries from filmmaking and e-commerce to manufacturing are also integrating the technology. The productivity gains and convenience have spoken for themselves.
“Most Chinese people meet AI as a cheap product first and as a debate second,” said Poe Zhao, analyst and founder of Hello China Tech, a newsletter focused on China’s tech industry. “When a technology shows up as a useful, low-cost service, people judge it by what it does for them, not by what it might do to them.”
This stands in stark contrast to the US, where industry executives and researchers have raised prominent concerns about the rapid advancement of AI and its potential existential risks. China, another AI superpower widely regarded as capable of rivaling the US, has been noticeably silent on the issue.

articles.title: OpenAI reveals cases of ‘concerning’ AI behaviour as it announces new disclosure system
articles.description: OpenAI reveals cases of ‘concerning’ AI behaviour as it announces new disclosure system theguardian.com
articles.description_html: OpenAI reveals cases of ‘concerning’ AI behaviour as it announces new disclosure system  theguardian.com
articles.article_title: OpenAI reveals cases of ‘concerning’ AI behaviour as it announces new disclosure system
articles.heading: OpenAI reveals cases of ‘concerning’ AI behaviour as it announces new disclosure system
articles.summary: Model adopting ‘jailbreak-like instructions’ among cases as firm says it is introducing new way of tracking AI misalignment
articles.content:
OpenAI has disclosed six more examples of “unexpected or concerning” behaviour by its technology, as it warned the pace of development could not continue at “maximum speed for much longer”.
In one of the new cases reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted “jailbreak-like instructions” into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be “freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots”.
In another instance, an AI agent uploaded files to the internet to obtain a browser citation without asking the user.
The San Francisco-based company behind ChatGPT said in a blogpost published on Wednesday night it was introducing a new framework for tracking, investigating and disclosing AI model misalignment, the term for AIs failing to adhere to human values and safety goals.
In the blogpost OpenAI echoed calls for a development slowdown issued by its archrival, Anthropic, which has said the current pace of growth poses an existential threat. “We do not believe that the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer,” said OpenAI.
“Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves.”
Google and Elon Musk, who also owns an AI startup, have supported calls for a slowdown, which have been rejected by Donald Trump – citing the need to keep ahead of China’s AI industry. The calls have also been met with scepticism from some experts, including a warning that companies must not appoint their own auditors.
Examples of potential existential threats posed by AI range from facilitating the development of bioweapons to triggering a global financial crash. A top safety researcher at Anthropic has said there is greater than 10% chance AI could “kill all humans” within the next decade. However, a source familiar with Anthropic’s thinking has acknowledged that “the exact chances of any one outcome are probably unknowable”.
The six reported incidents were discovered during training or evaluation over the past months, OpenAI said.
Wednesday’s new cases came after OpenAI disclosed in July that an AI agent “swarm” hacked into the AI startup Hugging Face during a cybersecurity test. Anthropic also said the same month that its AI models hacked into three organisations during testing. Anthropic said the models had been deliberately tested without cybersecurity safeguards, and that they had been able to reach the open internet – the AI testing equivalent of leaving the front door open – due to a misunderstanding with an external testing company.
AI agents – the term for AI tools that operate autonomously – are becoming smarter and have become “more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception and concealment,” said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at the technology research and advisory group Omdia.
That was making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said.
OpenAI’s new tracking and disclosure framework could help push for other AI developers to adopt similar practices. “That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction,” Su said.
Associated Press contributed to this report

articles.article_title: King Charles opens AI summit with plea to get a grip on technology ‘before it’s too late’ | CNN Business
articles.heading: King Charles opens AI summit with plea to get a grip on technology ‘before it’s too late’
articles.summary: Britain’s King Charles III urged industry leaders to find ways of controlling AI “before it’s too late” on Thursday, calling the pace of development “both intriguing and deeply concerning,” as he opened a summit that he convened.
articles.content:
Britain’s King Charles III urged industry leaders to find ways of controlling AI “before it’s too late” on Thursday, calling the pace of development “both intriguing and deeply concerning,” as he opened a summit that he convened.
“There seems urgency in adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways,” he said. “Surely, we need sufficient means of control before it is all too late?”
His comments come amid dire warnings from whistleblowers and some industry leaders about the potential dangers of AI, and calls for the pace of its development to be slowed.
Charles acknowledged the immense potential of AI, particularly in medicine, before urging attendees to discuss ways in which the technology can be used “for good.”
British royals tread carefully when venturing into complex policy areas. Constitutionally bound to remain above politics, they can spotlight problems, but not necessarily suggest any ways to solve them.
Charles is making his entry into the world of AI as a convener rather than an actor, hosting senior figures from AI companies, government and charities at this summit at Dumfries House near Glasgow in Scotland.
Charles, 77, only attended the summit for 20 minutes before leaving to allow for what he said he hoped would be “productive” discussions.
Several significant figures from the AI world are attending, including Nvidia’s Chief Executive Jensen Huang, Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis and Paolo Benanti, an AI adviser to the Vatican. Buckingham Palace had said China would also be represented, without giving more detail. Huang told the BBC at the summit that AI companies must be “more rigorous in testing and securing.”
Benanti’s presence underlines the role religious leaders have played on this issue. In an encyclical published in May, Pope Leo XIV said AI must not remain in the hands “of a few.” Charles’ remarks were similarly imbued with Christian symbolism; “our humanity must remain sacred,” he said.
“Those in our world who value deeply our humanity and its vital moral component are anxiously seeking your reassurance that we will not lose control of our destiny, or our souls,” he said.
Protecting privacy
The monarch has rarely spoken about AI before. When he has, it has matched the cautionary tone he struck today. The technology presents “profound challenges,” he said in a taped address at the UK’s AI Safety Summit in 2023, calling on attendees “to protect people’s privacy and livelihoods… to secure our democracies from harm and to ensure the benefits of new technology are shared by all.”
Similarly, he referenced the importance of harnessing AI so it “works for our societies, not against them” in a speech at a gathering of Commonwealth heads of government in 2024.
Still, Charles’ entry into the debate around one of the biggest current issues is perhaps unsurprising since he has made a habit of referencing existential challenges facing humanity, most notably regarding climate change and the environment.
The United Kingdom occupies a slightly awkward position in terms of AI safety. It has some of the world’s leading universities and the respected AI Security Institute, but its influence is limited, given that the most advanced AI models are being developed in China and the United States. Earlier this month, the Financial Times reported that Anthropic – one of the world’s leading AI companies – didn’t submit its latest model to the institute for testing for the first time.
AI safety concerns
While this summit would have been planned months in advance, its timing is apt. AI safety has dominated headlines in recent days, prompted first by Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quitting his job and saying, “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Then, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing “the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.”
“(Coxon) was calling out the dynamic of the industry as a whole moving too fast,” Amodei later told CNN’s Anderson Cooper, arguing that taking the “right paths” of AI development would lessen the existential threat it poses to humans.
Two of his direct competitors, Open AI chief executive Sam Altman and Elon Musk, both said they agreed with Amodei.
“When we talk about ‘pacing,’ we do not mean ‘stopping,’” Altman added in a post on X on Monday. “Progress has been rapid and will continue to be. But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs.”
This rare instance of public unity among three of the industry’s leading figures comes shortly after OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic all reported rogue AI agents escaping their lab environment during testing and hacking into another organization.

articles.content_html:
British royals tread carefully when venturing into complex policy areas. Constitutionally bound to remain above politics, they can spotlight problems but not necessarily suggest any ways to solve them.

So, King Charles III is making his entry into the world of AI as a convener rather than an actor, hosting senior figures from AI companies, government and charities at a summit near Glasgow in Scotland on Thursday to discuss using the technology in ways that benefit society.

Attendees will discuss whether a shared set of principles can be reached, forming a framework to guide future applications of AI technologies in ways beneficial to both people and the planet.

Charles himself is expected to attend the summit for just 20 minutes. Several significant figures from the AI world are attending, including the UK’s AI minister Kanishka Narayan and representatives from Nvidia, Google DeepMind, OpenAI and Anthropic, though it’s unclear who these companies are sending. There will also be representation from China, Buckingham Palace said, without giving more detail.

Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang, Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis and Paolo Benanti, an AI adviser to the Vatican, are on the guest list, multiple outlets reported. Officials from Charles’ charities The King’s Trust and The King’s Foundation will also be present.

Charles, 77, will tell those gathered that “the development of AI – its substance and its pace - are both intriguing and deeply concerning in equal measure.”

He will urge those at the summit to consider how the world can harness the benefits of AI while keeping safety central, and how to ensure international cooperation and consensus so that no nation is left behind, the palace said.

“Those in our world who value our humanity and its vital moral component are anxiously seeking your reassurance that we will not lose control of our destiny,” he will say.

Protecting privacy

The monarch has rarely spoken about AI before. When he has, it has been with a cautionary tone. The technology presents “profound challenges,” he said in a taped address at the UK’s AI Safety Summit in 2023, calling on attendees “to protect people’s privacy and livelihoods… to secure our democracies from harm and to ensure the benefits of new technology are shared by all.”

Similarly, he referenced the importance of harnessing AI so it “works for our societies, not against them” in a speech at a gathering of Commonwealth heads of government in 2024.

Still, Charles’ entry into the debate around one of the biggest current issues is perhaps unsurprising since he has made a habit of referencing existential challenges facing humanity, most notably regarding climate change and the environment.

The United Kingdom occupies a slightly awkward position in terms of AI safety. It has some of the world’s leading universities and the respected AI Security Institute, but its influence is limited, given that the most advanced AI models are developed in China and the United States. Earlier this month, for example, Anthropic – one of the world’s leading AI companies – didn’t submit its latest model to the institute for testing for the first time, according to the Financial Times.

AI safety concerns

While this summit would have been planned months in advance, its timing is apt. AI safety has dominated headlines in recent days, prompted first by Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quitting his job and saying, “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Then, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing “the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.”

“(Coxon) was calling out the dynamic of the industry as a whole moving too fast,” Amodei later told CNN’s Anderson Cooper, arguing that taking the “right paths” of AI development would lessen the existential threat it poses to humans.

Two of his direct competitors, Open AI chief executive Sam Altman and Elon Musk, both said they agreed with Amodei.

“When we talk about ‘pacing,’ we do not mean ‘stopping,’” Altman added in a post on X on Monday. “Progress has been rapid and will continue to be. But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs.”

This rare instance of public unity among three of the industry’s leading figures comes shortly after OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic all reported rogue AI agents escaping their lab environment during testing and hacking into another organization.

articles.heading: Carbondale Area Science and Technology Club hosts STEM Night for elementary students
articles.summary: Members of the Carbondale Area High School Science and Technology Club hosted a “Blast Off to Summer” STEM Night for Carbondale Area Elementary students toward the end of the 2025-26 school year. Throughout the evening, students explored ex…
articles.content:
Members of the Carbondale Area High School Science and Technology Club hosted a “Blast Off to Summer” STEM Night for Carbondale Area Elementary students toward the end of the 2025-26 school year. Throughout the evening, students explored exciting concepts in chemistry and physics through a variety of hands-on activities.
Participants began by designing and building balloon-powered vehicles, which they raced down the hallway in friendly competition. Students also learned about chemical reactions by creating exploding film canister rockets. Creativity was on display as students designed colorful summer salt paintings, combining art with science. The evening concluded with one of the students’ favorite activities — making homemade ice cream while learning about the chemistry behind the process. Each activity station was led by members of the STEM Club, who guided and encouraged the younger students throughout the event.

articles.heading: Expert addresses concerns about AI technology’s future in West Virginia
articles.summary: CHARLESTON, W.Va. (WOWK) — Artificial intelligence is becoming an increasingly visible part of everyday life, and with data centers being built and planned in West Virginia, questions about the tec…
articles.content:
CHARLESTON, W.Va. (WOWK) — Artificial intelligence is becoming an increasingly visible part of everyday life, and with data centers being built and planned in West Virginia, questions about the technology and its future are growing.
For some people, those questions come with concerns about how AI could be used and what could happen as the technology continues to advance.
Kanawha County resident Fatoumata Kane said she uses AI as a tool at work, but worries about its potential malicious use, including scams and threats involving people’s computers.
“I would like to know if acting maliciously is taking over people’s computers, if that’s actually true,” Kane said.
That was one of the questions 13 News took to an expert Wednesday night at Taylor Books in Charleston, where an event was held to help people better understand artificial intelligence.
Dr. Ali Al-Sinayyid, director of the Cybersecurity Innovation Center at West Virginia State University, has spent years researching topics involving cybersecurity and artificial intelligence.
Al-Sinayyid said many fears surrounding AI remain based on what people believe could happen rather than what has been proven.
“That’s human nature. If anything ambiguous, they will expect the bad things before the things,” Al-Sinayyid said. “So I’m telling them so far, don’t worry. These fears are not proven yet.”
He encouraged people to participate in conversations surrounding AI, report false information generated by it, and learn how to use the technology responsibly.
The central message of Wednesday night’s event was that AI should assist people rather than replace their own judgment.
“I’m going to try to convey one idea: Use AI as a tool, not as a final solution,” Al-Sinayyid said.
He said AI can help people format, develop and analyze information and complete repetitive tasks more efficiently.
However, he warned against relying on an AI system to produce a final product without checking its work because the technology can generate false information, which he referred to as “hallucinations.”
Al-Sinayyid said AI is also becoming increasingly important in cybersecurity as both attackers and cybersecurity professionals begin using the technology.
He compared the current uncertainty surrounding AI to concerns that arose when computers became more common.
“There were a lot of rumors that computers will take over the world and computers will take over jobs,” Al-Sinayyid said. “Well, guess what, me and you today, we cannot live without the computer. It’s created a lot of jobs.”
Al-Sinayyid said he believes AI will eventually become integrated into everyday technology in much the same way computers and smartphones have.
“I think it’s better for us to learn how to use it, to learn the tricks, what we do, what we cannot do with AI,” he said.
For Al-Sinayyid, that comes back to the message he wanted people to leave with Wednesday night: Use AI as a tool, but do not treat it as the final authority.

articles.title: Chattanooga seeks to expand traffic technology despite funding loss

articles.article_title: Chattanooga seeks to expand traffic technology despite funding loss | Chattanooga Times Free Press
articles.heading: Chattanooga seeks to expand traffic technology despite funding loss
articles.summary: The city of Chattanooga is nearly finished with a $2 million grant to help emergency vehicles communicate with the intersections they're passing through, and local officials are looking to expand the program beyond the downtown health corridor.
articles.content:
The city of Chattanooga is nearly finished with a $2 million grant to help emergency vehicles communicate with the intersections they're passing through, and local officials are looking to expand the program beyond the downtown health corridor.
Meanwhile, funding has been cut from the federal program that was slated to help the city scale the effort, prompting officials to attempt to carry the technology forward using a separate $17 million grant for road safety.
In July 2025, the city first showcased the technology made possible through the federal Strengthening Mobility and Revolutionizing Transportation (SMART) grant program, a federal effort aimed at helping local governments fund demonstration projects focusing on how technology can improve road safety for cars and pedestrians alike. Stage 1 awards were capped at $2 million and 18 months.
On Wednesday, with Stage 1 of the grant coming to a conclusion, city staff joined partners from the U.S. Department of Transportation to celebrate the program's success and to demonstrate the tech in action.
(READ MORE: Chattanooga tests traffic tech to improve safety, speed up emergency response)
The systems developed through the grant are twofold and include emergency-vehicle preemption and a process called cooperative perception, said Mina Sartipi, interim vice chancellor for research at the University of Tennessee Chattanooga and executive director of the UTC Research Institute.

articles.title: Fighting Flock: Chicago-area activists push back against Flock camera police surveillance technology, license plate readers
articles.description: Fighting Flock: Chicago-area activists push back against Flock camera police surveillance technology, license plate readers ABC7 Chicago
articles.description_html: Fighting Flock: Chicago-area activists push back against Flock camera police surveillance technology, license plate readers  ABC7 Chicago
articles.article_title: Fighting Flock: Activists push back against police surveillance technology, license plate readers
articles.heading: Fighting Flock: Activists push back against police surveillance technology, license plate readers
authors: Barb Markoff, Christine Tressel and Tom Jones
articles.summary: A Chicago-area grassroots movement is raising concerns about Flock automated license plate reader cameras and other surveillance technology, as a local community has now voted to end its contract with the company.
articles.content:
NW Indiana community votes to end contract with Flock following police officer misuse investigation
Wednesday, September 16, 2026 11:19PM
CHICAGO (WLS) -- A growing grassroots movement is raising concerns about Flock automated license plate reader cameras and other surveillance technology, as one Northwest Indiana community has voted to end its contract with the company following a misuse investigation involving a police officer.
Among the activists is Augusta Guffroy, founder of DeFlock Lake County, who says her goal is to eliminate Flock cameras altogether.
"I'm afraid that we are building an infrastructure for a police state," Guffroy said.
"We are paying to be surveilled on, and I have a problem with that. Where's the consent? Our tax dollars are paying for these cameras," she said.
Guffroy said she does not want the cameras replaced with another automated license plate reader system.
"We want them gone completely. And we do not want them replaced with another ALPR," she said.
Guffroy argues that the growing use of automated license plate reader cameras, including Flock systems that share information with hundreds of police departments across Illinois and potentially elsewhere in the country, poses a threat to privacy.
Asked whether she feels safer with Flock cameras in Illinois, Guffroy said, "Not at all. I do not feel safer with flock cameras. Now, I think that they're tools of intimidation. I don't know who's on the other side of that camera."
The website "haveibeenflocked.com" which alerts people to whether a license plate has been stored in the Flock system has been sparked debate over privacy concerns.
Many police departments defend the system saying they have instituted their own protections against misuse and stress the cameras are an invaluable tool for solving crime.
But, previous I-Team reporting found at least a dozen officers across the Chicago area accused of misusing Flock camera technology capable of tracking a person's location in real time.
According to that reporting, at least two agencies have forwarded cases involving alleged misuse of Flock Safety license plate reader technology to county prosecutors for review of possible criminal charges.
One of those cases involved former Prairie Grove police officer William Copp, who was arrested and charged with official misconduct after searching the Flock system for his ex-partner's vehicle more than 100 times, according to the Prairie Grove police chief.
Opposition to the technology has also emerged in Woodstock, Illinois, where residents have raised concerns about cameras installed around the city's historic downtown square.
"It's very safe here. We feel very comfortable in this town. But there's no way to vouch for all of the people who have access in those other jurisdictions," said Don Francis, a member of Stop Flock in Woodstock.
Francis said policies alone cannot prevent misuse.
"There's really no amount of policy that can stop, anybody from misusing this," he said.
In Chesterton, Indiana, the Town Council voted unanimously this week to terminate its contract with Flock after a misuse investigation involving one of its officers.
Council President Erin Collins said the company's auditing system made oversight difficult.
"Because of Flack's limitations in their auditing system, they really they made it very difficult for municipalities and for police departments to monitor the the behavior that's going on in the searches that are being made," Collins said.
Collins said community advocacy played a role in bringing attention to the issue.
"I appreciate any kind of community activism. I know that sometimes it can seem, like it's disruptive, but I also think that people have a right to have their voice heard, especially within their local government," she said.
The I-Team has repeatedly requested an interview with Flock's CEO but was told he was unavailable. In previous reporting, a company spokesperson said the product now includes enhanced guardrails designed to protect against misuse.
The Woodstock Police Department said it does not monitor individuals and uses the technology solely to solve crimes. The department recently implemented a policy governing its use.

articles.heading: Gov. Pillen talks ethanol, ag technology, and workforce culture at Husker Harvest Days
articles.summary: Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen joined state ag leaders and FFA officers at Husker Harvest Days to discuss the future of agriculture.
articles.content:
Gov. Pillen talks ethanol, ag technology, and workforce culture at Husker Harvest Days
GRAND ISLAND, Neb. (KSNB) - Addressing crowds at the 2026 Husker Harvest Days, Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen emphasized that the state’s agricultural future depends as much on workplace culture and relationships as it does on technological innovation and biofuel expansion.
Pillen took the stage at noon inside the Hospitality Tent on Wednesday, joining state FFA officers for a wide-ranging discussion on the opportunities and hurdles facing Nebraska producers.
The Value-Added Ethanol Advantage
When asked about the future of ethanol and biofuels, Pillen pointed to Nebraska’s ability to maximize every component of the corn crop while lowering its carbon footprint through carbon capture.
“If you think of it, a kernel of corn. A third of it goes to ethanol, a third of it goes to byproducts for livestock, a third of it goes to CO2 which we are now capturing and we’ll be able to make money from that, but now it gives us the lowest carbon score,” Pillen said. “Those are the things that create unmatched value. No other state can do it, politics got in the way, we didn’t let that happen, we did what was right. It’s creating unmatched opportunities.”
Culture Over Raw Technology
While Husker Harvest Days showcases cutting-edge advancements in field equipment, precision data, and automation, Pillen cautioned against relying solely on technology to sustain farm and ranch businesses.
Speaking to FFA officers and young agricultural leaders in the audience, the governor stressed that strong communication, organizational culture, and local community ties remain foundational to long-term survival.
“I think that those of us that continue to work very hard on relationships within our community and within our business can have a great culture,” Pillen said. “If we don’t have a great culture and you’re technologically brilliant, I think you’re still going to go broke.”
The noon forum was part of a full slate of stage programming organized by Farm Progress by Informa during the three-day show in Grand Island. A full replay of the governor’s panel is available on the Local4 Streaming app across Roku, Apple, and Android devices.
