articles.article_title: Advancing the Technology to Print Electronics on 3D Surfaces | Newswise
articles.heading: Advancing the Technology to Print Electronics on 3D Surfaces
articles.summary: Iowa State University's Ethan Secor is developing technologies and techniques to print electronics on curved and 3D surfaces.
articles.content:
Newswise — AMES, Iowa – The name of Ethan Secor’s startup company – “Contour Circuits” – is a great description of the technology he and his research group are developing.
They’re learning to print precise and complex electronic circuits on curved and 3D surfaces.
Step one of the process is understanding the mechanics and physics of a technology called aerosol jet printing, which, similar to an office inkjet printer, deposits droplets of ink to create a pattern defined by software.
Step two is monitoring and controlling the printing process in real time, as ink is atomized into a fine mist that’s carried by a gas flow and squeezed through a nozzle for printing at a resolution of just 10 to 100 millionths of a meter.
Step three is building custom printers and the software that controls them. One such printer is mounted to an articulated robotic arm, allowing the printer nozzle to work over a curved surface. That “introduces greater complexity for motion planning and alignment,” according to a summary of the technology.
“Right now, the work that’s getting me excited is the conformal printing,” said Secor, an Iowa State University associate professor of mechanical engineering. “For the next two to three years, that’s going to be a big effort. We’ll be pushing to develop applications for the technology.”
Those applications could include electronics for use by the energy, healthcare, manufacturing, aerospace, communications and security industries.
In recognition of that research program and other accomplishments – including early career awards from the U.S. National Science Foundation, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and the Office of Naval Research – Secor is being honored this fall with an Iowa State University Award for Early Achievement in Research.
‘The breadth of the work’
Secor describes his introduction to aerosol jet printing as an accident.
“In graduate school (at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois), I wanted to work on energy,” he said. “But the professor I wanted to work with (Mark C. Hersam) had a project involving printed electronics.”
Secor started by designing graphene inks for various printing technologies. That led to developing applications for graphene inks in flexible electronics, liquid metal electronics, microsupercapacitors and lithium-ion batteries. Those inks were promising enough to be distributed by Sigma-Aldrich Inc., and they’re still sold today.
Why not switch back to an energy project?
“What kept me there was the breadth of the work,” he said.
Working with printed electronics can mean pulling in collaborators from all over a university, including electrical engineers, mechanical engineers, materials scientists and chemists.
“There are a lot of different perspectives needed,” he said. “And that has kept me engaged and learning.”
One Iowa State collaborator is Adarsh Krishnamurthy, a professor of mechanical engineering and an associate director of the university’s Translational AI Center.
“In our work together, we have had to bring together expertise in materials, hardware, robotics, geometric modeling and computational methods to make aerosol jet printing work reliably on complex 3D curved surfaces,” he said. “Ethan is very good at envisioning how all of those pieces fit together.”
And, Krishnamurthy said, Secor knows how to work with a research team.
“He is also an excellent collaborator who is open to ideas from other disciplines, rigorous about technical details and focused on turning fundamental research into capabilities that can actually be demonstrated and used.”
Pursuing the practical
As an engineer, Secor is motivated to apply scientific research for practical benefits.
“Researchers have developed many creative and impressive demonstrations of printed hybrid electronics,” he said. “But to move those beyond a laboratory environment, reliability is key.”
Secor said there are two sides to that reliability: consistency of the manufacturing process itself, and stability of the printed devices. Secor’s lab is working on both.
Across five projects over the past six years, Secor’s team developed a sensor to monitor the printing process and automatically make corrections. His group has since installed these systems at several industry, government and academic sites from New York to California.
On the other side of reliability, a recent grant from the U.S. National Science Foundation has Secor studying new ink materials for printed electronics that hold up in the extreme environments of space, including high and low temperatures.
The challenge isn’t necessarily with the silicon-based chips that are essential to today’s electronics. The failures often occur at the interface between those semiconductors and larger circuits, Secor said.
Solve that problem, and we all could benefit:
“Electronic systems that can function in extreme environments are highly relevant for energy, infrastructure, aerospace, and space applications,” the researchers wrote in a project summary.
NASA is also interested in potential benefits for space electronics and has awarded the startup established by Secor and his former graduate student, Jeremy Rurup, with a $150,000 contract from the federal government’s Small Business Technology Transfer program that supports technology development and commercialization.
As the company incubates in its small space at the Roy J. Carver Co-Laboratory on the north side of campus, Secor is also looking ahead to future research ideas.
One idea that needs development is using aerosol jet printing to blend different materials during deposition, in a sense shifting from printing in black and white to gray scale, he said.
So yes, he’s confident there’s more to keep him engaged in the challenges of printed electronics.
He is, after all, the kind of engineer who’s ready to dive into a technology so he can advance a project.
As a post-doctoral researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy’s Sandia National Laboratories in New Mexico, “I learned how to build a printer and that opened up a lot of research directions,” Secor said. “Now we build and customize our own hardware. So, while other research groups are playing with a black box, we can open it up, understand how it works and improve on it.”

articles.title: Glenn Space Technology Symposium focuses on future of space exploration
articles.description: Glenn Space Technology Symposium focuses on future of space exploration Spectrum News
articles.description_html: Glenn Space Technology Symposium focuses on future of space exploration  Spectrum News
articles.article_title: Glenn Space Technology Symposium focuses on future of space exploration
articles.heading: Glenn Space Technology Symposium brings public, private sector together to discuss future of space
articles.summary: The 2026 Glenn Space Technology Symposium was hosted by the American Astronautical Society.
articles.content:
CLEVELAND — The Glenn Space Technology Symposium brings together leaders from the public and private sector to discuss the latest technological innovations and challenges facing the aerospace industry.
“The whole space enterprise is burgeoning, expanding, and evolving at unprecedented rates,” Ron Birk, the president of the American Astronautical Society, said. “There are reported to be over 10,000 space companies in the world, with over 5000 in the US.”
Private space ventures have proved integral in pushing the US space agenda forward. NASA’s Artemis missions are made possible through private and public partnerships, with the latest milestone being the successful completion of Artemis II.
Rickey Shyne, Director of Research and Engineering at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, said seeing the public’s reaction to Artemis II was particularly rewarding.
“Just the euphoria, the excitement, all of the hard work that so many people have done over the years to make that a reality,” Shyne said. “It was a flawless mission.”
Shyne, who attended the symposium, said any chance where the private and public sector can meaningfully connect is valuable in furthering aerospace development.
“Whenever we can leverage resources, whether or not the resources are subject matter experts through the people or through test facilities and other capabilities, I think it's a win-win for everyone,” Shyne said.
The 2026 Glenn Space Technology Symposium was hosted by the American Astronautical Society, in conjunction with Ohio Space Week, NASA Glenn Research Center and Cleveland State University.

articles.title: Arlington County ends use of Flock cameras and related technology
articles.description: Arlington County ends use of Flock cameras and related technology WTOP News
articles.description_html: Arlington County ends use of Flock cameras and related technology  WTOP News
articles.article_title: Arlington County ends use of Flock cameras and related technology – WTOP News
articles.heading: Arlington County ends use of Flock cameras and related technology
articles.summary: The Arlington County board in Virginia has discontinued the use of county-leased Flock Safety technology after a public meeting Tuesday.
articles.content:
The Arlington County board in Virginia has discontinued the use of county-leased Flock Safety technology after a public meeting Tuesday.
The board directed the county manager to begin removing all of the equipment the county uses that is related to Flock. Board members also directed that all data “not required for active criminal investigations” to be “deleted in accordance with applicable contractual, legal, and operational requirements.”
In total, Arlington County has 41 Flock Safety cameras, 26 Falcon license plate readers and 15 Condor point-tilt-zoom cameras.
Related stories
- DC police union raises questions about Flock cameras
- Dumfries pumps the brakes on Flock cameras rollout
- Va. governor says calls to ban Flock license reader cameras ‘overly simplistic’
Board Member Julius Spain told the “Tech Rundown Podcast” that the cameras would come down within the next 14 days.
“Effectively, immediately, our contract has ended with Flock. And the time when they’re going to come down, it may be Friday, it may be next week, but we were giving ourselves about a 14-day cushion,” Spain told podcast host Anna-Lysa Gayle.
The change comes as Flock cameras have been under scrutiny in the D.C. region and nationwide for the amount of information they collect without warning from people passing by.
D.C. Council member Brooke Pinto is seeking answers from the District’s police department about its use of Flock license plate reader technology, asking the D.C. police department 10 questions about the automated license plate reader system and requesting a response by the end of the business day Thursday.
Last week, Alexandria’s mayor said she wants the city to move away from using Flock Safety license plate readers amid growing concerns over privacy and how the cameras can be used to track people’s movements.
“This decision reflects concerns raised by Arlington residents regarding the use of Flock technology,” said Arlington County Board Chair Matt de Ferranti.
Spain said the board expects to share more with the public about where the cameras were located and what their purpose was during their meeting on Sept. 22.
“While Arlington has maintained strong safeguards to prevent the abuse of this technology throughout its use by the county, and there has been no report of misuse to date, the County Board takes seriously our obligation to maintain our community’s trust,” de Ferranti said in a news release. “The Board, the Manager, and our Public Safety staff will continue to evaluate the tools and technologies we use to ensure they align with the values and expectations of Arlington’s residents.”
Spain said that this type of technology has been helpful in solving crimes and locating missing persons and the county’s police department supports its use, but “we also respect the thoughts and concerns of our community and our constituents, who are really anxious right now about what’s going on with this level of technology.”
Flock cameras installed on private property are not impacted by the removal request because they are “not subject to county oversight,” the board said.

articles.title: Apple Weighs Return to Server Market with NVIDIA Networking Technology
articles.description: Apple Weighs Return to Server Market with NVIDIA Networking Technology TechPowerUp
articles.description_html: Apple Weighs Return to Server Market with NVIDIA Networking Technology  TechPowerUp
articles.article_title: Apple Weighs Return to Server Market with NVIDIA Networking Technology
articles.heading: Apple Weighs Return to Server Market with NVIDIA Networking Technology
articles.summary: Apple is reportedly considering a return to the server market, where the company was once active with its Xserve rack technology. According to The Information, Apple is developing AI-focused M-series chips, which could incorporate several NVIDIA components, including the NVLink Fusion portfolio...
articles.content:
Wednesday, September 16th 2026





Apple Weighs Return to Server Market with NVIDIA Networking Technology
Apple is reportedly considering a return to the server market, where the company was once active with its Xserve rack technology. According to The Information, Apple is developing AI-focused M-series chips, which could incorporate several NVIDIA components, including the NVLink Fusion portfolio of technologies and IP. This includes the possibility of interconnecting two or four Apple M8 Ultra chips using NVIDIA NVLink for socket-to-socket communication, while NVIDIA NVLink-C2C manages die-to-die interconnection. Currently planned for launch in 2029, this product would mark Apple's first entry into the server space since debuting Xserve in 2002 and discontinuing it in 2011. Nearly two decades later, Apple's server offering might be making a comeback, building on the success that the Mac mini and Mac Studio are experiencing among AI developers.
For instance, Apple's Mac lineup achieved a record $10.4 billion in sales last quarter, with strong demand from the AI community. Enterprises are even constructing custom racks, mounting multiple Mac Studios to set up local AI inferencing efforts. For the new server design, Apple would delegate every interconnect question to NVIDIA NVLink Fusion, while it focuses on the actual system-on-chip as before. The new rack design would target enterprises and governments, who may already be running Mac clusters locally.Readers might recall that Apple is already working on a custom AI inference accelerator with Broadcom, codenamed "Baltra." It reportedly uses TSMC's 3 nm N3E or N3P nodes and is scheduled for late 2026 or early 2027. Perhaps Apple, which also develops Apple Foundation Models (AFM), will use the "Baltra" AI accelerator to run large-scale inference and serve its massive customer base with its models using that chip, and later offer its M8 Ultra chips as standalone racks. However, for a company as secretive as Apple, schedules might change, and we could see more information in the future. With the new CEO John Ternus at the helm, hardware offerings might expand significantly.

articles.title: Ivey’s ed tech commission and use technology in schools
articles.description: Ivey’s ed tech commission and use technology in schools The Alabama Baptist
articles.description_html: Ivey’s ed tech commission and use technology in schools  The Alabama Baptist
articles.article_title: Ivey’s ed tech commission and use technology in schools | The Alabama Baptist
articles.heading: Ivey’s ed tech commission and use technology in schools
articles.summary: Alabama’s commission studying screen-based instruction is moving toward recommendations on when and how technology should be used in K-12 classrooms, with members focusing not simply on how much time students spend on screens ...
articles.content:
Alabama’s commission studying screen-based instruction is moving toward recommendations on when and how technology should be used in K-12 classrooms, with members focusing not simply on how much time students spend on screens but whether that technology serves an educational purpose and improves learning.
Rep. Jeana Ross, R-Guntersville, who chairs the Governor’s Commission on Screen-Based Instruction, said the group is making progress as it examines the many ways students and teachers use technology in classrooms. Members have broken into subcommittees and are beginning to narrow that work into recommendations.
The commission must submit recommendations to Gov. Kay Ivey by Dec. 1.
Support learning
Ross told Alabama Daily News after the meeting that she wants to make sure people understand what the commission is trying to do.
“This is not a ban on technology,” Ross said. “It is to just ensure that the technology that is being used with our students at school is effective and it’s implemented in the proper way, and it’s something that supports learning, not replaces that important teacher, adult-child interaction.”
Ivey in July directed the commission to study how classroom technology affects learning, student health and preparation for college or work, to compare Alabama’s practices with research and practices elsewhere and consider age-appropriate limits, guidance for educators and ways to make sure technology supports rather than replaces teacher-led instruction.
Tuesday’s discussion focused less on setting limits on screen time and more on what students are actually doing on screens and whether that use helps them learn.
Members repeatedly cautioned against a one-size-fits-all approach, noting that technology can serve very different purposes depending on a student’s age, subject, needs and access to teachers or courses.
“Technology is not going away,” Houston County Superintendent Brandy White said, adding that the commission’s goal should not be simply to increase or decrease screen time, but to determine how schools can use technology with “balance and purpose.”
Read more.
EDITOR’S NOTE — This story was written by Trisha Powell Crain and originally published by Alabama Daily News.

articles.title: “Technology is the equalizer”
articles.description: “Technology is the equalizer” MIT News
articles.description_html: “Technology is the equalizer”  MIT News
articles.source: MIT News | Massachusetts Institute of Technology
articles.article_title: “Technology is the equalizer”
articles.heading: “Technology is the equalizer”
articles.summary: Mohammad Imran Khan Mewati, an educator in rural India, builds apps using knowledge gained from MIT Open Learning to reach students who can’t make it to school.
articles.content:
Mohammad Imran Khan Mewati teaches grades 6-12 at a school in rural India. His students are largely from economically disadvantaged families, and the school itself has limited resources. But the biggest problem, he says, is absenteeism.
“If a student is not coming into your class, how are you going to teach?” says Mewati, a teacher for 26 years. “That’s why I’m using technology in my classroom and outside the classroom, so that they can learn a little bit using their smartphones.”
MIT Open Learning’s free educational resources have been a boon for Mewati as he develops Hindi-language digital resources for his students.
“I am a self-taught app developer,” he explains. “MIT Open Learning has had a deep and practical impact on my professional life as a teacher. Many concepts I learned influenced how I design digital learning activities, simple educational games, and classroom strategies. My students may not know they are indirectly benefiting from MIT, but they are.”
Through MIT Open Learning, Mewati has used in his classroom OpenCourseWare’s free, online library of educational resources from more than 2,500 courses spanning the MIT undergraduate and graduate curriculum. Learners can browse content at their own pace, watch lectures, read course notes, and hear from faculty experts. All materials can be downloaded for offline use, and the website is fully responsive for smartphone use. These materials are also available on MIT Learn, an AI-enabled platform for all of MIT’s lifelong learning opportunities.
Mewati started using OpenCourseWare resources in the early 2010s and cites programming courses as the most useful. He dove deep into Introduction to CS and Programming Using Python, Introduction to C and C++, and Introduction to Programming Using Java. Introduction to Computational Thinking helped him bring together problem-solving approaches from mathematics and computer science as he built apps.
Closing the gap with technology
Mewati’s school is located 15 miles from the city of Alwar in Rajasthan, a state in northwestern India. Most of the students do not have access to desktop or laptop computers, but the majority live in a home where at least one person has a smartphone. Taking advantage of this technology, Mewati creates classroom groups on WhatsApp so that he can share resources with his students, regardless of whether they can make it to class.
Mewati began incorporating technology into his teaching in the early 2010s, when he had to engage 180 students in a lesson about the moon landing and Neil Armstrong. Mewati created a simple HTML page that included many iconic images — the American flag planted on the moon, the Apollo 11 spacecraft, the footprint on the moon’s surface — with Hindi explanations. Once he created it, he could use it again and again. When he tested students on what they’d learned, they got better results than when he’d taught the material using his previous approach.
“This is the incident that confirmed to me that technology can play an important role in the lives of the students, and particularly for the rural students, for the students who do not have equal opportunities,” says Mewati. “Technology is the equalizer.”
That belief has driven Mewati’s efforts to build his school’s technological resources. Through crowdfunding, he secured 15 used computers to create a computer lab, and teachers now share the responsibility for creating mobile hotspots so students can connect to the internet. Mewati’s mobile apps provide additional opportunities for students to explore topics in greater depth or catch up on lessons they may have missed.
Referring to his apps as his favorite topic, Mewati explains that he has developed several types to meet a variety of goals. Some allow students to play games that develop their math skills, while others include syllabi, reading recommendations, and class notes. Other apps help students prepare for exams required for government jobs. He also builds apps for audiences beyond his school, such as an app that provides Hindi-language resources related to maternal health, a topic he says is not openly discussed in India. The app has been popular, he explains, because it provides honest information that people can view privately.
“If I see an issue, I think, ‘Yes, let’s create an app,’” he says.
Collaboration, open sharing, and lifelong learning
Mewati shares the apps he has created, and the MIT Open Learning resources that support him, with a network of teachers across India. He has connected with other educators through India’s National Teacher Awards and earlier this year, he traveled to Dubai for the Global Teacher Prize.
“We share things with each other,” he says. “We have a huge group — more than 1,000 teachers connected across India. So, if we see resources, or useful things for a class, we’ll share. All the time, I talk about open-source materials, like MIT courses, for educational purposes.”
Through this culture of collaboration and open sharing, Mewati is able to bring new learning opportunities to his students. The apps he has built — made possible by what he has learned through MIT Open Learning — help extend access to educational resources beyond the classroom. As an educator, he says he’s happy about that. But he is also a learner, and it’s his journey as a learner that he wants people to know.
“I am from a rural area. My parents are not educated at all. And I am a Fulbright Scholar. I can reach the Global Teacher Prize stage. The reason is simple,” he says. “It is because I continued my learning, whenever possible, with the use of technology and availability of free courses from MIT.”

articles.content_html:
Mohammad Imran Khan Mewati teaches grades 6-12 at a school in rural India. His students are largely from economically disadvantaged families, and the school itself has limited resources. But the biggest problem, he says, is absenteeism.

“If a student is not coming into your class, how are you going to teach?” says Mewati, a teacher for 26 years. “That’s why I’m using technology in my classroom and outside the classroom, so that they can learn a little bit using their smartphones.”

MIT Open Learning’s free educational resources have been a boon for Mewati as he develops Hindi-language digital resources for his students.

“I am a self-taught app developer,” he explains. “MIT Open Learning has had a deep and practical impact on my professional life as a teacher. Many concepts I learned influenced how I design digital learning activities, simple educational games, and classroom strategies. My students may not know they are indirectly benefiting from MIT, but they are.”

Through MIT Open Learning, Mewati has used in his classroom OpenCourseWare’s free, online library of educational resources from more than 2,500 courses spanning the MIT undergraduate and graduate curriculum. Learners can browse content at their own pace, watch lectures, read course notes, and hear from faculty experts. All materials can be downloaded for offline use, and the website is fully responsive for smartphone use. These materials are also available on MIT Learn, an AI-enabled platform for all of MIT’s lifelong learning opportunities.

Mewati started using OpenCourseWare resources in the early 2010s and cites programming courses as the most useful. He dove deep into Introduction to CS and Programming Using Python, Introduction to C and C++, and Introduction to Programming Using Java. Introduction to Computational Thinking helped him bring together problem-solving approaches from mathematics and computer science as he built apps.

Closing the gap with technology

Mewati’s school is located 15 miles from the city of Alwar in Rajasthan, a state in northwestern India. Most of the students do not have access to desktop or laptop computers, but the majority live in a home where at least one person has a smartphone. Taking advantage of this technology, Mewati creates classroom groups on WhatsApp so that he can share resources with his students, regardless of whether they can make it to class.

Mewati began incorporating technology into his teaching in the early 2010s, when he had to engage 180 students in a lesson about the moon landing and Neil Armstrong. Mewati created a simple HTML page that included many iconic images — the American flag planted on the moon, the Apollo 11 spacecraft, the footprint on the moon’s surface — with Hindi explanations. Once he created it, he could use it again and again. When he tested students on what they’d learned, they got better results than when he’d taught the material using his previous approach.

“This is the incident that confirmed to me that technology can play an important role in the lives of the students, and particularly for the rural students, for the students who do not have equal opportunities,” says Mewati. “Technology is the equalizer.”

That belief has driven Mewati’s efforts to build his school’s technological resources. Through crowdfunding, he secured 15 used computers to create a computer lab, and teachers now share the responsibility for creating mobile hotspots so students can connect to the internet. Mewati’s mobile apps provide additional opportunities for students to explore topics in greater depth or catch up on lessons they may have missed.

Referring to his apps as his favorite topic, Mewati explains that he has developed several types to meet a variety of goals. Some allow students to play games that develop their math skills, while others include syllabi, reading recommendations, and class notes. Other apps help students prepare for exams required for government jobs. He also builds apps for audiences beyond his school, such as an app that provides Hindi-language resources related to maternal health, a topic he says is not openly discussed in India. The app has been popular, he explains, because it provides honest information that people can view privately.

“If I see an issue, I think, ‘Yes, let’s create an app,’” he says.

Collaboration, open sharing, and lifelong learning

Mewati shares the apps he has created, and the MIT Open Learning resources that support him, with a network of teachers across India. He has connected with other educators through India’s National Teacher Awards and earlier this year, he traveled to Dubai for the Global Teacher Prize.

“We share things with each other,” he says. “We have a huge group — more than 1,000 teachers connected across India. So, if we see resources, or useful things for a class, we’ll share. All the time, I talk about open-source materials, like MIT courses, for educational purposes.”

Through this culture of collaboration and open sharing, Mewati is able to bring new learning opportunities to his students. The apps he has built — made possible by what he has learned through MIT Open Learning — help extend access to educational resources beyond the classroom. As an educator, he says he’s happy about that. But he is also a learner, and it’s his journey as a learner that he wants people to know.

“I am from a rural area. My parents are not educated at all. And I am a Fulbright Scholar. I can reach the Global Teacher Prize stage. The reason is simple,” he says. “It is because I continued my learning, whenever possible, with the use of technology and availability of free courses from MIT.”

To anyone who is curious, who wants to learn, to push themselves or build something new, he says that with MIT Open Learning, the resources are out there.

“We should use it, we should grab it, and we should share it as much as we can,” says Mewati. “Because that’s how humanity can flourish.”

ABERDEEN PROVING GROUND, MARYLAND, UNITED STATES

09.16.2026

Story by Robin Schumacher

U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Chemical Biological Center

Aberdeen Proving Ground, MD — This spring, the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Chemical Biological Center (DEVCOM CBC) participated in Rio Robotico, an annual integrated engineering and test event to evaluate the performance of Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) detection and autonomy payloads for unmanned systems in operationally relevant environments.

The event brought together numerous partners from government, industry, and academia to look at potential technology solutions for CBRN sensing. It was hosted by the Defense Threat Reduction Agency at the Eldorado Training Grounds in Eldorado, Texas.

Rio Robotico is a culmination of the work that happens throughout the year, mostly through cooperative research and development agreements, which allow DEVCOM CBC to partner with industry and universities to advance CBRN technologies. The ultimate goal of these agreements is speed and capability. This event provided a collaborative environment for operators and developers to foster those relationships, test the capabilities, and gather feedback on real-world application.

“Testing events like Rio Robotico can accelerate the deployment of new capabilities by several years,” said Chika Nzelibe, Product Design and Development Division chief at DEVCOM CBC. “It is a cost-efficient way to test the technology, which is key to getting it into the hands of the warfighter.”

Participants engaged in integration tests on both unmanned ground vehicle platforms and unmanned aircraft system platforms and with many different technologies, ranging in various lifecycle stages from early prototypes to ready to field. The data collected will be instrumental in accelerating the fielding of autonomous, modular payloads, as well as identifying mutual investment areas that could rapidly close capability gaps.

“Our main goal is to collaborate, develop, and push capability to the warfighter. To do that, we must continue to strategically develop these partnerships,” said Andrea Bechtel-Mathias, a technology transfer specialist at DEVCOM CBC. “The future lies in being able to combine the talents and efforts of distinct organizations that are all driving toward the same objectives.”

articles.summary: Professor Yasar Onel has received a research award from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) for his project, "Development of Secondary Emission Calorimetry." The award will support the development of a first-of-its-kind secondary emission calorimeter that combines ultra-fast timing, high precision...
articles.content:
Professor Yasar Onel has received a research award from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) for his project, "Development of Secondary Emission Calorimetry." The award will support the development of a first-of-its-kind secondary emission calorimeter that combines ultra-fast timing, high precision, and exceptional radiation resistance for applications in particle physics and advanced medical imaging. Building on a successful prototype, the project aims to create a highly segmented detector capable of operating in extreme radiation environments while requiring minimal power and maintenance. The research has the potential to advance next-generation collider experiments and innovative radiation detection technologies, positioning the University at the forefront of detector instrumentation and high-energy physics research.
Wednesday, September 16, 2026

articles.summary: For National Rehabilitation Week, we learned about technology offered at Encompass Health Rehabilitation Hospital of Bluffton.
articles.content:
Health Break: Bluffton rehabilitation hospital uses game-like technology for regaining mobility
BLUFFTON, Sc. (WTOC) - For National Rehabilitation Awareness Week, Encompass Health Rehabilitation Hospital of Bluffton showed Morning Break advance technology to help patients regain their independence.
Director of Therapy Operations Meg Foster showed Morning Break Host Camille Syed how to use a touch screen device helping stroke patient track visual progress. Foster also demonstrated the B.U.R.T. robotic machine, which was made to help stroke patients build their mobility. See how they work with the video above.
“We’re actually certified in three programs, Parkinson’s, stroke, and hip fracture,” Foster said. “So when patients come here, they get three hours of therapy a day.”
Medical Director Dr. Vincent Somaio says providing inpatient therapy allows their staff to prepare patients for the return to daily activities after a tragic incident or diagnosis.
“They need medical management and they also improve in function. We stay here between seven days and 21 days depending on their diagnosis. Our average length of stay is about 12 days,” Dr. Somaio said. “And they get good medical coverage. They have physicians that see them just about every day. Very different than a subacute facility where physicians are rarely there. And we have 24-7 nursing coverage. And the therapy is very intensive, 15 hours a week of therapy.”
For information about support groups and services, visit www.encompasshealth.com/locations/bluffton-rehab.

articles.content:
USA Skeleton and Carpenter Technology Renew Partnership for 2026-2027 Season
by Gregg Elkin
Carpenter Technologies
LAKE PLACID, N.Y. (Sept. 16, 2026) – USA Skeleton and Carpenter Technology Corporation have renewed their partnership for the 2026-2027 season, continuing a relationship built on innovation, performance, and engineering excellence.
Carpenter Technology, a leader in high-performance specialty alloys and process solutions, will keep supporting USA Skeleton's efforts to advance sled technology and athlete performance. The renewed agreement builds on a long history of collaboration between the two organizations.
"Carpenter Technology is proud to continue supporting the United States Skeleton Team as they pursue excellence at the highest level of competition,” said Carpenter Technology Chief Commercial Officer Marshall Akins. “This partnership reflects a shared commitment to performance and relentless innovation. We look forward to supporting these athletes as they prepare for the road ahead.”
Skeleton is one of the fastest and most technically demanding winter sports, where fractions of a second decide races. Carpenter Technology's expertise in advanced materials and metallurgy helps optimize sled components, improve stability, reduce drag, and sharpen responsiveness on the track.
"Carpenter Technology has been an invaluable partner in helping our athletes compete at the highest level," said Aron McGuire, CEO of USA Bobsled/Skeleton. "Every hundredth of a second matters in this sport, and access to their materials expertise gives our athletes a real edge on the track as we build on this partnership heading into the season."
Founded in 1889, Carpenter Technology develops premium titanium-, nickel-, and cobalt-based alloys for the aerospace, defense, medical, transportation, energy, and industrial markets. Its innovations translate directly to elite sport, where gains are measured in milliseconds.
The renewed partnership builds on advancements already made in sled development and performance. Both organizations plan to keep exploring new ways to apply materials science and engineering to help USA Skeleton stay competitive internationally.
Together, USA Skeleton and Carpenter Technology will continue pursuing innovation-driven performance, giving American athletes access to cutting-edge technology as they compete for podiums worldwide.

articles.content:
LANGHORNE, Pa., Sept. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TEN Holdings, Inc. (Nasdaq: XHLD) ("TEN Holdings" or the "Company"), through its subsidiary, Ten Events, Inc., a technology platform for enterprise-grade webcasts and virtual events, today announced that its Board of Directors has authorized a new share repurchase program of up to $2.0 million and approved the establishment of a strategic technology and engineering relationship with GLSoft Corp. ("GLSoft").
$2.0 Million Share Repurchase Program
Under the newly authorized share repurchase program, TEN Holdings may repurchase up to $2.0 million of its outstanding common stock through December 31, 2026. Repurchases may be made from time to time through open-market transactions, privately negotiated transactions or other transactions deemed appropriate by the Company, including pursuant to trading plans or arrangements intended to comply with Rule 10b5-1 and/or Rule 10b-18 under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended.
The timing, price and amount of any repurchases will be determined based on market conditions, the trading price of the Company's common stock, available liquidity, applicable securities laws, contractual restrictions and other relevant factors.
The authorization does not obligate the Company to repurchase any specific number or dollar amount of shares, and the program may be suspended, modified or discontinued at any time.
In connection with the authorization of the new program, the Board also approved the termination of the Company's existing share repurchase program administered through Bancroft Capital, LLC.
"We believe the authorization of this new share repurchase program provides us with an additional tool to strategically allocate capital while maintaining the flexibility necessary to continue investing in the growth of our business," said Virgilio Torres, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of TEN Holdings, Inc. "Following the strengthening of our balance sheet earlier this year, we believe it is important to maintain a disciplined approach to capital allocation. This authorization allows us to evaluate opportunistic repurchases when we believe they represent an attractive use of capital, while continuing to prioritize investments in technology, product development and long-term growth."
Strategic Technology Relationship with GLSoft Corp.
The Board has also authorized TEN Holdings to establish a strategic relationship with GLSoft, providing the Company with the ability to utilize GLSoft's engineering, software development and broader technology capabilities as opportunities arise.
The relationship is expected to provide TEN Holdings with additional flexibility to pursue product engineering, software and technology development, platform integrations, technical support, technology licensing, redistribution, resale and commercialization initiatives.
Rather than committing the Company to a specific project or minimum expenditure, the authorization enables management to identify and pursue individual development and technology initiatives with GLSoft when management determines that doing so is beneficial to the Company and consistent with its strategic objectives.
"Expanding our technology and engineering capabilities is a critical component of where we want to take TEN Holdings," Torres continued. "Our objective is to evolve beyond a traditional webinar and virtual-events offering and build a broader, more scalable technology platform. Having the ability to leverage additional engineering and development resources through relationships such as GLSoft gives us greater flexibility to accelerate product development, evaluate new technologies and bring additional capabilities to market."
The GLSoft authorization complements TEN Holdings' previously announced strategy to invest in expanded product functionality, automation, analytics, artificial intelligence and other technologies designed to increase the scalability of its platform and broaden its addressable market.

TEN Holdings, Inc. (Nasdaq: XHLD) is a technology company for enterprise-grade virtual events, offering a self-service platform through its subsidiary, Ten Events, Inc., that scales to over 100,000 concurrent attendees at 99.99% uptime. The Company is backed by more than a decade of experience producing mission-critical corporate broadcasts for Fortune 500 clients, and its roadmap extends this foundation with AI-driven capabilities in analytics, captioning, and intent data. Headquartered in Pennsylvania, TEN Holdings produces virtual, hybrid, and physical events supported by its Ten Events Pro platform. To learn more, visit www.tenholdingsinc.com.

articles.content:
MAD Security donates $100,000 to Alabama School of Cyber Technology and Engineering
HUNTSVILLE, Ala. (WAFF) - Leaders from Mad Security donated $100,000 to the Alabama School of Cyber Technology and Engineering in Huntsville this morning.
The donation comes as Mad Security opens a new headquarters in Huntsville.
The company’s CEO said the investment aligns with Mad Security’s overall philosophy of finding and training new talent in the cybersecurity field.
“It’s very hard to jump into an organization with just a degree. You need the experience. And a lot of organizations won’t take those types of risks associated with those junior employees. So we’re one of the few places that, like, somebody coming right out of college can get some experience and stuff in. So we take a lot of pride in that,” Jeremy Conway, Mad Security CEO, said.
Mad Security says it’s more than doubled its workforce in the past five years.

articles.summary: At the U.S. Fire Administrator's Summit on Fire Prevention and Control, Meridian Fire Chief Kris Blume said it's "important to never let technology master us."
articles.content:
Dr. Daniel T. Kistner, director of National Fallen Firefighters Foundation Institute for Firefighter Survivability, discussed wildfire issues at the U.S. Fire Administrator's Summit on Fire Prevention and Control.

EMMITSBURG, MD – Technology took center stage at the U.S. Fire Administrator’s Summit on Fire Prevention and Control here Tuesday.

To meet challenges like wildland urban interface, alternative energy sources and increased risks to firefighters’ health, U.S. Fire Administrator Paul Matheis said: “We are fortunate to have pioneering new technologies at our disposal, supported by a robust, dedicated network of practitioners, engineers and scientists who are fully committed to delivering modern, data-driven, science-based solutions to the problems we face.”

In addition to discussions about the impact of technology and science on responses, the attendees also heard some of the history of fire service.

While the United States is celebrating 250 years, the fire service is older as Ben Franklin helped create the Union Fire Company in Philadelphia in 1736.

Meridian, ID, Fire Chief Kris Blume reminded the nearly 140 attendees it’s “important to never let technology master us.”

He added that regardless of the technology, including drones and robotics, will never replace firefighters.

And, it’s imperative that firefighters have a seat at the table when officials are discussing land use decisions and deciding where to build as it’s the only way to protect personnel and the public, he noted.

Other issues he encouraged the group to address include recruitment and retention to insure there are personnel to continue to serve their communities and making sure behavioral health services are available and encouraged.

About the Author

Susan Nicol

News Editor

Susan Nicol is the news editor for Firehouse.com. She is a life member and active with the Brunswick Volunteer Ambulance & Rescue Company, Oxford Fire Company and Brunswick Vol. Fire Co. Susie has been an EMT in Maryland since 1976. Susie is vice-president of the Frederick County Fire/Rescue Museum. She is on the executive committee of Frederick County Volunteer Fire and Rescue Association. She also is part of the Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems (MIEMSS) Region II EMS Council. Susie is a board member of the American Trauma Society, Maryland Division. Prior to joining the Firehouse team, she was a staff writer for The Frederick News-Post, covering fire, law enforcement, court and legislative issues.

articles.heading: NSF announces 3 additional topics as part of the NSF X-Labs initiative to pursue generational breakthrough science and technology efforts
articles.summary: NSF X-Labs invites proposals from teams working in AI for physical systems and announces two forthcoming topics...
articles.content:
NSF announces 3 additional topics as part of the NSF X-Labs initiative to pursue generational breakthrough science and technology efforts
The U.S. National Science Foundation announced today three additional topics for NSF X-Labs as part of the $1.5 billion investment the agency initiated in May, completing the portfolio of topics for calendar year 2026. NSF's substantial, long-term investment in NSF X-Labs over the next decade aims to tackle pressing scientific and technological challenges through novel and innovative research partnerships.
The latest NSF X-Labs funding opportunity invites proposals in the technical domain of Artificial Intelligence for Physical Systems. NSF is also previewing two additional NSF X-Labs topics for which the agency anticipates inviting proposals later this calendar year: From Sequence to Function and Computation at the Limit of Physics.
"Science is moving faster than ever, and the challenges we face increasingly require new ways of working across disciplines and sectors," said Brian Stone, performing the duties of the NSF Director. "NSF X-Labs bring together researchers, engineers, and entrepreneurs to pursue ambitious scientific questions with the flexibility to test new ideas, learn quickly, and adapt along the way. This is part of NSF's broader effort to build the conditions for exceptional science to happen more often, more quickly and across a wider range of the research community, helping usher in a new era of American discovery and innovation."
NSF X-Labs — independent teams of researchers, engineers and entrepreneurs pursuing milestone-based federal funding to solve specific scientific challenges — reflect the interdisciplinary nature of today's modern science ecosystem.
"The NSF X-Labs initiative is investing in high-risk, high-impact research that requires substantial resources beyond traditional funding mechanisms, reducing the time it takes to go from insight to impact," said Erwin Gianchandani, NSF Assistant Director for Technology, Innovation and Partnerships (NSF TIP). "Today's announcement expands the pathways for a wide range of institutions and teams to identify and overcome key bottlenecks — advancing bold, innovative science and technology critical to U.S. competitiveness and economic leadership."
NSF X-Labs: AI for Physical Systems
Decades of progress in digital AI have positioned the U.S. to redefine how intelligent systems interact with the physical world. The next frontier of AI requires developing intelligent, adaptive, and scalable systems for complex physical environments. NSF is seeking NSF X-Labs teams to develop early-stage technologies that enable breakthroughs to accelerate entirely new forms of AI integration in physical systems, including advanced sensors, robotics, embodied systems, human-robot interfaces, and cyber-physical systems. Teams applying to this topic will produce innovative platform technologies that benefit a broad range of application domains critical to U.S. competitiveness and security, which may include healthcare, national defense, emergency response, advanced manufacturing, and scientific discovery.
Future NSF X-Labs topics
NSF is also releasing an early preview of two future NSF X-Labs topics — From Sequence to Function and Computation at the Limit of Physics — anticipated later this Fall, to help potential proposers anticipate upcoming opportunities requiring large, multidisciplinary teams to come together to accelerate bold research and development to, in turn, advance U.S. technological leadership. NSF is not accepting proposals for these topics at this time; rather, full details including proposal submission timelines and guidance will be provided in forthcoming topic announcements.
- NSF X-Labs: From Sequence to Function — By reliably linking protein sequence and structure to biological function, the U.S. can unlock a new era of biological engineering in which biological components are designed rather than discovered. NSF X-Labs in this topic will close the gap between predicting protein structure and understanding the dynamic behavior of proteins by creating platform technologies that enable the intentional design of individual proteins or entire genomes whose function is predictable and/or controllable.
- NSF X-Labs: Computation at the Limit of Physics — New technologies and paradigms are needed to pursue the computational efficiencies and capabilities required to drive U.S. innovation over the next half-century. NSF X-Labs in this topic will dramatically narrow the gap between the energy efficiency of conventional Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor-based computing and the inherent physical limits.
NSF issued a Request for Information seeking feedback on potential topics for future NSF X-Labs funding opportunities. Responses are due by Oct. 30, 2026.
The NSF X-Labs initiative is guided by the administration's mandate to revitalize and strengthen America's science and technology ecosystem by exploring innovative models for funding and sharing high-value scientific research infrastructure and results. The design choices underpinning these efforts are informed by thoughtful science policy scholarship and entrepreneurship from both established and emerging think tanks, metascience experts, congressionally chartered study commissions, and the broader scientific community.
To learn more about the AI for Physical Systems topic and how to apply, read the NSF X-Labs funding opportunity and topic announcement on the NSF X-Labs webpage. You may also plan to join an introductory webinar on Wed., Oct. 14, 2026, at 1 p.m. EDT. You must register online to join the webinar.
To learn about future NSF X-Labs topics and funding opportunities, sign up for NSF TIP emails.

"The NSF X-Labs initiative is investing in high-risk, high-impact research that requires substantial resources beyond traditional funding mechanisms, reducing the time it takes to go from insight to impact," said Erwin Gianchandani, NSF Assistant Director for Technology, Innovation and Partnerships (NSF TIP). "Today's announcement expands the pathways for a wide range of institutions and teams to identify and overcome key bottlenecks — advancing bold, innovative science and technology critical to U.S. competitiveness and economic leadership."

NSF X-Labs: AI for Physical Systems

Decades of progress in digital AI have positioned the U.S. to redefine how intelligent systems interact with the physical world. The next frontier of AI requires developing intelligent, adaptive, and scalable systems for complex physical environments. NSF is seeking NSF X-Labs teams to develop early-stage technologies that enable breakthroughs to accelerate entirely new forms of AI integration in physical systems, including advanced sensors, robotics, embodied systems, human-robot interfaces, and cyber-physical systems. Teams applying to this topic will produce innovative platform technologies that benefit a broad range of application domains critical to U.S. competitiveness and security, which may include healthcare, national defense, emergency response, advanced manufacturing, and scientific discovery.

Future NSF X-Labs topics

NSF is also releasing an early preview of two future NSF X-Labs topics — From Sequence to Function and Computation at the Limit of Physics — anticipated later this Fall, to help potential proposers anticipate upcoming opportunities requiring large, multidisciplinary teams to come together to accelerate bold research and development to, in turn, advance U.S. technological leadership. NSF is not accepting proposals for these topics at this time; rather, full details including proposal submission timelines and guidance will be provided in forthcoming topic announcements.

  • NSF X-Labs: From Sequence to Function — By reliably linking protein sequence and structure to biological function, the U.S. can unlock a new era of biological engineering in which biological components are designed rather than discovered. NSF X-Labs in this topic will close the gap between predicting protein structure and understanding the dynamic behavior of proteins by creating platform technologies that enable the intentional design of individual proteins or entire genomes whose function is predictable and/or controllable.
  • NSF X-Labs: Computation at the Limit of Physics — New technologies and paradigms are needed to pursue the computational efficiencies and capabilities required to drive U.S. innovation over the next half-century. NSF X-Labs in this topic will dramatically narrow the gap between the energy efficiency of conventional Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor-based computing and the inherent physical limits.

NSF issued a Request for Information seeking feedback on potential topics for future NSF X-Labs funding opportunities. Responses are due by Oct. 30, 2026.

The NSF X-Labs initiative is guided by the administration's mandate to revitalize and strengthen America's science and technology ecosystem by exploring innovative models for funding and sharing high-value scientific research infrastructure and results. The design choices underpinning these efforts are informed by thoughtful science policy scholarship and entrepreneurship from both established and emerging think tanks, metascience experts, congressionally chartered study commissions, and the broader scientific community.

To learn more about the AI for Physical Systems topic and how to apply, read the NSF X-Labs funding opportunity and topic announcement on the NSF X-Labs webpage. You may also plan to join an introductory webinar on Wed., Oct. 14, 2026, at 1 p.m. EDT. You must register online to join the webinar.

To learn about future NSF X-Labs topics and funding opportunities, sign up for NSF TIP emails.

articles.content:
Suffolk County delays plan to install Flock gunfire detection technology for a year
Suffolk County will delay installing new gunshot detection technology from Flock Safety for a year and instead continue using ShotSpotter, due to an "unforeseen circumstance."
The county will spend as much as $1.2 million on a one-year contract with SoundThinking, the company that operates ShotSpotter, for a deal that started Sept. 6 and runs through Sept. 5, 2027, records show.
On Wednesday, the county's RFP Waiver Committee, which approves requests for contracts that cut out the traditional competitive procurement process, approved the Suffolk County Police Department's request to revise its contract with SoundThinking "to temporarily continue coverage."
The county had been finalizing a five-year, $3.79 million with Flock Safety for its gunshot detection technology. Flock has generated nationwide controversy over its use technology that was found to have been improperly used by police departments.
"There has been some issues with the implementation of that program, so we need gap coverage so we don't lose any ShotSpotter gunshot detection availability within our gunshot areas," Det. Sgt. Dan Acer told the committee Wednesday.
Suffolk Police Commissioner Kevin Catalina wrote to the committee that the delay is due to "unforeseen circumstance in acquiring a new system for the Department."
SoundThinking's contract expired Sept. 5. The one-year coverage deal represents a savings of about $300,000, or 20%, compared to current annual subscription fee, according to the price proposal. The county would pay SoundThinking in quarterly installments of $308,700.
Acer told the committee the department anticipates it will take one year to transition to the new company.
The current gunshot detection covers 23.5 square miles; the Flock system was set to cover the same area. Suffolk lawmakers approved $1.8 million in funding for ShotSpotter in 2022 and Suffolk police began implementing the technology in 2023.
The Suffolk County District Attorney's Office and Suffolk police had pitched Flock Safety as an improved and cost savings technology system that can better differentiate sounds to pinpoint incidents that require a police response.
The Flock gunshot detection can also integrate into the company's vast network of license plate readers, which the company has advertised as a way for police to potentially locate fleeing suspects.
When a gunshot is detected, the Flock system "automatically queries all Flock LPR cameras in the surrounding area to surface every license plate captured within a configurable time window of the event," Flock Safety CEO Garrett Langley wrote in a March letter to Dara Martin, assistant deputy commissioner for Suffolk police.
Check back for updates on this developing story.
